0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans “the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel.” John Calvin wrote that “when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture.” Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over some thirteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his ministry as an apostle, probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, God’s sovereign choice of his people and his purpose for Israel, and how the redeemed are to live in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel’s own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity (pagan, moralist and Jew) stands guilty before the righteous God, with nothing of its own that could win acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

Who were the Christians in Rome? No apostle founded the church. Luke lists visitors from Rome in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), and the gospel probably reached the capital through Jewish believers like them. Some years before this letter Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), and for a time the congregations were largely Gentile. When Jewish believers returned after his death, they came back to churches whose leaders and habits had changed. That tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians lies behind much of the letter, especially chapters 9–11 and 14–15 (cf. 1:7).

And what of the New Perspective on Paul? Since the 1970s scholars such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright have argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation; that works of the law means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath; and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right that the unity of Jew and Gentile is a real concern of Romans (3:29–30; 15:7), and that Judaism has sometimes been described unfairly. But the more likely reading is the Reformation one. Paul’s charge in 1:18–3:20 is not that Jews kept Gentiles out but that all have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him, so that every mouth may be stopped (3:19). Justification answers that guilt. It is God’s verdict of acquittal, given freely to the ungodly (4:5) on the ground of Christ’s blood (5:9). Belonging to God’s people follows from that verdict; it is not what the verdict means.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin’s masterly commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller’s Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with a single Greek sentence of seven verses in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel and his Lord. By the end of the chapter the same pen has traced God’s wrath against human idolatry. The two belong together: the good news is only as good as the bad news is real.

Paul first sets out the gospel (vv. 1–17), then shows why everyone needs it (vv. 18–32). The world he describes in verses 18–32 is not only ancient Rome; it is every culture, and every heart, that suppresses the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In seven verses Paul calls himself a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God: a gospel promised in the Old Testament, concerning God’s Son, descended from David and declared Son of God in power by his resurrection.

The word euangelion, gospel, was used in the Roman world for public good news, such as the accession of a new emperor. Paul uses it for better news: Jesus Christ, Son of God and Lord, has been raised from the dead and reigns.

Before he asks anything of the church, he tells them who they are: loved by God and called to be saints.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Promised Beforehand

Paul insists that his gospel was “promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures.” It is not his invention or a Gentile novelty but the fulfilment of Israel’s own Scriptures: Jesus is David’s promised son (2 Samuel 7) and the Son of Psalm 2. Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul called himself a doulos, a slave, of Christ Jesus in a world where slavery meant degradation, and counted it his highest dignity. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy, the claim that the best life is one of belonging wholly to Christ still offends, and it still frees those who find that his yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans is Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel, written from Corinth around AD 57 to a church he had never visited. It lays out the whole plan of salvation: all are sinners under God’s wrath (1:18–3:20); God justifies the ungodly by faith in Christ alone (3:21–5:21); the justified are freed from sin’s power and given the Spirit (6–8); God’s purpose for Israel stands (9–11); and the gospel shapes a whole new way of life (12–16). Augustine, Luther and Wesley were among those converted through it. Chapter 1 opens with Paul’s greeting and theme, then begins the long argument: the wrath of God against a humanity that knew him and turned away.

Three names in one breath. Paul introduces himself three ways before his name is fully out of his mouth: a slave (doulos), called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel. The first is ownership: Paul belongs entirely to Christ. The second is commission: he did not volunteer; Christ stopped him on the Damascus road and sent him. The third is a single purpose: Paul has been reserved for one thing, the gospel of God.

A servant of Christ Jesus. Take the first word slowly, because we have made it sound tame. Most English Bibles render doulos as “servant”, and a servant is a man with a job. That is not what the word meant. A slave in the Roman world was not an employee but a possession, in law a thing and not a person. He owned nothing, and had no right to his own time, his own body or his own plans.

The word read aloud in Rome. Perhaps a quarter to a third of Rome was enslaved, and when this letter was read aloud in a house church there were slaves in the room, and probably people who owned them. Into that room the apostle introduces himself by the legal status of the lowest people present.

The highest title in Israel. Yet a Jewish reader would have heard something else in the same instant, and Paul intends both. “Servant of the LORD” is one of the great titles of the Old Testament. It belongs to Moses, to David, and supremely to the Servant of Isaiah. So in one word Paul takes the lowest rung on the Roman ladder and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures and says they are the same rung: to be owned by Christ is the highest honour there is. That is the pattern of the whole gospel he is about to explain.

Called to be an apostle. Not self-appointed (Galatians 1:1). An apostle is one sent with authority, an eyewitness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 9:1). And the Greek adjective, klētos, called, turns up twice more before the sentence is over: called to belong to Jesus Christ (v. 6), called to be saints (v. 7). Paul does not keep a special word for his own calling and a lesser one for everybody else’s. Whatever happened to him on the Damascus road and whatever happened to you are named with the same word: neither of you volunteered, and neither of you was consulted.

Set apart for the gospel of God. “Set apart” (aphōrismenos) echoes in Greek what the name Pharisee probably meant in Hebrew: the separated ones, a movement whose entire discipline was separation from everything and everyone that might defile. Many interpreters think Paul intends the echo. God takes the separated man and keeps him separated, but changes what the separation is for. He is no longer set apart from people; he is set apart for a message, and the message sends him straight to the Gentiles he had spent his life avoiding. Nothing about him was wasted. God took it over for his own use (Galatians 1:15). And “the gospel of God” means it comes from God: it is his good news before it is anyone’s message.

The title his Lord wore first. When Paul wants to describe what the Son of God did in coming to us, he reaches for this same word: Christ “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), the form of a doulos. Christ Jesus is Lord of all, and yet he knelt to wash his disciples’ feet (John 13:5) and was valued at the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32; Matthew 26:15). Paul is the slave of the one who became a slave. The Son who owned everything took the form of the one who owns nothing, so that people who belonged to sin could come to belong to him. And belonging to him is concrete: your time, body, money and plans are his to direct, you are not your own (1 Corinthians 6:19), and whether you live or die, you are the Lord’s (14:8).

What it does not mean. Paul is describing ownership, not exhaustion. The Master in question told his workers to come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31), and a church that quotes this verse at a tired person to extract more work has understood neither the slave nor the Master. Nor must every Christian have a dramatic calling like Paul’s. His assignment is not yours, but if you belong to Christ you were called, in exactly the sense he was.

Does the church still have apostles? Not in Paul’s sense. An apostle of Christ had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), and Paul calls himself the last to see him. The apostles laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and their teaching is now in the New Testament. Missionaries and church planters are sent ones in a general sense, but no one today carries an apostle’s authority. So when we want to hear an apostle, we open this letter. Some churches today give the title apostle to pioneering leaders; if they mean a sent missionary the word can bear it, but no such leader adds to the foundation or speaks with Paul’s authority.

In everyday life. A slave’s defining condition is that he does not own his own time, and the quickest way to find out what you believe about ownership is to listen to yourself when a day is interrupted. Listen for the word that arrives (my morning, my weekend) and for the resentment when someone spends it for you. That reaction is not a small sin to be scolded over; it shows who you really think owns your life.
verseByVerse.note: “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by his master. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oldest thing in the world. The gospel Paul preaches is not a novelty but the fulfilment of God’s promise in the Scriptures of Israel (Genesis 3:15; 12:3; Isaiah 53). And “promised beforehand” answers an objection the Roman church was certainly hearing. Rome respected age and distrusted new religions, so the charge was easy to make: a sect barely twenty-five years old, gathered round an executed provincial. Paul’s answer is that the gospel is as old as God’s first promise, and what happened outside Jerusalem was not the start of something new but the keeping of a promise.

Promised. A promise is only as good as the one who makes it, and the wait before it is kept is the test. In a garden God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head, and then let millennia pass. He swore to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in his offspring, and then the family went down to Egypt, stayed some four centuries, and ended in slavery. He told David that a son of his would have a throne for ever, and the line dwindled to a carpenter in a village nobody respected. The promise never lapsed. God’s delays run to centuries, and he has never yet failed to arrive. The word “promised” settles the character of God before a single doctrine is argued: he is the God who keeps his word across centuries.

Through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. Paul preached the gospel out of a book his hearers already owned; he had no New Testament. So any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point, and those three-quarters of your Bible, perhaps the part you find hardest, are not the run-up to the gospel. They are the gospel in promise. Jesus said as much on the road to Emmaus, when, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

How do I find Christ in the Old Testament without forcing it? Read each passage for its plain meaning first, in its own setting. Then ask where it is heading: which promise it carries forward (a seed, a king, a new covenant), which pattern it sets up that Christ fulfils (the Passover lamb, the priest, the temple), and which longing it leaves open that only he answers. The New Testament shows the way, because Jesus and the apostles read the Old Testament like this. You are not hunting for hidden codes. You are following a road to where it arrives.

Concerning his Son. The gospel is about a person. Not first a system, a method or a moral code, but God’s Son. Everything Paul will argue for fifteen chapters unfolds this one phrase. The good news is not first advice about what you should do, but news about what he has done: he lived, died for our sins and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Advice depends on you to carry it out. News is true whether or not you feel it, and you receive it by believing it.

According to the flesh. This means his human nature: a true man, born of David’s line, fulfilling the promise of a son of David who would reign for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). God’s Son entered a genealogy, a family with a documented history, and if you have read that family’s history you know what is in it. David, who arranged a man’s death to conceal an adultery; Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; a prostitute in Jericho. That is the family the Son of God consented to join, and he did not join it at a safe distance. He took their flesh.

A report, not a principle. Christianity is not a set of timeless spiritual principles that a thoughtful person could have discovered in any century. It is a report about something that happened, to a particular man, in a family whose line Scripture records. Which is why it could be false, and why, if it is true, it is not merely inspiring but binding.

parallels.desc: the promised son of David

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Declared, not made. The resurrection is the divine verdict on Jesus: he who was Son of God in weakness and humiliation has been publicly declared Son of God in power by his rising. “Declared” (horisthentos) means appointed, installed in the open. It does not mean made, as those argue who say God adopted the man Jesus as his Son at the resurrection. The answer is in the sentence itself. One verse earlier the gospel is “concerning his Son, who was descended from David”: the one born into David’s line was already God’s Son. He was the Son before he had a family tree to enter. A man cannot be promoted into a position he already held.

In power. What changed at the resurrection was not the Son but the public record. He moved from weakness to power, from humiliation to exaltation (Philippians 2:6–11). A verdict does not create the fact it announces: a man wrongly convicted and later exonerated was innocent throughout. The world had published its verdict on Jesus in the notice nailed above his cross, in three languages; then God overturned it, and not in private. The resurrection is the Father standing up in the courtroom of the world, after the sentence has been carried out and the body sealed in rock, and announcing that the accused was his Son the whole time. The Son who was never not the Son, who had the Father’s glory before there was a world to be glorious in, consented to be reduced to a corpse in a borrowed grave, so that the announcement could be made from the one place where no one could argue with it. Peter sets the two verdicts side by side: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36).

According to the Spirit of holiness. Both phrases describe the same person. “According to the flesh” describes Jesus in his earthly life, able to grow tired, to weep and to die; “according to the Spirit” describes him as he has been since Easter, risen, enthroned and pouring out the Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33). The Spirit of holiness is most probably the Holy Spirit, by whose power he was raised. And the Spirit is not incidental: the same Spirit who raised him is the one Paul says lives in you, so that “he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (8:11).

By his resurrection. The resurrection is the proof (Acts 13:33; 17:31). And it matters for the whole letter because Paul will say that Christ was raised for our justification (4:25). If the world’s verdict on the Son was overturned in public, the guilty verdict on everyone joined to him has been overturned with it. The empty tomb is God’s receipt: the debt was accepted as paid.

Jesus Christ our Lord. After such exalted titles, Paul ends on one small word, “our”. Not the Lord, but our Lord. Kyrios was what the Greek Old Testament used to render the divine name, and it was also a title the empire gave to Caesar; Paul claims both for Jesus at once. The one who holds the name above every name is spoken of, by a slave writing to a house church in the capital, as though he belongs to them.

In everyday life. Ask what you would say if someone told you tomorrow that they had found the body. Not whether you could refute it, but whether it would matter. If your faith is mainly a set of values, a way of being decent and hopeful, the news would be sad but survivable. Paul’s faith would not survive it for an hour, and he says so plainly: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:14–19). He staked everything on an event that could in principle be disproved by a corpse.

parallels.desc: you are my Son

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace and apostleship. Paul is almost certainly not listing two separate gifts. He means the grace that consisted in being made an apostle, and to feel why, remember who is writing. The man given the commission to preach had been arresting preachers, and he never got over it: “I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). So the commission was not a reward that followed the pardon. It was the pardon made visible. God did not merely forgive the persecutor; he handed him the message and sent him to the people he had been hunting.

To bring about the obedience of faith. A phrase that brackets the entire letter: it appears again at the very end (16:26), in a closing doxology that some ancient manuscripts place elsewhere in the letter but nearly all include. The grammar allows more than one reading. It may be the obedience that consists in faith, so that believing the gospel is itself the first act of obedience to God; or the obedience that springs from faith, the life that follows believing; or obedience to “the faith”, the body of Christian teaching. Paul would probably have been puzzled by our need to choose, and the decisive evidence is where he puts the phrase: as a pair of bookends, with everything between them as the explanation. This commentary’s view: faith is the first thing God commands, and the root from which every other obedience grows: not faith versus obedience, but faith working through love (Galatians 5:6).

Faith is not passive. The letter that insists most fiercely on justification by faith apart from works opens and closes by calling for obedience. Faith does not replace obedience, and obedience does not earn what faith receives. It costs nothing to admire Jesus or to agree that the gospel is probably true. What this phrase asks is that you stop relying on yourself and trust your whole life to Christ, and that is not a mild request. That is why the New Testament can call unbelief disobedience.

So am I saved by obeying? No. Paul will spend chapters 3 and 4 proving that no one is declared right with God by works (3:20, 28). Obedience is never the ground of our acceptance; Christ’s obedience is (5:19). But real faith never stays alone. The faith that rests on Christ is the same faith that begins to follow him, and the obedience that grows from it is the fruit of being accepted, not the price of it.

For the sake of his name. Not first for the nations or the church’s growth, but for the name, and the name has a history. The Father gave it to the Son who humbled himself to the death of a cross, the name above every name, so that every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:8–11). The Son declared in power by his resurrection (1:4) is the King of Psalm 2 (Acts 13:33), and to that King the Father says: ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). Paul’s mission is that promise being paid out. Every Gentile brought to the obedience of faith is part of the inheritance the Father promised his Son.

Among all the nations. The phrase echoes God’s promise that in Abraham’s offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 22:18). Paul’s travel plans are a promise sworn on Mount Moriah being kept on actual roads, by a man with a tentmaker’s hands.

Including you. The Christians in Rome are not the audience of this mission, watching it happen elsewhere. They are the thing itself, what “all the nations” looks like when the sentence stops being a plan and becomes a room with people in it. And note what they are called to: not to achieve, or to understand, or to be useful. Called to belong. You are called to belong to Jesus Christ, and the name for whose sake the whole world is being reached has been written over you.

parallels.desc: the obedience of faith

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who was in that room. This greeting is warmer than the situation was. Some years before, the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome; Luke mentions it in passing, which is how Priscilla and Aquila came to be in Corinth (Acts 18:2). The Jewish believers, probably including many of the founders, were gone, and for several years the Roman congregations were, it seems, largely Gentile. Then Claudius died in AD 54, the edict seems to have lapsed, and the exiles came home to churches that had learned to function without them, with other leaders and other customs. Hold that in mind and much of this letter stops being abstract, from Jew and Gentile equally justified to chapter 14 on the strong and the weak. Paul is writing into a congregation with a seam running through it, Jewish believers on one side and Gentile on the other, and he addresses them all with one description: loved by God, called, saints.

Loved by God. Before they are anything else, they are loved: not because they loved their way into God’s favour, and still after they have failed at a good deal. The letter will say it plainly: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (5:8). The love was at full strength at the worst possible moment. It cannot become greater than it already is.

Called to be saints. Not aspiring to be saints, but already saints by the call of God that placed them in Christ. Church usage has made the word mean a category of exceptional Christians, mostly dead, with stained glass. In the Old Testament it is used constantly of things, the holy vessels, and what made them holy was not their quality but the fact that they were set apart for God. A bowl in the tabernacle was not a better bowl. It was a bowl set aside for God, no longer available for anything else. So when Paul calls a mixed room of tradesmen, slaves and immigrants the holy ones, he is not describing their record. He is describing what has happened to them (Acts 9:13).

Be what you are. If holiness began as your achievement you would have to keep proving it. If holiness is God’s setting you apart for himself, then failure is a contradiction of what you are, not a disproof of it, because your standing rests on Christ’s perfect obedience, not on yours (5:19). That is exactly how Paul writes to the most disorderly church he knew, opening a letter about lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s table and a man sleeping with his stepmother by calling them saints (1 Corinthians 1:2). He does not withdraw the word in order to rebuke them; he rebukes them on the strength of it. To be called a saint is a comfort, and it is also a summons to treat your body and your life as his, never again as common property, and the Holy Spirit who now lives in that body is the one who makes that possible (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

How do I know I am called? Paul’s word means God’s effective summons, the call that actually brings a person to Christ (8:30). You do not need to remember a dramatic moment. If you trust Christ, rest your hope on him and want to follow him, that faith is the evidence that God called you, because no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44).

Grace to you and peace. Paul’s greeting joins the Greek and the Hebrew. Grace (charis) is a play on the standard Greek hello, chairein, and peace is the Jewish shalom: to a church with Greeks and Jews eyeing each other across a room, even his greeting brings the two together. Grace is God’s undeserved favour; peace is what that favour produces: reconciliation with God and wholeness of life. The order never reverses in Paul’s greetings: grace comes first, and peace follows from it. And Paul pronounces both before he has written a sentence of argument: the gospel is gift before it is demand.

From God our Father and the Lord. Jesus is set alongside the Father as the single source of grace and peace. Only God gives grace, so this is a quiet but clear statement of Christ’s deity. And this is the first time the letter says “God our Father”; by chapter 8 a room full of former slaves and shopkeepers will be crying “Abba! Father!” (8:15). The God who is about to spend a chapter and a half describing his own wrath is introduced to these people, by name, as their Father.

Peace across the seam. Into that divided room Paul speaks peace from the Lord Jesus Christ, and he does not mean a mood. Christ himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). That peace was made at a particular place, by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and it runs two ways at once: it reconciles the sinner to God, and because both are reconciled to the same God by the same blood, it reconciles him to the brother across the room. The greeting does not ask them to get on. It tells them the ground on which they already stand together.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people, that is, all believers. The church at Rome was not founded by Paul; he had never been there.

parallels.desc: visitors from Rome at Pentecost

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having greeted the church, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians constantly, longed to visit them, and been prevented more than once. The passage shows what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like: his longing for Rome is personal, not only strategic, and he expects to be encouraged by them as well as to strengthen them.

In verse 14 he calls himself a debtor to everyone: he owes them the message he received for nothing. And in verse 16 the understatement, “not ashamed”, says more than a boast would: he is eager to bring the gospel of a crucified Lord to the capital of the empire that crucified him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 shows that Paul’s mission cannot be separated from his affection for the church. The Roman Christians are not an audience for his theology or a resource for his travels, but brothers and sisters he longs to see. Mission comes from the church and builds the church, and Paul, for all his travelling, is an apostle within the body of Christ, not a lone evangelist.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s debt to Greeks and barbarians, the wise and the foolish, cut across every cultural and social rank: the gospel belonged to no class. Now: Churches are always tempted to shape the gospel for people already like themselves. Paul’s debtor language corrects that: the gospel is owed to everyone within our reach, whether or not they seem likely converts.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
First, I thank my God. This is Paul’s settled habit, even to the Corinthians; only Galatians has no thanksgiving at all, a sign that something was seriously wrong there. Here it is present, warm and first.

Through Jesus Christ. Easy to read as a formula, and it is not one. Paul cannot even say thank you to God on his own account. Gratitude goes up through the Mediator, because the problem the letter is about to describe is not merely that we sin but that we have no right of our own to come before God. So the smallest prayer in the Christian life travels the same road as the greatest. Every thank you before a meal is carried by the same blood that carried the thief into paradise.

Your faith is proclaimed. He thanks God not for their numbers or their strategic position but for their faith, and faith is itself God’s gift, so the Giver receives the thanks. Every road led to Rome and out again, and what travelled out along those roads was the news that these people believed God.

For God is my witness. Why swear to something as unremarkable as praying for people? Because they had no way of checking, and reason to wonder. Paul is writing to a church he did not found, in a city he hopes to use as a base for a mission further west (15:24), and someone in that room might conclude that the famous apostle’s sudden interest was strategic. So he calls God to witness what nobody else can verify: for years, unseen, they have been on his list.

Whom I serve. The word for serve, latreuō, is temple language, the word for priestly service: the sacrifices, the incense, the work done in the holy place by men in linen. Paul applies it to talking about Jesus in rented rooms, workshops and prisons (15:16): not something like worship, but worship itself. His prayer life and his preaching were not two compartments; they were one act of worship.

That without ceasing I mention you. Before this phrase crushes you: Paul was not praying every waking second; he made tents, argued in synagogues, sailed, ate and slept. The phrase was ordinary Greek for something regular and unremitting. It means these people never dropped off his list. A reader who takes it as a demand for continuous spoken prayer will conclude within a week that he cannot pray at all, which is exactly the result the verse was not written to produce.

How do I pray for people like this? Make it small enough to keep. Write down the names God has put on your heart, and pray for a few each day, so that every name comes round each week. Pray Paul’s own prayers for them (Ephesians 1:17–19; Philippians 1:9–11; Colossians 1:9–12), so that you are asking for what matters most, not only for problems to go away. And when you remember someone during the day, turn the thought into a sentence to God on the spot.

In everyday life. Look at what fills your praying. For most of us it is situations: the diagnosis, the interview, the money, the decision; when the situation resolves, the subject disappears. Paul’s prayer life was populated by people, most of them absent, some not yet met. In the last chapter he greets about two dozen of them by name in a city he had never visited.

For worship. Somewhere there is an old woman, or a friend from a church you left, or a parent, who mentions your name to God with a regularity you know nothing about. And above every one of them is the Son himself, who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and has never once let your name drop off his list.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now at last. These words are the sound of a man who has been waiting a long time: I have longed for many years to come to you (15:23). A plan formed for the best reasons had been blocked repeatedly, and he was still asking.

Somehow by God’s will. Paul did not know how. This is not the verbal tic that “if it be your will” often becomes, a disclaimer attached in advance so that nothing has really been asked. Paul asks for the specific thing, plainly and repeatedly, and then leaves the outcome with God (James 4:15).

Desire held within God’s sovereignty. He does not give up, or try to force the door. Most of us can manage desire without submission, which is impatience, or submission without desire, which is resignation wearing a pious face. Paul keeps both.

The delays are not neglect. Most delays feel like a door closing for no reason: the job that went to somebody else, the years of waiting for a child. Paul was not always told what the prevention was for (Acts 16:7). So the honest form of this doctrine is not that every delay has a visible reason you will eventually be shown. It is that the delays are not random and are not neglect. And in this case the proof is in your hands. If Paul had reached Rome when he first wanted to, we might well not have this letter. The fullest account of the gospel in the New Testament exists because a man could not get to the city he wanted to visit and had to write instead.

How do I know whether a closed door is God’s no, or something to push through? Do not try to read God’s will from circumstances alone; doors can close for many reasons. Ask first what Scripture says: God’s commands settle what is right, and no open door can make a wrong thing right. Within what is right, use wisdom, take counsel from mature believers, keep praying, and keep trying where it is wise to try, as Paul did for years. Then accept the outcome God gives. God’s providence (his ruling of all events) is understood by looking back. It is not a signal to steer by in advance. Paul did not know why Bithynia was closed until Macedonia opened.

Answered in his way. When the prayer was finally answered, it was answered in a form he had not asked for. He reached Rome as a prisoner, after arrest, two years in custody at Caesarea and a shipwreck, at the empire’s expense, chained to a soldier (Acts 27–28). He got the city. He did not get the itinerary. And the last verse of Acts leaves him there, proclaiming the kingdom of God with all boldness and without hindrance: exactly what this prayer had asked for.

The Lord who kept the timetable. Paul had learned from his Master to want things within the Father’s timing. Jesus lived by an hour that was not his to choose: “My time has not yet come,” he told his brothers (John 7:6), until the night he lifted his eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come” (John 17:1). And it was the risen Christ himself who answered this prayer for Rome. When Paul’s arrest in Jerusalem seemed to have closed the road for good, the Lord stood by him at night in the barracks and said: “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome” (Acts 23:11). The road to Rome ran under a promise from Christ’s own mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some spiritual gift. Paul begins confidently, with the gift running one way, from the apostle to the church. The phrase “spiritual gift” (charisma pneumatikon) does not describe a technique for handing over one of the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 like a parcel. Paul is deliberately vague: some gift, because he does not yet know what these particular people will need when he arrives, and he trusts the Giver to supply it then. “To strengthen” (stērichthēnai) is to make firm, as a building is made stable.

That is. Then he hears himself: “that is” is the sound of a man stopping mid-flow, hearing a note of condescension in his own draft, and reaching for a sentence in which the encouragement runs both ways. Even the apostle expected to receive from those to whom he ministered (Acts 28:15).

What the correction cost. Paul had seen the risen Christ and wrote Scripture; there was nothing ordinary believers in Rome could teach him about justification. But that is not what he says he needs from them. He expects to be encouraged by their faith, and faith is not expertise. A frightened woman still trusting God after a bad year has something the most learned man in the room cannot generate for himself by knowing more.

Strengthened by Christ preached. Paul wants to strengthen them, and in the last sentence of the letter he tells them how it is done. The same verb returns in the closing hymn of praise: “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ” (16:25). The strength is not Paul’s personality or learning but Jesus Christ set before them. So the mutual encouragement he longs for is not two groups admiring each other’s faith. It is two groups looking at the same Christ from different places, each seeing him more clearly for the other’s eyes.

The body has no passengers. If you are the one who normally teaches, leads, hosts or fixes, look at what Paul thinks a strong Christian is: not a man with no needs, but a man who knows he has them and says so, in plain words, to people less impressive than himself. And if you are newer, quieter, convinced you are in the room only to receive, the apostle to the Gentiles was looking forward to being helped by people exactly like you. The body of Christ has no passengers. Christ has so made his body that its greatest member cannot do without its least, and the faith he gives to the weakest believer is a gift to the strongest. That is why sitting with a believer who is suffering well can leave you steadier than a conference will.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want you to be unaware. This is a signal Paul uses when he is about to tell his readers something they might otherwise get wrong (11:25). Someone in Rome had almost certainly noticed the obvious: the apostle to the Gentiles has been working the eastern Mediterranean for years and has never once come to the capital of the Gentile world. The natural conclusion was unflattering, and Paul corrects it. The ESV notes that “brothers” includes sisters in the church.

But thus far have been prevented. He does not say he was too busy, which would have been true. He says he was prevented, and the word implies that someone was behind the obstacle. Part of the hindrance was the work elsewhere (15:22); and the same Spirit who forbade him Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7) had other work for him first. The account you give of a year changes how it feels to live inside it. “I never got round to it” leaves you the manager of a life that is not going well. “I was prevented” leaves you a servant whose Master has other arrangements.

Some harvest. Harvest (karpos, fruit): conversions and growth. Harvest is slow, and it is not manufactured: a farmer can plough, sow and water, and cannot make a single seed germinate: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). And it is seasonal, which is why he can be prevented for years without the work being lost. A field left unvisited is not a field abandoned. It is a field not yet ripe.

A field is never finished. Their faith is talked about all over the empire (v. 8), and Paul still expects a harvest among them. A building is completed and then maintained; a field is never finished, and is either being worked or going back to weeds.

The grain that made the harvest. Jesus gave the reason Gentile fruit exists on the day some Greeks came asking to see him: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). The harvest Paul hopes to reap in Rome is that fruit. Every Gentile believer comes from a single grain that went into the ground outside Jerusalem and came up on the third day. Paul ploughs and sows and waters, but he is gathering a crop that Christ’s death has already guaranteed.

In everyday life. Think of the situation you have privately written off: the relative who will never believe, the colleague who is too far gone, the part of your own character you have decided is simply how you are. Ask when you stopped expecting anything there. Not when you stopped trying; when you stopped expecting. And if you are the one doing the sowing and have seen nothing, the parent, the teacher or the colleague who has sown for years: often one sows and another reaps (John 4:37–38). The growing is not your department, and the absence of fruit in June says nothing about what is happening underground.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under obligation. Not willing, or burdened, or available: Paul is a debtor (opheiletēs). That is the language of the ledger: a man who owes something and has not yet paid it. How do you come to be in debt to strangers? Suppose someone hands you a sum of money to deliver to another man. You are then in debt to a person you have never met, for money that was never yours, until he has it in his hand. That is Paul’s position. On the Damascus road he was given something that was not for him: a message with a name on it, addressed to the nations. To withhold it would be theft.

Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. The first-century way of saying everyone: the cultured and the crude, the clever and the slow. Paul is naming the two groups a preacher instinctively avoids for opposite reasons: the sophisticated frighten us, and the unsophisticated seem unpromising. Paul says he is in debt to both. The church does not get to choose its creditors.

Where barbarian stands beside Greek. Paul’s word barbarian appears again in a list of divisions that Christ has ended: “Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11). That is why the debt runs to both ends of the human scale. The message is not a philosophy that suits the clever or a comfort that suits the simple, but a person. The Athenian and the Scythian are owed the same gospel because they need the same Christ, and in him they will sit at the same table.

Eager to preach. Even to believers: Christians need the gospel preached to them too. And Paul feels not guilt but eagerness. The debt has become a desire.

What it does not mean. A debt can be preached in a way that crushes. If you owe everybody, and the payment is their eternal life, then every conversation you did not have becomes an unpaid debt, and a sensitive Christian can be flattened by that arithmetic. But Paul is one man with one life who cannot reach Spain and Rome in the same year, and does not pretend otherwise. Your debt is to the people God has actually put in your reach: the ones whose names you know, whose kitchens you sit in, who work at the next desk. He never asked you to be the apostle to the Gentiles; that post is filled.

How do I pay the debt without being pushy? Begin with the people you already know, and with honesty about yourself. Live in a way that raises questions, and answer them gently and respectfully when they come (1 Peter 3:15). Pray for opportunities and notice them: a friend’s grief, a question about why you go to church, a conversation about what makes life worth living. Say simply what Christ has done, and leave the result to God. You are responsible to deliver the message, not to produce the response.

In the flow. Verses 8–15 are the letter’s personal frame, picked up again at 15:14–33, and this verse is the bridge into the letter’s theme. He is eager to preach the gospel in Rome, for he is not ashamed of it, for it is the power of God for salvation, for in it the righteousness of God is revealed (vv. 16–17): each step gives the reason for the one before. Until he can come in person, Romans is the gospel he would have preached to them.
verseByVerse.note: Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
These two verses are the thesis of the letter: nearly everything Paul argues later unfolds a phrase from them.

Martin Luther, who had understood “the righteousness of God” as the standard by which God condemns sinners, wrestled with the phrase until the light broke. “At last,” he wrote, “meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” Much of the Reformation grew from that discovery.

The gospel is power: not advice, but God himself at work to save. And it is for everyone who believes: faith is the one hand that receives what God freely gives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed interpreters have read “the righteousness of God” in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that comes from God and is given to the believing sinner. This is imputation: Christ’s perfect righteousness is credited to the believer’s account, so that God is both just (sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the “wonderful exchange”: Christ takes our sin, and we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther’s discovery of Romans 1:17 freed him, and many after him, from trying to earn salvation by merit and religious performance. Now: Every generation rebuilds the system of merit. These verses are its lasting answer: the gospel is not something you do but something done for you, received by faith from the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not ashamed. Paul would not say “not ashamed” unless the pull towards shame was real; we have had two thousand years to get used to the cross, and Paul’s readers had not. Crucifixion was not merely a cruel execution; it was a deliberately degrading one, reserved in practice for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, and Roman citizens were normally exempt from it by law. Cicero, arguing a case more than a century earlier, said the very word ought to be kept away not only from the body of a Roman citizen but from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears. And the message Paul is carrying into the capital has at its centre a Jewish provincial who was put to death that way: foolishness to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Alexamenos worships his god. Scratched into plaster on the Palatine in Rome, probably a century and a half after this letter arrived, someone drew a cartoon: a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a man beside it with his hand raised in worship. Underneath, in scrawled Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. It is exactly the social reality Paul is writing into: to confess this gospel in Rome was to be the person everyone else found faintly ridiculous.

A man who had felt the pull. Paul had private reasons for the sentence too. He had been beaten out of Philippi and mocked in Athens, and came to Corinth by his own admission “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). This is a man who has felt the pull repeatedly and decided where he stands.

The power of God for salvation. He does not say the gospel is true, though it is, or reasonable, though he will argue it for eleven chapters. He says it is power, and the grammar matters: not that the gospel has power or brings power, but that it is the power of God. The message is not a description of something powerful happening elsewhere; it is the instrument God uses to do the thing. Elsewhere Paul says the same of Christ himself: to those who are called, Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). The power in the message is the crucified and risen Lord at work through it. That is why ordinary Christians saying ordinary sentences about Christ keep producing results out of all proportion to the people involved. (The word, dynamis, means effective might, not “dynamite”.) “Salvation” is rescue from sin, wrath and death into eternal life.

Then why doesn’t everyone believe when it is preached? The same message that saves some is folly to others (1 Corinthians 1:18). The gospel is God’s power, but it is the power of a living God who works through it as he wills; the Spirit must open blind eyes (2 Corinthians 4:4–6; Acts 16:14). That is why we preach and pray together. We are never the power. We carry it, and ask God to use it.

To the Jew first. What does “first” (prōton) mean? Not that Jews are saved more easily or more fully, or by a different way: Paul will insist that there is no distinction, for all have sinned and all are justified the same way, by faith (3:22–23; 10:12). First means first in time and in the privilege of history. God made his promises to Israel; the Messiah came from Israel as Israel’s king; the gospel was preached first in Jerusalem, and in city after city Paul went first to the synagogue (Acts 13:46; 17:1–2). “Greek” means the whole Gentile world. And for a divided congregation Paul has already settled the thing that mattered most in that room: one power, one condition (faith), two peoples, and the same door.

Does it set a priority in mission today? Some Christians read “to the Jew first” as a standing rule that the church must take the gospel to Jewish people before others. The more likely reading is that it describes the order of salvation history, which Paul’s own practice followed. It does not put one people ahead of another in the queue. But it does forbid the opposite error. Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they may be saved (10:1), and a church that left Jewish people out of its witness would have forgotten whose promises it is preaching.

In the flow. The righteousness revealed from faith for faith is the argument of 3:21 to 4:25; the power of God for salvation is traced through chapters 5 to 8; the Jew first and also the Greek underlies chapters 9 to 11 and 14 to 15. Read the rest of Romans with these two verses open beside it.

In everyday life. Shame usually shows itself quietly, long before anyone questions you: the sentence you began and did not finish, the small disclaimer, “I’m not really religious, but”, attached in advance so that nobody takes you for a keen believer. Watch for those small edits this week. The answer is not to work up more nerve, because the verse ends not with a demand for courage but with an argument: for it is the power of God. And the Lord who “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), is not ashamed to call such people his brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteousness of God. Everything turns on what “the righteousness of God” means: an attribute (God’s own perfect rightness), an activity (God putting things right), or a gift (a righteous status God gives to people who have none). If the gospel reveals God’s standard, that is not good news; it is the problem restated more clearly. And this is where the verse becomes a biography.

The monk and the open gates. Martin Luther was a monk who took sin seriously enough to be destroyed by it. He fasted, kept vigils, confessed for hours at a stretch, and found no peace, and he later wrote that he had hated this phrase. Then the meaning broke open. He saw that the righteousness revealed in the gospel is not the standard God demands but the standing God gives; not the righteousness by which he condemns, but the righteousness with which he clothes (3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). He felt, he wrote, that he had entered paradise itself through open gates. Luther spent years trying to give God a righteousness God would accept. The gospel does not tell you how to produce a righteousness for God. It announces a righteousness from God, the spotless obedience of his own Son, put to the account of every sinner who trusts him.

An alien righteousness. The Reformers had a name for what Luther saw: iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, alien not as strange but as belonging to someone else. It is not produced in you; it is credited to you. Justification is a verdict, not a renovation: God declares a person righteous rather than making him so, as a judge pronounces sentence rather than reforms a character (Deuteronomy 25:1). Christ’s obedience is reckoned as yours; your sin was reckoned as his and dealt with at the cross. Luther called it the joyful exchange. And it is the only arrangement that lets God be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26): the debt paid, not waived, and the guilty acquitted, not excused. Imputed means counted to your account; imparted would mean worked into you. Justification is the first, complete the moment you believe; the second is the lifelong work of sanctification, God making you holy in fact, that follows (6:22).

If my righteousness is credited, does it matter how I live? Paul saw the question coming and gives chapter 6 to it: shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? By no means (6:1–2). The faith that receives Christ’s righteousness unites us to Christ himself, and no one can be joined to Christ and stay as he was. Holiness is not the payment for acceptance; it is the life of someone who has been accepted. You are not made right with God by how you live, but you will not stay comfortable living as if you were not.

Is revealed. Present tense, still happening. Every time this gospel is preached the curtain goes back again, and what Luther saw is shown to somebody else.

From faith for faith. The phrase (ek pisteōs eis pistin) has been read several ways: (1) from God’s faithfulness to our faith; (2) from the faith of the preacher to the faith of the hearer; (3) from Old Testament faith to New Testament faith; (4) faith growing from one degree to another; (5) faith from first to last. The ESV notes it can be rendered beginning and ending in faith. This commentary’s view: the fifth is most likely. The phrase is emphatic, like “from death to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16), meaning nothing but death. The righteousness God gives is received by faith, and by faith alone, from beginning to end, and Paul proves it at once with a text about faith. Not faith at the entry point followed by works for maintenance, and not faith plus works. The Christian life does not begin in grace and continue in effort; it is grace from first to last, received by faith from first to last.

Live by faith. From Habakkuk 2:4, and the prophet was not a man enjoying a settled faith. He had cried out to God about injustice and chaos, and God answered that the proud Babylonians would come, and fall, on a timetable Habakkuk would not choose; but the righteous would live by his faith, trusting God through the coming disaster. The Hebrew word can mean faithfulness as well as faith, but the faithfulness meant in Habakkuk is the steady trust of a person who relies on God’s word and waits for it, the trust Abraham showed (Genesis 15:6), so Paul is not changing its meaning but showing its heart. The Greek can be read as “the righteous shall live by faith” or “the one who is righteous by faith shall live”. Both are true, and the letter explains both: chapters 1–4 show how a person is righteous by faith, and chapters 5–8 show how the righteous person lives. The same faith that receives a righteousness you did not earn is the faith you go on living by in the dark, when nothing is visible.

Where Christians differ: what is the righteousness of God? Roman Catholic teaching sees it mainly as a righteousness God works into us over time, making us just. Some recent scholars (the New Perspective, a school that reads Paul’s debates as chiefly about how Jews and Gentiles belong together in God’s people) see it as God’s covenant faithfulness. This commentary’s view: it includes God’s faithfulness and his righteous character, but at its heart in Romans it is the gift of a righteous standing before God, credited to the believer on the basis of Christ’s work (3:21–26; 4:5–6; 5:17). We are justified by Christ’s righteousness imputed to us, not by our own righteousness imparted. This is the heart of the Reformation, and of the gospel.

In everyday life. If you were asked tonight why God should accept you, notice what actually rises first. If the answer includes “I try”, or “at least I never”, your account is being kept in your own name. The gospel’s answer contains no information about you at all, only about Christ, and the righteousness it gives does not fluctuate after a bad day, because you never generated it and cannot damage it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith,” and the quotation “The one who by faith is righteous shall live.”

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having announced the gospel, Paul shows why it is needed. God’s wrath is being revealed from heaven against people who suppress the truth. The problem is not ignorance but suppression: humanity knows God through creation and conscience, and holds that knowledge down.

The knowledge of God is suppressed (vv. 18–20); God is exchanged for images of creatures (vv. 21–23); and three times God gives people up (vv. 24, 26, 28) to the disorder that is both the result of their idolatry and his judgment on it.

This is not a portrait of the worst of humanity but of ordinary human life without the restraining grace of God, the kindness by which he holds evil back. Rome would have recognised itself here, and so will any honest heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has held that the wrath of God is real, personal and active. It is not merely the impersonal working out of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), but the holy, settled opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts his character. Leon Morris showed at length that in both Testaments God’s wrath is personal and purposeful. The gospel is fully good news only because this wrath is real: Christ bore it in our place (3:25), and those who are in him are saved from the wrath to come (5:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rome’s temples were full of gods in human form and deified emperors: creatures honoured in the Creator’s place, as verses 22–23 describe. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance: the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self. Any created thing made to bear the weight only God can carry produces futile thinking and darkened hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wrath of God. The first subject after the letter’s theme (vv. 16–17) is the wrath of God: before he explains the cure, he shows why we need it. And the word needs rescuing, because most people hear wrath and picture temper. The gods of Rome were famous for it: capricious, easily offended, dangerous chiefly because they were unpredictable. That is not what is described here. God’s wrath is not a mood he is in. It is his settled, personal, holy opposition to everything that ruins what he has made. It is not the opposite of his love but the form his love takes when it faces what is destroying those he loves. A parent who feels nothing on hearing what was done to their child has not achieved serenity. They have stopped loving the child.

Revealed now. The same verb as verse 17, in the present tense. The wrath is being uncovered now, as God gives people over to their sins (vv. 24, 26, 28), and will be revealed fully at the judgment (2:5). And it is revealed from heaven, the language of a throne. Some have proposed that wrath in Paul is only an impersonal process by which bad actions produce bad results. But consequences simply happen; this comes from heaven, and the whole argument leads to a cross that would be needless if the only problem were bad consequences. If nobody is angry, nobody needed to die.

Ungodliness and unrighteousness. Ungodliness is sin against God; unrighteousness is sin against people, and the rest of the chapter argues that the second grows out of the first: the morality problem is the symptom of a God problem. No subgroup is named: Paul is laying out the case against everyone, and the moment the list ends he turns on the reader who has been enjoying it (2:1).

Suppress the truth. “Suppress” (katechontōn) means to hold down by force, and it describes an action, not a condition. Think of holding a football under the surface of a swimming pool: the ball pushes up the whole time, and the moment your attention wanders it is on the surface again. That is Paul’s picture of unbelief: not an empty space where knowledge of God never arrived, not innocent ignorance, but a continuous effort to keep something submerged that keeps trying to rise.

Is God angry with me when I sin as a Christian? Not with the wrath of this verse. For those in Christ, that wrath was spent on the cross, and there is now no condemnation (8:1). God still grieves over our sin and disciplines us, but as a Father who corrects the children he loves, for our good (Hebrews 12:5–11). Discipline is not wrath in smaller doses. It is love making sure we share his holiness.

Where Christians differ: is God’s wrath real? Some say a loving God cannot be wrathful, or that wrath is only the natural consequence of sin. This commentary’s view: God’s wrath is personal and real, the reaction of his holiness to evil. Love and wrath are not opposites; a God who did not oppose evil would not be good. And the gospel is God’s answer: Christ bore that wrath (3:25; 5:9).

In the flow. The small word “For” at the start of verse 18 is the key to the next three chapters: a righteousness from God is revealed (v. 17) because the wrath of God is revealed against everyone (v. 18). Paul now builds the case, through the idolatrous world, the moralist and the Jew, until every mouth is stopped (3:19–20) and he can say “But now” (3:21).

In everyday life. Think of the moments when the pressure slips. A graveside; three in the morning after bad news. In those moments something surfaces, the sense that there is Someone, that you are known, and it is usually pushed back under within the hour. Paul’s claim is that nobody is short of evidence; we are all working very hard to hold it down. And the God you keep pushing down is not waiting to crush you when you stop: the next verses show his wrath, and the cross shows where it went.

For worship. Put verses 17 and 18 side by side: the righteousness of God revealed, and the wrath of God revealed. There is one place in history where both were revealed together. At the cross the wrath of God was displayed more terribly than in any judgment ever recorded, and it fell on the only man who had never once held the truth under. God put him forward as the propitiation (3:25), the sacrifice on which God’s wrath falls so that it does not fall on us, so that those who are his are saved by him from the wrath of God (5:9). The wrath has already arrived somewhere. For everyone who trusts him, that somewhere was not you. It was him.

verseByVerse.quote: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Plain to them. This is general revelation: God shows himself to everyone through creation (Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:17). Calvin called the world a theatre of God’s glory. Creation is not a set of clues God left lying about for those who care to investigate. It is his own voice, at conversational volume, everywhere, all the time.

His invisible attributes. The unseeable is clearly seen, the way you can see someone is exhausted: you are seeing a face, and reading it. And Paul is precise about how much it says. Two things: God’s eternal power (he must be powerful to make all this) and his divine nature (he is God, of an altogether different order from what he has made). It does not say that God is merciful or that there is forgiveness. Creation is enough light to know you are answerable. It is not enough light to be saved.

So they are without excuse. Anapologētos: having no defence to offer, a courtroom word. Paul is not claiming that nobody is ever honestly confused, or that everyone secretly believes and is lying. He is saying that when the case is heard, no one will stand up and say the evidence was insufficient. The claim is about what anyone will be able to say on the last day.

The Maker who came to be seen. The creation Paul describes has a Maker with a name. All things were made through the Son, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3); he is the image of the invisible God, and by him all things were created (Colossians 1:15–16). What creation could never say, he came to say in person. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (John 1:18). The God whose power is written across the sky did not leave us with the sky alone. He sent his Son, so that the God who could be known only as Maker could be known as Saviour.

What it does not mean. This is not a licence for contempt. If this passage has ever made you treat the sceptic at your table as a liar, you have taken a truth about the human race and used it as a weapon against one member of it. The suppression he describes is yours too: it is the reason you can know God is real and still live for stretches of a week as though he were not.

A question every reader asks: what about those who never heard? If creation reveals enough to condemn but not enough to save, what of people who never hear the gospel? Paul answers part of this and leaves the rest with God. People are not judged for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are judged for suppressing the light they did have, in creation and in conscience (2:12–16). God is perfectly just, and no one will be condemned unfairly (Genesis 18:25). If you carry a real grief about a particular person, this verse does not settle their case. It settles that God is not unjust in having a case at all. But that light cannot save, because no one responds to it rightly (3:10–12); salvation comes only through faith in Christ, and faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (10:13–17). That is why Paul was a missionary, and why the church must send the gospel to every nation.

Where Christians differ: can people be saved without hearing of Christ? Inclusivists hold that some who never hear the gospel may be saved by Christ’s work if they respond in faith to the light of creation, appealing to God’s justice and to believers outside Israel such as Melchizedek and Job. This commentary’s view: Scripture gives no warrant for that hope. General revelation leaves people without excuse (v. 20), not with a way of salvation; there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12); and Paul’s own logic assumes that people cannot call on one they have not heard of (10:14–15). God is free to work as he wills, and he can bring the gospel to anyone; but the church’s task is clear: go and tell. Those who hope more widely usually do so out of compassion, and the motive is a good one even where the reading does not persuade.

What about infants, and people who cannot understand? Paul is speaking of those who are able to perceive and suppress what God shows them. Infants who die, and people who were never able to understand, are in a different position. Scripture gives real hope here (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions say that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). They are not saved by innocence, but by the same Saviour as everyone else. If you have buried a little one, you may entrust that child to the Saviour who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

In everyday life. Take the last thing that genuinely stopped you: a night sky with no streetlights, a piece of music that went through you before you had decided anything about it, the face of someone you love asleep, the plain fact that there is something rather than nothing. Your first response was not an argument. It was awe, and awe is a response to a someone. That reflex, not the argument afterwards, is what Paul says is the knowledge of God arriving. Then watch what you habitually do with it thirty seconds later.

parallels.desc: the heavens declare the glory of God

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not honor him as God. The fall described here is first a fall of worship: humanity had the knowledge, the evidence and the obligation, and refused two things: to honour him and to thank him. To honour God is to give him his proper weight in the actual running of a life. You can believe in him and arrange your week, your money and your ambitions exactly as you would if he were not there. That is not atheism. It is knowing God and giving him no weight. Every sin begins here.

Or give thanks to him. Paul has begun a chapter that ends in murder, malice and ruthlessness, and the first item on the charge sheet is failing to say thank you. That looks out of all proportion until you see what gratitude is. To thank someone is to admit you have received something you did not produce. And nothing about you was produced by you, not even the intelligence you use to argue about God. Thanklessness is not rudeness. It is a claim about ownership, the quiet insistence that what I have, I hold by right. There is even a religious way to fail here. The Pharisee in the temple began by thanking God, and went on to thank him that he was not like other men (Luke 18:11). His thanks was really a compliment to himself: true thanks says I received it, and his said I deserved it.

The one man who gave thanks. Against this refusal stands one human life that never withheld either. Jesus gave God his full weight in every decision, down to the hour of his death. On the night he was betrayed he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, this is my body, which is for you (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). Where humanity began its ruin with ingratitude, the Saviour began its rescue with a thanksgiving.

Futile in their thinking. Emataiōthēsan: made empty, vain. In the Greek Old Testament this word group is often used of idols themselves: the vanities, the empty things, the nothings. So Jeremiah can make the pun that carries the whole indictment: your fathers went after worthlessness, and became worthless (Jeremiah 2:5). You catch the emptiness of what you serve. The Psalms give the mechanism: idols have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear, and those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Psalm 115:5–8). What you choose instead of God has no mouth to speak your name, no ears for anything you say to it in the dark, and nothing to give back, while the God who was set aside is the only one who was ever able to love you in return. Worship always changes the worshipper: you become like what you worship.

Foolish hearts darkened. The heart, the centre of the person, darkened, and the verb is passive: in view of what follows, the lights were most likely turned down by God, in judgment. It is the first hint of the phrase that will sound three times over the rest of the chapter: God gave them up. And a dark room is the one place where you cannot tell how dark it has become.

Claiming to be wise. The claim is not incidental to the foolishness; it is the evidence of it (1 Corinthians 1:20–21; Psalm 14:1). And Paul is not describing primitives, nor is he against learning (he quotes pagan poets when it suits him). He is writing to the capital of a civilisation with law courts, aqueducts, libraries and centuries of philosophy behind it, in which serious men carried food to statues.

In everyday life. You cannot usually see your own idol directly. But if we become like what we worship, look at what you are becoming and read backwards. More anxious and grasping? You may be worshipping something that can be taken from you. Exhausted and unable to rest? Something that never says “Enough, well done.” Your character is evidence of what you worship. But the same law runs the other way, and that is the hope: beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The cure for what you have become is not to stare at yourself but to look at Christ, and keep looking.

parallels.desc: they went after worthlessness

verseByVerse.quote: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exchanged. “Exchanged” is the word the chapter turns on (vv. 23, 25, 26), and it is a commercial word. An exchange is a transaction entered into deliberately, because at the moment of the trade you preferred what you were getting. Paul is not describing people who drifted or were misled, but a swap somebody wanted to make: God replaced with something less.

The terms of the trade. On one side, the glory (doxa) of the immortal God: the weight and blazing splendour of the One who cannot die. On the other, not even the creatures but likenesses of them: the living God traded for a picture of a lizard. Jeremiah put it as bewilderment: has a nation ever changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit. Be appalled, O heavens, at this (Jeremiah 2:11–12).

Creeping things. A staircase, and it only goes down: man, birds, four-footed beasts, reptiles, each step lower. And idolatry never levels out. Whatever a person puts in God’s place begins as something reasonably impressive, a career, a cause, a version of yourself, and the thing you serve keeps asking for slightly more and offering slightly less. Nobody sets out to worship a creeping thing. They set out to worship something a good deal higher up, and the staircase does the rest.

The golden calf. Paul writes with Israel’s own story in his ear. The nation had heard the voice of God out of the fire at Sinai, and within weeks had made a calf. The psalm describes it in almost these words: “They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass” (Psalm 106:20). So Paul is not indicting the pagan world from a safe distance: the people with the true revelation did this too, faster and with less excuse, which prepares for chapter 2, where he turns to the religious.
