2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a catalogue of Gentile vice that a first-century Jewish reader would have heard with some satisfaction. Chapter 2 turns on that same reader: the person who condemns the sins of others while practising the same things is not better placed than the Gentile; he is more to blame, because he knows better.

Paul’s target is the moralist, and especially the Jewish moralist who believes that belonging to God’s covenant people, with its religious privileges, shields him from God’s judgment. God judges impartially, rendering to each according to his works. The Gentile with only the law of conscience is judged by that; the Jew with the law of Moses is judged by that. Either way, all fall short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has described the moral ruin of the Gentile world, and now he turns on the reader who has been agreeing: the one who judges others is condemned by his own verdict.

He then sets out how God judges: according to truth (v. 2), according to works (v. 6), and without partiality (v. 11). God sees through performance to reality, the whole life is the evidence, and no ethnic or covenant privilege exempts anyone.

Verses 14–15 add the conscience as a moral witness: Gentiles without the law of Moses “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness.” Human beings are not morally blank, and so no one will have an excuse on the day of judgment.

Verse 4, the warmest in the passage and the most often misread, says that God’s kindness and patience are not evidence that he does not mind; they are “meant to lead you to repentance”. Each day on which judgment does not fall is an invitation held open. Verse 16 says who will judge and what: “on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus”. That is the most frightening sentence in the chapter, or the most freeing, since for those who are his, the one who will weigh what nobody else knows about them is the one who died for it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 can look like salvation by works, since God will give eternal life to those who persist in doing good. Reformed interpreters have read it as the principle of judgment (God judges the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). Works are the evidence of salvation, never its ground. Paul is not contradicting 1:16–17; he is setting out the standard of judgment that makes grace necessary for everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Many in Paul’s day trusted covenant privilege (circumcision, the law, the temple) to shield them: Gentiles might face judgment, but the covenant people were secure by their membership. Paul shows that it cannot. Now: The equivalent is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership or moral respectability instead of faith and repentance. God looks for a heart he has changed.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 2 turns from the openly wicked pagan world of chapter 1 to the moral, religious person who judges others, especially the Jew who has God’s law, and shows that he too is guilty. God judges by truth, not privilege, and he knows the secrets of the heart. Having the law, being circumcised, knowing God’s will: none of these saves a person who breaks the law. True circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit.

No excuse. This is the sentence chapter 1 was built to deliver. Paul spent fifteen verses on idolatry, sexual chaos, envy, gossip and the collapse of the family, knowing exactly what a religious reader does with such a passage: he agrees with it, warmly. And the agreement is the trap: a man who has been nodding for fifteen verses has persuaded himself that he stands above it all, as one who can tell right from wrong. Then “therefore” arrives, and the paragraph he has been applauding turns out to be a mirror. “No excuse” (anapologētos) is the same word as 1:20. The pagan had no defence; neither has the moralist.

O man. Chapter 1 was plural: they, them, humanity in the dock, comfortable enough to read. Here it is singular. Paul uses a device from the lecture halls, rounding on an imaginary objector, and the effect is that nobody can pass this verse along to somebody else. It is addressed to one person, and that person is holding the letter.

The very same things. The instinctive reply is: I have never done what that man did. Paul does not mean an identical list of acts. He means the same root disorder, living for self instead of for God, and the list of 1:29–31 includes respectable sins: envy, deceit, gossip, pride. By judging, you show you know right from wrong, and so you condemn yourself. We judge other people by their actions and ourselves by our intentions. Another man is short with his child and he is impatient; I am short with mine and I had a difficult day. Same act, filed under two different headings, and the filing is done before any conscious dishonesty, which is why it is so hard to catch.

The log in the eye. Our Lord gave this its permanent image. Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and not notice the log in your own (Matthew 7:3–5)? Because the log is in the eye. It is not on the table where it could be pointed out; it is lodged in the very organ you are using to look at him.

The only Judge without a log. Paul’s argument disqualifies every human judge, and he names the one who is left: “God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus” (2:16). The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), the one judge in history with no log in his eye. What he did with that sight is the gospel. “God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). The one person qualified to pass the sentence of this verse came down from the bench and took his place in the dock beside the accused.

Rightly. “Rightly” (kata alētheian): according to truth. God’s judgment, unlike the moralist’s, is based on reality, not appearances, and it has none of the self-exemptions we grant ourselves.

What it does not mean. Paul is not forbidding moral judgment. He has just spent a chapter making moral judgments of unusual severity, and later he will tell churches to deal with sin in their members. Jesus does not end with the log either: the speck is still to come out (Matthew 7:5). What changes is the order, and with it the whole character of the man doing the work: a person who has just removed a log from his own eye handles other people very differently.

So how do I correct someone without being the man in this verse? Start with yourself, honestly and first: what in me is like this? Then go to the person privately, not to others about him (Matthew 18:15). Go gently, as one who could fall the same way (Galatians 6:1), name the specific thing rather than the person’s character, and listen before you conclude. Ask whether you are hoping to win him or to be proved right. And if you find you enjoy it, wait: the pleasure is a sign the log is still there.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you suppose, O man, that you will escape the judgment of God? Paul asks it rather than asserting it, and the form matters. Nobody has ever said that sentence out loud. It is not a belief anyone holds consciously; it is an assumption underneath the beliefs, and Paul drags it into the daylight so the man hears it in his own voice. The man condemns a thing in someone else, does it himself, and expects a different outcome. He has no argument for this, only a settled sense that his case is somehow different.

Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience? “Presume” (kataphroneis) means to despise, look down on, take for granted. Three words for God’s goodness are stacked here. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is his active goodness, not mere tolerance. Forbearance is holding back what could justly be done. Patience (makrothumia) is long-temper, the opposite of a short fuse: the capacity to be provoked for a very long time and not act. So this is not a God who does not notice. He notices, is entitled to act, and does not, yet. The kindness in this verse has been running a very long time and has never once been hurried. It waited out the golden calf, the judges, the kings, the prophets who were stoned, and four hundred years of silence. It went on waiting while the men it was aimed at were sharpening the charges against his Son.

How presumption sounds. It almost never sounds like defiance. It sounds reasonable: it clearly cannot be that serious, or something would have happened by now; God knows what I am like and has evidently made his peace with it. Each argues from God’s silence, and each treats a delayed sentence as an acquittal. The prisoner whose appeal is pending is not free because the corridor is quiet.

Forbearance with a cross at the end of it. Paul does not leave the word forbearance hanging. He uses it once more in this letter, at the centre of the gospel: God put Christ forward as a propitiation (a sacrifice that turns away his wrath) by his blood, to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins (3:25). Here is why the patience of verse 4 was never indifference. For centuries God held back what sins deserved. He was waiting for the cross, where every sin he had patiently passed over would be dealt with in full. The kindness that leads to repentance has a face: when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared, he saved us (Titus 3:4–5).

Not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? The verse turns here. The verb is the ordinary word for leading someone somewhere. God’s goodness is not a neutral backdrop to your life; it is working on you, with a destination. The purpose of his patience is not to let you off but to give you time to repent (2 Peter 3:9). The mercies you have been enjoying are not evidence that the subject is closed. They are the means by which it is being reopened. His goodness should melt you, not make you comfortable. The same sun softens wax and hardens clay; so the same kindness softens one heart and hardens another.

What does repentance actually involve? Repentance is turning from sin to God. It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful to you but as offensive to him, and grieving over it. It takes hold of God’s mercy in Christ, because repentance without hope only drives a person away. And it turns: you forsake the sin and set yourself to walk with God in new obedience (the Westminster Confession 15.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 15.3). In practice that means naming the specific sin to God, not a vague apology; putting right what can be put right; removing what feeds it; and starting again the next time you fall, without waiting to feel worthy. It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life.

What it does not mean. Somebody will read “presuming on the riches of his kindness” and conclude that they have used up their allowance, that they are the one person for whom the offer has expired. Read the sentence again. It is not a warning that the kindness is running out; it is a complaint that it is being wasted, and you cannot waste something that has stopped being given. The fact that this frightens you is proof that the kindness is still doing its work. Presumption is a comfortable condition. It does not lie awake.

parallels.desc: slow to anger

verseByVerse.quote: But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hard and impenitent. Hardness (sklērotēs, from which we get sclerosis) is not a mood but a condition, and the honest picture is a callus. It forms slowly, in response to repeated friction, and its whole function is to stop you feeling what is happening at that spot. That is why hardness of heart is nearly impossible to diagnose from inside, and here it is the settled state of a religious man who has been listening to sermons for decades. If you are afraid this describes you, take the fear as good news: a callus does not worry about itself, and the fact that you ache shows feeling exactly where hardness would have none. Grief, depression and dry seasons are not hardness either.

Impenitent: remorse or repentance? Impenitent means refusing to repent, and most of us have never told apart two things that feel alike. Scripture keeps them apart by giving us two men in the same week. Judas was sorry enough to die of it, and Peter wept bitterly, and only one of them came back. The difference is not the amount of feeling. Remorse is mostly about me: what I have lost, how I look now, what this will cost. Repentance is about God: I agree with him about the thing, and I turn to him. Remorse can be enormously intense and leave a person exactly where it found him (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Storing up wrath. The verb is the one behind our word treasury, the same one Jesus used: do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, but lay up treasures in heaven (Matthew 6:19–20). Verse 4 spoke of the riches of God’s kindness; verse 5 says you are banking wrath. The picture is not of a man drifting toward a bad end but of a man making deposits. Yet the one thing this letter insists on is that the balance can be changed: not by a man improving his deposits, which is the only remedy he can think of and the one thing that cannot work, but by being credited with an account that was never his, Christ’s righteousness. For those who trust him, the wrath they had stored up was poured out at the cross, on the Son. The treasure they receive, they did not earn.

The day of wrath. The day of judgment, at Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). God’s wrath is not irritation or spite but his fixed and holy resistance to evil, as steady as his love (Psalm 7:11; Habakkuk 1:13). This is the third thing said to be “revealed” in barely twenty verses: the righteousness of God (1:17), the wrath of God (1:18), and now his righteous judgment.

The Judge who comes back for his own. The day of wrath is the day of the Lord Jesus, and the one who will render to each according to his works is the same Jesus who rescues his people from it. Paul tells believers that they wait for God’s Son from heaven, “whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come” (1 Thessalonians 1:10). The impenitent are storing up wrath against that day; those joined to Christ are waiting for it, because the Judge who comes is their Saviour coming back for them.

According to his works. Paul is quoting his Bible (Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12), and the psalm puts it in the same breath as something else: “to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work.” And “each one”: no one will be graded on a curve against the people around him or lost in a crowd, which is unnerving and is also the only arrangement that could be just (Matthew 16:27; Revelation 20:12).

Does judgment by works contradict justification by faith? No; they answer different questions. Works are what is produced in court as evidence, not what is paid at the counter. Nobody is saved by evidence, and there will be evidence. The tree is not made alive by its fruit, but at harvest the inspection is of fruit. And the only people who will be found with good evidence are those already justified freely by faith, whose lives the Spirit has begun to change.

Will Christians be judged too? Yes, but not to decide whether we belong to God: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). Their lives are opened and their work rewarded, and that should make us serious and not afraid. (See Acts 17:31 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. Take something you know is wrong in your life and ask what has actually happened about it in the last six months. Has anything changed, in some direction you could point to, or has there only been a cycle of failure, discomfort and private promises? A heart that repents moves; a heart that merely regrets goes in circles. If you find yourself in that circle, do not conclude you are lost: a believer can hate a sin and still fall to it for a long time (7:15–25), and the way out is the same Christ, sought again.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Patience in well-doing. Paul has said the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (1:16), and will say that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (3:28). Here he says God will give eternal life to those who persist in doing good. Taken alone, that sounds like salvation by works. “Patience” (hypomonē) is steady endurance under weight; “well-doing” is good work; “seek” means their lives are aimed at God’s glory and the immortality only he can give.

Where Christians differ: who receives eternal life in vv. 7, 10 and 13? There are two main readings among those who hold firmly to justification by faith alone. The first (taken, for example, by Douglas Moo) sees these verses as stating God’s standard in principle: if anyone did persist in doing good, they would receive eternal life; but Paul will show in 3:9–20 that no one does, so the verses shut every mouth and drive us to Christ. The terms are honest, like a scholarship advertised for candidates with a flawless record: the money is real, and the reason nobody collects is not that the committee is dishonest. The second (taken, for example, by C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner) sees them as describing real people: believers, whose lives, changed by the Spirit, show persevering good works, and whom God will vindicate on the last day. Support for this comes later in the same chapter, where the Gentile who keeps the law is one whose heart is circumcised by the Spirit (vv. 26–29), and from Paul’s teaching that those who sow to the Spirit will reap eternal life (Galatians 6:8). This commentary’s view: the second reading is most likely, and the first contains an important truth. God’s judgment will follow the evidence of a person’s life (v. 6). The only people who will be found persevering in good are those whom God has justified freely by faith and renewed by his Spirit (Ephesians 2:8–10; Philippians 1:6). Their good works are not the ground of their acceptance, which is Christ’s righteousness alone (3:21–26), but the fruit and evidence of it. And no one can reach this standard by the law in his own strength, which is exactly what Paul goes on to prove.

The direction of a life. Not achievement but patience, staying at something under weight; and seeking, not having arrived but still after it. Paul is describing not a spotless record but the direction a life faces over time. And he does not contrast the successful with the failing; he contrasts those who seek glory, honour and immortality with those who are self-seeking. Both are seeking; the last day asks what the life was after. And wanting glory, honour and immortality is not condemned as ambition. It is the right ambition. Our desires are not too strong but too weak: the self-seeking of verse 8 wanted glory for themselves, and settled for a cheap version of it.

Self-seeking. “Self-seeking” (eritheia) is selfish ambition, the spirit of faction and self-promotion. “Obey unrighteousness” shows sin not as mere weakness but as loyalty to another master, willingly served.

The one who kept these terms. If you have read this verse and concluded that you fall short of patient continuance in well-doing, you have read it correctly; the man who thinks he qualifies has misread it. Christ endured with patience, did good without a break, sought his Father’s glory and not his own, and never once obeyed unrighteousness. He met verse 7 in full, and the eternal life he merited is given to people who plainly did not merit it. Your patient well-doing is not the payment for it. It is the evidence that it has already been given to you.

I keep falling into the same sin. Does that mean I am not persevering in well-doing? No. Perseverance is not sinlessness; Paul assumes interruption, which is why his word is patience. The question is the direction of travel and what you do when you fall. A believer falls and gets up again, hates the sin, confesses it, and fights it, sometimes for years (7:15–25; 1 John 1:8–9). What Scripture warns against is the settled life that has made peace with sin and stopped fighting. If you are grieved by your sin and still running to Christ with it, that grief and that running are themselves the Spirit’s work in you.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tribulation and distress. Paul repeats verses 7 and 8 in reverse order: there it was good then evil; here it is evil then good. So the two destinies are set before the reader twice. And the words are concrete. Tribulation is pressure, the crushing of something under weight. Distress pictures a narrow space: being hemmed in, with no room to turn. Paul pictures the outcome of a life apart from God not as a distant fire but as a closing in.

The shape of sin. Every temptation presents itself as an enlargement: more freedom, more experience, and the people who declined were narrow and missed out. Then watch what it delivers over twenty years. The man ruled by drink ends with a world the size of one room. The bitter woman ends with a life organised around a single grievance she can no longer put down. The pornography habit that promised variety produces a man who cannot look at his own wife properly. Whatever is finally meant by tribulation and distress, it is this, continued, with the restraints gone.

Glory and honor and peace. Verse 7 promised immortality; here the third word is peace, shalom, not merely the absence of conflict but everything in its proper place, working. So the contrast is not pleasure against pain. It is expansion against contraction: a life given room to become what it was made for, or a life closing in until nothing is left but the thing it chose.

The Jew first and also the Greek. The same phrase as 1:16, now cutting the other way. There the Jew was first to be offered salvation; here he is first to face judgment. First in privilege, first in responsibility. Amos put it more bluntly: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). To whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48).

The light that walked their streets. The highest privilege Israel ever had was not the law or the temple. It was the Messiah himself, born of their race and sent first to them: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). And Jesus taught this verse before Paul wrote it. Woe to Chorazin and Bethsaida, he said, for if the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21–22). Every reader who has heard the gospel of that same Christ now sits in the seat of Chorazin and Bethsaida, and the seat is also a mercy: the light that increases the reckoning is the very gospel that has come to you.

Who is first today? The person raised in a Christian home who cannot remember not knowing the gospel. The one who has sat under good preaching for thirty years, owns four Bibles, could answer any doctrinal question, and has friends who pray for him by name. Every one of those is a mercy, and this verse quietly turns each into something to answer for. The most dangerous seat in any church is not the back row. It is the one occupied by somebody who has heard everything and been changed by very little.

verseByVerse.quote: For God shows no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God shows no partiality. The principle behind it all (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34). The Greek word is literally “face-receiving”. The picture is of a judge who lifts the bowed head of the man before him and favours him because he is somebody; Israel’s law forbade it (Leviticus 19:15). Paul is applying the oldest principle in Israel’s law to Israel. God will not lift your face because of anything you bring to court. Yet the psalmist could say, “you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (Psalm 3:3). By the end of this letter it is clear how a guilty man has his head lifted in that courtroom: not because the Judge was impressed by him, but because the Judge’s own Son stood in his place, and there was nothing left on the charge sheet to keep his eyes on the floor.

No face raised, no face lowered. We usually hear only one direction of this truth. Nothing you bring can raise your chin: not your family, not having been in church since you were four, not your giving, competence or reputation. But run it the other way, because this is the half that goes unpreached. If no advantage lifts a face, no disadvantage lowers one. God is not more ready to hear the articulate, the theologically trained, the emotionally stable, or those whose lives look tidy. The woman who cannot pray aloud, the man who came to Christ at sixty with a wrecked history, the believer with a criminal record: none of them is further down the list, because there is no list. Impartiality is terrifying to anyone trading on advantage, and the best news in the world to anyone who has none.

Peter learned it the hard way. It took a vision and a two-day journey. Standing in a Gentile’s house, he began: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). He was watching a wall come down that he had believed held up the roof.

Lord of all. Peter’s very next words put a name on God’s impartiality: he spoke of the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all (Acts 10:36). Paul says the same: the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him (10:12). And the impartiality could be seen in Christ before it was preached about him. Even his enemies said it, though they meant it as flattery: “you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances” (Matthew 22:16). He ate with tax collectors and touched lepers. Every face that comes to him meets the same welcome, because the only thing he looks for is the one thing he gives: faith in himself.

Does impartiality mean God loves everyone the same? It means no status can move his judgment, and his love cannot be bought. It does not mean he has no particular love for particular people; chapter 8 insists on the opposite in some of the warmest words Paul ever wrote. God has no favourites in judgment, and yet he has a people he loves with a special and extravagant love.

In the flow. This verse gives the reason for verses 6–10, and verses 12–16 will show how it works for people with the law and without it. The impartiality that closes every door in chapter 2 opens one door for everyone in chapter 3 (3:22–23).

In everyday life. James makes it a rule about Sunday morning: if a man in fine clothes is given the good seat and the poor man told to stand, have you not become judges with evil thoughts (James 2:1–4)? The modern version is who gets followed up after missing three weeks, whose name is remembered, which visitor is introduced to someone and which gets a handshake at the door. Take the last two conversations you had at church and ask what those people could do for you. Then, since Christ welcomed you when you could do nothing for him (15:7), seek out the person who can do nothing for you at all, and whose company is slightly hard work.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without the law. Paul builds a symmetry: sinned without the law, perish without the law; sinned under the law, judged by the law. Each person is measured by the light he was actually given, and there is real mercy in that: the tribesman who never heard of Sinai will not be tried by Sinai. But the mercy does not end where we would like. He is judged by less, and he still perishes, for sins against what he knew (1:20; 2:15). Fewer rules did not mean he kept them.

Not the hearers. “Hearers” (akroatai) would have stung a Jewish reader. Israel’s central confession begins “Hear, O Israel”, and every Sabbath in every synagogue in Rome the law was read aloud to people who had come specifically to hear it. And Paul says that the thing done faithfully every Sabbath for a lifetime will not make one person righteous. No generation has had such easy access to preaching, and the danger is the same, because hearing feels like doing. It is possible to feel recognition, warmth and resolve every week for a lifetime and be unaltered, which is why James says the hearer who does not do is deceiving himself (James 1:22).

The doers will be justified. “Will be justified” (dikaiōthēsontai): future, at the final judgment. This is the first appearance in the letter of the verb to justify, and Paul introduces it at full strength before he says who can meet its standard. The verb belongs in a law court. It means not to make someone good but to declare him in the right: Moses tells judges to acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty (Deuteronomy 25:1), and the Greek Old Testament uses this very verb for acquit. In principle a perfect law-keeper would be justified; but no one keeps it perfectly (3:10, 20, 23), so this shuts the mouth of anyone relying on having the law. Yet the verse also points forward: those justified by faith in Christ and given the Spirit begin truly to do what the law requires (8:4), and on the last day God will acknowledge them as righteous.

The one doer of the law. If only doers are justified and no one does, the verse would be a closed door, unless a doer could be found who stands for others. Paul names him three chapters later: “as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (5:19). Jesus is the doer of the law in the full sense of this verse: not a hearer who agreed with it but a man who did it, all of it, every day, from the manger to the cross, so that he could say: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). The doers of the last day are those clothed in his doing and changed by his Spirit, and their own doing, never perfect, is accepted for his sake.

Where Christians differ: does Paul teach salvation by works here? Roman Catholic teaching, and some recent scholars, read vv. 6–13 as teaching that final justification depends in part on the good works a person does with God’s help. This commentary’s view: no. Paul establishes that God judges according to deeds, and that hearing or possessing the law saves no one. He then shows that no one meets the law’s standard (3:9–20), so justification must be by faith apart from works (3:21–28; 4:4–5). The good works of believers are the evidence of a true and living faith, not its ground. We are justified by faith alone, and judged according to works that show whether that faith was real (James 2:14–26). There is no contradiction between Romans 2 and Romans 3: the first shows the standard and the evidence; the second shows the only ground of acceptance.

Two kinds of hearing. Paul says here that hearers are not justified; eight chapters later he says “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (10:17). Both are true, because there are two kinds of hearing. There is the hearing that receives information and files it, which changes nothing and can go on for a lifetime. And there is the hearing a drowning man does when someone on the bank tells him where the rope is. That second kind is not the opposite of doing. It is the first thing a man does, and it is the only kind that has ever justified anybody.

In everyday life. Listen for the sentence “yes, that is a good point” in your own mouth this week, after a sermon, a book, or a friend who told you the truth about yourself. It sounds like agreement, and it works as a full stop. A person who intends to act says “what do I do about that?” So after the next sermon, ask the Spirit to work that word into you, and before you leave the building name one specific thing you will do differently, and tell someone.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them
verseByVerse.commentary:
By nature. Pagans without Moses’ law still often honour parents, refuse murder and keep promises. This is common grace: the goodness God shows to all people, believers or not, by which he restrains evil and leaves a sense of right and wrong in every heart (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). Paul is not teaching that Gentiles can be saved by following their conscience; he is establishing that people without the written law still have a moral framework that makes them accountable.

They are a law to themselves. Not that they make up their own rules, but that their own nature carries God’s law within. The moral law is built into human nature as part of the image of God.

Their conscience. The word (syneidēsis) is built from two pieces meaning to know with: co-knowing. It names the strange fact that a human being can stand at a slight distance from himself and pass judgment on what he finds. A dog can fear consequences; it cannot lie awake at four in the morning because of what it said to somebody in 1998. Paul describes a courtroom: a witness, thoughts that accuse and thoughts that excuse. Even the excusing is revealing: nobody mounts a defence in a court he does not believe exists.

The defence the conscience cannot make. The word for “excuse” is the word for a defence in court. The conscience can argue a man’s case, but it cannot win it. The gospel does not tell the accused that his conscience is lying. It brings in a defence no conscience could mount, a Saviour who does not plead that the charges are false but pleads his own death: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, more than that, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (8:33–34).

Where Christians differ: who are these Gentiles? Some, from Augustine to Cranfield, take them to be Gentile Christians, in whom the new covenant writes the law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Others say Paul means unbelieving Gentiles who show moral awareness. This commentary’s view: the context points to unbelieving Gentiles. Paul is still proving that everyone is accountable (1:18–3:20); he speaks of what Gentiles do “by nature” and of a conscience that accuses (v. 15), and of people who “perish without the law” (v. 12). Jeremiah promised the law itself written on the heart; Paul speaks here of the work of the law, its demands. This is not saving obedience, but evidence of accountability.

Conscience is a witness, not the judge. It bears witness at a trial conducted by somebody else, and a witness can be mistaken: it can testify from a distorted upbringing, a frightening father, or a church that taught a rule God never made. There are two opposite failures. One is the conscience that will not stop accusing: believers who confess the same forgiven sin nightly for years and cannot receive assurance. To them Scripture says: “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20). He knows more than your accusing heart, including what his Son has done. The other is the conscience seared like scar tissue (1 Timothy 4:2), which is quiet, and whose quietness is its danger.

Should I always follow my conscience? Never act against it, but always be willing to have it corrected. To do what you believe is wrong is sin, even if the thing itself is allowed, because it is done without faith (14:23). But a conscience can be too strict or too loose, so it must be trained by Scripture. When your conscience troubles you about something God’s word does not forbid, do not simply override it: study what Scripture says, ask mature believers, and let the truth reshape it over time. When it is silent about something God’s word condemns, believe the word over the silence.

If the law is written on every heart, why do cultures disagree so much about right and wrong? They disagree less than it seems, and mostly about how to apply what they know. It is hard to find a culture that admired the man who betrays his friends, abandons his children or runs from battle laughing; every people has some form of honesty, justice, care for the weak and keeping of promises, even where it draws the circle of who counts far too small. And Paul has already explained the disagreement that remains: human beings suppress the truth they know (1:18), and a conscience resisted long enough grows callous (Ephesians 4:19). The remarkable thing is not that the writing has been smudged, but that it has never been rubbed out. Even the man who says all morality is relative protests the moment someone wrongs him.

In everyday life. Do not ask whether you feel guilty; that measures how loud your conscience is, not whether it is right. Take the last thing your conscience convicted you about and ask two questions. Can I name the command of God this broke? If so, that is real conviction, and the answer is repentance, not reassurance. If there is nothing behind it but a vague feeling of not being good enough, it may be a witness giving evidence it does not have. And does this drive me toward God or away from him? The Spirit’s conviction is specific and takes you to the cross. The accuser is vague, and always advises you to keep your distance for a while.
verseByVerse.note: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given to every person.

parallels.desc: I will write it on their hearts

verseByVerse.quote: on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secrets of men. God judges not only what we do in public, but hidden thoughts and motives (1 Corinthians 4:5; Hebrews 4:13).

In the flow. The chapter began with a man sitting as judge over others (v. 1); this movement ends with the true Judge, from whom no secret is hidden, and so prepares for 3:21–26: no one can be saved by a better-looking record, only by a righteousness God himself provides.

According to my gospel. Judgment is not the awkward small print at the end of the good news; Paul files it under the good news. The good news is not that there is no judgment, but that there is a way to be safe in it, and that the universe is just. Ask who the doctrine is good news for: the woman whose abuser was never charged and kept his job and his pew. A family whose village was burned by men who were promoted afterwards. The world has told every one of them that the file is closed. This verse says the file is open, the evidence is kept, and a date has been set. A universe with no judgment is not gentler. It is one in which the powerful got away with it permanently.

The hidden good. Jesus said: give in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4). If that day uncovers what was hidden, it does not uncover only hidden wrong. The eleven years of caring for a parent with dementia that nobody watched. The money given quietly by a man everyone thought was tight-fisted. None of it was recorded by anyone else, and none of it was lost. For a great many obscure people, that day will be the first time anyone has seen what they actually did with their lives.

By Christ Jesus. Jesus is the judge (Acts 17:31; John 5:22). The Father has given him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27): because he is human. He was poor, exhausted, misrepresented, betrayed by a friend, and tried in a rigged court himself. Nobody will be able to say the Judge did not understand the circumstances. And he will learn nothing new that day: he went to the cross already holding the complete file. You were found out long ago, and he came anyway.

Should I be afraid of that day as a Christian? Not afraid of condemnation, because your standing was settled in another court, at the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). What is assessed for a believer is his work, not his welcome, and Scripture is honest that some work will not survive the fire, while he himself will be saved (1 Corinthians 3:15). Loss is possible; losing Christ is not. So the right response is not dread but honesty now: bring your secrets into the light with God, confess them, and where it is right, to a trusted believer (James 5:16). What is confessed now is covered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now asks the Jewish hearer who has the law, teaches it and rests his identity on it: does he keep it himself? The law is not worthless, but it cannot save those who possess and teach it without obeying it from the heart.

The charge reaches its height in the words from Isaiah and Ezekiel: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.” Israel, called to be a light to the nations, had through its hypocrisy given the nations a reason to despise Israel’s God.

Paul’s answer is that “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (v. 29). This is the Old Testament’s own hope (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26), fulfilled in the new covenant, and it will become Paul’s great theme in chapters 6–8.

At verse 27 Paul goes further than saying that circumcision without obedience is worthless. The uncircumcised man who keeps the law will condemn the man who has the written law and the mark of circumcision and breaks the law: the outsider is called as witness for the prosecution. Our Lord made the same reversal with a Roman soldier (Matthew 8:10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the letter’s first extended treatment of what the law can and cannot do. Of the law’s three uses Calvin named (to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness, to guide the redeemed life), Paul is drawing on the first. The Jew who has the law has a clearer mirror than the Gentile, and so a clearer sight of his own failure. The law cannot save; it exposes the need for a Saviour, which is why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Circumcision was the defining covenant mark in Paul’s day, and to question its saving value was to question the whole shape of Jewish identity. Paul shows that the sign without the inward reality condemns rather than protects. Now: The equivalent is any Christian community that trusts outward marks (baptism, church attendance, sound doctrine, moral reputation) instead of the heart changed by the Spirit. God looks at the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you call yourself a Jew. Now Paul names his hearer directly: the Jew who has every privilege. Verses 17 to 20 are one long unfinished sentence, piling up claim after claim, and Paul does not complete it until the questions of verse 21 bring it all down. And the name carries a pun that many readers hear Paul spring at the end of the chapter: Jew comes from Judah, named by his mother with the words “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35). Hold that until verse 29.

Rely on the law. “Rely” (epanapauē) means to rest on, to lean back, to settle one’s weight. The law was given as a path to walk, and he has made furniture of it. A path only helps while you are moving along it; a chair helps most when you have stopped.

Where the weight can rest. The trouble is not that this man leans; everyone leans on something. It is that the law was never built to take the weight of a sinner. It tells him what God requires, and then has nothing to give him when he fails. Paul will name what it was pointing to: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (10:4). And the one the law points to offers exactly what this man was looking for in the wrong place: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). Paul’s word for rely and Jesus’ word for rest share the same root. The rest he wanted was a person all along.

Boast in God. Boasting in God can be good: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31), and we boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ (5:11). The fault is not that this man is proud of God, but that he is proud of having God. From inside they are hard to tell apart; from outside the difference is plain. Boasting in God makes a person smaller and warmer. Boasting in having God makes him larger and colder.

Approve what is excellent. The phrase is literally to test and distinguish the things that differ: the same verb as the mind that refused to test God (1:28) and the renewed mind that discerns his will (12:2). Paul credits this man with a trained sense of right and wrong, a real privilege (9:4–5). And it removes his last excuse, because his problem is plainly not that he cannot see.

In everyday life. When someone asks what you believe, listen to what comes out. Do you describe a position: what you hold, what your church teaches, where you stand relative to people who have it wrong? Or do you describe a Person? Both may be orthodox. Only one sounds like someone who has met him.

verseByVerse.quote: and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guide to the blind. Israel had been called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). So the titles this man gives himself describe a real calling. But he recites them as honours, and has stopped noticing that a calling makes demands. And every one of the four titles is a teaching role: not worshipper, servant or forgiven sinner, but a position relative to people who know less. Jesus called the Pharisees blind guides (Matthew 15:14; 23:16).

A teacher of children. Here is the occupational hazard of every teacher: parents, preachers, elders, Sunday school teachers, the person in the small group who always knows the answer. The danger is not error. It is that his relationship to the truth becomes professional. He reads a passage and his first thought is that it would make a good sermon; he hears a sermon and assesses it. None of this is dishonest, and all of it quietly puts him beside the word rather than under it. The Bible stops being a word addressed to him and becomes material.

The embodiment of knowledge. The law really did embody truth. The word (morphōsis) is the outline or shape of a thing, and here it is positive: the law is the outline of what God is like. But Paul uses the same word of the appearance of godliness without its power (2 Timothy 3:5). Everything depends on whether there is anything inside the shape. Having it is not obeying it.

Should I stop teaching if I fall short of what I teach? No. Paul does not tell this man to put the law down. He asks him a question: do you not teach yourself? The remedy for standing beside the word is not silence but getting back underneath it. Keep teaching, and let every passage you prepare speak to you first. Be honest with those you teach that you need it too; a teacher who admits his own struggle teaches grace better than one who seems to have none. If there is a sin you are living in, deal with it before God, and if it is serious, step back while it is put right. But the answer to hypocrisy is repentance, not resignation.

The true Guide. There is one Teacher who never stood beside the word, because he is the Word. The one true Guide to the blind did not stand in the dark giving instructions. He spat on the ground, made mud, anointed a blind man’s eyes and sent him to wash, and the man came back seeing (John 9:6–7). Then he said: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). The teachers who were sure they could see stayed blind, and the beggar who knew he was blind went home with eyes. He is the Teacher who does not hand the blind a lecture but gives them sight.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been called to be a light to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verseByVerse.commentary:
You then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? The question that brings the long boast of vv. 17–20 down. And the form matters: Paul does not say you steal; he asks. An accusation can be argued with: tell a man what he is and he starts building a case. A question leaves him alone in the room with the answer. It is the method God used on the first man who hid from him, who was not handed a list of charges but asked, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). God knew the answer. The question was so that the man would have to say it himself.

While you preach against stealing, do you steal? While you say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? Paul is not asserting that Jewish people were characteristically thieves and adulterers; he argues in the manner of the lecture hall, putting to an imagined objector the standard charges any moralist would recognise. He is a Jew himself, and seven chapters on he will say he could wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake. The point is that the law you teach condemns you too. And Jesus showed that the law reaches the heart: lust is adultery in the heart and anger is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–28).

You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? The most searching of the three. Israel was forbidden not only to worship idols but to profit from them: “You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves” (Deuteronomy 7:25). Pagan temples were full of precious metal, and there was money for anyone prepared to melt it down and ask no questions. The charge was live: the town clerk of Ephesus defends Paul’s companions as “neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess” (Acts 19:37), using the word for temple-robbers. So the accusation is exact: you denounce idolatry at the front and take the silver off it at the back. It may also point to robbing God himself (Malachi 3:8), as the Pharisees condemned idols while loving money (Luke 16:14).

The den of robbers. Paul’s three charges, stealing, adultery, idols, were not first his. Jeremiah stood at the temple gate and asked them: will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and then come and stand before me in this house and say, we are delivered? Has this house become a den of robbers in your eyes (Jeremiah 7:9–11)? Six centuries later Jesus overturned the tables in the same courts and turned that sentence on the men profiting from the worship of God: “you have made it a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17). He did not denounce the robbing of God’s house and take a share at the back. He cleared it; and John records that at a cleansing of the temple he spoke of the temple of his own body, which they would destroy and he would raise in three days (John 2:19–21).

The shape of our inconsistency. That third question is the shape most of our hypocrisy takes. We rarely do the thing we condemn. We benefit from it. You do not spread the gossip; you listen to all of it. You disapprove of how a colleague got the result, and you were glad of the result. You have views about where money comes from, and there are questions about your own you have decided not to ask. You genuinely do abhor the idol. You simply also take the gold.

The law as a mirror. The Reformers said that the law’s first use is to show a person what he really is. It is a mirror: superbly designed to show you the dirt on your face, and it has never once removed any of it. The error of the man in these verses is not that he owns a mirror. It is that he has framed it, hung it on the wall, and started showing it to visitors as evidence of how he looks. The mirror is meant to send us to the only place we can be washed.

verseByVerse.quote: You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dishonor God. The sentence closes a circle. The section opened with a man who boasts in God (v. 17) and ends with a man who boasts in the law, valued as a possession rather than a demand. And the verdict is one heavy word: he dishonours God, as humanity did in chapter 1 (1:21, 24). Now it is the religious man who does it. The pagan dishonours God by worshipping something else. The religious man dishonours him by claiming him loudly and living as though he were not there.

Why it is worse. A man who makes no profession and does wrong has damaged himself. A man who has told everyone he belongs to God, and does the same wrong, has attached God’s name to it. He has made a statement about what God is like, and other people will believe it, because a life is more persuasive than a doctrine. Taking the Lord’s name in vain is not chiefly about swearing; it is carrying his name and treating it as though it weighed nothing. And it needs no scandal. It is the Christian known at work for being sharp about money; the father whose family go quiet when he comes in; the believer whose neighbours have concluded, without discussing theology, that whatever he has does not seem to make him kinder.

I honour my Father. Accused in the temple of having a demon, Jesus answered: I do not have a demon, but I honour my Father, and you dishonour me (John 8:49). They carried the law and boasted in it, and dishonoured the Son; he carried the Father’s name through every hour of an ordinary life and never once took it in vain. At last the third commandment, against taking God’s name in vain, had someone who kept it.

Does my failure really damage God’s honour? Not God himself: he is not diminished by being misrepresented, any more than the sun is dimmed by a bad photograph of it. What is at stake is what the people around you are being shown. So the answer to failure is not to hide it, which adds a lie to the sin, but to own it. When you have dishonoured Christ in front of others, say so plainly to them, apologise without excuses, and put right what you can. Nothing honours God in front of unbelievers more than a Christian who admits he was wrong and shows where he goes for forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blasphemed among the Gentiles. From Isaiah 52:5 and Ezekiel 36:20. In the prophets the nations mocked God’s name because Israel had been defeated and exiled (Ezekiel 36:20); Paul applies the sentence to what is done by God’s people rather than to them. Either way the world forms its opinion of God from the people who carry his name. Christians who live badly cause the name of Christ to be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6:1; Titus 2:5).

Hypocrisy is not persecution. Say the modern form plainly. When a church covers up the abuse of children to protect its reputation, when a ministry’s finances turn out to be a private fortune, when a celebrated preacher was a different man off the platform, the contempt that follows is not persecution. It is an accurate response to the evidence, and Christians should be the last to confuse the two. Peter draws the line: if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer (1 Peter 4:15–16). Being despised for the cross is an honour. Being despised for hypocrisy is a debt we have earned. And when such things are exposed, the right response is truth, justice for the wronged and repentance, never protecting the institution.

Because of you. But do not let the headline scandals take this verse off your own shoulders. Paul writes “because of you”, the same singular man he has been questioning. Nobody in your street has met a famous pastor. They have met you. Their working theory of what God does to a person is assembled from two or three Christians they happen to know, in unguarded moments, and that sample includes you.

Ezekiel’s answer. Ezekiel 36 does not stop at verse 20. God announces the remedy in the same chapter: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), which is exactly where Paul is going in five verses (v. 29). His people had dragged his reputation through the nations, and God did not respond by demanding that they repair it. He undertook to repair it himself, and the way he chose was to change them from the inside. The name that was blasphemed because of us will finally be honoured because of what he does in us.

Isaiah’s answer. Isaiah 52 does not stop at verse 5 either. At the end of the same chapter the Servant appears: he shall be high and lifted up, his appearance marred beyond human semblance, and he shall sprinkle many nations (52:13–15; Paul quotes that last verse too, 15:21), the passage that runs straight into Isaiah 53. The name blasphemed among the nations because of Israel’s failure is vindicated among the nations by Israel’s Messiah, despised and rejected, who bore the sin of many. Ezekiel promises the new heart; Isaiah shows the Servant whose suffering pays for it.

parallels.desc: my name is continually despised

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of value. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17), the sign of belonging to God’s people. It was a permanent mark on the body, the one credential a Jewish man could not lose, and some Jewish teachers, in sayings preserved in later rabbinic writings, held that it guaranteed a place in the age to come. Paul grants it: God gave it, and it meant something. What he denies is that it works on its own, regardless of the life attached to it.

Circumcision becomes uncircumcision. The sign without the reality is worthless. And Paul is not spiritualising Moses away; he is following him. The command to circumcise the heart is in the law itself (Deuteronomy 10:16), and Jeremiah said it six hundred years earlier: the days are coming when God will punish all who are circumcised merely in the flesh, for all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26). A sign does not work automatically. A wedding ring has never kept anyone faithful; on the hand of a man conducting an affair it does not become neutral. It becomes a lie in metal.

So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? Who is this man? Some take him as hypothetical, like the doers of the law in v. 13. Others take him as a real person, a Gentile believer whose heart the Spirit has changed, so that the law’s requirement is beginning to be fulfilled in him (8:4). The second is more likely here, because Paul is moving toward the true circumcision of v. 29, which is by the Spirit. Such a man’s obedience is not perfect and is not the ground of his acceptance; it is the evidence of a heart God has circumcised. And the verb “regarded” matters: an accountant’s word, to credit to an account. It will dominate chapter 4, where Abraham believes God and it is counted to him as righteousness. Here, the first time the letter uses it of crediting, God is counting an outsider in.

The one on whom the sign was true. At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus (Luke 2:21). Born of woman, born under the law, he kept the covenant from the inside, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). On every other body the sign stood beside a broken law; on his it never lied. And because of him Paul can say: “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). The outsider is counted in because he is in Christ.

A lesson for baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The same applies to the signs Christ has given his church. They are valuable and commanded, but they do not save without faith. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, because in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith and declares them (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12); many faithful Christians baptise the infants of believers as a sign of God’s covenant promise, and they too insist that the sign never replaces faith. Very few people today trust in circumcision. Many trust in an event: a decision at fourteen at a summer camp, a card signed, a baptism, a week when everything seemed clear. The event may have been entirely genuine. Paul’s question is whether the thing it signified is present now.

What it does not mean. This is not an argument that the signs God has given are unimportant; Paul says the opposite in his first words. And some readers will now be examining a conversion they can barely remember and concluding that no vivid moment means no real faith. It does not. Assurance was never meant to rest on the quality of your memory of the beginning. Nobody proves he is alive by producing a birth certificate. A person who cannot date his conversion and loves Christ today is in an incomparably better position than one with a certificate and no pulse.

How can I know my faith is real? Look for present evidence, not only a past event. Do you trust Christ alone for forgiveness, not your record? Do you hate your sin and fight it, even when you lose? Do you love other believers and want to be with them (1 John 3:14)? Do you want to obey God, and grieve when you do not? Is Christ precious to you? None of these needs to be strong; each only needs to be real. And the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (8:16). If you find these marks, however weak, take comfort. If you find none, do not despair: go to Christ now, because he receives everyone who comes.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will condemn you. The man who has spent the chapter as a judge now faces the last witness he expected: the uncircumcised outsider he had been instructing. The outsider does not merely turn out to be acceptable; he condemns, and not by argument. His obedient life is itself the evidence. Jesus used the same device: the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they responded to less, and something greater is here (Matthew 12:41–42). They have done with a candle what others would not do with the sun.

The faith Jesus marvelled at. Jesus acted out this verse himself. When a Roman centurion, uncircumcised and without the law, trusted his word to heal a servant at a distance, Jesus marvelled and said: truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness (Matthew 8:10–12). The outsider condemns the insider not by being cleverer but by trusting the Christ the insider would not receive. The verdict of the last day turns on Christ.

The written code. “Written code” (gramma) is the letter: the outward, written law, without the Spirit. The code and the mark had become part of the problem, because they gave him a reason not to look at himself. A man with no credentials at least knows he has nothing to plead. Give him a credential and you have handed him somewhere to hide.

In everyday life. Think of a believer you find slightly irritating: the recent convert with no advantages, whose zeal seems naive and whose theology is thin, and whose obedience is not. Ask what the irritation is made of. Sometimes it is real discernment. Very often it is the discomfort of watching someone do easily what you have stopped doing, and the quickest way to manage that feeling is to find something in him to correct. Instead, thank God for him, and ask him what has been helping him.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not outwardly. Being a true member of God’s people is not a matter of race or ritual. Paul defines Jewish identity from the inside out, completing the logic of the Old Testament itself.

A matter of the heart. The Old Testament already said it (Jeremiah 4:4), and Moses says it twice with the same image: first as a command, circumcise the foreskin of your heart (Deuteronomy 10:16), and later, when it was plain no one had, as a promise: the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deuteronomy 30:6). The prophets never promised that Israel would try harder. They promised that God would operate. And circumcision was normally done to a man, not by him: an eight-day-old boy contributes nothing, and someone else holds the knife, which is why it produces no boast. And Moses says in the same verse what it is for: so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 30:6). The hard, unfeeling covering is cut away, and a person who once found God dull or threatening now loves him and wants to obey him.

The circumcision of Christ. The New Testament names where the operation is done: “In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11). It happens in union with Christ, and the Spirit he pours out (Acts 2:33) performs it. Christ’s death and resurrection, and his Spirit given to all who are joined to him, are the cutting away of the old life and the beginning of the new. The circumcision of verse 29 is not a better human effort. It is Christ’s work, applied.

By the Spirit, not by the letter. The Spirit does what the written law cannot: he changes the heart (2 Corinthians 3:6; Ezekiel 36:26–27). The contrast is not between spirit and law as such; it is between the outward written requirement and the inward power of the Spirit, who creates the obedience the law commands but cannot produce.

Where Christians differ: has the church replaced Israel? Some read this verse as saying that Gentile believers are now the true Jews, linking it with Philippians 3:3, we are the circumcision. This commentary’s view: that is not quite what this verse says. Paul is still speaking to the Jew of v. 17, and he is saying who is a Jew in the full sense: not everyone with the outward mark, but the one whose heart God has changed, as Moses and the prophets had said all along (compare 9:6). He does not erase Israel. In the next breath he asks what advantage the Jew has and answers, much in every way (3:1–2), and chapters 9–11 still speak of Israel as a people with a future in God’s purposes. Gentile believers belong to Abraham’s family by faith (4:11–12; Galatians 3:29), but this verse makes a narrower point: within Israel the outward mark never made anyone God’s.

Then do Jewish people today need Christ to be saved? Yes, and Paul says so with tears. The same heart-circumcision Moses promised comes only through the Spirit whom Christ gives, and there is no other name by which anyone is saved (Acts 4:12). That is why Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer for Israel was that they might be saved (10:1), and why he went to the synagogue first in city after city. Love for Jewish people, and gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, mean sharing him with them, humbly and gladly, never with contempt.

Praise from God. Remember what Jew means: Judah, named with the words “This time I will praise the LORD.” So the closing line is a definition delivered as a pun: the true Praise is the one whose praise comes from God. Jesus put the same question to the religious leaders of his day: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44). And the contrast is not between external and sincere; a merely private religion is no better than a merely public one, and chapters 12–16 will demand very visible obedience. The contrast is between what people can see and award, and what God sees and awards. Only God can see the circumcision Paul describes, so only God can praise it.

In the flow. Paul’s case against the religious man ends with the answer to the chapter’s question: only an inward work of God, by his Spirit, makes a man truly one of God’s people. That raises two objections Paul takes up at once (3:1, 3), and the Spirit named here in a single phrase will fill chapter 8.

For worship. The Christian nobody notices will not be asked at the end to produce the visible things: the platform, the record, the esteem of respectable people. Paul has spent a whole chapter taking away every commendation human beings can give, so that God can give one they cannot take back. It will come from the one who saw all of it, including what was done badly and what was done at cost and never noticed by a living soul, and it will be spoken because of his Son: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21). Nothing in it will be exaggerated, because he has no need to flatter, and nothing will be left out. It will be the first entirely accurate sentence ever spoken about your life.

parallels.desc: the LORD will circumcise your heart
