3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 moves in three steps. Paul answers objections about Israel’s advantage and God’s faithfulness (vv. 1–8); he closes the case against the whole human race from Israel’s own Scriptures (vv. 9–20); and then, with the words “But now” (v. 21), he announces a righteousness from God, apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe (vv. 21–31).

The order is deliberate. Paul gives the verdict before the remedy: no one is righteous. Only then does he show how a just God can justify the guilty. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If covenant privilege gives no shelter from judgment (chapter 2), was being a Jew worth anything? Paul answers that the advantage is great, above all that Israel was entrusted with the words of God, and that Israel’s unfaithfulness cannot cancel God’s faithfulness. These verses look ahead to chapters 9 to 11.

Verses 5–8 answer two objections that try to turn grace into licence: if my sin shows off God’s righteousness, why should he punish it, and why not do evil that good may come? People were saying that Paul taught exactly that. He refuses the objection here and gives the full answer in chapter 6.
verseByVerse.theology:
God’s faithfulness and human failure

Can human sin defeat God’s purposes? Romans 3:3–4 answers that it cannot. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. So a Christian’s standing does not rest on his faithfulness but on God’s. He who called us is faithful; he will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have welcomed Paul’s affirmation of Israel’s privileges and been troubled by his insistence that they gave no exemption from judgment. Now: Christians face the same tension. Scripture, preaching, baptism, the Lord’s Supper and prayer are real and great gifts, and none of them is a substitute for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 3 is the hinge of the letter. Paul answers objections about Israel’s advantage (vv. 1–8), then closes the case: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin, and every mouth is stopped (vv. 9–20). Then come the central verses of the letter on how God saves: a righteousness from God, given freely through faith in Christ, by a just God who is also the justifier (vv. 21–26). Boasting is excluded, and the law is upheld (vv. 27–31). The chapter that puts the whole human race in the dock ends with the Judge himself providing the righteousness the prisoners could never bring.

Then what advantage has the Jew? Paul has just argued that circumcision without obedience is worthless, and he knows exactly what the man in front of him is now thinking: then none of it meant anything, and two thousand years of covenant history were a waste of everyone’s time. Notice that Paul raises the question at all, and that it is a question against his own argument. A lesser writer would have let the misunderstanding stand rather than complicate a good argument. Paul stops the flow of his own case to answer it, which tells you something about the difference between winning a debate and telling the truth.

Much in every way. Paul does not retreat an inch from chapter 2, and he does not allow the privileges to be belittled; in chapter 9 he will list them with an ache in his voice: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, the Christ (9:4–5). A gift can be magnificent and insufficient to save the man holding it.

They were entrusted. The word Paul chooses is not the language of a possession but of a deposit: something handed to you which belongs to somebody else and about which you will be asked. A trustee does not own the fund; he is accountable for it. The advantage is real precisely because it is a trust, and a trust is the one kind of advantage that increases your liability rather than reducing it.

The oracles of God. The utterances, the things God actually said: the Scriptures, entrusted to Israel to keep and to pass on. Paul could have named the temple, the land or the throne. He names one thing: God had spoken, and they had it in writing. Every Gentile believer who has ever opened the Psalms is in debt to the scribes of Israel who copied them, letter by letter, for a thousand years.

A people with sentences. Every nation had priests who could tell you what the gods were thought to want, read from entrails, from stars, from the ambiguous mutterings of a woman at Delphi, and other peoples had hymns, myths and ritual lists. What Israel believed it had was words the living God himself had spoken, in a known language, that could be copied, memorised, checked, argued about, and read aloud to a child. The God of Israel did not leave the world to guess at him. He spoke, he put his words in writing, and he guarded them through exile, conquest and the slow centuries of copying. The God who could have remained silent chose to be the God who talks to his creatures, and the book on your table is the evidence that he has never stopped.

The trustee who kept the deposit. The trust was real, and so was the failure, for some were unfaithful (3:3). But the deposit did not stay unkept. One son of Israel received the oracles exactly as they were meant to be received: he answered the tempter from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:4) and went to his arrest saying that the Scriptures must be fulfilled (Mark 14:49). Then, risen, he opened the whole deposit to two disciples on a road and showed them what it had been about from the start: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). Israel was entrusted with the words. Christ is what the words were saying.

The advantage we hold. A Christian holds this advantage more fully than Israel did. You own, in a language you can read, more of God’s speech than Isaiah ever saw, and most of us keep several copies. But the deposit does not benefit a man who never opens it. There is no category in Scripture called owning the word of God. There is only hearing it and doing it, or hearing it and not.

Do Jewish people still have an advantage today? Paul’s answer to that belongs to chapters 9 to 11, and Christians who love those chapters read the details differently. But this much he says plainly: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (11:29), the privileges of 9:4–5 were never a mistake, and God has not rejected his people (11:1). What no privilege can do is justify. A Jewish heritage of Scripture, like a Christian upbringing, is a great mercy and a heavy responsibility, and it saves no one apart from faith in Christ. The proper response of a Gentile believer is gratitude, not arrogance (11:18), and a longing that the people who gave us the Bible should receive its Messiah.

Is the Old Testament still God’s word for me? Yes, every page of it. Paul calls it the oracles of God, the words God himself spoke, and he never treats them as out of date. Jesus said the Scriptures bear witness about him (John 5:39), and Paul says that whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope (15:4). Not every command applies to you in the same way: the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws governed a nation. But all of it is God speaking, all of it points to his Son, and all of it is for you.
verseByVerse.note: “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if some were unfaithful? If Israel failed, does God fail? Has he broken his promises? The sentence turns on a play on words that English cannot keep. Their faithlessness (apistia) and God’s faithfulness (pistis) are the same word in Greek, with a “not” in front of the first, as if to say: does their un-faith cancel the faith of God? Paul sets the two words against each other so that the answer is visible before it is argued. One is something real in God; the other is only something missing in us. Something missing cannot cancel something real. The dark in a room has never once put out a lamp.

By no means! Mē genoito: the strongest negative Paul has, used ten times in this letter when a conclusion is not merely wrong but intolerable. The older translations’ “God forbid” catches the tone: a man recoiling from a proposition, not weighing it.

Let God be true. God’s faithfulness does not depend on ours (2 Timothy 2:13): even if every human being failed, God would remain true. Kings have broken treaties, nations have broken covenants, friends have broken promises, and you have broken more vows to God than you can count. In a universe of human unreliability, he is true, and he will be true when every liar has fallen silent. Sooner or later what God has said and what you can see will fail to agree. He says he works all things for good, and you are standing in a hospital corridor. He says he is near to the brokenhearted, and you have felt nothing for eight months. He says his discipline is love, and it does not feel like love. In that moment one of two things has to give, and Paul tells you which: God is true. Your own eyes and your own heart at four in the morning are admitted as evidence, and they lose, not because your experience is unreal, but because a witness who has been wrong before is not permitted to overrule one who never has.

What it does not mean. It is not a call to pretend. Paul does not say, “Let God be true and every man be silent.” The Bible is full of people telling God exactly what they see, at length and without editing; half the Psalter does little else. You are allowed to say that it looks as though he has forgotten you. What you are not allowed to do is conclude it. Say the whole of what you see; then let his word, not what you see, have the last say.

Justified in your words. Psalm 51 is David after Bathsheba, after arranging for her husband, a loyal soldier, to be abandoned in the front line. That is the man who says, “Against you, you only, have I sinned”, and adds, “so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment” (Psalm 51:4). He is not defending himself. He is agreeing with the verdict in advance, without conditions, declaring that when God judges him, God will be in the right.

Displayed, not damaged. God’s truthfulness is not damaged by human failure but displayed by it: God had said that men are sinners, and David turned out to be exactly that.

The truthfulness of God in person. Paul later names where this rule was proved: Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs (15:8). God kept the promises by sending David’s Son, the one son of David who never needed a Psalm 51 of his own. And at the cross God was shown to be true in both his warnings and his promises. He was justified in his words, because sin was judged exactly as he had said it would be. And he kept his promise, because the judgment fell on that Son so that sinners like David could be forgiven.

Did God’s faithfulness mean every Israelite was saved anyway? No. God’s faithfulness is faithfulness to what he promised, and he never promised to save people who refused him. Paul answers this directly later: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (9:6). God kept his word by preserving a believing remnant, chosen by grace (11:5), and by sending the Messiah through Israel exactly as he had said. He also kept his word when he judged unbelief, because his covenant always carried warnings as well as promises. His faithfulness is not a guarantee that no one will be lost. It is a guarantee that nothing he has said will fail.

If I am faithless, will God still keep me? If you belong to Christ, yes. He remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13). But read the line before it too: if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Timothy 2:12). Paul is distinguishing the believer who wavers, doubts and fails, as Peter did on the night of the trial, from the person who finally and deliberately turns his back on Christ for good. The first is held, because what holds him is God’s faithfulness and not his own grip. The second shows he never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). If you are worried about your faithlessness and still turning to Christ, that worry is a sign of life, not of abandonment.

In everyday life. Take the last time you were rebuked, by Scripture, by a sermon, or by a person who loved you enough to say it. Did you come out of it agreeing with God, or explaining yourself, supplying the context, the tiredness, the other party’s share? David stops arguing and lets God be right about him. You can afford to: the verdict you are agreeing with has already fallen on David’s Son, and what comes back to you is forgiveness. So say the one specific thing to God in one plain sentence, with no clause beginning with but.

parallels.desc: so that you may be justified in your words
all mankind are liars

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? A twisted objection: if my sin makes God look good, why does he punish me? In modern dress it runs like this. God gets glory from forgiving sinners. No sinners, no forgiveness; no forgiveness, no glory. Therefore my sin is, in a roundabout way, a service, and it seems unfair of God to be furious about the very thing his reputation is built from. Nobody says this out loud. A great many people run some version of it quietly, and it is the oldest trick in the human repertoire: to find a way in which the thing you were going to do anyway turns out to be useful.

I speak in a human way. Paul flags his own sentence: he has just voiced an argument he considers close to blasphemy, and does not want it left in the air with his name attached. Then he refuses it, and instead of a philosophical rebuttal he asks a question.

By no means! “For then how could God judge the world?” That is not evasion; it is the argument. Every party to this conversation, Jew or Greek, agreed on one thing: God will judge the world. Abraham had said it long ago: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). It is the fixed point. And the objection, followed to its end, abolishes it, because if evil that serves God’s glory cannot be punished, and all evil somehow serves God’s glory, then nothing whatever can be punished, and there is no judgment of anything by anybody. The objector has not found a loophole. He has sawn off the branch he is sitting on, and Paul simply points at the saw. He assumes that a God who did not punish evil would be a worse God, not a kinder one, and that a Judge who could be argued out of a verdict by a clever man would be no protection to anybody. You cannot talk him out of a just verdict, and so neither can the person who wronged you; the widow, the orphan and the murdered have their hope in exactly that. And this same unbending Judge is the one who, in a few verses, will himself provide the sacrifice that turns his own wrath away (v. 25).

Good out of evil. God can and does bring good out of evil; that does not make him guilty of the evil, and it does not make the evil good. Joseph told his brothers exactly this and softened neither half: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Both clauses stand. The supreme instance is the cross, where the worst act in human history accomplished the salvation of the world, and Peter, preaching it, puts both truths in one sentence: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed him (Acts 2:23). Nobody at Pentecost heard that as an acquittal.

Does God cause sin, then, if he uses it? No. Scripture holds two truths together without apology: God rules over all things, including the evil acts of men, and God is never the author of sin, and the men who do it are fully responsible (Westminster Confession 3.1; 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; 5.4). Joseph’s brothers chose freely and wickedly; God overruled their choice for good. We cannot fully explain how both are true, any more than we can explain how a Person can be both God and man, but we can see both in the same story and refuse to give up either. The practical point is simple: God’s sovereignty is a comfort when you are sinned against, and never an excuse when you are the one sinning.

In everyday life. Watch when you reach for the sovereignty of God, because what matters is the tense. “God can bring good out of this”; “he knows my heart”: each is true in its place. Afterwards, looking back on something you regret, saying that God has brought something out of the wreckage is faith, and it is what Genesis 50:20 is for. Beforehand, while a decision is still open, the same sentence is a permission slip: the objection of verse 5 in your own voice. It is worship in the past tense and self-permission in the future one.

parallels.desc: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? The same objection, stated personally and then pushed to its extreme: if God’s glory is served by human sin, why not do evil that good may come, and maximise the glory by maximising the sin? Every attempt to turn God’s purposes into an excuse for sin ends here, if it is followed honestly, and Paul does not stop here to refute it at length.

Slanderously charged. The remarkable detail is the aside: people were claiming that this was Paul’s actual teaching. He had preached free grace so unreservedly, righteousness apart from works, God justifying the ungodly, nothing to bring and nothing to pay, that respectable religious people concluded he must be telling converts that sin no longer mattered (compare 6:1).

A test of preaching. Nobody seems to have accused the Pharisees of encouraging immorality, and a sermon about trying harder is seldom misheard as permission to sin. The charge of licence is only ever levelled at a message of grace so free that it sounds dangerous. A gospel nobody could possibly abuse is usually a gospel with a condition quietly attached.

The friend of sinners. The slander was laid against Paul’s Master first. When Jesus sat at table with tax collectors, the respectable muttered, “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2), and they called him “a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). Jesus answered the charge with the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son, and then went to a cross where sin was taken more seriously than any Pharisee had ever taken it. The grace that is slandered as licence is the grace that cost him his life.

Their condemnation is just. Paul answers with a verdict rather than an argument, and rightly. Some propositions are not to be debated but refused, because to argue them on their merits is already to concede that they might have some. A man who asks whether it might be good to do evil has not made an intellectual error you can correct with information. He has revealed what he wants, and dressed it up as logic.

Why the full answer waits. Paul will come back to this exact question in chapter 6, “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” (6:1), and the answer there is not a rule but a fact: you died to sin, so how can you still live in it? The full answer needs union with Christ, which he has not yet laid out, so here he simply blocks the road, and three chapters later he shows you the country on the other side of it.

This is forgivable. The everyday form is subtler. What a man thinks, at eleven at night, is: this is forgivable. And it is. That is the whole trouble. The doctrine of forgiveness is being used, in the moment before the act, to make the sin seem cheaper. That is the abuse not of a bad doctrine but of the best one there is, and it is possible only because grace really is that free. For a man who has understood the gospel, knowing what the forgiveness cost makes the sin more expensive, not less. He is not restrained by fear of punishment, because that was settled, but by something stronger: the difficulty of casually doing the thing that killed his friend.

I have used grace as an excuse before. Is there hope for me? Yes, and the very fact that it troubles you is part of the hope. The men of verse 8 were not troubled; they had turned grace into an argument. If you see that you have treated forgiveness as a discount and you are grieved by it, then grace is doing exactly what it does: it trains us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). Bring that very sin to Christ, the sin of presuming on him, and he will forgive it as freely as any other (1 John 1:9). Then let the cost of the forgiveness, not the fear of losing it, make the next temptation heavier. What Scripture warns against is not a Christian who has fallen this way, but a settled life that has made peace with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now seals the case with Israel’s own Scriptures. The chain of quotations in vv. 10–18, from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10 and 36 and Isaiah 59, leaves no exception.

The law was never meant to supply righteousness but to show its absence (v. 20). The verdict is universal so that the remedy can be universal too: all have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by grace (vv. 23–24). The section ends with every mouth stopped (v. 19), because a man still presenting his case cannot receive a gift.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the classic text for the doctrine of total depravity. It does not mean that every person is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every part of human nature: the mind (“no one understands”), the will (“no one seeks for God”), the affections, the speech and the conduct. That is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is given freely: there is nothing in us that could earn it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The psalms Paul quotes were sung in the temple and prayed in the synagogue, and Israel heard them turned on her own guilt. Now: Many prefer to speak of human potential and say little about the fall. Romans 3:9–20 corrects that. The doctrine of depravity is not pessimism but realism, and realism about the disease is what makes us grateful for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. Privileges, yes; a better verdict, no. Does this contradict verse 2, which answered “Much in every way”? No. The advantage was real: Israel had been entrusted with the oracles of God. But privilege is not a better standing before the Judge. In the courtroom, having the law only means being judged by it, and so Jew and Gentile stand together under sin.

For we have already charged. The word belongs to a prosecutor bringing a formal accusation: chapters 1 and 2 were the presentation of evidence, and the reader has been in a courtroom since 1:18.

Under sin. The charge, when it comes, is not the one we expect. Paul does not say that all have committed sins. He says that all are under sin: under its power and its guilt, the same construction you would use for a soldier under orders or a slave under a master (7:14; Galatians 3:22). The plural sins are the symptom; the singular Sin is the disease. If the problem is sins, then the problem is a record, and what a man needs is a pardon. If the problem is Sin, then the problem is a power he is under, and he needs to be rescued. This letter will say that God did both, and it will spend chapters 3 to 5 on the first and chapters 6 to 8 on the second.

Shut up to one door. Paul gives the purpose of this verdict in another letter: the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe (Galatians 3:22). Every other exit is walled up so that one door is left, and it opens onto a Person. Christ came under the very things we are under: born under the law to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5), made sin for us though he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). The verdict that shuts the whole human race in together sends the whole human race to the same Saviour.

But I know decent people. Of course. Paul has just conceded that Gentiles sometimes do by nature what the law requires (2:14). His claim is less visible and more serious: a man may be honest, generous, faithful to his wife, admired by everyone who knows him, and still be living his entire life without reference to the God who made him, and that is what being under sin looks like in a respectable neighbourhood. The chains are not always the kind that chafe.

As it is written. Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah (Psalm 14:1–3; 53:1–3; 5:9; 140:3; 10:7; Isaiah 59:7–8; Psalm 36:1), as the rabbis argued. Psalm 14 opens with the fool who says in his heart there is no God, and it was easy for Israel to sing it about other people: the evildoers who eat up my people (Psalm 14:4), the wicked outside. Paul turns it round on the very people who sang it, like a congregation being indicted by its own hymnbook: the words are familiar, everyone knows the tune, and this morning they are about you.

Not one. Paul closes the last exit, because the human mind, presented with a universal negative, hunts for the exception, usually itself.

What about babies, who have done nothing? Scripture teaches that we are sinners from birth, not only from our first wrong act: in sin did my mother conceive me (Psalm 51:5), and in Adam all were made sinners (5:12, 19). So no one, not even an infant, stands before God on the ground of innocence. That is exactly why the hope for little ones who die is grace, not their goodness. This commentary’s view, with the Reformed confessions, is that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster Confession 10.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3), and grieving parents may rest their child in the hands of the God who is rich in mercy and took little children in his arms (Mark 10:16).
verseByVerse.note: Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all are under sin.

parallels.desc: not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one understands. Three universal negations follow, and Paul begins with the mind. This is not a comment on intelligence. It is the claim that something is wrong with the faculty itself where God is concerned, which helps explain why brilliant people can come away unmoved while a person of no education grasps the gospel. Elsewhere he says that the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them (1 Corinthians 2:14). Not merely unwilling, but unable.

No one seeks for God. The world is full of seekers. How can Paul say nobody is looking? Because of what is actually being sought. Human beings look tirelessly for what God gives: meaning, peace, forgiveness, a sense that their life amounts to something, the assurance that they are loved. What nobody seeks, left to himself, is God on his own terms: a God with authority over him, who has the right to name his sin, who will not be edited, and whose company he cannot leave when it becomes inconvenient. We look for the benefits. We do not look for the Person, and religion is very often the most sophisticated method available for having the first without the second.

Behind a tree. In the garden, after the fall, God comes walking in the cool of the day, and the man is not looking for him; he is hiding among the trees (Genesis 3:8). The whole Bible is the record not of humanity’s search for God but of God’s search for humanity, and in the end our Lord defines his own mission in the same terms: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). If nobody is searching, then somebody has to come.

All have turned aside. Turned off the road. It is the shepherd’s picture Isaiah chose for the same condition: all we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way (Isaiah 53:6). The last phrase saves the doctrine from a caricature: nobody follows a common script; each turns to his own way. Depravity does not produce uniformity. It produces a world of highly individual people going, with great originality, in the same general direction.

Together they have become worthless. The word (ēchreiōthēsan) means become useless, good for nothing. Behind it is the Hebrew word of Psalm 14:3, which means gone bad, like milk that has turned. The creature made to bear God’s image and fill the earth with his glory has become, in the matter for which he was made, good for nothing.

No one does good, not even one. Not that no one does anything kind, but that no one does what is truly good before God: from a heart that loves him, in obedience to his word, for his glory.

Where Christians differ: how bad is human nature? Some believe people are basically good, or that fallen humans keep the ability to seek God on their own. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches total depravity: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that every part of human nature, mind, will and affections, is affected by sin, and no one can, by his own power, seek God or do spiritual good (8:7–8; Ephesians 2:1–3). This is why salvation must be entirely by grace. Many Christians who differ from this commentary elsewhere, such as Arminians (who hold that God’s grace enables every person to accept or refuse him), agree that without grace no one would seek God at all.

Then are the good deeds of unbelievers worthless? Not in every sense. When an unbeliever nurses the sick, tells the truth or gives to the poor, the deed itself may be right and is a real blessing to others, and God, in his common kindness, restrains sin and preserves a great deal of good in the world. What such deeds cannot do is please God as acceptable worship or earn his favour, because they do not come from a heart made right with him by faith, nor aim at his glory (Hebrews 11:6; Westminster Confession 16.7; 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.7). So we can honestly admire a good neighbour and still say he needs Christ. Admiration and evangelism are not in tension.

Is there any point in an unbeliever reading the Bible or coming to church? Every point. That no one seeks God by nature does not mean God does not use means to seek them. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (10:17). The Spirit works through the word read, preached and explained, and many have begun to read out of curiosity, or come to church to please a friend, and found that God was the one doing the seeking. The invitation of the gospel is sincere and goes to everyone. Keep inviting, keep praying, and keep the Bible open in front of the people you love.

In everyday life. Think of what you most want God to do for you at the moment. Now suppose he offered you that thing on condition that you would have nothing further to do with him: the healing, the restored relationship, the job, the peace of mind, delivered in full, and God himself off the table. Would you take it? This is the difference between seeking God’s hand and seeking his face, and Asaph settled it for himself in Psalm 73: with God in heaven as his portion, he found he wanted nothing else on earth (Psalm 73:25). If your honest answer troubles you, the trouble is itself a good sign: a heart that minds about wanting God more than his gifts is already being drawn to him.

For worship. If you are reading this and find that you do want God, that his existence is a comfort rather than a threat, that you would not take the gift without the Giver, then something has happened to you which this verse says does not happen naturally. The wanting is itself the sign of a work already done, which is why our Lord could say that no one can come to him unless the Father who sent him draws him (John 6:44). The seeking you are conscious of is the far end of a search that began with God, who came at last in his Son to find you behind your tree.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their throat is an open grave. Paul is walking down a body: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, then feet (v. 15), then eyes (v. 18). Four of the six are the organs of speech. Sin shows itself first in words.

Out of the abundance of the heart. Our Lord gave the reason: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34). Speech is where the inside becomes audible. You can conceal your character in almost every other department for years, but you cannot talk for long without giving yourself away. Which is why he added, in the same breath, that on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). He names the careless ones because those are the words we did not stop to edit.

An open grave. The image, from Psalm 5:9, carried two things for a Jewish reader. A tomb standing open gives off the smell of what is inside, and if what comes up out of a man smells of death, it tells you what is down inside him. And under the law, a man who so much as touched a grave was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). An open grave contaminated people who had done nothing but come near. Human speech does not stay with the speaker.

Tongues to deceive. The four organs are not four ways of saying one thing but a sequence. The throat is the source, what comes up from inside; the tongue is the method, and the verb describes a habit: they keep on deceiving.

Under their lips. From Psalm 140:3, and the sharpest of the four: speech that is lethal precisely because it is smooth. Not the shouted insult, which at least announces itself. The compliment with a hook in it. The concerned question that plants a doubt about somebody and leaves no fingerprints. The observation made in front of others that is perfectly accurate and perfectly timed to humiliate. None of it would stand out on a recording. All of it is under the lip.

Curses and bitterness. From Psalm 10:7, and the overflow: the point at which a man stops bothering to hide it. James calls the tongue a restless evil, full of deadly poison (James 3:8), and makes the observation that puts this verse in a church rather than a gutter: with the same mouth we bless our Lord and Father and curse people who are made in the likeness of God (James 3:9). The mouth that has been singing in the service is the mouth that dismantles somebody in the car afterwards, and it does not even change gear.

Every mouth turned on him. Once, the whole of this anatomy was aimed at one man: false witnesses at his trial, and at the cross passers-by, rulers, soldiers and robbers. Every organ in Paul’s list was at work that day, against the one man in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22). And from him came the opposite of every word in this chain. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and from the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34; a few early manuscripts lack this prayer, but most modern Bibles keep it). The bitterness of the human mouth was poured out on him, and he answered it with intercession for the people pouring it. This is the reversal the letter is heading for: the organ that chapter 3 calls an open grave is, in chapter 10, the mouth that confesses Jesus as Lord and is saved (10:9–10). The Word made flesh went down into a real open grave, so that graves like ours might be made into mouths of praise.

The open grave with a distribution network. Our generation has industrialised this. Most people in history spoke to a few dozen others; now a sentence composed in ninety seconds of irritation can reach thousands and still be sitting there in five years.

How do I actually change the way I speak? Start where Jesus starts, with the heart, because the mouth only reports what is there. Ask God to deal with the bitterness or contempt underneath, and pray David’s prayer before the day begins: set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips (Psalm 141:3). Then build small habits. Be quick to hear, slow to speak (James 1:19). Before you speak or post about someone, ask whether it is true, whether it is needed, and whether it builds them up (Ephesians 4:29). When you have wounded someone, go back and name it plainly rather than waiting for it to fade. And fill the mouth with better things: thanks, Scripture, encouragement, prayer.

In everyday life. Do not ask whether you swear. Think of one sentence you said this week that was entirely polite, that nobody in the room would have called unkind, and that you knew, as you were forming it, would land somewhere tender. That sentence is not on your lips. It is under them, and it is the one this verse is about. The blood of the one who answered every mocking mouth with intercession has covered that sentence too; go back, forgiven, and mend it.
