verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Swift to shed blood. From Isaiah 59:7. The list now moves from words to deeds: the mouth speaks, but the feet go and do. The disturbing word is swift. Speed is a measure of desire, and it is the eagerness rather than the violence that tells you what is in the runner.

Belonging. The same words echo the father in Proverbs 1 warning his son about the men who will invite him along: come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, we shall find all precious goods, throw in your lot among us. Then comes the father’s comment: their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood (Proverbs 1:11–16). The invitation is attractive: company, adventure and a share of the proceeds. Evil rarely presents itself as evil; it presents itself as belonging.

The sixth commandment at its root. A modern reader will want to file this verse under people unlike himself. Our Lord traced the sixth commandment back to its root: everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment, and whoever says “You fool!” will be liable to the hell of fire (Matthew 5:21–22). John said it flatly: everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). This is not a claim that a harsh word equals a killing in its consequences. It is a claim that the same thing lies at the root of both: the desire to see someone diminished, silenced, humiliated, ended. That desire is available to respectable people at their own kitchen tables. Most of us never reach the deed because we lack the opportunity, the nerve or the anonymity, which is a mercy but is not innocence.

Clean bloodshed. Bloodshed has always had its tidy forms, in which nobody’s feet appear to move at all. David never touched Uriah; he sent a letter and let the Ammonites do it. Ahab did not stone Naboth; a court was convened and witnesses were found. Pilate washed his hands in public and gave the order anyway. The distance between the decision and the death is the oldest device in the world for keeping one’s feet unmarked, and it works on the conscience without deceiving the Judge for a moment.

The swiftest feet of all. Every strand of this verse met on one Friday in Jerusalem, when Jesus was led to Pilate as soon as it was morning (Mark 15:1) and crucified before the day was done. Yet the one whose blood they hurried to shed had set his face to go to Jerusalem long before (Luke 9:51), walking toward that blood of his own will. Not long afterwards Peter told the same city that they had asked for a murderer and killed the Author of life (Acts 3:14–15), and in the same sermon offered them the blotting out of their sins (Acts 3:19). Scripture uses the identical image in the opposite direction. Isaiah pictured a runner coming over the mountains and wrote that his feet were beautiful, because of what he was carrying: good news, peace, salvation; and Paul quotes it later in this letter of the people who bring the gospel (Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15). Feet that ran to shed blood are not, in the end, cut off. They are sent somewhere else, in a hurry, carrying something worth the speed.

Is all anger sinful, then? No. Scripture says be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26), and Jesus himself was angry at hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). Righteous anger is aimed at what is genuinely evil, is grieved on God’s behalf rather than merely offended on mine, and wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored. The anger Jesus calls murder in seed form is different: it is about me, it nurses itself, and it wants the other person to be smaller. The test is what it wants. If your anger is pushing you to pray, to protect the vulnerable or to speak the truth in love, it may be right. If it is pushing you to rehearse speeches and enjoy imagining someone’s downfall, it has already crossed the line.

In everyday life. Watch what you move toward quickly. When somebody you resent is in difficulty, how fast do you pass the news on? When a story arrives that confirms what you already thought about someone, how long does it take you to believe it? What our feet hurry toward is evidence in this trial. Choose one of those and be slow, leaning on the Spirit of the Christ who set his face toward Jerusalem for you.

parallels.desc: their feet run to evil

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In their paths. From Isaiah 59:7–8. The ruin is not in front of them as a destination; it is in their paths, behind them, in the places they have already been. This line steps back and photographs the road the sinner has walked down.

The wreckage we cannot see. We experience our own lives from the inside, as a sequence of understandable decisions, so the wreckage is not in our field of vision. It is in other people: the child who grew up learning to read a father’s mood before coming into a room; the friend who stopped calling and was never asked why; the colleague made to look foolish in a meeting years ago who still thinks about it; the marriage that did not end but went quiet. None of that appears on the sinner’s own account of his life. All of it is in the path.

Ruin and misery. Ruin is breakage: something that was whole is now not. Misery is what the breakage costs the people living in it. Sin is never only an offence against God registered in heaven; it also lands somewhere on earth, and there is usually a person where it lands.

The way of peace. Peace here is not the absence of trouble but shalom: everything in its proper place, working, whole. And the wording is exact: not that they refuse the way of peace, but that they have not known it. The whole human race is trying to arrive somewhere it cannot find, which is why every generation produces its own confident method, better education, better systems, better technology, better politics, and why each produces a fresh crop of ruin along the way.

The arm that brought salvation. Paul’s quotation stops at the darkest line, but Isaiah 59 does not. The prophet goes on: the LORD saw that there was no one to intercede, and then his own arm brought him salvation (Isaiah 59:16). The chapter ends with the Redeemer who will come to Zion (Isaiah 59:20; Romans 11:26). The same chapter that says the human race cannot find the way of peace says that God himself would come and make it. And the New Testament tells us whose arm that was: when Israel would not believe the report about the arm of the LORD, John says Isaiah was speaking of Jesus (Isaiah 53:1; John 12:38–41). The way of peace was not known, so somebody had to come and be it: he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). The road nobody could find turned out not to be a road at all. It is a Person, the Prince of Peace, and he came looking for the people leaving ruin in their paths, and this letter will shortly say that he died for them while they were still doing it (5:8).

But many unbelievers seem to live peaceful lives? Many do, in the ordinary sense, and we should be thankful: God in his kindness restrains evil and gives order, friendship and quiet to people who do not know him. But the peace in view here is deeper. It is peace with God, which no one has apart from Christ (5:1), and the wholeness that flows from it. A life can be calm on the surface and still be at war with its Maker, and at death the surface calm comes to an end. Equally, a believer may live through great turmoil and still have the peace of God guarding his heart (Philippians 4:7). The question is not how quiet your life is but whether you have been reconciled.

Do I need to go back and put things right with people? Where you can, yes. Repentance in Scripture often involves other people and not only God. Zacchaeus did not merely confess; he worked out fourfold and promised to repay it (Luke 19:8). Our Lord told a man to leave his gift at the altar and go and be reconciled to his brother first (Matthew 5:23–24), interrupting an act of worship for the sake of a repair. But not every path can be walked back down. Some people are dead, some are unreachable, and some would be harmed by your return; there the road back is closed, and God’s forgiveness is not thereby withheld. Where it is open, walk it, humbly and without demanding a particular response. It is usually the last thing we want to do, and often the most freeing.

parallels.desc: the way of peace they do not know

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No fear of God. From Psalm 36:1, and the root of it all. With the eyes the body is complete. The earlier charges were symptoms; this one is the cause. Sin is, at bottom, a failure of worship before it is a failure of morality. Before a man does wrong things, he has already stopped treating God as God, which is how Paul began his charge: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him (1:21).

What the fear of God is. It does not mean terror, or cringing before a temperamental deity. “That boy has no fear of his father,” we say, and nobody hearing it thinks we mean the father ought to be frightening. We mean that the father’s reality does not weigh with the boy. He is not restrained by it, does not consult it, and behaves in his father’s presence exactly as he would in his absence. That is the charge here. God’s existence makes no practical difference to them at all: they have no reverence for him and no sense that they must answer to him.

Before their eyes. The phrase describes what a man keeps in view while he is deciding. Everyone knows a speed limit exists, yet the appearance of a patrol car in the mirror alters behaviour instantly. Nothing about the belief has changed; only what is in the frame. That is how it works with God, which is why it is hard to sin while consciously aware of him. The Christian’s problem is rarely that he stops believing. It is that at the moment of choosing, God is simply not in the picture, and the picture is what governs conduct.

The beginning of wisdom. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7), and the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10); its absence is the beginning of folly and sin. Verse 11 said no one understands; verse 18 says why. These people have removed from view the one fact that makes sense of every other, and a man reasoning about his life with God left out of the frame will reason with great sophistication to conclusions that are reliably wrong.

His delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. There has been one man of whom the opposite of this verse was wholly true. Isaiah, describing the shoot from the stump of Jesse, says the Spirit of the LORD would rest on him, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD, and that his delight would be in the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:2–3). Jesus lived every hour with his Father before his eyes: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). The fear of God missing from the whole human race was present, complete and joyful, in the Son, and he died for people with no fear of God before their eyes.

Is a Christian supposed to fear God? Yes, though not with the fear of punishment. John says that perfect love casts out fear, and he is careful about which fear, adding that fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The dread of being condemned is gone, and this letter will say so in the plainest words at 8:1. What is not gone, and grows, is the other thing. A child of a good father is not afraid of him and would not dream of being flippant about him; the boy is entirely at ease on his knee and would go white if he heard someone speak of his father with contempt. Both at once, and neither weakening the other. That is the fear this verse says is missing, and it is a covenant gift: I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me (Jeremiah 32:40). The fear is given as the thing that keeps a man. It is not the opposite of assurance; it is part of the means by which God holds on to his people.

How do I grow in the fear of God? Not by working yourself into a state of reverence, which does not last past Tuesday. Look at God as he has shown himself. Read the passages where his holiness is on display, Isaiah 6, Exodus 19 and 20, Revelation 4 and 5, and let them be large. Above all, look at the cross, because Scripture says something surprising: with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Psalm 130:4). Nothing makes God weightier to a forgiven sinner than knowing what his forgiveness cost. Then practise remembering him in the ordinary hours: a sentence of prayer before a hard conversation, a pause before you open something you should not. And ask him for it; he has promised to give it.

For worship. Paul’s last quotation carries its own cure. Psalm 36 opens with the wicked man who has no fear of God before his eyes, and then turns to say: your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds; for with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light (Psalm 36:5, 9). The psalm that diagnoses the eye supplies the light, and Paul knew where that light shines: in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), the one sight that, once seen, puts the fear of God before the eyes for ever.

parallels.desc: there is no fear of God before his eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever the law says. The first clause closes the last door. A Jewish reader could grant every quotation and conclude that the psalmist was describing the nations: bad people, elsewhere. Paul blocks it: those texts were addressed to the people who possess them. The word lands first on the people in the room, and you may not pass it along without receiving it yourself.

Every mouth stopped. The picture is a courtroom where the defendant, having heard the indictment, has nothing to say: no excuses, no protests, no plea of mitigating circumstances, no claim of comparative righteousness. A man does not become guilty when he stops arguing; he was guilty already. What the silence does is end the defence, and until the defence ends, nothing can be given. A man who is still presenting his case is asking for a verdict on his record, and grace has nothing to say to a man who still believes he might win. That is why religion can be the hardest place for grace to land. A moral person’s whole life can become one long speech for the defence, while the irreligious man often has fewer arguments to drop.

The whole world. Chapter 1 caught the pagan, chapter 2 the moralist and the man with the law; here the doors are shut and the room is full.

No human being will be justified. The conclusion of 1:18–3:20, echoing Psalm 143:2: enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you. At 2:7 Paul stated the standard: patience in well-doing, and God will give eternal life. At 2:13 he stated the rule: not the hearers of the law but the doers will be justified. Both left one question open: who has done it? Here is the verdict: no one. Chapter 2 was the statute; chapter 3 is the judgment.

The road is impassable. It does not say the law is bad, or that obedience does not matter, or that God has lowered the standard. It says that by this road no one arrives. The road is not condemned; it is reported to be impassable, and the report is made by the surveyor who laid it out. One man did walk it to the end. Jesus kept every commandment from the heart, and it is by his obedience, not ours, that the many will be made righteous (5:19). The road no one could travel was travelled once, by a substitute, for people who had failed on it.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars (the New Perspective on Paul) take them to mean mainly the Jewish identity markers. This commentary’s view: those markers are included, but the verse ends, through the law comes knowledge of sin: Paul means any obedience offered as a basis for acceptance, and no one keeps the law. (See Galatians 2:15–16 for the fuller answer.)

Knowledge of sin. The law’s purpose is not to save but to show sin (7:7). It is a mirror, not a washbasin. The word (epignōsis) is full recognition rather than vague awareness: the law turns a vague unease into a list of particular sins, and so drives us to Christ. That is why an honest reading of the Ten Commandments is more use to an unconverted man than any amount of encouragement: you cannot want a Saviour while your problem is only a vague feeling that something is wrong.

What about those who have never heard of Christ? This verse says the whole world is accountable, and Paul has already explained on what basis: those without the written law are judged by the light they had, creation and conscience, and they have not lived up to it (1:20; 2:12–15). No one will be condemned for failing to believe a gospel he never heard; he will be judged for real sin against real light. But no one is saved apart from Christ, and Paul is plain that people cannot call on one of whom they have never heard (10:14). The answer of this letter is not speculation but mission: the reason Paul was going to Spain. The question should send us to our knees and to our neighbours.

In everyday life. When Scripture shows you something true about yourself, where do you go next? Some go to despair, which is the law doing half its work and stopping. Some go to resolve, which is the law doing none of it: the man has heard that he cannot climb and responds by training harder. The law has done its full work only when a man stops climbing and starts looking for a rescue. Stop defending yourself before God. Let your mouth be stopped, and then open it to call on Christ.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
After three chapters of diagnosis come the words “But now” (v. 21): the righteousness of God has been revealed, apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, a sacrifice that turns away his wrath, so that he is both just, because sin has been punished in his Son, and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

Boasting is therefore excluded (v. 27). There is one God, and he justifies Jew and Gentile by the same faith. Paul ends with the question his critics were asking, whether faith overthrows the law (v. 31), and answers that it upholds it, which chapter 4 will show from Abraham.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation

In Romans 3:25 Paul calls Christ a hilastērion, a propitiation: an offering that turns away God’s wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris argued at length that this is the right reading, against C.H. Dodd's proposal to read it as expiation, which only removes sin, without reference to wrath. Christ bore the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God is both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). If Christ did not bear the whole of that wrath, some of it is still left for us, and the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Verses 24–25 echo the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when blood was sprinkled on the mercy seat for the sins of the people. What that day pointed to, Christ has accomplished once for all. Now: People still deal with guilt by ritual, moral effort, distraction or denial; Romans 3:21–31 says that the only remedy is the one God provided, the death of his own Son in our place, received by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now. Two small words, and the whole letter turns on them. Everything from 1:18 has been a closing down, until every mouth is stopped. And into that silence: but now. God has acted (Ephesians 2:13). Not a discount, or a reduced charge, or a quiet decision to overlook the file. A righteousness from God, apart from law, held out to the very people the law had that moment finished condemning, and priced at the life of the only innocent man who ever lived. Blessed be the God who did not wait for us to climb up to him, but came down, in his Son, with a righteousness already finished in his hands.

Not therefore. Paul writes “But now”, not “therefore”, because nothing in 1:18–3:20 leads on to grace. Paul presents the gospel not as the conclusion of an argument but as an interruption of one: an announcement from outside the courtroom, which is what gospel always meant, news, not advice.

Manifested. Not invented but brought into the open, and the tense describes something done once that still stands: it has happened, in public, and the announcement is catching up with it. This is the righteous standing that God gives (1:17), revealed in Christ, apart from law-keeping.

His character, or his gift? Paul holds both together. It is a righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, and so a status God gives: his verdict that a sinner is in the right with him (compare Philippians 3:9, the righteousness from God that depends on faith). Yet in vv. 25–26 the same cross shows God’s own righteousness, so that he is just and the justifier. Luther found the gospel when he saw that God’s righteousness in this letter is not only the standard that condemns us but the gift that clothes us. That is, God gives guilty people a right standing with himself that they did not earn, the standing that belongs to Christ, as a robe is given to someone with nothing fit to wear (Isaiah 61:10).

The Law and the Prophets bear witness. Apart from the law, and yet witnessed by it. The law never produced this righteousness, but it has been pointing at it from the beginning (Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4), and chapter 4 will prove it. Every sacrifice, every high priest going in on the Day of Atonement, every prophet who spoke of a servant wounded for our transgressions, was a signpost. Paul is not founding a new religion; he is announcing that the old one has arrived at what it was for.

For all who believe. Paul adds nothing after “believe”: no period of probation, no minimum standard of improvement, no requirement that you first become the sort of person to whom such an offer could decently be made. Paul has spent three chapters establishing that no such person exists, precisely so that the offer could be phrased this way. The offer is open to all and is received by faith alone, and faith is not an achievement God rewards but the empty hand that receives.

Where Christians differ: our faith in Jesus Christ, or his own faithfulness? The Greek (pisteōs Iēsou Christou) can mean faith in Jesus Christ or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, and some scholars prefer the second, emphasising Christ’s obedience unto death. This commentary’s view: Christ’s faithful obedience is indeed the ground of our justification (5:19), but here the phrase most naturally means faith in Christ, since Paul immediately adds for all who believe. We are justified by faith in Christ, whose faithful obedience is credited to us. Both truths stand, and nobody who holds both has lost anything.

No distinction. Jew and Gentile alike, the moralist and the pagan, the man with four Bibles and the man who has never opened one. The ground was levelled in vv. 9–20 so that one door could serve everyone.

Justification. To be justified is to be declared righteous by God as judge, on the basis of Christ’s work: a legal verdict, not a process of being made righteous. The word belongs to the courtroom: its opposite is to condemn (8:33–34), and no one thinks that to condemn a man means to make him wicked. Being made holy, which Scripture calls sanctification, really does begin at the same moment and always follows, but it is a different gift, and justification never rests on it.

Is that not a legal fiction, calling me righteous when I am not? No, because the verdict rests on something real. God does not pretend you have kept the law. He declares you righteous because you are joined to Christ by faith, and Christ really has kept it, and really has borne the penalty for your breaking it. His obedience is reckoned to your account as truly as your sin was reckoned to his (2 Corinthians 5:21). A fiction would be God saying the debt never existed. The gospel is God saying it has been paid, by the one who had the right to pay it. And the person God justifies he also begins to change, so the verdict is never left alone.

What exactly is faith? More than believing facts, though it includes them. Faith knows who Christ is and what he has done; it agrees that this is true and that it is true for me; and it trusts him, leaning the whole weight of your hope on him. The Westminster Confession calls it accepting, receiving and resting upon Christ alone for justification (Westminster 14.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 14.2). Think of a chair: knowing it is there, agreeing it would hold you, and then sitting down. Faith is the sitting down. It is not a feeling, and it is not the strength of your confidence; it is where you are resting.

In everyday life. Think of your worst week this year, the one with the failure in it that you have told nobody about. Now ask what changed about your standing with God during that week. If you suspect it dropped and has since partly recovered, then you are still living under chapter 2, whatever you believe about chapter 3. A righteousness manifested apart from the law is not affected by your performance under the law, because it never rested on it at any point.
verseByVerse.note: To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence. We are used to hearing verse 23 on its own, but in Paul it has no full stop: the next verse hangs on it. All have sinned, and are justified by his grace as a gift. The diagnosis and the remedy arrive in a single breath.

All. Paul has spent three chapters building a list long enough to catch everybody, so that this sentence lands as a description rather than an insult. Nobody has been singled out.

Fall short of the glory of God. It is not a moral score. The glory of God is what we were made to reflect, his image (Genesis 1:27), and what we were meant to share. We miss the mark, like an archer whose arrow drops short of the target. That explains the peculiar ache that comes with being human: the sense, available to everyone, of falling short of yourself. You know you were meant for more than you are: not more successful, but more truly what a human being should be. That intuition is accurate reporting, and this verse is its explanation.

Have sinned, and fall short. Have sinned is a completed fact. Fall short is present and continuous: it is describing this morning, for the Christian too. And the next clause, “are justified”, is in the same present tense: the believer who falls short today stands justified today.

As a gift. Grace is undeserved favour, and the word for gift (dōrean) means freely, for nothing, at no cost to the one who receives it. The same word turns up in a sentence our Lord applied to himself: “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). There was nothing in him to justify the hatred, and there is nothing in you to justify the gift.

Redemption. Redemption (apolytrōsis) belongs to the marketplace: the price paid to buy a slave’s freedom or release a prisoner of war. Christ paid the price to free us from sin (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18–19). It tells you what your position was: not a man with a poor record, but a man owned by somebody else. And grace was free to you, but not to the one who gave it. A gift that cost the giver nothing is a formality; a gift that cost him everything, given to someone who could not contribute a penny, is what this verse means by grace. The Lord of glory, whom we fell short of reflecting, came down to where we had fallen, and bought back his own image out of the slave market with his own blood.

Who received the price of our redemption? Some early Christian writers said it was paid to the devil, who held humanity captive. Scripture never says so. The debt was owed to God’s justice, which is why Paul goes straight on to propitiation (v. 25). The ransom picture tells us what our release cost and what it achieved; it is not meant to be pressed further.

Does all have sinned and are justified mean that everyone is saved? No. The all who are justified are the all who believe (v. 22); the sentence runs straight on from for all who believe, for there is no distinction. Every human being has sinned. Every believer, without exception, is justified. The gift is offered to all without distinction of race or record, and received only by faith. Paul will say the same in chapter 5: those who receive the abundance of grace reign in life (5:17). The good news is not that everyone is already forgiven, but that anyone, however far gone, who comes to Christ is.

In everyday life. Say this verse in the first person: I have sinned, and I fall short of the glory of God; and I am justified freely by his grace. Notice which half is harder to say without qualifying it. If it is the second, the reason is instructive: a diagnosis that puts us with everybody else is easier to accept than a gift that puts us in debt to somebody. Say both today, and add nothing to the second.
verseByVerse.note: “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
God put forward. God put Christ forward, and the initiative is entirely divine. It is not a reluctant God being persuaded by a loving Son; it is the loving God providing the means to satisfy his own justice. The love of God and the justice of God meet at the cross, not in opposition but in unity. God shows his love by giving his Son (5:8), and his justice by punishing sin in his Son.

Propitiation. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The word (hilastērion) is used in the Greek Old Testament for the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15; Hebrews 9:5). Christ is the true mercy seat, where God’s wrath against sin is satisfied and his mercy given. This letter has prepared for the word: wrath is real and being revealed (1:18; 2:5), and at the cross it was absorbed rather than deflected. God did not simply decide to stop being angry with sin; his anger fell, in full, on Christ, so that nothing of it is left to fall on those who trust him (5:9; 8:1).

Carried outside and shown to the crowd. In Israel the mercy seat stood in the innermost room, where once a year, in the dark, the high priest sprinkled blood over the covering of a box that held the law they had broken. Paul says God put Christ forward (the verb can also mean purposed, but most take it as set out in public): in the open, in daylight, on a hill outside a city wall, where anybody could see. The holiest thing in Israel had been hidden behind a curtain for centuries. At the cross it was carried outside and shown to the crowd.

Where Christians differ: propitiation or expiation? Some translate hilastērion as expiation, the removing of sin, and deny that God’s wrath needed to be satisfied; others prefer simply mercy seat. The mercy seat picture is real, since the same word is used in Hebrews 9:5. This commentary’s view: the context is God’s wrath (1:18; 2:5) and his justice (vv. 25–26), and in 5:9 Paul says that since we are justified by Christ’s blood, we shall be saved by him from the wrath of God. Christ’s death removes sin, yes, but by bearing the wrath it deserved. This is penal substitution: Christ suffered the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). It is the centre of the gospel. Christians who stress the cross as victory over evil or as the supreme example of love are right that it is all of that; this commentary holds that it is never less than this.

Passed over former sins. Why did the cross have to happen at all? Paul’s answer is not, first, that we needed rescuing, true as that is, but that God had a problem with his own record. For centuries he had been forgiving people. Abraham lied twice about his wife and remained the friend of God. David committed adultery and murder and was told that the LORD had put away his sin (2 Samuel 12:13). The whole sacrificial system ran on the blood of animals, which, as Hebrews says flatly, can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). On what grounds had all this been let through? The word here is not the ordinary word for forgiveness. It means to let go by, to leave unpunished for the present, and it puts God in the position of a judge who had been suspending sentences for two thousand years without explaining himself.

To show his righteousness. The cross is a demonstration, evidence produced in court: God was clearing his own name. The saints of the Old Testament were forgiven on credit, and at the cross the account was settled.

Just and the justifier. The heart of the gospel. A judge who acquits the guilty is not merciful; he is corrupt, and every legal system on earth knows it. Proverbs says so without qualification: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15). God’s own law forbade the very thing his gospel appears to do. The question of Romans is not how a loving God can forgive. It is how a just God can, and remain just. The answer: he punished sin in his Son. Nothing was waived. The sentence was carried out in full, on somebody else, by arrangement, with the Judge providing the substitute out of his own household.

Is it not unjust to punish an innocent person instead of the guilty? The charge would stick if God took an unwilling third party and punished him for others. That is not what happened. The one who bore the penalty is God himself in the person of the Son, who came willingly: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The Judge did not lay the cost on a stranger; he bore it in himself. And the substitute is not a stranger to us either: he took our nature and stands as the head of his people, so that what he did, he did as us and for us (5:12–19). The Father did not love us less than the Son did, nor the Son love justice less than the Father. Father, Son and Spirit together planned it, accomplished it and apply it.

In everyday life. Ask yourself why God accepts you, and listen for whether the answer leans on God’s kindness, his willingness to overlook, his understanding of your circumstances. If it does, your assurance rests on his character as you imagine it, and it will not hold on the worst night, because a God who overlooks things could presumably also change his mind about overlooking them. The answer this passage gives is harder and infinitely steadier: he accepts you because the debt was paid, and it would be unjust of him to collect it twice. Justice, the thing you feared, has become the ground you stand on.

Righteousness and peace kiss. “Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other” (Psalm 85:10). The psalmist sang it as a hope, and Calvary made it history. God did not balance love and justice in some compromise; he satisfied both, at his own expense, so that he might be at the same moment the Judge who does not bend and the Father who runs to the guilty.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the “mercy seat,” the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

parallels.desc: blood on the mercy seat

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. Boasting is claiming credit before God, and the word Paul uses is stronger than “excluded” suggests in modern English. It is the word for shutting a door: barred out, locked outside. Boasting is not discouraged, or moderated, or permitted in small quantities among mature believers. It has been put out of the building and the door has been closed behind it. If salvation is God’s gift, received by faith, no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 1:29–31). The proud Jew of 2:17, boasting in the law, and the proud moralist: all silenced.

By what kind of law? “By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith.” Law here means principle. A system of works would allow boasting; the principle of faith excludes it. Look at what has done the excluding, because it is not what we would expect. Paul does not say boasting is excluded by humility, or by a rule against it, or by a proper sense of proportion. It is excluded by the way salvation itself works. That matters in practice, because a man told to stop boasting will simply learn to boast more quietly, and self-congratulation driven underground becomes harder to detect and no less pleasant to indulge. What Paul describes is not a prohibition but a demolition: there is nothing left to boast about. You cannot be proud of a gift you did not choose, earn, deserve or contribute to. The impulse is not forbidden. It is unemployed.

Why has God arranged salvation this way? Why by faith and not by effort, when effort would at least keep people trying? Part of the answer is here. If any element of your standing rested on you, then somewhere in the last analysis you would have grounds for comparison, and comparison is the seedbed of everything Paul has denounced since chapter 2. God has closed off boasting not because he cannot bear rivals, but because boasting is a poison, and the only cure for it is a salvation in which no one has anything to show. And the deepest reason is his glory: he saves in such a way that the whole praise goes to the one who did the saving (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Justified by faith apart from works. The thesis of the Reformation. The verb translated “we hold” (logizometha) means we reckon, we count it settled, like a finding entered in the record. Nor does it clash with the judgment according to works in 2:6–8: the works weighed on that day are the fruit and evidence of the faith by which a person has already been justified, never the ground of the verdict.

Luther’s word. Luther translated the verse into German as “by faith alone” (allein), and was attacked for the rest of his life for adding a word. The word is not in the Greek, but it is exactly what the sentence means: if works are excluded, faith is the only thing left standing.

The tax collector went home justified. Paul did not invent this doctrine. Jesus told of two men who went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood and listed his record: not like other men, fasting twice a week, tithing everything. The tax collector would not lift his eyes, but beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” And Jesus gave the verdict: “this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other” (Luke 18:9–14). That is verses 27 and 28 told as a story. The Greek verb in his plea, “be merciful”, comes from the same word family as “propitiation” in verse 25, and the mercy he asked for is the mercy God put forward at the cross.

Where Christians differ: faith alone? The Council of Trent (1547), the Roman Catholic council that answered the Reformation, condemned the teaching that we are justified by faith alone. This commentary’s view: apart from works of the law leaves faith alone as the instrument. Not faith plus baptism, faith plus penance, or faith plus good works. Good works are the necessary fruit of justifying faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2), but they are not part of its ground. This is sola fide, the article on which the church stands or falls.

But does James not say the opposite? No: the apostles answer different questions. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is put right with God; James asks what kind of faith is real, and shows that a faith without works is dead. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. (See Romans 4:3–4 for the fuller answer.)

What about baptism? Is it not needed to be saved? Baptism matters greatly: Christ commanded it, and it is the sign of a believer’s union with him in his death and resurrection (6:3–4). This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that it is for those who profess faith, because in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12), and many paedobaptist brothers, with the Westminster Confession, baptise the children of believers too. But both agree on this verse: baptism is not the instrument of justification, and grace and salvation are not so tied to it that no one can be saved without it (Westminster 28.5). The thief on the cross was promised paradise unbaptised. Be baptised because Christ commands it, not in order to be justified.

What it does not mean. This is the point at which people become anxious about their faith instead of their works, which is the same disease at a new address. If you find yourself asking whether your faith is strong enough, sincere enough or free enough of doubt to count, you have begun to treat faith as a work: something you produce, of a certain quality, which God then rewards. It is not. A weak hand and a strong hand take hold of the same rope, and the rope does the holding. What saves is not the excellence of your grip but the strength of what you are gripping.

In everyday life. Listen to what you find yourself mentioning when you want somebody to think well of you spiritually: how long you have been a Christian, what you have read, what you gave up, how much you serve, the hardship you have borne well. Whatever the currency in your congregation, it is a boast, and this verse says the door it is trying to come in by has been locked. When you catch yourself, turn the sentence round and say something true about Christ instead.

The locked door. It is a kindness. Keeping score makes you anxious when you are losing and insufferable when you are winning, and Paul has removed the scoreboard. There is only one thing left to say: “far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). You have nothing to boast of before God except Christ, and in him you have everything, so that the mouth stopped in verse 19 is opened at last, not to plead its record, but to praise its Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? If salvation were by the law, only Jews could have it. The question is put as a question rather than an assertion, and that is deliberate. Nobody in the synagogue would have said aloud that God was the God of Jews only; the Scriptures they read every week said the opposite in a hundred places, from the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed to Isaiah’s house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7). Paul is not correcting their doctrine. He is showing them that their practice had quietly contradicted a creed they could recite in their sleep, which is a considerably more uncomfortable thing to be shown.

Since God is one. The phrase echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Feel the audacity of what Paul does with it. Devout Jews said those words morning and evening, and their obvious force had been separation: the nations have many gods, we have the one true God, and that is what makes us different. Paul takes the same words and turns them outward. If there is only one God, then he is not our God as opposed to theirs. He is theirs too, whether they know it or not, and a God who belongs to everybody cannot have arranged a way of salvation that only one group is able to use.

One God, one Lord, one new man. In another letter Paul sets Christ inside the very confession he echoes here: for us there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). The one God who justifies Jew and Gentile alike does it through that one Lord, and in his flesh Christ broke down the dividing wall between them, to create in himself one new man in place of the two and reconcile both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). The Shema had been the creed that set Israel apart. In Christ it becomes the creed that gathers the nations in. One day a multitude no one can number, from every nation, tribe, people and language, will stand before the throne crying out that salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10), and the Shema will be sung in every tongue.

By faith and through faith. Paul uses two different prepositions, most likely simply for variety. Both groups are justified by the same faith: two doors, the same width, and neither of them is a back entrance.

The fight that nearly tore the church apart. In Paul’s day this was far from settled. Whether Gentiles had to become Jews first, by taking on circumcision, the food laws and the calendar, before they could be Christians filled a council at Jerusalem (Acts 15), produced the letter to the Galatians, and put Paul in open conflict with Peter at a common table in Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). The question was on what terms Gentiles could be saved, and Paul saw, with a clarity that cost him dearly, that a gospel with a cultural entrance fee is not the gospel at all.

The modern form. It is rarely doctrinal, which makes it hard to see. No congregation holds that outsiders must first become like us. It simply turns out, over time, that the people who thrive there are the ones who already share the accent, the education, the politics, the family shape, the taste in music, the ease with a particular vocabulary. Nobody voted for this, and the tell is not what a church believes about who may come. It is who is comfortable once they have. Of the last person who came for a few weeks and did not return, did anyone find out why?

Does one God for all mean every religion leads to him? It means the opposite. Paul’s argument is that because God is one, there is one way to him for everyone, and that way is faith in Jesus Christ (v. 22). There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Jesus said no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14:6), and the apostles said there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12). Other religions are not different roads up the same mountain; they are human attempts, sometimes earnest, to reach a God who has come down to us by one road. That is not narrowness. It is the widest door in the world: open to every nation, every culture and every record, through the one Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? The obvious objection: if salvation is by faith, is the law pointless? This is not a stray thought at the end of a paragraph. It is Paul answering, at last, the slander he reported at 3:8, that he taught people to do evil so that good might come, a charge he there refused even to argue with. Now that the doctrine has been fully stated, he turns and faces it.

We uphold the law. The verb is a word for making something stand, setting it firmly on its feet. The claim is not that the law survives the gospel, but that it was never standing properly until now.

How the law is lowered. A man trying to be justified by the law must, if he is to have any peace, lower it. He cannot live with a standard that says “You shall not covet” and means it, so he quietly translates the commandments into things that can be achieved: no adultery becomes no affair, no murder becomes no violence, honour your father becomes a phone call at Christmas. He has kept the law in the sense that he has redefined it down to his own size. That is not upholding it. It is the most thorough disrespect the law ever suffers, and it is always done by its admirers.

How faith establishes it. The gospel does the reverse. It lets every commandment stand at full height: “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good”, Paul will say (7:12). Christ fulfilled the law’s demands and bore its penalty (8:3–4): nothing is discounted, and the sinner is justified without a single letter of the standard being adjusted in his favour. And those justified by faith are given the Spirit, who enables them to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement (8:4; 13:8–10). Only the man who has stopped needing the law to be manageable is free to see how magnificent it is.

The law itself testified. Faith also upholds the law in a second sense: the law itself, the books of Moses, teaches it. In chapter 4 Paul goes to Genesis and brings out Abraham, counted righteous by believing God before he was circumcised and centuries before the law was given. Justification by faith is not a novelty smuggled in past Moses. It is the oldest thing in the book.

So is a Christian still bound by the Ten Commandments? Yes, as a rule of life, though not as a way of earning life. The Reformed confessions distinguish the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in love for God and neighbour, which binds everyone always, from the ceremonial laws, fulfilled in Christ’s sacrifice, and the civil laws of Israel as a nation, which expired with that state (Westminster Confession 19.3–5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3–5). Christ does not cancel the moral law for believers; he frees us from its curse and writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Christians differ, honourably, on how the fourth commandment applies now that Christ has risen on the first day of the week, and this commentary sets out those views where the Sabbath is discussed, taking the view that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and that the Lord’s Day is a gift Christians gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not a law by which anyone may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17). But every Christian agrees that the law shows us how to love.

In everyday life. Read the Sermon on the Mount slowly this week and watch your own reaction. If your instinct is to soften it, “he cannot mean that literally”, “this is hyperbole”, “allowances must be made”, then something in you is still trying to pass, because only a candidate needs the exam to be easier. If you can let it stand at full height, agree with every word, and find that it does not frighten you, that is what this verse means by upholding the law. The man who is not being examined can afford to admire the standard.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?<sup>2</sup>Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.<sup>3</sup>What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?<sup>4</sup>By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.”<sup>5</sup>But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.)<sup>6</sup>By no means! Their condemnation is just.<sup>9</sup>What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For there is no distinction:<sup>23</sup>for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,<sup>24</sup>and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,<sup>25</sup>whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith.
