4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works, a Jewish reader would at once ask about Abraham, the father of the nation and the model of obedience. Romans 4 is Paul’s answer, from Genesis itself.

Abraham was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 comes before Genesis 17) and centuries before the law was given. So he is the model of justifying faith, and the father of Gentile believers as well as Jewish ones. The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul goes straight to Genesis 15:6, where righteousness is counted to Abraham because he believed: credited, not achieved. He adds a second witness, David in Psalm 32, who calls blessed not the man with a clean record but the man whose sins are forgiven. Then he settles the case by the calendar: Abraham was counted righteous years before he was circumcised, so circumcision was a seal of a righteousness he already had, and he is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not.

At the centre stands the phrase that God justifies the ungodly (v. 5), the very thing God’s own law forbade human judges to do. The cross has already answered the difficulty (3:25–26), and any reader who wonders whether he is too far gone should notice which people are being justified.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation

The verb logizomai (count, reckon, credit) appears eleven times in Romans 4. Imputation means that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account, and it is the hinge of justification. The righteousness is not infused into us (poured in so that we become righteous in ourselves), as Roman Catholic teaching holds, but credited to us. Luther called it an "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena): foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham was the strongest witness a Jewish opponent could call. If even he was justified by faith, the case for earning God’s favour has lost its founding father. Now: Every form of religious merit (I’m basically a good person, I go to church, I’ve never done anything really terrible) falls before Romans 4. Abraham stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise, and so must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 4 proves from the Old Testament that justification has always been by faith. Justification is a courtroom word: God the Judge declaring a person righteous, not making him good inside (Deuteronomy 25:1). Paul takes the greatest example in Jewish history, Abraham, and shows that he was counted righteous because he believed God, not because he worked, and before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile. His faith trusted the God who gives life to the dead, and ours trusts the God who raised Jesus. The chapter is the Old Testament foundation of “by faith alone”, and it ends at an empty tomb.

Why the whole chapter exists. Paul has just claimed that justification by faith upholds the law (3:31), and he calls the one witness no opponent could dismiss. If Abraham was justified by faith, the argument is over, because there is nobody further back to appeal to.

What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? This was a bolder move than it looks, because Abraham was not a neutral exhibit. Jewish teachers held him up as the great example of a righteous man, who kept the law before it was given and was tested and found faithful. If anyone was justified by works, surely Abraham was. One well-known book of the period, 1 Maccabees, quotes the very verse Paul is about to use and attaches it to the binding of Isaac: Abraham was found faithful when tested, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (1 Maccabees 2:52). On that reading, Genesis 15:6 is a verdict on Abraham’s proven obedience, which is very nearly the opposite of Paul’s point. He is not merely quoting a text. He is taking it back from an established interpretation, and his instrument will be the calendar: what Genesis 15 says, and when Genesis 15 happened.

Something to boast about. Paul does not say Abraham had nothing to show. At the human level the man had an extraordinary record. He left a settled city, a family and an inheritance on the strength of a word from a God he had not previously known. He pleaded with God for a wicked city, from fifty all the way down to ten (Genesis 18:22–33). And at the end he was willing to give up the one thing he had waited a lifetime for. Any tribunal on earth would have decorated him. Scripture three times calls him the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23).

But not before God. Paul grants the whole of it and then adds four words that take away its weight. The record is real, but it belongs to a different courtroom. Before other men Abraham towers. Before God he is a man counted righteous on the basis of having believed a promise, which is exactly the position of everybody else who has ever been counted righteous. The ground of boasting was never there (3:27), even in the strongest case anybody could produce. Paul leaves the man exactly as tall as he is, and then observes, quietly, that height was never the measurement being taken. Before the Holy One, the friend of God stands where the thief on the cross stands: with empty hands and a promise.

The one son of Abraham with a record. One descendant of Abraham could have stood before God on his record. In an argument about Abraham, Jesus asked which of them could convict him of sin, and then told them, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:46, 58). He is the only man who ever had something to boast about before God, and he did not boast. He spent his record instead, offering his obedience and his death for people whose record was empty. That is how Abraham, the greatest of the patriarchs, could be counted righteous at all: what was credited to him by faith was the righteousness of the offspring God had promised him.

Does God then not care about my good works? He cares very much, and delights in them. Scripture says he is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown for his name (Hebrews 6:10), and that labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). He even promises to reward it. But he receives your works as a Father receives the gifts of his children, not as an employer pays a wage. They are the fruit of your acceptance, made possible by his grace, never the price of it. That is why you can offer them gladly and without anxiety: they are not being weighed to decide whether you belong.

In everyday life. Write down the three things you would most want said about you at your funeral: the real ones, the achievements or qualities you quietly hope will be mentioned. Then read them again and ask what weight any of them would carry in a courtroom where the charge is that you have not loved God with all your heart and your neighbour as yourself. The list may be genuinely creditable, but everything on it is testimony in a different case. The greatest believers had nothing to boast of before God, and neither do you, which is freedom.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what does the Scripture say? Paul settles it by Scripture, not by tradition or argument. The question is not what the teachers have said about Abraham but what God has said.

Counted. From Genesis 15:6, the key verse of the chapter, quoted also in Galatians 3:6 and James 2:23. Counted (logizomai) is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account. Paul leans on it eleven times in these twenty-five verses: how does righteousness get onto a person’s account? God puts it there.

An old man under the stars. Abraham is old and childless, and God has just taken him outside at night and told him to number the stars if he can, and said: “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). There is no child and no evidence: an old man standing in the dark, looking up, with nothing in his hands and nothing in his future but a sentence somebody said to him. And the next line is: “he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Faith in the Bible is not a mood or a temperament. It is taking God at his word when the word is the only thing you have.

Wages. Either a sum is earned, in which case entering it is not generosity but bookkeeping, or it is credited from outside, and the recipient contributed nothing but an account number. Righteousness is credited as a gift. And if you ever find yourself feeling that God owes you something, after a hard season of faithfulness or a sacrifice nobody noticed, you have quietly moved yourself into the wages column, and the wages column has no grace in it anywhere.

What was not counted. Not Abraham’s obedience or his character. What was counted was that he believed God, which is why faith can never be reclassified as a small work that earns the rest. The hand that takes a parcel has not contributed to its contents. Faith justifies not because it is a fine quality but because of what it lays hold of.

Credited, not infused. God does not merely decline to count Abraham’s sins (vv. 6–8). Something positive is put on the account: righteousness, a standing the man did not have. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation. The righteousness is not infused into you like a medicine that gradually improves your condition; it is credited to you like a sum entered in a book. If it were infused, your standing would rise and fall with your progress. Because it is credited, it is complete on the day it is entered. A Christian ten minutes old and a Christian of fifty years stand in exactly the same righteousness, and neither has more of it than the other.

But does James not say the opposite? James 2:21–24 says that Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Readers rightly ask how Paul and James fit together. Three things resolve it. First, they are speaking of different moments in Abraham’s life: Paul quotes Genesis 15, when Abraham first believed and was counted righteous; James points to Genesis 22, perhaps thirty years later, when Abraham’s faith was tested and proved real. Second, they are answering different errors: Paul opposes those who think they can earn acceptance with God by works; James opposes those who think a faith that produces no works can save. Third, they use justified in different senses: Paul means declared righteous before God; James means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine before others (James 2:18, show me your faith). James himself quotes Genesis 15:6 and says Abraham’s works fulfilled it (James 2:23): his obedience showed what his faith had always been. So the two agree: the faith that rests on Christ alone is the same faith that goes on working through love (Galatians 5:6).

Was Abraham saved by believing in Christ, or only in a promise about children? By believing the promise, and the promise was Christ. God promised offspring, and Paul says the offspring in view was ultimately one person: and to your offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Jesus himself said that Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day (John 8:56). Abraham did not know the name Jesus or the details of the cross, but he trusted the God who promised to bless the world through his seed, and that seed came. Old Testament believers were saved exactly as we are, by grace through faith in God’s promised Redeemer; they looked forward to him, and we look back.

For worship. That night Abraham had a righteousness credited to him that he had done nothing whatever to produce. God did not enter the sum because the account looked promising; the account was empty. The same God has written the same entry against the name of every believer, and what he enters there is the spotless righteousness of his own Son, the very offspring promised under those stars. He determines the number of the stars and gives to all of them their names (Psalm 147:4), and he has never yet lost count of a single sinner he has counted righteous.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And to the one who does not work. Not that believers do no good works, but that they do not work in order to be justified. The qualification for being justified is having nothing to offer. That is why this is one of the hardest verses for respectable people. If you have been decent all your life, attended faithfully, given generously and raised your children well, you must still come to God on precisely the same terms as the man who has wrecked everything he ever touched: as one of the ungodly, working nothing, holding nothing out. Most people would rather be forgiven a great deal than be told their good record buys nothing.

Him who justifies the ungodly. The texts behind it are God’s own instructions to his own judges. “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15). “I will not acquit the wicked” (Exodus 23:7). Paul takes the phrase straight out of Israel’s working standard of justice and makes it a description of God: he is the one who justifies the ungodly. It is as if a man defined the Almighty by the one thing his own law calls an abomination. Set those words side by side and they ought not to be able to stand together: a holy God pronouncing right the people who are demonstrably wrong, and doing it without telling a lie. They stand because a cross is holding them up.

The ungodly. Paul does not soften the word. He does not say God justifies the weak, or the struggling, or the sincere but inconsistent. The word (asebēs) shares its root with the ungodliness of 1:18, the thing against which the wrath of God is revealed. The very people charged in 1:18 are the ones being acquitted: good news for the worst sinner.

How God can do it. God does it justly, because Christ bore their punishment (3:25–26). The guilt was not overlooked; it was transferred and dealt with. Justification is not God deciding that the ungodly are not so bad after all. It is God pronouncing a verdict that has already been paid for. The gospel is not the announcement that God is lenient: a judge who can be talked round can be talked round by your accuser as well. This is what Calvin and the Reformers loved to call the wonderful exchange: Christ takes our ungodliness, and we receive his righteousness.

Two readers. This verse is written for two opposite readers. If you are the one who has been quietly afraid that you are too far gone, that there is a thing in your past which puts you outside the ordinary offer, that God might save people like you in general but not you in particular, read the category again. He justifies the ungodly. Not the improved ungodly. If God only justified good people, your fear would be rational. And if you are the other reader, for whom none of this feels urgent because you have never done anything that would frighten a congregation, the word ungodly is yours too, and the letter spent three chapters establishing it. There is one door, and it is marked with a description you would not have chosen for yourself.

If I still feel ungodly after years as a Christian, was I ever justified? Feeling ungodly is not evidence against your justification; it is the condition God justifies. The verdict was never based on how godly you felt, and it does not move when your feelings do. What you are experiencing is the ongoing war of a justified sinner against remaining sin, which Paul himself describes with anguish (7:15–25). God declares you righteous in an instant, and then spends the rest of your life making you holy, slowly and truly. If you hate your sin and keep running to Christ with it, that is exactly what a justified person looks like from the inside. Keep looking at him, not at the feeling.

Is it fair that the decent and the wicked come in on the same terms? It would be unfair if God were marking on a curve, but he is not. Measured against a holy God, the decent man and the wicked man are both bankrupt, one owing more than the other, and neither able to pay (3:23). The real objection usually comes from the heart of the older brother in Jesus’ parable, who was angry that the father threw a feast for the son who had wasted everything (Luke 15:28–30). His complaint showed that he too had been serving for wages, not loving his father. Grace offends us only while we think we are owed something. Once you see that you are the ungodly too, the same terms are the best news you have ever heard.

parallels.desc: I will not acquit the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David also speaks. A second witness, from the Psalms, as the law required: “Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Paul has produced Abraham, the founder of the nation, from the age before the law. Now he produces David, the greatest of its kings, from the age under the law. Two men on opposite sides of Sinai, both counted righteous by God, not righteous by their own record.

Done nothing, and done something. There is a second reason David is the right witness. Abraham shows you that a man can be counted righteous without having earned it. David shows you that a man can be counted righteous after having forfeited it. Abraham answers the question, can God count a man righteous who has done nothing to earn it? David answers the harder one: can God count a man righteous who has done great evil?

Lawless deeds forgiven. From Psalm 32:1, traditionally read as written after David’s adultery and murder. Every instinct in a religious person says the blessed man is the man with a clean record. David says the blessed man is the one whose lawless deeds are forgiven, which means the blessed man is by definition a man with lawless deeds. His blessing lies precisely at the point of his worst failure, because that is where the forgiveness is. This psalm pronounces no blessing on anything David got right.

Covered. The two verbs answer two different fears. Forgiven is a word for lifting and carrying away: the load taken off a man’s back and removed. Covered means hidden from God’s judgment (Psalm 85:2). One word deals with the weight and the other with the exposure. If your trouble is that you cannot carry it, the first word is for you. If your trouble is that you cannot bear to have it seen, the second is. Paul has just named Christ as the true mercy seat (3:25), and what covers David’s sin, and yours, is his blood.

What it does not mean. Covered does not mean that God has agreed to look the other way, or that the file has been mislaid, or that enough time has passed. That kind of covering would be a fiction, and the psalm rules it out: David spends its opening verses describing what it was like before the covering: while he kept silent his bones wasted away, day and night God’s hand was heavy on him, his strength dried up as by the heat of summer (Psalm 32:3–4). The relief in this psalm is not the relief of a man who has decided to stop thinking about it. It is the relief of a man who said it out loud and discovered it had been dealt with.

Do I have to confess every single sin to be forgiven, even the ones I forget? Your justification does not hang on the completeness of your list. When you came to Christ, all your sins were forgiven and covered, including the ones you have forgotten and the ones you never noticed (Psalm 19:12). Confession is not a fresh payment each time; it is the honesty of a child with his Father, which keeps the relationship open and warm. God promises that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). So confess what you know, specifically and without excuses, and ask him to cleanse you from what you do not know. Then rest. The blood covers more than your memory does.

In everyday life. Take the thing in your life you would least want read aloud, and ask which you actually have: is it unmentioned, or is it covered? Unmentioned means nobody knows and you are managing it, and the arrangement holds as long as nothing surfaces. Covered means it has been brought out, named to God without qualification, and dealt with at the cost of blood, and a covered sin is safe precisely because it has already been fully seen. The difference between the two is the difference between Psalm 32:3–4 and Psalm 32:1–2. If it is only unmentioned, say it to God today.

parallels.desc: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will not count. Psalm 32:2, and the other side of God’s counting. The construction (ou mē logisētai) is the double negative Greek reserves for absolute denial: will never, under any circumstances. It is the same form our Lord used when he said that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and that his sheep will never perish (John 10:28). This is not a statement about God’s present mood. It is a door welded shut.

Not counted, and counted. God credits righteousness to the believer (v. 6) and does not credit his sin to him. Sin not counted against us, because it was counted against Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19–21). Righteousness counted to us, because Christ’s righteousness is ours. A man whose debts are cancelled has nothing; a man whose debts are cancelled and whose account is then filled from someone else’s fortune is rich. Justification is not being returned to zero. It is being given a standing you did not have even before you sinned.

What about the sins I have not committed yet? It is the question any honest Christian eventually asks, usually at night. A man converted at thirty has fifty years of failure in front of him, and it is natural to assume the past was dealt with at the cross and the future is on some kind of running account. But look at the tense of the promise. It does not say the Lord has not counted his sin. It says he will not count it: the verb faces forward. When Christ died, every sin you would ever commit was still future. The ones you committed last week were no more unknown to him then than the ones you committed as a child.

Then why do I still pray, forgive us our debts? Because you are now a child, not a defendant. Justification settles once for all that you will never be condemned. But a justified believer can still grieve his Father and fall under his fatherly displeasure, and needs to come back humbly, confess and ask for the joy of fellowship to be restored (Westminster Confession 11.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.5). David prayed restore to me the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12), not restore my salvation. So you pray the Lord’s Prayer not to be readmitted to the family, but because you are in it, and children who love their Father do not let wrongs sit unspoken between them.

What it does not mean. A verdict this absolute can be turned into permission, and Paul gives chapter 6 to the objection. He does not answer it by weakening the promise. He answers it by pointing to what has happened to the believer, who has died to sin with Christ (6:2). You do not respond to that kind of mercy by testing its limits, any more than a man pardoned at the scaffold spends the afternoon looking for another capital offence.

In everyday life. When you have failed badly and confessed it, do you then keep your distance for a few days, praying less, reading less, not quite able to sing on Sunday, until you feel you have re-established something? That interval is the tell. It is the behaviour of a man who believes his sins are not counted but suspects his standing must be earned back, and verses 6 and 8 together are the cure. There is nothing to re-establish. The righteousness on your account was never your own doing in the first place. If you are in Christ, God will never count your sin against you, today included, with no waiting period.

For worship. David wrote this from the bottom of his life, confronted by a prophet and with nothing to say, and that man wrote “blessed”, the same word the Psalter uses of the righteous man in Psalm 1. The sin David could never pay for was counted, in full, to his Son and Lord, and the Lord who counted it there will never count it anywhere else.

parallels.desc: blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? The key question for Jew and Gentile. Paul has just quoted David’s blessing, and blessings are the sort of thing people quietly assume belong to their own kind. The question is whether the forgiveness of Psalm 32 belongs to the household only, available to insiders through the proper channels. And the answer is settled not by an appeal to God’s generosity but by a date.

How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? A brilliant argument from the order of events, and the calendar argument promised at the start of the chapter. It is quietly devastating. Paul does not dispute a single word of the text his opponents value. He does not argue that circumcision was unimportant, or that Genesis has been misread, or that the covenant was provisional. He simply asks when. The whole case turns on the order of two chapters, and once the question is put there is no answer available, because Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17, and no amount of theology can move it.

Before, not after. Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, at least fourteen years later. Between them lie the birth of Ishmael and thirteen more years: the boy is thirteen when the command comes (Genesis 16:16; 17:24–25). For a decade and a half the man the whole nation traced itself to was justified before God and outwardly indistinguishable from any pagan in Canaan. So circumcision was not necessary for justification, and Gentiles can be justified without it.

Justified as a Gentile. Abraham was justified while he was, in every visible respect, a Gentile: a man from Mesopotamia, from a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2), with no law, no temple, no priesthood, no sign and no religious community whatever. The God of Abraham has never been the God of the insiders only. He went looking for a pagan in Ur, made him his friend under the open sky, and then built a nation around him so that, in the fullness of time, the door of that nation could be thrown open to the whole world through Abraham’s Son.

The gospel preached beforehand. The timing was the gospel announced in advance: the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed” (Galatians 3:8). The uncircumcised man under the stars was a preview of the nations coming in. And the blessing reaches them exactly as it reached him, through his offspring: in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith (Galatians 3:14).

The arrangement. The instinct Paul is dismantling is not only Jewish but human. It is the assumption that the blessing comes through belonging to the right arrangement: that the promises of Scripture are addressed, in practice, to people who are properly inside things, baptised, confirmed, on the roll, in the right church, taught by the right people. It is rarely stated. It shows up in the quiet confidence of those who have the arrangement, and in the hesitancy of those who do not.

What it does not mean. The sign is not thereby made worthless, as the next verse says; the argument is about which came first, not about value. What Paul has established is that the sign could not have produced what its owner already had, and that a man who has the sign and nothing else has the receipt without the purchase.

Does it matter which church I belong to, then? Yes, but not for this. Belonging to a faithful church matters a great deal: for sound teaching, for the Lord’s Supper and baptism rightly given, for care, discipline and love (Hebrews 10:24–25). Christ loves his church and you should too. But no church membership, however orthodox, justifies anyone, and no believer is shut out of God’s promises because he came to faith in an unremarkable congregation, or late, or alone. The church is the family the justified belong to, not the door by which they become justified. That door is Christ, received by faith.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, some years later.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sign and a seal. A sign points to something; a seal confirms it. A seal pressed into wax did not create the agreement; it authenticated one already made, and identified whose the thing was. Circumcision did not make Abraham righteous; it confirmed the righteousness he already had by faith. A seal on an empty page certifies nothing.

And our sign? Christians do not circumcise, so the obvious question is what our equivalent is, and whether this passage devalues it. It does not. Baptism stands in a similar relation to faith: commanded by God, genuinely meaningful, and never the thing itself. Paul’s argument cuts equally against a man who trusts his circumcision and a man who trusts his baptism, and it guards against the opposite error too. The sign is not nothing; it is given on Christ’s own authority and declares what he has done. What it cannot do is manufacture what it declares.

Where Christians differ: circumcision, baptism and infants. Paedobaptists argue that baptism replaces circumcision as the sign and seal of the covenant (Colossians 2:11–12), and since circumcision was given to infants, baptism should be too; they also point to the households baptised in Acts (16:15, 33). Those are serious arguments, held by many godly Christians. This commentary’s view: Paul says circumcision sealed the righteousness Abraham had by faith; it followed faith in Abraham’s case. Circumcision was given to every male of Abraham’s household and line, Ishmael as well as Isaac, believing or not. In the new covenant, all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and the sign is given to those who believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12), as Colossians itself says: buried with him in baptism, raised with him through faith (Colossians 2:12). Credobaptists hold that baptism belongs to believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters as fellow heirs of Abraham.

I was baptised as a baby, so should I be baptised now? If you hold, as this commentary does with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who profess faith, then being baptised now is not a second baptism but obedience to Christ’s command for the first time as a believer. Many Christians come to that conviction and take the step gladly. Others, persuaded of the paedobaptist view, believe their infant baptism was valid and that what they need is to own it by faith, which they do. Whatever you conclude, do it from Scripture and a clear conscience, after talking with your pastor, and never treat brothers and sisters who differ as anything less than fellow children of Abraham. The faith the sign points to matters more than either view of the sign.

The father of all who believe. Abraham is the father of Gentile believers by faith, not by blood (Galatians 3:7). Now Paul shows what the chronology was for. Because Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, he is not merely an example Gentiles may study from a distance; he is their father. The relationship is not a comparison. A believing Gentile is not like one of Abraham’s children. He is one.

A lineage. If you came to Christ out of a family with no faith in it, or a hostile one, or simply an indifferent one, if you are the first Christian anybody in your line can remember, this verse hands you a lineage. You are not a recent addition tolerated at the edge of somebody else’s story. Your family history runs back four thousand years to a man standing under the stars in Canaan, and Paul argues it not as sentiment but as fact.

The footsteps of the faith. He is father of believing Jews too, and Paul’s qualifier, “not merely circumcised”, does real work: possessing the sign does not by itself put a man in the family. And the picture is walking in footsteps, which is what a child does behind his father in a field, placing his feet where the bigger prints already are. Sonship is shown by direction of travel, not by paperwork.

Children through the one Offspring. God’s promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring, and Paul insists the word is singular: it means Christ (Galatians 3:16). So no one becomes Abraham’s child by being added to a family tree, but by being joined to the one Son in whom the whole family is gathered: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). The footsteps of faith all lead to him, and every believing Jew and Gentile who walks in them is walking toward the one Abraham was waiting for.

My faith feels far too small to walk in his footsteps. Paul is describing a pattern, not a standard of performance. He will shortly admit that Abraham considered his own body as good as dead, and Genesis records his lapses with complete honesty. The footsteps are not evidence of a great faith; they are evidence of a faith pointed at the same object. A child does not have to fill his father’s footprint. He only has to be going the same way.

In everyday life. Ask which of Abraham’s footprints your own feet are stepping in. He left security on the strength of a promise, waited twenty-five years, and believed what was physically impossible. Take one of those and ask where in your life there is anything like it: any point at which you are actually depending on something God has said, in a way that would look foolish if he turned out not to exist. If nothing comes to mind, bring that to the God who gave Abraham the faith that walked; he gives it still.

A family like the stars. The believing Gentile and the believing Jew turn out to be brothers, made so by the faith that came before the sign. And the God who once pressed a seal into Abraham’s flesh now seals his children with a seal no knife could make, the promised Holy Spirit, the guarantee of their inheritance (Ephesians 1:13–14), bought for them by the blood of Abraham’s Son. God promised Abraham a family like the stars, and he has been keeping that promise ever since, one name at a time, in every language under heaven.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine.

parallels.desc: the sign of the covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise that Abraham and his offspring would inherit the world never depended on the law, which brings wrath, but on faith, so that it rests on grace and is guaranteed to all who share Abraham’s faith, Jew and Gentile. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead, and faced his own body, as good as dead, without letting go of the promise. Paul ends by applying it to us: the same righteousness is counted to everyone who trusts the God who raised Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification to the resurrection. Christ was raised for our justification: his resurrection is not only proof of who he is but the Father’s public declaration that his atoning work was accepted. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that sin, death and wrath have been answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul reads the promise to Abraham in its full scope (v. 13): a redeemed humanity in a renewed creation, fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. Now: Abraham’s hope against hope (v. 18) is the model for faith wherever circumstances say it is impossible. The God who gave life to Abraham’s and Sarah’s bodies raises the dead still: spiritually in every conversion, and bodily at the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heir of the world. Genesis never uses that phrase. God promised Abraham a land (Genesis 12:7; 15:18), an innumerable offspring, and that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Paul reads the promise in its full scope: a blessing for all the families of the earth was never going to be exhausted by a strip of land. The land was a down payment on the new creation, and the heir is Abraham’s offspring, Christ, to whom God gives the nations as his heritage and the ends of the earth as his possession (Psalm 2:8).

Not through the law. The law came 430 years later (Galatians 3:17). The promise was made, ratified and believed long before Sinai, so it cannot have depended on the law.

Null and void. If inheritance depended on law-keeping, no one would inherit, since no one keeps it, and the promise would be empty. Null means emptied; void means put permanently out of use. Faith and promise would not be weakened but cancelled outright. If the estate goes to those who perform, then performance is what secures it, and faith is left as a mere feeling alongside, an ornament that holds nothing up.

A promise, not a contract. A contract binds two parties and is only as secure as the weaker signatory. A promise binds one party and names another as the recipient, whose conduct is not what keeps it in force.

The God who walked alone. Abraham had been shown that in the very chapter Paul keeps quoting. When he asked how he could know he would inherit, God told him to bring animals, cut them in half, and lay the pieces opposite each other (Genesis 15:9–10). In a covenant ceremony the parties walked between the severed halves, calling the same fate down on themselves if they broke the agreement (compare Jeremiah 34:18). Then a deep sleep fell on him, and when the sun had gone down a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch, the presence of God, passed between the pieces alone (Genesis 15:12, 17). Abraham was asleep for the ratification. God bound himself, took the entire liability, and left the other party lying on the ground.

Heir. Nobody earns an inheritance; an heir need only be named. And an inheritance takes effect by a death (Hebrews 9:16–17). The promise made over the divided animals in Genesis 15 was finally carried out when the God who had walked between them alone came in his Son and bore, in his own body, the death that ceremony threatened.

Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people? Christians answer this differently, and the question deserves care. Dispensational Christians (who see Israel and the church as distinct peoples in God’s plan) hold that it does: God promised Canaan to Abraham’s descendants as an everlasting possession (Genesis 17:8), and a promise of God cannot be cancelled. Many others, including this commentary, read it as not cancelled but enlarged. Paul says Abraham would be heir of the world; Hebrews says he was looking forward to the city that has foundations (Hebrews 11:10); Jesus says the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). On this reading Canaan was the down payment, and the renewed creation is the inheritance, belonging to all who are Christ’s, Jew and Gentile: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). What God will yet do for ethnic Israel Paul takes up in chapter 11.

In everyday life. Try to describe what you are actually going to inherit. If it comes out vague and largely elsewhere, a good place after death, notice that Paul says heir of the world, and he means it: this creation, healed; a body that works; work worth doing; the earth under a good King. If your hope is only an escape from this world, it is smaller than the promise, which ends with the dwelling place of God with man, on a new earth (Revelation 21:1–3). So treat the world now as an estate you will inherit, not a waiting room you will leave.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the law brings wrath. The law is good (7:12), but given to sinners it cannot give life; it exposes and condemns. It turns sin into transgression, and transgression brings God’s judgment (orgē, wrath). To people whose hope rested on possessing it, Paul says it does not bring the inheritance; it brings the charge sheet. Giving the law to sinners is like installing a speed camera on a road everyone was already speeding down. Nothing has been made worse. Everything has been made explicit, and the fines have started arriving.

No transgression. Transgression (parabasis) means stepping over a line. People without the law still sin and perish (2:12; 5:13–14), but transgression is a particular kind of sin: the deliberate breaking of a known, stated command. You can be lost without a map, but you cannot be a trespasser until somebody has put up a fence. When God gave the law, sin became wilful rebellion against his spoken word (5:20; 7:13). If the promise depended on the law, it would bring wrath, not blessing. That is why it must rest on faith and grace instead.

Rest on grace. Grace means God’s kindness given to people who have deserved the opposite, a gift with no wage in it anywhere (11:6), and faith receives what grace gives. Paul gives God’s purpose: he wanted a promise that was guaranteed, and so it had to depend on faith and rest on grace, because there is no other way to build a promise that cannot fail. Grace is the only option that produces certainty, since any arrangement involving human performance is only as reliable as the human, and we have three chapters of evidence about that.

Guaranteed. The word (bebaian) belonged to business and law: a title that would hold up, a deed that stands when challenged. Paul is not offering a warm hope but a valid title, and the difference is the difference between wanting something to be true and being able to produce the paperwork. Every human guarantee is only as good as the one who gives it, and every human guarantor dies. This one was given by the God who cannot lie, ratified in the blood of his Son, sealed by his Spirit, and stands as firm on your worst day as on your best.

Wrath borne, promise guaranteed. If the law brings wrath, a guaranteed promise needs someone to stand between the wrath and the heirs. Paul has already named him: God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (3:25), the sacrifice that turns wrath away. The law’s wrath was not cancelled; it was spent, on the Son. And so the guarantee has a face. Hebrews calls Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22), a priest who holds his office permanently because he continues for ever (Hebrews 7:24). The title to the inheritance is as secure as his life, and his life can never end.

Father of us all. Jew and Gentile believers alike, not one nation with an annexe for outsiders. The argument about law and promise lands on a family, which is what a promise, unlike a contract, is finally able to produce. God did not build salvation on the sand of our performance but on the rock of his own grace, so that every child of Abraham, from the weakest to the strongest, might stand on exactly the same ground.

Can I really be sure I am saved? Yes, and this verse is one of the reasons. Assurance does not come from looking at how well you are doing, but from three things God gives together: his promises, which cannot fail because they rest on grace; the fruit of his grace in you, however small, such as love for Christ and hatred of sin; and the witness of his Spirit with your spirit that you are a child of God (8:16; Westminster Confession 18.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2). A true believer may lose the feeling of assurance for a time and have to wait for it, but the title itself does not change. Doubt about your assurance is not the same as the loss of your salvation.

In everyday life. Think about how you feel when you approach God after a week in which you have done well: you prayed, you resisted something, you were generous. Now compare how you feel approaching him after a week in which you did none of it. If those feel very different, something has been fluctuating, and it is not the promise. That does not make you a hypocrite, but it locates the work still to be done, and the work is not more effort. It is learning to believe that the title is secure in both weeks.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have made you. From Genesis 17:5, when God renamed Abram, exalted father, as Abraham, father of a multitude. God does not say “I will make you”; he says “I have made you”, to a childless old man. He does not describe reality; he establishes it. So Abraham would have been addressed, by everyone he met, as father of a multitude while the promised son had not been born. Every conversation was a small act of faith or a small humiliation, depending on whether the One who named him could be relied on.

In the presence of God. Abraham is not a man reasoning his way to a conclusion about a distant deity. He is standing before someone. Faith in the Bible is never a calculation about probabilities; it is a posture in front of a Person, which is why it can survive evidence that a calculation could not.

Life to the dead. Paul picks these two descriptions of God because they cover the only two situations in which a human being has nothing whatever to contribute: when there is nothing there yet, and when what was there has died. A corpse cannot cooperate with its own raising, and nothing cannot assist in its own creation.

Both apply to Abraham literally. The offspring did not yet exist: nothing, waiting to be called. And the bodies through which they would come were finished: Abraham’s and Sarah’s, as good as dead (v. 19), waiting to be made alive. Later Abraham would receive Isaac back from the altar as if from the dead (Hebrews 11:19), and supremely he would give it to Jesus.

Hope against hope. With nothing in the situation to hope for, he hoped in God. This is not positive thinking, and it is not the refusal to admit facts; the next verse says outright that he faced them. Hope in Scripture is not a mood about the future but a settled expectation resting on something said. So the question is never how much hope you can generate. It is whether the One who spoke can do it.

So shall your offspring be. From Genesis 15:5. Paul is writing to people who will have to believe something at least as unlikely: that a man they never met, executed in a province they have never visited, is alive, and that his death has settled their account with God. So he gives them a father who was in exactly that position, whose faith rested not on any reason to expect a child, but on a God who does this sort of thing.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to promise people outcomes God never promised. Abraham had a specific word from God about a specific thing, and his faith was in that word, not in his own conviction that it ought to happen. Believing hard that a particular result will come is not the faith described here. Faith fastens on what God has said. Where he has spoken plainly, that he will forgive, that he will keep you, that he will raise the dead, that he works all things for the good of those who love him, you may believe against every appearance and you will not be put to shame. Where he has not spoken about your particular case, ask, leave the answer with him, and keep believing what he has said while you wait.

Will God really raise my believing loved ones who have died? Yes. This is exactly the God described here: the one who gives life to the dead. The Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies (8:11), and since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Their souls are already with the Lord, and their bodies will be raised, recognisable and glorious, when Christ returns. You may grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The grave is not a category God finds difficult.

In everyday life. Take the thing you are praying for and cannot see any way through: the marriage, the son, the diagnosis, the part of your own character that has not moved in twenty years. Ask which of the two descriptions in verse 17 your situation falls under. Is it something that does not exist and would have to be created? Or something that was alive and is now dead? Those are the specialities of the God you are praying to. There is no third category, no department for cases that are merely difficult, which suggests that difficulty was never the relevant measurement.

For worship. God is not described here as the God who improves things. He works with nothing and with the dead, so having nothing to work with is his usual raw material. He spoke, and a universe stood up out of nothing. He spoke, and a dead womb bore a son. He spoke, and on the third day a dead man walked out of a tomb. And that risen Son will speak once more, and all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28–29).

so shall your offspring be

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As good as dead. Faith is not ignoring reality. “Considered” is the verb for taking careful stock. Abraham faced the facts: he was about a hundred, and Sarah ninety and barren. He did the arithmetic, got the right answer, and believed God anyway. Some teaching implies that doubt comes from looking too hard at reality; Paul says the reverse. The KJV and NKJV read that he did not consider his body, following later manuscripts that add “not”; the earliest lack it, and either way his faith did not give way before the facts.

The deadness was the material. Verse 17 said God gives life to the dead; verse 19 says Abraham considered his own body as good as dead. He was standing inside the exact category God had just named. The deadness was not the obstacle to the promise. It was the material the promise was going to work with, and Abraham could see both facts at once.

No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God. A great many Christians have quietly used this sentence against themselves. Read alone it sounds like a man of unbroken confidence, and it produces a familiar despair: my faith wavers weekly, so I am not what Abraham was. But did Abraham not laugh, and take Hagar? He did. Genesis records that in these years he lied about his wife to save himself (Genesis 20), took Hagar because waiting had become unbearable (Genesis 16), and when God repeated the promise he fell on his face and laughed (Genesis 17:17), and said in his heart, “Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” Sarah laughed too, behind the tent door, and was asked about it. His faith was not perfect. But in the end it did not turn from the promise itself.

A man who staggers, not a man who defects. Paul is not rewriting the history; he is describing the direction of a life rather than auditing every hour of it. This is God’s summary of a long life, and the striking thing is not that God failed to notice the failures but that this is how he chooses to remember a believer (Hebrews 11:8–12).

He gave glory to God. Faith grows by looking at God, not at ourselves. It is not strengthened by trying to have more faith, which is like trying to fall asleep by concentrating: the harder you work at it, the more awake you are. It grows by attention to its object. Giving glory to God means saying back to him what he is like: that he keeps his word, that nothing is too hard for him, that he has never failed anyone yet. Faith gives glory to God simply by trusting him to keep his word, just as unbelief makes him out to be a liar (1 John 5:10).

The faith that never staggered. Abraham looked at a body as good as dead and trusted the God who gives life to the dead. One descendant of his looked at his own death, not as good as dead but certain, and trusted the same God to the end. Peter says David’s words, “you will not abandon my soul to Hades”, were spoken of Jesus (Acts 2:27–31, quoting Psalm 16:10), and Jesus’ last breath was an act of faith: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Abraham’s faith staggered and held. Christ’s held without staggering, and a staggering faith is safe because it is joined to his.

What should I do with my doubts? Bring them to God rather than hiding them from him. The father in the Gospel cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), and Jesus healed his son. Doubt is not the same as unbelief: unbelief refuses God, while doubt is faith struggling and asking. Talk to a mature Christian; doubts grow in the dark. Go back to the evidence God has given, above all the resurrection of Jesus and the promises of Scripture. And do what Abraham did: turn your attention from the size of your faith to the greatness of God, and praise him for what you know is true. Faith is often strengthened not by solving every question but by looking longer at him.

Does faith mean I should ignore medical facts or refuse help? No. Abraham considered the facts honestly; faith never requires pretending. Trusting God and using the means he provides go together: the same God who heals is the God who gave us doctors, medicine and wisdom (1 Timothy 5:23; Colossians 4:14). Refusing treatment to prove your faith is not faith but presumption, putting the Lord your God to the test (Matthew 4:7). Pray for healing, take the treatment, and leave the outcome with God. Faith says, God is able, and God is good, whatever he decides; it does not say that facts are lies.

A gentler pen. Twenty-five years of nothing happening, two episodes of frank cowardice, a laugh, and one line in the New Testament that says he did not waver. Abraham looked at his dead body, and then he looked at God, and the second look was the longer one. The God who wrote that line over Abraham’s life has a gentler pen than any of us, because every failure he leaves out of the record was written instead into the account of his Son, and paid.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Promise and power. Faith rests on two things, God’s promise and God’s power, not on our feelings or our ability. And the object of the conviction is narrow, which is the mercy of the verse. Abraham was not convinced that he understood what God was doing, but of one thing: that God was able to do what he had promised. That is far smaller and far harder than general spiritual confidence, and it is the whole of what is required.

Able, and willing. Our difficulty is often not about God’s ability at all. Could God heal the illness, restore the marriage, save the son, break the habit? Of course he could. The doubt sits somewhere else and is rarely said out loud: whether he will bother, whether he has particularly noticed, whether in this case he is inclined to. The letter answers that question elsewhere: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (8:32).

Fully convinced. The word (plērophorētheis) means fully persuaded, brought to complete conviction: not a decision made once but a settled state. Must a Christian who does not feel full of anything attain this before God will count anything to him? No. Faith does not justify because it reaches a certain intensity; it justifies because of what it is attached to. What Paul describes here is the direction his faith settled into over twenty-five years, the character it had by the end, not its state on the first morning. Full assurance of this kind is the fruit of a long walk with God, not the fee for beginning one.

What he had promised. Faith in Scripture is never free-floating. It always has a word behind it, and it can only go as far as that word goes. Abraham held on to a specific sentence God had spoken to him, and his confidence was exactly as wide as the promise. So when your faith is thin, do not try to generate more conviction; go and find the promise. This verse does not ask you to be strong. It asks you to be convinced about somebody else’s strength. The whole of Abraham’s greatness, in the end, was that he thought better of God than his circumstances did, and the God he trusted is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20).

How do I know which promises are really mine? Read them in context, and ask to whom they were made. Some promises were given to particular people for particular events: Abraham’s son, Gideon’s victory, Paul’s safe arrival in Rome. Those show you God’s character, but they are not addressed to you. Others are made to all who belong to Christ, and those are yours in full, for every promise God has made is confirmed in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). That he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), that nothing can separate you from his love (8:38–39): these are written to you. Learn them by heart, and lean on them by name.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–24a
verseByVerse.commentary:
Counted to him. Repeating Genesis 15:6, the sentence the whole chapter has been unfolding. The pattern for Abraham is the pattern for us: by faith, through grace, credited and not earned.

Not for his sake alone. Paul does not say merely that Abraham’s example is inspiring. He says the specific words, “it was counted to him”, had a second audience in view from the beginning.

For ours also. Scripture was written for us (15:4). When God did something for a childless man in Canaan, part of what he was doing was making a record that would hold your weight. You are not reading somebody else’s mail and hoping some of it fits. The letter has your name on it, and it was addressed before you existed, by the God who knew the end from the beginning and had you in mind when he took an old man outside to count the stars.

Not first a gallery of examples. This settles how to read Old Testament stories. Most of us were taught the narratives as moral examples: be brave like David, be faithful like Daniel, be patient like Job. That reading has two defects. It exhausts you, because you are asked to produce qualities you do not have. And it is not what the stories are first for. Paul does not say, “Be like Abraham.” He says the way God dealt with Abraham is the way God deals with you. The point of the story is not the patriarch’s faith but the Lord’s reckoning.

Moses wrote of me. The words were written for us because they were written, finally, about him. Jesus told his opponents that Moses “wrote of me” (John 5:46), and after his resurrection he told his disciples that everything written about him in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). The offspring promised under the stars is Christ, and the righteousness counted to Abraham is the righteousness Christ would bring. The record holds our weight because he stands inside it.

So should I never read Old Testament stories as examples? You should, but second, not first. Paul himself says that these things happened to them as an example, and were written down for our instruction (1 Corinthians 10:11), and Hebrews 11 sets the faith of the saints before us to imitate. The difference is the order. First ask what the story shows of God: his grace, his promises, his judgment, his patience, and how it points to Christ. Then ask what kind of response that God deserves, and you will find the example in its proper place: not a standard to reach in your own strength, but the shape of a life that trusts the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24b–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him who raised Jesus. This name for God closes the loop of the chapter. Abraham believed in the God who gives life to the dead (v. 17) and looked at a body that was as good as dead (v. 19). We believe in the God who gave life to the dead and look at a body that was truly dead, laid in a tomb until the third day. It is not an analogy. It is faith in the same God doing the same kind of thing, and the second instance is the one the first was pointing at.

Delivered up. The verb (paredothē): handed over, the word of Isaiah 53:12 in the Greek Old Testament, and of Judas’s betrayal. And it is the same verb that fell three times like a gavel when God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to dishonourable passions, to a debased mind (1:24, 26, 28). There, God handed sinners over to what they had chosen. Here, God hands his own Son over to what they deserved. The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful one are the same word, and one handing over is the answer to the other.

Who handed Jesus over, Judas, the rulers, Pilate or God? All of them, in different ways and with opposite purposes. Judas handed him over for money, the rulers out of envy, Pilate out of cowardice, and each was guilty. Yet Peter says he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and the church prayed that Herod, Pilate and the peoples did whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Above them all, the Father gave him up for us all (8:32), and the Son gave himself: the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Men meant it for evil; God meant it for the salvation of the world.

Raised for our justification. The same small word, “for”, stands in both halves, which suggests that our trespasses were the reason he went to the cross, and our justification, accomplished there, was the reason he came out of the grave. He was raised because the work was done, and the living Christ applies his righteousness to us (5:10; 8:34).

The receipt. Without the empty tomb, a man dies claiming to bear the sins of the world, and stays dead. There is then no way to know whether the payment was accepted. Death releasing him is the public statement that there was nothing left to hold him for. A payment can be doubted at three in the morning: was it enough, for me? The resurrection is God’s own signature on the transaction, given before witnesses who would not stop saying so even under threat of death. The Father does not raise men whose work is unfinished.

Why does the resurrection matter for my justification, and not only the cross? Because the cross is where the debt was paid, and the resurrection is where God declared it paid. Without the resurrection, Paul says, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The risen Christ is also the one who now lives to apply what he won: he is at the right hand of God, interceding for us (8:34), and it is to a living Saviour, not a dead martyr, that faith is joined. So the gospel is not only Christ died for our sins, but that he was buried and raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Both halves belong in your confidence.

In the flow. This verse closes the case Paul opened at 3:21; chapter 5 begins to show what the verdict brings, starting with peace with God (5:1).

In everyday life. When you have sinned badly and the accusation arrives, “You cannot possibly be forgiven for that”, listen to what you say in reply. If it is your repentance, or how sorry you are, or a resolution about the future, the accusation will win, because none of those is strong enough and you know it. The answer this verse puts in your hand is a historical event you had nothing to do with: he was raised. Nothing you have done this week can un-empty that tomb. Say it back to the accuser, and to yourself: he was delivered up for my trespasses, and raised for my justification.

For worship. An old man in Canaan and a grave in Jerusalem are joined by one sentence: it was counted to him; it will be counted to us. Between the two lies the only event that makes the accounting honest, a Son handed over by his Father and handed back. On that one weekend the standing of everyone who would ever believe hung on the Father’s verdict concerning his Son, and the verdict was life.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh?<sup>2</sup>For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.<sup>3</sup>For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>4</sup>Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.<sup>5</sup>And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,<sup>6</sup>just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:<sup>7</sup>“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;<sup>8</sup>blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.”<sup>9</sup>Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.<sup>10</sup>How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.<sup>11</sup>He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well,<sup>12</sup>and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.<sup>13</sup>For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.<sup>14</sup>For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.<sup>15</sup>For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression.<sup>16</sup>That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring—not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,<sup>17</sup>as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations”—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.<sup>18</sup>In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”<sup>19</sup>He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb.<sup>20</sup>No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,<sup>21</sup>fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.<sup>22</sup>That is why his faith was “counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>23</sup>But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone,<sup>24</sup>but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,<sup>25</sup>who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Romans 5 stands at a turning point in the letter. Behind it lie three chapters of diagnosis and one of remedy; ahead lie three chapters on the Christian life. Paul first sets out what justification brings (vv. 1–11), then places it within the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose acts decided the standing of all who belong to them (vv. 12–21).

Because we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God, access to grace, hope of glory, joy even in suffering, and the love of God poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Peace, Access, Hope, and the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
After three chapters of guilt comes peace, because the hostility has been dealt with at the cross. To peace Paul adds access (v. 2) and a standing in grace that does not move with our feelings or performance. Then the most surprising claim: we rejoice even in sufferings, because God uses them to produce endurance, character and hope, and that hope is safe because God’s love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit (vv. 3–5).

Paul then proves that love from the cross. Christ died for us while we were still weak, ungodly and sinners (vv. 6–8), and if God did that for enemies, he will certainly keep his friends (vv. 9–10). The section ends not with the benefits but with the Giver: we rejoice in God himself (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peace with God and assurance

Romans 5:1 is a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The believer’s peace with God is not the peace he feels on good days but the settled peace established by Christ’s finished work and received by faith. The Reformers taught this against the Roman Catholic view that a believer cannot ordinarily be certain of his justification: when God has spoken the verdict, to doubt it is to question his word. As Calvin taught, faith without assurance is not the faith of the New Testament.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world met suffering by gritting its teeth, as the Stoics taught, or by avoiding pain, as the Epicureans taught; neither set it within the love of a personal God. Paul’s rejoicing in suffering (vv. 3–5) was new: suffering has a direction, and it ends in a hope the Spirit guarantees. Now: Many today treat suffering simply as the enemy of a good life, to be avoided at all costs. Romans 5:3–5 does not call suffering good, but it shows that God uses it to make his children steady and hopeful. A Christian who suffers and keeps holding on is not an oddity but a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Justification brings peace with God, access, hope of glory, joy in suffering and the love of God poured into our hearts, and God, who loved us as enemies, will surely save us as friends (vv. 1–11). Then Adam and Christ (vv. 12–21): through one man’s sin, condemnation and death; through one man’s obedience, righteousness and life. The chapter that begins with a man at peace with God ends with grace seated on a throne, and both are the work of one Man.

Therefore. The first word carries four chapters, and the whole letter swings on it. Everything from 1:18 has been a court case. Chapters 1 to 4 establish the verdict. Chapters 5 to 8 describe what it is like to live inside it. Paul is no longer arguing that you can be justified. He is telling you what is now true of you because you are.

Justified by faith. A completed fact: the verdict has been pronounced and the court has risen. To be justified means that God, the Judge, has declared you righteous in his sight: not guilty, and more than that, accepted, because Christ’s righteousness has been credited to you (4:5–6). Everything that follows in this chapter rests on this, and none of it rests on anything else.

Peace with God. Peace with God is not first a feeling of calm. It is a fact: the hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature has ended. The war is over. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The hostility ran in both directions, and not in the same way. On our side it was real enmity: we were “alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds” (Colossians 1:21). On God’s side it was not bad temper but the settled opposition of a just Judge to evil, his wrath, which chapter 1 said is being revealed from heaven. Our hostility could be overcome by God winning our hearts, but his holy wrath could not be talked away; it had to be satisfied, and Christ bore it. That is why the word is peace and not ceasefire. A ceasefire can be revoked on an afternoon’s notice; a peace treaty settles the terms, and this one was signed in blood by the offended party. Peace was not negotiated by us and is not maintained by us. It was made by him, and it stands as long as he stands.

We have, or let us have? A brief word about a footnote you may find in your Bible, since it can be unsettling to discover that the manuscripts differ here. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace”. The difference is a single letter in Greek, a long o for a short one, and the two were pronounced identically in Paul’s day, so a scribe taking dictation could easily write one for the other. The “let us have” reading has strong support in early manuscripts, but most modern translations read “we have”, and rightly: the context is a list of what we have, and Paul is drawing a conclusion from the argument he has just finished, not urging us to do something. And even on the other reading the peace would still be a fact. It would mean “let us enjoy the peace we have”, never “let us try to obtain it”.

Access. The word (prosagōgē) means access by introduction, and a related word named the official who brought visitors into a king’s presence. Nobody simply walked in to see a king; you were brought in, by someone with the standing to bring you. And the Greek tense describes a finished act whose result lasts: we have obtained access. The introduction has already been made. You are not applying each morning to see whether today is a day on which you may approach.

This grace in which we stand. Grace here is not a mood or a transaction but a place: something you can be standing on, which means it is underneath you and bearing your weight. The tense is the same again: we took our stand and we are still standing. The man who has understood this verse does not have to re-establish his position with God every morning, any more than he has to re-lay the floorboards before he can cross the room.

Hope of the glory of God. The verb for rejoice (kauchōmetha) means boast, exult: the same word as the boasting that was excluded in 3:27. The boasting of the man who trusted his own record has been shut out, and a right boasting has taken its place, in God’s glory, which we will share (8:18, 30). The charge sheet against the human race reached its summary in exactly these words: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23). Paul has taken the precise phrase in which our ruin was stated and made it the description of our future. The thing we lost is the thing we are promised: not merely forgiveness for having fallen short of the glory, but the glory itself. The glory of God is the shining out of what God is, and we were made to reflect it, as a mirror reflects the sun. Sin turned the mirror away. In Christ we are already being changed into his likeness, and when he appears we shall be like him (2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 John 3:2).

Hope is not wishful thinking. In ordinary speech, hope means “I would like it but I am not sure”: “I hope it does not rain.” In the New Testament it means confident expectation of something God has promised and not yet delivered. The uncertainty is only about the date, never about the thing.

If I have peace with God, why do I still feel anxious or guilty? Because feelings report on many things, and the verdict of God is not one of the things they are good at reporting. Your peace with God is a fact about God’s judgment of you, settled in Christ, and it is not reopened by a bad night. Guilt you still feel may be pointing to something real you need to confess, and then the answer is to confess it and believe 1 John 1:9. Or it may be the leftover echo of sins already forgiven, and then the answer is to argue with it from this verse. Anxiety may be temperament, tiredness or illness, none of which alters your standing. Do not try to feel your way into peace. Look at the verdict, and let the feelings follow when they can.

In everyday life. Which of these two sentences describes your normal week: “I am trying to get right with God”, or “I am right with God”?
