If the background hum of your spiritual life is effortful and slightly anxious, a project not yet completed, the word to hear is Paul’s first one: therefore. The case is closed. Pray today not as a man applying for an audience but as one who has been brought in and is still standing there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.”

parallels.desc: the effect of righteousness will be peace

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In our sufferings. “Not only that” suggests that this rejoicing is as natural to the Christian as the first: not just in spite of sufferings, but in them, and the verb is the same. The joy of verse 2 looks at the future; the joy of verse 3 is found in the middle of the present at its worst (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

What it does not mean. Two things need saying before the chain, or this passage will do damage. First, Paul does not say suffering is good, or that it should be sought; the Lord himself wept at a grave he was about to empty. And he does not say rejoice because of your sufferings. The word is “in”: joy located inside a situation that remains bad, on account of something else that is true about it. Second, this is not a formula and not a promise about outcomes. Paul knows better, as does anybody who has watched a man come out of a hard decade smaller and harder than he went in. Suffering by itself does not produce endurance. It produces bitterness at least as often, and the difference is not the quantity of the pain but what the sufferer is holding on to while it lasts. That is why the paragraph ends where it does, at the love of God poured into the heart by the Spirit (v. 5).

Endurance. “Suffering” (thlipsis) is pressure, affliction, the crushing of something under weight. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is not passive resignation. The Greek word is made of two parts that together mean “remaining under”: staying put beneath a load rather than crawling out from under it. Hardly anyone has become patient in a comfortable year, and several of the qualities we most want are only manufactured in conditions we would never choose.

Character. The Greek word (dokimē) comes from the testing of metals: the quality of metal that has been through the refiner’s test and come out proved genuine. It shares its root with the failed test at 1:28, where those who would not acknowledge God were given up to a mind that, like bad metal, did not pass. Here the metal passes. A proving does not create the quality; it demonstrates it, to the man himself. Most of us do not know what we believe until something has tried to take it away from us. Trouble also shows what we were really leaning on: when health, money or reputation is taken, we find out whether it was a gift we enjoyed or a god we trusted.

Hope. The surprising link: we would expect hope to enable endurance, but Paul says hope is the result. The reason a tested believer hopes is that he has evidence: he has been in the place where he was certain he could not go on, and he went on, and looking back he can see that he was carried. Hope is not optimism about the future; it is a conclusion drawn from the past.

The road the Son walked first. Paul’s chain is not a technique he discovered; it is the road Christ walked. The risen Lord told two disciples on the way to Emmaus that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26), and the order of those words is the order of these verses: affliction first, glory after. The Father vindicated him by raising him, and that is why Paul can say later that we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (8:17). A believer’s affliction is not a detour from Christ’s road. It is a share in it, and it ends where his ended.

If I cannot feel any joy in this. If you are suffering now and can find no joy in it whatever, you have not failed this passage. Paul is describing a direction of travel over years, not a mood you can produce on demand. Endurance mostly looks like simply not leaving. If today you have not walked away from God, if you are still, in some ragged fashion, holding on, then the first link of this chain is being forged in you at this moment, and it will not feel like anything at all while it happens.

Does this include suffering I brought on myself? Yes, though differently. Peter distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering for doing wrong (1 Peter 2:20), and the second calls first for repentance, not celebration. But God does not waste even the consequences of our own folly. The man reaping what he sowed, the woman living with the results of a bad decision she cannot undo: once the sin has been confessed and forgiven, the pressure that remains is still pressure, and the same God still works endurance, character and hope through it. Paul’s word covers every kind of affliction a believer carries, including the ones with his own fingerprints on them. Grace is not too proud to work with the wreckage.

Does God send suffering, then? Scripture holds two things together without embarrassment. Suffering is an intruder in God’s world, the fruit of the fall that this very chapter goes on to describe, and God takes no pleasure in it for its own sake (Lamentations 3:33). And nothing reaches a believer that has not passed through his hands, and he works all of it for good (8:28). Joseph could say to his brothers that they meant it for evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), in the same sentence, about the same event. You do not have to call the thing good. You may call God good in it.

In everyday life. Write down, specifically, the three hardest things you have been through since becoming a Christian. Beside each one, write what you were afraid would happen: that you would lose your faith, that you would not cope, that you would never be happy again. Then write what actually happened. If you cannot reconstruct how you got through, you were carried. That list is the raw material of hope, and this is exactly how Paul says hope gets made. Keep it, and read it at the start of the next hard thing.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hope does not put us to shame. The phrase is not primarily about embarrassment. In the Old Testament, to be put to shame is what happens to a man whose confidence turns out to have been misplaced: the one who trusted an ally that did not come, or a god that could not answer. It is the shame of having backed the wrong thing in public (Psalm 25:3). Every hope is a bet, and most eventually expose the person who made them. Paul says this one will not, not because we hope sincerely, but because of what is holding the other end.

Poured into our hearts. The reason he gives is not the one we would expect. He has just said that tested character produces hope, but he does not rest the reliability of hope on our character. He rests it on something given. The chain of verses 3 and 4 is real, but it is not what makes hope safe. What makes it safe is that God has already done something inside you.

Whose love? Note the direction of the love, since it can be read either way and the difference is everything. This is not first our love for God, welling up. It is his love for us, poured in and made real to the heart, so that we do not only work out that he loves us but know it. Paul is not describing a doctrine you hold; he is describing something that has happened to you.

Poured. The verb (ekkechytai) is extravagant. It is the word for something emptied out without measuring, used of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:17) and of the blood of the covenant poured out for many (Matthew 26:28). And the Greek tense describes a finished act whose results remain: it “has been poured”. The reservoir was filled before today, and a bad week does not empty it.

The Spirit given to us. Every believer has the Spirit, given at conversion (8:9), and it is the Spirit who assures us of God’s love, so that we cry Abba, Father (8:15–16). He is the first instalment of the coming glory (8:23), God’s own pledge that the hope will be honoured.

The stone that will not shame. Paul has a prophet’s promise in mind, and later in this letter he tells us whom it is about. Isaiah 28:16 spoke of a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion, and Paul applies it directly to Christ: no one who believes in him will be put to shame (9:33; 10:11). And the love poured into us does not come by a different route from the cross: it was the exalted Christ who, having received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit, poured him out on his people (Acts 2:33). The hope that will not disappoint rests on a stone laid in Zion and a gift sent from a throne, and both are Christ.

What if I have never felt anything of the kind? A great many faithful Christians read a verse like this and conclude that whatever Paul is describing has not happened to them. So three things, carefully. First, this is not describing a particular kind of experience: not a single moment, not one kind of feeling, not the sort of thing that could be arranged at a meeting. It shows up in more ways than one. It is in the man who finds, to his surprise, that he wants to pray. It is in the sudden and inexplicable conviction, halfway through an ordinary Tuesday, that you are not facing your life alone. It is in tears at a line of a hymn you have sung a hundred times. It is in the fact that you mind about your sin at all. None of those announces itself as the love of God being poured out, and all of them are.

Temperament and health are real. Second, some people feel everything strongly and some feel very little, and the difference is largely how they were made and how they slept. There are believers who have loved Christ for forty years with the emotional volume permanently low, and others whose capacity for felt experience has been flattened by depression or exhaustion or grief. Scripture never treats intensity of feeling as the measure of anything, and a man whose illness has taken his feelings has not thereby lost the Spirit who was given to him.

The evidence is not only inward. Third, and most usefully: Paul says the love was poured in through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, and the presence of that Spirit is demonstrable in ways that do not depend on your feelings today. Do you call God Father, and mean it? That is the Spirit (8:15). Do you want holiness, even while failing at it? Is Christ precious to you in a way he was not at nineteen? Those are not achievements. They are signs that he is there.

Does every Christian have the Spirit, or is he a later blessing for some? Every Christian has him. Paul says plainly that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (8:9), and here he speaks of the Spirit as given to us, all of us, the whole church in Rome. There is no second class of believers who have been given him and a first class who are still waiting. Christians may be filled afresh, strengthened and led more deeply as they grow (Ephesians 5:18), and you should ask for that. Many Pentecostal and charismatic brothers speak of a later baptism in the Spirit, and their hunger for more of God is right; this commentary reads the New Testament as giving the Spirit to every believer at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13), with fresh fillings after. But you do not need to seek the Spirit as though you lacked him. You need to believe what he has already been given to do in you.

parallels.desc: in you they trusted and were not put to shame

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary:
While we were still weak. Paul now offers proof of the love he has just asserted. A sceptic, or a Christian on a bad night, might answer that inward feelings are not evidence of anything. So Paul goes outside us altogether: the proof is a death, in public, at a datable moment, and its force lies in when it happened. “Weak” (asthenōn) does not mean doing our best in difficult circumstances. It means without strength, the word used of the sick, like the invalid at the pool who could not get himself into the water (John 5:7): a man who could not have contributed to his own rescue if he had wanted to.

At the right time. The phrase (kata kairon) means the crucifixion was not an accident of history. God had planned it from eternity, and it came “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4), exactly when we were helpless. And “for the ungodly” means in their place, on their behalf: not for those who had earned divine favour, but for those in active opposition to God. It is the same word as 4:5, where God justifies the ungodly. If Christ had died for the repentant, the cross would prove that God responds well to repentance. If he had died for the promising, it would prove God has an eye for potential. He died for people who were at that moment incapable, opposed and guilty, which proves something about God and nothing whatever about us.

Scarcely for a righteous person. Paul is going out into human experience to find the highest instance of love he can, so as to measure God’s against it. For a righteous man, the upright, correct, admirable sort, one will scarcely die.

Perhaps for a good person. Then he corrects himself: perhaps for a good man, the warm and generous kind, a benefactor you would actually be fond of, someone might dare it. Even that is hedged with perhaps and dare. People do die for others: a mother for her child, a soldier for the man beside him, occasionally a stranger in a river. But there is almost always a condition: something in the object that draws it out. Love, in us, is a response to worth or to belonging. Hardly anyone lays down his life for a man he finds contemptible, who had wronged him, and who would not be grateful. That is not cynicism; it is where our ceiling is. Christ died for neither the righteous nor the good. He died for the ungodly.

A different kind of love. These verses establish that divine love is a different kind of thing, not a larger quantity of the same thing. Ours is drawn out by something in the person loved; his begins in himself. Ours responds to something lovely; his makes lovely what it will later delight in. And that is why the question “What does God see in me?” has no answer: not because the answer is disappointing, but because the question assumes that his love works like ours. He was not looking for something to see. A love with a reason can lose its reason. But the love demonstrated at a specific hour, for people who were at that hour helpless and hostile, has nothing in us to lose.

Does this mean Christ died for me in particular? Paul writes we and us: he is speaking to believers about what Christ did for them. But look at the description: weak, ungodly. Those are not the names of a select class you might fail to qualify for. They are the names of everyone, and the gospel is offered freely to every one of them. No one who comes to Christ will discover that he was not included. If you are trusting him, you may say with Paul that he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and if you are not yet, the only qualification for coming is the one you already have: being ungodly.

In everyday life. When you try to believe that God loves you, ask what you offer yourself as the reason. Even unspoken, it is usually something: that we have been trying, that we mean well, that we are not as bad as we might be, that at least we care about this. Now take whatever you produced and set it against verse 6. Christ died for the weak and the ungodly: people who have not a single reason to offer. Whatever you were holding was not what secured this and cannot be what maintains it. Put it down.

parallels.desc: when the fullness of time had come

verseByVerse.quote: but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows his love. The verb (synistēsin) is not the word for announcing something. It means to exhibit, to present, to prove by putting on display, and the tense is present: God goes on demonstrating his love in this. The cross is not a historical fact from which we may infer that God was once well disposed. It is a standing exhibit.

The demonstration he chose. God could have shown his love by a statement, and he has made many. He shows it in what he provides: he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matthew 5:45). That proves his kindness, but not this. When he set out to prove that he loved people who hated him, the only thing sufficient was the death of his Son.

His own love. God shows his own love, not a love delegated to someone else, and later in the letter Paul makes plain what it cost him: he who did not spare his own Son (8:32). It is not the loving Son appeasing an angry Father; it is the Father showing his love by giving his Son (John 3:16). The cost fell inside the Trinity. Anybody can be generous with somebody else’s son.

How can it be loving to punish an innocent man in the place of the guilty? This verse answers a question people ask honestly and are rarely answered on. Stated that way it sounds like a miscarriage of justice with a cheerful gloss. But the sentence does not describe a third party being conscripted. The Judge did not find a substitute; he became one. The one who was owed the debt is the one who paid it, in the person of his Son, by agreement within the Godhead before the world began. The Son was not volunteered against his will; he laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). That is not injustice. It is the only arrangement in which mercy costs the person extending it, and in which justice is fully satisfied and the guilty fully freed.

While we were still sinners. The word is “still”. Christ did not wait until we had begun to change; he died for us while we were in the middle of our sinning. Whatever there was in your life at its worst, the cross was aimed at precisely that. It was not aimed at the person you have since become, and it is not waiting on the person you hope to be.

The two moments to reach for this verse. They are opposite. The first is when you have failed badly and cannot bring yourself to pray. The accusation at that hour says: “Not after this.” The answer is that the love was demonstrated when you were doing exactly this, and worse. Your failure this week is not a new development. God already knew it when the price was paid. The second is subtler and catches the respectable. There are believers who have never doubted that God loves them and have quietly concluded that this is reasonable enough: they are, after all, the sort of person who goes to church, gives, prays, means well. That confidence rests on an assessment of themselves, and an assessment can be revised. Verse 8 takes it away, which feels at first like a loss and is the only route to a peace that does not depend on how the year has gone.

If God loves me like this, why does my life feel as though he does not? Because Paul does not point you to your circumstances as the proof of God’s love; he points you to the cross. Circumstances are mixed in a fallen world, and they shift every week; read on their own, they will tell you God loves you on Monday and has forgotten you by Thursday. The cross does not shift. It is the one fixed point from which everything else is to be interpreted: the God who gave his Son for you while you were his enemy has not stopped caring because your job was lost or the treatment failed. He who did not spare his own Son will, with him, graciously give us all things (8:32). Read your life by the cross, never the cross by your life.

For worship. God goes on demonstrating his love, and the exhibit is not a memory. The hands that were nailed at the hour of our worst were raised with the marks still in them and shown to a doubting disciple (John 20:27), and the Lamb at the centre of the throne still stands as though he had been slain (Revelation 5:6). The proof of the Father’s love was carried into heaven and set at the centre of everything. He has never needed a second demonstration, because the first one has never ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Justified by his blood. “By his blood” means by his sacrificial death, the sacrifice that turned God’s wrath away from us (3:25). And Paul now reasons from the harder case to the easier, as Jewish teachers often did. If a man has given you his house, he is not going to quibble about the key.

Much more. The wrath of God is the Judge’s just and measured sentence against evil, stored up for a day when it will be revealed in full (2:5), and no sinner could stand in it for a moment. Instinctively we assume the hard part is still ahead: the cross is settled, but will we make it? Paul says we have it exactly the wrong way round. The hard part was justifying enemies. That is done. What is left is the comparatively minor matter of God keeping his friends safe on the day of wrath, and it is unthinkable that he would fail at the easy end of his own work.

Enemies. Paul has been escalating for four verses, helpless, ungodly, sinners, and now enemies, hostile to God (8:7), the strongest and least flattering word. Christianity does not teach that God found us lost and pitied us. It teaches that he found us in arms against him and made peace at his own expense. That is why the word is reconciled, and God took the initiative: it is God who reconciled us to himself through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). We did not come to the table. He came to us.

Saved by his life. We were reconciled by his death; we shall be saved by his life. Our future does not rest on something a dead man once did, but on a living Saviour, who always lives to plead with God for those who draw near through him (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). So the security of your Christian life does not depend on the strength of your grip on Christ. It depends on a man who is alive at this moment and whose present occupation is you. The Son who died for his enemies now lives for his friends, and he has never lost one whom the Father gave him (John 6:39).

Assurance and perseverance. These verses are a foundation for the perseverance of the saints, the teaching that God keeps every true believer to the end. They answer a fear many serious Christians carry and rarely say: I might not last, because I know myself. That fear is reasonable if the finishing depends on you. This argument removes it from your hands entirely: the one who did the hard part when you were his enemy is the one doing the rest now that you are his child.

What it does not mean. This is not an invitation to drift; chapter 6 and chapters 12 to 16 spell out what is required. Paul is saying where the guarantee is located. The Christian is still called to endure, and he can, because the outcome does not hang on the quality of his enduring, and the Spirit given to him (v. 5) is the strength he rows with. A man rowing a boat that is also under tow rows better, not worse.

If I am already saved, what does saved from wrath mean? Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses. You have been saved from the penalty of sin, at the moment you were justified (Ephesians 2:8). You are being saved from its power, day by day, as the Spirit makes you holy (1 Corinthians 1:18). And you will be saved from its presence and from the wrath to come on the last day (1 Thessalonians 1:10). Paul is speaking here of the third: the final rescue when Christ returns. It has not happened yet, and it is not in doubt, because it was paid for in the first.

But what about the warnings, and people who seem to fall away? The New Testament does warn believers, seriously, against drifting and unbelief (Hebrews 3:12–14), and some who professed faith did leave. John explains them: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Their departure showed that the root was never there, not that God failed to keep someone who was his. The warnings are one of the means by which God keeps his people: a believer who hears them and turns back to Christ is persevering. So if you are frightened that you might be one who falls away, the fear itself, and the turning to Christ that it produces, are signs of life. Those who fall away are not usually worried about it.

verseByVerse.quote: More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We also rejoice in God. Three rejoicings make a staircase: in hope of glory (v. 2), joy about the future; in sufferings (v. 3), joy in the present at its worst; and now in God himself, the top step. The goal of salvation is not a set of benefits. It is God.

The gifts and the Giver. It is entirely possible to be delighted with the benefits of Christianity while having little appetite for God. A man can be glad about forgiveness, relieved about judgment, attached to his church, and all of it can be love of the gifts. That is not hypocrisy; the gifts were meant to be enjoyed. But it can be tested: would the benefits be enough without the Benefactor, if God gave you everything you have asked and were himself absent? If something essential would be missing from such a world, you have found what verse 11 is about, and that preference is the surest evidence in the chapter that something real has happened to you. If your honest answer troubles you, bring the trouble to him: grieving that you want him too little is itself a way of wanting him.

Received reconciliation. Not achieved, not even entered, but received: something done for us and handed to us, as salvation is all through this letter. Reconciliation is not a settlement negotiated between two aggrieved parties who each move some way. One party was entirely in the wrong and did not want terms; the other party made peace, at his own cost, and then handed the completed reconciliation to the offender as a gift.

Now. The small word is Paul’s drumbeat through the section: now justified (v. 9), now reconciled (v. 10), now received (v. 11). Not at the last day, not pending review. Whatever remains outstanding in the Christian life, and chapters 6 to 8 will be honest about how much does, the relationship itself is settled.

Joy in God through a Man. Paul does not say we rejoice in God and then add Christ as the route. The words “through our Lord Jesus Christ” belong to the whole sentence, because God is enjoyed only where he is seen, and he is seen in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father (John 14:9). So the joy at the top of the staircase is a share in the Son’s own delight in his Father: Jesus prayed that the love with which the Father loved him before the foundation of the world might be in his people (John 17:24, 26). We rejoice in God by being brought inside that joy.

What does rejoicing in God actually look like? It looks like enjoying God for who he is, not only for what he does. In practice it shows in praise that dwells on his attributes, his holiness, faithfulness, wisdom and mercy, and not only on the week’s answers to prayer. It shows in prayer that sometimes asks for nothing and simply stays in his company. It shows in reading Scripture to see him, not only to find instructions. And it shows in a quiet steadiness when the gifts are thin, because the chief good has not gone anywhere. It does not need to be loud. Asaph had watched the wicked prosper until his feet almost slipped, and he ended his psalm by finding that, with God as his portion, he wanted nothing else in heaven or on earth (Psalm 73:25–26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Death in Adam, Life in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From v. 12 Paul steps back from the individual believer to the whole human story: two men, Adam and Christ, each acting as head for those who belong to him.

The parallel is real but uneven, because grace exceeds sin at every point (vv. 15–17). Adam’s one trespass brought condemnation and death; Christ’s obedience brings justification and life to all who are in him, and where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (v. 20). The section ends with two reigns, sin reigning in death and grace reigning through righteousness to eternal life (v. 21), and the believer has been moved from the first to the second.
verseByVerse.theology:
Federal headship

Romans 5:12–21 is the main biblical basis for the Reformed doctrine of original sin. Death spread to all because all sinned in Adam, not merely by imitating him but by being represented by him: he was the covenant head of humanity, appointed by God to act for us all. That is why all die, even infants (v. 14). And the parallel with Christ is the point: as we were condemned in Adam, so we are justified in Christ, in the same way, by one man acting for all who belong to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish writers of Paul’s day already saw Adam as the one through whom ruin came to humanity, and Paul uses that shared starting point to show how universal sin is and how wide the gospel’s offer is. Now: Every generation supplies fresh evidence that something has gone wrong with the human race at its root. Romans 5:12–21 names where it began, in Adam, and offers the remedy, Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through one man. “One man” is Adam (Genesis 3). Sin entered human history through him, and death came in behind it. Paul treats him as a real, historical man, and he tells his story here for one reason: the Man who was to come (v. 14). The whole paragraph is built as a comparison, and Adam is in it because Christ is.

A sentence left unfinished. Paul begins a comparison, “just as sin came into the world through one man”, and then breaks off. The matching half, the “so”, does not arrive until verse 18. Verses 13 to 17 are an aside, and knowing that makes the whole paragraph easier to follow.

Death through sin. Death is not natural; it is the penalty of sin (Genesis 2:17; Romans 6:23). And the death that spread is more than the grave. God had warned Adam that in the day he ate he would surely die. He died at once in his relationship with God, and in his body years later. So death here includes physical death, the spiritual death of being cut off from God (Ephesians 2:1), and, apart from Christ, the eternal death that is the wages of sin (6:23). That is why the answer at the end of the chapter is not only resurrection but eternal life (v. 21).

Death spread to all. Paul’s evidence is not a doctrine but a fact anybody can check: death spread to all, with no exception anywhere in the record, every civilisation, every temperament, every infant. He is pointing at a fact and asking what could account for it.

Because all sinned. “Because” translates eph’ hō, and everything turns on it. Augustine, reading the Latin translation (in quo, in whom), took it as “in whom all sinned”, that is, in Adam. Most scholars now agree the Greek means “because”, but the question remains: in what sense did all sin?

Where Christians differ: two readings of “all sinned”. The first says all die because each person sins personally, following Adam’s example. The second says all sinned in Adam, when he sinned as the representative head of the human race. This commentary’s view: the second, for three reasons Paul gives in the passage itself. First, death reigned even over those who did not sin as Adam did (v. 14), including infants, who have committed no personal sins; so their death must come from Adam’s sin. Second, Paul says five times that condemnation and death came through one man’s one trespass (vv. 15–19), not through each person’s many sins. Third, verse 19 says that by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners: a passive construction, in which Adam’s act, not our own, is the ground of our sinner-status. Personal sins follow, and they are real and add to our guilt; but the root is our union with Adam. This is what theologians call original sin: we inherit both Adam’s guilt, counted to us, and his corrupted nature (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3).

Federal headship. The Reformed tradition calls this federal headship, from the Latin for covenant (foedus). Adam stood as covenant head of the race, and his sin is counted to all his descendants just as Christ’s obedience is counted to believers (Westminster Confession 6.3). Another older view, natural headship, says we sinned in Adam because all human nature was present in him. Both reject the idea that Adam merely set a bad example, and the federal view best explains the exact symmetry Paul draws between the two men.

Where Christians differ: was Adam a real person? Some Christians, seeking to harmonise Genesis with evolutionary theories of human origins, hold that Adam is a symbol of humanity rather than a real first man. This commentary’s view: Paul’s argument requires a real, historical Adam. He sets one man against one man, one trespass against one act of righteousness, and a real history of death reigning from Adam to Moses (v. 14). If there was no real Adam whose sin brought condemnation, Paul’s parallel with the real Christ whose obedience brings justification falls apart, and so does the comfort, because Christ’s obedience was a real act in history. Paul treats Adam the same way elsewhere (1 Corinthians 15:22; 1 Timothy 2:13–14). Jesus too treated Adam and Eve as real (Matthew 19:4–5), and Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back to Adam (Luke 3:38). Christians who take the symbolic view are often wrestling honestly with real scientific questions, and those questions deserve patient answers; but the argument of this chapter stands or falls with a real Adam.

Before the law. “Counted” (ellogeitai) is charged to an account, as in a ledger. Between Adam and Moses there was no written law, so people’s sins were not charged as transgressions of a stated command in the way Adam’s was (see 4:15). Yet they still died, and death is the penalty of sin, so Adam’s sin must have been counted to them. This also shows that the written law did not create sin. It only put into words what was already wrong: sin was real before Sinai.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagians (followers of Pelagius, a monk of the early fifth century) taught that Adam only set a bad example, and each person sins freely on their own. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that Adam’s sin was counted to the whole human race, so that all are born guilty and corrupt (vv. 18–19; Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3). Adam was the federal head of humanity, and his fall became ours. This is hard, but it is the background of the gospel: in the same way, Christ’s righteousness is counted to all who are in him.

Is it fair to be condemned for Adam’s sin? This is the question every reader asks, and it is usually felt not as a dispute about doctrine but as: “I never voted for Adam.” Paul does not run from it, and several things help. Representation is how God has always related to humanity: the head acts for those in him. It is the fabric of ordinary life too. A country goes to war on the decision of a government most of its citizens did not choose. Children inherit the language, the nationality, the debts and the reputation their parents handed them. We accept the inherited goods readily and object loudly to the inherited liability. Adam was the best representative humanity could ever have had, placed in a perfect world with every advantage; no one can say they would have done better. Each of us confirms Adam’s choice by our own sins, every day: every human being has stood where Adam stood, with what God has said on one side and his own preference on the other, and has chosen as he chose. That is why Paul can say both that we were made sinners by one man’s disobedience and that all sinned, without contradiction. And most importantly, if we reject the principle of representation, we lose the gospel, because we are saved in exactly the same way: by another man’s obedience counted to us (vv. 18–19). We cannot accept the second Adam and refuse to understand the first. The question is not whether we will be represented, but by whom: Adam or Christ.

Standing alone. Pressed all the way, the objection argues against itself. Insist on standing alone, with no representative and judged strictly on your own record, and you would be free of Adam’s guilt, but left with your own, and this letter has spent three chapters describing how great that is. Both men acted before you were consulted. Only one of them acted deliberately for your good.

Does original sin mean I am not really responsible for my sins? No. Original sin explains where the disease came from; it does not excuse what you do with it. Scripture always holds people accountable for their own choices (Ezekiel 18:20; Romans 2:6), and nobody sins against his will; we sin because we want to. The doctrine actually deepens responsibility rather than removing it, because it shows that the problem is not a few bad decisions you could put right with effort but a heart turned from God at the root. That is bad news for self-improvement and very good news for the gospel. You need not a better example but a new head and a new heart, and both are offered in Christ.

In everyday life. Ask yourself what you actually believe death is. Many will say it is natural, yet nobody stands at a funeral thinking this is how it should be. We grieve as though a person has been taken rather than merely ceasing, and Scripture agrees with your instinct rather than your theory: death is an enemy, the last enemy to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). The next time you stand at a grave, let your grief say what Paul says, and then let your hope say what he goes on to say.

For worship. One man opened the door, and death came in after him, and no one born since has been able to shut it. Then another Man was born into that same world. The eternal Son took the flesh of Adam’s children, without Adam’s sin, stood where Adam stood, and did not fall; and he walked into the death Adam let loose, not dragged but willing, and on the third day walked out of it holding the keys (Revelation 1:18).
verseByVerse.note: “One man” is Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death reigned. The verb is the striking thing. Death did not merely occur; it reigned, the word for a king exercising dominion, which Paul will use four more times before the chapter closes. Death is not only the moment a body stops; it is a power with a territory and subjects, and it governs a life long before it arrives: it sets the limit on every plan and gives every love its ache. It reigned for thousands of years, over infants and kings, and in all that time not one grave escaped it. And then One came into its territory who owed it nothing, let it take him, and broke its rule from the inside.

Not like Adam’s transgression. Adam broke an explicit command knowingly. Between him and Moses there was no such published command to charge people under, and they died anyway, because of Adam (v. 13).

What about infants and those who could never sin knowingly? This brings a great many readers, rightly, to a question that is not academic: the infant, the stillborn, the profoundly disabled, anyone who dies before there is anything to charge. It is usually asked by somebody with a name and a date in mind, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a systematic one. Start with what this verse does say, because it is sobering: it says they die. Scripture does not exempt anybody from the ruin we all share in Adam, and the theology of this passage is the reason infants are mortal at all. But see what the verse does not say. It does not say they are condemned. Paul’s subject here is death’s dominion, not the final destiny of individuals, and it is a serious mistake, one that has caused enormous grief, to read a paragraph about the reign of death as though it were a roll of the lost.

The ground of hope. Scripture gives real ground for hope, without giving a formula. David’s child died, and David stopped fasting, washed, worshipped, and said: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Samuel 12:23), words of expectation, not resignation, from a man who elsewhere says he will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever (Psalm 23:6). Our Lord took children in his arms and said the kingdom of God belongs to such as these (Mark 10:14–16). The Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and he judges according to the light given (2:12). The Westminster Confession speaks of elect infants dying in infancy as regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3), and many Reformed teachers, among them Charles Spurgeon, Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, have held that all who die in infancy are among them. They are saved not on the ground of an innocence this chapter denies them, but by sovereign mercy, through the same Christ, though they were not able to believe consciously. Scripture does not state that in so many words, and it would be wrong to pretend it does. It is a hope that rests on the character of God, which is the only place a hope was ever safe.

If you are reading this with a grave in mind. Hear the two halves in the right order. Yes, this passage explains why that death happened at all: it is the reign Paul is describing, death is an enemy, and your grief is not a failure of faith but an accurate response to an intruder. And no, this passage is not a verdict on that child. The one who will decide is the one who wept at a friend’s tomb while fully intending to empty it, and who himself became an infant.

A type. The word (typos) is a pattern, a mould, a foreshadowing. Everything we have been told of Adam is catastrophe, and Paul calls him a preliminary sketch of Christ. Not in his sin, obviously, but in the position he held: one man, whose one act decided the standing of all who belong to him. Two men, two heads, two families: Adam is the pattern Christ reverses (1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49).

The mechanism kept. God did not respond to the disaster by abolishing the mechanism that produced it. He built representation into the structure of humanity from the first day, and the arrangement that ruined us was the arrangement through which we would be rescued. He sent a second Man to stand at the head of it, so that the very thing you would have complained about in Eden turns out to be the thing that makes your salvation possible. Adam was never merely a warning. He was a rough draft, and the finished work was already in view.

How do I know which family I am in? Not by birth, church background or how you feel. Everyone begins in Adam; nobody is born into Christ. You come into the second family by being joined to its head through faith: trusting Christ himself, not your record, for acceptance with God. If you are resting on him, you are in him, whatever your past. If you are not sure, do not wait to be sure: come to him now, as you are. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

In everyday life. Watch this week how much of what you do is quietly shaped by death’s reign: the plans you make to feel secure, the fear behind the money, the dread of a diagnosis, the need to leave a mark. Then name each one before Christ, and say plainly that you belong to another King. Death still has its day in your body, but it has lost its throne over your life.
verseByVerse.note: A “type” is a pattern or foreshadowing: Adam, head of the old humanity, foreshadows Christ, head of the new.

parallels.desc: the first man Adam, the last Adam

verseByVerse.quote: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not like the trespass. Similar in pattern, but not equal in power. Paul has set the two men side by side, one man, one act, a whole race affected, and now twice he says the two sides do not balance. If they balanced, Christ would merely undo Adam and we would be back where we started. The comparison is real, but the two sides are nothing like the same size, because God put his own Son on one of them.

Much more. This is the heart of it: grace is stronger than sin. The word for abounded means to overflow, to exceed the container. The gospel is not the restoration of Eden. Adam lost a garden; we are promised a city. Adam had innocence, which is a fragile thing and was lost in an afternoon; the believer has a righteousness that is not his own and therefore cannot be forfeited by him. Adam could fall. The man in Christ cannot finally fall, because he is not standing on his own record. We do not end where Adam began; we end further on, redeemed rather than merely restored.

The grace of that one man Jesus Christ. The gift is named twice: the grace of God, and the free gift by the grace of one man. The Father’s grace and the Son’s are one grace. And it comes through a man: the eternal Son had to become one of us to stand at the head of a new humanity, as Adam stood at the head of the old.

One trespass, many trespasses. The first imbalance is in the arithmetic. Adam faced one command and broke it: a single trespass, and condemnation followed. Christ faced the accumulated mass of every sin of every person he came to save, a mountain of them, and justification followed. You would assume that a great many sins would be proportionately harder to deal with than one. It is exactly the reverse: one was enough to condemn, and the countless were not too many to forgive.

Can he forgive this much? That answers a fear a great many Christians live with privately. Not can God forgive sin? That is settled. But can he forgive this much of it? The man converted at fifty who cannot stop counting the years. The believer who keeps returning to the same failure and has begun to suspect there must be a limit somewhere. This verse is the answer. The gift is not measured out to match the size of the debt, enough for a certain quantity of sin and running short beyond that. Grace was never measured against the sin in the first place. It is measured against the worth of the one who gives it.

If I am forgiven, why do I still feel the weight of sins I have confessed? Because memory and conscience are slower than the verdict. God has removed your transgressions as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12); your memory has not, and it is not meant to be the judge. When an old sin returns, do not confess it again as though the first confession failed. Thank God that it was forgiven, and use the memory to humble you and make you gentle with others. Where a wrong you did to someone can still be put right, put it right, because forgiveness from God does not cancel the duty of restitution. And where it cannot, leave it with the Christ who bore it. Feelings of guilt over forgiven sin are not God’s voice; the gospel is.

In everyday life. After your last serious failure, did you find yourself calculating: how much ground have I lost, how long before things are normal again, how many good weeks does this cost me? That calculation is Adam’s arithmetic, reasonable inside his system, where everything runs on your record, and you are not in that system. There is no ground to make up, because the ground was never yours, and there is no quantity at which the gift becomes insufficient, because it was never being weighed against you. Confess it, receive the gift, and get up.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death reigned through one man. Death reigned through one man’s trespass, so we expect the matching clause to be that life will reign through Jesus Christ. That is the tidy version, and it is not what Paul says.

Reign in life. The parallel breaks again, and it breaks upward. Paul does not say that life will reign where death reigned; he says that people will. Under Adam we were the territory being ruled. Under Christ we are not merely liberated subjects; we are given a throne. Believers become kings, sharing Christ’s rule (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). This is the destiny Genesis described when the creature made in God’s image was told to have dominion. Adam was made to rule and ended as a subject of death. The man in Christ was a subject of death and ends by ruling. The King of kings did not merely free his people from the tyrant. He emptied the tyrant’s throne and set them beside himself.

Will reign. Will reign is future, and anybody who cannot find much evidence of sovereignty in his own life is reading it correctly. But the word beside it is in the present tense: those who are receiving the abundance of grace. So the receiving is now and the reigning is later, which is exactly the shape of the Christian life: a king in exile, whose title is already granted, whose coronation is on a date he does not know.

Receive. There is a single condition, stated in one word. It is the only thing in the sentence that we do, and it adds nothing to the gift. Everything else is done by somebody else: the grace is given, the righteousness is credited to us as a gift, not a quality we produce, and the reign is conferred. And Paul chooses his nouns to make refusal look absurd: not grace but the abundance of grace, not righteousness but the free gift of righteousness.

How do I receive it? By faith, which is the empty hand of the beggar. You receive the gift of righteousness by trusting Christ: believing that what he did is enough, and resting your whole case with God on him rather than on yourself. It is not a feeling you must work up or a prayer with the right words; it is a reliance. You go on receiving it in the same way, every day, by coming back to him as the only ground of your acceptance, especially on the days you have failed. A man in a burning building does not earn his rescue by climbing the ladder. He does have to climb it, and the climbing is simply letting the rescuer have him.

What it does not mean. The language of reigning has been badly misused. This is not a promise that faith gives you command now over illness, finances or other people. The verb is future, the men who wrote these letters were beaten, imprisoned and executed, and Paul himself is about to describe the whole creation groaning and Christians groaning with it (8:22–23). Reigning in life is a destination. What does begin now is freedom from sin’s rule, which chapter 6 will describe.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. — Romans 5:18–19
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence finished. The comparison Paul began in verse 12 and broke off is at last completed; everything between was an aside.

Justification and life for all. Read alone, the phrase appears to say everybody is saved. But Paul has just said the gift belongs to those who receive it (v. 17), a limiting phrase he had no reason to insert if everyone receives it regardless. It is all who are in Christ, as all in Adam are condemned.

Where Christians differ: are all saved? Universalists read justification and life for all men as meaning every person will be saved. This commentary’s view: Paul limits it to those who receive (v. 17), believers. In the very next sentence all men becomes the many in both halves: he is using the phrases interchangeably, contrasting two humanities, not counting heads. As all in Adam die, so all in Christ are made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22). The all is all who belong to each head. And a sentence must be read with its author: the same apostle wrote chapter 2 on the day of wrath and chapter 9 on vessels of wrath, and Scripture clearly teaches that some perish eternally (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46). The longing behind universalism, that mercy should triumph, is right in itself; Scripture answers it with a multitude no one can number (Revelation 7:9), not with the salvation of all.

The completeness of each head. The two acts have the same universality within their own spheres. Adam’s trespass reaches every person in Adam, and Christ’s obedience reaches, with exactly the same completeness, every person in Christ. Neither head leaves out anybody who belongs to him, which is precisely what you would want to know if you were wondering whether you might be an exception at the edges of the second group. You are not.

Made sinners. The verb (katestathēsan) means constituted, appointed, put in the category of. It is a legal word. It describes where a person stands before God, not first what he is like in character. Adam’s disobedience was counted to all in him.

Made righteous. Christ’s obedience is counted to all in him, and here Paul names a part of Christ’s work that is often left untaught. Paul does not say here that Christ died for our sins, though he believes it. He says obedience: his whole life of perfect obedience to God’s law, culminating in obedience to death on the cross (Philippians 2:8). All his years count, not merely the six hours on the cross: the temptations refused in a wilderness, the ordinary decades in a workshop, every commandment kept in the only human life that ever kept them.

Active and passive obedience. Theologians call these his active obedience (he kept the law perfectly for us) and his passive obedience (he bore its penalty for us). Both are credited to believers. That is why justification is more than pardon. A pardon cancels a record and leaves the man with none: forgiven, and possessing nothing. The New Testament describes an exchange: your record reckoned to him and his to you, so that you stand before God as one who has kept the law entirely. The Son of God lived every hour of a human life in perfect love for his Father, and then gave that life up on the cross, and both the life and the death are yours. And this is the believer’s rest on the days his own obedience falls short, which is every day: we all stumble in many ways (James 3:2), and even our best works are mixed. Our standing never rested on them. Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours, and so our imperfect obedience is accepted for his sake, offered to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). Failure does not undo that standing. This never excuses sin; it is what sets a forgiven child free to obey gladly.

Is being made righteous the same as becoming good? No, though the one always leads to the other. Being made righteous here is justification: God’s verdict that you are righteous in his sight because Christ’s obedience is counted to you. It is complete the moment you believe, and it does not grow. Becoming good in heart and behaviour is sanctification: the Spirit’s patient work, through the whole of life, of changing you into Christ’s likeness. It is real, it grows, and it is never complete in this life. Confusing them is dangerous in both directions. If you make your acceptance depend on your progress, you will never have peace. If you think acceptance needs no progress, you have not understood the grace that accepted you, as chapter 6 is about to show.

In everyday life. Ask which sentence you actually believe about yourself: “God has forgiven me”, or “God accepts me in the righteousness of Jesus Christ, as fully as he accepts his Son”. The second may sound like presumption, and it is the plain implication of verse 19. The gap between them is the amount of this verse you have not yet believed. Say the second one today, and pray from it.

parallels.desc: shall my servant make many to be accounted righteous

verseByVerse.quote: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 5:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law came in. One of the strangest statements in Scripture, and it is a statement of purpose: God gave the law at Sinai in order that the trespass might increase. And the word for the law’s arrival (pareisēlthen) is telling: it came in alongside, as by a side entrance, a verb suggesting something entering a situation already underway. The law is not the main plot. It arrived after Adam and before Christ with a defined job to do. That was a bold thing to say to people who had built their national identity around the law.

How does the law increase trespass? Not by making people worse in themselves. Chapter 4 has already set out the first way: “where there is no law there is no transgression” (4:15), so once the line is drawn, wrongdoing becomes the breaking of a known command. The law shows sin as sin. But there is a second and more uncomfortable way, which Paul will describe from his own experience in chapter 7: a prohibition provokes (7:7–13). Tell a man “do not” and something in him wakes up that was asleep a moment earlier. Every parent knows this, and every one of us has felt it: the cupboard you had no interest in until you were told not to open it. The law does not create the appetite. It exposes it, and in exposing it inflames it, because the disease is rebellion, and rebellion rises when it is told no.

Why would God do that? Because a sin that is vague is never brought to be forgiven: not because God cannot forgive it, but because nobody asks. A man with a general sense that he is not all he should be does not go anywhere in particular with it. The law’s work is to take that fog and turn it into an itemised bill, so that the man is finally holding something specific enough to bring to a Saviour. It was not given to save but to expose our need. Sin had to be made visible before grace could be seen to be sufficient.

Is the law bad, then? No. Paul will say emphatically that the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (7:12). The fault is not in the law but in us: it is like a straight edge laid against a crooked wall, which does not make the wall crooked but shows how crooked it is. For the believer the law remains a good guide to the life that pleases God, and its moral commands are summed up in love (13:8–10). What it cannot do is give the life it describes. That is what grace does.

Grace abounded all the more. Sin increased; grace super-abounded (hypereperisseusen), an already strong verb made stronger still, found elsewhere in the New Testament only at 2 Corinthians 7:4. Wherever sin has gone, grace has gone further, and it did not arrive with a measure in its hand.

For the one who thinks he is the exception. The comfort is aimed at people who think they are outside it: the one who came late, having done damage that cannot be repaired, or the person with one thing in his past he has never said aloud. This verse is about the places where sin went deepest, and it says grace went further. Bring the thing by name to Christ today, and, if it would help you to be free, to one trusted, mature believer as well (James 5:16).

Then why not sin more, so that grace abounds more? Paul knows exactly what a certain kind of mind will do with the sentence he has just written, and he answers it in the first line of the next chapter: by no means (6:1–2). He does not soften the statement to prevent the abuse; he lets it stand at full strength. But the answer is already embedded here. Grace reigns through righteousness. It does not reign by suspending righteousness or negotiating with it. So a man who concludes from this verse that he may now sin freely has misunderstood the kind of king he is dealing with. Grace is not permission; it is a rule you live under, and its rule is righteous. Someone who wants grace in order to keep sinning has not yet wanted grace at all, only escape.

Two kings. Sin reigning through death, grace reigning through righteousness. A reign is a government you live under; you do not negotiate with it; you are transferred out of one reign into another, the great theme of chapters 6 to 8. The justified person is no longer defined by Adam’s inheritance or his own accumulated failures. He is under the reign of grace, moving toward eternal life, claimed and kept by the God who abounds.

Through Jesus Christ our Lord. The refrain that ends each section of chapters 5 to 8 (5:11, 21; 6:23; 7:25; 8:39). Ten verses on two men end on a name. The law came in alongside. He came in to reign.

For worship. Grace reigns. Not grace permits or overlooks: grace reigns, the language of a throne. Sin had a reign too, and it ended in a graveyard the size of the world. The new King took his throne by dying, and the first thing he did with the crown was to spend it giving life away, eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>2</sup>Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God.<sup>3</sup>Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance,<sup>4</sup>and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,<sup>5</sup>and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.<sup>6</sup>For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.<sup>7</sup>For one will scarcely die for a righteous person—though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die—<sup>8</sup>but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.<sup>9</sup>Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God.<sup>10</sup>For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.<sup>11</sup>More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned—<sup>13</sup>for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.<sup>14</sup>Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.<sup>15</sup>But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many.<sup>16</sup>And the free gift is not like the result of that one man’s sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.<sup>17</sup>For if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men.<sup>19</sup>For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.<sup>20</sup>Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,<sup>21</sup>so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

6.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.overview:
Romans 6 answers the question Paul’s gospel provokes: if grace covers all sin, why not go on sinning? His reply is a flat refusal, grounded not first in a rule but in a fact: believers have been joined to Christ in his death and resurrection, so sin no longer has the right to rule them.

The commands come only after that fact: count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God, refuse sin its old reign in your body, and give yourselves to God. Holiness here is not a way to earn what grace gives; it is living from what is already true in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — United with Christ in Death and Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul points to baptism, the sign of union with Christ: joined to him, we died with him, were buried with him and were raised with him to a new life. Sin is still present (chapter 7 will be honest about that), but it no longer reigns.

Our security rests first on what happened to Christ: he died to sin once for all and, raised from the dead, will never die again (vv. 9–10). Only then come the commands of vv. 11–14, and the section ends on a promise rather than a target: sin will not be master, because we are under grace, not under law.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ: The Foundation of Sanctification

Romans 6 grounds holiness in union with Christ, not in moral effort alone. Reformed teachers have held that justification and sanctification are distinct but never separated, because both come from being joined to Christ. John Murray, in Redemption Accomplished and Applied, argued that union with Christ is not one blessing among others but the root of them all.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The objection Paul answers, sin so that grace may abound, was a real slander against his preaching (3:8). He does not retreat into moralism; he goes deeper into the gospel. Now: The same objection still comes whenever grace is preached plainly, and Paul’s answer still stands: grace does not make people careless about sin; it joins them to the Christ who died and rose.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 6 answers the obvious objection to grace: if grace abounds where sin increases (5:20), why not sin more? Because believers have died to sin. Union with Christ means we died and were raised with him, so sin is no longer our master. We must count ourselves dead to sin and alive to God, and offer our bodies to him as instruments of righteousness. Justification never leaves a person in sin; it joins him to Christ, who breaks sin’s power. The chapter that begins with a question about sin ends with a gift and a name, and the name is Lord.

What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? Before the answer, consider that the question exists at all, and that Paul has heard it before. He reported it as an actual slander back at 3:8, where people were saying that he taught, in effect, “why not do evil that good may come”. So this is not a hypothetical objection invented for the sake of argument. It is what his preaching provoked in real congregations, and it is worth asking why. Nobody ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. You only get this objection if you have said something that sounds dangerously like “God accepts the ungodly and their record contributes nothing”, which is precisely what Paul has been saying for five chapters. A gospel that has never once been misheard this way may not yet have been stated clearly.

Continue in sin. The verb is more specific than English suggests. It means to remain, to go on dwelling somewhere. Paul is not asking whether a Christian ever sins; chapter 7 is painfully clear about that. He is asking whether a Christian takes up residence in it. The question is not whether you have trespassed but whether you have built a house on the property.

By no means! Mē genoito: Paul’s most emphatic way of rejecting a thought, something like “perish the thought”. Having provoked the objection, he does not retreat an inch from 5:20, and the shape of his answer is the whole point.

How can we who died to sin still live in it? The answer in one question. He does not say “you must not”. He asks “How can we?” Those are different kinds of sentence. One puts up a fence; the other says the thing no longer fits who you are. You do not tell a man released from a life sentence that he is forbidden to sleep in his old cell. You ask him why on earth he would want to. Paul’s answer is not a rule but a fact: those who have died to sin cannot go on living in it, not because they are forced from outside but because being joined to Christ has changed their whole relationship to sin. It is not that sin has died in us, or that we no longer feel it, but that we died to its reign.

What “died to sin” does not mean. It does not mean that believers no longer feel the pull of sin, or that sin has been removed from them, or that they have become unable to sin. Paul goes on to command them not to let sin reign (v. 12), which would be pointless if they could no longer sin; and chapter 7 describes the believer’s real struggle with it. Nor is it a command (die to sin!); it is a past fact (we died): a completed act, done to you rather than achieved by you, dated at a cross and applied to you when you were united to Christ. It is the fact from which the whole Christian life proceeds, which is why every command in this chapter comes after it and not before.

What it does mean. The key is verse 10, which says that Christ also died to sin. Christ never had sin in him, so dying to sin cannot mean sin was rooted out of him. It means he died to sin’s realm and claim: he came under the reign of sin and death for our sake, bore its penalty, and through death passed out of that realm for ever. Believers, united to him, have died with him to that same reign. Sin was once our master, holding a legal claim on us; that ended when we died with Christ, and we now belong to a different realm, the reign of grace (5:21).

A jurisdiction ended. Death ends a court’s authority over a man: a dead man is beyond the reach of the court that had a warrant out for him. So think of sin as a former employer, not as a feeling that has gone away. He still has your number and he still rings, often, and he knows exactly what to say. What he has lost is not his voice but his authority: he can make suggestions, but he cannot give you an instruction you are obliged to carry out, and the reason is not that you have grown stronger but that you no longer work there.

Then why do I still sin? Because sin’s reign has been broken, but its presence remains until the resurrection. The old regime has been overthrown, but its forces still fight in the land. Sin still lives in our mortal bodies and pulls at us (vv. 12–13; 7:20–23); but it is no longer our rightful master, and it has no right to our obedience. That is why Paul can command us to resist it: we are not slaves trying to escape, but free people refusing to go back. The fight is real, but it is fought from victory.

What is the difference between falling into sin and living in it? Falling is when you are overtaken: you sin, and you know it, and it grieves you, and you go back to God and fight again (Galatians 6:1; 1 John 2:1). Living in it is when you have made peace with it: you no longer call it sin, or you call it sin and have stopped resisting, and you have arranged your life so that it can continue. A believer can fall often, and badly, and still be fighting. What Paul calls impossible for the Christian is the settled residence. If you are not sure which describes you, ask whether you are still bringing the thing to God honestly. If you are, you are not at home in it. If you have stopped, start today: the door out is still open.

For worship. Sin’s house was where we lived, and its rent was death. Christ came into that house, took its whole debt on himself, died there, and carried us out with him when he rose. He did not pardon us and leave us under the same roof; he ended the tenancy, and the old address is no longer ours.
verseByVerse.note: Paul answers a charge his teaching of grace invited.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know? Paul opens with a reminder. He is not teaching them something new. He is reminding them of something they were told at the beginning and have evidently not been using, which is the commonest condition in the Christian life. Most of us are not short of information. We are short of the habit of standing on what we already have.

Into his death. “Baptised into Christ” means united with him. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, and especially with his death: when he died, we died with him. The word that matters most is “into”: not a benefit transferred at a distance, but your being placed inside an event. What happened to Christ is reckoned to have happened to you, because you are in him, which is why this letter can say you died, and were buried, and were raised, of things that occurred in Judea before you existed.

Buried with him. Baptism pictures burial: going under the water, as into the grave (Colossians 2:12). Immersion makes the picture vivid. Burial is what a society does to confirm that a death is real and final: a man in a coma may recover; a man in the ground has been publicly given up on. Paul wants no possibility left open that the old life is merely convalescing somewhere. And Christ went down into that death first, alone, under the full weight of our sin, and lay in a borrowed grave.

By the glory of the Father. A strange phrase. Not by the power of the Father, which is what we would have written. Glory is the weight and blazing reality of who God is, so the raising of Jesus was not merely an exercise of strength but an expression of the Father’s whole character, his verdict on his Son made visible. And the same glory stands behind your newness of life. The energy available for an ordinary Christian’s Tuesday is the energy that emptied the tomb.

Newness of life. Rising from the water pictures rising with Christ. Paul does not say we were raised in order to feel new, but in order that we might walk: daily conduct, the least dramatic verb available, ordinary and repetitive, and it gets you somewhere over time. “Newness” is a new quality of life, the life of the resurrection. The new life shows itself not in one dramatic event but in the way you walk, day after day.

Where Christians differ: what does baptism do? Some see baptism as the moment when union with Christ actually happens (baptismal regeneration): Roman Catholic and Lutheran Christians say that in the rite God gives new birth and joins the person to Christ. Others, Martyn Lloyd-Jones among them, think Paul means not water baptism at all but the Spirit’s baptism into Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). This commentary’s view: Paul means water baptism, but as the sign of a union God brings about by the Spirit through faith. Paul assumes that those he addresses are believers, for whom baptism expressed their faith. Union with Christ is by faith, wrought by the Spirit (Galatians 3:26–27; Ephesians 3:17); that is why Colossians says we were raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God (Colossians 2:12), and why Abraham’s sign followed his faith (4:11). Even when Peter says that baptism now saves you, he explains at once: not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience (1 Peter 3:21). The water does not save; Christ does. The reality is union with Christ; baptism is its God-given picture. Credobaptists, who baptise only those who profess faith, see this as strong support for believers’ baptism by immersion, picturing death, burial and resurrection, and fitting a person who has already come to faith. Christians who baptise infants, many of them our dear brothers, see the sign as God’s promise to the children of believers (compare 4:11); but the dying and rising Paul describes here is something the baptised have entered by faith.

I was baptised as an infant, or I have never been baptised. What should I do? If you trust Christ and have never been baptised, be baptised: it is the Lord’s command for every disciple (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38), and this passage shows how rich a gift it is. Speak to your church’s pastor. If you were baptised as an infant and have since come to faith, this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, and so would encourage you to be baptised as a believer. Do it humbly, without contempt for the parents and church who brought you as a child in love and obedience as they understood it. Either way, the main thing is not the water but the union it declares: if you are in Christ, you have died and risen with him.

In everyday life. Take the sin you fight most often, and notice what you say to yourself in the moment of temptation. If it is only “I must not”, that is a fence, and fences are climbed. Paul’s argument supplies a different sentence: “I am not that man any longer; that man is buried.” It is not a stronger effort; it is a truer description. Remember your baptism today.

parallels.desc: buried with him in baptism

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
United with him. The word Paul chooses for our union (symphytoi) is not a legal term at all. It means closely joined, and it comes from a verb for growing together, so the picture is of living things, as when a shoot is grafted into the stock of another tree and the two come to share one life. What happens to the tree happens to the branch, because the branch is now living on sap it did not produce. His death is your death for the same reason that his life is your life.
