A resurrection like his. Both now, in new life, and at the last day, in a resurrection body. The second clause follows from the first without further condition: you cannot be grafted into a living tree and share only its dying. Nobody has ever been joined to Christ for the funeral and excluded from the resurrection.

Our old self. The “old self” (palaios anthrōpos, literally old man) is the person we were in Adam, before conversion (Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9). The idea is simpler than the phrase: Adam acted for the whole human race, so everyone born of him shares his guilt and his bent away from God (5:12, 19); the old self is simply you as you were in that family, before God joined you to Christ. Paul does not say the old self is being crucified gradually. It “was crucified with him” (compare Galatians 2:20): a completed fact. Christ took our old self with him to Golgotha and did not bring it back.

If my old self was crucified, why does it keep getting up? The question every honest reader asks. Paul says the old man is dead. My experience says he was in the kitchen this morning, in a bad temper, saying something unkind. Either the doctrine is false or something has been misunderstood. Two distinctions clear it. The first is between the old self and remaining sin. The old self is not a part of you, like a compartment or a shadow self that survives alongside the new one. Paul’s phrase means the entire person you were, defined by Adam. That person is dead: you no longer stand in Adam, the old authority over you has ended, the man who belonged to Adam has been executed. What remains is not the old self but the habits, appetites and reflexes he trained into a body over many years, and those are a different thing. A country can change its government overnight; the officials who served the old regime are still in their offices on Monday morning, still know the procedures, and will carry on running things exactly as before unless somebody stops them. Their authority is gone. Their filing cabinets are not.

Brought to nothing. The second distinction is in Paul’s own words. “Body of sin” is the person as controlled by sin. “Brought to nothing” (katargēthē) means rendered powerless, put out of action, put out of a job. Not annihilated, but stripped of its power. Paul is careful. He does not say sin is gone, or that its pull has ceased, or that you will not lose to it this week. He says it has been deposed. And a deposed power that still has adherents in the country is exactly what you experience every day: real fighting, genuine losses, and a war whose outcome is not in question.

The fight is evidence of life. This changes what the struggle means, and here lies the comfort for a reader discouraged by his own life. The presence of a fight is not evidence that the doctrine has failed; it is evidence that there are two parties. A man wholly under sin’s dominion does not fight it. He is not conflicted about it; he simply lives, and the accusations that trouble you would not trouble him. So the very thing that makes you doubt this passage, that you find yourself resisting, grieving, getting up again, is the thing the passage predicts. You are not failing to be dead. You are experiencing the resistance of a regime that has already lost.

No longer enslaved. Freedom is the aim, not merely forgiveness. The verse is not describing a man who has been pardoned and left in the same condition. It is describing a man who has been taken out of service, freed from an owner who has not yet accepted the verdict.

Will the struggle ever end? Yes. In this life it changes: battles that were fierce at the beginning often become quieter as the Spirit works and old habits are starved, though new ones appear, and some believers fight one besetting sin for decades. But the fight is not permanent. When a believer dies, his soul is made perfect in holiness and goes at once to be with Christ (Hebrews 12:23; Philippians 1:23), and at the resurrection his body is raised incorruptible (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Then the presence of sin will be gone as completely as its reign is gone now. Every resisted temptation today is the rehearsal of that freedom. The war you are in has an end date, and it is fixed by the God who has already won it.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set free from sin. “Set free” (dedikaiōtai) is literally “has been justified”, the court word of chapters 3 to 5. A dead man is released from all claims; the law has nothing more to say to him. Ancient law took it for granted that death dissolves obligation: a creditor may pursue a debtor across three provinces and has no case against a corpse. Because we have died with Christ, sin has no more legal claim on us.

Stronger than a debt written off. We tend to imagine forgiveness as a debt written off by a generous creditor, which is true. But Paul’s point here is stronger: the debtor has died. Sin is not standing at the counter having its claim graciously waived; it is standing at the counter discovering that the man it came for is not available, and never will be.

We believe. Union with his death guarantees union with his life. Then Paul’s tone changes: after arguing from baptism, burial and grafting, he says “we believe”. The death is behind us and can be argued from; the life with him is ahead and has to be trusted. The difficulty is believing that this ends well for you, that there is a life on the far side of your own grave, with him, in a body. Paul offers a link: if the first is true of you, the second follows, and the two cannot be separated because they are one union with one Person. He lives, and he will not live without those he died for.

Dated and undated. The promise is future, but it hangs on a past event. Your death with Christ has a date, the day he died. Your life with him beyond the grave has no date yet, and is no less certain.

When will I live with him: now, at death, or at the resurrection? All three, in order. Now, you share his risen life by the Spirit (v. 4; Ephesians 2:5–6). At death, your soul goes immediately to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8); there is no sleep of the soul and no purgatory in between. And at his return, your body will be raised and you will live with him, body and soul, for ever in the new creation (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Paul’s we will also live with him reaches all the way to that last day, but it begins the moment you are joined to him. Death interrupts the body’s part in it; it never interrupts your being with him.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at Christ. Paul has been making claims about us, and a reader might ask how firm they are. So he spends two verses on Christ: everything the chapter asserts about your security rests on facts about somebody else’s history. If you want to know how permanent your position is, do not examine your position. Examine his.

Never die again. That had never been true of anyone before. Lazarus came out of a tomb and in time died again; every previous raising in Scripture was a reprieve. The resurrection of Jesus is the only one in history that did not end in a second funeral. Death has been in charge of every human story ever told, and it lost one, permanently. He has conquered death for ever, and holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

No longer dominion. Death exercised its authority over him from the Friday until the third day, and then lost it for ever.

He died to sin. The phrase cannot mean for him exactly what it means for us. We die to sin as men leaving a dominion that owned us. He had never sinned and was never owned. He entered its territory voluntarily, bore its full penalty, and when it was paid, that transaction was complete and is now permanently behind him. Sin has no further business with him at all. That is why the same words can be used of believers in verse 2: joined to him, they too have passed out of sin’s realm, though sin still lives in them until the resurrection.

Once for all. Ephapax: a single, final act, never to be repeated (Hebrews 7:27; 9:12; 10:10). Not once so far, but once and therefore never again; and a thing that must be repeated has not worked. The old sacrificial system ran on repetition precisely because nothing was ever finished; priests stood day after day offering the same sacrifices, which could never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11), and the queue outside was made of the same people. This death ended the queue.

Why it matters for you. If you are in him, then sin’s claim on you was settled in the same transaction, and it cannot be reopened for the same reason it cannot be reopened against him. Your security is not that you have moved beyond sin’s reach by your own progress. It is that the account was closed on a Friday in Jerusalem and the receipt was issued on the Sunday, and neither can be recalled.

If Christ died once for all, what are we doing at the Lord’s Supper? Remembering and proclaiming that death, not repeating it. The Supper is not a fresh offering of Christ, as the Roman Catholic Mass teaches; Hebrews insists that he offered himself once, and that where there is forgiveness there is no longer any offering for sin (Hebrews 10:10–18). At the table the church proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), and believers feed on Christ by faith, receiving afresh the benefits of a sacrifice already finished. The bread and cup do not add to the cross. They point to it, and the Spirit uses them to strengthen your hold on what it accomplished.

To God. Not against sin, not in reaction to it: to God. His dealing with sin is finished; what remains is a life lived wholly towards his Father.

In everyday life. When you are anxious about your standing with God, notice where you go looking: at the state of your faith, the quality of last week. Those things fluctuate, so the anxiety never settles. The next time the accusation comes, the question is not “How am I doing?” but “Is he still risen?” There is only one possible answer, and it does not depend on your week.

For worship. The risen Lord has no second death ahead of him. He lives now wholly to his Father, he lives for ever, and everyone in him lives with him. The wounds are still on him. They are the only scars in existence that no longer mean anything is wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider yourselves. The first of the letter’s great commands to believers. “Consider” (logizesthe) is the accountant’s word: to reckon, enter in the books. The same verb ran through chapter 4, eleven times in twenty-five verses, where Abraham believed God and it was “counted to him as righteousness”. Now Paul takes the same verb and turns it round: God has been doing the reckoning all this time, and here he tells you to do some.

Not pretending, but counting on what is true. It is not visualisation or talking yourself into a mood. An accountant who enters a sum that is not in the account is committing fraud; the entry is only honest if the money is there. So Paul is not asking you to pretend you are dead to sin. He is telling you to write down what is already the case, the same operation God performed when he credited righteousness that was genuinely Christ’s to people who genuinely had none. Reckoning never creates the fact. It aligns the books with it. The books have been correct in heaven since the cross, and the One who keeps them has written our names beside his Son’s.

The first command. Ten verses of what is true of you, and only then something to do, and it is an act of the mind: not “become what you are not”, but “be what you are”. Paul begins not with “fight harder” but with “believe something about yourself”, on the grounds that a man who does not know who he is will fight the wrong war his whole life.

Alive to God. The two halves must be held together. Most attempts at holiness are only about giving things up, and they fail, because a life cannot be built around what is missing from it. Paul’s reckoning has a positive half: you are alive to God, which means available to him, responsive to him, in the room with him. The man who fights sin without cultivating that will find sin winning on ground he has left empty. And all of it is in Christ Jesus: not a state you hold by yourself, but what you are in him.

Let not sin reign. The sober half: the command assumes that sin, though overthrown, tries every day to take back its rule. What is forbidden is not the presence of sin (chapter 7 shows why that is not yet on offer) but its reign: whether it is giving orders that are being obeyed. A defeated army in the hills is a serious nuisance and a genuine danger. It is not the government. “Mortal body” means the body still subject to death and temptation, not yet glorified.

Its passions. Passions are sinful desires, and Paul shows how sin uses them. Sin has no power to compel a Christian; what it has is persuasion, and its method is to present a desire as though it were an instruction. That is why temptation so rarely feels like a summons from an enemy and so often feels like simply wanting something. The lie is not usually about the thing desired. It is about you: the suggestion that you have no real choice, that this is just how you are, that resistance is theoretical.

Is my body the problem? No. The body is God’s good creation, the Son of God took one, and it will be raised (8:11, 23). Paul is not teaching that the physical is evil, as some ancient philosophies did. He calls it the mortal body because it is still subject to death and is the arena where the daily battle is fought: sin works through bodily appetites, habits and senses. So the answer is not contempt for the body but rule over it, for God. Sleep, food, exercise and avoiding needless temptation are not unspiritual; they are part of keeping the battlefield in good order. Your body is not the enemy. It is the ground both sides want.

In everyday life. Next time you are tempted, do not begin by measuring how strong the pull is. Say two sentences to yourself, in words: “I am dead to this. I am alive to God in Christ.” Then see what happens to the temptation when it has been named as an ex-employer making a request rather than a master issuing an order. It may not evaporate, but it will have been correctly classified, and a great deal of the Christian fight is simply refusing to accept a false description of who you are. Then turn to God with the next thing you do, leaning not on your resolve but on the Spirit of him who raised Jesus, who now lives in you (8:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two tenses. The two commands have different tenses in Greek. The first is a standing prohibition: do not go on presenting your members to sin, describing a habit already in progress that must be broken. The second is a decisive act: present yourselves to God, once and definitely. One is the daily refusal of an old habit; the other is a handing over that a man can name and date.

Members. The word is not a vague term for the self; it means the parts of the body, and Paul means them literally: hands, eyes, tongue, feet, the physical equipment you actually sin and serve with. Holiness in Romans 6 is not primarily a state of mind. It is what your hands did this afternoon.

Instruments. The other word (hopla) can mean tools, but in Paul it more often means weapons: the equipment issued to a soldier. Your body is not neutral territory; it will be used by one side or the other today, and there is no third option in which it is used by nobody. Do not put it at sin’s service.

Brought from death to life. A phrase about corpses. A man does not present a dead body to God for useful service; the thing has to be raised first, and it has been. So the surrender Paul asks for is the natural act of somebody who has been given a life he did not have and is now deciding what to do with it.

How do I actually present my members to God? Make it as concrete as Paul does, and go through them. Your eyes: what you choose to look at tonight, and what you refuse; whether you notice the lonely person at church. Your tongue: the conversation you will not join, the encouragement you will speak, the truth you will tell. Your hands: the work done honestly, the help given, the phone put down. Your feet: where you go and where you will not go. Begin the day by offering them to God in a sentence of prayer (12:1), and when you fail, offer them again rather than giving up. The act is renewed daily, but it is not complicated.

No dominion. After the commands, a promise: not “sin ought not to have dominion”, but sin “will have no dominion”. You will still struggle with it (7:14–25), but it will not rule you. That is a sentence to take to bed on the evening of a bad failure.

Not under law but under grace. The reason is the opposite of what any serious person would expect. Every instinct says that a man who sins needs more law. Paul says law, as the way to be right with God, is precisely what keeps sin in power. It tells you what is right and supplies no ability to do it; it provokes what it forbids (5:20); and it leaves you under a condemnation that makes real repentance almost impossible, because a man who believes he is one failure away from being finished cannot afford to look honestly at himself. Grace dismantles that arrangement. To be under grace is to live under God’s favour, which both forgives and gives strength. The King who brought us from death to life does not stand over us with a list and a whip; he asks for our hands and eyes and tongues because he has already given us his own.

In the flow. The words “not under law but under grace” at once provoke the second objection (v. 15), and the larger question of what the law was for, which chapter 7 answers.

Where Christians differ: not under law? Antinomians (from the Greek for against law) take this to mean believers have no obligation to God’s moral law. This commentary’s view: the very next verse asks, are we to sin because we are not under law? and answers, by no means! Not under law means not under its condemnation or as the means of justification. Believers are under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21) and fulfil the law by love (13:8–10). Paul has just given three commands in two verses, and he will give many more before the letter ends.

What it does not mean. Being under grace does not mean you will not sin. It means that your standing does not depend on your performance, and therefore your failures cannot destroy you, and therefore you are finally free to fight them without terror, which is the only condition in which anybody has ever fought them successfully.

In everyday life. When you fail badly, notice what you reach for as the remedy: a tightened rule, a new system, a resolution with more teeth, a private undertaking to be stricter. Paul’s remedy runs the other way: go back to what is true of you, brought from death to life, not under law, and present the same members again today. It feels too easy because it costs nothing in self-punishment, the one payment sin is always happy to accept.
verseByVerse.note: “Members” means the parts of the body, such as hands, eyes and tongue, used for good or evil.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Slaves of Righteousness: Freedom and Its Direction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verse 15 asks the question again in a new form: if we are not under law, may we sin now and then? Paul again refuses: everyone serves someone, either sin, which leads to death, or God, whose service leads to holiness and eternal life. The section ends with the contrast between a wage and a gift: death is earned, eternal life is given, and it is given only in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace and the New Obedience

Romans 6:15–23 shows that grace does not produce lawlessness but a new obedience, one that comes from a changed heart rather than from fear. Calvin insisted that the justified are not released from obedience but freed for it. The law no longer condemns them; it guides them, as the will of the God they now love.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Slavery was part of everyday life in the Roman world, so Paul’s first readers knew at once what it meant to be owned. His point is arresting: you were a slave before and you are a slave now; the only question is whose. Now: Our culture prizes the right to answer to no one. Romans 6 says everyone serves something, whether appetite, ambition, approval or comfort. The gospel does not offer escape from every master; it offers the one Master worth serving.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! A second form of the objection (v. 1), and the difference matters. There the question was “Are we to continue in sin”: shall we stay where we are? Here it is “Are we to sin”: not live in sin, but commit a single act, take an occasional liberty. It is the reasonable-sounding idea that if the law is no longer my master then the odd indulgence costs nothing. It is the more plausible objection of the two, and it usually comes in the form “this once will not matter”. It receives the same categorical answer.

What obedience does. Paul does not argue about the size of the act. You belong to what you obey, because that is what obedience is. Each act of yielding is a small act of enlistment. So the question “Can I get away with this once?” is the wrong question entirely: the issue was never whether you would be caught but what you were becoming while you did it. Hardly anyone decides to become an alcoholic; whatever else contributes, a man decides, several thousand times, to have a drink. Habits are formed not by decisions about habits but by decisions about single occasions.

There is no third option. Everyone serves someone. There is no neutral freedom (Matthew 6:24; John 8:34). Paul offers two masters and no independent territory; serving nothing is not presented as a possibility at all. The man who has thrown off every external authority is not thereby unruled; he is ruled by his appetites, and appetites are the least merciful masters available, because they never say thank you and never say enough.

The Son who sets slaves free. Jesus reasoned this way before Paul did. Everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, he said; the slave does not remain in the house for ever, but the son remains for ever, and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). And the Son did it by becoming the obedient servant himself: he took the form of a slave and was obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:7–8), and that obedience is the righteousness counted to his people (5:19).

Two destinations. We use freedom to mean the absence of constraint. Paul uses it to mean being under the right authority: being owned by the one for whom you were made, which is the only condition in which any creature functions properly. A fish in a net is constrained; a fish on a riverbank is free of the water and dying of it.

Can a Christian give himself back to sin and so lose his salvation? Arminian Christians (who hold that a true believer can finally fall away) read the verse that way: a believer who keeps presenting himself to sin becomes its slave again, and the end of that road is death. But Paul is describing two kinds of people, not one person changing sides. He goes straight on: you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart (v. 17). A Christian still sins, sometimes badly, but sin is no longer his master (v. 14). Someone who gives himself to sin without struggle or repentance is not showing that he has lost his salvation; he is raising the question whether he ever had it (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and God uses it to keep his own, from whose love nothing can separate them (8:38–39). Many Arminian Christians love Christ deeply, and this difference is held among brothers. And if you are afraid that you are the person this warns, that very fear shows you are not at peace with sin, which is the mark of those he keeps.

In everyday life. Over the last month, what actually decided your choices at the points where it cost you something? Trace three or four real decisions back to their reasons: the evening, the money, the awkward conversation. Whatever turns up repeatedly at the end of those chains is a master, whether or not you would ever have used the word. Bring what you find to Christ, and give the next of those decisions to him.

For worship. Everyone serves a master, and ours bought us. We were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), and the price was the blood of the Master himself, who died for the slave. He purchased us to keep, and the service he asks is the service of sons in their Father’s house. Sin took our obedience and paid in death; he takes it and gives back life.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God. A spontaneous doxology in the middle of an argument. These Christians have turned from a wicked past and now obey from the heart, and Paul does not congratulate them. He thanks God. It follows from everything the chapter has argued: a slave does not transfer himself, and a dead man does not decide to be raised. If they are obeying from the heart, it is because they were given a different heart, and the right response to somebody else’s work is gratitude rather than applause.

From the heart. Not outward conformity, but inner obedience, the new covenant promised by the prophets, the law written on the heart and a new spirit within (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27). Slaves in the ancient world obeyed with their hands; nobody expected a slave to agree. Paul says these slaves obey from the heart, which no picture of slavery can hold, and that is exactly his point. The new Master has done something no owner has ever managed: he has changed what the servant wants.

The standard of teaching. “Standard” (typos) is a pattern, a mould: the die into which molten metal is poured, or the stamp that leaves its shape on a coin. We would say the teaching was delivered to them; Paul says they were handed over to the teaching. The gospel is not a substance you take possession of and store; it is a shape you are poured into, and what comes out bears the impression of the mould.

Doctrine as a mould. If teaching is a mould, what you steadily attend to will steadily form you, whether or not you are trying. That is why a Christian cannot be indifferent to what is taught where he attends: he is being shaped by it.

The likeness the mould leaves. The pattern of teaching is not a list of statements with no person behind it. Its centre is Christ crucified and risen, and the shape it presses into those poured into it is his. That is where this letter is heading: those God foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (8:29). So obedience from the heart is not a believer reproducing a code. It is the features of the Son beginning to show in an ordinary life, as the image on a die comes up on the coin.

Slaves of righteousness. Christian freedom is not independence but a new, good slavery to the Master who made us for himself. Doing right is no longer an optional extra you may decline, as it was when you served sin (v. 20). It now has a claim on you, the claim of the One you belong to, and because he has changed your heart you increasingly find you want to answer it (Ezekiel 36:27).

What if my obedience feels mostly like duty? Almost nobody obeys from the heart perfectly or consistently; motives in this life come mixed, and a man who waits until his are pure before he acts will never act at all. Doing the right thing when you do not feel like it is not hypocrisy; it is often love choosing God over a mood. The right response to discovering mixed motives is not to stop obeying but to bring them, mixed, to the God who is changing them, and to ask him to make you love what he commands. And notice, as evidence, that you mind about the mixture at all. A slave who merely complies does not lie awake examining his sincerity.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In human terms. Paul has built an entire argument on slavery, and now he half-withdraws it, not because the metaphor is wrong but because it is inadequate in one direction. Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the Roman church were probably slaves or former slaves (several names in chapter 16 were common among slaves), and Paul uses an image they knew. But no image drawn from a brutal human institution can carry what it is like to belong to God. Slavery communicates ownership, obligation and total claim, all of which are true. It cannot communicate that the Master is a Father, that the service is freedom, or that the slave is loved. That is a useful rule for reading every biblical image: find what it was chosen to convey, and do not make it say what it was never built to say.

Because of your natural limitations. Literally, “the weakness of your flesh”, that is, your human weakness. He is not insulting them: we are creatures who think in pictures, and God has arranged his book accordingly: it is full of vineyards, sheep, courtrooms, marriages and slaves rather than definitions.

More lawlessness. A diagnosis of how sin works over time: the result of serving impurity was not satisfaction but more lawlessness. Sin escalates. What served last year does not serve this year; the dose that once produced an effect produces nothing, and the appetite that was fed has grown by being fed. Anyone who has watched an addiction recognises the mechanism, and it is not confined to the obvious vices. Pornography is the plainest modern example because the escalation is so measurable, and it is the same law that operates in a man’s ambition or his temper. Sin cannot be kept at a fixed level by an act of will, because growing is not something that goes wrong with sin. It is what sin does.

Leading to sanctification. The other direction has a slope too. Righteousness leads to sanctification: growing holiness, the gradual turning of the whole person towards God. Holiness also builds on itself. The thing you resisted with difficulty at thirty is not the same size at fifty, not because you have become impressive but because the Spirit, through ten thousand small refusals, has worn a channel. Neither slope is fast. Both are real. And the God who made us did not leave us on the downward one: he came down it himself, all the way to the bottom, and lifted us onto another road, where his grace compounds as surely as sin once did.

Free in regard to righteousness. Paul speaks with bitter irony: as slaves of sin you were “free”, but only in the sense that righteousness had no hold on you. That was the freedom on offer, and the previous verse has described where it was heading. Remember it the next time freedom is presented as an escape from God’s claims.

Is it demeaning to call ourselves slaves of God? It would be if the Master were like human masters. He is not. Human slavery, especially as it was practised in Rome and later in the Atlantic trade, was a terrible evil, and Paul knows its cruelty. He borrows only one thing from it: total belonging. Everything else the Bible says about this Master reverses the institution. He bought his slaves with his own blood, he calls them friends (John 15:15) and sons (8:15), he serves them at table (Luke 12:37), and his yoke is easy (Matthew 11:30). To be his is not to lose your dignity but to find it, because you were made for him. The only truly degrading slavery is the one Paul has just described.

In everyday life. Measure direction rather than position. Take something you struggle with and compare it not with last week but with five years ago. Is it costing you more to sin than it used to, or less? Does it take more to satisfy it, or less? And on the other side: is there anything that used to be a battle and is now largely settled, not because you gave up, but because it stopped being a live question? Those two answers together will tell you which slope you are standing on far more accurately than an audit of the last seven days.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the church were slaves or former slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? Paul invites a backward look, and he does it by asking, not lecturing: the answer is meant to come from the reader. It is the question sin never invites you to ask, because sin lives entirely in the future tense. Its whole method is anticipation: what this will feel like, what it will settle, how much better the evening will be. It has nothing whatever to say about the morning after, and it never volunteers a retrospective. So Paul makes them look backwards, and the answer he expects is not a list of pleasures regretted but something starker: nothing. The Greek can be read so that the honest answer to his question is that there was none. Not bad fruit: no fruit. Sin is not an alternative crop; it is a season of work with an empty barn at the end of it, and the only thing left in the hand is the shame.

The honest inventory. Everyone reading this has the material. Think of something you did that you would not want said aloud. Now ask what it actually yielded. Not what it promised: what you have, now, as a result. Almost always the honest inventory reads the same way: an hour that no longer exists, a relationship altered by a degree nobody else noticed, a memory that arrives uninvited years later while you are doing something else. That is the harvest, and it is why Paul does not need to argue the point; he only has to ask the question and wait. It is worth writing down before the next temptation comes, because sin will only ever tell you about tonight.

Ashamed. The word is chosen carefully, because shame has a particular character that guilt does not. Guilt says I did something bad; shame says I cannot look at it. It is the impulse to turn the face away, which is exactly what Adam did in the garden, and exactly why sin requires concealment to survive. A man does not hide what has done him good.

The shame he carried. Shame was the one thing sin left in our hands, and Christ took it out of them. Crucifixion was designed to shame, the death of slaves. Jesus endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), not because it did not hurt but because he counted it worth bearing for the joy set before him. That is why a believer can look back at what he is now ashamed of without being destroyed by it: the shame is real, but it has been carried, and the face Adam turned away in the garden can be lifted to God again.

What it does not mean. A backward look can be turned into a weapon against the wrong person. Paul describes Christians looking back at a life they have left, in one sentence, and moves on to the fruit they are bearing now. If you are a believer who cannot stop rehearsing an old sin, replaying it at night, unable to let it be finished, this verse is not asking that of you. The shame here has a purpose, and the purpose is not to punish you. It is meant to make the old master look like what he is, and then you are meant to look at the new one. Chapter 8 will say “There is therefore now no condemnation”, and it will not add “except for that”.

Slaves of God. The same four stages run in both directions: a master, a service, a fruit, and an end, shame and death, or sanctification and eternal life. Only the master changes, and everything after follows from that. That is why this chapter has spent twenty verses on ownership rather than on techniques for behaving better. Change the master and the rest of the chain changes with him.

Two harvests. Sanctification is the road; eternal life is the end. No one reaches the end without the road (Hebrews 12:14). And the image is agricultural: fruit is slow, and it is not produced by the branch straining. It appears because the tree is alive and attached and has been standing in the right place for long enough, which is the honest answer to any Christian discouraged by how gradual his own sanctification looks. You are growing, and growth is not visible on the timescale at which we tend to inspect ourselves.

Then is eternal life earned by holiness? No. Paul will say in the very next verse that eternal life is a gift. Holiness is not the price of heaven but the road that leads there, and God himself lays the road. Those he justifies he also sanctifies (8:29–30; Philippians 1:6), so that no one who is truly his arrives at the end without having been changed on the way. That is the point of Hebrews 12:14: not that we must become holy enough to deserve to see the Lord, but that the people who see him are people he has been making holy. If you are in Christ, the fruit is coming, slowly and surely, because the life in the branch is his.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 6:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wages. The word for wages (opsōnia) was often used of a soldier’s pay: the ration money paid out to troops, issued at intervals, the small regular allowance a man drew for his service. Sin pays, and its pay is death: physical, spiritual, eternal. If Paul has the soldier’s pay in view, sin does not pay its people in a single catastrophic settlement at the end. It pays them in instalments, on time, throughout the campaign.

Paid as you go. We imagine death as the bill arriving at the end of a long life. But sin has been paying you all along, in the currency it deals in: the friendship that thinned and was never repaired, the capacity for wonder that dulled, the prayer that got harder to say, the person you can no longer be honest with. They are the wage, paid in small coin, on schedule; the final payment is the same currency, in full.

Is death really what every sin deserves, and does it mean hell? Yes, and the reason is not the size of the act but the greatness of the One sinned against. Every sin is treason against the infinitely holy God, the Fountain of all life, and turning from him is turning from life itself. So the death sin earns is not only the grave. It is the second death (Revelation 20:14), conscious and eternal separation from God’s goodness under his just wrath, which Jesus himself described more often than anyone (Matthew 25:46; Mark 9:48). That is sobering, and it should be. But Paul does not state the wage to crush you. He states it so that you will see the size of the gift beside it.

The free gift. Paul breaks his own parallel, as in chapter 5. Nobody has ever earned a wage of eternal life, so he changes the noun. Not wages, but a gift (charisma, a gift of grace). Death is earned; life is given. And what God gives is not merely a longer life or a better one but his own Son, and with him eternal life, the very life of God shared with the creature who had earned only death. The two halves of the sentence do not balance, and the whole gospel is in the imbalance.

Hell is earned and heaven is not. So the two ends are not reached in the same way. Nobody will be in hell who did not earn it, and nobody will be in heaven who did. That sentence offends most people the first time they meet it, but it is the only arrangement in which God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, which is precisely what this letter has been arguing since 3:26.

In Christ Jesus our Lord. The verse ends not with a benefit but with a name. Eternal life is not a commodity God hands over for you to possess independently, like a sum of money taken home. It is in a Person, the One who is himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). To receive eternal life is to receive Christ; whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). It is not stored anywhere you could lose it. To have it, you must have him; and if you have him, you cannot have less of it than he has.

Our Lord. The last word of the chapter is Lord, and it is not a flourish. After two masters, two slaveries, two harvests and two ends, Paul names the owner. The chapter has been about who you belong to, and it closes by saying so.

In the flow. Paul brings chapters 5, 6, 7 and 8 each to its climax on almost the same words, Jesus Christ our Lord (5:21; 6:23; 7:25; 8:39), as if justification, holiness, the law and the Spirit all come home to the same Person. What then of the law? Chapter 7 takes it up.

How do I receive the gift? The way any gift is received: by taking it, not by paying for it. Turn from trusting yourself, and trust Christ Jesus, who died for sinners and rose again, as your Saviour and your Lord. Tell him so, in your own words. You do not need to tidy your life first; a gift that required qualifications would be a wage. The gift is as hard for the respectable to take as for the guilty, because it means admitting that a lifetime of decency has bought nothing; and it is as open to the worst as to the best. And if you have already received him, go on receiving: the gift is not a single transaction you once completed but a Person you live with, and every day you may come back to him and find that life in him is still yours.

In everyday life. Ask which half of the verse you expect to receive, and why. If your reason contains anything about yourself, that you have tried, that you believe the right things, that you are not as bad as some, you have answered from the first half of the sentence, where things are earned. The only answer the verse permits is a name that is not yours, and that name is enough. Then look at the people around you: each is drawing a wage or receiving a gift. Pray for one of them by name, and be ready to tell them where the gift is found.
verseByVerse.note: Wages were the regular pay of a soldier or labourer: what is earned. A gift is not.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?<sup>2</sup>By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?<sup>3</sup>Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?<sup>4</sup>We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.<sup>5</sup>For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.<sup>6</sup>We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.<sup>7</sup>For one who has died has been set free from sin.<sup>8</sup>Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.<sup>9</sup>We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.<sup>10</sup>For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.<sup>11</sup>So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.<sup>12</sup>Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.<sup>13</sup>Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness.<sup>14</sup>For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.<sup>15</sup>What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!<sup>16</sup>Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?<sup>17</sup>But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed,<sup>18</sup>and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.<sup>19</sup>I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification.<sup>20</sup>For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.<sup>21</sup>But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.<sup>22</sup>But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.<sup>23</sup>For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 has two parts. Verses 1–6 use marriage to explain the believer’s release from the law: death ends a marriage, and through Christ’s death believers have died to the law’s claim, so that they now belong to the risen Christ. Verses 7–25 defend the law as holy and good, show how sin used it, and describe with great honesty a man who loves God’s law and still finds sin at work in him.

Christians have long debated whether that man is Paul before or after his conversion. Following Augustine in his later writings, Luther and Calvin, this commentary reads him as a believer: no unconverted person delights in God’s law in his inner being (v. 22). The chapter ends with thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A wife is bound to her husband while he lives, and free to marry again if he dies. In the same way, believers have died to the law through Christ’s death. They belong to Christ, raised from the dead, so that they may bear fruit for God.

The law is not bad, but it was never the means of life: meeting a sinful heart, it provokes what it forbids; it can show sin but cannot remove it. Now believers serve in the new way of the Spirit, the new covenant in which God writes his law on the heart, and the motive has changed from fear to love.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

Dying to the law (vv. 4, 6) does not release the Christian from its moral content; chapters 12–15 will show that love fulfils the law (13:8–10). What has changed is the believer’s relationship to it. Calvin called this the third use of the law: a guide for the redeemed, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s readers knew marriage law well, so the illustration needed no explaining. The startling part was the death that ended the marriage: the believer’s death with Christ. Now: Many Christians still live as though married to the law, haunted by condemnation and worn out by religious duty. These verses declare their freedom: serve Christ from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Believers have died to the law through Christ, as a widow is released from her marriage, so that they belong to Christ and serve in the new way of the Spirit (vv. 1–6). The law is holy, righteous and good, but sin used it to provoke and kill (vv. 7–13). Then Paul describes one who loves God’s law but still finds sin at work in him, and cries out for deliverance (vv. 14–25). The chapter that goes deepest into the misery of the human heart ends not with a method but with a person: Jesus Christ our Lord (v. 25).

Those who know the law. Jews, and God-fearing Gentiles familiar with Moses. Paul argues from something his readers already grant, and that respect runs through the chapter: he will insist that the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). Whatever he says about being released from the law, he is not disparaging it. He is explaining how a good thing can be the wrong thing to be married to.

In the flow. Chapter 7 explains the phrase of 6:14, “not under law but under grace”. Chapter 6 showed that a believer died to sin; now Paul shows that he died to the law too, which a Jewish reader would find the harder saying. Verse 5 is opened out in verses 7–25, and verse 6 in chapter 8. The law cannot make us right with God (3:20), and it cannot make us holy either; only Christ and his Spirit can.

Only as long as he lives. A basic legal principle, ancient and modern: death ends a person’s legal obligations.

Why marriage? Paul has debt and slavery available and has used both already in this letter. He picks marriage, which is the Old Testament’s own picture of God’s covenant with his people. The Lord is the husband, Israel is the wife, and her idolatry is adultery; Hosea was told to marry a woman who would betray him so the nation could see what it had done. So the illustration carries what a lesson about debt could not: exclusive belonging, a covenant rather than a contract, and, as verse 4 will say, fruitfulness. Marriages are meant to produce something.

The pieces do not line up, and need not. In the illustration the husband dies and the wife goes free; in the application it is not the law that dies: “you also have died to the law” (v. 4). Paul is not building an allegory in which every detail matches. He is establishing one principle, that death dissolves legal obligation, and applying it. Whoever does the dying, the bond is over.

Married to the law. A great many Christians are, in practice, still married to the law, and people living in that marriage rarely name it. It is life with a spouse who is never satisfied. He is not wrong; every criticism he makes is accurate. He notices everything you fail at, never says well done, and offers no help. And you cannot leave, because he is entirely in the right and you have nothing to plead. That is religion under law, and it produces exactly what you would expect: a conscientious person, permanently tired, who cannot enjoy God and cannot admit it.

A husband born under the law. The remedy is not that the first spouse lowers his standards; the law is holy and stays holy. The remedy is that the marriage has ended by a death, and you are joined to another, “to him who has been raised from the dead” (v. 4). God sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). Christ stepped inside the very bond that held us. He lived under that exacting spouse all his life without a single complaint against him, and then bore the curse the law pronounces on everyone who fails it (Galatians 3:13). The one we now belong to is not waiting to be satisfied. He has already satisfied everything the first husband required.

So do the Ten Commandments no longer apply to me? They still apply, but not as a husband you must satisfy to be accepted. Through Christ you died to the law as a covenant of works: its demand that you earn life by keeping it, and its sentence of condemnation when you do not. That relationship is over. But the moral law has not been abolished. It still shows what love for God and neighbour looks like, and Paul will quote the commandments to Christians as the shape of the life they now live (13:8–10). The difference is that you now keep them as a wife who is loved, by the Spirit’s help (8:4), and not as a debtor trying to stay in credit. The Reformers called this the third use of the law: a guide for the redeemed, not the price of heaven.

In everyday life. A woman long married to a severe man often goes on bracing for his criticism years after the funeral. So take an ordinary act of obedience this week, your praying, your giving, your Sunday, and ask honestly which husband it is being done for. To stay in credit, or because you belong to somebody and want to be with him? The act is identical in both marriages. In Christ you died to the law’s condemnation; whatever is left of the old marriage in you, bring it to the new husband, who is not waiting to be satisfied.

parallels.desc: a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adulteress. Not a technical irregularity, but the strongest word available for covenant betrayal. The law’s claim is that serious.

If her husband dies. The same act is treachery in one circumstance and blameless in the other, and the only thing that has changed is a death. Her character and history are the same; what has changed is her standing before the law, and that is not a matter of degree. She is either bound or free. Christians are not people whom the law is gradually letting off as they improve: the change is a change of category, complete on the day of the death.

Free to belong. The woman is “free from that law”: not from all law, not from marriage, and certainly not free to belong to nobody. She is free to be married again. Freedom in this passage is always freedom to be attached to someone new.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Some use these verses to say remarriage after divorce is never allowed while a former spouse lives. This commentary’s view: Paul is using marriage as an illustration, not giving a full teaching on divorce. Marriage is meant to be for life. Elsewhere Scripture allows divorce for adultery (Matthew 19:9) and for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (1 Corinthians 7:15), and in those cases the innocent party may remarry. This is the Westminster position (Westminster 24.5–6). Whether persistent, serious abuse amounts to such desertion is for the elders to weigh in each case; but the abused should seek safety at once, no one is ever required to stay where they or their children are in danger, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered. Divorce is always a tragedy, to be avoided where possible.

I am divorced and remarried, and not on those grounds. What now? Do not undo your present marriage. It is a real marriage, made with vows before God, and the way forward is to keep it faithfully, not to break a second covenant to atone for the first (compare Deuteronomy 24:1–4, where returning to a former spouse is forbidden). If there was sin in how the first marriage ended or the second began, name it to God plainly, put right what can still be put right, such as care for children or honesty with those you wronged, and then believe the gospel about it. The blood of Christ cleanses that sin as fully as any other (1 John 1:7). And speak with your pastor; you should not carry it alone.

Lawful, not tolerated. Some Christians carry a low-level sense that their happiness in Christ is somehow illegitimate, that a stricter accounting would find them out. Look at the woman in her second marriage: she is not being tolerated. Your standing with Christ is not a generous arrangement that would collapse under scrutiny. It is lawful. It would survive any court in the universe, because the death that made it lawful has already taken place.

Overlooked or resolved? That is the difference between two ways of holding the gospel. One says: God has kindly overlooked the problem. The other says: the problem has been legally resolved and there is nothing left to overlook. Only the second can be rested on at three in the morning, since a thing that has been overlooked can always be looked at again. This is why Paul has said that God is both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26). The cross did not set justice aside. It satisfied it.

Widowed, not divorced. The woman did not walk out on an obligation she found burdensome; she was widowed. That is Paul’s claim for every Christian: not that you escaped the law, but that the bond was ended by a death, and the death was Christ’s (v. 4).

In everyday life. Marriage is meant for life, and Christ keeps his vows to his bride, so honour your own and pray by name for a marriage you know is under strain.

For worship. Adulteress was the name the prophets gave God’s own people, and they had earned it. Yet the Lord told Hosea to go again and love his unfaithful wife, and Hosea bought her back with silver and barley (Hosea 3:1–2). Christ fulfils that picture: he loved a bride who had gone after other lovers, gave himself up for her, and washes her until she stands before him without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Her joy in him is not stolen. It was bought, lawfully, at the full price.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The application. Death ends the old relationship. Through Christ’s death, his body on the cross, we died to the law as a covenant of works and as a condemning master.

Through a body. Not through a decision or a ceremony, but through an execution at a particular hour on a particular hill. Your release from the law is not a spiritual principle you have grasped; it is a consequence of what happened to somebody’s body, and you were in him when it happened (6:3–6).

Belong to another. A new marriage. Freed from the law, we are married to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25–32). The church is his bride. And this is the point of the death: not liberty for its own sake, but belonging to someone new. The whole purpose was a second marriage.

Raised from the dead. Paul names the resurrection, because the illustration requires it. The first marriage ended by a death; the second cannot end the same way. This husband has been through death already and come out the other side, which means the wife is not going to be widowed twice. “Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again” (6:9). The Son of God gave his body to be broken so that he could have a bride, and he rose so that she would never be widowed.

Fruit for God. Fruit of a marriage: children. Fruit of union with Christ: good works, holiness. But fruit is not manufactured by the wife through effort. It is the natural consequence of a union, which is why the New Testament so rarely tells Christians simply to try harder and so often tells them to abide, remain, stay joined (John 15:4–5).

In the flesh. The phrase means our unconverted state, before the Spirit: not merely having a body, but living as fallen human nature lives, without God at the centre. Paul uses the past tense. For a Christian, this is a condition left behind, and that matters for reading the present tense of verses 14 to 25.

Fruit for death. The law did not restrain our sinful passions; it aroused them (5:20). When the law meets a sinful nature, it first provokes sin, then comes failure, and the end is death. Both marriages are fertile. That is the horror of the first one: it was not barren, it was productive, and you have the children to prove it.

What does fruit for God actually look like? Paul names it elsewhere: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and the righteous deeds that flow from them (Philippians 1:11). It is usually less dramatic than we expect. A temper that has become slower. A man who now gives quietly. A woman who can forgive a sister she once avoided. Repentance that comes sooner after a sin. Prayer that has become less a duty and more a conversation. It is also slow, like all fruit, and it is often seen more clearly by others than by yourself. If you want to know whether it is there, ask someone who has known you for years.

In everyday life. Under the first husband the pattern is a rule, a period of success, a collapse, and then either despair or a quiet lowering of the standard. Under the second it is slower: something you did not particularly work at has quietly changed, and you noticed afterwards. So spend this week less on the resolution and more on the union: time with Christ in his word, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the company of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now. The same two words turned the letter from sin to the gospel at 3:21. Both times they follow a state we could not escape. “Released” is the word used of the widow freed from the marriage law (v. 2).

Held us captive. The language of being gripped, kept in custody. It is why Paul spends the rest of the chapter clearing the law of blame: it was not the jailer by design. It became a prison because we were sinners under its condemnation, in the way that a mirror becomes unbearable to a man who cannot change his face.

The covenant in his blood. The new way is not a new idea but a new covenant, which Christ himself began. On the night he was betrayed he took the cup and called it the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), the covenant Jeremiah had promised, in which the law is written on the heart. Then, risen and exalted, he poured out the promised Spirit (Acts 2:33). So the new way of the Spirit is the way Christ opened with his death and supplies from his throne.

So that we serve. Not freed to do nothing: we serve differently. The question was never whether a Christian obeys, but what moves him to obey.

The new way of the Spirit. It is not a contrast between the Old Testament and the New, and it is certainly not a contrast between law as bad and Spirit as good. The written code is God’s own word. What Paul is contrasting is two ways of serving: by external rules written on stone, or by the Spirit, from a changed heart (2 Corinthians 3:6). Chapter 8 explains it.

A rule outside, a life inside. A written code can tell you what is required and can do nothing whatever to make you want it. That is not a fault in the code; it is all that written words can do. What the new covenant promised is not clearer instructions but a changed heart. God said he would put his law within them and write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and put his Spirit within them and cause them to walk in his statutes (Ezekiel 36:27). The statutes do not change. The walking does. God does not merely tell his people what is good; he comes to live in them and makes them love it, and the law that once stood outside us accusing is written inside us by the hand of God.

Pushing the car. Christians easily slip into the old way without deciding to: I must, I should, I ought, I will try. It produces a life disciplined and quietly joyless. The new way does not abolish the shoulds; it puts the power to do them inside you. The difference is between a man driving a car and a man pushing one, and from the outside on a flat road the two can look remarkably similar for quite a long way.

Does serving by the Spirit mean I wait until I feel like obeying? No. The Spirit does not usually work by replacing obedience with feelings; he works through your will, giving you both the desire and the strength to do what God says (Philippians 2:13). Often the desire follows the obedience rather than preceding it. So do the right thing on the dull days too, but do it as someone who belongs to Christ, asking his help, rather than as someone earning his place. The new way is not obedience minus effort. It is effort with a different source and a different motive: not to be accepted, but because you are.

parallels.desc: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now defends the law. It is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is sin, which seized the commandment as a foothold: the command not to covet woke the very covetousness it forbade. The law did not kill Paul; sin did, using what is good, so that sin might be exposed as sinful beyond measure (v. 13).

From verse 14 Paul speaks in the present tense of a man who wants the good, delights in God’s law and still finds another law waging war in his members and taking him captive. The cry for rescue is answered at once, and the struggle itself is evidence of the Spirit’s work.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 underlies the Reformed teaching that sanctification is a lifelong struggle rather than a single crisis in which sin is removed. John Wesley taught that a believer may be made perfect in love in this life, and parts of the later Holiness movement spoke of the sinful nature being eradicated. Augustine, Luther and Calvin held that indwelling sin remains until glory. That is realism, not defeatism: a Christian who knows it will not be crushed by the fight, and will fight with the means God gives, the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of believers.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ancient writers knew this experience too. Ovid gives Medea the famous line: “I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse.” But the philosophers’ answer, more reason and more willpower, is exactly what Paul finds inadequate. The trouble is not ignorance but the power of indwelling sin, and the answer is not a philosophy but a Person, Jesus Christ our Lord (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has tried harder and still found the same sins returning is not a failure but a normal Christian. The answer is not more effort but more of Christ, and chapter 8 follows.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say? “That the law is sin? By no means!” Paul is answering a question his own argument has created. He has just said the law arouses sinful passions (v. 5) and that we have been released from it (v. 6). A reader might fairly conclude that the law is the problem. Paul reaches for his strongest denial, and then spends the rest of the chapter defending the law he has just said held us captive.

I would not have known sin. The law reveals sin (3:20), as an X-ray shows the disease but cannot cure it.

To covet. The tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17), and the choice is not accidental. He takes the one commandment that cannot be seen being broken: coveting happens entirely inside a man. As a Pharisee Paul could say that as to righteousness under the law he was blameless (Philippians 3:6), and he meant it. He seems to have believed he had kept the other nine. It was the tenth that got in past his defences, because it is the one that asks what you want.

Seizing an opportunity. “Opportunity” (aphormē) could be a military term for a base of operations, the bridgehead from which a campaign is launched. Sin does not merely react to the commandment; it sets up camp on it and attacks from there.

The wet-paint sign. A wet-paint sign creates an impulse to touch that did not exist a moment before. It would be easy to blame the sign, but the sign does not corrupt the child. It brings into daylight something that was in him all along and had never been provoked into showing itself.

Sin lies dead. Dormant, not yet stirred up; not absent. A quiet conscience is not necessarily evidence of a clean heart. It may only be evidence that nothing has yet come along to wake what is sleeping. It is easy to think well of our own patience until we live with someone who tries it.

So should I avoid giving rules to my children, or to myself? No. Paul is not against commandments; he is about to call this one holy and righteous and good (v. 12). Children need clear boundaries, and adults need them too. What this passage teaches is what rules can and cannot do. They can show what is right, restrain the worst outward evil, and expose what is in the heart. They cannot change the heart. So give the rule, and with it give the gospel: explain why God’s way is good, show the child that you also break rules and need forgiveness, and point to the Saviour who gives a new heart. A home with rules and no grace breeds either rebels or Pharisees. A home with grace and no rules breeds neither love nor wisdom.

What the commandment taught him to want. The tenth commandment stripped Paul of his confidence in himself, and that was the beginning of grace. The blameless Pharisee who found that he could not stop wanting was the man who would later write that he counted everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:7–8). The law could not cure his wanting, but it drove him to the one person worth wanting with the whole heart. That is what the law was given to do: to shut every other door until the sinner runs to Christ (Galatians 3:22–24). And Christ, who owned all things and was content with a manger and a cross, kept the tenth commandment in our place, in every desire of his heart. Covetousness is desire with the wrong object, and the gospel does not abolish desire. It gives it Christ.

In everyday life. Do not only examine your behaviour; you may well pass. Examine what you want. Over the last week, what did you want in a way that made your own life look thinner: somebody’s marriage, their ease, their platform, their health? When you find it, name it to God, and then thank him for one specific thing he has given you instead. Contentment is learned (Philippians 4:11), in the strength Christ gives (4:13), and gratitude is how it is learned.
verseByVerse.note: Coveting is the one commandment that concerns only the heart.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once alive. Who is the “I”? Perhaps Paul as a child before he understood the law; or Paul speaking for Adam, who lived before the command; or for Israel before Sinai. Most probably Paul’s own experience, told in a way that echoes Adam and Israel: he felt alive, self-satisfied.

One story told three times. All three readings are possible because the same three steps (alive, then the commandment, then death) happened in Eden; at Sinai, where Israel made a golden calf before Moses was down the mountain; and in a devout boy when the tenth commandment reached him. Paul is telling one story that has happened to the first man, to a nation and to himself.

Alive? How could Paul, blameless as a Pharisee (Philippians 3:6), say he was once alive apart from the law? He could call himself alive, not because he had never heard the law, but because he had never felt its weight. He knew its outward demands and kept them. The commandment came to him when he saw that the law also forbids coveting (v. 7), a sin of the heart he could not stop. Then he died: his confidence in his own righteousness was finished. “Alive” does not mean he was really safe. He is describing how it felt, not how it was, and that is the condition of everyone whose conscience has not yet been woken. Such a person does not believe he is in danger, not because he has examined the matter, but because the question has never been pressed on him. There is a kind of peace that comes only from not knowing.

Does this mean children are innocent until they understand the law? No. Paul has already said that all die in Adam, even those who did not sin as Adam did (5:12–14); alive describes how things seemed, not his standing before God. Scripture gives no age of accountability. But it gives good ground for hope for those who die in infancy: David expected to go to his child (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). As the 1689 London Baptist Confession (10.3) puts it, elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases. A parent who has lost a little one may rest that grief on the Saviour who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

Sin came alive. When the law’s demand pierced his conscience, sin revived, and he saw himself as spiritually dead, condemned. Sin had been dormant (v. 8) and now it is the living party; the man who thought himself alive is the corpse. The arrival of the commandment did not change the amount of sin in him. It changed which of the two was standing up. In this verse, dying is progress: God’s way of saving people is to let a commandment kill them first, and then to raise them with his Son. He kills and he makes alive; he wounds and he heals (Deuteronomy 32:39).

Proved to be death. The law promised life to those who keep it: keep my statutes and live (Leviticus 18:5). But to a sinner, it brings death. He does not say the commandment is death; he says it proved to be death “to me”, and those two words are his whole defence of the law in this chapter. The same word that would be life to a man who kept it is death to a man who cannot.

Sunlight and water. The same sunlight that ripens fruit blisters skin that cannot take it; the same water that a swimmer moves through drowns a man who cannot swim. The fault is in what meets them. That is why every attempt to fix the human problem with better teaching has failed: the trouble was never the quality of the teaching.

Did anyone ever receive the life the law promised? One man did. Jesus Christ kept every statute, from the heart, every day of his life, and the life the law promised was rightly his. Then he went to the death the law threatens, not for any sin of his own but for ours (Galatians 3:13). So the promise of Leviticus 18:5 was not empty; it was kept by the only person who could keep it, and his life is credited to all who trust him. The law cannot give life to you. But Christ, who earned it under the law, gives it to you as a gift.

In everyday life. Ask when the commandment came to you: when a sentence of God’s became an accusation with your name on it. Some can date it; for others it came slowly. A churchgoer who has always regarded himself as broadly all right, and has never been alarmed by anything God has said, should consider whether he is still “alive apart from the law”, in the first half of verse 9. But if you are reading this anxiously, afraid your conviction was never deep enough, that anxiety is itself the commandment’s work: the complacent do not ask the question. Read one commandment slowly this week, and ask God to let it find you and then send you to Christ, who kept it for you.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deceived me. “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve. Eve said the serpent deceived her and she ate (Genesis 3:13), and Paul uses here the same strong word for “deceived” that he uses of Eve elsewhere (2 Corinthians 11:3). Sin lies: it says the forbidden thing will satisfy and that God is holding back good, and so it used God’s good command to kill.

The serpent’s method. The method has not changed. The serpent did not begin by denying the commandment; he began by misquoting it, asking whether God had really said not to eat of any tree, inflating the prohibition until God looked mean. Then he attacked God’s motive: God knows that when you eat you will be like him, which is to say, he is keeping something good from you. And only then the flat denial: you will not surely die (Genesis 3:1–5).

Still in service. All three moves are still in use: the commandment exaggerated until God seems to forbid things for the sake of it, the Giver’s motive questioned, and the consequence quietly denied: not disproved, only made to feel unreal.

Sin misinforms. Sin’s primary work is not to overpower you; it is to misinform you. The lie in temptation is usually about what the sin will give and what it will cost: that this will satisfy, that it will not cost much, that you will be able to stop, that God is being unreasonable. Which is why the counter to temptation is so often simply telling yourself the truth, out loud if necessary, since what is under attack is what you believe to be true.

Where the serpent met his match. The deceiver who used the commandment against Eve came to the last Adam in the wilderness with the same kind of lie, that God’s word could be bent and his care doubted, and this time it failed. Jesus was hungry, alone and offered every shortcut, and he answered each lie with a commandment from Deuteronomy, the very law sin had turned into a weapon (Matthew 4:1–11). In his mouth the word was not an occasion for sin but a sword against it. Where Adam believed the slander and died, Christ believed his Father and lived.
