Then he went further: he took on himself the death that sin had dealt through the commandment, and in dying crushed the serpent’s head, as was promised in the garden (Genesis 3:15).

How do I actually fight sin’s lies? Do what Jesus did in the wilderness: answer the lie with what God has said (Matthew 4:1–11). That means having particular verses ready for particular temptations, learned in advance, not hunted for in the moment. Ask the arithmetic questions sin hopes you will not ask: what will this cost tomorrow, and who else will pay? Say the truth aloud: this will not satisfy; God is not holding out on me; he gave his Son, so he will not withhold any good thing (8:32). Tell a trusted Christian friend, because lies thrive in secret. And remember that being tempted is not sinning; Christ was tempted in every way, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

Holy and righteous and good. The law is not the problem; sin is. After five verses on how the commandment was used to kill him, Paul uses three adjectives where one would have done, defending the law warmly. The law is not a set of rules God happened to choose. It comes from the Holy One and mirrors him: its demands are his own purity put into words. That is why breaking it is never mere rule-breaking but an offence against God himself (Psalm 51:4), and why the holy law is so terrible to sinners and so precious to the redeemed. The holy, righteous and good law, which sin used to kill us, found in Christ the one who loved it perfectly and kept it perfectly.

A wounded man’s verdict. Paul was wounded by the commandment and says so, and he will not let his experience be evidence against God. We tend to do the reverse and blame the command, a conclusion that always flatters us. The problem is not in the doctor’s prescription but in the patient’s condition.

In everyday life. Think of a commandment of God that has cost you something: the one that has stood in the way of what you wanted, or that you have failed at so often you have stopped hoping. Is there a quiet sense that God was asking too much, that a reasonable God would have made an exception for your case? That resentment is the serpent’s second move, still working. Name it, and look at the cross: nobody who sees the Father give up his own Son for us all (8:32) can go on believing that the Giver of the commandment is mean.
verseByVerse.note: “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? “By no means!” The law did not kill; sin did. This verse is where Paul’s account of his own experience (vv. 7–12) has been heading, and it answers a question that ought to trouble a thoughtful reader. If God knew the law would provoke sin rather than restrain it, why give it? Paul does not say it was a miscalculation. He says it was the purpose.

Shown to be sin. The law was given, among other things, to make the disease declare itself. Nobody goes to a physician for a condition he cannot feel, and the commandment forced a hidden thing to produce symptoms, violent enough that the patient finally went for help.

Sinful beyond measure. The phrase (kath’ hyperbolēn) is the phrase behind our word hyperbole. Sin earns it not by producing something spectacular but by what it is willing to use: it took the holiest thing God had given, a good commandment from a good God designed for life, and turned it into an instrument of death.

Sin has a strategy. We think of sin as weakness. Paul describes something with a strategy, ready to turn the best things to its own use. Doctrine can be used this way: a man may use accurate theology to avoid God, and many do. Even repentance can be, when it becomes a show of sorrow that eases the guilt without ever dealing with the sin that caused it. The man who has fought an obvious sin for twenty years is often caught by one he never thought to watch.

The best thing sin ever seized. Sin showed itself most fully when it laid hold of the best gift God ever gave. The Son of God came, holy and righteous and good, the living picture of all that the law commands, and sin used God’s own law, in the mouths of the leaders of God’s own people, to put him to death: we have a law, they said, and by that law he ought to die (John 19:7). At Calvary sin was unmasked as never before. And there God turned its masterstroke against it: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin in the flesh (8:3). The place where sin did its worst is the place where it received its sentence.

Do I need to feel terrible about my sin before I can come to Christ? No. The law shows us sin so that we will come, not so that we will first earn the right to come by feeling bad enough. Conviction is not measured by the depth of the misery but by where it sends you. Some people are brought to Christ through long terror of conscience; others through a quiet, clear seeing that they need him. Both are the Spirit’s work. If you see enough of your sin to know that you cannot save yourself, you see enough to come. Christ invites the weary and heavy-laden, not the sufficiently weary (Matthew 11:28).

In everyday life. Ask what good thing in your life is currently being used against you. Your work, which is a gift, and which has become the place you go to avoid a difficulty at home. Your theological knowledge, which is real, and which has become a way of being superior to other Christians. Your service, which helps people, and which has become how you avoid asking whether anybody knows you. Pick one good thing this week and inspect it, and ask God to show you how sinful sin is, so that you will treasure his grace.

For worship. Sin may be sinful beyond measure, but it is not the only thing beyond measure in Paul’s vocabulary. He uses the same phrase for the eternal weight of glory being prepared for the people of God (2 Corinthians 4:17). “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (5:20). God’s mercy has outrun his people’s sin at every turn, and it ends in a glory that outweighs all of it together.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is spiritual. Not vague or only inward, but from the Spirit of God, carrying his holiness. That is why a person of the flesh cannot keep it, and why those who walk by the Spirit begin to fulfil it (8:4).

Of the flesh. Sarkinos: made of flesh, human, weak. From here Paul writes in the present tense (“I am”), and so begins one of the most debated and most comforting passages in Scripture.

In the flow. Verses 7–13 cleared the law of being sin; verses 14–25 show that it cannot make a man holy either, because even a man who loves it finds it powerless against the sin still living in him. That prepares the great sentence of 8:3: what the law could not do, weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son.

Sold, and bought back. “Sold under sin” is slave-market language, and the New Testament answers it in the same market. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). So the believer who still feels the old master’s grip in his flesh no longer belongs to the old master. The sale to sin was real, but Christ’s purchase is the one that stands. The struggle of these verses is the struggle of a slave who has been bought by a new Lord and is still learning to walk out of the old house.

I do not understand. He does not say he regrets them or cannot justify them: he cannot make sense of them. Anybody who has fought a recurring sin knows that the strangest thing about it is not its power but that it makes no sense: afterwards you cannot say why you did it. The man in this verse is not making excuses. He is baffled.

The very thing I hate. He does not do what he wants, which means he wants the right thing. This is not a man making a show of reluctance while enjoying his sin; the wanting is real, and it is the source of the anguish. A man who wanted only the wrong thing would have no conflict and nothing to report.

Where Christians differ: who is the “I” of verses 14–25? Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer. Some (many early Greek fathers, Wesley, and many modern scholars) see an unbeliever under the law, or Paul before conversion. This commentary’s view: with Augustine (in his later writings), Luther, Calvin and the Reformed tradition, this best describes a believer. The present tense; the delight in God’s law in the inner being (v. 22), which no unbeliever has (8:7); the hatred of sin (v. 15); the cry for deliverance and thanks for it (vv. 24–25): all fit a regenerate person who still has indwelling sin. It describes the struggle, not the whole Christian life; chapter 8 shows the victory by the Spirit. Mature believers often feel this struggle most keenly, because they love God’s law most.

The case on the other side. The other reading has real arguments on its side: “sold under sin” (taken up below), and the fact that verse 5 puts “living in the flesh” in the past, while these present-tense verses sound like that same condition. But the present tenses run unbroken for twelve verses, and the delight of verse 22 remains the hardest thing for that reading to explain, since 8:7 says the unconverted mind cannot submit to God’s law. A person who has not been born again lives in his sin without this distress.

But how can a believer be “sold under sin”? This is the strongest objection to reading verses 14 to 25 as the experience of a Christian, and it deserves an honest answer. In 6:17–18 Paul says believers have been set free from sin; here he says he is “sold under sin”. Three things help. First, Paul carefully limits where this is true: “nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (v. 18); “with my flesh I serve the law of sin” (v. 25). He is describing what remains of the old nature, not the whole person, whose inner being delights in God’s law (v. 22). Second, he is describing the believer measured against the law alone, considered apart from the Spirit’s help: as far as the law’s power goes, even a believer cannot overcome sin; the law can command but not enable. That is why chapter 8, where the Spirit is named again and again, follows immediately. Third, the language of captivity describes real defeats in a real war (v. 23), not surrender: losing a battle is not the same as deserting.

A mediating view. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in his great sermons on Romans, argued for a third option: a person awakened by the law to his sin and distressed, but not yet born again and resting in Christ. Others hold that Paul describes his past as a Jew under the law, seen with Christian eyes. These readings take the strong language of verses 14 and 23 seriously, but the Reformed reading remains the most natural, and the most true to what believers experience.

The comfort survives either reading. If Paul is describing the Christian, then your experience of failure is normal and you are not disqualified. If he is describing life under law before Christ, then the passage is telling you what you have been rescued from and where to look instead of at yourself. In both cases the answer arrives in the same breath: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (v. 25).

What it does not mean. This passage has been misused in both directions. It is not a licence: a man who quotes Romans 7 to excuse a sin he has stopped fighting has taken a description of anguish and used it as a permission slip, and the anguish is precisely what he no longer has. And it is not a ceiling: chapters 6 and 8 insist that the Christian grows in holiness (6:19–22; 8:13). This chapter describes the floor of Christian experience: you may find yourself there at any time, and you are not lost because you are.

Should I expect to feel like this all the time? No. The conflict is constant in the sense that indwelling sin is always present until glory, but the experience of it varies. There are seasons of real victory and quiet joy, when old sins have lost their grip and the war feels far away, and seasons when the struggle is fierce. What Paul describes here is what the believer finds when he measures himself honestly against the law: he never does the good as fully as he wants. Chapter 8 describes the same believer looking at Christ and the Spirit, and finding no condemnation, real power, and sure hope. A healthy Christian lives in both chapters at once, and spends more of his attention on the second.

For worship. The holy law could only show us the gap between what we are and what we ought to be, and the Son of God came into that gap. He took our flesh, yet was never sold under sin; he always did the things that pleased his Father (John 8:29). Tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), he pities those still fighting. He remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14), and he is not ashamed to call such strugglers his brothers (Hebrews 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer; many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read it as the believer’s experience.

parallels.desc: the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I agree with the law. His very unwillingness shows he sides with the law; his deepest self agrees with God. Paul’s final evidence for the law is his own failure: his conscience has voted for the commandment while his hands voted against it. Guilt, uncomfortable as it is, is a person admitting that God’s law is right just after he has broken it.

Sin that dwells within me. Not an excuse, but a diagnosis. Paul’s true self, the new self, does not want sin. “Dwells” (oikousa): lives, makes its home. Sin is still present, though no longer the master. The believer is responsible for his sins, but they do not express who he truly is in Christ.

No longer I. Paul can speak of an “I” distinct from his sin because something has happened to that “I”. Our old self was crucified with Christ (6:6), and he says the same of himself elsewhere: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The real Paul is the man joined to Christ, who died with him and was raised with him. Who a Christian is, is settled not by his worst day but by Christ’s death and resurrection, and knowing that is what gives him the courage to call his remaining sin an enemy.

Not the oldest excuse in the world. Read carelessly, this verse is the oldest excuse in the world. Paul is not saying, “It was not me”; he has spent a chapter accepting responsibility. If you catch yourself saying, “That was not the real me”, you are misusing the verse. The difference is easy to see. Paul’s sentence produces anguish and a cry for deliverance. The excuse produces relief and no cry at all.

A lodger with a room. Paul distinguishes what he is from what is in him, and the word is uncomfortable: sin dwells, a settled inhabitant rather than a visitor. It has a room, knows the layout, and is not paying rent. That explains why sin in a believer so often looks like a habit rather than a decision: a lodger does not need to be invited each time. But sin may dwell in a believer; it does not own him. The deed of the house was bought with blood, and the Spirit of God has taken up residence in the same rooms where sin still lurks, and he is the stronger occupant.

Holding both. The distinction gives a Christian a way to hold two things that otherwise tear him apart: “I did that”, and “that is not who I am”. Hold the first alone and you get despair; hold the second alone and you get evasion. Paul holds both in a single sentence: full responsibility, and an identity that is not defined by the failure. The first keeps you honest; the second keeps you standing.

Is guilt not just something to be got over? Many today are told that guilt is a leftover of upbringing, to be managed rather than heard. Some guilt is false, attached to rules God never gave, and the gospel frees us from that too (Colossians 2:20–23). But the guilt of this verse is conscience agreeing with a law that is good (v. 16), and silencing it is like disconnecting a smoke alarm because the noise is unpleasant. True guilt is not cured by denial but by having the wrong dealt with, and only a God who is both just and merciful can do that. He does not call the sin nothing. He condemned it in the flesh of his Son (8:3), so that the guilty may be forgiven without the wrong being pretended away.

How does this fit with John’s word that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning (1 John 3:9)? John is describing the settled direction of a life, not a sinless one; the same letter says that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1 John 1:8). Paul’s man hates the sin he does and fights it. What John rules out is the man who has made peace with it.

Will God punish me for the sins I commit as a Christian? Not with condemnation. Every sin you will ever commit was laid on Christ and paid for at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). But God does discipline his children, as a father and not as a judge (Hebrews 12:5–11). He may let you feel the bitterness of a sin, withdraw the felt sense of his nearness for a time, or allow consequences to stand, and he does it to make you share his holiness, not to make you pay. So confess your sins to him freely, as a child to a father who has already forgiven the debt (1 John 1:9), and expect his correction to be love.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing good dwells in me. Paul corrects himself mid-sentence, and the correction matters: he will not let the first half stand alone. Something good does dwell in a believer, the Spirit (8:9) and the delight of verse 22, so he narrows the statement to the flesh, which is not the whole of him.

Copy the correction. Christians sometimes make the statement Paul refused to make: “There is nothing good in me at all.” It sounds humble and it is not accurate. A man who believes there is nothing good in him anywhere has no basis for hope, and no explanation for the fact that he minds about his sin. Paul is precise: the flesh has not improved and cannot be improved, but the flesh is not the whole man.

What is the flesh? “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the physical body. English misleads, because it suggests that physical appetites are the problem while the mind is clean. But the vice lists in this letter are full of pride, envy, gossip and malice, sins with no bodily component at all (1:29–31). Flesh is the whole self as it lived before grace arrived, without God at the centre, and what is left of that in a believer. That is why a man who denies himself every bodily pleasure can be entirely fleshly, and a man enjoying his dinner with thanksgiving need not be. The body is not the enemy. The body will be raised.

Desire without ability. He is willing, but not able in his own strength; only the Spirit gives the ability (8:4, 13). That discovery undoes every self-improvement scheme. Most moral advice assumes that what is missing is the wanting, and so it supplies motivation. Paul has the motivation. He is drowning anyway. Nobody discovers this by reading about it; he discovers it on the fifth occasion of resolving the same thing with complete sincerity and failing by Thursday.

What I keep on doing. Not that he never does good, but that he never does it as fully as he wants, and evil keeps breaking through. The verb describes something that goes on happening: not a bad week but the shape of a lifetime, which makes this passage either depressing or liberating, depending entirely on what comes next.

No technique. Paul offers no method. He states the problem in its full hopelessness and lets it stand, because the answer to this condition is not a better strategy but a person, Jesus Christ our Lord (v. 25), and he wants you to have exhausted every alternative before he names him.

Willing and doing in one man. There has been one human life in which the desire to do right and the ability to carry it out never once came apart. “My food is to do the will of him who sent me,” Jesus said, “and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). In Gethsemane the struggle was real, and still the willing and the doing held together: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). What verse 18 cannot find in us was found whole in him. By that one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (5:19), and the good he did is counted to everyone who trusts him, while his Spirit begins in them the same union of wanting and doing.

If I cannot do it, why try at all? Because the ability Paul lacks in himself is given by the Spirit, and the Spirit works through your effort, not instead of it. Paul will say that by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body (8:13): you do it, and you do it by him. Work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). So you still fight: you pray, you flee, you confess, you form new habits. But you fight as someone who has given up on his own strength and is leaning his full weight on another. Despair of yourself is the beginning of victory, not the end of trying.

In everyday life. Take the sin you return to and ask which of these two is actually true of you: “I do not really want to stop”, or “I want to stop and cannot”. They require different medicine. If it is the first, the problem is that you still love the sin, and the answer is repentance. If it is the second, you are where verse 18 is, and your wanting is evidence that God has already been at work in you: you did not manufacture it. Often you will find both at once, and the part of you that hates the sin is the Spirit’s work (Galatians 5:17).
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the body as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Word for word. Paul repeats his diagnosis from verse 17 deliberately, driving it home before he names the pattern: the sin is his, yet it is a resident enemy and not his true self.

A law. “Law” here means principle, a fixed pattern. Paul uses the word as we speak of the law of gravity: something that always happens and makes no exceptions for people who are trying hard. Temptation is always close; sin was crouching at the door for Cain (Genesis 4:7).

Summoned by the good. Evil turns up just when the good is wanted, as if the wanting had called it. You resolve to pray more, and the following week is the busiest in a year. You determine to be patient with a particular person, and that person becomes markedly more irritating within about thirty-six hours. It is easy to conclude that the resolve was insincere, or that God is not helping.

The friction of moving. But Paul says it is a law. The opposition does not show that your resolve was false; it shows that it was real. A man walking with the current does not feel the river; only the one who turns against it does.

Opposed at every step toward the good. Jesus knew this law at its fiercest, from the side of perfect obedience. At his baptism the Father declared his delight in him, and at once the Spirit led him into the wilderness to be tempted (Matthew 3:17–4:1). When he began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer, the opposition came through Peter, one of his closest friends, and he had to say, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:21–23). Every step he took toward the Father’s will was opposed, and he never once gave way. Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

What it does not mean. Not every difficulty that follows a good decision is a spiritual assault, and reading life that way makes people strange and frightened. Sometimes the week really was busy. Paul describes a pattern, not a key for explaining every event, and a Christian who begins interpreting every inconvenience as warfare will exhaust himself and misjudge his neighbours.

So what do I do when the counter-attack comes? Keep going, and do the next small right thing. Expect resistance, so that it does not surprise you into quitting. Pray about it plainly, naming the resolve and the opposition to God. Shrink the resolution if necessary, from an hour of prayer to ten honest minutes, rather than abandoning it. Tell another Christian what you are attempting, because resolutions kept alone are easily dropped. And when you fail, start again the same day, not next Monday. The evil may lie close at hand, but the Lord is closer: he is at hand (Philippians 4:5), and he is the one who is able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 24).

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I delight. “Delight” (synēdomai): rejoice with, take pleasure in. He does not merely approve of God’s law; he delights in it, the language of the psalmist (Psalm 1:2; 119:97). And it is precisely what the next chapter says the unconverted cannot do: the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God and does not submit to God’s law, indeed it cannot (8:7). Whatever else is disputed here, the man of verse 22 is not the man of 8:7. “Inner being” is the inner self, renewed by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 4:16; Ephesians 3:16).

Whose delight this is. The delight of verse 22 has a source. Psalm 40 says, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8), and Hebrews hears that psalm on the lips of Christ, “I have come to do your will”, as he comes into the world to offer his body once for all (Hebrews 10:5–10). A few verses later Hebrews quotes the new covenant promise: “I will put my laws on their hearts” (Hebrews 10:16). The order is the gospel: first the law was in the heart of the Son; then, because of that offering, it is written in the hearts of his people. The believer’s delight in God’s law is a share in Christ’s own.

Waging war. The believer is a battlefield: the flesh against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17). Not peace yet, but war, and the verb describes a sustained campaign with strategy and objectives, not a series of accidents.

Captive. Taken prisoner at times: not total defeat, but painful losses, like a soldier taken alive after a lost battle and marched off where the victor chooses. Paul admits not merely to being tempted but to being taken prisoner: more humiliating, and more honest.

Where the battle is fought. The fighting is located in his members: hands, eyes, tongue, the body with its trained reflexes. The delight is in the inner being; the defeat happens where the habits live, which is the shape of most Christian failure. A Christian rarely sins because he stopped believing the truth that morning; his beliefs were sound, but the battle was being fought in his habits.

Fortify the right position. If the war is fought in the members, that is where the defences belong. Hence the New Testament so often tells people to do physical, unspiritual-sounding things: flee (1 Corinthians 6:18), cut it off (Matthew 5:30), make no provision for the flesh (13:14). They are commands about your hands, your feet and your evening, and the Spirit who lives in you is the strength to obey them (8:13). A man who prays about a temptation and takes no practical steps has fortified the wrong position. In practice that may mean the phone that stays out of the bedroom, the route home that does not pass the shop, the drink not poured, the account closed, the friend who has permission to ask.

Both real. A Christian who recognises himself in the captivity often concludes that his delight must be false. Paul puts both in the same sentence, happening in different places: one in the inner being, one in the members. A prisoner of war has not changed sides. He is in enemy hands, and he is still loyal, and everything now depends on whether anybody is coming for him. Somebody is coming for the prisoner. Christ has already fought the decisive battle and won it, disarming the rulers and authorities and triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15); the war is real, but the outcome was settled on a hill outside Jerusalem.

What should I do straight after I have lost a battle? Go to God at once, not after a decent interval of feeling bad. Confess the specific sin plainly; he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9), because Christ’s blood has already paid for it. Do not try to earn your way back with extra devotion; you are received on the same ground as before, which is Christ. Put right anything you have damaged with others. Ask what made the defeat easier, and change that. Then get up and carry on, because the war is not lost when a battle is. The devil wants a fall to become a retreat. The gospel turns it into a return.

In everyday life. If you suspect your own delight, do not ask whether you always obey; verse 23 has already answered that. Ask what you feel about the commandment you keep breaking. When you consider the standard you have failed, does anything in you say, “That is good, and I wish I were like that”? An unconverted man thinks the standard unreasonable. If you find yourself agreeing with the very law that is currently defeating you, that agreement is not nothing. It is the deepest thing in you, and it was put there.

parallels.desc: his delight is in the law of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wretched man that I am! A cry of anguish: not despair, but deep longing. The word translated “wretched” does not express self-pity. It describes a person worn out by a struggle that has gone on too long. The risen Christ uses it of the church at Laodicea, who did not know it applied to them (Revelation 3:17). Paul knows. The difference in this man is that he has stopped making excuses for himself.

Who will deliver me from this body of death? “Who,” not “what.” Not a technique, but a person. “This body of death”: this body subject to death and to sin’s pull. The Roman poet Virgil tells of the tyrant Mezentius, who punished men by binding the living to the dead, face to face and hand to hand, and leaving them to die in that embrace, and commentators have recalled the image here for centuries. Whether or not Paul had it in mind, it is exactly right for what he has described: something dead, strapped to a living man, which he cannot reach round to untie and cannot outrun. He does not ask to be improved. He asks to be delivered, which is what you ask when the problem is attached to you.

Thanks be to God! The answer bursts out at once. Nothing stands between the cry and the answer but a question mark. In the end the chapter is not about how long the misery lasts but about how near the deliverer is. Jesus Christ delivers: now in part, by the Spirit (8:2), and fully at the resurrection, when this body of death is changed (8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:57). The KJV has “I thank God”, the reading of many manuscripts; others, followed by most modern Bibles, read “Thanks be to God”, and the meaning is the same.

Thanks, not a request. He asked, “Who will deliver me”, looking to the future, and the reply is gratitude, in the present, for something already true, even while he waits for its completion.

The design of the chapter. The chapter was written to bring a man to the end of himself while he is still holding on to God, because the cry of verse 24 is the last thing a self-reliant man will say and the first thing a rescued man remembers saying. Wretched, and thanking God in the same breath: that is a Christian.

So then. Between conversion and glory the believer is both things at once: not yet sinless, but no longer sin’s slave at heart. After his burst of praise Paul states the war again: the deliverance is certain but not yet complete. Chapter 8 opens on that same man, and its first word to him is that there is now no condemnation.

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some holiness teachers claim believers can reach a state of sinless perfection in this life; some in the Wesleyan and Holiness traditions teach that a believer can be so filled with love that he no longer sins deliberately, and often read 7:14–25 as life before conversion or before that second blessing (a later, distinct work of grace). This commentary’s view: Paul, an apostle, still struggled. John says that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Believers grow in holiness and win real victories, but sinless perfection comes only at glorification (Philippians 3:12; 1 John 3:2). Sin’s rule is broken now; its presence ends only when we are glorified. Those who hold the other view are often earnest Christians hungry for holiness, and that hunger is right; the question is only whether Scripture promises its fulfilment before glory.

When will the struggle end? At death, for the soul, and at the resurrection, for the body. When a believer dies, his soul is made perfect in holiness and goes immediately into the presence of Christ (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1; Philippians 1:23; Hebrews 12:23). There is no purgatory to finish the job; Christ’s work has already finished it. And on the last day the body itself, the very place where this war has been fought, will be raised imperishable and glorious, with no law of sin left in its members (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). So the struggle is not for ever. It is the last chapter of the old life, not the first chapter of the endless one.

Is it right for a Christian to call himself wretched? As an honest cry about his remaining sin, yes; as his settled identity, no. Paul says “Wretched man that I am!” in the same breath as “Thanks be to God”, and he calls every believer a saint, beloved, a child of God (1:7; 8:16). The cry is the voice of a man who sees his sin clearly and longs to be rid of it, and that clear sight is itself a gift. But it is not the whole truth about him, and he does not stop there. If you find yourself saying the first half of verse 24 and never the first half of verse 25, you have taken the lament without the answer.

In everyday life. Ask what you have been asking for. If your prayers about your besetting sin are requests for assistance, “help me try harder”, then you are still asking “what” and not “who”. The prayer of this verse is the cry of a man who has given up on himself entirely and wants a person to come and get him. Often that prayer comes only when the other kind has been exhausted, which may be why God lets his people be exhausted. And when you next make the cry of verse 24, answer it at once with the thanksgiving of verse 25.

For worship. The living man was bound to a corpse and could not cut himself free, so the Son of God came and let our death be bound to him. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). He rose in a body death can never touch, and he will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). No discipline could have untied the knot; a Person severed it, with hands that were pierced to do it.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Or do you not know, brothers —for I am speaking to those who know the law—that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?<sup>2</sup>For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.<sup>3</sup>Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.<sup>4</sup>Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.<sup>5</sup>For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.<sup>6</sup>But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.<sup>7</sup>What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”<sup>8</sup>But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.<sup>9</sup>I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.<sup>10</sup>The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.<sup>11</sup>For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.<sup>12</sup>So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.<sup>13</sup>Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.<sup>14</sup>For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin.<sup>15</sup>For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.<sup>16</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good.<sup>17</sup>So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>18</sup>For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.<sup>19</sup>For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.<sup>20</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>21</sup>So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.<sup>22</sup>For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being,<sup>23</sup>but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.<sup>24</sup>Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?<sup>25</sup>Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Romans 8 is the summit of the letter. It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with no separation, and between the two it gives a full account of the Christian life: the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation, the golden chain of God's purpose, and the love of God from which nothing can separate us.

The chapter moves from liberation (vv. 1–17) through present suffering (vv. 18–27) to security (vv. 28–39). In each movement the Spirit is central: he frees (vv. 1–11), he adopts (vv. 14–17), he intercedes (vv. 26–27). Over all of it stands the love of a God who foreknew, predestined, called, justified and will glorify, a chain with no broken link.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first verse gives the whole of the gospel's comfort in one sentence: not less condemnation, but none. The verdict rests not on the believer's life on any given day but on the finished work of Christ and on union with him by faith.

The reason is that a new power, the Spirit who gives life, has set the believer free from the power of sin that ends in death (v. 2). God condemned sin in the flesh of his Son (v. 3), so that the law's righteous requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit (v. 4). In vv. 5–11 flesh and Spirit are not body and soul: they are a life organised around the self and a life ruled by God's Spirit, and the Christian belongs to the second (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification and Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The absence of condemnation for those in Christ is total: nothing past, present or future can bring it back, because justification is not a process but a verdict, given once and not reversed. A Christian may sin grievously and be disciplined for it, but she is not in danger of condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's readers knew condemnation as a court's verdict of guilty, with its sentence. In the court of God, no condemnation means the case is closed, the penalty paid, and the accused free for good. Now: Many Christians hold the doctrine of justification and still live under a cloud, haunted by past sins and unable to receive grace without qualifying it. Romans 8:1 speaks to exactly that: not reduced condemnation, but none.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 8 is the summit of the letter, and perhaps of the whole Bible. It begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation. In between stands the Holy Spirit, mentioned about twenty times, who frees us from sin’s power, gives life, makes us God’s children, helps us pray, and guarantees our future glory.

Therefore. This word reaches back to Christ’s work (3:21–5:21) and the believer’s deliverance (7:25), and not to a triumphant paragraph about victory over sin. It reaches back to a man crying out that he is wretched and cannot do what he wants and keeps doing what he hates. That is the person this sentence is addressed to. He has not improved, resolved anything, or turned a corner. He has cried out, and the answer is: “There is therefore now no condemnation.”

Now. Already, not someday, and not when the struggle has been resolved. Now: in the middle of it, on the same page as the groaning, to a man who has just described his own life as captivity. If Paul had wanted to make this a reward for progress he had every opportunity, and he put the word “now” in instead. The verdict of the last day has been given in advance, and the Judge has spoken in our favour.

No condemnation. In the Greek the sentence opens with the word “no” (ouden): in effect, “None, therefore, now, condemnation.” None at all: not reduced, not probationary. Katakrima, the word for condemnation, is not merely the guilty verdict; it carries the sentence that follows from it, the penalty to be served. So Paul is not only saying the charge has been dropped. He is saying there is nothing left to serve. A man can be acquitted and still be ruined by the costs; this is an acquittal with nothing of any kind left to pay.

In Christ Jesus. United to him. His standing is ours: faith has joined you to him, so that your sin was counted to him and his righteousness is counted to you (2 Corinthians 5:21). The believer is not in herself, where condemnation would be entirely deserved. She is in Christ: hidden in him, clothed in his righteousness, sharing his verdict, “righteous”, before the Father. The condemnation has already fallen, on the Son of God, in full, on a hill outside Jerusalem; it cannot fall again on those who are found in him.

In the flow. Chapter 8 returns to the promise of 5:1–11, after the questions of chapters 6 and 7, and builds it into full assurance: no condemnation at the start (8:1), no separation at the end (8:39), and the Holy Spirit as the reason in between.

The law of the Spirit of life. Verse 2 explains why there is no condemnation. It raises a fair question: Paul usually means the law of Moses when he says law, so how can a reader be confident that here it means a power or a principle? There are four good reasons.

Why “law” here can mean a ruling power. First, Paul has just used the word this way, several times, in the paragraph immediately before. In 7:21 he says, “I find it to be a law”: that is, a regular pattern, a fixed principle, that when he wants to do right, evil lies close at hand. In 7:23 he sees another law in his members waging war against the law of his mind and making him captive to the law of sin. A law that wages war and takes prisoners is not a written code; it is a power that rules. The law of sin and death in 8:2 is plainly the same law of sin of 7:23 and 7:25. Second, Paul had already stretched the word the same way in 3:27, where boasting is excluded not by a law of works but by the law of faith: the principle or order of faith. Third, ordinary Greek, like ordinary English, used law for a fixed rule of how things work, as we speak of the law of gravity. Fourth, the two laws in v. 2 are set against each other as rival masters, one freeing from the other. The law of Moses is holy, righteous and good (7:12); it cannot be the law of sin and death in the sense of something evil. So the law of sin and death is the ruling power of sin, which always ends in death; and the law of the Spirit of life is the ruling power of the Holy Spirit, who gives life.

Where Christians differ: does “law” here still mean the law of Moses? Some scholars (for example James Dunn, and in his own way N. T. Wright) argue that both laws are the Mosaic law seen two ways: the law used by sin to produce death (7:8–11), and the same law, now empowered by the Spirit, leading to life. This commentary’s view: there is a real play on words, and Paul is aware that he is using his key word in a surprising way. But the most natural reading, and that of most careful commentators (Calvin, Murray, Moo among them), is that law here means the governing power or authority under which a person lives. Two regimes, two rulers: the reign of sin leading to death, and the reign of the Spirit giving life. This also fits 5:21, where sin reigned in death but grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life.

Has set you free. The tense marks a decisive act, done once: not a process that may or may not succeed, but a liberation that has happened, and it has happened in Christ Jesus, to whom we are joined. The chains are broken, not by the prisoner’s effort, but by the liberating power of the Spirit of God.

How did the one power set me free from the other? Paul answers in vv. 3–4, which begin with “For”. The liberation has two sides, and both matter. First, the legal side: sin’s claim on us was cancelled. Sin rules in death because the law’s sentence against the sinner stands; God condemned sin in the flesh of his Son (v. 3), so the sentence has been carried out and sin has no legal right left to hold us. This is why v. 2 can explain v. 1: no condemnation, because sin’s grip, which rested on our guilt, has been broken. Second, the living side: the Spirit, who is life, now lives in us (vv. 9–11). By uniting us to Christ in his death and resurrection, the Spirit has ended sin’s reign over us (6:6–7, 14: sin will have no dominion over you), and has given us a new heart with new desires (Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that we now want God and can resist sin. A useful picture, often used by preachers: the law of gravity is not repealed when an aircraft flies, but a stronger law, the lift of the wing, overcomes it, as long as the aircraft flies in that power. Sin still pulls; the Spirit is the stronger power.

What it does not mean. Freedom from the law of sin does not mean that sin is no longer present, or that the believer no longer struggles. Romans 7:14–25 and Galatians 5:17 describe that struggle honestly. It means sin is no longer the master. We were slaves who had no choice; now we are free people who fight, and who are on the winning side. Nor does it mean freedom from God’s moral law as a guide for life (v. 4; 13:8–10).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh” to v. 1, and the King James and New King James Versions follow them. This was probably copied from v. 4, and makes “no condemnation” sound conditional on our walk. The earliest manuscripts don’t have it. No condemnation rests on being in Christ, not on our performance. In v. 2, the manuscripts vary between “set you free” (singular, as in the ESV), “set me free” (as in the King James Version) and “set us free”. The singular “you” is probably original: Paul turns from the “I” of chapter 7 and speaks directly to each reader.

Living under a cloud. This verse has to be preached to Christians and not only to unbelievers, because a great many believers hold the doctrine and live underneath a cloud of something else. They cannot hear a promise of God without adding a condition to it. They approach God in prayer as though re-applying each time. They find it easier to believe they are forgiven than that they are welcome. And when something goes wrong, their first instinct is to ask what they are being punished for. That instinct treats what God sends as punishment, under a verdict that has been cancelled. Whatever the hard thing in your life is, it is not that. It may be discipline, it may be consequence, it may be the ordinary friction of living in a world that is groaning, but it is not God collecting on a debt, because there is no debt outstanding.

Three things often confused. Condemnation is gone entirely. Discipline remains, and is evidence of sonship rather than of wrath: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). And consequences remain, often in full: a man may be completely forgiven and still lose the marriage. Telling him his forgiveness must be doubtful because his circumstances are hard is one of the cruellest mistakes a Christian can make.

If there is no condemnation, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings are slower than verdicts, and because a conscience trained for years under the old marriage to the law (7:1–4) keeps its habits for a while. Some guilt is the Spirit convicting you of a real sin you have not yet confessed: then confess it, plainly and specifically, and receive the forgiveness already bought (1 John 1:9). But much of what Christians feel is accusation, not conviction. Conviction is specific, leads to Christ and leaves you lighter; accusation is vague, drives you away from God and leaves you heavier. When the feeling persists after you have confessed, do not wait for it to lift before you believe. Answer it with this verse, out loud if necessary. God’s verdict is the fact; your feeling is weather.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and that some read “me” for “you.”

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the law could not do. The law couldn’t save, not because it was bad, but because we were too weak to keep it (7:14–25). It could tell us what is right and condemn us for doing wrong, but it could not give us the power to obey or the forgiveness we need. Then the subject of the sentence changes: “God has done”. The law could not; the flesh could not; the man of chapter 7 could not. Everything after those words is in a different tense: not what must be attempted, but what has been accomplished, in real flesh, by somebody else.

Where the blame lies. Paul has been assigning the blame carefully since chapter 7, and here he does it in a single clause. The weakness was not in the law; it was in us, the material the law had to work with. The law failed the way a ladder fails a man who cannot climb, which is to say, it did not fail at all.

What Paul means by “the flesh”. The word runs through vv. 3–13. “Flesh” (sarx) can mean the body’s tissue, human descent (1:3), or human frailty (3:20). But in Romans 7–8 and Galatians 5 it means human nature as it is since the fall, living from itself and for itself, turned away from God. It is not the body as such: Christ came in flesh, and our bodies will be raised (v. 11). The flesh includes the mind (v. 6), the will and the desires; its works include jealousy, rivalry and anger (Galatians 5:19–21), and even religion done in our own strength, which Paul calls “confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3–6). It is the whole self organised around self. Paul also uses it for a realm: the old order of life under Adam. So to be “in the flesh” (vv. 8–9) is to be unconverted, and believers are no longer in it (v. 9); yet the flesh is still present in them as a pull, against which they fight by the Spirit (v. 13; Galatians 5:16–17).

His own Son. The Son existed before he came: he was sent from heaven, and became truly human: subject to weakness, temptation and death, yet without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). He entered the very realm where sin ruled, in order to defeat it there.

One word out of place. Watch how precisely Paul places the word “likeness”. He does not write that Christ came in the likeness of flesh: that would make the incarnation a costume. Nor does he write that he came in sinful flesh, which would put sin in the Son. He writes “likeness of sinful flesh”: real flesh, genuinely ours, in the same condition of weakness and mortality that ours is in, and without the sin. If the flesh he took was not truly ours, he did not redeem ours; as the old Fathers said, what is not assumed (taken on by the Son) is not healed. If it was sinful, he would have needed saving himself. He had to be near enough to be genuinely one of us and clean enough to be of use, and this one clause holds both.

Was Jesus really tempted, if he never sinned? Yes, truly. He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). He felt hunger in the wilderness, the pull of an easier road, and in Gethsemane the full horror of the cup. Sinlessness does not make temptation lighter; it makes it heavier. A man who gives way at the first push never learns how strong the pressure can become; only one who never yields feels its full weight to the end. So when you go to him with your temptations, you are not going to someone who cannot understand. You are going to the only person who has felt the whole force of temptation and stood, and who is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

He condemned sin in the flesh. The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering”, like those laid down in Leviticus 4; Isaiah 53:10 foretold the Servant’s life made an offering for guilt. “Condemned” (katekrinen) is the verb that matches the noun “condemnation” in v. 1. Sin was condemned, sentenced and punished, in Christ’s flesh on the cross. This is penal substitution. Penal means it was a penalty, the punishment God’s law pronounces on sin; substitution means it fell on someone in our place. Christ did not merely suffer alongside sinners: he bore the sentence that was theirs, so that it is no longer waiting for them (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24).

Where the condemnation went. Here is where the condemnation of verse 1 went. It was not waived; it was carried out. The condemnation that is not on you fell somewhere, and Paul names the place: the flesh of God’s own Son. The reason there is none in verse 1 is that there was some in verse 3.

On sin’s own ground. Note also the words “in the flesh”: they name the place where the battle was fought. Sin had made its home in human nature and had never been beaten there. God did not defeat sin from a distance by decree; he came into the territory sin had held since Eden and beat it there. This is Christ, the second Adam, winning on our ground what the first Adam lost on it.

The righteous requirement. “Righteous requirement” (to dikaiōma, singular: the just requirement, the righteous demand). Not the many commandments, but the law’s one total demand, the whole of what it requires. “Might be fulfilled” is passive: not that we might fulfil it, but that it might be fulfilled “in us”, not “by us”.

Where Christians differ: what does it mean that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in us? Readers have long wondered whether Paul means the law’s demand for punishment, carried out on Christ; or the law’s demand for a righteous life, now lived by believers; or both. There are three main views. The first is forensic: the law demanded perfect righteousness, and that demand is fully met for us in Christ, whose obedience and death are counted as ours. Calvin took it this way, and so does Douglas Moo: the passive verb, the singular “requirement”, the word “fulfilled”, and the link with no condemnation all point to something God does, completely, rather than our partial obedience. The second is ethical: the Spirit now enables believers to live the life the law always aimed at, love for God and neighbour. C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner take this view, pointing out that the verse ends by describing the walk of those in whom it is fulfilled, and that v. 4 explains why God sent his Son: not only to forgive us but to change us (Ezekiel 36:27; Jeremiah 31:33). The third holds both together. The requirement is not mainly punishment: the law’s real demand is righteousness, and the punishment falls on those who fail to give it. Christ met that demand both by his perfect obedience and by bearing the penalty for our disobedience. This commentary’s view: the best reading holds the two together, with the forensic sense as the foundation. In Christ, the law’s whole requirement has been fully met for us, which is why Paul can say “fulfilled” without any qualification, and why it is passive and “in us”: we are in Christ, and what is true of him is counted true of us. And the same union with Christ brings the Spirit, who begins to produce in us the very righteousness the law requires. That is why the verse ends with how we walk. Justification (the verdict, given once, that we are righteous in Christ) and sanctification (the Spirit’s steady remaking of us in holiness) are never separated: no one has the first without beginning the second.

But how can it be fulfilled if my obedience is still imperfect? The forensic side answers most of this: in Christ the requirement is fully met now, and nothing can be added to it. But even the ethical side does not claim perfection. Paul says in 13:8–10 that the one who loves another has fulfilled the law, using the same verb, without suggesting that any believer loves perfectly. He means that love is the kind of life the law describes, and that a life of Spirit-produced love is genuinely, if not yet completely, the law’s fulfilment. It is real now, and growing; it will be perfect at glorification, when we are conformed to the image of the Son (v. 29; Philippians 1:6; 1 John 3:2). So Paul looks back to the cross, around at the Spirit’s present work, and forward to glory, all at once.

Who walk. To walk is to live, to conduct one’s life step by step. This is not a condition we must meet in order for the requirement to be fulfilled; it is a description of the people in whom it is fulfilled. Everyone in Christ walks by the Spirit, imperfectly but truly.

Not a technique. Do not turn this into a technique, because Paul does not, and this chapter will not say how it is done until verse 13. What he establishes here is that the resources have changed, and the walking follows from the gift rather than producing it. The problem in chapter 7 was a man with the desire and not the ability, and here the ability arrives from outside him. The Father sent his own Son; the Son took our flesh and bore our sentence; the Spirit now writes in us the very righteousness the law required.

In everyday life. When you face a sin you have repeatedly lost to, what do you instinctively reach for? If the answer is your own determination, a firmer resolve, a better system, a promise to yourself, you are working with the resources of chapter 7, and chapter 7 records how that ends. Ask instead what has been given to you that you are not using. The Spirit is not a reserve to be summoned in emergencies; he lives in every Christian, all the time. So begin today’s fight by remembering that sin has already been condemned in Christ, and ask the Spirit for the walking.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering.”

verseByVerse.quote: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two kinds of people. Those who live by the flesh (unconverted) and those who live by the Spirit (converted). What you think about, value and pursue shows who you are.

A compass, not a moment. The phrase to get hold of is “set the mind”, because it is doing all the work. The Greek word (phronousin) covers more than thinking: it takes in what you are interested in, what you care about, what you are inclined toward, the whole disposition of a person. It is not his opinion, nor the stray thought on a train; it is where he goes when nothing requires him to be anywhere. Paul is describing a compass rather than a moment: the direction the needle returns to when it is left alone.

Settings are visible in the gaps. You find out where your mind is set not in what you do at church or at work, where the agenda is set for you, but in the unstructured minutes. What do you reach for when you wake in the night? What occupies the ten minutes in a queue, the drive with the radio off, the moment your hand goes to your phone before you have decided anything? Those gaps show where the mind is set. A man’s mind, when released, goes where it lives.

The things of the Spirit. The Spirit-led mind cares about what God cares about (Colossians 3:1–2; Philippians 4:8): Christ, his word, holiness, his people, his kingdom.

Is death. In the Bible, death is first of all separation: physical death separates the soul from the body; spiritual death separates the person from God, the source of life. A mind set on the flesh is already in that state now: alive in the body, but dead toward God, unable to know, love or please him (Ephesians 2:1–3, dead in trespasses and sins, while walking in them; 1 Timothy 5:6, she is dead even while she lives). Unless God intervenes, this present death ends in physical death and finally in the second death (6:23; Revelation 20:14): separation from God now becomes separation for ever.

Not leads to, but is. The verdict is stated with startling flatness. Paul is not describing a penalty attached at the end but a condition already in effect. A life organised around the self is not awaiting a sentence; cut off from God, it is already death, in the same way that drowning is not a punishment for being underwater: it is what being underwater does.

Life and peace. Life is the life of God shared with us: knowing God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3), begun now and completed in the resurrection (vv. 10–11). Peace is first peace with God: the war is over (5:1, 10), whereas the mind of the flesh is still hostile to God (v. 7). Then peace within, the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, a life put right (Philippians 4:7).

Why peace? Note that second word, because it is not the one we would have chosen. We would have written life and holiness, or life and usefulness. Paul writes peace, and it is the exact answer to chapter 7. That was a chapter of war: a law waging war, a man taken captive, a self divided against itself. What ends the war is not a stronger will but a mind that is no longer set on the flesh, the very thing that was fighting against it.

What the Spirit sets the mind on. The things of the Spirit are not a vague cloud of religious topics. The Spirit’s own work, Jesus said, is to glorify him, taking what is Christ’s and declaring it to us (John 16:14). So a mind set on the Spirit is, in the end, a mind set on Christ, and there has been one human mind set on the things of the Spirit without a wandering minute: the Son, whose food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34). That is why Paul can write, “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). Life and peace are his, and the Spirit turns our minds to him so that they become ours: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). The Prince of Peace made that peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and the Spirit of peace now draws our wandering minds home to it.

A guard for the tender conscience. This verse can be turned into a whip for the wrong person. Paul is describing two categories of people, not grading Christians on their concentration. The believer whose mind wanders in prayer, who finds Scripture hard going this month, who is distractible and knows it, is not the man whose mind is set on the flesh. The proof is that it troubles him. A mind genuinely set on the flesh does not lie awake troubled by how little it wants God; it does not want God and is not troubled. Wanting to want him is already the needle pointing the right way, however unsteadily.

So how do I actually set my mind on the Spirit? By choosing what you look at, repeatedly, until the needle learns. Seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Colossians 3:1–2): give the first minutes of the day to his word rather than the news, even if only a psalm. Carry one verse with you and return to it in the gaps. Pray in sentences through the day. Think on whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely and commendable (Philippians 4:8), which means also choosing what not to watch and read. Gladly give the Lord’s Day to worship with his people, because minds are set in company. And when you notice your mind has drifted, do not scold yourself; simply turn it back. Every turning is the Spirit at work.

verseByVerse.quote: For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hostile, not merely indifferent. The unconverted mind is at war with God (5:10; Colossians 1:21), and the word is stronger than most readers allow. Paul is not saying that everyone outside Christ hates God consciously; a great many are perfectly polite about him, and some are religious. He is describing an orientation rather than an emotion, like one magnet set against another: the closer God comes the more it turns away. Watch what happens in a conversation when God stops being a topic and starts making a claim. Discussed as an idea, he is interesting; introduced as someone with rights over the person listening, the temperature changes. That shift is not rudeness and it is often unconscious. It is the thing Paul is naming.

Indeed, it cannot. Not only does not, but cannot. Theologians call this total inability: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that no part of fallen human nature can turn itself to God (1 Corinthians 2:14; John 6:44). “Cannot” is a statement about ability, and it is the claim that makes the Christian faith unlike every programme of moral improvement: the natural man is not equipped to obey, in the way that a stone is not equipped to float. It also bears on chapter 7: the man who delights in God’s law in his inner being (7:22) is doing what the mind of the flesh cannot, which is one reason to see him as a believer.

Inability is not an excuse. This is easily misheard. Inability of this kind does not reduce guilt, because it is not a disability imposed from outside. It is the inability of a man who cannot bring himself to love someone he has decided to despise: real, total, and entirely his own fault. And the hostility can wear religious clothes. A person can keep God’s rules in order to keep God at a distance, obeying so that God will owe him and leave him in charge of his own life. That is the flesh too, and Paul knew it from the inside (Philippians 3:4–7).

Cannot please God. Nothing an unconverted person does pleases God, because it doesn’t come from faith and love for him (Hebrews 11:6).

The one Man who pleased God. Verse 8 describes every human being since Adam, with one exception. Over the Jordan the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and Jesus could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). He said it in real human flesh, without sin, his will submitted to the Father all the way to the cross. So the gospel does not tell the natural man to improve until God is pleased with him. It joins him to the One with whom God is already well pleased, and makes him accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6).

Are the good deeds of unbelievers worthless, then? Not worthless to people: an unbelieving doctor who heals, a neighbour who is honest, a father who provides, all do things God commands and that bless others, and they are far better done than neglected. God restrains evil and gives such kindness through them by his common grace. But they cannot please God in the sense Paul means, because they do not come from a heart made right by faith, and are not done in love for him or for his glory (Hebrews 11:6). The Westminster Confession says this carefully: such works may be good things in themselves and useful to others, yet they cannot please God or make a person fit to receive grace (Westminster 16.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.7). So we honour the good we see in unbelievers, and we never tell them it will bring them to God.

Where Christians differ: free will. Arminian Christians (those who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted, and that he chooses those he foresees will believe) teach that God gives everyone enough grace, which they call prevenient grace, to choose to believe. They too confess that no one comes to God without grace, and they are brothers and sisters in Christ. This commentary’s view: Paul says the fleshly mind cannot submit to God. Only the Spirit’s regenerating work makes faith possible (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). This is why salvation is entirely God’s work: he must give new life before we can respond.

Why your arguments did not work. If unbelief were merely a shortage of information, the cleverest people would always be the first to believe, which they are not. Paul says the problem is inability, which is why conversion is described as new birth, resurrection, and a heart of flesh for a heart of stone. So when you have explained it, lived it and answered every objection to someone you love, and still they do not believe, it is not that you argued badly. The work is God’s, it is exactly the sort of thing he does, and the person you pray for is not a harder case than you were. Keep praying, loving and speaking; God gives new life through his word (James 1:18).

A stone made to float. This bleak paragraph stands immediately before the words “You, however” (v. 9), so that you know what it cost to be able to read verse 9 and find yourself in it. Verse 8 plainly described you once, and it was not your own effort that changed that. When we were hostile, God loved us: while we were enemies we were reconciled to him by the death of his Son (5:10). When we could not submit, the Son submitted for us, all the way to the cross. When we could not please him, he made us pleasing to him in his Son. Every Christian is a stone that God has made to float, and the praise belongs entirely to him.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Spirit. Believers no longer belong to the old realm of the flesh but to the realm of the Spirit, because the Spirit dwells in them. “Dwells” (oikei): lives at home, permanently. “If in fact” (eiper): here probably not a doubt, but a reminder: since, as is the case.

Does not belong to him. Every Christian has the Spirit; there is no Christian without him. And the Spirit of God (v. 9a) is the Spirit of Christ (v. 9b): he is sent by the Father and by the Son (John 14:26; 15:26). Christ can call God’s own Spirit his Spirit only because Christ is God.

Three names in two verses. Paul packs a great deal into a short space. The Spirit of God dwells in you; anyone without the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him; and then, in the same breath, Christ is in you. The New Testament assumes the Trinity here rather than arguing for it, and the pastoral consequence is that to have the Spirit is to have Christ. You are not dealing with a lesser third party sent as a substitute while the Lord is elsewhere. The indwelling of the Spirit is how the risen Christ is present with his people.

Read by the wrong person. This sentence is one of the great dividing lines, but it is regularly read by exactly the wrong person: the anxious believer, who takes it as an examination he is probably failing, while the man who ought to be searched by it reads past it without a flicker. The verse does not say “anyone who does not feel the Spirit”, or who has not had a particular experience, or who cannot point to a datable moment. Paul is not describing a sensation. He is describing a possession, and possessions can be verified by their effects rather than by how vividly they are felt.

How would I know? Not by looking inward at your feelings, which mostly reports on your temperament and how you slept. Look for effects, and the New Testament names them plainly. Do you call God Father and mean it, not as a formula but as an address (v. 15)? Do you find yourself loving Christian people you have nothing else in common with (1 John 3:14)? Do you mind about your sin, and mind more than you used to (the whole of chapter 7)? Is Christ precious to you in a way he once was not? None of those is spectacular. All of them are supernatural, in the sense that nothing in the flesh produces them (vv. 7–8).

Is there a second experience of the Spirit that ordinary Christians lack? No. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There are no two classes of Christians, the ones who merely believe and the ones who have the Spirit. What Scripture does call for is being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a continual, repeated yielding to the one who already lives in you, shown in worship, thanksgiving and humble service, not in a single crisis experience. So if you trust Christ, do not go looking for the Spirit as though he had not yet arrived. Ask him to fill the rooms he already owns. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers speak of a later baptism in the Spirit, and their zeal for Christ is often real and humbling; this commentary honours them, but reads 1 Corinthians 12:13 as saying that every believer has already been given the Spirit, so that later experiences are best understood as fresh fillings of the one who has come to stay.

But if Christ is in you. The Spirit in you is Christ in you, and with the Son comes the Father: “we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23).

The body is dead. Not a corpse, but mortal: under the sentence of death. Death entered the world through sin (5:12), and even the believer’s body still carries that sentence. Christians still grow old, fall ill and die.

An honest admission. Paul does not pretend that the indwelling Spirit fixes everything now. Your body is ageing as you read, and it will fail, and any teaching which implies that enough faith should keep a believer well has not read this verse.

The Spirit is life. Many readers find this phrase difficult, and translations differ. The 1984 NIV reads it as the human spirit: “your spirit is alive”. The ESV, the 2011 NIV (“the Spirit gives life”) and the CSB read it as the Holy Spirit. Which is right?

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or the human spirit? The case for the human spirit: Paul contrasts body and spirit, two parts of the person, and the believer’s body is dead while their inner self is alive. This commentary’s view: Paul means the Holy Spirit, for four reasons. First, he does not say the spirit is alive (zōn), which would suit the human spirit, but that the Spirit is life (zōē), a noun: the Spirit is life itself, its source. Second, the Spirit has just been called the Spirit of life (v. 2). Third, every other use of spirit in vv. 9–11 means the Holy Spirit, and v. 11, which continues the thought, says that the same Spirit will give life to your mortal bodies. Fourth, Paul’s contrast is not between two parts of a person, but between two powers: sin brings death, the Spirit brings life. So the meaning is: your body is still marked for death because of sin, but the Spirit who lives in you is life, and he gives you life now, which will reach even your body at the resurrection. The result is that the believer, as a whole person, is alive to God already (6:11). So the two readings meet in experience: we are alive inwardly because the Holy Spirit, who is life, lives in us.

Because of righteousness. The phrase is set in parallel with “because of sin”. As sin brought death, so righteousness brings life. Here this is mainly the righteousness of justification, God’s verdict that we are righteous in Christ (5:17–21: grace reigns through righteousness leading to eternal life). Because we are justified, the Spirit gives us life.

Decaying and being renewed. The two halves stand in the same sentence: the body dead, the Spirit life. Both true at once, which is the shape of the whole Christian experience: a man who is decaying and being renewed simultaneously, and who can feel both on the same afternoon (2 Corinthians 4:16). And the Lord of heaven has taken up residence in bodies that are wearing out, not because they are worthy of him, but because he has declared us righteous in his Son. He did not wait for a better house. He moved into this one, and he means to rebuild it.
