verseByVerse.quote: If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name God is given. Paul could have named God in many ways, and he says this: “him who raised Jesus from the dead”. Not the Almighty, not the Creator, but the one who did that particular thing on that particular morning. He says it twice in one sentence, fixing the reader’s attention on a single historical act and then telling him that the same power is at this moment resident in his own body. If that Spirit dwells in you, as verse 9 says he does in every Christian, then the God who has already done the harder thing, raising Jesus, has placed inside you the Spirit by whom he will do the easier one, raising you. The difficult case is behind us. What remains follows.

Will also give life. The promise of bodily resurrection. As Jesus rose bodily, so will we: salvation includes the body (v. 23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). Matter matters to God: he made it, his Son took it, and he will raise it in glory.

The body back, repaired. Not to some refined essence of you that survives the wreck, but to the body that is currently reading this: the one with the bad knee and the thinning hair and the scan results, the one that gets tired at four in the afternoon. That is the object of the promise. Christianity does not offer escape from the body; it offers the body back, repaired.

Closer to Plato than to Paul. Ask a congregation what happens when a believer dies and you will hear about the soul going to be with the Lord, which is true and is not the main thing the New Testament says. The hope in this letter is not disembodied: a soul leaving the body behind for ever is the hope of the Greek philosopher Plato, not of Paul. It is a raised body, in a renewed creation, and this verse says the deposit on it is already lodged in the very flesh that is wearing out.

Your body now. This has something to say about how you regard your own body. If it is destined to be raised, it is not a shell to be endured, resented or despised, nor, at the other extreme, worshipped and defended against time. If you are ill, or watching someone you love decline, the promise is not that the body does not matter, but that it matters so much that God intends to raise it. That is a steadier place to stand than either the contempt or the panic our culture offers.

Through his Spirit who dwells in you. The indwelling Spirit is the guarantee of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14). Paul’s word there, arrabōn, means a down payment: the first instalment, which binds the one who pays it to pay the rest. So the Spirit in you now is the Spirit of the God who emptied that tomb on the first Easter morning, and he is not there as a comfort during the decline. He is there as the deposit that guarantees its reversal. That is why the promise is stated in the future and the guarantee in the present. Nothing in this verse asks you to hold on tightly enough to qualify: the one who raised Jesus has put his Spirit in your body, and a God who has gone to that trouble is not going to lose track of the address.

What happens to a believer between death and the resurrection? At death the believer’s body returns to the dust, but the soul does not sleep or wait in some shadowy place. It goes at once to be with Christ, conscious and at rest, which Paul calls far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43). The souls of the righteous are then made perfect in holiness and received into heaven, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). There is no purgatory. And the waiting is not the end: on the last day the same Spirit who raised Jesus will raise their bodies, and soul and body will be joined again, glorious and imperishable.

Does it matter whether a Christian is buried or cremated? Not for the resurrection. The God who will raise bodies long since turned to dust, lost at sea or burned by martyrs’ fires is not hindered by the method of a funeral. Christians have historically preferred burial, because it pictures what we believe: the body laid down like a seed, waiting to be raised (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and Jesus himself was buried. That is a good reason to choose it where you can, but it is not a command, and no believer should fear for a loved one who was cremated. The promise of this verse rests on the Spirit’s power, not on the condition of the remains.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Heirs with Christ: The Spirit of Adoption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The section opens by cancelling an obligation: we are debtors, but not to the flesh, which has no further claim on us. Then comes the one command in the passage: by the Spirit, put to death the deeds of the body (v. 13). This is the answer to the defeat of chapter 7: the killing is genuinely ours to do, and the power is the Spirit's. Putting sin to death is not the price of sonship but the family likeness of those being led.

The Spirit establishes our identity as God's children. Abba is the Aramaic word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and his Spirit now gives it to his adopted brothers and sisters. Adoption is a legal status and also a present relationship: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, even when God feels distant.

As children we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (v. 17): the inheritance is God himself, shared with the Son, which is why Paul can say elsewhere that all things are ours (1 Corinthians 3:21). Suffering with him is the road to that glory, not an obstacle to it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption and Assurance

Adoption is one of J.I. Packer's great themes in Knowing God: he argues that it is a higher privilege than justification, because justification changes our standing before the court while adoption brings us into the family. The Spirit draws the child into the love the Father and the Son share, so that she can cry Abba as the Son always has. Assurance at its deepest is not confidence in our own faith or experience but the Spirit-given knowledge that we are the Father's beloved children.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Roman law an adopted son received full legal rights, his old debts were cancelled, and the inheritance was secured: no probation, full sonship from the moment of adoption. Now: The spirit of slavery (v. 15) is the sense that God is mainly a demanding judge to be appeased and that our place at his table depends on our performance. Romans 8:15 answers it: not slaves but sons, not fear but Abba, not earning but inheriting.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. — Romans 8:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Debtors. People under obligation, and the obligation is not to the flesh. We owe the flesh nothing because we owe Christ everything, and God has given us life by his Spirit.

The unfinished sentence. Paul never finishes it: we are debtors, not to the flesh, and he leaves the reader to supply “but to the Spirit”. The flesh is the old master whose debt has been cancelled by Christ. It still exerts a pull, as chapter 7 admitted, but it has no rightful claim on the person who is in Christ. Every demand it still makes on you comes from a creditor whose debt was settled and who is now simply hoping you have not read the paperwork.

You will die. A warning. A life ruled by the flesh shows a person is not truly in Christ, and leads to eternal death.

Put to death the deeds of the body. The old word for this is mortification, from the Latin for killing. The deeds of the body are the sinful practices carried out through the body under the flesh’s rule, not the body itself. “By the Spirit” means that the Spirit is the power by which it is done. And the life promised is the life of v. 6, life with God now and eternal life.

A violent word, a continuous tense. This is the one command in the passage, and Paul chooses a violent word for it. Put to death: not manage, not moderate, not keep under review. And the tense is continuous: keep putting to death, as an ongoing occupation rather than a decisive event. There is no version of this in which the thing is dealt with once and never returns.

What does it mean to put sin to death by the Spirit? Many readers are unsure, and a common view is something like this: the Spirit shows me through God’s word that something is wrong; since the Spirit lives in me, it is now my job to say no; and by saying no I put the deed to death. That is right as far as it goes. There is real, active effort involved: Paul says you put to death, not that you wait for the Spirit to do it while you do nothing. And the Spirit does use his word to show us sin. But the great teachers on this verse add some important things.

John Owen. The fullest treatment of this verse in English is John Owen’s Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656), a short book written entirely on Romans 8:13. Owen made several points. Mortification is not merely stopping an outward act, hiding a sin, or exchanging one sin for another; it is a lifelong weakening of sin’s root, its inner desires, so that it loses its strength and its hold on the heart. It is not achieved by our own vows, rules and resolutions alone, which he said only drive sin underground. It is the Spirit’s work, and the Spirit does it by showing us the guilt and danger of the sin, by setting Christ crucified before us, by giving us faith to rely on Christ’s death and power, and by strengthening us with grace. Yet the Spirit does not do it without us: in Owen’s words, he works in us and with us, not against us or without us. So we must be active: hating the sin, watching for its approach, refusing its first stirrings, and above all, as Owen put it, setting faith to work on Christ for the killing of your sin. His most quoted line sums it up: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

Other voices. Thomas Chalmers, in his famous sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection, argued that the heart cannot simply be emptied of a love; it can only be freed from one love by a greater love taking its place. Tim Keller often drew on Chalmers: since sin is at root idolatry, loving something more than God, it is put to death most deeply not by gritted teeth alone but by seeing and rejoicing in the greater beauty of Christ, so that the idol loses its attraction. Preachers in Owen’s line stress that the Spirit’s main instrument is the word of God, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and that mortification is daily, practical and never finished in this life.

The means the Spirit uses. Scripture: knowing God’s word, so that the Spirit can use it to expose and resist sin (Psalm 119:11; Hebrews 4:12). Faith in Christ’s death: counting yourself dead to sin and alive to God because you are united to him (6:6, 11). Prayer: asking for the Spirit’s strength, and confessing sin honestly (1 John 1:9). Refusing early: saying no to the first thought, not the last (James 1:14–15). Cutting off opportunities: “make no provision for the flesh” (13:14; Matthew 5:29–30). Replacing, not only removing: putting on the new self, its love, gratitude and service (Colossians 3:5–14; Ephesians 4:22–32). And fellowship: other believers who know your struggle and pray for you (Hebrews 3:13; James 5:16).

Map the chain. Be concrete. Most sin is not a decision; it is the last link in a chain, and by the time you reach the decision the outcome was settled several links earlier. So the fight is not mainly at the moment of temptation, where you are weakest, but upstream of it. Take the sin you keep returning to and ask what reliably precedes it: the hour of the day, the room, the device, the state you are in, tired, alone, resentful, answerable to no one, having just been criticised, having just succeeded. A sin that is never traced upstream is lost the same way for years.

Attack the chain, not the last link. That is what our Lord meant by the startlingly physical language of cutting off and tearing out (Matthew 5:29–30): not mutilation, but the removal of access, which is nearly always possible and nearly always inconvenient. And it is why the New Testament so often says flee rather than resist (1 Corinthians 6:18; 2 Timothy 2:22). There are temptations you are meant to stand and fight, and there are temptations where standing to fight is itself the mistake.

By the Spirit, not by willpower. This is what keeps all of that from being self-improvement. The difference is not in the steps, which an unbeliever could also take, but in whether they are taken in dependence on God: whether you are praying while you do them, and whether the thing you actually want is not merely to stop failing but to please a Person. A man can lock his phone away in the strength of the flesh, and the flesh will find another route within a month. The same act, done in prayer, by a man asking God for the desire he does not yet have and looking to Christ crucified, is mortification.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by our success in killing sin. Even our best mortification is stained, but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours (5:19), and our imperfect fight is accepted for his sake (Westminster 16.6). Those who belong to him will do this, imperfectly but truly. Nor does it mean harming the body, or rigid self-denial for its own sake (Colossians 2:20–23). And it does not mean waiting passively for the Spirit to take temptation away; by the Spirit, you put to death.

Can a Christian lose his salvation by living according to the flesh? No, but the warning is real and meant to be heeded. Verse 13 alarms people who ought not to be alarmed, so read it carefully. Paul describes a direction of life, not a tally of failures, and he has already settled in this letter what our standing with God rests on. The question is not whether you have lost battles; the whole chapter assumes you have. It is which way you are facing. A man who is putting sin to death badly and repeatedly is doing the thing this verse describes. A man who has stopped, and made his peace with his sin, should be alarmed, because he shows no sign of belonging to Christ. God uses warnings like this one to keep his people, whom nothing can separate from his love (vv. 38–39), and those who are truly his will heed them. Many Christians in the Arminian tradition read the warning as a real possibility of a believer falling away; this commentary reads it alongside the unbroken chain of verses 29 and 30. And if this verse frightens you, the fear itself is a sign of life: the Spirit is already at work in someone who cares this much.

In everyday life. Name the sin you most need to put to death, write down what usually happens before it, and make one of those links harder this week. Ask the Spirit for strength, look at Christ crucified for that very sin, and do not negotiate with it.

Both halves stand. In your own strength you will fail, as chapter 7 showed; and if you wait to be delivered without lifting a hand, nothing will happen either. The Spirit does not do it instead of you. He does it through you, and the hands are yours. Nor is the fight a lonely one. Christ took the sin we fight and bore its death on the cross, so that we would not have to die for it; and he sends his Spirit to kill in us what was already condemned in his flesh (v. 3). The war we wage is a mopping-up operation after a victory already won.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Led by the Spirit. Verse 14 explains verse 13: those who by the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body are those who are led by the Spirit. The verb is passive and continuous: the Spirit is the one who leads, and we are being led. “All” means every believer, not a spiritual elite. In context, being led by the Spirit means being led in holiness, away from the flesh (as in Galatians 5:16–25).

Evidence, not a threshold. The direction of verse 14 is nearly always read backwards. Paul does not say that those who are led by the Spirit become sons. He says those who are led by the Spirit are sons: the leading is the symptom, and the sonship is the condition producing it. Read the other way it becomes a treadmill: a standard you must keep reaching before you may call yourself a son. Paul is offering evidence of sonship, not an entrance test. A Christian who has never had a strong impression about a career move and who has been slowly and unglamorously turning away from the same sin for ten years is precisely the person this verse is describing.

What it does not mean. Being led by the Spirit here does not mean receiving detailed inner guidance for life’s decisions: which job to take, which house to buy, which person to marry. Many believers read it that way, and then worry that they are not hearing the Spirit, or treat their impressions as his voice. Paul is describing what every child of God already experiences: the Spirit drawing them, through his word, to trust Christ, to hate sin and to live for God. God does guide our lives by his providence, and gives wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5); we decide by obeying his revealed word, praying, seeking good counsel, and choosing freely within his will. A believer who is unsure which car to buy is not therefore unsure whether he is a child of God.

The spirit of slavery. What we received is not the fear of a slave before a master, or of a criminal before a judge, which is how people relate to God under the law without grace.

Back. Paul is describing a relapse, a return to a former condition, and it is the standing temptation of the Christian life. It happens by drift, and it has a recognisable feel: the sense that you are on probation; that God is broadly disappointed; that the relationship is under review and this week’s performance is the evidence. That is the spirit of slavery, the constant anxiety of a slave who never knows whether today brings punishment, and this verse says it is not what you received.

The Spirit of adoption. In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, and his status changed for ever: he passed out of his old family and wholly into the new father’s household. “Sons”: in the ancient world, sons inherited. Women believers too are “sons” in this sense: full heirs (Galatians 3:26–28).

What does adoption add to being justified? Justification is the courtroom: God the Judge declares the guilty righteous for Christ’s sake. Adoption is the family: God the Father takes those he has acquitted into his household as his own children. A judge can acquit a man and never see him again; this Judge takes the acquitted man home. Adoption brings the Father’s name, his love, his access, his care, his discipline and his inheritance (the Westminster Confession 12.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 12.1). That is why Paul moves from no condemnation to Abba. The first tells you that you will not be punished. The second tells you that you are wanted.

A word left untranslated. Abba is the Aramaic word for father, and a household word: the one used in a house, at a table, by a child who has not yet learned to be careful. It is not baby-talk, as is sometimes said; grown men used it of their fathers all their lives. What it is, is unguarded. Paul leaves it untranslated for Greek-speakers in Rome, probably because they were already using it: somebody had taught these Gentile converts an Aramaic word they had no other use for, and the reason is not hard to find.

The word he used in the dark. Jesus used it. In Gethsemane, face down, with the cup in front of him, our Lord prayed “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). That is the only place in the Gospels where the Aramaic word itself is recorded on his lips, and it is at one of the darkest hours of his life. So it was never a term for the good days. It is what the Son said in the dark, and the Spirit puts it in your mouth in the same conditions. And the verb is “cry”. Not a recitation but something closer to a shout, the sound a person makes involuntarily. The evidence of adoption is what comes out of you when you are frightened. The eternal Son, who has called God Father from before the foundation of the world, has shared his own word with us. He was forsaken so that we might be welcomed; he cried out in the dark so that we might cry Abba in ours and be heard. And the Father now turns to every adopted child with the same love he has for his only Son (John 17:23). We are not slaves on probation. We are sons and daughters at home.

What if my own father makes this word hard to say? The word father is not neutral for everybody. If your own father was frightening, absent or cruel, then this verse asks you to use the warmest word in the language and hands you a cold one. Two things. First, Scripture knows: it is God who is called the father of the fatherless (Psalm 68:5), which is not a metaphor borrowed from good fathers but a claim made in the absence of them. Second, the direction of the comparison is the reverse of what we assume. Your father was not the original of which God is a copy. God is the original, and every human father is a more or less faithful attempt at him. Yours may have been a poor likeness. That tells you nothing whatever about the original, and this verse is an invitation to meet him.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, as if born into the family. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

parallels.desc: sons of the living God

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Setting and background. A Roman adoption was performed before witnesses, who could testify if it were ever challenged. Paul has just spoken of the Spirit of adoption (v. 15), and here are two witnesses to it.

Bears witness with our spirit. Two witnesses: the Holy Spirit, and our own spirit, our inner self. “Himself”: the Spirit in person (the King James Version’s “itself” only follows the grammar of the Greek word for Spirit, which is neuter; it does not make him a thing).

A second witness. The need for two witnesses comes from the law of Israel: a charge was established by two or three witnesses and never by one (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Paul has been writing in courtroom terms since chapter 1. So when he says the Spirit bears witness with our spirit, he is describing testimony that meets the legal standard. Your own sense of being God’s child would not be sufficient evidence on its own; you are, after all, an interested party, someone who gains by the verdict. A second witness has been called, and he is not.

The witness first given at the Jordan. This testimony has been heard before. When Jesus came up out of the water, the Spirit descended on him like a dove and the Father’s voice declared, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (Mark 1:10–11). Now the same Spirit, the Spirit of his Son (Galatians 4:6), bears witness in us that we are children of God, and he can say it only because it is true of the Son first. We are not children in our own right but because we are in him: the Spirit’s testimony is the Jordan verdict extended to everyone joined to the beloved Son. That is why it never points to our record. It points to whose we are.

Where Christians differ: to whom does the Spirit testify? Many Christians struggle with this verse because they are not sure they hear or feel anything, and wonder whether they lack the Spirit’s witness. One suggested way out is to read it as the Spirit testifying to God the Father that we are his children, rather than testifying to us. It is a thoughtful suggestion, and it has a real foothold: a few verses later the Spirit does speak to the Father on our behalf, interceding for us (vv. 26–27). This commentary’s view: in this verse, though, the witness is given to us. First, the verb means to testify together with: the Spirit’s testimony joins our spirit’s testimony, which only makes sense if our own spirit is also hearing and confessing the truth. Even if the Greek is read as the Spirit testifying to our spirit, the hearer is still us, not the Father. Second, the Father does not need to be told who his children are; the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19), since he chose them (v. 29). Third, the context is about our fear and assurance: the Spirit of slavery led to fear, but the Spirit of adoption leads us to cry Abba (v. 15). The witness is for our sake.

What does this feel like? Every honest reader asks, and it is better asked than left sitting: how would I know if it had happened to me? A great many faithful Christians read a verse like this and conclude that whatever Paul is describing has evidently passed them by. So be clear about what is not being claimed. Paul does not describe a voice, or an experience with a date attached, or an event you could arrange in a meeting. And the tense is worth noticing: the Spirit bears witness, present and continuous, not bore witness at some crisis you ought to be able to point to. It is a testimony that has been going on quietly underneath your Christian life, most of it below the level at which you notice anything.

How does the Spirit’s witness work? This is the most helpful answer for those who struggle. The witness is not usually a voice, a vision or a special feeling. Look at v. 15: by the Spirit we cry, Abba, Father. Galatians 4:6 says the same: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The Spirit’s witness is mainly the cry he produces in us: a real, if sometimes weak, trust in God as our Father, a desire to come to him, and confidence that he will receive us for Christ’s sake. When you pray, Father, forgive me for Jesus’ sake, and you mean it, the Spirit is bearing witness with your spirit. He works through the gospel promises, giving us faith to believe them (1 John 5:10–13), and through the new life he produces: love for God’s people (1 John 3:14), obedience (1 John 2:3), and hatred of sin (v. 13). The Westminster Confession puts it this way (Westminster 18.2): assurance rests on the divine truth of the promises of salvation, the inward evidence of the graces those promises speak of, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption witnessing with our spirits that we are the children of God. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (18.2) says the same.

A settledness. What the witness produces is usually not a feeling but a settledness: the ability to read a promise of God addressed to his children and take it as meant for you, without having to argue yourself into it; the instinct, when trouble comes, to pray before you have decided to; the fact that you care whether God is pleased with you at all. None of that announces itself as a witness. All of it is one, heard not alongside your thoughts but in them. You have been looking for a second witness while the second witness was speaking with your mouth. The Holy Spirit of God, who searches the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10), stoops to tell anxious children that they belong. The Father does not merely tolerate his children; he wants them to know that they are his.

Where Christians differ: a direct witness? Some teachers, including the Puritan Thomas Goodwin, John Wesley and Martyn Lloyd-Jones, held that besides this ordinary witness the Spirit sometimes gives a direct, immediate assurance, an overwhelming sense of God’s love, and they encouraged believers to seek it. This commentary’s view: God may give seasons of special joy and assurance, and believers may thank him for them. But the verse does not make such experiences the test of whether we are God’s children. The normal witness of the Spirit is the one every believer has: faith in Christ’s promises, the cry of Abba, and the fruit of the new life. Do not wait for a feeling before you believe you are God’s child; believe God’s promise, and the Spirit will witness through it.

Where Christians differ: can we be sure? Roman Catholic teaching (the sixteenth-century Council of Trent) holds that, apart from special revelation, no one can be certain of being in grace. This commentary’s view: the Spirit himself testifies that we are God’s children. Assurance is the birthright of believers (1 John 5:13; Westminster 18.1; 1689 18.1). It may be shaken or weak at times, but it is God’s will that his children know they are his. The concern behind the Catholic view, that no one should presume on God, is a fair one; but the answer to presumption is the Spirit’s witness, not a lifelong uncertainty.

Two cautions about the Spirit’s witness. First, it cannot be manufactured: teaching that presses people to claim an inner assurance they do not have produces despair or pretence. Second, it is not a licence to ignore evidence. John supplied tests (do you love the brothers, keep his commandments, confess the Son) so that people might know (1 John 5:13). A man who claims a deep inner assurance and whose life shows nothing of Christ has only one witness, himself, and he is the interested party.

What if I have no assurance at all? Then you are not the first, and you are not thereby lost. The Westminster Confession says plainly that assurance is not of the essence of faith, so that a true believer may wait long and struggle hard before he has it, and may have it shaken by sin, temptation or God’s seeming withdrawal (Westminster 18.3–4; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.3–4). Faith that rests on Christ saves, even when it is too weak to feel sure of itself. So do not look first at your assurance; look at Christ, and keep looking. Keep hearing the word, coming to the Lord’s Table, praying, confessing sin, and walking in obedience, because these are the ordinary means by which God strengthens assurance. Talk to a pastor. And keep calling God Father, even when the word feels thin.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. — Romans 8:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then heirs. Children inherit. Fellow heirs with Christ: we share his inheritance, the whole world (4:13), the new creation. Everything that belongs to Christ is ours (1 Corinthians 3:21–23).

In the flow. With the last clause of verse 17, “provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him”, Paul announces the two themes of verses 18 to 30, present suffering and coming glory.

Heirs of God. The phrase is stranger than it looks. An heir normally inherits what the deceased owned. Paul does not say we are heirs to God’s possessions. He says heirs of God. The inheritance is not a set of possessions; it is God himself.

All Levites now. This is not a new arrangement, and Israel had a picture of it. When the land was divided, Levi was handed no territory of its own, only towns scattered among the other tribes (Numbers 35:1–8). And the reason given was not a slight but an honour: “the LORD is their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18:2). The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God. Every adopted child of God is a Levite now. Everything else you possess can be taken from you, by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply by time. An inheritance that is God cannot be repossessed.

Fellow heirs. This is the more staggering half. Paul does not say we inherit in some junior capacity. The word is joint-heirs, which means the measure of what you will receive is not measured by your service, your maturity, or how well your Christian life has gone. It is measured by his. Everything the Son inherits by right of being the Son, the adopted receive by right of adoption, and there is no clause anywhere reducing the portion of the ones who came in late or did badly. The Son would not inherit without his brothers. He endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and now he shares the joy with those who share his road.

If we are all fellow heirs, are there still rewards? Yes, and both truths stand. Every believer receives the whole inheritance, because it is Christ’s and we have it in him. Scripture also speaks of rewards for faithful service (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Matthew 25:21; 2 Corinthians 5:10). But these are not wages earned alongside grace; they are God crowning his own gifts in us, and there will be no envy in that kingdom, only joy. A thimble and a bucket can both be full. So serve faithfully, knowing that nothing done for him is forgotten, but never imagine that your place at the table depends on it.

Provided we suffer with him. The road to glory goes through suffering, as it did for Christ (Luke 24:26; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Peter 4:13). Does this make the inheritance depend on how much we suffer? No. Paul is not setting a price, but describing the family path: the children share their brother’s road. It covers all that comes to believers because they belong to Christ: opposition, the cost of obedience, and the groaning of living in a fallen world while waiting for glory (vv. 18–23).

With him. The clause has frightened people it was never aimed at. The reader who is frightened by it is nearly always the one currently suffering, and what he hears is a demand for more. Paul does not write “provided you suffer enough”. He writes “suffer with him”, and the whole weight is in the last word. It is not the quantity that qualifies anything; it is the company. The question is not how much you are bearing but who is bearing it alongside you, and the answer this chapter gives is that he is not observing your suffering from a distance. He is in it, and he has been in worse.

What it does not mean. This verse is sometimes used to sanctify things that ought to be resisted. Suffering with Christ does not mean accepting every affliction as sent and staying where you are. It does not mean a woman should remain in a house where she is being harmed: abuse is never to be tolerated, and she should seek safety and help at once. It does not mean an illness should not be treated, or that an injustice should be borne quietly when it could be addressed. Paul himself avoided danger repeatedly, appealed to Caesar, and was lowered over a wall in a basket. The verse describes the shape of the road, not a duty to seek out wounds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Future Glory: Groaning, Intercession, and the Golden Chain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Present sufferings are real, and Paul does not minimise them, but they are not worth comparing with the coming glory (v. 18). Creation groans for its liberation, believers groan for the redemption of the body, and the Spirit groans in intercession for us: three groans, all pointing to the glory of God's children in the new creation.

Verse 28 does not promise that everything will feel good or produce an obvious benefit. It promises that God is at work in all things, the painful as well as the joyful, for the good of those he has called, and verse 29 defines that good as likeness to his Son.

The golden chain of vv. 29–30 runs from foreknowledge to glory: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified, with no link missing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Effectual Calling and the Golden Chain

Romans 8:29–30 is a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of election and effectual calling. Foreknowledge here is not mere prior knowledge but prior, choosing love, the sense in which God knew Israel (Amos 3:2) and the Shepherd knows his sheep (John 10:14). Every link of the chain is God's work, and the calling is inward and effectual: it brings about the faith it calls for. No one finally falls from grace, not because believers are strong enough to hold on, but because God is able to keep what he has begun.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The groaning of creation in vv. 19–22 draws on the Jewish understanding that the natural world was affected by human sin (Genesis 3:17–18) and would be renewed in the age to come. The gospel is not only the rescue of souls but the renewal of all things. Now: Romans 8:28 is sometimes pressed on people in fresh catastrophe. Used rightly, it does not promise that things will work out as we hope; it promises that a sovereign God is working toward his purpose in all things, and that his purpose is better than our preferences.

verseByVerse.quote: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I consider. The verb (logizomai) means to calculate, the bookkeeping word that has run through this letter. Paul is not saying he feels the sufferings are light; he has done the sum, and he knew the suffering side of it from the inside: beaten five times with thirty-nine lashes, three times with rods, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), and, as the early church remembered, not many years from a Roman execution.

In the flow. Verse 18 opens the section that runs to verse 30: three groans, of creation (v. 22), of believers (v. 23) and of the Spirit (v. 26), ending in God’s unbreakable purpose (vv. 28–30).

Not worth comparing. The word is doing something precise. Paul does not say the sufferings are small; he says they are not in the same category as the glory: the two cannot usefully be set side by side, the way you cannot weigh a colour against a sound. We tend to say the good will eventually outweigh the bad, and a grieving person feels the falseness of it at once: no quantity of future pleasantness makes a dead child worth it. Paul is not proposing a trade. He is saying the coming thing is of an order that makes the comparison itself break down.

This present time. The sufferings are of this present time, a phrase with a boundary in it: they belong to an age that is ending. And the glory is “to be revealed”, a word that means drawing back a covering. It exists now, in Christ, out of sight, which is why the honest thing to say about the present is not that it is fine but that the curtain is still down.

The glory has a face. The glory exists already, in a Person. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus asked, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). His sufferings came first and his glory followed, and ours are joined to his in the same order (v. 17). So the curtain will be drawn back on him: “When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). What tips Paul’s scales is not a better climate but the appearing of the Son, whose glory his people will share. He did not ask us to walk a road he had not walked; he walked it first, and he walked it further. And the God who weighs our sufferings knows their exact weight: he keeps count of every tear (Psalm 56:8).

Revealed to us. Or “in us”: we will share it. Not merely a better world to look at, but a transformation of the person looking: conformed to the image of the Son (v. 29).

What it does not mean. A verse like this can be used as a stick, quoted at a woman who has just buried her husband as though the right response to grief were to stop making so much of it. That is not what the verse does, and the surrounding paragraph proves it: within eight verses Paul has creation groaning, believers groaning, and the Spirit himself groaning. He is not asking anyone to minimise. And timing matters. This verse is not a reply to somebody’s pain in the first week. It is ammunition to be stored in advance and used later, by the sufferer himself, on the days when the trouble threatens to fill his whole view. Paul writes it in the first person, as the conclusion he reached about his own troubles.

Is it wrong to grieve, if the glory is so great? No. Jesus wept at the tomb of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35). Paul tells the Thessalonians not that they should not grieve, but that they should not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is the right response to real loss in a fallen world, and the glory to come does not make the loss less real; it makes it not final. Christian grief and Christian hope live in the same heart at the same time. Weep, and hope while you weep.

What exactly is the glory? Not a vague brightness. Scripture names it. We will see Christ as he is and be like him (1 John 3:2). We will have bodies raised imperishable and glorious, like his (Philippians 3:21). We will be free of sin for ever, not only its guilt but its presence. We will live with God in a renewed creation, where he wipes away every tear and death is no more (Revelation 21:3–4). We will know him, worship him, serve him and reign with him, with the whole family of God from every nation. And at the centre of it all is not a place but a Person: the Lamb who was slain, whose face we shall see (Revelation 22:3–4).

In everyday life. Paul’s sum needs both figures, and if “glory” is only a vague word to you, it will feel hollow when weighed against a vivid ache. So this week, read one passage about the glory (Revelation 21–22 or 1 Corinthians 15), and let it fill in the other side of the scales.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
verseByVerse.commentary:
Craning its neck. The word for eager longing is a picture rather than a concept. Apokaradokia is built from the word for a head: it describes someone craning on a station platform, watching the point where the train will appear. That is what the physical universe is doing, and the surprise is what it waits for. Creation is craning for the revealing of the sons of God: it is watching for us. Its own liberation is attached to ours. It went down when we did, and it comes up the same way. The whole universe stands on tiptoe because its Maker has promised to come back for it.

Does creation really long for anything? No. Rocks, rivers and stars do not have minds or feelings. Paul is using personification: a figure of speech that speaks of non-human things as if they were people, to help us feel a truth. The Bible does this often. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1). The earth mourns (Isaiah 24:4). The mountains and hills break into singing, and the trees clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12). The sea roars and the fields exult because the Lord is coming to judge the earth (Psalm 96:11–13), which is the very hope Paul has in view here. And Jesus said that if his disciples were silent, the stones would cry out (Luke 19:40).

Poetic, but not unreal. The picture describes something true. Creation is in bondage to decay (v. 21), and its future is tied to ours. We say a dry field is crying out for rain; the field feels nothing, but the need is real. Paul lends creation human longing so that we will feel how much is at stake, and long too (v. 23).

Subjected to futility. Futility is exactly the right word for what we actually experience. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses again and again in Ecclesiastes for vanity, which in Hebrew means breath, vapour, the thing that will not hold still. It is why the beautiful thing decays and the body that was strong at thirty is not at seventy. Paul is not being pessimistic; he is describing the condition of a world under sentence, and everybody knows it whether or not they have a theology for it.

Him who subjected it. Almost certainly not Adam, who had no power to subject creation to anything, nor Satan, who could not do it in hope. It is God, who pronounced the curse on the ground because of Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17–19). Creation did not choose its frustration; it was bound up with humanity’s fall, because humanity was meant to rule it. And God subjected it in hope, with its liberation already planned. The curse was never meant to be final.

A hard sentence, and a mercy in it. The thorns of Genesis 3, the decay, the earthquakes, the diseases that kill children in countries that did nothing in particular to deserve them: Paul does not attribute any of that to blind chance. He traces it to a judicial act of God following Adam’s rebellion. It does not mean that any particular child’s illness is a punishment for anyone’s particular sin (John 9:3); it is the condition of the whole fallen world. And this truth saves you from despair. If the disorder of the world is an act of God, then it is meaningful and it is bounded. A universe damaged by accident has nobody to appeal to and no reason to expect a repair. A universe placed under futility by a Judge can be released by the same Judge, and the sentence has an end date. That is why Paul adds “in hope”: the sentence was passed with a view to the release.

The Man who will rule it. Creation went down with Adam because Adam was set over it: Psalm 8 says God put all things under man’s feet. Hebrews takes up that psalm and admits that at present we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:8–9). The Man who was always meant to rule the earth well has arrived. The Son through whom all things were made entered his own creation, wore its thorns as a crown, and rose as the first piece of the world made new; and through him God is reconciling all things to himself (Colossians 1:20). He is the hope in which creation was subjected, and it waits for the sons of God to be revealed with him.

Your ache is agreement. The sense that something is wrong with the way things are, the grief at a landscape ruined, the anger at a disease that should not exist, the refusal to be reconciled to the fact that everything you love is temporary, is not a failure to be spiritual. It is agreement with the apostle. Creation is groaning; you are supposed to hear it.
verseByVerse.note: The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin.

parallels.desc: cursed is the ground because of you

verseByVerse.quote: that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set free. Creation itself will be liberated. Not destroyed and replaced, but renewed (Acts 3:21; Revelation 21:1–5; Isaiah 65:17). Decay, death and disorder will end.

Bondage to corruption. Corruption here is not moral wickedness but decay: the process by which things come apart. The iron rusts, the photograph fades, the strong man weakens, and every living thing is on a schedule it did not choose. Paul calls that a slavery: a condition nothing here can escape.

What is abolished. Decay will not be slowed but ended. No more funerals, because there will be nothing left to bury. No more scans, no waiting rooms, no results delivered by a doctor who has learned how to arrange his face. No more photographs of people you cannot ring. No more of the particular grief of watching a mind go while the body remains, or a body go while the mind remains. The thing this verse abolishes is the machinery by which everything good is taken away from you. What you love is not going to be taken from you for ever; it is going to be given back, without the decay attached. Every leaf that falls this autumn falls in a world that has been promised its spring.

The freedom of the glory. Creation’s destiny is tied to ours. When God’s children are glorified, creation will be set free with them. This will happen when Christ returns, at the same time as the resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:23, 51–54). Then God will make the new heavens and the new earth (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1).

The family estate restored. Creation is not given a separate freedom of its own. It is brought into the very liberty that belongs to God’s glorified children, as though the family estate were being restored along with the family. That is the Genesis arrangement running backwards: the ground was cursed because of a man (Genesis 3:17), and it is released because of God’s redeemed children; both times mankind and its home go together.

What are the new heavens and the new earth? The phrase comes from Isaiah (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22) and is taken up by Peter and John (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1). “The heavens and the earth” is the Bible’s way of saying the whole universe, as in Genesis 1:1: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. So the promise is a whole renewed creation, not just a better place for souls.

New in what sense? The Greek word for “new” here (kainos) is often said to mean new in quality rather than brand-new from nothing, though that distinction should not be pressed. Our resurrection bodies are the better guide. They will be our bodies, raised and transformed: sown perishable, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The risen Jesus still bore the marks of the nails (John 20:27). In the same way, the new creation will be this creation, set free (v. 21), and yet so changed that it is truly new. Peter speaks of fire (2 Peter 3:10–12), but he also compares it with the flood, when the world of that time perished (2 Peter 3:6), yet the earth itself remained. The fire purifies and remakes; it does not simply erase. In 2 Peter 3:10 the King James Version says the earth will be burned up; the earliest manuscripts say it will be exposed, as the ESV has it.

What will it be like? Scripture gives us glimpses, not a map. God himself will dwell with his people: heaven and earth joined (Revelation 21:3). There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4), and no more curse (Revelation 22:3). It will be a home of righteousness (2 Peter 3:13). We will have real, resurrected bodies, and eat at the feast of the kingdom (Matthew 8:11; 26:29). God’s servants will serve him and reign (Revelation 22:3–5). The river and the tree of life are there (Revelation 22:1–2): Eden restored, and more than restored, because it is now a city full of the nations, who bring their glory into it (Revelation 21:24–26).

A garden at both ends. The Bible opens in a garden and closes in a garden city, with a river and a tree and leaves for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:1–2). It does not open in a garden and close in a cloud. The end of the story is physical, and any version of the Christian hope in which believers finally leave the material world behind has got the last chapter wrong.

Where Christians differ: the future of creation. Some believe the earth will be annihilated and believers will live in a purely spiritual heaven; others (premillennialists) expect a renewed earth in a thousand-year kingdom before the final state, and some of them a secret rapture of the church beforehand. This commentary’s view: Scripture promises that this creation will be set free and renewed at Christ’s return: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Not escape from the material world, but its redemption. The amillennial view (which reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of the present age between Christ’s two comings) sees this as the final state, following Christ’s single return. The reason is texts like this one: creation is set free when the children of God are revealed, at the resurrection, with no further age in between (also 2 Peter 3:10–13). Many faithful believers see it otherwise, and this commentary holds its view as brothers and sisters together waiting for the same Lord.

Work on material things. If God intends to redeem the material creation rather than discard it, then work done on material things is not a lower kind of work. The farmer, the surgeon, the engineer, the man who repairs things properly: they are, in a small way, doing to a corner of creation what God intends to do to all of it. That does not make their labour permanent; the building will still fall down eventually. It makes it a signpost to the world God will make new, which is a serious thing to be.

Will animals be there? Scripture pictures the new creation with animals in it: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6). Whether a particular pet will be raised, Scripture does not say, and we should not claim more than it does. But the hope of renewal shapes how we treat the world now. God put man in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15), and that rules out both worshipping the earth and wasting it carelessly. And if you are grieving an animal you loved, the grief is not foolish: not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29).

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Birth pains. Not death throes, but birth pains. The groaning of creation, earthquakes, storms, disease, is not meaningless. It is labour, leading to new birth (Matthew 24:8).

Two kinds of screaming. There are two kinds of screaming in a hospital, and they can sound alike to somebody in the corridor. One is coming from a ward where something is ending; the other from a delivery room where something is beginning. Nothing in the sound itself tells you which is which. Paul says the groan of this world is the second kind. The image does not say the pain is small or brief; it says the pain is going somewhere. And labour gets worse before it ends. Nobody in Scripture promises that the groaning of this age will taper off gently.

Does creation really groan? Not literally. Creation is not a person: the earth has no mind, and it does not feel pain as a mother in labour does. Paul is using poetic language, personification: speaking of creation as if it were a person, to help us feel a truth. The picture of childbirth says two true things at once. The pain is real: creation really is broken, subject to decay, disease and disaster. And the pain is not pointless: like labour, it is leading somewhere, to the birth of a new creation (v. 21). Then the poetry turns to us: we, who really do feel, groan too (v. 23).

The firstfruits of the Spirit. The firstfruits were given to God as a pledge that the rest of the harvest would follow (Leviticus 23:10).

Groaning because of the Spirit. Paul puts Christians in the same sentence as the earthquakes, and the ones groaning are not the weak in faith but those who have the firstfruits of the Spirit. The groaning is not evidence that something has gone wrong with your Christianity. It is evidence that the Spirit is in you. The first sheaf is truly part of the harvest, but not the whole of it. A man who has never tasted anything does not know what he is missing; the taste is what creates the hunger. So the Spirit makes you less at home in the present world: the longing is the appetite the first course produced.

Homesick saints. That is why the ache goes up rather than down as a Christian matures, and why the most godly people you have known were often the most homesick. If you have found that the older you get in the faith the less this world satisfies you, you have not lost ground. You have been given more of the firstfruits. You are not malfunctioning. You are in labour, along with everything else God has made, so turn the ache into a prayer: Come, Lord Jesus.

The paperwork is signed. It is odd to read of adoption still awaited after verse 15 said we have received it, but both are true. The adoption is complete in law and only partly experienced: you are a son now, and you are still living in a body that is failing. The paperwork is signed. The child has not yet come home. And the last words are the ones to hold: the redemption of our bodies, not only of our souls. The body is the one part of you that is visibly losing. Your soul is not the part of you that has a diagnosis.

The firstborn of the new creation. The labour has already produced its first child. Christ is the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). So the groaning of creation and of believers is not a guess about whether a new world will come: one body has already passed through the grave into the age to come, and it is the body of our Lord. The Spirit in us is the firstfruits of what we will receive; the risen Christ is the firstfruits of what we will become. That is why Paul waits for the redemption of the body. He has seen what God does with a body on the third day. And the God who began the harvest with one sheaf has never yet left a field ungathered.

Does this groaning mean I should not seek help for depression? No. The groaning of this verse is the longing of every believer for the redemption of the body, and it is healthy. Depression is something else: an illness of a body and mind that are part of this groaning creation, and like any illness it may need a doctor, medicine or counselling as well as prayer. Seeking that help is not a lack of faith, any more than setting a broken leg is. Elijah under the broom tree was given sleep and food before he was given a word (1 Kings 19:4–8). Tell your pastor and a trusted friend, see your doctor, keep coming to Christ, and if you ever think of ending your life, tell someone today.
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come.

verseByVerse.quote: For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saved into hope. The verb is past tense, completed. Our rescue is not something still in doubt; it has happened. But it happened “in this hope”, with the best part still to come: a Christian has been saved into a situation that is not yet finished.

Hope is a strong word. In ordinary English hope is the weakest word we have for the future: “I hope it does not rain”, meaning I have no idea and no control. In Scripture it is one of the strongest: a settled expectation of something certain that has not yet arrived. The uncertainty is entirely in the timing and entirely absent from the outcome. A man waiting at an airport for a plane that has already taken off is not hoping in the English sense. He does not know the minute; he knows the plane is in the air.

Invisibility is the arrangement. Nobody hopes for what he sees, so the invisibility of the thing is not an objection to the hope but a condition of it. The very feature of the Christian life that most troubles us, that the promises are not visible, that God does not produce evidence on demand, is not a flaw in the arrangement. It is the arrangement. You are not failing because you cannot see it. You would be failing if you needed to.

Remaining under. The word for patience (as in 5:3–4) is built from remaining under: endurance, the capacity to stay put beneath a weight that is not lifting. Paul does not say we wait with serenity. So the honest shape of the Christian life in this passage is this: saved, certainly; groaning, genuinely; seeing nothing, at present; and staying put. That is a considerably less triumphant account than the one often preached, and it is a great relief to anybody whose experience has not matched the advertised version. The waiting is not the interval before the Christian life begins. It is the Christian life, conducted in the dark, by people who have been given every reason to believe the lights are about to come on.

A hope anchored in what was seen. We do not see what we hope for, but the hope rests on something that was seen: the risen Jesus appeared to Peter, to the Twelve, and to more than five hundred at one time (1 Corinthians 15:5–6). God has caused us to be born again to a living hope through his resurrection (1 Peter 1:3). What we wait for has already happened once, to him, in history and before witnesses. And the hope is not only about him; it is him: Christ Jesus our hope (1 Timothy 1:1), who has gone ahead of us behind the curtain, where the anchor of our soul is fastened (Hebrews 6:19–20). We cannot see where it holds. We know who fixed it there.

What if I find it hard even to want heaven? Then say so to God, and ask him for the longing; it is a prayer he delights to answer. Desire for glory grows the way appetite grows: by tasting. Spend time with what Scripture says about the age to come, and especially with Christ himself, because heaven is wanted most by those who want him most. Many Christians do not want heaven because they picture it wrongly, as a thin and ghostly place; the real promise is a raised body in a renewed world with the Lord. And do not despise the small longing you already have. The firstfruits of the Spirit are small by definition.

In everyday life. Hope is not optimism, a temperament that rises and falls with sleep and collapses when the facts turn. Hope is a conviction about an outcome guaranteed by somebody else, and it is entirely compatible with feeling terrible. So ask: if you were told today that the thing you are waiting for will not come in your lifetime, the prodigal will not return before you die, the illness will not lift, the marriage will not mend, would you still be a Christian on Sunday? An optimist could not survive that sentence. Hope can, because hope was never resting on the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other end of the load. The word for helps (synantilambanetai) is a picture of two people and a load. It means to take hold of something together with somebody, from the other side; Martha uses it when she asks the Lord to tell Mary to help her (Luke 10:40). It is somebody coming to the other end of a thing too heavy for one person and lifting. The Holy Spirit, who is God, kneels, as it were, beside the weakest believer and takes the other end. And the help is applied not first to our circumstances but to our weakness, and Paul names a particular one.

We do not know. That is a remarkable admission, and the apostle includes himself. In suffering especially, we do not know what is best. The problem is not technique; it is that we genuinely cannot see far enough to know what is good. You pray for the illness to be lifted, and it may be the illness that saves your life in a way you cannot yet imagine. You pray for the door to open, and you do not know what is behind it. Paul himself prayed three times for a thorn to be removed and was told no, and the no turned out to be the better answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

The third groan. The Spirit does not merely improve our praying. He prays, from within. This is the third and deepest groan, after creation’s and ours. The Trinity is not a spectator of the ache of the world.

What does “too deep for words” mean? The Greek is two words: stenagmois alalētois, “groanings” that are alalētos, literally “not spoken”. It can mean wordless, never put into speech, or unutterable, too deep to be put into speech. Either way, the point is not that God cannot understand them, or that the Spirit is short of words. The point is that this praying happens below the level of our words. Our words fail; his intercession does not. And it is perfectly understood: the Father, who searches hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit (v. 27).

Whose groanings are they? Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes. But he has just said that we groan inwardly (v. 23), and the Spirit is the Spirit who lives in us (vv. 9–11). So many, including Calvin, understand it this way: the Spirit stirs up in our hearts the deep, wordless longings that we cannot express, and takes them up as his own intercession before the Father. Others stress that the Spirit intercedes for us in a way hidden from us altogether. Both agree on the heart of it: the Spirit is praying for us, within us, in line with God’s will. Groaning is also a word borrowed from our experience. It speaks of deep, earnest desire, not of the Spirit being in distress or unable to cope.

What it means in real life. You sit by a hospital bed and cannot find a single sentence to pray. You wake at night with a weight you cannot name, and all you can say is, O God. Your grief over a child, a marriage or your own sin comes out as a sigh or tears. That is not failed prayer. The Spirit takes that wordless longing, and before the Father it becomes a prayer that is exactly right, because the Spirit always asks according to the will of God. You do not have to find the right words to be heard.

The Son who knew this weakness. Our Lord knows from the inside what it is to stand before the Father with a heart too heavy for easy words. Facing the cross he said, “Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say?” (John 12:27). In Gethsemane his prayer came to rest where every true prayer must: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The Spirit who intercedes for us according to the will of God is the Spirit of that Son. He carries to the Father, in line with the Father’s will, the groan of a believer who does not know what to ask, and in Christ that broken praying is heard, as the Son was heard (Hebrews 5:7).

The whole circuit. The Father searches hearts and reads what the Spirit is saying in you. The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God. So a prayer that begins as an inarticulate ache in a believer is taken up by God the Spirit, presented to God the Father, in perfect accordance with the will of God, and Christ is at the right hand interceding as well (v. 34). Every person of the Trinity is engaged in your prayer, and the only weak link in the chain, your own faltering words, is the one the Spirit has taken in hand.

The praying has changed hands. If prayer has become almost impossible, because the grief is too heavy or you have prayed so long about one thing that you cannot bear to raise it again, this verse says the praying has not stopped. It has changed hands. The groan you cannot put into words is itself being carried, and it arrives at the Father in perfect condition. So do not stay away until you have something worth saying: go and sit down with nothing, and say so. On the authority of this verse, that may be the truest praying you have done all year. It is not an experience to be attained; it is a fact to be leaned on.

Where Christians differ: are these groanings tongues? Some see these groanings as speaking in tongues; many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read them as a private prayer language given by the Spirit. This commentary’s view: no. They are “too deep for words”, not spoken in any language, and they belong to every believer, since Paul is speaking of all who have the Spirit (vv. 9, 14). Tongues were a spoken gift given to some, not to all (1 Corinthians 12:30). Paul says it is the Spirit who intercedes, and that his groanings are too deep for words, which is the opposite of an utterance. This is the Spirit’s hidden intercession for all God’s children, and the comfort is meant for every believer who cannot find words to pray. Brothers and sisters who pray in tongues need not feel dismissed: whatever view one takes of that gift, this verse’s comfort is theirs too.

parallels.desc: you have searched me and known me

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. — Romans 8:28
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we know. This is not optimism but apostolic certainty: a fact about the way God operates, over suffering, betrayal, disease and death. Because this is one of the most misused verses in the chapter, it is worth being exact about what it does not say before enjoying what it does.

All things work together for good. All things: not just good things, but suffering, loss, failure, even sin. Not that all things are good, but that God works them together for good. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.” Either way, God is the one at work. “Good”: defined by v. 29, being made like Christ. Not necessarily comfort, but Christlikeness.

Called according to his purpose. The promise is for those who love God, and they love him because he called them. His purpose comes first. God’s calling here is effectual: it does what it says and brings people to faith (v. 30). It is not only the invitation of the gospel, which many hear and refuse, but God’s summons through that gospel, which opens blind eyes and makes the hearer willing to come (John 6:44; 2 Corinthians 4:6).

Not that all things are good. After ten verses of groaning, Paul is not now saying it was fine all along. The cancer is not good. The betrayal is not good. The child’s death is not good, and God does not call it good: he calls death an enemy, and the last enemy at that (1 Corinthians 15:26). What the verse says is that God works in all things, which assumes that these things, in themselves, are not good.

Not on our timetable. Nor does it say that all things work together for what you would recognise as good, or that the good will be visible on any particular timetable, or that a reason will be supplied. Joseph waited more than twenty years to be able to say what God had been doing (Genesis 50:20), and many of the people in Scripture who suffered were never told anything at all. As far as the book tells us, Job never learned about the conversation between God and Satan in chapter 1.

Not of everyone. Twice in one sentence Paul draws the circle: for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose. This is a promise made to a family, not a general observation about how the universe treats people. To offer it to somebody outside that circle is not comfort; it is a false assurance, and they will find out. The right thing to offer them is the gospel, which invites them into the circle.

Not for the hospital corridor. As with verse 18, this is not a sentence to be deployed at a funeral, or in a hospital corridor, or in the first weeks after a marriage ends. Not because it is untrue then. But in the mouth of the sufferer it is a handhold, while in the mouth of a bystander it sounds like an instruction to stop making a fuss, as though the pain has already been accounted for and can therefore be set down. It belongs to the people inside the trouble (we know), and the right thing to do with someone in fresh grief is what Job’s friends did for seven days, sitting with him in silence (Job 2:13), before they opened their mouths and ruined everything.

All means all. The verse is stronger than the version we usually preach. All includes the things done to you by other people’s malice, which is the hardest category, and Genesis says so without flinching: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The brothers’ intention was evil, and it is never called anything else; God’s intention, in the very same event, was good. It also includes your own sins and stupidities: not that they were good, but that God’s working reaches even them. And it includes the wasted years: the decade in the wrong job, the season you were too ill or too lost to be of use to anyone.

Work together. This is the right image, because it is not a claim that each item is individually beneficial. Ingredients are not individually pleasant; nobody eats flour, raw egg is unappetising, and salt on its own is unbearable. The promise is not that every element tastes good but that the baker knows what he is doing and there will be a cake.

The proof case at Calvary. Whether God can work all things together for good has already been settled in public. The crucifixion of Jesus was the worst thing human beings have ever done: betrayal, false witness, cowardice and murder, aimed at the Son of God. Yet Peter preached that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same sentence called his killers “lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Their sin was still sin; yet through it God worked the salvation of the world. So this verse is the cross applied to everyone who is in Christ: if God could bring life out of Good Friday, he can work in all things for those he has called.

What good? The very next verse supplies the definition, and it changes everything. The good in view is not comfort, or resolution, or the outcome you asked for. It is being conformed to the image of his Son (v. 29). That is a considerably higher good than the one we would have chosen, and it explains why so many prayers get answered sideways: you asked for the circumstance to change and God is at work on the person in the circumstance.

If God works even my sins for good, why should I not sin? Because God works good out of sin in spite of what sin is, not because it is any less evil. Paul has already rejected this exact argument: shall we sin that grace may abound? By no means (6:1–2). Sin still grieves the Father, wounds others and scars you, and David’s forgiven adultery still cost him a child and a divided house. A son who wrecks his father’s car is not entitled to call it good because his father later teaches him through it. What this verse gives you after a fall is hope, that God has not abandoned you to your worst decisions. It never gives you permission for the next one.

In everyday life. Take the worst thing that has happened to you and ask, not whether you can see the good, because you very often cannot, but whether you are more like Christ than you were before it. More patient, less confident in yourself, quicker to pray, kinder to those in the same trouble. If any of that is true, you have found the good, and it did not look like good at the time. If you cannot see it yet, the working is still his, and he has not stopped. The verse does not say we see. It says we know: the word for a thing held on to in the dark, on the authority of somebody who can see the whole of it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.”

parallels.desc: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good

verseByVerse.quote: For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son... And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. — Romans 8:29–30
verseByVerse.commentary:
Foreknowledge as love. “Foreknew” carries the full biblical weight of the word “know” as God uses it: not mere awareness or prediction, but intimate, prior love. When God tells Israel he has known them only, of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2), he means he chose them with covenant love; so too with Jeremiah, known before he was formed in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5). Foreknowledge is not God looking down the corridor of time and selecting those he predicts will believe; it is God’s prior sovereign love that is the very ground of their believing.

Predestined to a likeness. Paul does not say predestined to heaven, or to be on a list. To predestine is to decide beforehand, and he says predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. The destination is a likeness, the good of the previous verse. God’s settled intention concerning you, formed before the world existed, is that you should end up like Jesus Christ.

A family for the Son. “Firstborn” here is not about origin; it is the language of rank and inheritance, the pre-eminent one in a family. So the whole vast work of election, calling, justification and glory exists to produce a family for the Son. God was not merely rescuing individuals from a fire; he was gathering brothers and sisters for his Son, and family resemblance is the goal.

Called, justified. The call here is effectual: it brings people to faith. To be justified is to be acquitted and accepted by God the Judge: not made sinless on the spot, but pronounced righteous in Christ, a gift received by faith alone (3:24–26; 4:5).

He also glorified. The golden chain: foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Every person in the first link is in the last, and “glorified” (raised and made fully like Christ) is in the past tense, though future for us: so certain that God speaks of it as done. Your glorification is not a possibility but a certainty, not because you are strong but because he is faithful.

Every verb is God’s. He foreknew, he predestined, he called, he justified, he glorified; the human person appears only as the object. That is not fatalism but faithfulness: the chain holds because every link is God’s work, not ours. It was begun before the world was made and ends in eternity to come, and every link of it was forged by love.

The missing link. Look at what is missing from the chain. Foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and then straight to glorified. There is no link for “sanctified”, made holy in life. Not because sanctification is unimportant. But if progress in holiness were a link in this chain, the chain would be exactly as strong as your last six months, and every believer would have grounds for terror. Paul’s chain contains no link that depends on you. Your growth in holiness is what God himself is doing between the fourth link and the fifth, not a condition you must meet to get from one to the other, and because he does it, it will be done.

Where Christians differ: foreknowledge and predestination. Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s choice rests on his foreknowledge of our faith, and that his grace can be resisted) teach that God foreknew who would believe and predestined them on that basis. This commentary’s view: Paul says God foreknew persons, not their choices; “foreknew” in biblical usage means to set one’s love on beforehand. And the chain is unbroken: all who are called are justified, so the call must be effectual, not merely an invitation many refuse. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2 Timothy 1:9). This is unconditional election (God’s choice resting on his own love, not on anything he foresaw in us), and it is the ground of perfect assurance: if God began it in eternity, he will finish it in glory.

The Arminian case, heard fairly. Arminian Christians, who love the same Saviour, point to the ordinary sense of the word, knowing in advance, and to Peter’s description of believers as elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father (1 Peter 1:2). But Paul says God foreknew people, those whom he foreknew, not facts about them. He uses the same verb in 11:2, of his people whom he foreknew, where it means God’s choosing love for Israel. And faith itself is God’s gift: it has been granted to you to believe (Philippians 1:29). If God chose us because he saw we would believe, the chain would begin with us.
