Is it unfair? It would be unfair only if anyone deserved to be chosen. No one is condemned who did not deserve it, and everyone who is saved owes it to mercy (9:14–16). The question is not why God does not save everyone, which Scripture leaves in his wisdom, but why he saves anyone, which Scripture answers: because he loved them, freely, in Christ. Election does not make heaven smaller than it would have been; left to ourselves none of us would come, and election is how it fills.

How do I know I am in this? The question should be asked out loud rather than left to trouble people privately. The first link is in eternity past and you cannot read it. Nobody has ever been given access to the decrees of God, and every attempt to peer into them ends either in presumption or despair. So do not start there. Of the five links, the first two and the last are out of sight, but the middle two are visible. Have you been called: not merely invited by a preacher, but drawn, so that Christ came to matter to you in a way he had not before, whether or not you can date the moment? Are you justified: when you consider standing before God, are you resting on Christ rather than on your record? Those are answerable questions. And a chain does not have a middle without both ends. If you can find yourself at link three or four, links one and five are settled, and they were settled without consulting you.

What if I am afraid I am not elect? The anxiety itself is a kind of answer. Nobody who is indifferent to God lies awake worrying about this. The desire is not the qualification, but it is evidence of the drawing, and the door has never been shut on anyone who came: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). You are never asked to find your name in eternity past before you come to Christ. You are asked to come, and those who come find they were expected.

If God has chosen, why evangelise or pray? Because the God who chose the end also chose the means. Those he predestined he called, and he calls through the gospel preached by people like you: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard (10:14)? Election is not a reason to stay silent; it is the reason evangelism will not fail. Paul kept going in Corinth because the Lord told him he had many people in that city (Acts 18:10). You do not know who the elect are, so offer Christ freely to everyone, and pray, because prayer is one of the ways God brings about what he has purposed.

What it does not mean. A doctrine this strong is regularly turned into passivity, but Paul has already commanded you to put sin to death (v. 13) and will spend four chapters on obedience. The chain does not tell you what to do. It tells you why what you do will not finally fail. Nor does it give anyone a reason to look down on others. A doctrine that says you were chosen for no merit of your own leaves you nothing to boast about, and every reason to be gentle with those who do not yet believe (1 Corinthians 1:26–31; 1 Corinthians 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: “Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time: God set his love on them beforehand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — Nothing Can Separate Us from the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends in a series of questions, each answered in triumph, and a list of everything that might be imagined to separate the Christian from the love of God, only to declare that none of it can. This is the conclusion of everything Paul has argued since 1:16: the God who did not spare his own Son will not abandon those for whom his Son died.

If God is for us, it does not follow that no one will be against us: Paul names tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger and sword (v. 35). The enemies are real, but none can prevail. To the troubled conscience's questions, who shall bring any charge and who is to condemn (vv. 33–34), Paul does not deny there is anything to charge; he names who occupies the seats that matter: God who justifies, and the Christ who died, was raised and now intercedes. And we are more than conquerors in all these things (v. 37), inside the trouble rather than by escaping it.

The closing list covers death and life, every unseen power, all of time and all of space, and anything else in all creation. God's love is not a feeling that rises and falls with our spiritual temperature but his settled commitment in Christ, and it will not let us go, because it never depended on us to begin with.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Perseverance of the Saints

Romans 8:31–39 anchors the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance, or preservation, of the saints. The saints persevere not because they are strong but because God keeps them. Nothing in all creation, ourselves included, can sever the love that chose us before we existed and bought us at the cost of the Son. Perseverance is God's gift, the last link in the golden chain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The hardships of v. 35 were not hypothetical for the first readers. Within about a decade the Roman church would face Nero's persecution, when some believers were torn by dogs and some burned as torches in his gardens. Now: A Christian in comfort reads Romans 8:35–39 as help in ordinary difficulties; a Christian in the persecuted church reads it as the word needed to die well. Both readings are right, and the grace that sustained the martyrs is the same grace that sustains every believer, whatever is still to come.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say to these things? Paul draws the conclusion of everything he has said, and the question is looking further back than we usually notice. These things are not merely the golden chain of the previous verse. The phrase reaches back through the whole letter: the wrath revealed, every mouth stopped, the propitiation (the sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath) set forth in public, the ungodly justified, peace with God, the reign of grace, no condemnation, the Spirit given, the groaning, the chain. Paul has finished arguing. What follows is not another proof but a challenge thrown out to the universe.

If God is for us, who can be against us? Not that no one opposes us, since many do, but that no opposition can succeed against those God is for.

Since, not if. The “if” is not tentative. The Greek treats it as true, so it is better heard as since God is for us: the established fact of eight chapters. And “for us” does not mean on our side, as though God were choosing between two teams. It means that God himself is our advocate, our champion, our protector.

Abraham’s sentence, spoken of God. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb, “did not spare”, in a scene every reader would have recalled. On the mountain, with the knife raised over Isaac, the voice from heaven says to Abraham that now he knows Abraham fears God, seeing he has not withheld his son, his only son (Genesis 22:12, 16). Paul takes the sentence God spoke to Abraham and applies it to God.

No ram in the thicket. The whole verse rests on this. Abraham was stopped: a voice, a hand caught before it fell, and a ram in the thicket so that the son could walk down the mountain alive. At Calvary there was no voice; there was no ram in the thicket, because this time the Son was the ram. God asked Abraham for something he did not in the end require of him, and then did it himself. Abraham climbed a mountain with his son and came down with him. God climbed the same kind of hill and came down alone, and the whole security of every Christian rests on the fact that nobody stopped him.

The same verb. The word for what he did is the one that has been running through this letter like a dark thread: “gave him up”, the same word used three times in chapter 1 of God handing sinners over to what they had chosen (1:24, 26, 28). The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful one are the same verb, and here it reaches its destination. The Father handed over the Son so that he would never have to hand us over.

Was it cruel of the Father to give up his Son? No, and the objection misses who is giving. The Son was not an unwilling victim pushed forward by an angry Father. He laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18), and Paul can say both that the Father gave him up and that the Son gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Father and Son are one God with one will and one love. At the cross God did not make someone else pay; he paid himself, in the person of his Son, which is the very opposite of cruelty. It is the costliest kindness there has ever been.

How will he not also with him graciously give us all things? The argument from greater to lesser. If God gave the greatest gift, his Son, he will not withhold anything lesser that we need. Every good thing comes with Christ.

The arithmetic is settled. If God has already paid out the greatest sum he could, his own Son, no later request will strain his account. The question of his generosity was answered publicly, at Golgotha; everything else is a smaller ask. The Father who did not spare his own Son has nothing left to prove about his love. The verb is “graciously give”, built on the word for grace. And “all things” is the same phrase as in verse 28: the all things that work together for good are the all things he will freely give.

What it does not mean. This verse has been made into a blank cheque. It does not promise that God will give you whatever you ask for. All things here is bounded by what has just been defined as the good, conformity to the image of his Son (v. 29), and the chapter has already admitted that we often do not know what to pray for (v. 26). The promise is that nothing you truly need will be withheld, and that the God supplying you is the one who has already proved he does not hold back the things that cost him.

Then why do I lack things I ask for? Because a good Father gives what is good, which is not always what is asked, and because he sees further than we do. Sometimes he withholds a thing because it would harm us, sometimes because something better is coming, and sometimes for reasons we will not learn in this life. What you can be sure of is the direction of his heart. Ask freely and specifically; Jesus tells you to (Matthew 7:7–11). But when the answer is no or not yet, do not read it as stinginess. A God who gave his Son is not saving money on you.

In everyday life. Name something good that you want and have quietly concluded God is not willing to give you: the healing, the child, the work, the release from the thing that has you. As evidence that he is unwilling you will generally find a long silence and a feeling. As evidence that he is willing you have the execution of his own Son, on your behalf, while you were his enemy. Whatever he withholds, he does not withhold it because he is unwilling to be good to you.

parallels.desc: the LORD is on my side; I will not fear
you have not withheld your son

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? A courtroom scene. “God’s elect”: those chosen by God. Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), conscience accuses, others accuse. Can any charge stand?

Outranked, not denied. Asked who shall bring any charge, the natural reply is nobody: there is nothing to charge. Paul could not say that: the first three chapters of this letter were the charge sheet, and every word of it stands. He answers a question about the prosecution by naming the judge. The charges may be entirely accurate. They have already been heard by the only court with authority to judge, and the verdict is in. The accusation is not denied but outranked: the question is who is sitting on the bench.

Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, more than that, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us. The question takes us back to the first verse of the chapter, no condemnation, and now gives the full reason for it. Paul answers with a creed in four clauses, each one raising the ground higher. He died: the penalty has been carried. He was raised: the payment was accepted, publicly receipted. He is at the right hand: the one with the right to condemn is the one already seated as sovereign. He is interceding: and he is using that position, at this moment, on your behalf, pleading his finished work (Hebrews 7:25).

A doctrine often neglected. Christians think a great deal about what Christ did and far less about what he is doing: interceding, present tense, now. Not that he is pleading with a reluctant Father, as though the Father needed persuading; the Father is the one who gave him. It means the case is permanently before the court with counsel permanently present. John puts it in the plainest possible terms for people who have just failed: “if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). There has not been a moment since he took his seat at the Father’s right hand in which the Son of God was not speaking to his Father about people who do not deserve to be mentioned.

Who sits where. The Judge is the one who justifies. The counsel for the defence is the one who might have condemned. There is no seat left for the prosecution that carries any weight, which is why Scripture can call the enemy the accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night before our God (Revelation 12:10), and still treat him as thrown down. He is not necessarily lying about you. He simply has no right to be heard in this court. Every seat that matters in it is occupied by someone on your side. The Advocate is also the one who died for your sins, which is a far more serious view of them than the accuser has, and he speaks for you not out of sentiment but because he has the receipts.

What do I do when my conscience accuses me of something true? Agree with it about the sin, and disagree with it about the verdict. If the charge is true, confess it to God plainly; do not argue, minimise or blame. Then take your stand where this verse stands: it is God who justifies, and Christ has died for this very sin. Even when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20). If you have wronged someone, put it right. But do not let a true charge become a false sentence. The sin was real; so was the payment.

In everyday life. When the accusation comes, usually at night and usually after a failure, listen to your own reply. If it begins with “but I”, “but I am trying”, “but I have repented”, “but I did well last week”, you have accepted the prosecution’s framing and are conducting your own defence, and your record cannot bear the weight. The reply this passage gives contains no information about you whatever: it is God who justifies; Christ Jesus died, was raised, is at the right hand, and is speaking for me now. Four facts, none of them about your week.

parallels.desc: he who vindicates me is near; who will contend with me?

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, "For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? The final question. Can anything break Christ’s love for us?

The thing under guarantee. Paul has narrowed the question, and the narrowing is the comfort. He does not ask whether these things can separate us from a sense of God’s nearness, or from peace of mind, or from comfort, any of which suffering demonstrably can disturb. He asks whether they can separate us from the love of Christ. That is the thing under guarantee. Your feelings about God will be knocked about badly by famine and danger and the sword; his love for you is not among the casualties.

Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? Seven trials, most of which Paul himself endured (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). The sword: the early church remembered that Paul was later beheaded in Rome.

Reading out his diary. Every item on the list had a face for Paul: he is reading out his diary. Nor was it hypothetical for the people receiving the letter. Within a few years of this being read aloud in Rome, Nero would be using Christians as entertainment, some torn by dogs, some crucified, some set alight in the imperial gardens. Paul was writing these sentences for people who would need them. The verse is not too grand for your difficulties. It was simply built to bear a great deal more.

Sheep to be slaughtered. Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned us. It has always been the lot of God’s people. Believers are not spared suffering, but they are never separated from Christ’s love in it.

A psalm of complaint. The quotation is from Psalm 44:22. At the summit of his argument for the believer’s security, Paul quotes not a psalm of triumph but a complaint. The nation is being slaughtered and cannot understand why: all this has come upon them, though they have not forgotten God; and near its end it cries out to heaven, “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:17, 23). Paul is not claiming that the Christian life will look like victory from the outside. It will often look exactly like abandonment, sheep in a queue at the slaughterhouse, and he says so by quoting the complaint rather than answering it. The security he is describing is not visible in the circumstances. If it were, he would not have needed the psalm.

For your sake. “Regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” is how it looks and not how it is. And the psalm gives three words for why: for your sake. This is not meaningless loss. Even at the slaughterhouse the sheep belong to somebody, and their being there has to do with him.

The love that went through the list. It is the love of Christ that cannot be broken, and that love has a history. Before these things touched Paul, they touched his Lord: hungry in the wilderness, hunted by rulers, sorrowful even to death in Gethsemane, stripped by soldiers who gambled for his clothes, and brought to the end of the list not by the sword but on a cross. The Good Shepherd himself became the lamb that is led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), so that no sheep of his would ever face the slaughter alone. His love went through the whole of Paul’s list and came out the other side with nail-scarred hands still holding his own; nothing that comes to us now is a new test for it.

Is it wrong to ask God why? No. Paul has just quoted from a psalm that asks him why, and God put it in the Bible. Lament is not unbelief; it is faith that talks to God when it does not understand him, rather than turning away. The psalmist asks why and still calls God his own, and still appeals to his steadfast love (Psalm 44:26). Jesus himself cried out from the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). So bring your questions to God, not away from him. What you must not do is turn the unanswered why into a verdict against his love. The cross has already settled that.

In everyday life. In the middle of something hard it is natural to reason from the circumstance: “if he loved me, this would not be happening”. Paul reasons the other way round, from the evidence of verse 32. The measure of Christ’s love for you is not the state of your life this year but a cross, fixed, dated, and unaffected by anything now happening to you; and the same love holds those who are being killed for his sake today, whom you can name in prayer this week (Hebrews 13:3).

parallels.desc: for your sake we are killed all the day long

verseByVerse.quote: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word Paul may have built. The word for more than conquerors (hypernikōmen) looks as though Paul made it up, and he may well have. He has put hyper on the front of the verb to conquer: over-conquer. And the first words are the ones to hold: “in all these things”, not out of them or after them. The sword of verse 35 is not confiscated before it falls. Paul is describing a victory that happens with the sword still in the room.

Living on a finished act. “Through him who loved us” is the phrase that keeps the whole thing from becoming a boast about Christian resilience. The tense is past: loved, pointing at a completed act rather than a passing sentiment. The strength you are conquering by is not being generated in you now; it was expended at a particular moment in history, outside a city wall, and you are living on it. That is a great relief to anyone who has ever read a verse like this and quietly concluded that real Christians must be stronger than they are.

What do we conquer? Not people. Paul will soon tell us to bless those who persecute us (12:14), and our enemies are to be loved, not defeated (12:20–21). What we conquer are “all these things”: the list in verse 35 (tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword) and the list in verses 38–39 (death and life, angels and rulers, present and future, powers, height and depth). Behind them stands the accusation of verses 33–34: who shall bring any charge, who is to condemn? Each of these threatens to do one thing: to separate us from the love of Christ, to break our faith, or to prove that God has abandoned us. To conquer them is for them to fail at that.

In what way do we conquer? Not in the way the world means. Verse 36 has just quoted Psalm 44: for your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered. Sheep led to slaughter do not look like conquerors. Yet that is exactly who Paul calls conquerors. We win, not by escaping these things, but in them. Three things happen.

1. They cannot separate us from God’s love. A persecutor can take your freedom, your health or your life, but not your Saviour (vv. 38–39). The thing these enemies were trying to do, they cannot do.

2. They are made to serve us. God works all things together for good (v. 28). Suffering produces endurance, character and hope (5:3–5), and our light, momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). The enemy is turned into a servant.

3. Even death becomes gain. For Paul, to die was to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:21–23). The last enemy, which seems to win, opens the door home (1 Corinthians 15:54–57).

Why “more than” conquerors? An ordinary conqueror wins the battle but is often wounded by it, and loses something. The believer loses nothing that finally matters, and gains from the very battle: the enemy ends up serving him. And the victory is secure before the battle even starts, because Christ has already won it: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33; Colossians 2:15). Revelation gives the same picture: the saints conquered the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (Revelation 12:11). They conquered by dying faithful.

The lion did not make them let go. This is the chapter’s own argument arriving: all things work together for good (v. 28), the good of being made like the Son (v. 29). Adversity that would have destroyed you is conscripted into making you like Christ, which was the point of your existence. The enemy is not merely defeated. He is put to work. That is why the martyrs are not tragic figures. The lions of the arena did not defeat them; the lion did not even manage to make them let go, and in the attempt it sent them home. That is how their Champion won before them. The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and when John turned to look at him he saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:5–6): he conquered by being slain, and he makes his people conquerors in the same way.

What it looks like. A Christian with cancer whose body weakens while her trust in Christ grows deeper. Believers in prison for their faith who sing, as Paul and Silas did at midnight (Acts 16:25). Paul himself, in chains, probably in Rome, writing Philippians, the most joyful of his letters. None of them escaped. All of them conquered.

What it does not mean. Not triumphalism: that Christians will be healthy, wealthy and successful, or that the church will win every battle in society. Not that we will always feel victorious: Paul once despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Our feelings may say defeat while the fact is victory. And not that the victory is our own strength or courage. It is through him who loved us. Christ’s love holds us; we do not hold ourselves. A Christian weeping in a hospital corridor is not failing this verse. He is standing inside it, in the dark, being carried by a love that does not require him to notice it in order to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 8:38–39
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who has tested the rope. Paul ends his great chapter with a personal declaration: “I am sure”. He has been through the catalogue of verse 35 personally. The certainty is not presumption: he has tested the rope and found it holds. None of it reached the thing that mattered.

A list in pairs. The list comes in pairs, each covering a whole field by its two extremes. Death nor life: every possible state a creature can be in; there is no third option. Angels nor rulers nor powers: the entire unseen order, good or evil, whatever ranks it holds. Things present nor things to come: all of time, in both directions. Height nor depth: the whole of space, and also astrologers’ terms for the highest and lowest points of a star’s course. Paul is going through the ancient world’s inventory of powers that determine a human fate and crossing them off.

Whatever you were about to raise. Having covered states, spirits, time and space, Paul adds nor anything else in all creation, the clause that closes every remaining door. It is the sentence of a man who has stopped to think whether he has missed anything and has decided to make it impossible to name one. Whatever you were about to raise, your own temperament, your family history, a sin you have not mentioned to anybody, the thing you are most afraid will one day undo you, is in that clause. If it is part of creation, it is on the list of things that cannot separate you. The apostle went looking for something in the universe strong enough to break the grip of God on one of his children, and came back having found nothing at all.

The one thing not on the list. There is one being in the universe who is not part of creation, and that is God himself. Paul has listed everything that cannot separate you from the love of God, and the only possible remaining threat would be God changing his mind, which is precisely what the whole letter has been arguing he will not and cannot do, because the love was fixed before you existed and secured at the cost of his Son.

Love in a Person. The very last words locate it exactly: the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Not a benevolence in the sky which we hope covers us, but love in a Person, held for you in someone who died and was raised and is at the right hand interceding. Which means the question “could I lose it?” is really the question “could he be dislodged?” And that is a considerably easier question to answer.

But could I not separate myself? It is the question every honest reader asks at this point, and it deserves a straight answer. Two things. First, you are part of creation, and Paul’s catch-all does not make an exception for the reader. Second, and better: the whole chapter has already answered it, because the chain of verses 29 and 30 contains no link that depends on you. If your remaining in the love of God rested on your grip, the honest verdict on every one of us would be that we will let go, probably before Friday. The security here is not that we hold on well. It is that the holding is being done from the other end.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Some hold that, though nothing outside us can separate us, we can separate ourselves by turning away. This commentary’s view: “nor anything else in all creation” includes us. And the chain of vv. 29–30 ensures that all who are justified are glorified. This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his own, and they persevere because he keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). It is not a licence for carelessness, but the ground of joyful, confident obedience.

The warnings of Hebrews. Arminian Christians, whose concern that confidence should never breed carelessness is a fair one, answer that a believer may still turn away by his own choice, pointing to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). The warnings are real and must be heard, but they are among the means by which God keeps his people (as at v. 13). Those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19). If you fear that you have fallen away, come back to Christ, who casts out no one who comes (John 6:37).

What of a Christian who takes his own life? Suicide is a grave sin, and no one should read this verse as making it light. But it is not the unforgivable sin, and Scripture never says it is. A believer’s safety rests on Christ’s grip, not on the state of his mind in his last hour, and death heads Paul’s list. Those who mourn a believer who died this way may grieve with hope. And anyone tempted to it should tell someone today, a friend, a pastor or a doctor, and hold on to the love that will not let him go.

In everyday life. Say the sentence with your own name and the thing you fear most in it: neither death, nor the diagnosis, nor what I did all those years ago, nor my father’s illness in me, nor the years I wasted, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate me from the love of God in Christ Jesus my Lord. Whatever makes that sentence hard to say is the thing you have been treating as stronger than the cross, and there is no such thing.

No condemnation, no separation. Nothing against you at the beginning; nothing between you at the end. Because a just Judge has justified (3:26), the last word of this chapter is not a sentiment but a verdict, entered in a court, and unappealable. The love that chose us before creation cannot be overcome by anything within it. Here the gospel argument comes to rest, and so does the believer: in the love of God, in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Paul names every kind of power, time and place, whether seen or unseen.

By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,<sup>4</sup>in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.<sup>5</sup>For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.<sup>6</sup>For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.<sup>7</sup>For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot.<sup>8</sup>Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.<sup>9</sup>You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. 9.title: The Sovereignty of God in Election
9.overview:
Romans 9 is one of the most debated chapters in the Bible. Chapter 8 ended with the promise that nothing can separate the called from the love of God. Then why have most of God’s covenant people rejected their Messiah? Has the word of God failed (v. 6)? For Paul the question is personal before it is theological: he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his kinsmen (v. 2).

He answers on two levels. From Israel’s own history he shows that God has always worked by choosing within the covenant family: Isaac, not Ishmael; Jacob, not Esau. Then he defends God’s justice and freedom in that choosing, from Exodus and from the prophets’ picture of the potter and the clay. These are hard pages, and Paul does not soften them; but he writes them with tears, and he ends the chapter with an open door for whoever believes (v. 33).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before Paul takes up the question, he opens his heart: if it were possible, he would be cut off from Christ for the sake of his kinsmen. The apostle who will argue for God’s sovereign choice without flinching weeps for the lost.

Then he lists Israel’s privileges: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and last and highest the Christ himself, who is God over all, blessed forever (vv. 4–5). The tragedy Paul mourns is that the Messiah came from Israel and was refused by most of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology:
Evangelistic passion and doctrinal conviction

Romans 9:1–3 shows that a firm belief in God’s sovereign choice need not make anyone indifferent to the lost. Paul believed in unconditional election (v. 11) and still ached for the people he loved. Election encourages mission: we preach because God has people everywhere (Acts 18:10), and he calls them through the preaching of the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges blocks any easy dismissal of Jewish unbelief, as though Israel had simply missed something obvious. Now: Someone who has grown up in a Christian home, heard the gospel from childhood and been surrounded by every means of grace, yet has never trusted Christ, stands where Paul’s Israel stood. Privilege does not save; it deepens accountability, and it keeps the invitation within reach.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit— — Romans 9:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 9–11 answers the question chapter 8 raises: if nothing can separate God’s elect from his love, what about Israel, to whom God made promises and most of whom have rejected their Messiah? If God’s word failed for them, how can we trust it for us? In chapter 9 Paul shows that God’s word has not failed: his promise was always to the children of promise, chosen by his free mercy (vv. 6–13); God is not unjust in choosing (vv. 14–24); and the prophets foretold both the calling of Gentiles and the saving of a remnant of Israel (vv. 25–29). Chapter 10 shows Israel responsible for its unbelief, and chapter 11 that God has not rejected his people. Chapter 9 is the Bible’s most sustained teaching on God’s sovereign election (his free choice of whom to save), and Paul writes it with tears.

The setting. Paul was a Jew, a Pharisee, and the apostle to the Gentiles. Some Jews accused him of abandoning his people and teaching against the law (Acts 21:21, 28). The Roman church had Jewish and Gentile believers, and Gentiles were tempted to look down on Jews (11:18–20). So Paul opens with a solemn oath of love for Israel before he says hard things.

I am not lying. A double oath, positive and negative. “In Christ” means as one united to Christ, speaking in his presence. Why does a man need witnesses to say that he is sad? Because in every synagogue from Antioch to Corinth he is the man who went over to the other side, who eats with Gentiles and says the law cannot save anybody. To his own people he is a defector, and a defector’s tears are cheap. So before he says one word about election he raises his hand in court.

My conscience. Conscience is the inner moral awareness that judges your own conduct, a witness that can accuse or defend you (2:15), though it is never the final judge (1 Corinthians 4:4). The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); Paul brings Christ, his conscience and the Holy Spirit, three witnesses for one sentence about sorrow, because he fully expects not to be believed.

No step down from the summit. There is no transition between chapter 8 and chapter 9. The highest line in the letter, that nothing can separate us from the love of God, is followed at once by “great sorrow and unceasing anguish”. Paul does not climb down off the summit to write this. He writes it standing on the summit. The assurance and the grief are in one man’s chest at the same hour, and neither is pretending.

The Spirit who groans. Paul calls the Holy Spirit to testify to a grief. A chapter ago that same Spirit was interceding with groanings too deep for words (8:26); here the groan has surfaced and has names attached to it: brothers, kinsmen, a whole people. Chapter 9 shows what the love of chapter 8 does to a man once it has hold of him. It does not seal him up, safe and unbothered, at a distance from the lost. It puts him in tears over people, many of whom would gladly see him dead (Acts 23:12).

The truth in Christ. Paul swears in Christ, and that phrase tells you whose sorrow this is. He speaks as one joined to the Lord who looked at Jerusalem and said, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). No one knew the Father’s purposes as the Son did, and that knowledge did not dry his eyes. Paul’s anguish is not his temperament breaking through his theology. It is the heart of Christ beating in a servant of Christ.

Why does Paul need to say this before teaching election? Because doctrine heard from someone who does not love you sounds like contempt, and Paul is about to say the hardest things in the letter about his own people. If he began with the potter and the clay, his Jewish readers would assume he was gloating, and his Gentile readers might be tempted to gloat themselves (11:18–20). So he shows his heart first. There is a lesson in the order. The truth of election is not softened by love, but it can only be rightly heard where love is plainly present. Whoever teaches it with a shrug has not been taught it by Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unceasing anguish. Sorrow, and anguish like the pain of a wound, that never stop. The anguish is unceasing (adialeiptos), and the only other place Paul uses the word in this letter, in its adverb form, is 1:9, where it describes his praying: “without ceasing I mention you always in my prayers”. In Paul the grief and the praying are not two things: his grief is the form his praying takes. If you have prayed the same name every morning for thirty years, a son, a sister, a husband who will not come, and you have wondered whether the fact that it still hurts means your faith is thin, this verse says the reverse. That hurt is what unceasing prayer feels like from the inside.

Accursed. The word is anathema, something devoted to God for destruction, the thing under the ban that Israel was forbidden to keep back (Joshua 6:17). Paul would take the sentence himself. Chapter 8 has just listed everything that cannot separate us from the love of Christ. With the ink barely dry, the man who wrote that list offers to be its one exception: he would sooner be cut off from Christ, the very thing chapter 8 says cannot happen, than watch his people perish.

I could wish. The verb is chosen with care. Paul does not write “I wish” but “I could wish” (ēuchomēn): most likely a wish stated and withdrawn in the same breath, a thing he would ask for if it could be asked for. He knows it is not on offer, and says it anyway, because it is the only measure he has for how much this costs him.

My kinsmen. Fellow Jews, his own flesh and blood. In chapters 7 and 8 “the flesh” meant our sinful nature; here “according to the flesh” means nothing worse than family, by natural descent. Grace did not dissolve those ties or lift him above them; it made him love his own people more fiercely. If you have been made to feel that desperation over your own household is a lower love a mature Christian should have risen above, Paul puts the most intense sentence in this letter on exactly that ground.

Moses before him. Moses made the same offer at Sinai, after the golden calf: “blot me out of your book that you have written” (Exodus 32:32). The answer was no. Paul’s offer is refused too, and for the same reason. A sinner cannot be accursed on behalf of sinners; he has nothing to spare. There is exactly one man in history whose being cut off could save anybody, and he has already been cut off. Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), a different word for the same reality, and the darkness at noon and the cry “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” are what Paul’s wish looks like when it is granted to someone who could carry it. So the deepest thing this verse tells you is not how much Paul loves Israel. It is that his love, at full stretch and offering everything, is a shadow of a love that actually went through with it.

Grief, doctrine, prayer, hope. You may be about to read a chapter on election with a name in your throat: a child who walked away, a husband who is kind and unbelieving. Read verse 3 first, as your own permission. The man who says God has mercy on whomever he wills is weeping while he says it, and in chapter 10 he is still praying for them (10:1), and in chapter 11 saying God has the power to graft them in again (11:23).

Where election must not be misused. First, election is never a diagnosis you are permitted to run on another person. Nowhere does Scripture allow you to conclude that because someone has not come yet, they were never going to. Paul’s own kinsmen are the unbelievers in question, and he spends three chapters refusing to write them off. You do not know who is elect. You know who to pray for. Second, the guard runs the other way: this is not a guarantee that everyone you love will be saved in the end, and pretending otherwise would be a comfort that breaks when tested. What you are given is not a prediction. It is a warrant to keep asking, from a God who is free, which is exactly why the asking is worth anything at all.

Is it wrong to grieve this much if I trust God’s sovereignty? No. Paul held God’s sovereignty more firmly than anyone, and he grieved without ceasing. Jesus, who knew the Father’s plan perfectly, wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Grief for the lost is not unbelief; it is love agreeing with God that perishing is terrible. What sovereignty adds is not numbness but hope: because salvation depends on God and not on the sinner, no one you pray for is beyond his reach. Grieve, and let the grief drive you to prayer rather than to despair. The two belong together in a healthy heart.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — devoted to destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are Israelites. Not just Jews, the word Paul used all through chapter 2, but Israelites, the honoured covenant name. It is what a man is called after God has met him in the dark and refused to let him go without giving him a new name (Genesis 32:28). Two verses on, Paul will show that the name has a wider and a narrower sense: “not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel” (v. 6). He lists the privileges (vv. 4–5) not to belittle them but in wonder, and the grief he feels is proportioned to the size of the gift.

The adoption. Israel was God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1), a national sonship that was both a privilege and a picture of the sonship believers receive in Christ. Adoption means being taken into a family you were not born into and given a son’s name, standing and inheritance (Galatians 4:5–7).

The glory. The Shekinah, God’s visible glorious presence, in the cloud and fire, the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34). Every item on the list has a date and eyewitnesses: the day the cloud filled the house of the LORD so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11), and the night the fire stood over the camp so that a child could wake in the desert and see by it.

The covenants. Plural: with Abraham, at Sinai, with David, and the promised new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). Some early manuscripts read the singular, the covenant, but the plural is well supported and fits the list.

The giving of the law. One Greek word, nomothesia: the event at Sinai when God spoke his law to them. No other nation had statutes and rules so righteous (Deuteronomy 4:8).

The worship. Latreia: the priestly service of tabernacle and temple, the sacrifices God himself had appointed.

And the promises. Above all, the promises of the Messiah and of salvation. They were not optimism; they were sentences with names in them, spoken to particular men in particular fields. Whatever else Israel lacked, they were never guessing. They had been told plainly what God would do.

The words of chapter 8. Read the list with chapter 8 open beside it. Adoption: the word Paul has just used for the Spirit-given cry of sons (8:15, 23). Glory: the thing we rejoice in hope of and are being conformed to (5:2; 8:18, 30). Covenants and promises: the whole argument of chapter 4. The words Paul used in chapter 8 for the Christian’s highest blessings belonged first to a people who have now refused the Messiah, which is why he cannot be comforted by their privileges. It is the privileges that are breaking his heart.

Six gifts with one face. Hold each of verse 4’s gifts up to the light and Christ is standing inside it. The son God called out of Egypt (Hosea 11:1) is the Son Matthew sees coming back from Egypt (Matthew 2:15). The glory that filled the tabernacle shines in him, for he is the radiance of the glory of God (Hebrews 1:3). The covenants run on to the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). The law he came not to abolish but to fulfil (Matthew 5:17). The worship of altar and priest is gathered up in the one who is both priest and sacrifice (Hebrews 9:11–14). And the promises are promises about him. Israel was not handed six unrelated gifts. It was handed six portraits of one person, and the grief of this chapter is that when he came, the family that owned the portraits did not know the face.

To them belong. The Greek has no verb, and the natural sense is present, hence belong, not belonged. A generation after the crucifixion, Paul does not put one item of the list into the past. That present tense is the seed of chapter 11: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (11:29). Paul is grieving, but he is not writing an obituary.

What it does not mean. This verse is not written to convince the person raised in church that his case is now hopeless. Paul’s point is not that privilege damns; it is that privilege does not save, which is a different sentence entirely. What condemned Israel was refusing the Christ the covenants pointed to, and the invitation stayed open (chapter 10). If you are the churched reader reading this with a cold hand on your chest, that alarm is not the verdict. It is the kindness of God, still doing what 2:4 says it is meant to do: lead you to repentance.

If privileges do not save, why are they called privileges? Because they are real gifts that bring you near to the truth. Paul says the Jews’ advantage was much in every way, chiefly that they were entrusted with the words of God (3:1–2). A Christian upbringing, a Bible, a faithful church: these put the gospel within reach, and God often uses them to bring people to faith. But they are means, not the thing itself. A map is a great privilege to a lost traveller; it does him no good if he never follows it. The privilege is meant to lead you to Christ, and it becomes a greater responsibility if you refuse him.
verseByVerse.note: “The glory” is God’s glorious presence among his people, as in the tabernacle and temple.

verseByVerse.quote: To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. — Romans 9:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
The patriarchs. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers to whom God made the promises, and with whom the rest of this chapter is about to deal.

According to the flesh. The greatest privilege. The Messiah was a Jew. “According to the flesh” means by his human descent (1:3), and implies there is more to him. God over all has a family tree, with names and awkward histories. Of all the privileges on the list, this is the one that cannot be revoked or repeated: one nation, out of every nation on earth, supplied the human nature of God. The blood is Jewish blood. Whatever the church has said about Israel in its uglier centuries, it has had to say it about the relatives of its own Lord.

God over all. A clear statement that Christ is God. The incarnation does not diminish his deity; it expresses it in the most unexpected way. The kinsman according to the flesh is God over all, and both halves of that sentence are true; the church has spent two thousand years learning not to drop either one. This is the ultimate privilege and the ultimate tragedy: the God of Israel came to Israel, and Israel largely did not receive him. So the one who is over all has already been on the receiving end of the exact refusal you may be grieving. And Paul does not stop to defend the statement. Nine chapters into one of the most closely argued letters ever written, the argument simply gives out and turns into praise. He states it, blesses Christ for it, and signs it with an Amen.

Textual note: the punctuation. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so the sentence can be divided in more than one way. The ESV text reads it as referring to Christ. Its footnote gives alternatives that make it a separate praise of God the Father, such as: Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever. This is a real grammatical possibility, not an invention by people avoiding the deity of Christ, and it should be admitted honestly. This commentary’s view: The ESV text is right. The natural flow of the Greek joins “who is” to the Christ just named. “According to the flesh” is a limiting phrase that calls for its counterpart, exactly as in 1:3–4, where descended from David according to the flesh is answered by Son of God in power; cut the sentence in half and the limitation dangles with nothing to limit. Paul’s separate blessings of God normally put “blessed” first (2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3; compare Luke 1:68), which here it does not. And a sudden burst of praise to the Father sits oddly in the middle of a lament, whereas a final and highest item at the end of a list of privileges sits perfectly. Most of the church fathers read it this way. It fits the New Testament’s plain teaching that Jesus is God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8). The traditional reading is not merely the pious one; it is the natural one.

Whose hands are these? Now see where Paul has put this sentence, because it is not decoration. He is about to spend twenty verses defending the freedom of God: mercy on whomever he wills, a potter with rights over the clay, Pharaoh raised up for a purpose. That argument frightens people, and it should not be softened. But Paul establishes who this sovereign is before he shows what this sovereign may do. So when the potter’s hands appear in verse 21, you already know whose hands they are. They are not the hands of raw power, or fate, or a will with no character behind it. They are the hands of the one who took the flesh of the very people he chooses among, who came into the world through a womb in his own creation, and who, when he finally held the clay, did it with hands that bear the nail marks. The doctrine of election is only unbearable while God is anonymous. Verse 5 makes sure he is not.

Amen. At the end of the worst grief in the letter, Paul blesses God forever, and he will do it again when chapter 11 closes with “To him be glory forever” (11:36). The grief is bracketed by worship at both ends: unresolved sorrow, not explained away, but held inside praise.

How can Jesus be a man descended from Israel and also God over all? Because the eternal Son, who is God, took a full human nature to himself when he was conceived by the Spirit in Mary (John 1:14; Galatians 4:4). He did not stop being God, and he did not merely appear to be human. He is one person with two natures, as the church confessed at the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451): truly God, truly man, without confusion and without division. So the baby in Bethlehem was God over all, and the man on the cross was the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). That is why his death can save: a man died, and the one who died was God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes alternative punctuations, such as “Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever”; the ESV text calls Christ God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–29 — God's Sovereign Choice: Election and the Potter's Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s answer begins by reframing the problem. Israel’s unbelief does not show that God’s word has failed, because the promise never ran by descent alone: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (v. 6). Isaac, not Ishmael; Jacob, not Esau, chosen before either had done anything, so that God’s purpose would rest on his call and not on works (vv. 7–13).

Then come two objections, raised by Paul himself. Is God unjust (v. 14)? Paul answers with the words God spoke to Moses after the golden calf, when Israel deserved destruction: mercy is God’s to give, and no one has a claim on it (v. 15). Pharaoh shows the other side, hardening, and Exodus says both that God hardened his heart and that Pharaoh hardened it himself (vv. 17–18). Why then does God still find fault (v. 19)? Paul offers no theory; he reminds the creature that he cannot put his Maker on trial (vv. 20–21).

The section turns on verses 22–24. God has endured the vessels of wrath with much patience, and the vessels of mercy are named at last: us, called from Jews and Gentiles alike. Hosea and Isaiah close the section (vv. 25–29): without God’s mercy no one would be left at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unconditional election

Romans 9:6–29 is the main New Testament passage for the Reformed teaching of unconditional election: God’s choice of individuals for salvation, made before the foundation of the world, resting not on foreseen faith or merit but on his own good pleasure. Calvin argues (Institutes III.21–24) that to make election depend on foreseen faith turns grace into a reward for human initiative. Election that rests on God’s own love, and works through human response rather than around it, gives all the glory to God and puts all the hope in him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau came from stories every Jewish reader knew: God’s free choosing was there in Israel’s own beginnings. Now: This teaching tends to draw one of two responses: “That is not fair,” or “Why me, Lord?” The second is the right one. The person who asks why he was chosen and finds no answer in himself has understood the doctrine, and is on his knees.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but "Through Isaac shall your offspring be named."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has God’s word failed. This is the theme of chapters 9–11. To chapter 8’s promise a reader of the Old Testament has an obvious reply: God said things like that to Israel too, and look at them now. Israel is the test case for chapter 8. If God’s word to them fell over, then no promise of his is worth the weight you are putting on it, and your assurance is a sentiment. Paul is defending the only ground you have for believing anything he told you in the previous chapter.

Failed. The verb is ekpiptō, used of a ship driven off its course and onto the rocks (Acts 27:17, 26, 29) and of a flower falling from its stem. It is the word for something that has come adrift, and Paul flatly denies that this has happened to God’s word. He is answering a reader who stands on the shoreline looking at what appears to be wreckage, and telling him he is looking at a ship still under way.

Two Israels. Paul uses the word Israel in two senses in one sentence: the physical nation descended from Jacob, and within it an Israel in the full sense of the promise, those chosen and called by God. The promise was always to the second. Paul made a similar move at 2:28–29, where he distinguished the outward Jew from the one whose circumcision is of the heart. There the outward thing was a sign, circumcision. Here it is descent itself: the same distinction, pressed further.

How do we know this is true? This is a big claim, and Paul does not simply assert it. He proves it, and the Old Testament had been saying it all along. Five lines of evidence:

First, the sentence itself. Literally: not all who are from Israel are Israel. The same word cannot mean the same thing both times, or the sentence would contradict itself. The first Israel is the man Jacob and his physical descendants; the second must be something narrower. Paul defines it two verses later: it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring (v. 8).

Second, the first generations of the family. Paul’s proof comes straight from Genesis (vv. 7–13). Of Abraham’s two sons, only Isaac carried the promise (Genesis 17:19–21; 21:12); of Rebekah’s twins, conceived together, God chose Jacob before they were born (Genesis 25:23). From the very beginning, being born into the family did not by itself make someone an heir of the promise.

Third, the remnant. The prophets repeatedly spoke of a faithful remnant within the nation, and Paul will quote Isaiah on it in verses 27 and 29. In Elijah’s day, when the nation had turned to Baal, God kept seven thousand who had not bowed the knee (1 Kings 19:18), and Paul says the same is true at the present time: there is a remnant, chosen by grace (11:2–5). An Israel within Israel is not Paul’s invention; it is the prophets’ teaching.

Fourth, the circumcision of the heart. Moses himself told Israel to circumcise their hearts, and promised that God would one day do it (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). Jeremiah said that the whole house of Israel was uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26). So the Old Testament already distinguished outward membership, marked by circumcision, from inward reality, a heart given to God. That is exactly Paul’s point in 2:28–29.

Fifth, John the Baptist and Jesus. John warned his hearers not to presume to say, “We have Abraham as our father” (Matthew 3:9). Jesus told some who claimed Abraham as their father that if they were his children, they would do what Abraham did (John 8:39–44). And he called Nathanael “an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47): an Israelite in the true sense, not only by birth.

Who belongs to this true Israel? In this verse Paul is speaking of Jews: the believing remnant chosen within the nation (v. 27; 11:5), such as Paul himself (11:1). Elsewhere he teaches that believing Gentiles also become Abraham’s offspring and are grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 4:11–12; 11:17), and in verse 24 he goes on to say that God has called his people not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles. Whether Paul ever calls the church as a whole “Israel” is debated (Galatians 6:16). But the principle is the same: membership in God’s true people comes by promise and faith, not by birth alone.

Where Christians differ: the two Israels. Dispensationalists (who see God’s dealings with Israel and with the church as distinct, with distinct promises) hold that “Israel” in Scripture always refers to ethnic Israel, so the true Israel here is believing Jews only, and God’s promises to the nation remain separate from his purposes for the church. Covenant theologians (who read the whole Bible as one unfolding covenant of grace) see in this verse the principle that runs through the whole Bible: the true people of God are the chosen and believing, Jew and Gentile together in Christ. This commentary’s view: in Romans 9:6 itself, both sides largely agree: the true Israel is the elect, believing remnant within the Jewish nation. The wider truth, that believing Gentiles share fully in Abraham’s family, is taught clearly elsewhere (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22), and makes one people of God, not two. But Paul does not therefore write off ethnic Israel. He keeps calling the nation Israel (9:31; 10:21; 11:7), says they are still beloved for the sake of their forefathers (11:28–29), and holds out the hope that all Israel will be saved (11:25–26), which many read as a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ and others as the full gathering of God’s people.

Ishmael. Abraham already has a son, Ishmael, thirteen years in the house (Genesis 17:25). When God promises a son by Sarah, Abraham pleads for the child he has: “Oh that Ishmael might live before you!” (Genesis 17:18). In other words: I already love this one.

Not cursed, not discarded. God’s answer is no, and in the same breath he promises to bless Ishmael, make him fruitful and multiply him greatly (Genesis 17:20). He is simply not the one the promise runs through, and it helps to see this early in a chapter that will get much harder: being outside the line of promise is not the same as being outside God’s kindness.

Through Isaac. Paul quotes Genesis 21:12, and it comes from a hard page. It was spoken to Abraham when Sarah demanded that Hagar and the boy be sent away, and the text has just said that “the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son” (Genesis 21:11). Paul knows where the sentence comes from: a household in tears. Paul’s claim is not that God changed his mind about Israel. It is that God’s promise was always narrower and more particular than descent: from the first generation it ran through one named son and not the other, as any reader of Genesis could see. Abraham’s promise never ran through the son he already had. It ran through the son who did not exist yet, born to two people long past the age of producing him. The word of God cannot fall off course, because it never depended on what Abraham had available. It depended on what God had said he would do.

The offspring who is one. Follow the narrowing and see where it ends. Not all Abraham’s children, but Isaac; not both of Isaac’s sons, but Jacob; not all Jacob’s descendants, but a remnant. In Galatians Paul names the last step himself: the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and Scripture says offspring, not offsprings, referring to one, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The line of promise runs down the generations until it becomes a single man, and then it widens again: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). So the true Israel is not first a membership list. It is Christ, and everyone who is in him. To be in him is to be joined to him by faith, so that his standing, sonship and inheritance are counted yours. God’s word did not fail when the nation said no. It arrived, in person, at Bethlehem.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s promise to Israel was a trick, or that being a physical Jew counts for nothing (3:1–2; 11:28–29). Nor does it mean that the church has simply replaced Israel, so that the Jewish people no longer matter to God (11:1–2). The narrowing is not something new that happened to Israel from outside; it is the principle that was operating inside Israel from Abraham onward, and in chapter 11 Paul insists it is still the same tree with the same root. God never promised to save every descendant of Abraham, and so the unbelief of many Jews does not cancel his word.

Does this apply to people who grew up in the church? Yes, the principle does. Being born into a Christian family, baptised and brought up in church does not by itself make a person a child of God, any more than being born a Jew did. Each person must be born again (John 3:3) and come to Christ in faith. That is not a reason for alarm for those who trust him, nor a reason to despise a Christian upbringing, which God often uses to bring children to faith. It is a reason never to assume. Parents should pray for and speak to their children as people who need Christ, not as people who already have him because of their family.

parallels.desc: through Isaac shall your offspring be named

verseByVerse.quote: This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. For this is what the promise said: "About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children of the flesh. Ishmael was a child of the flesh: born by ordinary human means, when Abraham and Sarah tried to obtain the promised son by their own plan through Hagar (Genesis 16). Natural birth does not make a child of God. “Flesh” here is not contempt for Jewish descent; Paul has just wept over his brothers. It means what human capacity can produce on its own: not ethnicity but ability.

Counted as offspring. Isaac was born by God’s promise and power, to a barren woman past age (Galatians 4:23, 28). Abraham’s body was as good as dead (4:19), which is what marks it as a birth of promise. “Counted” is logizomai, the accountant’s word of chapter 4. There the thing reckoned was righteousness credited to a man; here it is a person entered into a family, from outside, in. You did not qualify for this household on the strength of your paperwork. You were counted into it. And reckoning is not pretending: God is not overlooking the fact that you are not related, he is stating what is now the case.

I will return. Paul quotes Genesis 18:10 and 14. God put a date on his own word, in a house where the one thing that had run out was time. And the promise is not merely that a child will appear but that God will return. He does not post the miracle from a distance; he says he will be there, in person, at the tent, in a year. The promises of God keep turning out to have God himself inside them.

Is anything too hard for the LORD? Attached to that date is the question the whole of Genesis 18 turns on (Genesis 18:14). It is put as a question, not an announcement. God invites them to do the sum. He is not asking Abraham and Sarah to ignore their age; he is asking them to add in the one who made the promise. The pattern set in Isaac points forward to the new birth itself: the children of God are born because God acts, not because nature is able (John 1:12–13). And he has done the same in you: he spoke, and a heart that could produce nothing living began to believe.

Nothing will be impossible with God. The question asked at Sarah’s tent was answered again at a door in Nazareth. When the angel told Mary she would bear a son though she had no husband, he gave her the reply of Genesis 18:14 in new words: nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). Isaac came from a womb that was dead; Jesus from a womb that had never known a man. Both births were announced in advance, and both children were named before they were conceived. But Isaac was a child of the promise, and Jesus is the one the promise was about. Everyone counted into Abraham’s family is counted in him.

What it does not mean. Isaac is not a guarantee that God will do the particular impossible thing you have in mind: the marriage restored, the diagnosis reversed, the son home by Christmas. Sarah was given a son; plenty of faithful women in Scripture were not. What Isaac establishes is not a promise about your circumstances but evidence about your God: this is the kind of God who acts where there is nothing to act with.

My conversion was ordinary. Am I really a child of promise? Very likely, yes. Isaac’s birth was a miracle, and it still took nine months. No lightning, no voice, no visible interruption of the world: just a woman growing larger through a winter and a baby in the spring. So if you came to Christ with no drama at all, a friend who kept asking, a hard year, a sermon you barely remember, and one day you noticed you believed it, do not conclude you are a child of the flesh because the wiring did not show. The most supernatural birth in the Old Testament looked, from outside the tent, like an ordinary confinement. The question is not how dramatic your beginning was but whether you now trust Christ.

In everyday life. Trace your Christian life backwards as far as it goes: past the decision, the church you happened to walk into, the person who would not leave you alone about it, the household you were born into. Mark the point where the chain stops consisting of things you arranged. It ends somewhere you did not put yourself. And when you plan, work and strive, do it gladly, but do not mistake what your own strength produces for what only God’s word can create. The flesh did produce a son, Ishmael; what it could not produce was the one the promise had named.

parallels.desc: Sarah shall have a son

verseByVerse.quote: And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not only so. A stronger example, and it closes a loophole. A reader could say the real difference between Isaac and Ishmael was Hagar. So Paul reaches for one father, one mother, one conception: twins (Genesis 25:21–26). Every variable that could be offered as the hidden reason has been removed, and the difference remains.

A frightened mother. The scene is not a seminar. Rebekah is pregnant and in pain. The children struggle together within her until she says, If it is thus, why is this happening to me? and goes to inquire of the LORD (Genesis 25:22). One of the most contested doctrines in the Bible arrives as an answer to a frightened woman asking why her pregnancy hurts.

Not yet born. Before the boys had a character, a history, a temperament or a single act to their name, the distinction was set, so God’s choice cannot have rested on their deeds. Whatever else the doctrine of election is, it is the news that the most important thing ever decided about you was settled before you were in a position to spoil it.

In order that. “God’s purpose of election” is his plan (as in 8:28), carried out by his choosing; “continue” means that it stands firm. And the small phrase “in order that” carries the argument: God made the choice early on purpose. God arranged for this decision to be announced at the one moment when nobody could mistake what it rested on.

Him who calls. The basis of election is not anything in the person, but God who calls. Calling here is God’s effective summons, as in 8:30.

Where Christians differ: election based on foreseen faith. Arminian teachers (Christians who hold that God’s saving grace can finally be resisted) say God chose people because he foresaw that they would believe; others say election here is only about nations or roles in history, not individual salvation. The first view deserves a straight answer rather than a dismissal, because faith is not a work, and so not because of works does not by itself settle it. This commentary’s view: Paul’s point excludes foreseen faith. If God had chosen Jacob because he foresaw Jacob’s faith, Paul would simply say so, and the objection of verse 14 (is God unjust?) would never arise. Paul says the choice was made before they had done anything, good or bad, and not by works but by him who calls; his alternative to works is not foreseen faith but the caller. Five verses later he says it flatly: it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy (v. 16). Foreseen willing is still willing. Faith is not the cause of election but its fruit (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). And though Jacob and Esau stand at the head of nations, Paul uses them to answer a question about individual salvation: why some Jews are saved and others are not (vv. 1–6, 24, 27). This is unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.5; Canons of Dort 1.7–10). Arminian brothers who read the verse otherwise want to guard God’s fairness and the reality of human response; Paul guards both as well, in his own way, in verses 14 to 24 and in chapter 10.

Chosen in him. Paul’s fullest statement of this truth adds two words this verse leaves unspoken: “he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). Election was never a bare decision about names on a list. It is election in Christ. The Father’s first and greatest choice is his Son, whom he calls my Chosen One (Luke 9:35; Isaiah 42:1), and every other choosing happens in him. That is why the choice could be made before the twins were born without being arbitrary, and why it stands: God’s purpose rests not on Jacob, nor on you, but on the one in whom it was made, and he cannot fail. We cannot read God’s decree, but we can look at Christ, the Chosen One, and come to him.

The comfort on the underside. Turn the verse over: if nothing good you did was ever the reason, then nothing bad you do can be the disqualification. God’s choice never rested on your record, so your record cannot overturn it. That is why this doctrine, which frightens people at first hearing, has comforted so many Christians on their deathbeds. It is the only ground of assurance that your own performance is unable to erode.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is arbitrary or that his choice is random. His reasons are hidden in his own wisdom and love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). It does not mean human choices do not matter; Esau truly despised his birthright (Hebrews 12:16). And it is not a licence to sin (6:1–2): behaviour is not irrelevant, but it was never the foundation.

If election is unconditional, how can I know I am elect? Not by peering into God’s secret decree, which is not revealed, but by looking where God has pointed you: to Christ and to his promise. Do you trust Christ? Then you have been called, and those he called he predestined (8:30). Faith is the fruit of election, so the fruit tells you about the root. Peter tells believers to make their calling and election sure by growing in godliness (2 Peter 1:10), not as the ground of acceptance but as its evidence. Look first to Christ, not to yourself. Assurance grows as you rest on his promise and see his work in you.

verseByVerse.quote: she was told, "The older will serve the younger." As it is written, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The older and the younger. From Genesis 25:23. God reversed the normal order, in which the firstborn has the leading place. Esau was born first, but Jacob received the blessing. This never visibly came true in the two men’s lifetimes: when they finally meet, it is Jacob who bows to the ground seven times and calls his brother my lord (Genesis 33:3, 8). The oracle was fulfilled at the level of nations, centuries later, when Edom became subject to David (2 Samuel 8:14).

Jacob I loved. Malachi 1:2–3 was written more than a thousand years after Rebekah’s pregnancy, when God pointed to his covenant love for Israel (Jacob’s descendants) and his judgment on Edom (Esau’s descendants). Paul uses it to confirm that God’s choice of Jacob was his free, sovereign love.

Hated. In Hebrew idiom, “love” and “hate” in a comparison can mean choosing one and not the other, loving one and loving the other less. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and the next verse says Leah was hated (Genesis 29:30–31); Jesus speaks the same way of hating father and mother (Luke 14:26). So “hated” here means first of all that God did not choose Esau for covenant love.

But not merely neutral. Yet “hated” must not be softened into mere indifference. Malachi goes on: I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals; they may build, but I will tear down (Malachi 1:3–4). And Malachi’s verdict lands on a real record. Edom stood at the roadside and watched Jerusalem burn, and did more than watch: gloating over the ruin, cutting off the fugitives, handing over survivors (Obadiah 10–14). So verse 12 quotes what God said before the twins were born, and verse 13 quotes his verdict, centuries later, on a nation with a long history of wickedness. Both are true. Nobody should be told that God announced hatred over a foetus, because that is not what the text Paul quotes says.

Where Christians differ: individuals or nations. Some say verses 10–13 speak only of nations (Israel and Edom) and earthly roles, not eternal salvation. The case is stronger than it is usually given credit for: Genesis 25:23 says in so many words two nations are in your womb, and Malachi means Israel and Edom, not two men. What that reading gets right is a needed corrective: Paul is arguing about how God constitutes a people, and he never hands anybody a device for sorting the individuals around him. This commentary’s view: The original prophecies did concern the nations that came from the two brothers. But Paul applies the principle to individuals and to salvation, because that is his question: why some Israelites are saved and others are not (vv. 3, 6, 22–24). And nations are made up of individuals. Jacob and Esau themselves illustrate God’s choice of persons. Within a few verses Paul moves to two named individuals, Moses and Pharaoh, and then to even us whom he has called (v. 24). The objection that follows (v. 14) only makes sense if Paul is teaching unconditional individual election.

The man God chose. Jacob bought his brother’s birthright with a bowl of stew from a man who came in from the field exhausted. He lied to his blind father’s face to steal a blessing. And when he finally had to face Esau and his four hundred men, he lined up his household in order of how much he valued them: the servant women and their children in front, Leah and hers behind them, Rachel and Joseph at the back (Genesis 33:1–2). And the brother God passed over? Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept (Genesis 33:4). If election were a reward for character, this verdict is upside down. That is exactly why Paul chose the example. The evidence runs so obviously the wrong way that no one can pretend the choice was made on merit.

A ladder for the heel-grabber. Follow the chosen man one night past the stolen blessing. Jacob is running for his life from the brother he cheated, sleeping in the open with a stone for a pillow, and God does not rebuke him.
