He shows him a ladder set up on the earth with its top in heaven, the angels going up and down on it, and repeats to the deceiver the promises made to Abraham (Genesis 28:12–15). Jesus tells Nathanael that he himself is that ladder: “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). So the love that chose Jacob was never fondness for a likeable boy. It was the love that would build a way between heaven and an undeserving sinner, and the way is Christ. And the same God met him again, twenty years on, in a night of wrestling until daybreak, when he refused to let go without a blessing. He went into that night called Jacob, the heel-grabber, and came out of it limping and called Israel, which is the name this chapter is arguing about. The God of Jacob wounds and renames, and will not let his chosen go.

What if I am an Esau? Look at what actually marks Esau, because Genesis is not vague. I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me? (Genesis 25:32), and the narrator’s summary: Esau despised his birthright (25:34). The defining thing about him is not that he longed for God and was shut out. It is that he did not want it. He had it, and sold it for one hot meal, because the future was less interesting than his appetite. So do not ask whether you feel chosen. Ask what you actually want. A man terrified of being Esau is showing the opposite of Esau’s defining trait. Contempt is not anxious. Nobody ever lay awake grieving over a birthright he despised. If you want Christ, come to him; he turns no one away (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Hated” in Hebrew idiom can mean “loved less” or “passed over” — here, not chosen.

parallels.desc: the older shall serve the younger
I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! For he says to Moses, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? The natural objection. If God chooses one twin and not the other, before either has done anything, isn’t that unfair? The fact that Paul raises this objection strongly suggests he is teaching unconditional election. Few would accuse God of injustice for choosing those he foresaw would believe. A version of election that has never made anybody ask whether it is fair is milder than the one Paul is teaching. The question is evidence that you have understood, not evidence that you are resisting.

By no means! Mē genoito, Paul’s strongest denial (as in 3:4; 6:2). God cannot be unjust. Paul rejects the conclusion; he does not scorn the person who asks.

For he says to Moses. Paul answers from God’s own words in Exodus 33:19. He quotes a sentence that is not about justice at all but about mercy, and that switch is his argument. Injustice would mean somebody received less than he was owed. So ask what is owed. At the foot of the mountain where these words were spoken, what was owed was destruction, and everybody knew it. The question is not whether God is unjust. It is whether God is obliged. Paul is not defending God against the charge of giving somebody too little. He is answering people who have not yet grasped that the whole story, from the mountain onward, is God giving somebody far too much.

The scene at Sinai. While Moses receives the law, the people dance round a metal calf, a few months after watching the sea open. The covenant is in pieces before the ink is dry (Exodus 32). Then God tells Moses to go up to the land but says he will not go with them himself, “lest I consume you on the way” (Exodus 33:3). Moses will not accept it: “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). Better no promised land than a promised land without God. And then, with the nation still smelling of the fire, he asks for something astonishing: “Please show me your glory” (Exodus 33:18).

I will have mercy. Here is what God answered: “I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name”. And then the sentence Paul quotes. A man asks to see the glory of God, and what God shows him is his freedom to be merciful. Not power or the fire on the mountain; those had been on display for months. The hardest-sounding sentence in Romans 9 is, in its own place, the definition of divine glory: mercy that answers to nothing outside itself. The sentence loops back on itself exactly like “I AM WHO I AM” at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14): once about his being, once about his mercy, and both times nothing outside God determines it. So God is not unjust when he gives mercy to some and not to others. No one is treated worse than he deserves; some are treated far better.

The glory Moses asked to see. Moses was hidden in a cleft of the rock and saw only the back of the glory as it passed (Exodus 33:22–23). John tells us where the rest of that request was answered. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, full of grace and truth (John 1:14), the very name proclaimed on the mountain, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). So the free mercy announced at Sinai has a face. Watch Jesus call a tax collector from his booth, or promise paradise to one of the two criminals crucified beside him (Luke 23:39–43), and you are watching God have mercy on whom he has mercy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has no reasons, or that he enjoys the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). It means the reason for his mercy lies in himself, not in us. And nothing here entitles anyone to say to a frightened person, “Perhaps he has not chosen you.” That sentence appears nowhere in this chapter. “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” entered the Bible as a reprieve for a nation that had earned annihilation. If you hear it as a door swinging shut, that says more about what you expect of God than about what the verse says.

Then is God fair? Is it fair that some receive mercy and others do not? If fair means everyone gets what he deserves, God is perfectly fair to all who are lost: no one in hell will be punished beyond his sin. But no one in heaven will be there because it was fair. They will be there because God was merciful, and mercy cannot be demanded. Think of a judge who pays the fine of one guilty man out of his own pocket. The others have not been wronged; they received justice. The one has received a gift. Grace is not a matter of being fair, and that is the best news there is, because fairness would condemn us all.

For worship. After the golden calf, justice would have meant destruction; everything Israel received after that was mercy. And it was never cheap. The God who proclaimed himself to Moses as merciful, and as one who “will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7), stayed true to both when the guilty were spared: he laid their judgment on his Son. God’s freedom to have mercy is the freedom to pay for sin himself. He is the LORD, gracious to whom he will be gracious: no one can demand his mercy, no one can exhaust it, and he has put it beyond doubt for all who come to him in Christ.

parallels.desc: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious

verseByVerse.quote: So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will or exertion. Literally, not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, and the running is a race. Wanting it enough and trying hard enough are both excluded in one clause. Esau wanted the blessing and ran to hunt game for it (Genesis 27), but did not get it.

God, who has mercy. Salvation rests finally on God’s mercy. We do will and run, but only because God has first worked in us both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). What Paul denies is that willing and running are the cause. He once put both halves in one sentence: “I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own” (Philippians 3:12). The pressing on is real, and it comes second. You do not run in order to be laid hold of. You run because you were.

Relief for the exhausted. If salvation did depend on will and exertion, the honest follow-up question would be: how much? How much wanting counts as enough, how much effort clears the bar? Nobody could ever rest. Verse 16 removes a measurement no one has ever passed, and it is hard news only for the heart that would rather keep running than be carried.

The Scripture says to Pharaoh. The other side: hardening. Paul writes the Scripture says where Exodus has God speaking: what Scripture says, God says. Read Exodus 9:15–16 whole: by now God could have put out his hand and struck Pharaoh and his people with pestilence, and they would have been cut off from the earth, but for this purpose he raised him up. So the verse explains to a man six plagues into a contest he has lost why he is still alive.

Raised up. God brought Pharaoh onto the stage of history, made him king, and kept him standing through the plagues. Pharaoh’s whole career was ordered by God’s purpose: not as approval of his wickedness, but as the stage on which God’s power would be displayed to the nations.

My name in all the earth. It happened. Forty years later, in Jericho, a Canaanite prostitute told two Israelite spies why she had hidden them: we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you, and our hearts melted (Joshua 2:10–11). And it saved Rahab. She and her household came out of Jericho alive, and her name stands in the first chapter of Matthew, in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. It does not depend on the one who wills or runs: Pharaoh willed and ran harder than anyone in the story, and it moved nothing. It depends on God, who has mercy: and the mercy reached the last person in the region anyone would have picked, by way of the hardest heart in it.

Another ruler, another purpose. The pattern of Pharaoh returns at the centre of history. Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus, and the church confessed that they did only what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Pilate, like Pharaoh, was fully responsible in his cowardice, yet through the worst thing rulers ever did God showed his power as nowhere else. The Red Sea was the rehearsal. The empty tomb is the display of power the whole earth was meant to hear about.

If it does not depend on my will, should I just wait for God to act? No. God’s mercy does not bypass your will; it renews it, so that you willingly come. The gospel calls you to repent and believe now (Acts 17:30; 2 Corinthians 6:2), and Paul will say in the next chapter that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (10:13). If you want Christ, that desire is already the sign of God’s mercy at work. Do not sit waiting for a feeling. Call on him, read his word, go where it is preached, and pray, Lord, have mercy on me. No one who ever came to him was refused.

parallels.desc: for this purpose I have raised you up

verseByVerse.quote: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mercy and hardening. The two sides of God’s sovereignty, drawn from the two quotations: mercy (Moses) and hardening (Pharaoh). To harden is to make stubborn and unresponsive. The two are not presented as equals: mercy is what God declares about himself (Exodus 33:19), while hardening is Paul’s conclusion from the story of Pharaoh. Scripture gives mercy the greater weight, and so does this chapter, most clearly at verses 22–23.

How God hardens. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (Exodus 9:12; 10:20), and God foretold it before any plague (Exodus 4:21). Both are true. The order matters: not until the sixth plague does the account say the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart (9:12), after Pharaoh had repeatedly done it himself. That does not soften the doctrine, but it shows its shape. God does not put evil into a good heart. He hardens by withholding the softening grace that would melt the heart, and by giving sinners over to the sin they already love (1:24, 26, 28). Pharaoh is Romans 1 in a single man: he freely chose his stubbornness, and God, as a judge passing sentence, handed him over to the choice he kept making.

Jesus said it first. The truth of verse 18 was spoken, in substance, by Jesus himself, and he said it as a prayer of joy: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will” (Matthew 11:25–26). He rejoiced in the Father’s freedom to hide and to reveal. And in the next breath he turned to the crowd: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). No one understood the sovereignty of God better than the Son, and it did not make him sparing with his invitation. Whoever wants to know how verse 18 should sound must hear it in his voice.

You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” The second objection. If God decides who is hardened, how can he blame anyone? Again, the objection only arises because Paul really is teaching that God decides. No one asks this of an election based on foreseen faith. And let the objection stand at full height, because there is no point answering a weak version of it. If God’s will cannot be resisted, and if what I am is finally traceable to that will, then blaming me is like blaming a stone for falling. Every honest reader of this chapter has felt it, and Paul writes the sentence for exactly that reader: you will say to me then. He knows this is where his argument leads a thinking person.

Paul declines to solve it. Paul does not answer this objection with an argument. What follows in verse 20 is not a rebuttal but a question about who is asking. He could have distinguished what God decrees from what he permits, and does not. If you came wanting the logic resolved, you will not get it here. But declining is not evading. Paul is doing what God did with Job. Job asked for a hearing, got questions about the sea and the ostrich, and was satisfied: not because he received the information, but because he received the one speaking. A God whose decisions you could fully audit would be a God the size of your understanding. People want that God right up until they are in trouble, and then they want a bigger one.

The chapter does not stop at the potter. Paul does eventually give a cause for Israel’s failure, and it is not a decree. It is Israel: “they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works” (v. 32). And in the next chapter God holds out his hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21). Paul refuses to explain the mechanism, and then places the responsibility exactly where the objector feared it could not be placed. Anyone who quotes verse 20 as though it settled the question of human responsibility has stopped reading eleven verses too early.

Has God hardened me? If that question frightens you, look at what the fear itself shows. Pharaoh never once asked it. Hardness does not lie awake wondering whether it is hard; that is the whole trouble with it. Alarm about your own heart is a sign of feeling in it. And the remedy was never introspection. A heart of stone is not repaired by being examined more closely. It is replaced, and God promised to do exactly that: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26). You do not soften your own heart. You ask for the one thing you cannot manufacture, and you ask the God who gives it. And the God who need not have mercy on anyone has had mercy on multitudes, softening hearts of stone, opening blind eyes, and drawing rebels who once hardened themselves against him.

Is this not just fatalism? No. Fatalism says an impersonal force fixes the outcome whatever anyone does, so nothing you do matters. Scripture says a personal God, holy and good, rules all things and works through what people do, not around it. He ordains the end and also the means: the preacher, the prayer, the hearing, the believing (10:14–15). That is why Paul, who wrote this verse, did not shrug. He prayed for Israel (10:1), preached to them in city after city, and hoped that some would be saved (11:14). A fatalist sits still. A believer in this God gets up and prays, because the God who decides also hears.

In everyday life. Do not play with sin, thinking you can repent later. Repeatedly refusing God hardens the heart, and God may give you over to it: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). Whatever is true about the eternal decree, no one has ever stood before God able to say, I wanted you and you turned me away. And if your struggle with sin grieves you, that grief is not hardness. It is the Spirit at war with the flesh in you (Galatians 5:17), and he finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6).
verseByVerse.note: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it.

verseByVerse.quote: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, "Why have you made me like this?" Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Paul does not give a philosophical answer. He rebukes the attitude behind the question. O man: the same address Paul used at 2:1 to the reader who was enjoying chapter 1. It is not an insult. It is a reminder of what you are, and that is the answer: whatever else you are, you are a creature, having this conversation from inside the made world, not outside it. Then the verb. “Answer back” (antapokrinomai) means to reply against, to contradict, to talk back, arguing with God as if he owed us an account. It is the posture of cross-examining, not of asking. Job learned the same lesson (Job 38–42; 40:2).

Questions are not forbidden. Paul asked two of the hardest questions himself (vv. 14, 19), and Scripture is full of people who put hard questions to God: Habakkuk asked how long; Jeremiah said, “Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you” (Jeremiah 12:1). So if this verse has ever been used on you to shut down an honest question, in grief or doubt, it was misused. What Paul rebukes is the posture of summoning God to the stand as a defendant and making yourself his judge.

Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” From Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9. A clay pot has no rights against its potter. We are creatures; God is the Creator. He is not answerable to us, and the creature does not sit in judgment on the Creator.

The potter in the dust. Once in the Gospels the question of verse 20 is asked out loud, about a man born blind. “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” the disciples ask, and Jesus answers that it was so that the works of God might be displayed in him (John 9:2–3). Then the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3) stoops, makes clay with his own hands, and gives the man his sight (9:6). The potter who once formed man from the dust of the ground has taken up dust a second time. Jesus does not take the question away from the potter. He answers it as the potter, with a purpose no one had guessed, and the purpose is mercy. The one with every right over the clay is the one who stooped to the dust to remake it.

The potter’s right. The image comes from Jeremiah 18, and people often make it say the opposite of what Jeremiah saw. The vessel was spoiled in the potter’s hand, and he did not throw it out: he reworked it into another vessel (Jeremiah 18:4). And the application God draws is an appeal: if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, he will relent of the disaster (Jeremiah 18:7–8). That does not blunt Paul; he cites the potter for the potter’s right, and the right is real. But it tells you what kind of potter has that right. Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9 also sit within promises of restoration. The image can also speak of judgment, as when Jeremiah smashes a flask that can never be mended (Jeremiah 19:11), so the potter’s right is no empty word. But not one of these passages shows a God who does not care.

The same lump. Most Reformed interpreters take the lump as all humanity, alike sinful in Adam (5:12). From it God makes some vessels for honour (salvation) and leaves others for dishonour (judgment). The lump is not innocent clay; it is fallen humanity, already deserving wrath. God wrongs no one by showing mercy to some. And there is no better grade of clay: the difference lies entirely in the potter’s intention. One caution about pressing the picture further than Paul does: in a household, honourable and dishonourable use means the fine dish and the common pot; the final destinies come in verses 22–23. Elsewhere Paul uses the same image and has a person cleanse himself to become a vessel for honourable use (2 Timothy 2:20–21).

Where Christians differ: double predestination. Some say God chooses only to save, and the lost simply choose damnation without any decree. Others (hyper-Calvinists, a fringe view that most Reformed churches reject) say God creates people in order to damn them and causes their sin in the same way he causes faith. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that God decrees both: he elects some to life, and he passes by the rest and ordains them to wrath for their sin (Westminster Confession 3.3, 3.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.3 puts it more gently: the rest are left to act in their sin to their just condemnation). But the two are not symmetrical. God works faith in the elect by his Spirit; he does not work sin in the reprobate, those he passes by. The saved owe everything to grace; the lost owe their condemnation entirely to their own sin. Many believers who rejoice in grace still hesitate here, and their hesitation is a fair warning to speak of it as Paul does. Hold the mystery with humility, as Paul does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is a tyrant who enjoys destruction. Nor is this a call to stoicism. Not knowing why is a real grief, and Scripture never tells you to pretend otherwise. You are not required to feel resolved. You are required not to sit in judgment on God.

Does this mean we are just pots, without dignity? No. The image is about authority, not worth. Paul is not saying people are mere objects; Scripture says we are made in God’s image and crowned with glory and honour (Psalm 8:5). The point is the relationship: we cannot stand over God and judge him, because he made us and we did not make him. And the potter who has this right is the one who reshapes spoiled clay rather than throwing it away, and whose own Son took human clay in the incarnation. To be clay in such hands is not humiliation. It is the safest place a creature can be.

parallels.desc: shall the potter be regarded as the clay?

verseByVerse.quote: What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory —
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if God. God means his holy wrath against sin and his power to be seen, as with Pharaoh. And the sentence begins “What if God”, and never finishes. At the hardest point in his hardest chapter Paul does not assert; he puts a question and leaves it with you. If he will not close this sentence, nobody preaching it should close it harder than he did.

But why would God want his wrath to be seen? A fair question, and Paul answers it in the very next verse. Five reasons, from this passage and the rest of Scripture.

First, because it is true of him. God’s glory is God made known as he really is. When he showed Moses his glory, he named himself merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity, and also one who will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:6–7). Justice is part of who he is. A God who hid it would be hiding himself. And a God who did nothing about evil would not be good: we would not call a judge good who let a child abuser walk free.

Second, because evil must not have the last word. Pharaoh was enslaving and killing God’s people. The plagues that showed God’s power were also the rescue of the oppressed. The cry of every victim, how long, O Lord? (Revelation 6:10; Psalm 94:3), is answered by God’s wrath. His judgment tells the world that cruelty and injustice will not win.

Third, so that his name would reach the nations. God raised Pharaoh up so that his name might be proclaimed in all the earth (v. 17), and the report of the Red Sea reached Jericho and saved Rahab (Joshua 2:9–11). The display of God’s power against Pharaoh became mercy for a Gentile. That is the pattern of this chapter.

Fourth, so that mercy is seen as mercy. This is Paul’s own answer: in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy (v. 23). Mercy only means something where judgment is deserved. Those who are saved see what they were saved from, and so they see the riches of grace: we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. But God, being rich in mercy … (Ephesians 2:3–4). The one who is forgiven much, loves much (Luke 7:47).

Fifth and supremely, at the cross. The place where God shows both his wrath and his mercy most fully is Calvary. God put Christ forward as a propitiation, to show his righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:25–26). Propitiation means that God’s own Son stands where the sinner stood and bears the anger the sinner deserved, so that none is left. There wrath against sin is fully shown, and fully borne, by the Son, for the vessels of mercy.

What this does not mean. Not that God enjoys destroying: As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Not that his wrath is a loss of temper; it is his settled, holy opposition to evil. And not that God shows his glory out of vanity or insecurity, as a person might. For us, living for our own glory is pride, because we are not the greatest good. For God it is the opposite: he is the greatest good, so making himself known is the best thing he can give his creatures. God tells us enough to trust him, and calls us to humility where we cannot see further (v. 20; 11:33–36).

Much patience. In the middle of the sentence sits the phrase that ruins every caricature of this passage. God endured with much patience, at length: the word is makrothumia, slowness to anger, the same quality this letter said at 2:4 is meant to lead you to repentance. And the patience in this verse is spent on the ones headed for destruction; if the only aim were to display wrath, there would be no reason to wait. Peter uses the same word for the same behaviour and tells you what is inside it: the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Whatever Romans 9 is doing, it is not describing a God in a hurry to condemn.

Prepared for destruction. The Greek word (katērtismena) is passive: they “were prepared”, and Paul does not say by whom. Many read it as ripe for destruction, fitted for it by their own sin. Contrast the next phrase, where Paul says God prepared the vessels of mercy.

Vessels of mercy. The ultimate goal. God’s patience with the wicked and his judgment of them show the vessels of mercy what they were saved from, and so make his grace shine brighter. And here the verses become personal: God’s patience with the vessels of wrath gives time for mercy to reach the vessels of mercy. Every Christian was on the wrong side of that sentence for a while. The waiting was not happening around you while you stood safely elsewhere. You were inside it. The delay people demand an explanation for is the delay they were saved during.

Prepared beforehand. Here the verb is active, and God is the subject: he prepared them beforehand (proētoimasen), as in Ephesians 2:10. The difference in grammar is deliberate: God is the author of salvation, but not the author of sin. And glory here is not a vague word for heaven. It is what chapter 8 promised: being glorified with Christ, made like him in body and character, and living for ever in the presence of the God whose wrath we once deserved (8:17–18, 29–30).

Three differences in one sentence. Of the vessels of mercy: an active verb, God named as the one who acts, and a prefix meaning beforehand, so the preparing is dated before the vessel existed. Of the vessels of wrath: a passive verb, no one named as doing it, no beforehand. Paul had every word he needed to make the halves match. Be careful not to claim more than that: a passive with no stated agent can still have God’s decree behind it, and careful readers in this tradition have said so. But anyone who presents election and reprobation as two identical acts, worked the same way by the same hand, is being more symmetrical than the apostle and the Reformed confessions (see this commentary’s view at verses 20–21). And watch where the weight of the sentence falls: on verse 23, on riches, on glory, on mercy prepared beforehand. Wrath is the thing God is said to endure. Mercy is the thing he is said to prepare.

Could the person I love be a vessel of wrath? You cannot know, and you are not asked to know. The categories are not visible, and the patience described here has not run out, not for the person you have given up on and not for you. Paul himself was once a persecutor who looked for all the world like a vessel of wrath, and God showed him mercy so that he might display his perfect patience as an example (1 Timothy 1:16). As long as it is called today (Hebrews 3:13), God’s patience is still at work, and the invitation still stands. Your task is not to sort people but to pray for them and to tell them about Christ.

In everyday life. Work out roughly how long it was between the first thing you did that you knew was wrong and the day you came to Christ. Whatever the number, that interval is much patience, measured from the inside. You have already lived in it, for years, and were not consumed. That is not a theory; it is your own history. So when someone tries your patience today, remember how long God endured you.

verseByVerse.quote: even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even us. The vessels of mercy are identified: we, whom God has effectually called (8:30). An effectual call is not only an invitation but a summons that brings the person: God speaks through the gospel, and his Spirit gives the hearer life to answer (John 6:44; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). For twenty verses everything has been in the third person: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Moses, Pharaoh, a potter, two vessels. Then, without warning, Paul writes us, like a hand on the shoulder. The vessels of mercy prepared beforehand for glory are not a category. They are the people in the room where this letter is being read aloud.

Called. The verb has been running quietly under the whole passage. “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named” (v. 7; in Greek, “called”). “Not because of works but because of him who calls” (v. 11). “Called ‘sons of the living God’” (v. 26). And in the previous chapter, those whom he predestined he also called (8:30). That matters, because you cannot observe an eternal decree, and staring at it has driven serious people to despair. But a call is a thing that happens in time, to a person, at an address. It leaves marks.

Not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles? God’s choice crosses the boundary of race. This brings Paul back to his question about Israel: God’s purpose never was to save every Jew, but to call out a people from Jews and Gentiles alike. The inclusion of the Gentiles is not a fallback plan after Israel’s rejection; it was always in the promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Look too at the preposition: called out of the Jews and out of the Gentiles. Out of both. Neither group is summoned wholesale. So the narrowing Paul described inside Israel at verse 6 is now running inside the Gentile world as well. No one is carried in by belonging to a group. Any Gentile Christian who has been reading this chapter with quiet satisfaction about Israel has just been included in its terms, and Paul will tell him to his face: “do not be arrogant toward the branches” (11:18).

A church with a seam down the middle. The letter went to a congregation with a seam down the middle: Jewish believers who had been expelled from Rome under Claudius and had come back (Acts 18:2; compare Romans 16:3), and Gentile believers who had, it seems, kept the church going in their absence. Into that room Paul sends a sentence that gives neither group first place: both were simply called. Election turns out to be the one thing that can settle an argument about who ranks where. The chapter began with a man weeping because his own people would not come. It ends its argument by naming the people who did: a mixed, unlikely, quarrelling congregation in the capital of the empire that would one day kill him, called out of both halves of a divided world by the God who has been doing exactly this since Isaac.

One new man. What joins the two halves of that church is not a treaty but a person. Paul says it to another mixed congregation: Christ himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility, so that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two (Ephesians 2:14–15). Jew and Gentile are not merged into a compromise; each is brought to the same cross and the same risen Lord, and finds the other already there. That is why Paul can write us without strain: the us is Christ’s body.

How do I know if I have been called? Look not for a voice but for a summons you have answered. God’s effectual call comes through the gospel: you heard the message about Christ, and something in you, against your old inclinations, found it true and came to him (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). If you now trust Christ, want to know him, and find yourself, however unevenly, turning from sin, those are the marks of the call. It may have been sudden or gradual; that does not matter. What matters is that you have come to Christ and are still coming. If you are unsure, do not stare at yourself. Answer the call now, and keep answering it.

In everyday life. Did you count yourself in the word us? Romans 9 is easily read from the gallery, weighing God’s conduct; Paul wrote it as a member. If the chapter has felt like a court case you are watching rather than a mercy you are inside, this verse puts you inside it. And the same call seated beside you the people in your church you find hardest to sit beside.

verseByVerse.quote: As indeed he says in Hosea, "Those who were not my people I will call 'my people,' and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved.'" "And in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they will be called 'sons of the living God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As indeed he says in Hosea. Paul now shows that the Old Testament foretold both the calling of Gentiles (vv. 25–26) and the saving of only a remnant of Israel (vv. 27–29). He quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10. And he is quoting the names of a man’s children.

Lo-ammi. God told Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him, and he did, and she was. They had three children, and God named them. The second was a daughter: Lo-ruhamah, No Mercy, or not loved. The third was a son: Lo-ammi, Not My People (Hosea 1:6, 9). The sermon was his family. So when Paul quotes “her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved’”, he is quoting a little girl’s name being taken off her. God does not hand out replacement names; the lo, the “not”, comes off. No Mercy becomes Mercy. Not My People becomes My People. If mercy can reach that house, the question of whether it can reach Rome or you is already settled.

How Paul uses Hosea. Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel, who by their idolatry had become like pagans. Paul applies the words to Gentiles. This is not misuse. Israel had become like the nations, and so the principle is the same: God can make a people out of those who are not a people, by sheer grace. Peter applies the same words to his readers, many of them probably Gentile believers: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people” (1 Peter 2:10).

In the very place. God’s grace reaches the very place of rejection and makes outsiders sons. Not somewhere new where the story is not known, but at the same address where the disowning was announced. And the promise climbs higher than my people again: Hosea says “sons of the living God”: not merely readmitted, but family. And the God whose sons they are is the living one, over against the dead idols they had left him for.

What did the renaming cost? Everything, and Hosea shows it. God sent him back to buy his wife out of what she had sold herself into, and Scripture records the price, down to the barley (Hosea 3:2). That is the shape of every renaming God does: somebody goes and pays for the one who left. Hosea was rehearsing, in a small way and at his own cost, what it would take. The final price was paid by Christ, the beloved Son, who on the cross was forsaken and treated as an outcast, so that those who were not God’s people could be called sons of the living God (Galatians 4:4–5). Your new name is free to you because it was not free to him.

In everyday life. You may carry a name for yourself that surfaces when the house is quiet, often one of these two: not wanted, or not forgiven. Put beside it the name God gives everyone in Christ: beloved, my people, a child of the living God. Do not argue that the old name was never true. Agree that it was, and that God has taken the not off it. Then live today under the new name, among the very people who knew the old one.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel; Paul applies the words to the Gentiles too.

parallels.desc: I will say to Not My People, “You are my people”

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah cries out. The word is a shout: a man raising his voice about his own nation. Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22–23, mainly from the Greek translation, though his opening words, the number of the sons of Israel, are borrowed from Hosea 1:10, the verse he has just quoted.

A boy named Remnant. Isaiah had a son called Shear-jashub, which means a remnant shall return (Isaiah 7:3). Hosea’s children were the judgment; Isaiah’s son was the hope, and it cut both ways. A remnant shall return can be read with the stress on either word, and both readings are true. Only a remnant: that is the threat. A remnant shall return: that is the promise. To a man secure in his numbers and his ancestry, the word is only. To a man who has counted the faithful and thinks he has reached the end of them, the word is a remnant: there is one.

As the sand of the sea. An echo of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). Paul is not saying the multitude promised to Abraham was cancelled and replaced by a handful; he is saying the multitude was never going to arrive by descent. Paul goes on to speak of a future fullness for Israel (11:12, 25–26), so this verse is not his last word on it.

Only a remnant. A small number preserved through judgment. In Isaiah, only a remnant would come through the Assyrian disaster and return to God. The principle runs through the Old Testament, from Noah to Elijah’s seven thousand (11:4). So the fact that most Jews have rejected Christ is not a surprise; the prophets foretold it. And read the sentence just before the one Paul quotes, because it defines the remnant: a remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God (Isaiah 10:21). The remnant is not defined by having survived. It is defined by having returned to God.

The mighty God. That title is not chosen at random. The remnant returns to the mighty God, and a chapter earlier Isaiah gave the same Hebrew name to a child: for to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God (Isaiah 9:6). The God to whom the remnant returns is the God who would be born a son of David. So the remnant has a head. Christ is the true and faithful Israel (Isaiah 49:3), who went through judgment and came out of the grave, and everyone who returns to God returns through him.

Fully and without delay. God will do what he has said, decisively. The Greek of this line is genuinely difficult. The KJV, following later manuscripts, has a longer form of the verse; the earliest have the shorter one that most modern Bibles print. The sense is that God will bring his word to completion and will not let it drag. There is mercy even in that: God does not leave a people suspended for centuries in a judgment that never arrives and never lifts.

In the flow. Verses 25–29 take up the two halves of verse 24 in reverse order: Hosea speaks of outsiders brought in, Isaiah of Israel narrowed to a remnant. So the unbelief of many Jews is not God’s word failing (v. 6) but coming true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the remnant were saved because they were better. Chapter 11 says it is a remnant chosen by grace (11:5). And remnant language is the natural vocabulary of every small, self-congratulating group that has decided everyone else has compromised. Isaiah’s remnant is survivors of a catastrophe, people who came out of a burning country with nothing, whose only distinction is that God kept them. The moment remnant becomes a compliment you pay yourself, it has stopped describing you.

Our church is small. Does that mean we are the faithful remnant? Not necessarily, and the question itself can be a trap. Size proves nothing either way. Large churches can be faithful and small ones proud, and the reverse. A small congregation that is preaching Christ faithfully can take comfort from this verse: God has often worked through few, and he is keeping his word. But it must never become a badge, as if being few made you better. The remnant is marked not by smallness but by returning to God, by grace alone. Be faithful, pray for growth, and leave the counting to God.

parallels.desc: only a remnant will return

verseByVerse.quote: And as Isaiah predicted, "If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as Isaiah predicted. Paul quotes Isaiah 1:9, the final scriptural witness of the section.

The Lord of hosts. The Lord of the armies of heaven, all-powerful. And the sentence is about what would have happened and did not: if the Lord had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom. It is not a lament about how few were kept. Everything up to here has pressed a question about the people passed over. Isaiah asks the rarer one: why is there anybody here at all? He is standing in the wreckage, one of the survivors, saying we should not be here.

Offspring. The word is sperma, seed, and the verse turns on it. A remnant is what is left over; a seed is put into the ground on purpose. Isaiah is not saying God salvaged a few but that he planted, and Paul closes the section on a word that means a future.

A shoot from the stump. Isaiah keeps returning to this picture. When the land is burned and felled like an oak, the holy seed is its stump (Isaiah 6:13), and out of a stump comes the hope: there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit (Isaiah 11:1). The seed God left in Jerusalem was not kept for its own sake. It was kept because the Messiah had to come from somewhere, and God would not let the line be cut off before he came. The survivors of Isaiah 1:9 were the soil in which that shoot would one day grow.

Like Sodom. The cities were wiped out completely for their sin (Genesis 19), and Israel deserved the same. And the comparison is more brutal than it sounds. One verse further, Isaiah says: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” (Isaiah 1:10). He is calling Jerusalem, with its temple operating, Sodom to its face. So the difference between Jerusalem and Sodom, on Isaiah’s own account, was not the behaviour. It was that one had seed left in it and the other did not. Abraham pleaded, and ten righteous men could not be found in Sodom. Lot was pulled out by the hand. Sodom is what a place looks like when nothing has been kept back: no seed, no next generation, no morning after.

Does this mean the church today is only kept alive by God? Yes, and that is a comfort, not a threat. Every generation of believers exists because the Lord of hosts has left a seed. The church has survived persecution, heresy and its own failures not because it was strong but because Christ said he would build it and the gates of hell would not prevail (Matthew 16:18). When you see churches shrinking or a nation turning from God, do not despair as though the gospel were dying out. God has never let his seed be wiped out, and he will not now. Pray, and keep sowing.

In everyday life. Finish Isaiah’s sentence about yourself: If the Lord of hosts had not left me ______, I would have been ______. A friend who would not give up on you. A conscience that would not settle. An illness that stopped you just before the irreparable thing. Left to ourselves we count what we lack; Isaiah counts what he was spared, as someone who knows what he escaped.

parallels.desc: if the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–33 — The Stumbling Stone: Israel's Pursuit and Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by turning from God’s side to Israel’s. Gentiles who were not pursuing righteousness have received it by faith; Israel pursued the law and did not reach it, because they pursued it as if it were by works (vv. 30–32). They stumbled over the stone God laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16), which is Christ. Their problem was not lack of zeal (10:2) but its direction: seeking a righteousness of their own instead of God’s.
verseByVerse.theology:
The stone and the two ways

The stone of Romans 9:33 is one of the New Testament’s central pictures of Christ (1 Peter 2:6–8; Matthew 21:42–44). He is the cornerstone for all who believe and the stone of stumbling for all who refuse. The gospel is never neutral: to one it is a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life (2 Corinthians 2:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel’s pursuit of righteousness by works was not insincere; it was zealous and disciplined. Now: Misdirected zeal can be harder to reach than apathy: in any church, people with much invested in their own religious record can find it hardest to stand before God empty-handed; yet the stone is laid for them too, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say, then? Paul now turns from God’s sovereignty to human responsibility. Both are true. Election explains why some believe; unbelief explains why others are lost. This section runs to the end of chapter 10.

Pursue and attain. A paradox. Pursue is a hunting or racing word, to chase something down; “attain” is to overtake it and lay hold of it. The Gentiles were not chasing a right standing with God, yet they caught it. The result board makes no sense: the people at the finish never entered the race. They were somewhere else entirely, doing the things chapter 1 described.

By faith. The righteousness of chapters 3–4: God’s gift of a right standing, received by faith in Christ. The Gentiles were handed the prize though no one would have bet on them. As a gift is the only way anyone has ever received it.

Did not reach that law. The ones who tried hardest missed, because they ran on the wrong track. Paul does not say Israel pursued righteousness and failed to reach righteousness. He says they pursued a law and did not reach that law. The people who studied it and died rather than break it did not get to the law, because the law was leading to a person, and they treated it as a list of requirements to complete. Paul will say it outright in a few verses: Christ is the end of the law (10:4).

Not a lack of zeal. The diagnosis is never insincerity. Paul says plainly in the next chapter that they have a zeal for God (10:2). And misdirected zeal is harder to reach than apathy. The indifferent man has nothing invested. The devout man has forty years invested, and every one of those years argues against the one thing being asked of him. It is often the person who has not missed a Sunday in fifty years who finds grace impossible, because to receive righteousness as a gift he has to agree that the fifty years bought him nothing.

A runner who stopped. Paul is describing his own life. He had been the fastest man on Israel’s track: circumcised on the eighth day, a Pharisee, as to righteousness under the law blameless (Philippians 3:5–6). Then he met the risen Christ, counted the whole race as loss, and wanted only to be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith (Philippians 3:9). That is the righteousness by faith of this verse. It is not a better technique. It is a person, Christ himself, who became our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30). He ran the course without a stumble, and his obedience is counted to outsiders who never entered and to exhausted runners who never finished, the moment they stop running for it and receive it.

How can I tell if I am pursuing righteousness by works? Ask what you are resting on when you come to God. If your confidence before him rises after a good week and collapses after a bad one, you are probably trusting your performance. If you think God owes you something for your faithfulness, or you look down on less disciplined Christians, the same root is showing. Faith rests on Christ’s righteousness, credited to you, which does not change with your week. That does not make you careless; it frees you to obey out of gratitude rather than fear. The remedy is not to try less but to look away from yourself to Christ every day.

verseByVerse.quote: Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. The reason. Israel pursued the law like a runner chasing a prize to be won by effort, rather than receiving God’s promise by faith. “As if”: works were never the true way. Even in the Old Testament, people were justified, declared right with God, by faith (4:1–8). And notice the first word. Why? Paul asks for a reason, and the reason he gives is not the potter, not the hidden will of God, not the clay’s lack of standing. It lies squarely in Israel. Twelve verses ago Paul refused to answer the question of fault by argument, and that refusal stands. But it was not his last word. Here, at the end of the same chapter, Paul names a cause for Israel’s fall, and the cause is what Israel did.

The stumbling stone. The stone is Christ. A crucified Messiah offended them (1 Corinthians 1:23). He tells them their works cannot save; that is the offence. And Deuteronomy 21:23 says that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God, so a crucified Messiah was a contradiction in terms. Yet at verse 3 Paul wished he could be accursed and cut off for his people, and could not. The stone they tripped over is the one person who could do the thing Paul wanted to do, and did it. The curse he bore on the cross, which made him unthinkable to them as Messiah, is the very thing that saves.

As it is written. Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 (a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion) with Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling). The same stone is a foundation for those who trust it and a stumbling block for those who do not. Peter uses the same combination (1 Peter 2:6–8). In Isaiah 8 the LORD himself becomes a sanctuary and a stone of offence in the same breath. The difference is not in the masonry but in the approach: come to it as a threshold and it holds you up; come at it in the dark, looking elsewhere, and it takes your feet from under you. It was not rubble in the road. It was placed, deliberately, in Zion, at the front of the building, where nobody could get in without meeting it. The builders looked at the stone, could not see a use for it, and threw it aside (Psalm 118:22). It is holding up everything.

Whoever believes. Believing in him is the way. Not put to shame means never disappointed or disgraced at the judgment. “Whoever” opens the door to anyone, Jew or Gentile. This leads into chapter 10, where everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved. After nearly thirty verses of narrowing, it is the widest sentence in the chapter: it asks for no lineage and no proof of having been chosen. It is the one sentence in Romans 9 that a frightened reader can act on directly, and Paul has deliberately put it last. And shame is the word Paul used of himself at the start of the letter: I am not ashamed of the gospel (1:16). Shame is the very thing this stone takes away. Paul, who has just written one of the most uncompromising passages on election in the Bible, ends it by throwing the door open and standing back.

Where Christians differ: sovereignty and responsibility. Some think that if God elects, human responsibility vanishes; others think that if humans are responsible, God cannot be fully sovereign. This commentary’s view: Paul holds both in the same chapter without apology. Israel’s unbelief is truly their fault (vv. 30–33; 10:21), and salvation is truly God’s sovereign mercy (vv. 6–24). We cannot fully reconcile them in our minds, but Scripture teaches both, and we must too (Westminster Confession 3.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; Acts 2:23). Sovereign mercy is why anyone is in. Unbelief is why anyone is out. A reader who can only carry one of them will misrepresent Paul whichever one he keeps.

If God chooses, can I be sure the invitation is really for me? Yes. The promise says whoever believes, and God does not make offers he does not mean. You are never asked to find out first whether you are elect and then believe; you are asked to believe, and in believing you will discover that you were chosen. Jesus said that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Election is the reason anyone comes, not a barrier at the door. If you want Christ, nothing in God’s decree stands between you and him. Come, and you will not be put to shame.

In everyday life. Name your stone: the thing about Christ you have to get past rather than merely accept. His exclusive claim, the wrath in chapter 1, the cross itself, or the requirement to arrive with nothing in your hands after a lifetime of being competent. It was laid as the foundation, not an obstruction to edge around. The thing you are stumbling over is not in front of the door. It is the door.

parallels.desc: a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone
a stone of offence

9.text: <sup>1</sup>I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—<sup>2</sup>that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.<sup>3</sup>For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.<sup>5</sup>To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!<sup>15</sup>For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”<sup>16</sup>So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.<sup>17</sup>For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”<sup>18</sup>So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.<sup>19</sup>You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?”<sup>21</sup>Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?<sup>22</sup>What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,<sup>23</sup>in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—<sup>24</sup>even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?<sup>25</sup>As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ’my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ’beloved.’”<sup>26</sup>“And in the very place where it was said to them, ’You are not my people,’ there they will be called ’sons of the living God.’”<sup>27</sup>And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved,<sup>28</sup>for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”<sup>29</sup>And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”<sup>30</sup>What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith;<sup>31</sup>but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.<sup>32</sup>Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,<sup>33</sup>as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Romans 10 turns from God’s choosing (chapter 9) to the human side: faith, confession and the preaching that carries the gospel. Paul’s heart is again on view; his heart’s desire and prayer for Israel is that they be saved. Their problem is not a lack of religious commitment but its direction: a zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, and a pursuit of their own righteousness that will not submit to the righteousness God gives.

Verses 9–15 run from confession and faith, to calling on the name of the Lord, back to the preachers who are sent with good news. The gospel does not reach people automatically; it reaches them through people who are sent and who speak. The chapter ends with Israel’s own Scriptures as witness: they have heard and have not believed, and still God holds out his hands to them all day long (v. 21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s longing for Israel’s salvation (v. 1) is the key to the chapter. He writes not as a detached analyst of their failure but as a grieving brother who knows what his people are missing and keeps praying for them. His diagnosis is zeal without knowledge (v. 2): sincere, disciplined and wrong.

Verse 3 is the hinge: a righteousness that comes as a gift has to be received on the giver’s terms, and receiving is what a capable, self-respecting person finds hardest. Verses 5–13 read Deuteronomy 30, where God’s word is near, in the mouth and the heart, as a description of the gospel itself. And the word “everyone” runs through verses 11–13: the gospel shuts out no nation and no class of person.
verseByVerse.theology:
The confession of lordship

Romans 10:9 makes the confession “Jesus is Lord” the central act of Christian profession. In the Roman world, “Lord” was Caesar’s title, the one to whom final allegiance was owed, so the confession was never only a private opinion. Every true confession of Christ still declares a transfer of final allegiance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses spoke of the nearness of God’s word (Deuteronomy 30) on the plains of Moab, just before Israel entered the land; Paul applies it to the gospel, a near word proclaimed by the apostles and received by faith. Now: Romans 10:9 is a standing rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. It requires no theology degree, record of achievement or elaborate ritual, only the honest confession of a changed allegiance and real faith in the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 10 explains Israel’s unbelief (begun at 9:30) from the human side: chapter 9 showed God’s sovereign choice, chapter 10 shows Israel’s responsibility. The righteousness of faith needs no climb to heaven and no descent into the grave, for Christ has come down and risen up; it is near, in the gospel word. Election never makes preaching unnecessary; it makes it hopeful.

Prayer after doctrine. Chapter 9 ended on a stone laid in Zion and a nation tripping over it, and the very next thing Paul does is pray for them. He finishes the argument and goes to his knees about it. Grief at 9:2–3, doctrine through 9:6–29, prayer here, and by 11:23 hope: one man, and no contradiction between them.

Heart’s desire. The phrase is stronger than English usually carries. It is eudokia: good pleasure, delight, the thing you would choose if you could have whatever you wanted. It is the word used elsewhere of God’s own good pleasure (Ephesians 1:5, 9). Paul’s delight, the outcome he would pick above every other, is that these people should be saved. Not that they should be proved wrong, which was well within his powers. Saved. He is talking to brothers, and the church in Rome was by now probably mostly Gentile. He asks them to care about Israel’s salvation by opening his own heart rather than by issuing an instruction. In the next chapter he will warn these same readers not to be arrogant toward the branches that were broken off (11:18). The work of that warning starts here.

Tears learned from the Lord of Israel. Paul did not invent this prayer. He caught it from the Lord he now serves. Jesus came to his own people and they did not receive him (John 1:11), and he did not answer that refusal with contempt. He wept over Jerusalem as he approached it (Luke 19:41–42), and from the cross he prayed for the men who put him there: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Some early manuscripts of Luke lack this prayer, but many others have it and most Bibles print it. At 9:3 Paul could only wish himself cut off for his people. Christ did more than wish it: he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Every prayer for an unbelieving Israel is an echo of his.

I bear them witness. Courtroom language: Paul appears for the defence. This is the man who advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age, being extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Galatians 1:14), and who listed among his credentials, as to zeal, a persecutor of the church (Philippians 3:6; Acts 22:3–4). When Paul writes of zeal not according to knowledge, he is describing his own younger self, and that keeps the verse from contempt. He is not a healthy man diagnosing a disease he never had. He is a survivor of it, and he remembers exactly how right it felt.

Not according to knowledge. Knowledge here is true, full understanding. Sincerity is not enough, and this is genuinely frightening: it is possible to be sincere, disciplined, costly, lifelong and wrong. Israel’s zeal was not a pose; it produced martyrs. Paul’s zeal was not a pose; it had him guarding the coats at Stephen’s stoning (Acts 7:58) and carrying arrest warrants to Damascus (Acts 9:1–2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is wrong, or that sincere people are saved because they are sincere: sincere, zealous people can be lost if they reject God’s way of righteousness. Nor does it license contempt for people of other convictions, as though they were simply stupid. Paul credits their zeal, bears witness to it, and wants them saved rather than defeated. And the cure is not cool accuracy instead of hot error. The remedy for zeal without knowledge has never been knowledge without zeal. Remember how Paul’s own case was resolved. Nobody argued him out of it. He was stopped on a road and shown, in person, the one he had been so zealous against. Zeal without knowledge is cured by meeting the one you were serving so badly.

If God has already chosen, why should I pray for someone’s salvation? Because God has chosen to work through prayer, and he commands it (1 Timothy 2:1–4). Election is God’s purpose; prayer is one of the means by which he carries it out, just as preaching is. You do not know whom God has chosen, so you pray for everyone you love, as Paul did for a people who had rejected the gospel. And election is what makes such prayer hopeful. If salvation depended on the sinner’s own will, praying for a hardened heart would be useless. Because it depends on God, who can open any heart, no one is beyond his reach.

In everyday life. There is a better question than whether you are sincere, since you already know you are. When did you last change your mind about something in your faith because Scripture required it and not because it suited you? Zeal that is according to knowledge can be corrected, because it answers to something outside itself. Zeal without knowledge has no way of revising itself; it can only grow warmer.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ignorant. Not ignorant that God is righteous, but of the righteousness that God gives, the gift of right standing revealed in the gospel (1:17; 3:21–22). They did not understand that God himself provides the righteousness he demands. Paul’s diagnosis comes in three verbs, in order: they were ignorant, they sought to establish, they did not submit. Ignorant is the mildest and the most surprising, because these were not people who had neglected the subject. They were a people steeped in the Scriptures, which were read aloud to them every Sabbath (Acts 15:21), and they had been entrusted with the oracles of God (3:2). The word is not about stupidity but about failing to recognise what was in front of them.

To establish their own. Establish means set up, make stand, like building a monument. Their own righteousness: a record of law-keeping that they hoped would stand before God (Philippians 3:9). Hold that verb against the one at the end of the sentence: submit, to place yourself underneath. One is a man putting up a structure with his own name on it. The other is a man getting under something somebody else built. You cannot do both at once, and what stops a man doing the second is not chiefly a failure of understanding. It is that he has spent thirty years on the first and it is nearly finished, and pride refuses to admit it counts for nothing.

What it looks like from inside. Picture the man Paul has in mind. He tithes. He has never been unfaithful to his wife. He looks after his mother, keeps his word, gives to people in need, and has not missed a service in eleven years, and every bit of that is genuinely good. Ask him what stands between him and God and he will not sneer at grace or deny that he needs mercy. He will simply begin, somewhere in his answer, to describe himself. That is what establishing your own righteousness looks like from the inside. It does not feel like arrogance. It feels like diligence.

The end of the law. End is telos, which can mean the termination, or the goal and fulfilment (the ESV note mentions goal). The picture that holds both is a finishing tape. It ends the race, so that nobody runs on past it, and it is also the whole reason the race was run. And Christ did not merely stand at the tape. He ran the course. Born under the law (Galatians 4:4), he kept every command Israel had broken, became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8), and at the finish bore the curse the law pronounces on those who fail it (Galatians 3:13). That is why he can be the law’s end for others: he is the only one who ever reached it.

For righteousness. The qualifier keeps this from becoming lawlessness: the end of the law for righteousness. It is the law’s role as the route to a right standing that has ended, not the law as God’s word, nor its power to show you what you are. Nobody is being told to stop reading Leviticus, only to stop trying to climb it. Paul has already ruled out the other reading: “Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law” (3:31).

Where Christians differ: end or goal. Some take telos to mean that the law is entirely finished for Christians, with no ongoing role. Others take it to mean only that the law pointed to Christ. This commentary’s view: Both senses are present, and they belong together. Christ is the goal the law aimed at: its sacrifices, promises and demands all pointed to him (3:21; Galatians 3:24). And so he is the end of the law as a way to gain righteousness: for everyone who believes, the attempt to be justified by law-keeping is over. But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains the rule of life for the believer, fulfilled by those who walk by the Spirit (8:4; 13:8–10; Westminster Confession 19.5–6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.5–6). This is often called the third use of the law: not a ladder up to God but a guide for those already brought home. Some faithful Christians prefer to call the law of Christ, rather than the Ten Commandments as such, the believer’s rule, and they too hold that grace produces glad obedience.

If I am not saved by keeping the law, why should I try to obey? Because obedience is now the fruit of salvation, not its price. You do not obey in order to be accepted; you obey because you have been accepted, out of love for the one who saved you (John 14:15). The law shows a believer what love looks like, and the Spirit gives the desire and power to walk in it (8:4). And obedience is good for you: God’s commands are the instructions of a wise Father, not the hoops of a suspicious examiner. A justified person who does not care to obey has not understood what he has been given (6:1–2).

In everyday life. Finish this sentence without thinking too hard: I would say I have had a good week with God if I had ______. If the answer is a list of activities, prayed more, read more, been more patient, not lost my temper on Wednesday, look at what that list is: scaffolding, the sign of a man still building his own righteousness. The habit survives even in people whose doctrine of grace is entirely correct. Christ is your righteousness. You will never keep the law perfectly, not even in your best week; he did, in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours (5:19). So your imperfect obedience is accepted for his sake, and a bad Wednesday does not undo your standing. Let this week’s obedience, worked in you by his Spirit (8:4), be thanks, not construction.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 4 can also be read “Christ is the end of the law, that everyone who believes may be justified.” “End” can mean goal as well as termination.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses writes. Paul contrasts two ways of righteousness, both described by Moses.

Do, and live. Leviticus 18:5, which Paul also quotes in Galatians 3:12. The principle of law: do, and live. Paul is not accusing Moses of a trick: it is a genuine offer, and the terms are honourable. The difficulty was never the offer. It was the doer. If you kept the law perfectly, you would live. But no sinner can (3:20; Galatians 3:10). So as a way to life, the law brings only death to sinners.

The righteousness of faith speaks. Its words come from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, where Moses told Israel that God’s word was not far off or too hard. Paul is not raiding Deuteronomy out of context, which is the usual charge. Look at where chapter 30 stands. It comes after the covenant curses of chapter 28, after the exile has been described in advance, and straight after God promises to circumcise the hearts of his people so that they will love him and live (Deuteronomy 30:6). The nearness Moses speaks of belongs to a passage about restoration after failure and about surgery performed by God on the human heart.

Who will ascend. “Do not say in your heart” echoes Deuteronomy 9:4, where Moses warned Israel not to think God gave them the land because of their righteousness, and 8:17, where he forbade them to say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.” It is a formula aimed at private thoughts, the sentence nobody speaks aloud. Its modern form is short, and many Christians have said it: “There must be something more I have to do.” That is the ascent: hearing the gospel, believing it in principle, and then quietly assembling a ladder, more discipline, more feeling, a better run of weeks, as though Christ needed fetching down and the fetching were your job. He has already come down. The Son of God became man of his own accord, without being fetched, and came down into a stable and onto a cross, so that sinners who could never ascend could be lifted up with him. You do not have to make salvation happen.

Was anyone in the Old Testament saved by keeping the law? No. The law’s promise of life for perfect obedience was real, but no sinner ever met it. Old Testament believers were saved the same way we are: by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer he would send. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (4:3), and David rejoiced in the forgiveness of sins (4:6–8). The sacrifices pointed them to the coming Lamb. Only one man ever did the commandments perfectly and lived by them: Jesus Christ, and he did it for us.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live
who will ascend to heaven for us?

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who will descend. Deuteronomy 30:13 says “beyond the sea”. Paul has deliberately changed it to “the abyss”, the deep, the realm of the dead (compare Psalm 107:26; Jonah 2), and he signals each application with “that is”: he is applying the passage, as Jewish teachers of his day often did, not reciting it. Over the sea is merely far. The abyss is the place from which nobody returns, and it is the second of the only two directions a human being could travel to reach God: up, and down. Paul closes both, because Christ has been to both and come back from both.

The sentence from below. If the ascent says, “There must be something more I have to do,” the descent is its opposite, and it is spoken by a different kind of reader: “What he did cannot reach as far down as I have gone.” That sentence keeps many people from Christ who would never call themselves unbelievers. It does not deny the gospel. It simply holds that this particular case is beneath its reach: the thing done at nineteen, the years nobody knows about, the marriage wrecked on purpose. And Paul answers it by pointing to where Christ has been. He went down into death itself, and came up again.

But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” From Deuteronomy 30:14. Salvation is not far away. It is as close as the word you hear and speak. Measure that against where people instinctively put it. Nearer than the church building. Nearer than the minister. Nearer than the next conference, the next book, the next season when things have calmed down enough to think properly. The gospel is not somewhere you must get to. On Paul’s account it is already in the room, closer than the furniture. Christ came down from heaven and went down into death, and rose from both to stand beside us in the word. The whole distance a sinner now stands from God is the width of an open mouth.
