The word of faith. The near word is the gospel message, the word that calls for faith. And this clause stops nearness from becoming mysticism. The word did not become near by drifting. It got near because somebody said it out loud. Paul builds six verses on that (vv. 14–17). The nearness of verse 8 and the preacher of verse 15 are the same fact seen from the two ends.

What it does not mean. The near word must still be believed and confessed. And in your heart does not mean the word is your own inner voice, or that you should look inside yourself to find it. It is near because it was brought and spoken, from outside, by someone sent. What is inside you is where it has landed, not where it came from.

What if I feel that God is far away? Feelings of distance are real, and many believers have known them (Psalm 13:1; 42:9). But the nearness of verse 8 is not a feeling; it is a fact about the word. Christ has come down and risen, and the gospel that offers him is as near as your Bible and your mouth. So when God feels far, do not try to climb up or dig down to find him. Go to the near word: read it, hear it preached, say it back to him in prayer. Feelings follow slowly. The promise does not wait for them.
verseByVerse.note: Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the message about Christ.

parallels.desc: the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is Lord. Confess means to say the same thing, to agree, to declare openly: to agree with God about his Son, where it can be heard. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s name, the LORD. To confess Jesus as Lord is to confess him as God and to bow to his rule.

What two words cost. In Greek the whole confession was two words: Kyrios Iēsous. Around AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the Emperor Trajan about Christians and described the test he had settled on. They were brought in, told to offer incense and wine before the emperor’s image, and to curse Christ. Those who did were released. A capital examination came down to one sentence, said where witnesses could hear. That is why the mouth is named. Not because God needs to hear syllables, since he has already read the heart, but because the mouth is the organ that costs. Kyrios was Caesar’s own title, the word for the one who held the final right over your life. To give it to a crucified Galilean was to take it from somebody else. Confession is a transfer of allegiance. To say Jesus is Lord is to say that he now has the last word over my life, my body, my money and my plans, ahead of any employer, government or desire of my own: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

God raised him. Believing the resurrection is not just accepting a historical fact. It is trusting in the living Christ whom God vindicated (4:24–25). Calvin called saving faith a firm and certain knowledge of God’s kindness toward us, founded on the promise freely given in Christ, revealed to our minds and sealed on our hearts by the Holy Spirit. And why the resurrection, of everything that might have been named? Because you cannot call a dead man Lord. The raising is God’s own verdict on the crucifixion: the Son declared to be the Son of God in power (1:4), and raised for our justification (4:25). The event you are asked to believe and the ground on which you are declared right are the same event.

You will be saved. A promise, firm and simple. “Will be saved” is a future tense, and it should be left future: it points to the day of judgment. But the verdict for that day is not kept waiting until then. It has already been given to everyone who believes: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (8:1).

Heart and mouth. Paul reverses the order. In verse 9 he follows Moses’ order, in your mouth and in your heart (v. 8); in verse 10 he sets them in the order in which they happen. Faith in the heart receives righteousness; confession with the mouth is its outward expression: one faith described twice, once from within, where it is trust, and once from without, where it is audible. Nor are justified and saved two prizes, a smaller one for believing and a better one for speaking. They are one rescue named twice: once by what it does to your standing before the Judge, once by what it does to your future. Justified means that the Judge has spoken in your favour: you are not made sinless on the spot, but pardoned and accepted for Christ’s sake (4:5–6). True faith does not stay silent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that saying the words is a magic formula, or that someone who cannot speak cannot be saved. Faith receives; Christ saves. Jesus blocked the magical reading before Paul wrote the sentence: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21), the very words of the confession, on lips he does not know. No one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The confession is not what causes the new life. It is the first sound the new life makes.

I cannot remember a moment when I confessed Christ. Am I saved? Look at the verb. With the mouth one confesses is a present tense and a description, not a ceremony: not an event you may have failed to perform, but what a believer’s mouth goes on doing. Someone converted alone in a hospital bed, someone who came to faith so gradually there is no date to write down, someone who cannot speak at all: none is shut out. You have confessed every time you prayed to him, every time you called him Lord in a room where that was awkward, every time you told the truth about whose you are when a shorter answer was available. The question is not whether there was a moment, but whether your mouth now agrees with your heart.

Should I be baptised as part of confessing Christ? Yes. In the New Testament, baptism is the first public confession a believer makes, the moment he says with his whole body that Jesus is Lord (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:36–38). It does not save; faith in Christ saves. But it is Christ’s command to all who believe, and it marks you out before the church and the world as his. If you trust Christ and have not yet been baptised as a believer, speak to your church about it. Many faithful brothers baptise infants, and we honour them, but the pattern of Scripture is confession first, then the water. They baptise infants because they see baptism, like circumcision, as the sign of God’s promise to believers and their children; this commentary is persuaded that in the New Testament the sign follows faith, as in the baptisms Acts describes, but this is a difference between brothers who share one Lord.

For worship. The argument of this letter reached its lowest point in chapter 3, in a silent courtroom: the law speaks so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God (3:19). That is where Romans left the human mouth: shut, with nothing to plead. Seven chapters later, the first thing the gospel does with a stopped mouth is give it something to say. And what it is given to say is not a defence. It is a name. Blessed be Jesus, the Lord, whom God raised from the dead, who opens the mouths of the condemned to confess him and fills their hearts with the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession. “Lord” is the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The added word. This is Isaiah 28:16, which Paul quoted at 9:33 without the word everyone. Isaiah does not have it (the Greek Old Testament says whoever believes). Paul put it there. The paragraph is built on that word, and he says it twice more.

The stone that bore the shame. The him of this verse is the stone God laid in Zion, a tested and precious cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16), and the New Testament names it: Jesus, the stone the builders rejected (1 Peter 2:6–7). Why can no one who leans on him be put to shame? Because he took the shame himself. Calvary was the exposure of the guilty before the eyes of all: the Son of God stripped, mocked and hung up in public as a criminal. He endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2). The disgrace a believer’s sins deserve has already been publicly spent on Christ, so there is none left over to fall on the one who trusts him.

No distinction. In 3:22–23 there was no distinction in sin; here there is no distinction in salvation. In chapter 3 the phrase introduced the worst news in the letter and was a leveller: it swept away every advantage anyone had counted on and left the whole world standing on one floor. Here the words that closed every door now open one. Nobody is far enough in to be exempt from needing this, and nobody is far enough out to be barred from having it. The gospel can be for everybody only because the ruin was.

The same Lord. One Lord, Jesus, over Jews and Gentiles alike (3:29–30; Acts 10:36). The ground Paul gives is not a warm feeling about including everyone; it is that there is only one God. One Lord means one door, and it also means that a Gentile calling on Jesus is not being admitted as a guest to somebody else’s God. He is calling on his own Maker. That can sound narrow. But if each people had its own god and its own way, your way in would depend on where you were born. One Lord over all means that the Jew with his Scriptures and the pagan with his idols come in by the same door, on the same terms, to the same welcome.

Rich toward all. The riches are those of his grace and glory (2:4; 9:23; 11:33). The Greek says he is “being rich” toward all who call: a continuing generosity, not a fixed sum divided among claimants. That matters to the reader who came late, or came out of wasted years, and carries the settled impression that what is left for him will be the reduced portion. There is no reduced portion. Nobody arriving now is served what earlier arrivals did not finish.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that everyone will in fact be saved. The riches are for all who call on him. One distinction is left standing, and not the one anybody was arguing about: those who call on him, and those who do not. And that is not a line anyone is born on the wrong side of.

Does “no distinction” mean the Jewish people no longer matter? No. There is no distinction in the way of salvation: Jew and Gentile alike are justified by faith in the one Lord. But Paul still speaks of Israel’s special history and future (3:1–2; 11:28–29), and he began the letter with the gospel going to the Jew first (1:16). No distinction means no one has a separate road to God and no one is excluded from the one road. It does not erase God’s faithfulness to Israel, and it gives Gentile Christians no ground for looking down on Jewish people.

parallels.desc: whoever believes will not be in haste

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name of the Lord. Paul quotes Joel 2:32, which Peter also quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:21). In Joel, the Lord is the LORD, Yahweh. Paul applies it to Jesus, whom he has just called Lord (v. 9). To call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh. In the Hebrew, the name of the LORD is the name given at the burning bush, four consonants that by Paul’s day a synagogue reader would not pronounce, saying Adonai instead so that the name itself never crossed his lips. Paul takes that sentence, about that name, and applies it without a word of justification to Jesus of Nazareth.

Reasoning from it, not to it. A man trained as a Pharisee, who had handled the sacred name with that much care all his life, hands it to a Galilean executed outside Jerusalem within his own adult lifetime, and does it in passing, in a clause that begins with “for”, as proof of something else. He is not arguing that Jesus is divine; he takes it as settled and argues from it. The highest claim in the chapter is made in its quietest sentence.

What does Joel’s promise save us from? Joel is worth reading for what saved means, because the promise is not vague. It stands at the end of a passage about the day of the LORD, the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before that great and awesome day comes. Then the promise. That is rescue with a date and a named danger. Romans has named the same danger already: the wrath revealed from heaven (1:18), and the day of wrath a hard heart is storing up for itself (2:5). This verse is the way out of that day, and all it asks is that you call.

To call. To pray to him, appeal to him, trust in him, worship him (Genesis 4:26; 12:8). It is faith speaking: not eloquence or correctness, but what a person does who has no other options left and one name to say. It became, almost at once, a description of Christians: Paul writes to all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:2), and in Damascus the disciples knew Saul was coming to bind all who call on your name (Acts 9:14). One of the church’s earliest names for itself was a verb.

Everyone. No sinner who calls will be turned away. This free offer of the gospel is real, and it fits with God’s sovereign election: the elect are those who are brought to call, and none who call are turned away (John 6:37). The clearest case in the Gospels is a man being executed, with no time to make amends, no changed life to point to, and his hands not even free. What he has is a mouth and a name, and he uses them: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). He is told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The name a reader of Paul’s day would not pronounce is here the one thing a dying man can still get out, and it has been put within reach of any mouth on earth, in any language, at any hour, without an appointment and without anyone standing in the way. Paul’s everyone is at least that wide.

I called on him, but I felt nothing. Did it count? Read the promise again. It says will be saved, not will feel saved. What God attaches himself to here is the calling, not the sensation that may or may not come with it. Many of the calls he has answered were made by people who were sure at the time that they had spoken into an empty room. If you called on Christ in faith, he heard you, and his word stands whether your feelings agree today or not. Keep calling on him; that is what believers do all their lives. And let the promise, not your pulse, tell you where you stand.

In everyday life. Try to remember, not the best prayer you ever prayed, but the shortest one you ever meant: two or three words, probably, at an hour you would rather not describe. That is the verb in this verse, and it is the whole of what is asked. Pray it again today, and pray it for someone else by name.

parallels.desc: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Sent Preacher and Israel's Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The promise of verse 13 raises a question, and Paul answers it with a chain that runs backwards: calling needs believing, believing needs hearing, hearing needs a preacher, and preaching needs someone sent (vv. 14–15). Isaiah’s beautiful feet are lovely because of what they carry. God’s choosing does not make preaching unnecessary; it is the means by which he calls his people, for faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (v. 17).

For Israel every link held but one: not all obeyed (v. 16), as Isaiah foresaw (Isaiah 53:1). Israel cannot plead that it never heard or never understood (vv. 18–20). The chapter ends with God’s hands held out all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (v. 21): the refusal is theirs, and the love remains his.
verseByVerse.theology:
The necessity of preaching

Romans 10:14–17 is a key New Testament text on preaching. Preaching is the means God has appointed for bringing people to faith. The Spirit works through the word proclaimed and heard to create the faith that saves. That is why the Reformed tradition gives preaching a central place in worship, not as a performance or a lecture, but as a means of grace through which God speaks to his people. And because hearing needs a preacher and a preacher needs sending, the call to mission is built into the logic of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The beautiful feet of Isaiah 52:7 brought Jerusalem news that the exile was over; Paul applies the picture to the heralds of a greater exodus. Now: A kind and honest life matters, but it does not tell anyone who Christ is or what he has done. People come to faith by hearing the word of Christ, so the church must keep speaking it, in pulpits and in ordinary conversation, because faith comes from hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!' — Romans 10:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? A chain of questions, working backwards. Calling requires believing. Paul has just said that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. So he asks what must already have happened for anybody to be in a position to call, and works upstream one link at a time, until he arrives somewhere surprising.

And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? Believing requires hearing. Some read it “him whom they have never heard”: in the preaching, Christ himself speaks (Ephesians 2:17).

And how are they to hear without someone preaching? Hearing requires a preacher (kēryssō, to herald, announce publicly). And this is where the promise of verse 8 is paid. The word is near you, Paul said, in your mouth and in your heart. But it did not become near by drifting there. Ask how it got into your mouth, and the answer is that it was in somebody else’s first.

And how are they to preach unless they are sent? Preaching requires sending (apostellō, the root of apostle). God sends preachers, and the church sends missionaries (Acts 13:2–3). The chain does not stop at the preacher. It stops at “unless they are sent”: somebody else has to act first. Nobody in this sequence appoints himself, and the sending does not finally begin with a committee. It is God’s own initiative arriving in ordinary shoe leather. And that settles the objection often raised here, that if God has chosen his people, preaching is a formality. Paul argues the reverse. The God who appointed the harvest appointed the plough, and no farmer certain of a crop leaves the seed in the barn. Election does not make proclamation optional; it makes it worth doing, because God’s word will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

Beautiful feet. From Isaiah 52:7, describing the messengers who ran across the mountains with news of Israel’s return from exile. (The KJV, following later manuscripts, adds the gospel of peace in Romans 10:15; the earliest lack it, and the sense is the same.) Word travelled at the speed of a man’s legs, and the watchmen on the wall had no other way to learn how the war had gone. Feet were the filthiest part of a person, the part a household slave was given to wash, and Isaiah calls them lovely anyway, because of what they carry. And look at what the herald shouts: peace, good news, salvation, and then the line the whole scene is built for, “Your God reigns.” There has been a change of government, and you can go home. The herald on the ridge cries “Your God reigns”; the believer at the foot of the hill says “Jesus is Lord” (v. 9).

The first Herald and the great Sender. The chain of sending begins in heaven. The Father sent the Son, and Hebrews calls Jesus the apostle and high priest of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), the first Sent One. He came as Isaiah’s herald in person: Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God and saying, the kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1:14–15). Your God reigns, said the runner on the ridge; the kingdom is here, said the King, and he was the news he carried. Then, risen, he sent others: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). Every pair of beautiful feet since has been running on his errand, with his message.

In the flow. These verses are rightly read as a missionary text, but their first job is about Israel: for Israel every link but one was in place (vv. 16–21), and the broken link was believing. So the chain clears God of any charge that Israel never had a chance, and lays the failure where verse 3 laid it, at a refusal to submit.

Where Christians differ: those who never hear. Some say people who never hear the gospel can be saved through other religions; this is usually called pluralism. Others, often called inclusivists, hold a wider hope, that God may save through Christ people who never heard of him but responded to the light of creation or conscience, pointing to Cornelius (Acts 10), to 2:14–16, and to Psalm 19, which Paul quotes in verse 18. Those who hold it usually do so out of real love for the unreached and concern for God’s fairness. This commentary’s view: Paul’s chain says otherwise: calling requires believing, and believing requires hearing of Christ. There is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). This is why missions matter so much. Cornelius is in fact the strongest case against the wider hope: devout as he was, an angel told him to send for Peter, who would declare a message by which he would be saved (Acts 11:14). Creation is enough light to leave a man without excuse (1:20) and not enough to save him. God may use many means to bring the word, but salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Westminster Confession 10.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.4). Infants dying in infancy, and those incapable of being outwardly called, are in God’s hands and saved by Christ through the Spirit as he pleases (Westminster 10.3; 1689 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest that child in the hands of the God who gave him, as David did (2 Samuel 12:23).

Who are the sent, and must I go? Paul has in mind heralds sent to proclaim publicly, and the church still recognises and sends such people, as the church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1–3). Not every Christian is called to be a preacher or missionary. But ordinary Christians need no commission to speak of Christ. When persecution scattered the Jerusalem church, those who were scattered went about preaching the word (Acts 8:4), and every believer is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). So everyone has a part: some go, many send by prayer and giving, and all speak of Christ to the people around them.

Is it fair that people who never hear of Christ are lost? The question deserves an honest answer, not a shrug. No one is condemned for failing to believe a message he never heard. People are judged for what they did with the light they had, the creation around them and the conscience within them (1:20; 2:12–16), and Paul has shown that no one has lived up to that light (3:9–10). The gospel is not the reason anyone is lost; it is the rescue sent to people who were lost already. And look at what God does about those who have not heard. He does not leave the question hanging in the air; he sends. The fitting answer to this verse is not to accuse God of unfairness but to join him in the sending, so that more may hear.

In everyday life. Who told you? Not who taught you afterwards: who first put it into words in your hearing? Perhaps someone who said it badly and said it anyway. The beauty was not in how they said it but in what they carried, and it made them lovely all the way down to the dust on their shoes. You are standing at the end of a long line of feet, and you can usually name the last pair. Then ask who is waiting to hear it from you. Pray for preachers and missionaries, give to send them, and open your own mouth: your feet can be beautiful too.

parallels.desc: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?' — Romans 10:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not all. The problem is not that Israel lacked preachers. Paul writes not all, and the qualification carries weight: it leaves the remnant standing, it is why chapter 11 can ask whether God has rejected his people and answer with a flat no, and it stops this verse becoming a verdict on a whole nation. Three times in verses 11–13 Paul has said “everyone” or “all”; here the same Greek word comes back with “not” in front of it. The word that carried the promise now measures the response, and the response falls short.

Obeyed. The gospel is a command as well as an offer: repent and believe (1:5; Acts 17:30). The Greek for obey is built on the verb hear; in use it simply means obey, but in a passage about hearing Paul surely wants the echo: hearing that submits. Nobody obeys a weather forecast; but news of a change of government does not merely inform you, it puts you under someone. That is why unbelief in this chapter is described in the language of refusal rather than mere error: they did not submit (v. 3), they have not obeyed (v. 16), they are disobedient and contrary (v. 21).

Who has believed. Isaiah 53:1 opens the great passage on the suffering servant. John quotes it too, of the Jews who saw Jesus’ signs and did not believe (John 12:38). And the location sharpens the grief. The very next lines speak of a man with no form or majesty that we should look at him, despised and rejected. So the question is the preface to a report about a crucified man. The difficulty was never that the message was badly delivered. It is what the message says, the same thing chapter 9 called a stone people trip over. Yet the servant whose report was not believed is the same servant who was wounded for the transgressions of those who did not believe, and who will yet see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10). His word is not defeated by unbelief; he bore the very rejection the prophet grieved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel has failed when people reject it; Isaiah foresaw it. Nor does it mean results do not matter to God’s servants. “Results belong to God” is true, and it is also the standard excuse of the lazy and the cold. Isaiah does not shrug; he brings his grief to God: “Lord, who has believed?” And Paul’s response to his people’s unbelief, at the top of this chapter, was to pray for them.

I have shared the gospel for years and no one has believed. Have I failed? Not if you have been faithful. Look at what Isaiah was sent to do. When God commissioned him, the commission itself described the outcome: keep on hearing, but do not understand (Isaiah 6:9). Isaiah asked how long, and was told, until cities lie waste. If faithfulness were measured by response, Isaiah failed for a lifetime, and so did Paul with his own people. Your task is to speak truly, live consistently, and pray persistently. The opening of hearts is God’s work. Many who seemed deaf for years have believed in the end, sometimes after the one who prayed had gone to glory.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. — Romans 10:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
From hearing. Faith is born when the message is heard. Hearing (akoē) can mean the act of hearing or the message heard. God creates faith through his word. “So” draws the conclusion from Isaiah’s question, where the noun is the same akoē, the report: faith is what comes by the report. This sentence is the theology of preaching in a single verse. Faith is not finally produced by argument, emotion or social influence, though God may use them, but by the word, which the Holy Spirit uses as his instrument.

The word of Christ. The word of Christ is the message about Christ, and also Christ’s own word, for he speaks through his messengers. Some manuscripts read “word of God,” as the ESV note says, but “word of Christ” is the better reading. Faith comes through a specific message, not religious atmosphere. That is why the faithful exposition of what Scripture actually says has always stood at the centre of Reformed worship. It is the word of Christ that creates faith, and the preacher’s task is to get out of the way. Christ preached peace to people in Asia Minor who had never seen him (Ephesians 2:17), and he still does. So the sermon you will hear next Sunday, imperfectly delivered by a tired man with a cold, is not merely a report about a distant event. It is the risen Christ still speaking to people who were not born when he was crucified.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is our own achievement after hearing: the Spirit uses the word to give new birth and faith (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). Nor does it exclude reading. Akoē is about a message reaching a person, not about ears: the housebound believer with an open Bible, the deaf believer watching an interpreter, the prisoner reading a page in his cell all receive the word of Christ, and it does there exactly what it does in a crowded church. And hearing is not automatic. Sitting under preaching is not the same as receiving it, and a person can do the first for forty years.

How can I get more faith? Not by squeezing harder inside. People who long for more faith almost always try to solve it inwardly, by concentrating, resolving, trying to feel more certain. It does not work, because faith is not a substance you can press on; it is a response, and a response needs something to respond to. Faith grows as it feeds on Christ in his word. Sit under faithful preaching. Read the Gospels and let Christ speak. Memorise promises and pray them back to God. Take the Lord’s Supper, where the word is made visible. And ask God for faith; he gives it (Mark 9:24; Ephesians 2:8).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the word of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for "Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have. Israel cannot excuse itself by saying it never heard. Paul is not claiming that every human being has now heard the gospel. He tells the same church that his ambition is to preach where Christ has not been named (15:20–21). The question belongs to the argument he is running: it is Israel who cannot plead that the message never reached them. It had been announced in their own synagogues, in their own language, by their own countrymen, for some twenty-five years.

Their voice has gone out. Psalm 19:4 is about the heavens declaring God’s glory. Paul borrows the words to describe how widely the gospel had spread: through synagogues across the Roman world, the message had reached Jews everywhere (Colossians 1:6, 23). He is not proving from a psalm about stars that the gospel has been preached in every village. The announcement has gone out the way daylight goes out. And that closes a circle from the opening of the letter, where the sky was enough to leave a man without excuse (1:20); now the message that can actually save him has travelled the same roads.

But I ask, did Israel not understand? Maybe they did not grasp it? But Scripture itself had told them that God would turn to the Gentiles. Paul calls his witnesses in order: first Moses, then Isaiah.

I will make you jealous. From Deuteronomy 32:21, in the Song of Moses. Israel made God jealous with idols, no-gods; so God would make them jealous with a no-people, the Gentiles. It is measure for measure. And the detail that makes the question unanswerable: Moses was told to teach this song to Israel and put it in their mouths before they ever entered the land, so that it would stand as a witness against them in a future they had not yet lived (Deuteronomy 31:19–21). The prophecy of their own refusal, and of the outsiders brought in over it, was in their hymnbook. Did Israel not understand? It had been put in their mouths.

Jealousy meant to win them back. This theme returns in 11:11–14. It is not spite: God does not say he will replace them but make them jealous, which is only worth doing if you intend to get somebody back. The jealousy is not a punishment. It is God’s way of drawing them back.

What the no-people were given. What could make Israel jealous of Gentiles? Not Gentile virtue: Moses calls them no people and a foolish nation. What the outsiders were given was Israel’s own treasure. From Israel, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (9:5), and now men in Corinth and Rome and Galatia call on him by name, sing Israel’s psalms to him, and call Abraham their father. The words that went out to the ends of the world went out on the orders of Israel’s risen Messiah: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8). The jealousy Moses foresaw is the ache of seeing your own King loved by strangers.

A foolish nation. A nation without understanding, without the law. Here is a guard for the Gentile reader: the Gentiles are not chosen as the better party, but as the ones nobody counted. The branch grafted in has no grounds for looking down the trunk at the branch broken off, which is the warning Paul is about to spend a chapter delivering.

What about people today who have heard the gospel many times? They are in Israel’s position, and it is serious. Having heard is not a safe place to stay; it is greater light and greater responsibility (Luke 12:48; Hebrews 2:1–3). But it is also a mercy, because the word is still near. If that is you, do not tell yourself you will understand it better later. You have heard enough to come now. And if you are a believer with friends or family who have heard it all before, do not stop: keep praying, keep loving, and let your life make them jealous for what you have in Christ.

parallels.desc: their voice goes out through all the earth
I will make them jealous with those who are no people

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." But of Israel he says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So bold. Paul quotes Isaiah 65:1–2. The verb means to throw caution aside: the prophet knew he was saying an outrageous thing. The outrage was not that God saves Gentiles; Isaiah says that many times. It was the way he does it: he is found by people who never looked for him.

Found by those who did not seek. The Gentiles: God took the initiative and let himself be found by people who were not looking for him (compare 9:30). For a certain reader this is the best sentence in the chapter. Some read chapter 9 and came away frightened, quietly sure they are not among the chosen, and the evidence they bring against themselves is nearly always the same: I did not really want this. I came to it late, or badly, or for the wrong reasons. I was not seeking. Verse 20 takes that evidence off the table. Not seeking is the very description of the people God says he was found by.

All day long. A moving picture: God, like a parent, standing with hands stretched out all day, pleading with his children to come home. “Disobedient” (apeitheō, refusing to be persuaded) and “contrary” (antilegō, speaking against). He held out his hands, and they refused. The second word means answering back: exactly what 9:20 said the clay has no right to do, and exactly what Israel did. Hold your own arms straight out and see how long before the shoulders burn. All day long, says God: a parent in a doorway with arms open from morning until dark while a child walks past, again and again, and does not stop.

Side by side in Isaiah. Verse 20 is Isaiah 65:1 and verse 21 is Isaiah 65:2. They are consecutive. Paul did not hunt through the Scriptures for a counterweight; he simply kept reading, and sovereign grace and human refusal were already lying side by side in one paragraph. That corrects any reading of chapter 9 that stops at the potter and the clay. A chapter later the same apostle ends with God in a doorway with his arms out, and puts the loss down to a people who would not come. Paul softens neither, and neither should anyone using him. The Lord Jesus said the same about the same city, in the street: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34). He does not say they could not come; he says they would not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has given up on Israel. The next chapter answers that at once. Nor is his patience endless indifference (2:4–5). A day has an evening. All day long is a measure of extraordinary endurance, not a promise that the arms will never come down.

Where Christians differ: the sincerity of the offer. Some argue that if God has elected only some, his offer of salvation to the non-elect cannot be sincere. This commentary’s view: God’s outstretched hands are real. He truly calls all who hear the gospel to come, and he is grieved by their refusal (Ezekiel 33:11; Matthew 23:37). His secret purpose in election and his revealed will in the gospel do not cancel each other. We do not fully understand how they fit together, but Scripture teaches both, and we must preach freely to all (Canons of Dort 2.5; 3/4.8).

I have drifted from God for years. Will he take me back? Yes. Look at the posture this verse describes: hands held out all day, to people who were refusing him at the very time. When you think of coming back after a long stretch of neglect, most people picture folded arms, a turned back, or at best a cool, formal patience. The text has already described God’s posture, and it is not the one you are bracing for. Think of the father in Jesus’ parable, who saw his son a long way off and ran (Luke 15:20). Come today. Confess plainly, return to his word and his people, and do not wait until you feel worthy.

For worship. Chapter 10 does not end with a door bolted but with arms held open, and Paul’s next sentence asks whether God has rejected his people and answers no. Isaiah was not writing about the cross, yet a Christian cannot read him without seeing where those hands went at last: on a Friday outside the walls of the city they were held out to, his incarnate Son stretched out his own on a cross, in public, for the very people refusing him. Blessed be the God who found us when we were not looking, and who has still not lowered his hands.

parallels.desc: I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me
I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people

And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?<sup>15</sup>And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”<sup>16</sup>But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?”<sup>17</sup>So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.<sup>18</sup>But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”<sup>19</sup>But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry.”<sup>20</sup>Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.”<sup>21</sup>But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

11.title: The Mystery of Israel and the Doxology of Grace
11.overview:
Romans 11 completes the argument about Israel that began in chapter 9. Paul asks whether God has rejected his people, and answers with his strongest negative. The first evidence is Paul himself, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin who has believed: the remnant is real.

Then the chapter moves beyond the remnant to a mystery. Israel’s hardening has served the coming in of the Gentiles, whose blessing is meant to provoke Israel to faith, and the olive tree (vv. 17–24) holds the argument together. The chapter ends not in rejection but in the promise that all Israel will be saved (v. 26), and then in praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Remnant: God Has Not Rejected His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s first evidence that God has not rejected his people is himself, the former persecutor of the church. As in Elijah’s day, there is a remnant chosen by grace, not by works or ancestry.

The harder half follows in the same breath (vv. 7–10): the elect obtained what Israel sought; the rest were hardened. Paul holds both sentences together. But this is not the section’s last word: the next verse asks whether they stumbled in order to fall, and answers no.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remnant Principle in Scripture

The remnant runs through the whole Old Testament: the remnant of Israel in Isaiah (Isaiah 10:20–22), the remnant of Jacob in Micah, the seven thousand in Elijah’s day. God has never saved the whole nation simply because they were born into it; he has always worked through a called, believing remnant within it, chosen by grace and not self-selected. The new covenant does not change God’s way of saving; it makes it plain and fulfils it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal were invisible to Elijah. The prophet who declares the cause lost may be wrong. Now: When the church seems to be in steep decline, the statistics grim and the culture running the other way, the temptation is Elijah’s: “I alone am left.” The church is always smaller than it should be and larger than it appears, and God keeps what he has promised to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 11 finishes Paul’s answer about Israel, and it finishes with hope: God has not rejected his people. There is a remnant now, chosen by grace; Israel’s stumble is not final; Gentile believers grafted into the olive tree must not be proud; and the hardening lasts until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. The chapter that asks whether God abandons people ends with everything in existence going home to him.

I ask, then, has God rejected his people? This is not an academic question Paul has invented in order to answer it. It is the question his own argument has just forced. Chapter 10 ended with God holding out his hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21), and any reader who has followed the argument that far is already forming the sentence: then that is the end of them. Paul asks it aloud before anyone else can, which is what an honest teacher does with the conclusion his last paragraph invites. The word “rejected” (apōtheomai) means to thrust away, to push off. And Paul’s wording deliberately echoes an old promise: the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name’s sake (1 Samuel 12:22; Psalm 94:14). The very form of the question in Greek expects the answer no.

By no means! And the recoil is violent. Mē genoito is one of the strongest negatives Paul has, and he keeps it for conclusions that would wreck the gospel if they were allowed to stand: shall we sin that grace may abound (6:1–2), is there injustice with God (9:14), does faith overthrow the law (3:31). It is not yet an argument. It is a man flinching.

For I myself am an Israelite. He points at himself, not at the thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem (Acts 21:20). And of all the specimens available he selects the one with the worst history in the room: the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their coats while Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58; 8:1), and who then went from house to house dragging believers off to prison. The proof that God has not finished with Israel is a Jew who had done his level best to finish the church.

An Israelite at the right hand of God. Paul is only the nearest proof. From Israel, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (9:5). The Son of God was born a son of Abraham and a son of David (Matthew 1:1), circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), and raised in that same body, and he still names himself the root and the descendant of David (Revelation 22:16). God cannot have thrust away the people whose flesh his Son took up into heaven. And it was this risen Israelite who came down the Damascus road to meet the persecuting Israelite and made him his apostle. Paul’s own conversion is the Messiah of Israel refusing to give up on Israel.

The least of the tribes. Benjamin was the smallest tribe in Israel (1 Samuel 9:21), and the one that stayed with Judah when the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:21), itself a kind of remnant. Smallness has never been evidence that God has left the building.

Whom he foreknew. “Foreknew” does not mean that God knew in advance how they would turn out. He did know, and what he saw was their unbelief, which is the very problem. To know, in the Bible’s vocabulary, is to set your love on someone: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). It is the same verb (proginōskō) that began the chain of God’s saving acts in 8:29: God set his love on them beforehand. His people here are the nation he chose in love; within it, as the next verses show, is the elect remnant. The relationship did not begin with them, so it does not end with them either. Whatever holds Israel, it is plainly not Israel’s grip. It is the grip of the God who set his love on a people before they had done anything, and kept it through the wilderness, the judges, the kings and the exile. His faithfulness is not a reaction to ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every Jew is saved, or that God has two ways of salvation, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. There is one way, faith in Christ, for there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all (10:12). Paul establishes here only a remnant, proved by Jewish people who believe in Jesus; the larger claim comes at v. 26, and he makes no claim about territory or politics at all.

Why does a chapter about Israel matter to an ordinary Gentile Christian? Because your own salvation hangs on the same question. Romans 8 ended with promises that nothing can separate God’s people from his love. If God could make promises to Abraham’s children, set his love on them, and then quietly walk away when they failed, the promises of Romans 8 would be worth nothing either. Chapters 9 to 11 are Paul’s answer to the question of whether God keeps his word. Every Gentile believer has an interest in the answer being yes. And there is a family interest too: your Bible, your Saviour and your promises all came to you through Israel, and Paul will shortly tell you that you are a branch on their tree.

So what if I feel that God has finished with me? Watch how Paul answers this question, because you can use his method for your own fear, even though his subject is Israel. He does not go inward. He does not take the temperature of Israel’s devotion, or of his own, and he offers no reassurance about anyone’s feelings. He points to a Person and a history: something God did, at a date, to a man who was not looking for it. When the fear comes that you are finished, the instinct is to go and look at our feelings, which is like checking the weather to find out whether you are married. Look instead at what God has done: the promise he made, the Son he gave, the call that reached you. Those do not move when you do.

In everyday life. Somewhere today a mother will pray again for a son who has not been inside a church for twenty years, and part of her will wonder whether she is wasting her breath. This verse is for her. If God has not given up on Israel after centuries of unbelief, and if the most violent enemy of the early church became its apostle, then the long, unanswered prayer is not foolish. It is in line with the way God has always worked: slowly, and then on a date nobody saw coming.

parallels.desc: the LORD will not forsake his people

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." But what is God's reply to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the Scripture says of Elijah. Paul turns to 1 Kings 19, and where this cry falls in Elijah’s life is the most useful thing about it. He has just come off Carmel, the greatest public victory in the Old Testament, fire out of a clear sky onto a soaked altar. Then a single messenger arrives from Jezebel with a threat, and the man who faced down a nation runs for his life, goes a day’s journey into the wilderness, sits under a broom tree and asks God to let him die.

After the triumph. The collapse comes after the triumph, not after a defeat. The dangerous ground is the week after the thing went well, when the adrenaline drains, there is nothing left in the tank, and one small piece of bad news arrives. Anyone who has crashed on a Monday after a Sunday that went beautifully has sat under that tree.

A nap and a meal. What God does first is not what a religious instinct would predict. He does not correct the theology first. He lets him sleep, sends food, lets him sleep again, and sends food again (1 Kings 19:5–8). Only later, after forty days of walking to Horeb, comes the low whisper and the number. God’s answer to “I alone am left” began with a nap and a meal. Some of what presents itself as a crisis of faith is a body that has not been fed or rested, and God treats it accordingly before he treats anything else. Exhaustion and depression are not the same as unbelief, and he is gentle with both.

How he appeals to God against Israel. Paul’s verb is pointed. “Appeals” (entynchanō) is the word used of the Spirit’s intercession for the saints (8:27). Here Elijah uses it against Israel. A prophet’s calling was to stand between God and the people and plead for them; Elijah stands in the same place and accuses them. Despair rarely stays private. Given long enough it starts building a case, and the people it builds the case against are usually the very ones you were called to serve.

I alone am left. The detail is checkable. One chapter earlier Obadiah had told Elijah to his face that he had hidden a hundred prophets of the LORD in caves, fifty to a cave, and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:13). Elijah had been told, and on the mountain he still says he is the only one left; the text gives no hint that the hundred had perished since. Despair does not merely misread the evidence; it leaves out the evidence that does not fit.

But what is God’s reply to him? “Reply” is chrēmatismos, a divine answer, an oracle. Elijah has spoken his complaint; God speaks his verdict, and it is the only word in the exchange that is entirely accurate.

I have kept for myself. God’s reply puts the verb where it belongs. He does not say that seven thousand have stood firm. He says, “I have kept for myself.” Their survival is not a report on their stamina; it is a statement about his grip.

The one who truly was left alone. Elijah’s “I alone am left” was false: seven thousand stood with him. There was one man of whom it was true. Jesus told his disciples, “you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone” (John 16:32), and they did. At Gethsemane they all left him and fled (Mark 14:50), and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). Israel’s faithful remnant narrowed to a single servant, and he was abandoned so that none of his would be. That is why God can say “I have kept for myself” and mean it. On the night he was left alone, Jesus prayed, “I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost” (John 17:12).

Faithfulness in the negative. Consider what these seven thousand had actually done. Nothing, visibly. Their faithfulness is described entirely in the negative: they had not bowed the knee to Baal. If your own obedience feels like nothing more than a series of things you did not do, the gossip you did not pass on, the compromise you did not make, that is the very kind of faithfulness God chose to count.

What it does not mean. The point is that God always keeps a people, even when faith seems to have died out. And the remnant doctrine has a smug cousin. Elijah’s error was self-pity, and the error next door is self-congratulation: the small faithful group that has begun to enjoy being small, and reads the seven thousand as a compliment. Nobody in that seven thousand knew they were being counted, and the man who was sure he had the roll call was the one who had it wrong.

What if I really am the only Christian at work, or in my family? Then you are in the place where Elijah felt he was, and God’s answer still holds: you can see far less of the board than you think. There are almost certainly believers nearer than you know, and God has never felt obliged to introduce you to all of them. Ask him to show you one. Meanwhile, do not try to stand alone: be faithfully joined to a local church, so that the isolation of Monday is answered by the fellowship of Sunday. And remember that even where you are visibly alone, you are not unaccompanied. The one who kept the seven thousand for himself is keeping you, and he is in the room.

For worship. God’s answer did not end with the number. He sent Elijah back down the mountain with errands (1 Kings 19:15–16). Such is the tenderness of our God: he answers despair with truth rather than scolding, and gives the broken servant work again. The Shepherd knows his seven thousand by name when the prophet cannot find one.

parallels.desc: I, even I only, am left
seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

verseByVerse.quote: So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. — Romans 11:5–6
verseByVerse.commentary:
A remnant at the present time. What was true on that mountain is still happening in Paul’s own decade. “Remnant” (leimma) means what is left over, and the thousands of Jews who believed in Jerusalem (Acts 2:41; 21:20) were this remnant. The remnant is not an emergency measure God resorts to when a generation goes wrong. It is the ordinary shape of how he has always saved: never the whole nation by birth, always a kept people within it.

Chosen by grace. Literally the phrase reads according to the election (eklogē, choosing) of grace. The choosing is itself an act of grace: God chose them freely, not for merit. The remnant is not the group that turned out to be better. It is the group that was chosen, by a God whose choosing is gift all the way down. Nobody in it can point to anything in himself as the reason he is there. That is what makes it a remnant rather than an elite.

Chosen in the Chosen One. God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), by a grace given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began (2 Timothy 1:9). Christ is the Chosen One himself: the Father’s voice called him my Son, my Chosen One (Luke 9:35), and Peter calls him the living stone, chosen and precious in the sight of God (1 Peter 2:4). The remnant is chosen in him, and so its grace has a face. What God freely gave was his Son, and all that is his. Nobody earns a place in Christ. He is the gift.

No longer on the basis of works. If God chose because of works, it would be wages, and wages are a debt, not a gift (4:4). Paul is closing off the compromise every religious person reaches for: mostly grace, with some contribution of our own. The two cannot be mixed, because they are rival accounts of where the outcome came from, and only one of them can be true of the same thing.

Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. Grace (charis) is free, undeserved favour. Mix in merit and it stops being grace. Think of the difference between being given a house and being sold one at a discount. Take the discount to ninety-nine per cent: the deed still says sold, and the buyer can still say what he paid. Grace is not a very large discount. It is a different kind of transaction, and the moment anything is owed the paperwork changes. God did not discount salvation; he gave it. He did not meet us halfway; he came all the way, in his Son, to people who were not coming. A textual note: some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add a further sentence, that if it is by works it is no longer grace, otherwise work is no longer work. The earliest manuscripts do not have it, so most modern Bibles omit it; the meaning is the same.

Why say something so obvious? It is fair to ask why an apostle needs to state this to people who already believe it. Because the instinct to earn is inexhaustible. Grace is the one doctrine that will not stay where you put it: agreed to on Sunday, quietly renegotiated by Wednesday, and the renegotiation almost never announces itself. It comes disguised as seriousness. And it usually surfaces where people do not look for it. Listen to how you explain other people’s faith. She was always a seeker. He had a good upbringing. They were the sort who would respond. Every one of those sentences is a small denial of verse 6, an attempt to locate something in the person that accounts for the outcome. The same instinct running the other way explains those who have not come: he was always hard, that family was never going to. This is the seed of the arrogance Paul will confront twelve verses from now, when the Gentile reader starts explaining why the branches were broken off.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the remnant are passive. They believe and obey. But their faith is the fruit of grace, not its cause. None of this makes obedience optional: the man who writes verse 6 writes chapter 12 a page later. Works are the evidence and never the ground, as Paul showed at 2:7–8. What verse 6 forbids is not effort. It is sending God the bill for it.

If God chooses by grace, how can I know whether I am chosen? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, which is not given to you, but by doing what the gospel commands: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Election is never revealed in advance as a list; it is discovered from the inside, as faith. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (10:13), and no one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37). So if you are coming, trusting him, you have your answer, because nobody comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Election is meant to be a comfort to those who believe, not a riddle that keeps people from believing. Make your calling and election sure by looking at Christ, not by looking for your name.

Is it unfair that God chooses some and not others? Paul has already faced that question head-on in 9:14–24, and his answer begins with the fact that no one is owed mercy. If God gave everyone what they asked for by their works, no one would be saved. That anyone is chosen is astonishing; that grace is free means it cannot be claimed. And in this verse election is the reason there is hope at all in a dark time. In Elijah’s day, and in Paul’s, the nation as a whole had turned away. Left to themselves, none would have remained. The remnant exists because God chose to keep one.

In everyday life. When you are tempted, after a good week, to feel that God must be pleased with you now, or after a bad week that he must be finished with you, say verse 6 aloud. Both feelings treat God’s favour as wages, and grace has never worked that way.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The first clause carries the grief of the whole section. Seeking. These were the people still at it, still in the synagogue, still keeping the calendar, still possessed, as Paul put it a chapter ago, of a zeal for God (10:2). Israel was seeking righteousness before God (9:31; 10:3), and did not get it. And set that beside the words Paul quoted from Isaiah a few verses earlier, where God says he was found by those who did not seek him (10:20). Together the two sentences make a bleak irony. The party that was searching missed it; the party that was not searching was found.

Where the failure happened. A person can look very hard in a direction where he has already decided the answer must lie. Paul has said twice where the failure happened: they pursued righteousness as if it were based on works (9:32), and would not submit to a righteousness that came as a gift (10:3). And the gift arrived in a form they had ruled out in advance: a carpenter from Nazareth, crucified. Jesus put the tragedy in one sentence to the most earnest seekers of his day: you search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life (John 5:39–40). They were holding the map and walking past the treasure.

The elect obtained it. The elect are the remnant chosen by grace, and they obtained righteousness through faith in Christ. Paul does not say they sought better. The difference between the two groups lies not in the quality of their searching but in the grace that chose and gave.

But the rest were hardened. “Hardened” (pōroō) means to make callous, like the hard skin that forms over a wound, and the wording “were hardened” implies that God did it, as he hardened Pharaoh (9:18). The next line says so outright: “God gave them a spirit of stupor.” It is an act of judgment: God gives over to blindness those who refuse the light, the pattern of giving over that the letter set out at 1:24–28.

A spirit of stupor. A blend of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. A “spirit of stupor” (katanyxis) is numbness, deep sleep, spiritual insensibility. Isaiah pictures people who stagger and cannot say why, drunk but not with wine, because the LORD has poured on them a spirit of deep sleep (Isaiah 29:9–10). Not a blindness that knows itself, but the fog of a man certain he is thinking clearly. Jesus quoted similar words from Isaiah 6 about those who would not understand his parables (Matthew 13:14–15).

A heart that has to be given. The other half of the citation, from Moses, says the same thing from the opposite side: to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear (Deuteronomy 29:4). What is described there is not something added but something withheld. A heart that understands is a thing that has to be given, which means it was always a gift and not standard equipment, and the judgment, at its most terrible, is God declining to supply what was never owed. So if you see Christ, it is because God opened your eyes. You did not have better eyesight than the people around you; you were given sight. The same God who could justly leave the whole race in its stupor has spoken light into hearts that loved the dark, saying, as at creation, let light shine out of darkness (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Could I be hardened without knowing it? The person who asks that question with real anxiety is showing the opposite of the stupor Paul describes. Hardening, as Scripture paints it, is comfortable: it does not lie awake worrying about God. If you are troubled about your heart, the trouble itself is a sign that God is at work in you, and the remedy is not to analyse yourself but to come to Christ now, today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13). The real danger is the opposite: hearing the gospel again and again and quietly deciding there is no hurry. So whatever you do with this verse, do not postpone. The door Paul describes is open to anyone who will stop continuing in unbelief.

Is it fair for God to harden people? God never hardens an innocent heart that wants him. He hands people over to what they have chosen. In the story of the plagues we read that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) before we read that the LORD hardened it (9:12), though God had told Moses from the start that he would (4:21); and Israel had resisted the prophets for centuries before Paul quotes this verse. Hardening is God giving people the thing they insisted on: a life without the light they refused. That is just. What is not owed to anyone is the softening, and every softened heart is a mercy. So the right response to this verse is not to accuse God, but to thank him if your eyes have been opened and to pray for those whose eyes are still shut.

parallels.desc: the LORD has not given you eyes to see
a spirit of deep sleep

verseByVerse.quote: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David says. Paul quotes Psalm 69:22–23, a psalm of the suffering righteous man, and a modern reader flinches. David asks God to darken people’s eyes and bend their backs, and an apostle quotes it with approval. It is fair to find that hard, and pretending the psalm is gentler does not answer it.

Three things make it bearable. First, the man praying is not nursing a private grudge; he says earlier in the psalm that it is for God’s sake he has borne reproach (Psalm 69:7, 9). The hostility he is under is aimed past him at God. Second, an imprecation, a prayer that calls down God’s judgment, is the opposite of vengeance: it is a refusal to act, a man handing the case to the one Judge entitled to hear it and then doing nothing himself. Third, Paul is not issuing a prayer for us to aim at our neighbours. He is producing evidence: Scripture said this would happen, and it is happening.

The psalm of the cross. The choice of psalm is not incidental. The New Testament applies Psalm 69 to Christ again and again: zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17), the reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (15:3), and the sour wine handed up on a sponge to a thirsty man (John 19:28–29; Matthew 27:34, 48). The psalm that supplied the vinegar at Golgotha supplies the verdict here, and the judgment falls on those who rejected God’s anointed.

A snare and a trap. A snare is not set out in open country. It is set where the animal habitually feeds, on the path it takes without thinking, at the place it has learned is safe. The table here is their feasts, their comforts, and especially their religious privileges and the law in which they trusted: the sacrifices, the Passover, the whole apparatus by which God had fed them for centuries. The trap is in the dining room.

Bend their backs forever. Bend their backs is the shape of a man under a load he cannot put down: the back of a slave. That is bitter, since the law opens by reminding Israel that God brought them out of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2). The commandments that were a rescue have become a weight. “Forever” (dia pantos) here means continually, not necessarily eternally. Paul is quoting a lament, not announcing a verdict on Israel’s last day; they can be grafted in again (v. 23).

Who noticed the bent back. Remember who saw that back and offered to do something about it. Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; take my yoke upon you, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30). That is not a general invitation to tired people. It is addressed to exactly the posture this psalm describes, by the very one the psalm was about. And he went further than offering rest to bent backs: he took the curse onto his own back, was darkened under it at noon, and carried it into the grave, so that the table could become a feast again. Now there is a table spread by him, where the bread is his body and the cup is his blood, and it is no snare to anyone who comes in faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse Jews or anyone else. David’s prayer is a cry for God’s justice against those who persecuted his anointed king, fulfilled in God’s judgment on those who rejected Christ, and Christians are told to bless those who persecute them (12:14). Nor does it justify the shameful history of Christian hatred of Jews, which this chapter, read to its end, condemns.

May a Christian pray the cursing psalms today? Yes, in the way the psalms themselves teach, though with care. They are part of God’s word, and they give voice to a longing for justice that is right: that evil will not have the last word. When a Christian prays them, he hands vengeance to God rather than taking it himself (12:19), and he prays first against the powers of evil, sin and Satan, and against unrepentant cruelty, rather than against personal enemies. Above all, he prays them at the foot of the cross, where Christ bore the curse for those who would believe (Galatians 3:13), and so he joins to his cry for justice a prayer for his enemies’ repentance, as Jesus did from the cross (Luke 23:34). What he must never do is use them to bless his own grudges.

In everyday life. What traps a settled Christian is seldom the thing he already knows is dangerous. It is the privilege: the Bible knowledge that has quietly made him unteachable, the role at church that has become the name he answers to, the doctrinal precision that began as reverence and now runs mostly on contempt. All of it good; all of it his table. So this week ask which part of your religious life you have never examined because it is so obviously good, and bring it back to the Lord who gave it.

parallels.desc: let their own table before them become a snare

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Olive Tree: Gentiles Grafted In, Israel Recoverable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A stumble is something you get up from, and Paul denies that Israel’s stumble is final (v. 11). Their trespass has brought salvation to the Gentiles, and that salvation is aimed back at Israel, to make them jealous; if their failure meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion, an argument that only works if a fullness is still to come.

In the olive tree, the cultivated tree is the one people of God, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs: unbelieving Jews are branches broken off, believing Gentiles wild branches grafted in against nature (v. 24). So the Gentile believer must not be arrogant toward the broken branches. God is able to graft them back in (v. 23), and the mercy shown to Gentiles is part of how he means to fulfil his purposes for Israel, not a reversal of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Olive Tree and Replacement Theology

Romans 11:17–24 is central to the debate over supersessionism (the view that the church has simply replaced Israel, so that God has no further purpose for the Jewish people). The text resists that reading: unbelieving Jews are broken branches, not dead stumps, and can be grafted back in. The Reformed tradition has generally held that the church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, one tree and not two, while refusing the conclusion that God’s purposes for ethnic Israel are exhausted. Verses 25–29 take this further.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some Gentile believers in Rome were in danger of looking down on Jewish unbelief. Paul’s answer is immediate: you stand only by faith, and the God who broke off natural branches can break off wild ones too. Now: The church has too often fallen into exactly the arrogance Paul warned against: contempt for Jewish people, sometimes dressed in theological language, and the assumption that God has finished with them. Romans 11 stands against it. God has not abandoned the people he foreknew.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? The question is built on two verbs, and the whole hope of the chapter sits in the gap between them. A stumble happens on the way somewhere; it is an interruption in a journey, and the man who trips is still going where he was going. A fall, in the sense being denied here, is going down and not getting up, the end of the travelling. And note the little words in order that. Paul is not denying that the stumble had a purpose. He is denying that the purpose was the fall. What they tripped over has already been named: the stone laid in Zion, which is a refuge to the one who trusts in it and a stumbling stone to the one who will not (9:32–33). Paul answers with the chapter’s second mē genoito, by no means: the stumble is not the end of the story.

In the flow. Verses 1 to 10 answered whether God has rejected his people by pointing to the present remnant. Verse 11 asks about the future: is the stumble of the rest final? Paul answers step by step, until at verse 26 he says outright that all Israel will be saved.

Through their trespass. God brought good out of Israel’s sin, and this had been happening, city by city, for a decade. Paul goes to the synagogue first, is thrown out, and turns to the Gentiles: at Pisidian Antioch, at Corinth, and later in Rome itself (Acts 13:46; 18:6; 28:28). What this verse describes happened in real, named cities.

Riches from a rejected King. The trespass at its sharpest was Israel handing over its own Messiah to be crucified, and that is where the riches came from. Rejected by his own, Christ bore the sins of the world, and the gospel of a crucified and risen King went out to the nations. Paul calls his message to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ (Ephesians 3:8): not a consolation prize won from Israel’s loss, but Christ himself, who though he was rich, for your sake became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The riches for the world are a Person, given to the world by the people who refused him.

So as to make Israel jealous. The purpose, from Deuteronomy 32:21, already quoted at 10:19. Jealousy is not an emotion you can feel about a stranger: for the provocation to work, the affection has to still be there underneath. So the very emotion God intends to stir is evidence of a bond that was never cut. You cannot make someone jealous of a house he was glad to leave.

Their full inclusion. “Full inclusion” is plērōma, fullness, and Paul will use the word once more at v. 25, there of the Gentiles, here of Israel: two fullnesses, one at each end of the mystery. If their loss brought such blessing, their fullness will bring far more, whether it is a great future turning of Israel to Christ, as many read it, or the full number of believing Jews gathered in through the age. The argument reasons from the lesser to the greater, as in 5:9–10.

If God brings good out of sin, does that make the sin less bad? No, and Paul’s grammar refuses that conclusion. He calls it trespass and riches in one breath. Many of us have an episode we have become unable to name honestly precisely because good came out of it: the marriage that ended, the betrayal, the failure that redirected a life. Because God used it, we start calling it a blessing in disguise, and something in us knows that is not true and quietly stops trusting the whole account. The biblical way is to say both sentences, in that order: that was wrong; God brought this out of it. That is the guard that Romans 8:28 needs and is rarely given. God working all things for good never turns evil into good. It means evil does not get the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Paul turns to face one part of the room, and there was a reason. The emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome some years earlier (Acts 18:2), and when the edict lapsed, probably at his death in AD 54, many seem to have come back to a church that had carried on without them and had become largely Gentile in the meantime. That tension between Jewish and Gentile believers probably lies behind much of this letter. Paul is speaking to Gentile believers who needed to understand that Israel’s story is their story too, and who were in danger of despising the Jewish believers sitting near them.

I magnify my ministry. Magnify (doxazō) is glorify: he honours his work among the Gentiles and gives himself to it fully, and immediately tells you what that is for. He wants his work to look like something worth having, because there are people watching it whom no argument will reach.

To save some of them. “My fellow Jews” is literally my flesh. Paul’s Gentile ministry had a Jewish goal: as Gentiles came to faith, he hoped some Jews would be stirred to seek their Messiah. “Save” means to be God’s instrument in saving them (1 Corinthians 9:22). And then the most quietly moving word in the two verses: some. This is the man who wished himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his people (9:3), and his working expectation is a few. Both belong to a healthy servant of God: a hope with no ceiling on it, and an estimate with no fantasy in it.

A light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. Paul can magnify this ministry without vanity because it is not finally his (15:18). And the double aim of these two verses, Gentiles brought in so that Israel might be won, is the aim of Christ himself. When old Simeon took the infant Jesus in his arms in the temple, he called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel (Luke 2:32).
