Paul’s mission is that sentence at work, city by city: the light going out to the nations so that Israel might yet see its own glory in the face of its own Messiah.

Should Christians still share the gospel with Jewish people? Yes, gladly and humbly, as Paul did. Some today say it is unkind or even anti-Jewish to evangelise Jewish people, because they have their own covenant. Paul, a Jew, says the opposite: his heart’s desire and prayer was that they might be saved (10:1), and here he shapes his whole ministry around that hope. It would be a strange love that kept from Jewish friends the Messiah who came from their own people. But it must be done in Paul’s spirit: with grief over the church’s history of contempt, with respect, with patience, and above all with lives that make the gospel look like the fulfilment of their Scriptures rather than a foreign religion.

In everyday life. Paul’s hardest audience was people who had grown up with the faith and concluded they knew exactly what it was. Their counterparts today are the one raised in church who is finished with it, the minister’s son, the woman who can quote more of the Bible than you can. They have had the arguments. What reaches them is people visibly better off for the thing they walked away from: not a performance of happiness, which they will detect at once, but lives changed by grace, over years, in the parts they can see. Think of the friend who has heard it all, and ask what has passed between you recently: argument, or evidence?

verseByVerse.quote: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reconciliation of the world. Their rejection (apobolē, casting away) is God’s setting aside of Israel for unbelief. Through it the gospel went to the nations, and the world was reconciled to God, who in Christ was reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5:19). Enemies are made friends, not because God overlooked sin, but because Christ took it away by his death (5:10–11). The setting aside of one people became the bringing near of every people.

What will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? Their acceptance (proslēmpsis, being received back) will mean life from the dead. It is worth admitting that Paul does not explain the phrase, and careful readers have taken it two ways. Some take it as the final resurrection: Israel’s turning stands so close to the end that the general resurrection follows it. Others take it as the strongest figure available for a great spiritual revival in the world, a quickening so far beyond ordinary revival that no smaller word would carry it, like the dry bones of Ezekiel 37 standing up in a valley. In favour of the second, Paul does not use his usual phrase for the resurrection of the dead, and the riches for the world of v. 12 suggest an outpouring of new life among the nations. In favour of the first, the phrase is very strong, and Paul links Israel’s salvation closely with the Deliverer’s coming (v. 26). Hold the question with an open hand. Either way, Israel’s return will be wonderful.

The note of the phrase. What is not in doubt is its tone, and a parable of Jesus shows it. A father explains to a resentful elder son why there is music coming from the house: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:32). That is the note. Not a chart of the last things so much as a door opening on a feast that somebody had stopped expecting.

Life only the risen Christ can give. Whatever the phrase finally means, such life can come from one place only. Jesus said, I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), and Paul has told these readers that the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead gives life to mortal bodies (8:11). Israel’s acceptance, whenever and however it comes, will be Israel receiving her own risen Messiah. The phrase points past every strategy of the church to an empty tomb outside Jerusalem.

The firstfruits and the lump. From Numbers 15:17–21, and the picture is domestic. A woman making bread from the new harvest takes a cake from the first batch and gives it to God before any of it is eaten. From that moment the whole batch is holy, set apart to him: not because each loaf was separately consecrated, but because the first piece stood for the rest. The firstfruits are probably the patriarchs, or perhaps the believing remnant. Because God consecrated them, Israel as a whole remains set apart in his purpose.

If the root is holy. The root is the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom the promises were made, as Paul confirms when he says Israel is beloved for the sake of their forefathers (v. 28); and behind them stands the God who swore by himself because there was nobody greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). The image prepares for the olive tree, and the change of metaphor matters. A lump of dough is inert; a root is alive. What flows through it is not merely a status but sap. God keeps a root alive through centuries of winter, and he has never yet failed to bring spring.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Jew is personally holy or saved. “Holy” here means set apart by God’s covenant purpose, in the way the children of a believer are called holy in 1 Corinthians 7:14: belonging to a people God has marked out as his own, not personally born again. Each branch must still be joined by faith, as the next verses show.

I came to faith late, with no Christian family. Is my faith second-hand? No. The holiness in view never came up out of any branch. It comes through the root. A branch attached last Tuesday is drawing on exactly the same sap as one that has been there sixty years. Some believers carry a quiet sense that their faith is not quite the real thing: no heritage, converted out of nothing much, always aware of others who have had it since childhood and seem to hold it more naturally. But nobody in God’s family is there by pedigree, and nobody draws life from his own history. Everyone draws it from Christ and the promise. Your family tree does not hold you up. His tree does.
verseByVerse.note: The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy. The “root” is the patriarchs.

parallels.desc: a loaf from the first of your dough

verseByVerse.quote: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. — Romans 11:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
The olive tree. Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree, green and beautiful with good fruit (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6). There is one tree: the one people of God, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. It is not that Israel is one tree and the church another.

Some of the branches. Unbelieving Jews. And mark the restraint: some. Not the tree felled, but some of them: Paul is exact about quantities (vv. 14, 25) in a chapter where every reader on both sides reaches for totals.

A wild olive shoot. Gentile believers, wild by nature, once strangers to the promises and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:11–12), now grafted in by faith among the believing Jews. And the oddity of the horticulture is deliberate. Ordinary practice ran the other way: you joined a cultivated cutting onto hardy wild stock. (Ancient writers do mention grafting a wild shoot into a tired old tree to revive it, but that was the exception.) Paul is not making a mistake about farming; he is pointing at the one feature of the picture nobody would have done on purpose, which is the feature that makes it grace. God did not plant a new tree for us; he grafted us into the old one, wild shoots cut from a barren hillside and set, against all good gardening, into the richest root on earth.

The nourishing root. Literally the root of fatness, the rich sap of the tree. Gentiles share in the blessings promised to Abraham, so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:14, 29). And the sap of that root has a name. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and the offspring, Paul says, is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Every promise in the root was a promise about him, so to be grafted into this tree by faith is to be joined to Christ, and to draw from him everything God swore to the fathers.

Do not be arrogant toward the branches. “Arrogant” (katakauchaomai) is to boast against, to crow over. The form of the command means “stop doing this”: the boasting was already under way among the Gentile believers in Rome. The broken-off branches are not enemies to be despised but kinsmen to be mourned and prayed for, and Paul’s own posture at the start of chapter 9 is the model: grief, not gloating.

The root that supports you. The church owes its life to Israel’s root: salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Picture it and the boasting is absurd: a branch held up by a root it did not make, and could not survive ten minutes without, is proud of its own contribution.

An inventory. Everything the branch has arrives through a join it did not make. Name something in your faith that you invented. The Scriptures came through Israel. The God you pray to introduced himself to Abraham, Moses and the prophets. The words you use when you have no words of your own are usually a psalm written by a Jewish king. The Messiah you belong to was a son of David, born under the law (Galatians 4:4). Nothing on the list is yours; all of it arrived down the trunk.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Classic dispensationalists (who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, or dispensations, and expect a future national restoration of Israel) teach that God has two distinct peoples with two programmes, Israel and the church. Others teach that the church has simply replaced Israel, so ethnic Israel has no further place. Both views are held by Christians who love the Scriptures, and the dispensational concern that God keep his promises to Israel is one Paul plainly shares. This commentary’s view: The olive tree shows one people of God across both testaments, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. Gentiles do not form a new tree; they are grafted into the old one, and they do not grow beside it either. So there are not two peoples. But neither has God finished with ethnic Israel: the natural branches can be grafted back into their own tree whenever they believe (vv. 23–24), and many Reformed teachers read verses 25–26 as promising a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, while others read all Israel there as the whole people of God. The church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, not a separate plan, which is how Paul can tell Gentile believers that they are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19).

Should Gentile Christians keep Jewish feasts or customs, then? They are free to learn from them, but they are not required to keep them, and must never make them a badge of a higher Christianity. The feasts and food laws were a shadow of things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper, not the Seder, is the meal he commanded his church to keep. Studying the feasts can deepen your grasp of the gospel; celebrating a Passover meal to understand the Last Supper can be a fine way to teach children. But Paul fought hard against Gentiles being told they must take on the law to be full members (Galatians 5:1–6). Honour the root by trusting the Messiah it bore, not by adopting its shadows.

The church did not heed this. It has to be said plainly. The specific sin Paul forbids here, Gentile Christians holding Jewish people in contempt, became over the centuries a settled habit of Christendom, dressed in theological language and eventually in far worse than language: expulsions, forced baptisms, massacres, and the ground prepared for the horrors of the twentieth century. Whatever else Romans 11 is, it is a warning given early, in writing, by an apostle, and disregarded. A commentary that expounds the metaphor and passes over that in silence has not really read the verse.

In everyday life. Never speak of the Jewish people with contempt, and do not laugh along when others do; if you have Jewish friends or neighbours, love them and pray for them by name.
verseByVerse.note: Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree.

parallels.desc: a green olive tree

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in." That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you will say. Paul puts the boast into the Gentile’s mouth for him: they were removed to make room for me.

That is true. Paul grants the fact and refuses the conclusion drawn from it: the sentence is accurate, but the pride it produced is wrong. So correct doctrine is no protection. A man can have the doctrine of election exactly right, be able to defend it from the text, and still be drawing from it a conclusion that Paul answers with the word fear.

Through faith. The real reason was unbelief, not ethnicity, and you stand only by faith, not by merit. Not because of your faith, as though faith were the qualification that replaced their lineage, but through it. Faith is the empty hand that receives, and it gives no ground for boasting (3:27). Nobody stands on his own grip. He stands because of what he is gripping.

The one who did not fall. And what faith grips is a Person who stood where Israel fell. In the wilderness the generation of the exodus was cut off through unbelief (Hebrews 3:19). In the wilderness Jesus stood, answering each temptation with Moses’ own words from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1–11), and where the branches proved faithless he was faithful to the point of death. To stand through faith is to stand in him, in a faithfulness never ours yet counted to us. He is the one who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). No grafted branch has ever stood on any other ground.

So do not become proud, but fear. Literally, do not think high thoughts. Fear here is reverent awe and humble watchfulness (Philippians 2:12; Proverbs 3:7). And the command is startling in this letter of all letters. Three chapters ago Paul told these same readers they had not received a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear (8:15). He is not contradicting himself. The fear he forbade is the fear of a slave who does not know whether he is owned. The fear he commands is the alertness of someone standing somewhere high who has understood exactly what is holding him up. The right posture is not the swagger of a branch that thinks it chose the tree, but the awe of a branch that knows it was chosen, cut and joined by a hand that did not have to reach for it.

How can I fear God and still be sure of my salvation? Because the fear Paul commands is aimed at pride, not at God’s promises. The one who stands by faith looks away from himself to Christ, and that is exactly where assurance comes from. What Paul wants you to fear is the thought that you are standing in your own strength, or that you are better than those who fell. A child holding his father’s hand near a cliff edge is both perfectly safe and very careful, and the carefulness is part of the safety. If your fear drives you to Christ, it is the right kind. If it drives you away from him into anxious self-inspection, it is the wrong kind, and the answer is to look at his grip, not yours (John 10:28–29).

In everyday life. Take a position you hold and are confident is biblically right: about who is in and who is out, about a group that has gone wrong, about the tradition you left. Ask what it makes you feel toward the people it excludes. If you find anything like satisfaction, Paul’s reply is the one he gave in verse 20: yes, that is true, and now be afraid. Then let the fear do its proper work: turn it into prayer for those people, and into thanksgiving that you stand at all.

parallels.desc: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither will he spare you. Many once-flourishing churches have been cut off: think of the churches of North Africa, home of Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, and of Asia Minor, where all seven churches of Revelation stood. The risen Christ warned Ephesus that he would remove its lampstand unless it repented (Revelation 2:5), and in time there was no lampstand there.

Note then the kindness and the severity of God. “Note then” is literally “look”: Paul makes the reader look at both. Kindness (chrēstotēs, goodness, generosity) is the word Paul used at 2:4 of the kindness meant to lead a man to repentance. Severity (apotomia) is a rare word, related to the verb to cut off; its adjective could describe a sheer face of rock, in a paragraph about branches being cut off.

A God who is only one of them. It is easy to have a God who is one of these and not the other. The one whose God is all kindness has a religion that cannot account for a cross: there was no crisis grave enough to require it. The one whose God is all severity has a religion that cannot account for his own continued existence, and lives braced for the blow. A God who is only one of them is not the God who is there. And the place where you see both at once, at full strength, is Calvary: severity toward sin, poured out on the Son; kindness toward sinners, poured out from him. Here is a God severe enough to cut off his own branches and kind enough to graft in wild ones; holy enough that sin must be judged, and loving enough to bear the judgment himself.

Provided you continue in his kindness. A conditional warning. Continuing (epimenō, remain, persevere) in God’s kindness means continuing to trust it, not trusting yourself, and the warning is against the very unbelief that broke the natural branches. The you is singular, as throughout the olive tree: Paul addresses the Gentile reader as one representative branch, so that the warning reaches each person who reads it.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this verse to show that a truly saved person can lose salvation, as Arminian Christians (who hold that grace can be finally resisted and a real believer can fall away) often do; they are brothers who take the warning seriously, and that is to their credit. This commentary’s view: Paul speaks here mainly of Gentiles as a group, a branch of the tree, not of each individual’s election. And the warning is one of God’s means of keeping his elect. Those who are truly in Christ will continue, because God keeps them (8:30, 38–39; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). Those who fall away show that they were not truly of us, for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and true believers heed it. This is the perseverance of the saints (the Westminster Confession 17.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1). Romans 11:22 is not meant to frighten a trusting believer out of the kingdom; a good many drowsy ones have been woken up by it.

How do I know I am continuing in his kindness? Not by a perfect record, but by where you keep returning. Continuing means that, through falls and dry seasons, you keep coming back to God’s mercy in Christ as your only hope, rather than drifting into either self-trust or indifference. Signs of it are simple: you still want him; you still grieve over sin and confess it; you still hold to the gospel when you are tempted to rest on something else; you stay among his people and under his word. A believer may be weak in all of these and still be continuing. The danger sign is not struggle but settled carelessness, the life that has stopped caring whether it is near God at all.

Could my own church be cut off? A local church or a whole denomination can lose the gospel and cease, in any real sense, to be a church of Christ, and history is full of them. It rarely happens with a dramatic decision. It happens when the church starts to stand on something other than faith in God’s kindness: its tradition, its respectability, its size, its culture, its moral campaigns. The remedy is not panic but the same one Christ gave Ephesus: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first (Revelation 2:5). Pray for your church’s leaders, love the gospel at the centre of its life, and do not assume that a past of faithfulness guarantees a future.

verseByVerse.quote: And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even they. The way back is open. Their unbelief, not their ancestry, cut them off, and faith will graft them back in. And the condition is merciful: continuing in unbelief is the only thing named as keeping anyone out, and it is the one thing that can stop.

God has the power. Humanly, a broken branch cannot be put back, and the unspoken assumption about a hardened person is that the case has become too difficult. Paul answers by stating that God is able, because the real doubt was never about the person. It was about God’s power. The gardener of this passage is not a man coaxing reluctant wood; he is the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (4:17). He did it for you when you were wild.

Contrary to nature. God did something unnatural in bringing Gentiles in, and it quietly demolishes Gentile confidence: the Gentile believer has already granted the harder of the two miracles. Putting a branch back onto the tree it grew on is not the astonishing operation. His own presence there is.

Their own olive tree. If God did the unnatural thing, how much easier the natural one. And a phrase here ought to be read slowly by anyone inclined to arrogance: their own olive tree. The tree still belongs to them. The guest has been given a great deal; he has not been given the deeds.

Coming home to Israel’s King. A natural branch grafted back is a Jew coming to Jesus, and that is not leaving Israel’s tree but coming home to its fruit. Jesus called Nathanael an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit, and within minutes Nathanael answered, Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel! (John 1:47–49). The Messiah is not a foreign Lord but Israel’s own King, and to receive him is to receive what the tree was always growing.

Someone I love was raised in the faith and has left it. May I hope? Yes, and this verse gives you good reason. Many readers have someone in mind who grew up inside the faith and is now outside it, and about whom a quiet verdict has been reached: too far in, too long out. Read verse 24 again with that person in view. The branch that once grew on the tree is the case Paul calls easier. He is not promising you an outcome, and it would be cruel to pretend he is; some never return. But he tells you this is the easier kind of case, and he tells you God is able. So keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open without nagging, and let your own life be the kind of evidence that makes them jealous.

If they must believe, what does God’s power have to do with it? Everything, because the faith that grafts them in is itself God’s gift. A branch cannot graft itself back. When someone who has long resisted Christ comes to believe, it is because God has given him new eyes and a new heart, as he did for Paul on the Damascus road. That is why we pray for unbelievers and do not merely argue with them. Their coming to faith is real and personal, and they will be fully responsible and fully willing in it, but it is God who makes the dead branch willing. Prayer for the hardest case is therefore never wasted: it is addressed to the only one with the power.
verseByVerse.note: Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock; grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is, as Paul says, “contrary to nature.”

parallels.desc: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — The Mystery, the Promise, and the Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reveals a mystery so that the Gentile believers will not become proud: Israel’s hardening is partial and lasts until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved. Israel is at once opposed to the gospel for the Gentiles’ sake and loved for the patriarchs’ sake, for God does not take back his gifts and calling. God has shut all up in disobedience in order to have mercy on all. Then the argument turns to praise of the God whose ways no one can trace or advise, from whom, through whom and to whom are all things.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Irrevocability of God’s Covenant Purposes

Verse 29 is the capstone of chapters 9–11: God does not change his mind about what he has given and whom he has called. For Israel, whatever “all Israel will be saved” finally means (v. 26), it means at least that God will not abandon the people he chose. For the individual Christian, the calling and justification God has given her will not be revoked. The chain of 8:29–30, from foreknowing to glorifying, and 11:29 say the same thing: what God begins he does not take back.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The doxology of verses 33–36 was Paul’s own response to the argument he had just made. He does not end with a summary but with worship. Now: When we want every mystery resolved into a tidy system, these verses remind us that we are not God. The depths of his wisdom and knowledge are beyond what our minds can hold, and the fitting posture before the mystery of election and salvation is Paul’s: to him be glory forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, "The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob"; — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest you be wise in your own sight. The phrase echoes Proverbs 3:7, and it gives Paul’s reason for telling them this. The greatest disclosure about the future in the whole letter is handed over to stop a group of Christians thinking too well of themselves. The doctrine is medicine for conceit. A reader who comes away with a firmer grip on a timetable and no change in how he regards anybody has taken the medicine and kept the disease.

This mystery. A “mystery” (mystērion) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (16:25; Ephesians 3:3–6): not a puzzle for clever readers, but a secret God has chosen to tell.

In the flow. The mystery crowns the olive tree. In verses 23 and 24 Paul argued that God is able to graft Israel back in; now he says that God will, as a truth God has revealed, and so gives the fullest answer to the opening question (v. 1).

A partial hardening has come upon Israel. Partial: not every Jew is hardened, for the remnant believes. All through this chapter the apostle writes in fractions, not totals. And the hardening is also limited in time.

Until the fullness. The single most important word in the sentence is “until”. The very clause that announces the hardening also sets its limit, which a permanent rejection would not have. The fullness of the Gentiles is the full number of elect Gentiles that God intends to save, coming into the people of God.

In this way. “In this way” (houtōs) means in this manner, by this process: through the hardening of part of Israel, the coming in of the Gentiles, and the jealousy that provokes Israel to faith. Some hear a sense of sequence too, but the stress falls on how God brings it about.

The Deliverer will come from Zion. From Isaiah 59:20–21, with words from Isaiah 27:9. The Deliverer is Christ. Paul’s word (ho rhyomenos, the one who rescues) is the same he uses of Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10). In the Hebrew of Isaiah the Redeemer comes to Zion (the Greek Old Testament has for the sake of Zion); Paul says from Zion, and readers differ over whether he means Christ’s first coming, whose gospel went out from Jerusalem, or his return from the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). Either way, what the Deliverer does is the gospel itself (compare Acts 3:26): ungodliness is banished, and sins are taken away. That rules out the popular idea that Israel has a separate way of salvation, by its covenant alone and without Christ. The hope of v. 26 is enormous, and it is the same hope by the same Saviour as everybody else’s.

Where Christians differ: who is all Israel? Three main views are held among Reformed Christians. First, all Israel is the whole church, Jew and Gentile, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16); this was Calvin’s view. Those who hold it point also to 9:6, not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and to the words in this way, which describe how Israel is saved rather than when. Second, all Israel is the total of elect Jews saved throughout history, the remnant in every generation, as in vv. 1–10. Third, all Israel is the Jewish people as a whole, who will turn to Christ in large numbers in the future, before his return. Dispensationalists (who divide history into distinct eras and keep God’s plan for Israel distinct from his plan for the church) add a separate future plan for national Israel in a thousand-year kingdom; many of them are earnest Bible readers whose love for the Jewish people this commentary shares. This commentary’s view: it does not press one reading, because godly Reformed teachers have held each. Many find the third the most natural reading of verses 25–26, and it is held here with humility: in verse 25 Israel means ethnic Israel, distinguished from the Gentiles, and it would be strange for the word to change meaning in the next sentence; the contrast of now and then (vv. 12, 15, 23–24, 30–31) and the full inclusion of v. 12 seem to look for something greater than a remnant. Those who hold the first view, with Calvin, answer that in this way describes the manner and not the time, and that Paul has already widened the name Israel in 9:6; those who hold the second stress that the remnant is how God has always saved Israel. On every reading, any Jew is saved exactly as any Gentile is: through the gospel, by faith in Christ, into the one olive tree, the church. It is not a separate plan of salvation, and it does not require a rebuilt temple or a thousand-year earthly kingdom. It fits the amillennial view, which this commentary holds: the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign, and the church age ends with his one visible return, the resurrection and the judgment, with no secret rapture (an unseen coming to remove believers before a final tribulation). Premillennial Christians, who expect an earthly reign after his return, read the order of events differently, and they are honoured brothers. All Israel need not mean every individual Jew. The Westminster Larger Catechism teaches us to pray for the calling of the Jews (Q. 191), and no reading permits contempt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews can be saved without Christ, and it gives no ground whatever for anti-Jewish hatred. Nor does it mean any modern political state fulfils this prophecy; Paul speaks of conversion to Christ, and what he promises is forgiveness (v. 27), not territory. Christians may pray for the Jewish people and judge the policies of the modern state as they would any other nation’s.

When will this happen, and should we watch for signs? Scripture gives no date, and Paul gives none. He says until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and only God knows when that number is complete. So we should not try to read it off the news, or treat events in the Middle East as a countdown. Our task is the one Paul gives in this chapter: to preach the gospel to the nations, to love and pray for Jewish people, and to stay humble. The Lord will return visibly, at a day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36), and his people will be ready by being faithful, not by being well informed about a timetable. Scripture does name things that come before his return, such as the gospel reaching the nations (Matthew 24:14) and a final rebellion (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and on many readings this turning of Israel is one of them; but none is given to us as a date.

Does all Israel mean every Jewish person who has ever lived? No. In the Old Testament the phrase usually means Israel as a whole, the nation as a body, without implying every single person (1 Samuel 7:5; 2 Chronicles 12:1). When the nation gathered at Mizpah, it was all Israel, though not every individual was present. So on the reading that expects a future turning, Paul’s hope is that the Jewish people as a people, in great numbers, will turn to Christ; on the reading that takes all Israel as the whole people of God, it is the full number of the saved, Jew and Gentile. It does not mean that Jews who die rejecting him are saved, any more than Gentiles who reject him are. There is one Saviour for all, and the way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike is faith in him.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God. Interpreters differ over whether “all Israel” means the Jewish people as a whole before the end, or the whole company of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The more natural reading in context is the first: a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

parallels.desc: a Redeemer will come to Zion

verseByVerse.quote: "and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins." As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I take away their sins. Isaiah 59:21 joined with Isaiah 27:9, echoing the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33–34. The promise is not of territory or a political settlement. What God guarantees is forgiveness of sins in Christ, the heart of the new covenant (Hebrews 8:8–12), the same thing Paul has been offering to everybody since chapter 3.

Enemies for your sake. In relation to the gospel, unbelieving Israel stands opposed to the message and under God’s displeasure, and their rejection opened the door for the Gentiles. That phrase, for your sake, ought to stop a proud Gentile reader: the hostility he might feel superior to is the hostility that opened the door he walked through. There is no posture left to him but gratitude, and gratitude cannot be combined with contempt.

Beloved for the sake of their forefathers. God loved the fathers and chose their offspring after them (Deuteronomy 4:37; 7:8). They are loved on somebody else’s account: not for anything in the present generation, which Paul has spent two chapters describing, but because of promises made to men who had been dead for nearly two thousand years. Our God does not lose track of a promise, and he does not let a covenant lapse.

Loved for another’s sake. Before anyone finds that arbitrary: it is the only way anyone in this letter is loved. Every Christian who has ever lived is loved for the sake of another: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (5:19). Israel’s case is no exception to the gospel. It is the gospel applied to a nation, and the promises made to its fathers were always promises about Christ.

How can people be God’s enemies and beloved at the same time? Because God’s relation to people has more than one side, and Scripture speaks of both honestly. As long as someone rejects Christ, he stands under God’s displeasure; that is the enemy side. Yet God may at the same time have purposes of love toward him that he has not yet carried out, as he had toward every believer before conversion: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (5:10). Every Christian was once both. So this verse should keep us from two errors: pretending unbelief does not matter, and writing off those who are presently against the gospel. God has not written them off.

In everyday life. Paul holds two true things about the same people in one sentence and refuses to let either cancel the other. Take the person you are most tangled with and put both halves down in one line, joined by and rather than but: what is actually wrong, and what is actually true of them and of your bond. Paul managed it about people who had tried to have him killed, because God had held both halves about him: once an enemy, and beloved (5:10).

parallels.desc: when he takes away his sin

verseByVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Irrevocable. “Irrevocable” (ametamelētos) is built on the verb to regret, with the negative in front: without regret, never taken back. God has no second thoughts about what he has given. The gifts are the privileges of 9:4–5, the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the promises; the calling is God’s choosing of Israel as his people.

No regret in God. Everyone knows what it is to give generously and regret it afterwards. Paul says there is none of it in God. Someone may object that Scripture says the LORD regretted making Saul king (1 Samuel 15:11). It does, and the same chapter adds that the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man (15:29). The first speaks of God’s real grief over sin as it unfolds in history; the second of his purpose, which never changes. God can be grieved by what his people do. He is never caught out by it.

He loved them to the end. The clearest picture of gifts given without regret is an upper room. Jesus knew what the night held: one of the twelve had already agreed to betray him, and the boldest of them would deny him before dawn. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1), and he knelt and washed their feet. He called Peter knowing about the courtyard and the fire, and after the resurrection he came looking for him by the lake to give him his commission again (John 21:15–17). That is irrevocable calling with a human face.

A comfort for every believer. In context the sentence is about Israel. Extending it to the individual believer is legitimate, because the same logic produced the chain of 8:29–30, and the comfort is enormous. If God does not take back his calling of a nation that refused his own Son, he will not take back his call to you on the day you fail him. Before the foundation of the world he knew everything his people would do, every failure and every betrayal, and he chose them anyway. He did not regret Abraham, or Jacob, or David, or you. His Son went to the cross knowing exactly whom he was dying for, and he does not look back on it with regret.

Does irrevocable mean a minister who falls into serious sin keeps his calling to office? No, this verse is not about that. Paul is speaking of God’s covenant choice of Israel and, by extension, of his saving call to his people. He is not saying that anyone who once held church office or had a gift for ministry must always be allowed to exercise it. Scripture sets qualifications for elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9), and a man who disqualifies himself must step down, whatever his gifts. God may restore such a man to fellowship and use him again, but the church must not quote Romans 11:29 to shield a leader from discipline or to protect the institution at the expense of those he has wronged.

In everyday life. If you carry a private theory about what would finally exhaust God’s patience, some specific thing you suspect would be the end of it, name it. Verse 29 does not weigh whether that thing would be bad enough. It says that for those God has called there is no such thing. Bring the thing to him in confession, and leave it with the God who has no regrets about you.

parallels.desc: God is not man, that he should lie

verseByVerse.quote: so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they also may now receive mercy. The pattern reverses. Jewish disobedience brought mercy to Gentiles; mercy to Gentiles will bring mercy to Jews, and neither group is the senior partner. A textual note: some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, omit the second now, as the ESV notes. If it stands, it means that the time of mercy for Israel is the present gospel age, and mercy can reach them now.

Consigned all to disobedience. “Consigned” (synkleiō) means to shut in, to lock in with no way out. Luke uses it of fish trapped in a net (Luke 5:6), and Paul uses it when he says the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin (Galatians 3:22). The image is not a courtroom but a cell with the whole human race in it, Jew and Gentile together, every exit tried and found locked.

That he may have mercy on all. He locked them in so that he might have mercy. God closed every other door so that the only one left would be the one that opens from outside. Paul’s other use of the word shows who that door is: the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe (Galatians 3:22). I am the door, Jesus said; if anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9). God sent his Son into the cell to carry the sentence and walk out with the key. Not one prisoner comes out by his own merit, and so not one can boast; every one comes out by mercy, and so every one can sing. “All” here means all kinds, Jew and Gentile alike.

In the flow. Verse 32 retells the whole letter so far: God has consigned all to disobedience is the verdict of 1:18 to 3:20; that he may have mercy on all is the message of 3:21 to 8:39; and the Jew and Gentile held together in that all have been the subject of chapters 9 to 11. The only place left to go is worship (vv. 33–36).

Where Christians differ: universal salvation. Some read “mercy on all” as meaning that every human being will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: The context is about two groups, Jews and Gentiles, not every individual. Paul has just spoken of branches cut off and of God’s severity (v. 22), and elsewhere of eternal destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:9). He hopes to save some of his countrymen (v. 14), and he opened chapter 9 in anguish over people he expects to be lost. The two alls are the same width, and the whole argument since chapter 9 has told us what that width is: two categories, not every person. God shows mercy on both groups without distinction, but not all individuals are saved. Hell is real and conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46).

Did God make people disobey? No. God is never the author of sin, and no one is forced to disobey against his will (James 1:13). The disobedience was entirely ours, freely chosen, as chapter 1 showed. What God did was to shut the doors: he gave the law, which exposed sin; he let both Jew and Gentile go their own way and prove what was in them; and he closed off every route to salvation by merit, so that the only door left is mercy. It is the way a doctor might let a patient see the full results of the tests before he offers the cure, not because he caused the disease, but so that the cure is received as a cure.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the second “now.”

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The doxology. After eleven chapters of some of the deepest theology in Scripture, Paul does not end with a conclusion but with worship. Doctrine is meant to lead to doxology, from doxa, glory.

Oh, the depth! Three depths. The riches of his grace and mercy (2:4; 9:23; 10:12). The wisdom of his plan, which uses even sin and hardening to bring salvation to the world, for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). The knowledge by which he foreknew his people and sees all things. Eleven chapters of close reasoning do not end in a conclusion. They end with a man running out of language in front of God and saying so.

How unsearchable are his judgments. “Unsearchable” (anexeraunētos) means what cannot be fully investigated. His decisions and decrees go beyond our understanding. You can follow them a long way, as Paul has just done, but you will not reach the bottom.

And how inscrutable his ways! “Inscrutable” (anexichniastos) carries a picture that English hides. It is built on ichnos, a footprint: literally, his ways cannot be tracked, like footprints that cannot be followed (the same word Paul uses for the unsearchable riches of Christ, Ephesians 3:8, so the depth that cannot be traced has a name: Christ). You can see where he has been, and you cannot reconstruct the route. Israel’s own hymnbook said so about the greatest thing God ever did for them: your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen (Psalm 77:19). The defining act of the nation’s history left no tracks. He made a path through the sea and left no footprints, and he made a path to the cross that no one could have predicted and no one can now undo.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is irrational or that we can know nothing about him. He has revealed much, as Romans shows, and what he has revealed opens onto a depth no creature can fathom. This verse is often used to shut down hard questions, but nobody reasons harder than the man who wrote chapters 9 to 11. The doxology stands at the end of the argument, not instead of it.

A depth, not a muddle. See what Paul does with the questions he never resolved. He leaves some standing: why these and not those, how the hardening and human responsibility fit together, what exactly life from the dead means. He looks at the unexplained remainder and calls it depth, which is a word of praise. That is the difference between a mystery and a muddle. A muddle is something you have failed to sort out; a depth is something you have come to the edge of. We do not reach the bottom of him and we never will, and that is our joy: we will spend eternity discovering that he is more than we thought.

Is it wrong to be troubled by chapters 9 to 11? No. Paul himself was troubled; he began this section with great sorrow and unceasing anguish (9:2). Hard questions about election, hardening and Israel are not a sign of unbelief, and you should not pretend to feel no difficulty. But look at the direction Paul’s troubled mind travelled. He took the questions to Scripture, reasoned through them as far as God had revealed, and then, at the edge of what he could see, he worshipped rather than accused. The same road is open to you. Ask your questions honestly, study, talk to mature believers, and when you reach the limit, let the remaining mystery make God bigger in your eyes, not smaller.

parallels.desc: my thoughts are not your thoughts

verseByVerse.quote: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mind of the Lord. From Isaiah 40:13, in the great chapter on God’s incomparable greatness. The verse is usually quoted to silence people who question God, but Isaiah spoke it to comfort. Isaiah 40 is addressed to exiles, a beaten, deported people whose complaint is quoted a few verses later: “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God” (Isaiah 40:27). They are not complaining that God is too free. They are afraid he has lost track of them.

One who has known. Among creatures the answer is no one. But the New Testament knows one exception, and he is not a creature. No one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matthew 11:27). No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (John 1:18). The mind no creature could search came to us in a Person who has always known it from within, and so Paul can say, astonishingly, we have the mind of Christ (1 Corinthians 2:16).

Or who has been his counselor? No one advised God when he planned salvation. He did not need help or input. His plan comes from his own wisdom alone (Job 15:8; Jeremiah 23:18). And to those exiles the news that nobody has ever instructed God is comfort, not rebuke. It means his handling of their case has not been delegated, or advised, or worked out from partial information. It has a quieter mercy in it still: if nobody has ever been God’s counsellor, then nobody has ever successfully briefed him against you. No one got to him first. There is no version of your file that he has been given by someone else. And this is the mind that decided, without anyone needing to suggest it, to save the ungodly at the cost of his own Son. No one could have advised it; no one would have dared.

Built, not blurted. The three questions of vv. 34–35 are not a random pile. They answer the three nouns of v. 33 in reverse order: his knowledge (who has known his mind), his wisdom (who has been his counsellor), his riches (who has given to him). Paul is no less careful in worship than he was in argument.

If no one advises God, why pray? Because God has ordained prayer as one of the means by which he carries out his plans, and he delights to hear his children. When you pray, you are not informing God of something he did not know, or persuading him to be kinder than he was. You are a child bringing his needs to a Father who has promised to act through the prayers of his people (James 5:16; Matthew 7:7–11). Prayer changes things because God has decided that it will; and it changes the one who prays, bringing his will into line with God’s. Pray boldly, and leave the counsel to him.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? From Job 41:11 (see also Job 35:7). The setting of the quotation gives it its weight. Job 41 is God speaking out of the whirlwind, near the end of one of the longest and least comfortable answers in Scripture, and the line runs: who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine. No one has ever put God in debt. No one can claim that God owes him salvation. Everything we have, including the faith we give him, he first gave us: what do you have that you did not receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7). This sums up the message of Romans: salvation is by grace, not earned.

The ledger nailed to a cross. There is a ledger in the gospel, but it runs the other way. God was never our debtor; we were his, with a debt no one could pay. And he dealt with it himself, cancelling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, setting it aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The only one who ever gave to God everything he owed was the Son, who became obedient to the point of death, and he gave it not to put the Father in his debt but to clear ours. Verse 35 says no one can make God owe him. The cross says God chose to pay what we owed. He needed nothing from us, and yet he gave us his Son, his Spirit, his kingdom and himself.

The background hum. The instinct this verse kills is rarely admitted aloud. It shows up as the faint sense, after a stretch of obedience, that something is now owed: that the year of faithful service has bought a measure of protection, that God should not let this particular thing happen to someone who has been doing what you have been doing. It is not usually a belief. It is a background hum, and it becomes audible the moment life goes wrong.

What if God did owe you? Turn the question round and let it land. You would have a claim, and enforceable claims are excellent things to have. But a debt paid is not a gift given, and a God who was settling an account with you would not be loving you. Think of the difference between the friend who visits because he owes you and the friend who visits because he wanted to see you. Everything that makes the second visit worth anything is the absence of obligation. That is what verse 35 protects. It is not only a statement about God’s independence, though it is that. It is the guarantee that nothing you have ever received from him was a payment.

But do we not give to God when we give money, time or service? We do, and he receives it gladly; but every gift we bring was his before it was ours. David said it when Israel gave lavishly for the temple: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving to God is not making a deposit that puts him in our debt; it is returning a small part of what he lent us, as an act of thanks and love. That is why Christian giving should be cheerful, not calculating (2 Corinthians 9:7). We give because he first gave, and we can never out-give him.

In everyday life. The background hum is loudest on the day something goes wrong after a good stretch, and the question rises by itself: after all I have done? Nothing you did put God in your debt, so nothing that happens to you is God defaulting on one. And everything good in your day came without a ledger, so you are free to give that way too, to someone who cannot repay you.

parallels.desc: who has first given to me, that I should repay him?

verseByVerse.quote: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From him, through him, to him. The whole of reality in one sentence, salvation included: planned by him, carried out through him, and ending in his praise. And Paul gives these same prepositions to the Son: one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6); all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). Christ stands at the centre of this doxology. Each preposition closes a door. From him: nothing that exists brought itself. Through him: nothing that exists is keeping itself going. To him: nothing that exists is its own point.

The frame of three chapters. Chapter 9 opened with Paul in grief, breaking off to bless the Christ who came from Israel: God over all, blessed forever. Amen (9:5). Here at the far end he says Amen again. Paul does not arrive at praise because his difficulties dissolved; he arrives at praise because the God he could not fully trace turned out, when the argument was finished, to be more merciful than the argument had made him fear: a God who shut everyone in so that he could let everyone out, and who has not taken back a single thing he ever gave.

To him be glory forever. Amen. The right response to all of this. Glory (doxa) is honour, praise, weight. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever (Q. 1). Amen: so be it, truly. This Amen is not merely the close of a prayer. It is Paul putting his name to everything God has done.

Does all things include evil and suffering? Yes, in the sense that nothing happens outside God’s rule and purpose, but not in the sense that he does evil. Scripture teaches that God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet in such a way that he is not the author of sin, and the responsibility of creatures is not taken away (the Westminster Confession 3.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1). Joseph’s brothers sold him, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The cross was the greatest evil ever done, and it was through him and to his glory. So when suffering comes, you are not in the hands of chance or of the devil. You are in the hands of the God from whom, through whom and to whom all things are, who is working even this toward his glory and your good.

For worship. From him, and through him, and to him, are all things. Every galaxy and every atom of it. Every hour of every life that has ever been lived. The election of Abraham, the hardening of Pharaoh, the seven thousand, the remnant, the olive tree, the cross and the empty tomb, the fullness of the Gentiles and the salvation of all Israel. It began in him, it is being carried by him, and it is going home to him, and there is no fourth preposition, and nothing anywhere that falls outside the three. To him be glory forever. Amen.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.<sup>2</sup>God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?<sup>3</sup>“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.”<sup>4</sup>But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”<sup>5</sup>So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.<sup>6</sup>But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.<sup>7</sup>What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,<sup>8</sup>as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”<sup>9</sup>And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;<sup>10</sup>let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”<sup>11</sup>So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.<sup>12</sup>Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!<sup>13</sup>Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry<sup>14</sup>in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.<sup>15</sup>For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?<sup>16</sup>If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.<sup>17</sup>But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree,<sup>18</sup>do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.<sup>19</sup>Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”<sup>20</sup>That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.<sup>21</sup>For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.<sup>22</sup>Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.<sup>23</sup>And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again.<sup>24</sup>For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.<sup>25</sup>Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.<sup>26</sup>And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;<sup>27</sup>“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.”<sup>28</sup>As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.<sup>29</sup>For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.<sup>30</sup>For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,<sup>31</sup>so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy.<sup>32</sup>For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.<sup>33</sup>Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!<sup>34</sup>“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”<sup>35</sup>“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”<sup>36</sup>For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

12.title: The Transformed Life
12.overview:
Romans 12 begins the practical part of the letter, and its first word ties it to everything before it: therefore. The mercies of God set out in chapters 1–11 are the ground, and the life of chapters 12–16 grows out of them. Paul does not turn from doctrine to duty as if they were two subjects; the way of life he describes is what the gospel looks like when it is believed.

The call to present your bodies as a living sacrifice and to be renewed in mind (vv. 1–2) is then shown at work: in a sober view of yourself and your gifts (vv. 3–8), and in genuine love that reaches at last to enemies (vv. 9–21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Living Sacrifice and the Renewed Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul appeals to the church by the mercies of God, not by its obligations. Everything God has given in chapters 1–11 is what moves the believer to give himself back to God: his body, his whole life as it is lived in the world.

The change Paul asks for is something God does in him, renewing his mind through the Spirit and the word. The believer puts himself under the means God uses, and the fruit is a mind that can recognise what is good and acceptable and perfect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body as Instrument of Worship

Romans 12:1 refuses to divide life into a sacred part that belongs to God and a secular part that does not. The body presented to God as a living sacrifice is itself where worship happens, so daily work, rest, eating and drinking, money and marriage can all be offered to God in faith. The Reformers drew much of their teaching on the holiness of ordinary callings from passages like this. John Calvin saw the whole creation as the theatre of God’s glory; Paul places that vision in the offered body of the believer.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish and Gentile readers alike knew what a sacrifice was: an offering brought to an altar and given up to God. Now the Christian’s whole life is the offering, brought to God day by day. Now: Every culture, including the church’s own subculture, presses its assumptions on us about worth, success and meaning. The renewal of the mind is God’s answer to that pressure: learning to see life through Scripture and the mercies of God until the world’s measures lose their hold.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. — Romans 12:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 12 begins the practical part of the letter (chapters 12–16): not ethics as a separate subject but the gospel being lived. The foundation is a whole self given to God and a renewed mind (vv. 1–2); then life in the church, with a sober view of yourself and your gift (vv. 3–8); then genuine love, within the church, toward outsiders and toward enemies (vv. 9–21).

I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God. Everything in this chapter hangs on a word that is easy to step over: “therefore”. It joins the commands that follow to all that Paul has said so far. “Appeal” (parakaleō: urge, exhort, encourage) is a pastor’s pleading, not a cold order. And Paul says what the therefore points back to: not the law, not what you owe, but the mercies of God, eleven chapters of them. Justification as a free gift (3:24), no condemnation (8:1), a Spirit who prays when praying is beyond us (8:26), nothing able to separate us from his love (8:39): that is the ground he stands on to ask for anything at all.

The mercies. The plural is deliberate. “Mercies” (oiktirmoi) is the Greek Old Testament’s word for God’s compassions, translating a Hebrew family of words related to the word for a womb: the ache of a parent over a child. It is God’s settled attitude, not one act of pardon, and every one of these mercies is given in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood (3:24–25): the offering that takes God’s righteous anger on itself, so that it no longer falls on us. And they set the order of Christian obedience, which most of us reverse. Very little is asked of anyone in this letter until chapter 12 (the appeals of chapter 6 are the main exception); mercy comes first, and obedience follows as a response, never as a way to earn it. A Christian life that begins with the appeal and treats the mercies as background music will not run for long.

To present your bodies as a living sacrifice. “Present” (paristēmi) is the regular word for bringing an offering forward and setting it down at the altar. Paul used it at 6:13 and 19; this is the same instruction with the whole letter now behind it. And what is brought is your bodies: your whole self as you live in the world, eyes, hands, tongue and time. Intentions can be offered from an armchair and cost nothing. Your body is the one part of you that has to actually turn up, and it leaves a record.

A body prepared for him. Before God asked for our bodies, he had received one. When Christ came into the world, Hebrews says, he took up the words of Psalm 40: a body have you prepared for me, and, I have come to do your will, O God; and by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:5–10). (Hebrews follows the Greek translation of Psalm 40:6, which is why your English Old Testament reads differently there: “you have given me an open ear”.) His whole bodily life was a presented life: hands laid on lepers, feet set towards Jerusalem, a back given to those who struck him, and at the last a body laid on the cross. Our living sacrifice is not a second atonement beside his. It is our response, which his offering makes possible: bodies that belong to God because his body was given for them.

A living sacrifice. In the Old Testament, sacrifices were killed. Ours is offered alive, not to atone, for that was finished once for all (Hebrews 10:14), but in thanksgiving. A dead sacrifice stays where it is put. A living one has legs. The difficulty is not that the offering is hard to make, but that it can get up afterwards and walk off, usually without deciding to. So the offering is not one moment but a daily presenting, in the living of an ordinary life.

Holy and acceptable to God. Holy: set apart for God. Acceptable: well-pleasing to him. Under the law an animal once set apart for the altar could not be exchanged or taken back, because it now belonged to the LORD (Leviticus 27:9–10). A life presented to God is no longer ours to reclaim on Monday. Our offerings are never without blemish, yet through Christ they please God, for we are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). The Father receives a stammering, half-hearted life because it comes through his Son, who offered the one unblemished life in our place and whose obedience is counted as ours (5:19).

Which is your spiritual worship. “Spiritual” is logikos: rational, reasonable, fitting (the ESV note offers rational). “Worship” is latreia, the priestly service of the temple (9:4). In view of God’s mercies, giving your whole life to him is not extreme devotion but the only reasonable response; to receive so much and offer so little would be the irrational thing. Worship is the whole of life given to God, not only what we do on Sunday.

Do not be conformed to this world. “Conformed” (syschēmatizō) means pressed into the shape of, like dough in a mould. And “this world” is literally this age (aiōn), the present evil age with its values, opposed to God (Galatians 1:4). You cannot get away from an age by moving house or joining a smaller church; the pressure is in the water, and the mould is made of the things everyone around you assumes without ever arguing for them: that you are what you earn, that your body is your own, that a good life is a comfortable one. You are not to set in that shape, because the world is passing away with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides for ever (1 John 2:17).

But be transformed by the renewal of your mind. “Transformed” is metamorphoō, the word the Gospels use of Jesus on the mountain, when he was transfigured before them and his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2), and the word Paul uses of believers being changed into Christ’s image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). Not improvement: a change of form. The form of both verbs means something that keeps on being done to you: keep on being transformed, by the Spirit’s work in you. But that does not mean you are idle. You cannot transform yourself, but you can decide what you put your mind under: what you read, whose company you keep, what you rehearse while driving. Nobody drifts into a renewed mind. They drift into the world’s shape.

That by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. “Testing” (dokimazō) means to prove, to approve after testing, the word used of assaying metal. It closes a circle opened in chapter 1, where those who did not see fit (did not, on testing, approve) to acknowledge God were given up to a debased mind, adokimos, failed and rejected metal (1:28). The sound judgment lost at 1:28 is given back at 12:2. The will of God here is his moral will, revealed in Scripture, not secret guidance: good (morally right), acceptable (pleasing to God) and perfect (complete, lacking nothing).

A competence, not a signal. The verse does not promise a signal, an impression or a door that opens at the right moment. It promises a competence: a mind so remade that it can weigh a situation and recognise what is good in it. God’s more usual answer to “What should I do?” is not an instruction. He changes the person who is deciding.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must withdraw from the world; Jesus prayed not that his Father would take us out of the world but that he would keep us from the evil one (John 17:15). The change Paul asks for happens from the inside, in the middle of ordinary life.

How do I make a big decision, like a job, a move or whom to marry? Begin with what God has already revealed. Many decisions are settled by his moral will: marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39), do not take a job that requires you to sin, keep your promises. Within those bounds, God usually gives freedom, and he expects you to use the renewed mind this verse describes. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Ask which option will help you love God and others better, use your gifts, and keep you under good teaching in a faithful church. Take counsel from mature believers who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God with the outcome. You do not need a sign to obey; and if you have honestly sought to please him, you have not missed his will.

What does renewing my mind look like in practice? It is slow and ordinary. Read Scripture regularly, not only for information but to let it reshape what you love and how you see. Sit under faithful preaching each Lord’s Day, and let one truth from it go with you into the week. Memorise a few verses and turn to them when anxious or tempted. Notice which voices shape your thinking most hours of the week, from your phone, the news, entertainment and friends, and change the balance. Pray Scripture back to God. And expect change to be gradual: like the growth of a tree, you rarely see it happen, but you see it has happened.

In everyday life. Start the day by offering yourself to God, your body, your work, your words, before the day has a chance to claim them, and feed your mind on his word. When you wonder whether anything is changing, look back rather than in: if you can now see something you could not see five years ago, that is this verse at work. And where you see less change than you hoped, the offering still stands, because the Father receives it for his Son’s sake, not for its quality.
verseByVerse.note: “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, then the response. The ESV notes that “spiritual worship” can also be rendered “rational service.”

parallels.desc: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — Gifts of Grace: Sober Self-Assessment in the Body
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first fruit of a renewed mind is an honest view of yourself: neither pride nor false modesty, but a glad recognition that every gift was given. In the one body difference is the design and not a defect, and the gifts of vv. 6–8, a sample rather than a full list, mostly come with a manner: give with generosity, lead with zeal, show mercy with cheerfulness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charismata: Gifts of the Spirit for the Common Good

The gifts of Romans 12 are what Paul elsewhere calls charismata, gifts of grace. Each is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7), not to make its owner more admired. A gift that is not used in service is like a lamp put under a basket.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first churches mixed slaves and free, Jews and Greeks, the educated and the unlettered, and the Spirit’s gifts crossed every one of those lines: a slave might teach, and an educated Greek might serve tables. Now: Churches still drift toward two opposite errors: prizing the visible, up-front gifts until a hierarchy forms, or overlooking the ordinary gifts until people conclude they have nothing to give. Romans 12:6–8 holds the balance: every gift, faithfully used, is grace from God and service to the body.

verseByVerse.quote: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. — Romans 12:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by the grace given to me. Paul speaks with apostolic authority, which itself was a gift of grace (1:5; 15:15). He speaks from the same received grace he is commending.

I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think. Paul uses words built on the verb think (phroneō) four times in one line: do not over-think (hyperphroneō) yourself beyond what you ought to think, but think so as to be sound-minded (sōphroneō). The first fruit of a renewed mind is a right view of yourself. And it is addressed to everyone among you, not only the leaders or the gifted, because Paul expects to find pride in every person in the room.

Why this comes first. Pride is often the last thing in a person to be renewed and the first to corrupt everything else, and Paul goes straight on to describe the church as a body (v. 4). A body cannot function if every member has privately concluded it is the head. The same verb returns as the love section closes, do not think high things and never be wise in your own sight (v. 16), so humility stands at the beginning and the end of everything Paul says about the church in verses 3–16.

But to think with sober judgment. To think soberly (sōphroneō) is to have a sound, sensible mind: not solemn, but realistic, neither inflated nor falsely humble, an estimate of yourself that is not under the influence of anything. The man who says he is no good at anything is not being humble but inaccurate, and often he is fishing for a compliment. False modesty is still pride: it has learned that running yourself down wins more praise than boasting. A sober mind can say “I am good at this” in a level voice, because the sentence is a fact about a gift rather than a claim about a person.

The mind that was in Christ. Paul’s verb here, phroneō, is the one he reaches for to describe the mind of Christ himself: have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:5–6). There is sober thinking in its perfect form. Christ alone could have thought of himself as highly as possible without exaggeration, and his true knowledge of himself made him stoop, all the way to the cross. And the cross makes sober thinking possible for us. Whoever has stood there knows what he was worth without grace and what he was worth to God, and those two facts kill pride from opposite sides.

Each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. “Measure” (metron) is portion, allotment. Some take the measure of faith as the standard of faith, the same for all: the gospel itself. Others take it as the amount of faith or gifting given to each. Either way, what you have was given, so there is no room for boasting: what do you have that you did not receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7). And it rules out comparing yourself with others: let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbour (Galatians 6:4). The measure was assigned to you. Nobody else was issued yours.

Does God give different amounts of saving faith? No. Saving faith is not graded; the weakest faith in Christ saves as surely as the strongest, because it is Christ who saves, not the strength of your grip on him. A trembling hand receives the gift as truly as a steady one. The measure of faith here is the portion God has given each believer for the service he has called him to, which is why Paul goes straight on to the different gifts (vv. 4–8; 1 Corinthians 12:11).
