So never conclude that because your faith feels small, you are less saved than someone else. You may be less mature, and you should want to grow; but you are not less justified.

How can I tell healthy confidence from pride? Pride needs to be noticed and compared; sober confidence does not. Ask a few honest questions. When someone else is praised for the thing you do well, are you glad or stung? When you are corrected, do you listen or defend? Do you use your gift to serve others, or to be seen? Can you thank God for your ability without needing anyone else to mention it? Healthy confidence knows its gift, uses it, and is happy for others to have greater ones. Pride is restless until it is ranked. The cure for both pride and false modesty is the same: look at what you have as given, and at the Giver as worthy.
verseByVerse.note: A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphronein) but to think with sober judgment (sōphronein).

verseByVerse.quote: For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as in one body we have many members. One of Paul’s favourite pictures of the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 4:15–16). A body is one, yet has many parts, and the metaphor carries a bluntness we tend to soften: parts of a body are not detachable. A hand that leaves the arm does not become an independent hand with its own plans; it becomes a dead hand, quite quickly, and the arm does not do well either. Separation is an injury to two parties.

And the members do not all have the same function. “Function” (praxis) is activity, work. An eye sees; a hand works. Difference is not a problem but the design, and that is worth saying to the person who has quietly concluded he is peripheral. Almost everything keeping your own body alive at this moment is something you have never thought about, could not point to, and would not miss until it stopped.

So we, though many, are one body in Christ. Our unity is real, because we are all joined to the same Christ, and the Supper makes it visible. The bread is a participation in the body of Christ, and because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread (1 Corinthians 10:16–17). The church is one body because one body was given for it. We were gathered round a broken body, not shared interests. So no member may write off another: Christ did not die for a club, but for a body he means to keep whole. He did not save us one by one and leave us to find our own way; he made us a body, his body, with his life running through every member.

And individually members one of another. The last phrase is stranger than it sounds. Paul does not say we are members of the body, which would be tidy, but members of one another. The belonging runs directly between people. You need them, and they need you.

Do I really need to join a local church? Yes, if you can. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who belong to Christ but to no congregation. Believers were baptised and added to a church (Acts 2:41–42), they had elders who watched over them (Hebrews 13:17), and they met together, which Hebrews tells us not to neglect (Hebrews 10:24–25). Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you, correct you, or receive your gifts. Commit to a faithful local church where the gospel is preached, the ordinances are kept, and members care for one another. If illness or circumstances keep you housebound, ask the church to bring its fellowship to you.

What if a church has hurt me? Then you are not alone, and your pain is real. Some churches have wounded people badly, and where there was abuse it must be named, reported where it is a crime, and never covered up. But the answer to a sick body is not to live as a severed hand; it is, in time, to find a healthy body. Take your time, pray, and look for a church where the gospel is clear, leaders are accountable, and people are gentle. Tell a pastor there what happened. Christ has not given up on his church, and he has not given up on healing you within it.

In everyday life. The useful question is not whether you are one of the parts people can name. It is whether anything would stop if you did. In most congregations there are two or three people about whom nobody thinks and without whom nothing would happen by Thursday. Find out who they are in your church and thank them this week. And if you are one of them, take heart: the body knows what it would lose, even if it never says so.

verseByVerse.quote: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us. “Gifts” (charismata) come from “grace” (charis): a gift is a piece of grace, made specific and handed to a named person for building up the body. It is not earned and not chosen by us, for the Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). The ability you have is not a reward for the grace you received. It is more grace.

Let us use them. The Greek has no verb, but the sense is clear. Gifts are for using, not admiring. Possessing a gift without exercising it is a failure of stewardship, like a servant burying his master’s money in the ground (Matthew 25:25).

Spoils from an ascended King. When Christ ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8). In Psalm 68 the conqueror goes up and receives tribute; Paul sees the risen Christ, having won, handing the spoils out. He goes on giving them, so that no congregation is ever left without what it needs to be built up. Every gift in a congregation is a piece of the victory of Easter. The deacon who mends the boiler and the woman who knows which widow needs a visit were given by a Lord who gives because he has conquered, not because we have earned.

If prophecy, in proportion to our faith. Prophecy (prophēteia) in the New Testament was speaking a message revealed by God for the church (1 Corinthians 14:3, 29–31). In proportion to our faith is literally according to the analogy (analogia) of the faith. It may mean according to the measure of faith given to the prophet (v. 3), or in agreement with the faith, the body of truth already revealed. From the second, Reformed interpreters drew the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture, and no teaching may contradict the rest of God’s word. Both readings keep the gift under an authority outside the gifted person.

Where Christians differ: does prophecy continue today? Continuationists (Christians who believe all the gifts of the New Testament church continue today) believe the gift of prophecy continues in the church, giving new messages from God, usually understood as words prompted by the Spirit, to be weighed by the church (1 Corinthians 14:29) and never equal to Scripture. This commentary’s view: The gift of prophecy, in the sense of new revelation from God, belonged to the foundation period of the church, laid by apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). With the completion of Scripture, the canon is closed, and no new revelation is to be added (Hebrews 1:1–2; the Westminster Confession 1.1, 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.1, 1.6). Continuationists answer that New Testament prophecy was a fallible human report of the Spirit’s prompting, to be weighed; but a word truly from God cannot be fallible, and a church that receives new words alongside Scripture will soon be ruled by them. Today the prophetic function continues in a secondary sense through faithful preaching, which applies Scripture to the church with power, as one who speaks oracles of God (1 Peter 4:11). This view is held charitably: many continuationist brothers and sisters love Christ, and their churches are often marked by warm prayer and evangelistic zeal; and everyone agrees that any claimed word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

How do I find my gift? Not chiefly by a questionnaire, but by serving. Begin where there is need: the crèche rota, the welcome team, visiting the sick, the washing-up after church. Notice what bears fruit and what others in the church recognise in you, and keep going. Gifts are given to serve one another as good stewards of God’s varied grace (1 Peter 4:10), so they are found in the serving, not before it. And look at what is not on Paul’s list. There is no gift of being impressive, and nothing here that would look like much from a distance. Serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, being kind to people in trouble: that is the inventory, and most of it happens where nobody is watching. If you have concluded you have no gift, check whether you have been searching the wrong list.

Are natural talents spiritual gifts? Often God uses the abilities he gave you at birth, for he is the Creator as well as the Redeemer; a gifted organiser or a natural carer may find that the Spirit takes up those abilities for the church. But a talent becomes a gift to the body when it is given over to Christ and used in love to build others up. Some abilities appear only after conversion, and some natural talents are never meant for church use at all. The test is not where the ability came from, but whether it is being used to serve the body by grace, in humility.

verseByVerse.quote: ...if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. — Romans 12:7–8
verseByVerse.commentary:
If service, in our serving. “Service” (diakonia) is practical help, the root of our word deacon. And the list changes shape halfway through. The first items simply repeat themselves: the one who serves, in his serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching. That sounds like saying the same thing twice, but it is a correction. A great deal of activity can gather around a gift without being the gift: meetings about the serving, and opinions about it. Paul’s instruction is to get on with the thing itself.

The one who teaches, in his teaching. Explaining and applying God’s truth (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 2:2). The teacher is called to teach, not to perform or to be admired for teaching.

The one who exhorts, in his exhortation. “Exhorts” is parakaleō, the same word as the appeal of v. 1. Teaching informs the mind; exhortation moves the will. The church needs the one who comes alongside and says, now do it, and I will help you.

The one who contributes, in generosity. Giving to others’ needs. “Generosity” (haplotēs) means simplicity, single-mindedness: a gift with one motive in it and no second agenda folded underneath, giving without hidden motives or holding back (2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11).

The one who leads, with zeal. “Leads” (proistēmi, stands before, presides) is used of elders (1 Thessalonians 5:12; 1 Timothy 5:17). Lead with diligence and earnestness, not laziness. Because it stands between giving and mercy, some take it in its other sense, to give aid.

The one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. Caring for the sick, poor and suffering. “Cheerfulness” (hilarotēs) is a glad, willing heart, not a grudging one (our word hilarity comes from it, but it means gladness, not laughter), and Paul uses its cousin when he says God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Mercy done with a martyr’s air does more harm than good.

The manner can cancel the gift. The last three items do not repeat themselves. Each names a manner: generosity, zeal, cheerfulness. And this is where gifts most often go wrong. A person can exercise the right gift in a way that damages the person receiving it. Everyone has met the merciful helper who leaves you feeling like a case, or the giver whose gift arrives with strings. The gift was real; the manner cancelled it.

The manner of the Lord. Every gift on this list was exercised first, and perfectly, by Christ, and in the very manner Paul names. Paul calls him a servant (diakonos) (15:8). He gave, not a portion with strings attached, but himself (Galatians 2:20). He leads his flock as the great shepherd of the sheep (Hebrews 13:20). And his mercy never wore a martyr’s air: in his own parable the shepherd who finds the lost sheep lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:5). That is why the manner matters so much. A gift exercised grudgingly does not only disappoint the person receiving it; it misrepresents the Lord whose gift it is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean this is a complete list of gifts (compare 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Peter 4:10–11). Nor does it mean that those without a particular gift are excused from the duty. All must serve, give and show mercy. The gifted do so in a special way.

What if I serve but feel no cheerfulness? Do not stop serving; ask God to change the heart behind the hands. Cheerfulness is not a mood you can switch on, but it grows from remembering why you serve: Christ came not to be served but to serve and to give his life (Mark 10:45), and he served you first. Sometimes the lack of joy is a sign of tiredness, and you need rest or to share the load; sometimes it is a sign that you are serving to be noticed, and the remedy is to serve somewhere no one will see. Pray before you serve, think of the person rather than the task, and give thanks afterwards. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it.

For worship. Nothing on this list needs a stage: the Son of God did most of his work with a towel and a basin. And he has not finished serving. He said that when the master comes home and finds his servants awake, he will dress himself for service, have them recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). That is the Lord whose gifts we hold: the King of glory, who means one day to wait on his servants at his own table.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — Love in Action: The Ethics of the Transformed Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–21 are a run of short commands, and they begin and end with love: let love be genuine (v. 9), and overcome evil with good (v. 21). Between them love widens from the church to outsiders and at last to enemies: not a programme for earning anything but the shape of a life grace has taken hold of.

The burning coals of v. 20 are not a promise that kindness will make your enemy suffer more; they are most naturally read as the shame that leads to repentance. The aim is not a defeated enemy but one who has stopped being one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ethic of the Cross in Daily Life

Romans 12:9–21 shows what the cross looks like in daily life. The crucified Christ did not retaliate; he prayed for those who crucified him and overcame evil by giving himself. The believer who blesses his persecutor is not merely keeping a rule. He knows he was once God’s enemy and has been loved into the family, and he is doing to others what was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman church held slaves and freedmen, members of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22), wealthy patrons and poor migrants, and friction between them was a daily danger. Now: Churches are still divided by income, education, race and status. The question is not whether a church approves of diversity in principle but whether its members weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice across every line the world draws.

verseByVerse.quote: Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. — Romans 12:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let love be genuine. The heading of verses 9–21. “Love” is agapē, self-giving love. “Genuine” (anypokritos) comes from the theatre: a hypokritēs was an actor speaking his lines from behind a mask. Love that is anypokritos is love with the mask off: not love that is always warm, which no one can manage, but love that is not performing a warmth it does not have. There was once a love entirely without a mask. The Son of God came among us and never performed a warmth he did not have: every word to the leper, every look at Peter, every tear at Lazarus’ tomb was real.

In the flow. Paul moves from gifts (vv. 6–8) straight to love, as in 1 Corinthians 12 and 13, because gifts without love are noise. Verse 9 is the heading, and verses 10–21 fill it in, widening ring by ring from the church to the enemy: the mercies of God (v. 1) passed on to other people.

Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. This keeps love from turning into a mood, and both verbs are violent. “Abhor” (apostygeō) is to loathe, to shudder at. “Hold fast” (kollaō) is to join closely, to cleave, the word used of a man holding fast to his wife (Matthew 19:5): two things so joined that they tear if you separate them. The sentimental version, which treats love as universal acceptance, cannot abhor anything, and so it cannot hold fast to anything either. Real love hates what harms the beloved, and a love with no hatreds in it is not deep enough to hold anybody.

Love one another with brotherly affection. Verse 10 stacks two family words: philadelphia, love of brothers and sisters, and philostorgos, built on storgē, the unchosen affection of people who belong to each other by birth. The church is not being asked to be a pleasant society. It is being asked to have the texture of a family, including the part where you did not pick them.

Brothers of the firstborn. The church can be asked for family affection because it really is a family, and it is one because of Christ. God predestined his people to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers (8:29), and the Son is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He did not choose us for our compatibility; he brought each of us, unlikely and unlovely, into his Father’s house by the same door. To withhold warmth from the person in the next pew is to treat as a stranger someone Christ calls his brother.

Outdo one another in showing honor. The verb can also mean to go first, or to prefer one another in honour (Philippians 2:3). In a status-conscious culture Paul does not tell the church to stop competing. He changes the contest: the winner is the one who honours others first, before anyone has earned it.

How can I love people in church I do not naturally like? Begin with what love does, not with what you feel. Agapē is not liking; it is willing and doing someone’s good. You can pray for his good, speak well of him, greet him warmly, ask about his week, and help him when he needs it, all while your feelings lag behind. Very often feelings follow. Remember too that you belong to him and he to you, by the same blood of Christ, and that God chose you both knowing exactly what you are like. If there is a real wrong between you, deal with it honestly (Matthew 18:15). If it is simply that he grates on you, he is probably one of God’s chosen tools for making you more like Christ.

Does hating evil mean hating people who do evil? No. Paul says hate what is evil, not who. A Christian hates sin most of all in himself, and he hates what sin does to those he loves. But he is to love his neighbour, and even his enemy, as this chapter goes on to say (vv. 14, 20). Think of a doctor who hates cancer precisely because he loves his patient. In the same way, the more you love someone, the more you hate the lies, the addictions and the cruelties that are destroying him. Love that refuses to hate evil cannot help anyone, and hatred of evil without love becomes a kind of evil itself.

In everyday life. Find someone in your church today and be the first to honour them: a word of thanks, a note, a meal, a real compliment. And if, when a friend is praised for the very thing you also do, you catch a flicker of something sour before you have arranged your face, that flicker is what the mask in this verse covers. Confess it, for Christ has already forgiven it, and then go and honour that friend.

parallels.desc: hate evil, and love good

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be slothful in zeal. The phrase joins two words that ought not to fit. “Slothful” (oknēros: hesitant, sluggish) is Proverbs’ word for the sluggard, and “zeal” (spoudē) is diligence, eagerness. How is a person lazy at zeal? Very easily; it is a common condition in a long-standing Christian. Nothing has been renounced and no doctrine abandoned; the effort has simply stopped, gradually, without a decision. This is not the same as exhaustion, grief or depression, which can drain a faithful believer of all feeling while his faith holds; those call for rest, care and help, not rebuke.

Be fervent in spirit. “Fervent” (zeō) means to boil. The ESV notes that this can also be read as fervent in the Spirit, and both are true. Luke uses the same word of Apollos, fervent in spirit as he taught accurately the things concerning Jesus (Acts 18:25). The opposite is not coldness. Most people who need this command are lukewarm, a temperature that takes no energy to maintain, and which the risen Christ finds sickening (Revelation 3:16).

Serve the Lord. As slaves (douleuō) of the Lord Jesus, not of our own projects. Zeal without this direction can be dangerous; Paul himself had once been zealous for God in persecuting the church (Philippians 3:6). A few manuscripts read serve the time, but serve the Lord is the better reading.

Rejoice in hope. The hope of glory (5:2; 8:24–25). The three clauses are not three separate topics but one situation handled three ways, and the situation is trouble. Rejoice in hope looks forward to how it ends.

Be patient in tribulation. “Patient” (hypomenō) is to endure, to remain under the load, and there is a great difference between remaining under something and merely waiting for it to pass. Tribulation (thlipsis: pressure, affliction) is expected (5:3).

Be constant in prayer. “Constant” (proskartereō) is to persist, to devote yourself to, with the sense of stubbornly not letting go. It is the word used of the first church devoting itself to the prayers (Acts 2:42). Prayer talks to God about the trouble throughout, and it is how hope and patience are kept alive.

The Lord who never cooled. The Lord we serve is the one person in whom every clause of these verses was true without a lapse. When he cleared the temple his disciples remembered the psalm, zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17; Psalm 69:9), a psalm Paul applies to Christ in this letter (15:3). For the joy set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2): hope rejoicing, and patience under the heaviest tribulation ever carried. He prayed in Gethsemane while his friends slept. So Christian zeal is not a temperament. It is likeness to a Master who was never lukewarm for one hour, and who served us before he asked us to serve him.

What do I do when my zeal has gone cold? Do not wait to feel fervent before you return. Go back to the means God uses to light the fire: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, and the fellowship of warm believers. Remember the mercies of verse 1; zeal is fed by grace, not by guilt. Ask whether something has crept in to cool you, an unconfessed sin, an idol, exhaustion, or a grievance, and deal with it. Ask the Spirit to set your heart alight again, as he did at the first; Christ told a cooling church to remember from where it had fallen, repent, and do the works it did at first (Revelation 2:5). And be patient: embers can be fanned into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

What if prayer feels dead? Keep praying anyway, because constancy, not feeling, is the command. Use the Psalms, which give words to every state of soul, including the dry ones (Psalm 42; 63). Pray short, honest prayers through the day rather than waiting for a perfect hour. Pray with others, for their warmth can carry you. And remember that prayer is not measured by how it feels to you but by who hears it: your Father hears, the Son intercedes for you (8:34), and the Spirit helps you in your weakness when you do not know what to pray (8:26).

For worship. The fire that keeps a Christian warm was not lit by the Christian. John the Baptist said of the One coming after him that he would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11), and the risen Christ, exalted at the right hand of God, poured out the promised Spirit on his waiting church (Acts 2:33). Every tired saint still praying in the dark is carrying a coal from that fire. And the One who kindled it tends it still: a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3; Matthew 12:20). Our fervour runs low; his love for us never has.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “fervent in spirit” can also be read “fervent in the Spirit.”

verseByVerse.quote: Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Contribute to the needs of the saints. “Contribute” (koinōneō) is to share, to have fellowship. Christians share their goods with Christians in need (Acts 2:44–45; Galatians 6:10). Paul himself was collecting for the poor believers in Jerusalem as he wrote (15:25–26). The movement from the inward life of vv. 11–12 to the outward life is immediate: a boiling spirit shows itself in an open purse.

And seek to show hospitality. “Seek” (diōkō) is to pursue, to chase, and Paul uses the same word in the very next clause for those who persecute you. Some are hunting you; you are to be out hunting for strangers to feed. Hospitality (philoxenia) is literally love of strangers, not of friends; the stranger is the test. In a world of poor and dangerous inns, opening your home to travelling believers was vital and costly (Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5–8). This is the hospitality of God. We were strangers and enemies, and he did not wait for us to turn up; he came looking for us, pursued us, and set a table for us in his house.

Bless those who persecute you. A turn toward outsiders, and Paul is not laying down a rule of his own. He is echoing his Master: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28; Matthew 5:44). To bless (eulogeō) is to speak well of, and to ask God’s good for.

The persecutor who was blessed. Paul knew this command from the receiving end. Diōkō, the verb for persecute, is the word the risen Christ used on the Damascus road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The man hunting the church was met by the Lord he was hunting, and Christ did not curse him. He left him blind for three days, then sent a disciple to lay hands on him, call him brother, and give him back his sight (Acts 9:17). Every time Paul told a church to bless its persecutors, he was describing how he had been treated. A Christian who blesses an enemy is passing on the kindness that found him.

Bless and do not curse them. Do not call down harm on enemies. Jesus prayed for his executioners (Luke 23:34); Stephen did the same as the stones fell (Acts 7:60). And there is mercy in the verb. To bless is to speak well, so the command is first about what you say, not what you feel, and that is something you can do this afternoon while feeling nothing appropriate whatsoever. Say something true and good about them to God, and leave unsaid what you were going to say about them to somebody else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring injustice or refusing to seek legal protection. Blessing a persecutor is something you do with your mouth about a person; it is not a requirement to stay within his reach or to call what was done acceptable (see vv. 17–18).

How does this fit with the psalms that call down curses on enemies? Those prayers hand the enemy over to God’s justice rather than taking revenge, which is exactly what Paul commands a few verses later (v. 19). The Christian may still pray that God will stop the wicked and do right, and cry out for justice for the oppressed. What he may not do is wish evil on a person in his own name. His word to and about his persecutor is blessing, and his deepest prayer for him is that he will repent and be saved, as Saul the persecutor was.

Does hospitality need a big house or a lot of money? No. Hospitality is a matter of an open heart, not a large kitchen. A pot of soup, a cup of tea, a lift to church, a seat beside you after the service, or an invitation to join your family’s ordinary meal can all be hospitality. Hospitality in the early church was not only for the wealthy: the Macedonians gave out of extreme poverty (2 Corinthians 8:2), and a table can be generous without being grand. Start small and simple: invite the newcomer, the international student, the widow, the single person who goes home alone. The aim is not to impress, which turns hospitality into entertaining, but to welcome, as Christ has welcomed you (15:7).
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travelling believers was vital in a world of poor, unsafe inns.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Weeping with the weeping is often called the harder half. But there is a case for the other order. Grief invites sympathy, an emotion we are practised at; there is even a quiet satisfaction in being the one who sat with someone. Another person’s good news invites comparison instead, and it usually arrives exactly where you wanted news of your own: the pregnancy, the job, the child doing well. Rejoicing with the rejoicing can be the harder half, and nobody notices you doing it. Both ask you to take your emotional cue from somebody else’s life rather than your own. Love does both, for if one member suffers, all suffer together, and if one member is honoured, all rejoice together (1 Corinthians 12:26).

Live in harmony with one another. Literally, think the same thing toward one another: be of one mind, not in every opinion, but in shared purpose and care.

Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. “Haughty” is literally thinking high things. “Associate with” (synapagō) means to be carried along with, the word used of Barnabas being carried away by others’ hypocrisy (Galatians 2:13): losing your footing and going where the current goes. Paul turns it into a virtue and points it downward. The instruction is not to be kind to people beneath you, which leaves you above them, but to let yourself be carried into their company and concerns until the phrase “beneath you” stops meaning anything.

The friend of the lowly. Every clause here describes Christ before it describes us. He went to a wedding and kept its joy from running dry (John 2:1–11), and when he met a widow following her only son’s coffin, he had compassion on her (Luke 7:13). He did not think high things. He let himself be carried into the company of fishermen, tax collectors, lepers and children, until his enemies’ sneer, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19), became one of his truest titles. The Lord of glory chose the company of the lowly, and a church that will not sit with them has not yet understood whose body it is.

Never be wise in your own sight. From Proverbs 3:7, and Paul used the phrase a chapter ago, when he revealed the mystery of Israel so that Gentile believers would not be wise in their own sight (11:25). There it guarded the church against contempt for outsiders. Here the same words guard it against contempt for the people in the next seat.

What do I say to someone who is grieving? Often very little. Job’s friends did best in the first seven days, when they sat with him in silence (Job 2:13), and worst when they began to explain. Go, sit, listen, and let them talk about the one they have lost. Say you are sorry and that you love them. Do not rush to explain the loss, compare it with your own, or tell them how they should feel. Weep if you weep; Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). Then keep coming back, weeks and months later, when everyone else has moved on. Practical help, a meal, a lift, a note on the anniversary, often speaks more than words.

What if I cannot feel glad about someone else’s good news? Be honest with God about it; envy confessed is already losing its grip. Then act in love before the feeling arrives: congratulate them sincerely, thank God aloud for their blessing, and pray for them. Remind yourself that their blessing was not taken from you; God is not poorer for giving to them, and his plans for you are not smaller. And look at what envy is: a quiet complaint against God’s generosity (Matthew 20:15). The more you rest in Christ as your treasure, the freer you become to be glad when others receive good things.

parallels.desc: be not wise in your own eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repay no one evil for evil. The instinct to pay back is strong; the Christian breaks the cycle (Matthew 5:38–39; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 1 Peter 3:9). What is forbidden is repayment, evil for evil, not the pursuit of justice, which Paul will soon place in the hands of the magistrate. The two must be kept apart, because confusing them has done real harm to people who were told that reporting a crime was unchristian.

When he was reviled. Peter sets this same command in front of the cross. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). And Peter will not let it be only an example. In the next breath he says that Christ “himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Christ could absorb evil without returning it because he was carrying it away. So we can refuse to settle accounts: ours was settled at the cross, and every other will be settled by the One who judges justly.

But give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. “Give thought” (pronoeō) is a verb of forward planning. Honourable means what even unbelievers recognise as good and noble (Proverbs 3:4; 2 Corinthians 8:21), and such conduct commends the gospel. It does not happen by accident. It is arranged beforehand by someone who has decided in a calm hour what he will do in a hot one.

If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. The command carries two careful limits, and they are there out of kindness. If possible: sometimes peace is impossible without betraying truth. So far as it depends on you: you cannot control others, only yourself. He concedes that some relationships cannot be at peace, and that this will sometimes not be your fault. That matters enormously to the person who takes the whole weight of every broken relationship onto himself. Your responsibility ends where your conduct ends; it does not extend to an outcome that needs another person’s cooperation. And that cuts the other way too: if peace fails, the honest question is whether you had first done everything that depended on you. God himself did everything that depended on him, and more, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). He did not repay our evil with evil; he repaid it with the good of his Son.

Does living at peace mean I must reconcile with someone who abused me? No, not in the sense of restoring closeness or trust. Forgiveness, letting go of revenge and handing the case to God, is commanded of every Christian. Reconciliation, the rebuilding of a relationship, takes two, and it requires real repentance and changed behaviour on the other side. With someone who has abused you, safety comes first, and it may be right to keep your distance permanently, to report what happened, and to involve the authorities. As far as it depends on you means you do not seek his harm and you do not stir up conflict; it never means you must put yourself or others back in harm’s way. Abuse is never to be tolerated in the name of peace.

What about conflicts in church, especially over truth? Seek peace earnestly, but never by abandoning the gospel. Paul, who wrote this verse, opposed Peter to his face when the gospel was at stake (Galatians 2:11–14). Most church conflicts, though, are not about the gospel. They are about preferences, personalities, money and hurt pride, and these call for humility, patience, speaking directly to the person rather than about him (Matthew 18:15), and a readiness to give way. Ask before any conflict: is this a matter of Scripture, or of my preference? Hold firmly to the first, and hold the second lightly.

In everyday life. Is there someone you are at odds with? Apologise for your share, plainly, without adding a but, and leave the rest to God; the Spirit whose fruit is peace (Galatians 5:22) lives in you for exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." To the contrary, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, never avenge yourselves. Paul chooses this moment, of all the moments in the chapter, to call them beloved. It is the only word of affection in these thirteen verses, and it lands immediately before the hardest thing he asks. People are not argued out of revenge. Affection can do what argument cannot.

But leave it to the wrath of God. Literally, give place to wrath: step aside and make room, like someone standing in a doorway who is told to move because something else is coming through. You are not being told the wrong was small enough to absorb. The matter is too serious to be left with the injured party, the one person guaranteed to judge it badly: far too harshly or, just as often, far too leniently, because he wants it all to stop. It is being moved to a competent court, for justice belongs to God, and he will do it perfectly, in part through the governing authorities of the next chapter.

For it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. From Deuteronomy 32:35, the Song of Moses, which Paul has already used at 10:19: the song God gave Israel to sing about their own future, and it contains both the mercy to the Gentiles that provokes Israel to jealousy and the vengeance that lets the wronged leave justice with God.

Where the vengeance goes. God does not say vengeance will be dropped. He says it is his, and the New Testament tells us what he has done with it. For everyone who trusts Christ it has already fallen, on the Son whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood (3:25), so that every wrong a believer has done, including every wrong done by one believer to another, was paid for at the cross. For the rest it waits for the day when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). Either way it is in his hands. No one escapes justice because you held back; the only question is whether his sin is answered at Calvary or at the judgment seat, and you are free to pray that it will be Calvary. So you can let go.

To the contrary, if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. From Proverbs 25:21–22, and this is where most people quietly stop reading. The instruction is concrete: food and drink, the two things a body needs today. Paul does not ask for a change of heart before you act. He asks for a meal, which you can give while your heart is still exactly where it was.

For by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head. This probably means bringing the enemy to shame and repentance through unexpected kindness: the burning pain of conscience. Some connect it with an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried a pan of coals on his head as a sign of remorse. Both point the same way, and Proverbs ends the couplet not with the enemy’s ruin but with the promise that the LORD will reward you. Kindness is not a clever way to hurt your enemy more. The goal is not an enemy outmanoeuvred by your virtue but an enemy who stops being one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean crime should go unpunished: reporting a crime or leaving a dangerous house is not vengeance but one of the ways God answers this verse.

Where Christians differ: does this forbid self-defence? Some Christians, from the Anabaptists (the radical wing of the Reformation, whose heirs include the Mennonites) to modern pacifists, hold that a follower of Jesus must never use force, and they cite our Lord’s command to turn to him the other also (Matthew 5:39). This commentary’s view: Vengeance comes after the harm, to pay it back; defence comes during it, to stop it. The law allowed a householder to strike a thief breaking in at night (Exodus 22:2), and Scripture commands us to rescue those who are being taken away to death (Proverbs 24:11). In Matthew 5 Jesus speaks of an insult, a slap on the cheek, not an attack on life. So Christians may use proportionate force to protect themselves and especially others, and the state may wield the sword. What they may not do is retaliate. Christians who hold the pacifist view are to be respected as brothers who are trying to follow Christ’s word.

Is a God who takes vengeance not a cruel God? No: it is a God who refuses to shrug at evil. Picture a man whose family was murdered. If God simply overlooked it, that would not be kindness but indifference, and it would leave the victim alone with his rage. Because God will repay, the wronged person can put down the weapon; he no longer has to carry justice himself. And God’s vengeance is never spite. It is the holy Judge doing right (Genesis 18:25), slow to anger, taking no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and he has already borne its full weight himself, at the cross, for everyone who will come to him.

Must I forgive someone who has not said sorry? In your heart, yes: lay down revenge and wish him good, as Jesus prayed for those crucifying him; full reconciliation waits on his repentance (Luke 17:3). (See Luke 23:34 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. We were his enemies once, hungry and thirsty and without excuse, and God did to us what this verse tells us to do. He did not starve us out. He fed us with the bread of life and gave us living water to drink (John 6:35; 4:14), and the coals of that kindness were heaped on our heads until we burned with shame and turned to him. Every believer is an enemy who was given a meal instead of a sentence. The vengeance that was his by right, he kept in his own hands, and then he opened those hands to feed us.
verseByVerse.note: Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and a change of heart through kindness.

parallels.desc: vengeance is mine
if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be overcome by evil. “Overcome” is nikaō, conquer, used twice in one line, and in the first half you are the one conquered. The danger named first is not that you will do something wrong but that a wrong done to you will go on working in you after the deed is over. Evil can win a match inside a person long after the original injury is over. Being wronged is not defeat; becoming like the wrongdoer is.

A familiar condition renamed. The verse renames something we all recognise. The man who was genuinely wronged, who was right about it, and who is now permanently harder, sharper with his family, quicker to assume the worst, unable to speak about a whole category of people without an edge, has not been defeated by an argument. He has been overcome, in exactly Paul’s sense. The wrong done to him has gone on to do a second wrong: it has changed him.

But overcome evil with good. Goodness is the weapon that defeats evil. This is not a retreat into niceness: return evil and you have agreed to fight on ground the enemy chose. This is how Christ conquered: by suffering, forgiving, and doing good to his enemies. God did not overcome the world’s evil with mere force but with sacrificial love, for while we were still sinners, while we were enemies, Christ died for us (5:8, 10). The cross is not only the supreme example of this; it is the victory itself. Evil threw everything it had at Christ and was overcome, not by a greater violence but by a greater love.

In the flow. Verse 21 gathers up verses 14–21 and reaches back to verse 2: the call not to be conformed to this age ends in the refusal to be conformed to your enemy. And good and evil come back at once in 13:3–4: the private person overcomes evil with good, and God has also appointed public hands to restrain it (12:19; 13:4). The chapter that opened by asking for a body on an altar closes by asking for a body that does not hit back, and both requests are made by the mercies of God.

What if the evil keeps going and good seems to change nothing? Then keep doing good, and remember that the outcome belongs to God. Overcoming evil with good does not always change the other person; sometimes it only keeps evil from changing you, and that is already a victory. The cross looked like defeat on Friday. Joseph waited years before he saw what God had done with his brothers’ evil. Do not grow weary of doing good, for in due season you will reap, if you do not give up (Galatians 6:9). Where the evil is ongoing harm, doing good may mean protecting the vulnerable, telling the truth and calling in the authorities. Good is not the same as giving in.

In everyday life. When someone does you wrong today, ask what good you can do in return. And bring the older wrongs to Christ as well: name one way the worst thing done to you has changed you, and ask him whether it is a wound to be healed or a hold to be broken. He does both, and he does not wait for you to have sorted out which it is before he begins.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.<sup>2</sup>Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.<sup>3</sup>For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.<sup>4</sup>For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,<sup>5</sup>so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.<sup>6</sup>Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;<sup>7</sup>if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching;<sup>8</sup>the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness.<sup>9</sup>Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.<sup>10</sup>Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.<sup>11</sup>Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord.<sup>12</sup>Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.<sup>13</sup>Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality.<sup>14</sup>Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.<sup>15</sup>Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.<sup>16</sup>Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.<sup>17</sup>Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all.<sup>18</sup>If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.<sup>19</sup>Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”<sup>20</sup>To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”<sup>21</sup>Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

13.title: Citizens of Two Kingdoms
13.overview:
Romans 13 turns to two parts of the Christian’s life in the world that seem unrelated but belong together: the governing authorities (vv. 1–7) and the debt of love that fulfils the law (vv. 8–14). Both apply the renewed mind of 12:2 to ordinary social life: the Christian lives inside a civil order and a moral order, and both place real obligations on her.

The passage on government has been badly misused, both to demand passive submission to every kind of power and to excuse every kind of resistance. Paul teaches neither. He grounds civil authority in God’s own ordering of human society.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Governing Authorities: God's Servant for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Civil government is not a human invention that God merely tolerates. He established it for the good of human beings, and in their lawful work the magistrate, the soldier and the tax official are his servants, to keep order, punish evil and commend good.

Paul is not asking the Roman Christians to approve every policy of the emperor. He is asking them not to treat their citizenship in God’s kingdom as permission to ignore the civil order God has set up. The limits of submission come from the rest of Scripture (Acts 5:29), but the normal posture is submission. Watch for three things as you read: the warning of judgment in verse 2, the link between the avenger of verse 4 and the forbidden revenge of 12:19, and the motive of conscience in verse 5.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kingdoms and Civil Authority

The Reformers taught the doctrine of the two kingdoms as a framework for passages like Romans 13: the kingdom of God’s left hand (civil government) and of his right hand (the church). God governs civil life through natural law (the sense of right and wrong he has given all people) and common grace (his kindness to believer and unbeliever alike), and the church through his Word and Spirit. The two are distinct but not separate, and the Christian belongs to both: Caesar has his domain, Christ has his, and the two must never be confused.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman Christians had obvious reasons to view the imperial state with suspicion: it had crucified their Lord and would one day persecute them. Paul’s command to submit was not naive but grounded in God. Now: In a democracy, Romans 13 means paying taxes, respecting lawful authority, and working through lawful channels for justice. It does not require silent compliance with injustice; the Christian who uses those lawful means to oppose evil is not breaking verse 1 but serving verse 4’s picture of government as a servant of good.

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 12 forbade personal revenge and told the wronged Christian to leave it to the wrath of God; chapter 13 shows one way God carries out that wrath in this age: through the governing authorities. The Christian is a good citizen, a loving neighbour whose only standing debt is love, and a person dressed for the coming day. And the chapter that begins with Caesar on his throne ends with Christ as the believer’s clothing: every throne in it is under God, and the last word belongs to the King who is coming.

The setting. Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his reign, before his persecution of Christians in AD 64. Claudius had earlier expelled the Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2), Priscilla and Aquila among them (16:3). A small congregation that confessed Jesus, not Caesar, as Lord could easily be seen as a nest of rebels. Paul makes clear that the gospel does not make Christians revolutionaries, and he does it without flattering Rome for a moment: his whole argument rests on God, not on the emperor.

Be subject. “Every person” is literally every soul: no exceptions, apostles included. Paul could have written hypakouō, obey, the word he uses elsewhere of children and slaves. Instead he writes hypotassō, a word about rank and order: to take your place under an arrangement. A person can be genuinely subject to an arrangement and still decline a particular command inside it, which is precisely what the Christian martyrs did when they refused to offer incense to the emperor. They did not raise a hand against the arrest, the court or the sentence. They simply would not sin.

Instituted by God. “Instituted” (tassō, appointed, set in order) has the same root as the verb for “be subject”: God set the authorities in place, and we take our place under them. Government is God’s idea before it is anyone’s policy, and human authority is borrowed authority. Jesus told Pilate, who boasted of his power to release or crucify, that he would have no authority over him at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). Nebuchadnezzar had to learn that the Most High rules the kingdom of men (Daniel 4:32). The state’s proper work, order, justice and protection, serves God’s purposes even when the state itself does not acknowledge him. That is common grace, God’s kindness to believer and unbeliever alike. On leadership and order as God’s gift in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Whoever resists. “Resists” (antitassō) is a military word: to range yourself in battle order against something, the opposite of the ordering in verse 1. Paul is not describing a citizen who campaigns or votes against the government, or refuses one specific unjust demand. He is describing settled hostility to ordered authority itself, on the grounds that a person who now belongs to another kingdom has been released from this one. That temptation appears on the political right and on the left, with the same reasoning: my citizenship is in heaven, so these arrangements have no claim on me. Paul’s answer is that they have a claim on you because they have an Author, and that the alternative to imperfect order is not freedom but the strong doing as they please with the weak.

Will incur judgment. Judgment here comes in two ways: from God, whose order has been opposed, and through the state’s own punishment, which is one of the means God uses.

Thrones made through the Son. By the Son all things were created, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities: all things were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16). And since his resurrection he sits at the Father’s right hand, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion (Ephesians 1:20–21). So the order Paul tells us to respect is not a rival kingdom to Christ’s but a lower office within his. The Christian who submits to the magistrate is not trading one lord for another, and he knows that the magistrate himself has a Master. The Lord who told Pilate that his power came from above did not use his own power to escape Pilate. He submitted to an unjust court, a corrupt governor and a Roman cross, so that rebels against the throne of heaven could be pardoned. So the Christian can be the calmest citizen in the land: not because the rulers are good, but because the King is.

What it does not mean. This passage has been made to say all of the following. It does not say every ruler is good or every command must be carried out, or that rulers are above God’s law. It does not say a government may not be criticised, voted out, or taken to court, or that Christians may not vote, speak out, protest lawfully, or work to change laws.

Scripture refuses the absolutist reading. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed a direct royal order to kill baby boys, and God dealt well with them (Exodus 1:17–20). Three young men declined to bow to a state-erected image and said so to the king’s face (Daniel 3:18). Daniel went on praying against an explicit statute (Daniel 6:10). The apostles told the supreme council of their own nation, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). None of these is treated as a lapse. And in Revelation 13 power of the same kind appears as a beast rising out of the sea, making war on the saints (Revelation 13:7). A state is an ordinance of God and can become a monster, and the Christian is required to know which one he is looking at.

Where Christians differ: obedience and resistance. Some say Christians must obey the state in everything. Others say Christians may overthrow any unjust government. This commentary’s view: Christians must submit to the governing authorities in all lawful things, even when rulers are unbelievers or unjust (1 Peter 2:13–18). But no human authority can command what God forbids or forbid what God commands, and then we must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Such disobedience should be open, peaceful, and willing to accept the consequences, as the apostles accepted their beating and went away rejoicing (Acts 5:40–41). Reformed tradition has also taught that when rulers become tyrants who destroy the very purpose for which God gave them authority, lesser lawful magistrates may lead lawful resistance. Calvin allowed that lower magistrates, such as estates and parliaments, have a duty to restrain a king who savagely oppresses his people (Institutes 4.20.31), and later Reformed writers such as Samuel Rutherford built on that to justify resistance led by lawful authorities. Private Christians are not to take up arms against their government on their own authority. But where lawful authorities resist a ruler who has turned against the good he exists to serve (v. 4), they are not resisting God’s ordinance but upholding it. Such cases are rare and grave, a last resort, and never a private person’s revenge; the Westminster Confession (23.4) insists that even an unbelieving ruler’s lawful authority stands. Paul wrote these words under Nero, and his point here is the normal duty: submission.

Even wicked rulers? A reader naturally asks: was Nero instituted by God? Was a tyrant? Paul is speaking of two things at once. First, the office: government as such is God’s ordinance, his gift to restrain evil in a fallen world; anarchy is never his will. Second, God’s providence: no ruler comes to power apart from God’s sovereign rule, which sets up kings and removes them (Daniel 2:21; 4:17). Sometimes he gives a nation a wicked ruler as a judgment, as he used Assyria and Babylon (Isaiah 10:5; Jeremiah 27:6). That a ruler holds power by God’s providence does not mean God approves of what he does with it, any more than God approved of Pilate condemning Jesus (John 19:11). The ruler is accountable to God for every abuse, and will answer for it.

A guard that must be said aloud. This passage has been used by slaveholders against abolitionists, by governments against the people they were crushing, and, closer to home and more often, by individuals telling someone under their power that resistance is a sin. That is a misuse, and the text itself supplies the refutation. Verse 4 defines authority by its service to your good, and the ordering Paul tells you to submit to is one whose own laws forbid what is being done to you. A husband, a pastor or an employer who abuses is not the governing authority of Romans 13; he is the wrongdoer of Romans 13. Reporting a crime is not resisting the ordinance of God. It is using it.

How do I know whether a law actually requires me to sin? Ask whether it commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, not merely whether it is foolish, costly or unfair. Being made to pay a tax you think wasteful does not require sin. Being ordered to sign a false statement, to stop telling people about Christ, to deny him, to take part in harming the innocent, or to abandon the gathering of God’s people altogether would. Most cases are easy; the hard ones are rarer than our rhetoric suggests. When you are unsure, search the Scriptures, talk to your elders, and pray before you act. And if you must refuse, refuse respectfully and openly, without contempt, and be ready to bear the cost as Daniel was.

Does this still apply in a democracy, where the people choose the government? Yes, and in some ways it is easier to keep. In a democracy the governing authority is the whole lawful order: the constitution, the courts, the parliament and the officials it appoints. When you vote, write to your representative, campaign or take a case to court, you are not resisting that order; you are using the means it gives you. What Paul forbids is the attitude that treats the order itself as having no claim on you, whether that shows itself in quiet law-breaking, in contempt for those elected, or in refusing to accept a lawful result because your side lost.

In everyday life. Take the thing you are angriest at your government about and ask which of three it is: something you dislike, something that is unjust, or something that requires you personally to sin. The first is politics. The second calls for every lawful means you have. Only the third is the martyr’s question, and a Christian who treats the first as though it were the third has spent the credibility he will need if the third ever arrives.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his rule. Jesus had said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

parallels.desc: by me kings reign

verseByVerse.quote: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a terror to good conduct. Paul now says what government is for: to restrain evil and protect good. He describes what rulers are meant to be, and generally are, since even a bad government usually punishes theft and murder. When a ruler becomes a terror to good conduct, he is doing the opposite of what is described here, and Paul’s argument cannot be stretched to bless him. The passage tells us where authority comes from. It does not shield a ruler who abuses it.

Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? “Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval.” The way to live without fear of the police is to do right. And the small word “approval” deserves attention, because it is the half of the sentence nobody quotes. “Approval” (epainos) is praise. The state is not described here only as a punisher. It is also expected to commend what is good: the magistrate as an institution that notices decency and honours it, the award for bravery, the citizen thanked for handing in what he found. Any account of government drawn from this passage that produces only fear has read only one of its two halves.

God’s servant for your good. “Servant” is diakonos, minister, the same word used of deacons in the church and of Paul himself (1 Corinthians 3:5). The ruler is God’s minister whether he knows it or not, as the pagan Cyrus was (Isaiah 45:1). And his work is for your good: peace, order and justice, the safe street and the honest market, the conditions in which families can be raised and the gospel can be preached (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

Not in vain. The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including the power of death (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). God gave it real authority to use force. And Paul wrote this about the government that, by the church’s consistent tradition, later executed him with that very sword, on no just charge, under the same emperor. The sentence was never a compliment paid to Rome. It was a claim about God.

An avenger. In 12:19 Paul told the wronged Christian never to avenge himself but to leave it to the wrath of God. Here the magistrate is an avenger (ekdikos): the same word family in Greek, and the same wrath. So the state may do what the individual may not.

Where the wrath went. Wrath was never cancelled when it was taken out of your hands. You were asked to stop being the one who settles it, and here Paul tells you where some of it has gone: to the courts and the police, who have an address, a payroll and an office in your own city. Together 12:19 and 13:4 say something precise: justice is real, it matters enormously, and you personally are not the one authorised to administer it.

The sword and the innocent man. Once the servant of God bore the sword against the only innocent man who ever stood in his court. Pilate found no guilt in him and sentenced him anyway, the state doing the very opposite of verse 4. Yet under that injustice God was carrying out a justice deeper than Rome could see. The wrath that the magistrate carries out only in part fell in full on God’s own Son, so that it would never fall on those who trust him (3:25; 8:1). The cross is where the sword of earthly justice and the wrath of heaven met in one body, and both were turned into mercy. At the cross God showed himself both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26). He can declare the guilty righteous without corrupting justice only because the sentence has been carried out, on his Son.

If I have forgiven someone, should I still go to the police? Yes, if a crime has been committed. Going to the police is not a failure of Romans 12 and not a lapse in forgiveness. Paul has just called that officer God’s servant. Forgiveness means you give up your own right to repay, hate or punish; it does not mean you shield the wrongdoer from the authority God has appointed, still less that you leave others in danger. This is especially true where there has been abuse of a child or of a spouse: the church must never hide it, and the victim must never be told that silence is the Christian thing. You are not taking the matter into your own hands; you are handing it to the hands appointed for it.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong, reading the sword more generally as the state’s power to punish, and pointing out that courts make mistakes and that Christ calls us to mercy. This commentary’s view: Scripture gives the state the right to use the sword, including the death penalty for the gravest crimes such as murder (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). Behind it stands God’s word to Noah, given before Moses and to the whole human race: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. The penalty rests on the dignity of the human made in God’s image, not on contempt for it. Christians may disagree on whether, in a given country with its legal system, the death penalty should be used, given the risk of error and injustice; Scripture permits it rather than requiring it in every case, and it requires that it be done justly. But it is not wrong in principle. This is not personal revenge, which is forbidden; it is God’s justice carried out by lawful authority.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. If the ruler is God’s servant in bearing the sword, a believer may serve in that office. When soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do, he did not tell them to leave the army but to stop extorting and be content with their wages (Luke 3:14), and Jesus praised the faith of a centurion above anything he had found in Israel (Matthew 8:10). Christian pacifists cite the saying that all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52), but that was a rebuke to Peter for using it to resist God’s plan, not a ruling on lawful office. The same principle underlies the long Christian teaching on just war: force may be used by lawful authority, for a just cause, as a last resort. A Christian in uniform must still refuse an unjust order, and serve with the restraint of a man who knows whose servant he is.

What if the police or the courts themselves are corrupt? Then they are failing at the very thing Paul says they exist for, and Christians may say so and work to put it right by lawful means: complaint, appeal, the press, the ballot, the higher court. Corruption in an office does not abolish the office; it calls for its reform. Meanwhile, keep doing good, keep your own hands clean, and remember that every corrupt judge has a Judge. The psalmist pictures God standing in the assembly of the rulers and holding judgment among them (Psalm 82:1). No injustice done under colour of law escapes him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the state may use the sword to compel faith or to punish true worship. Its sphere is civil justice, not the conscience before God. The magistrate may punish the thief; he has no authority to tell the church what to believe or whom to worship, and the long history of Christians persecuting Christians in the name of this verse is a history of the sword used in vain.
verseByVerse.note: The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including capital punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. — Romans 13:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
One must be in subjection. “Must” (anankē) is necessity. And Paul gives two reasons, the second deeper than the first.

Not only to avoid God’s wrath. Wrath here is the punishment the state carries out on God’s behalf (v. 4). Fear of consequence is a real motive, and Paul lists it first. But on its own it produces a citizen who keeps the law only when he might be caught: a man who is calculating, not obeying.

But also for the sake of conscience. The word is syneidēsis, the inner sense of right and wrong that accuses or excuses us (2:14–15). The conscience of a Christian knows that government is God’s ordinance, so he keeps the law even when no one is watching and he could get away with breaking it.

The empty junction. An empty road at three in the morning, a red light, no cameras and no other car within a mile. What you do at that junction is one of the few completely honest facts you have about yourself, because there is nobody to perform for. Conscience produces the same conduct at the empty junction as at the busy one.

The same conscience sets the limit. This verse and Acts 5:29 (“We must obey God rather than men”) are the same principle. The reason Peter could refuse the council is the same reason Paul can tell you to pay your taxes without being watched: in both cases the man is answering to Somebody who is not in the room. That is why conscience makes both the best citizen and the one citizen who cannot be bought or bullied into sin.

Is it really a sin to break a small law, like going a little over the speed limit? In principle, yes, because Paul ties obedience to conscience, not to the size of the penalty. The question is not whether anyone will mind but whether God has placed you under this order, and he has. That does not mean you should live in anxious scrupulosity over every unclear regulation, or treat a genuine accident as a crime. It means you do not make a private exception for laws you find inconvenient. If you have been careless here, confess it simply, receive his forgiveness, and start keeping the rule cheerfully, as a small daily act of worship.

What if my conscience objects to something other Christians think is fine? Do not act against your conscience, but do bring it to Scripture. Conscience is not infallible; it can be too tight or too loose, and it needs to be taught by God’s Word. Where a matter is a genuine question of sin, obey God. Where it is a matter of personal scruple, follow your conscience without condemning brothers who see it differently, which is exactly the subject Paul turns to in the next chapter (14:5, 22–23). Talk it through with a wise older Christian or an elder.

For worship. There is a Witness at every empty junction. He sees three in the morning as clearly as noon, for darkness is not dark to him (Psalm 139:12). Once a man lived his whole life in that light without needing to hide: Jesus could say of his Father, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and it was as true in the unseen hours as in the temple courts. We never keep the law like that; even our best obedience is patchy. But by his obedience the many are made righteous (5:19): his obedience is counted as ours, and our imperfect obedience is accepted for his sake. So the eyes that see everything look on the believer and see the obedience of the Son, and the empty road at three in the morning is not a place of exposure but of fellowship.

verseByVerse.quote: For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. — Romans 13:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also pay taxes. Because government is God’s servant, it has a right to be funded. Jesus had already settled the principle with a coin (Mark 12:17).

Ministers of God. In verse 4 the authorities were diakonoi, servants. Here they are leitourgoi, the word behind our liturgy. In everyday Greek it meant anyone who performed a public service, but the Greek Old Testament often uses it of priests and Levites, and Paul later uses it of his own gospel ministry (15:16). He chose a word with the temple in it: the clerk processing a tax return is rendering, without knowing it, a service to God.

Attending to this very thing. The verb (proskartereō, to devote yourself to, to persist at) is the one used in 12:12 of the Christian constant in prayer. It is an extraordinarily high view of an extraordinarily dull job.

The setting of the command. The Roman historian Tacitus records serious public complaint over indirect taxes in AD 58, with Nero considering abolishing them outright, and Romans was written within a year or so of it. Paul tells a small, suspect congregation to keep paying into a treasury that funded the games, the temples of the gods, and eventually the machinery that would kill them.

Pay to all what is owed. “Pay” (apodidōmi) means to give back, to render what is due: not a gift but a debt. But there is a limit inside the command: “what is owed” implies that not everything demanded is owed. The saying of Jesus behind it has the same shape and is usually quoted only halfway. “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” is not the whole sentence; the second half, “and to God the things that are God’s”, sets a limit on the first. Caesar may have the coin with his image on it. He may not have the man made in the image of God.

The Son who paid what he did not owe. Collectors once asked Peter whether his teacher paid the temple tax. Jesus answered that the sons of a king are free, and the tax was for his Father’s house; yet so as not to give offence, he paid it, with a coin from a fish’s mouth, for himself and for Peter (Matthew 17:24–27). The One to whom every tribute in the universe is owed paid what he did not owe, and then paid in full at the cross the debt we could never pay. So the Christian can hand Caesar what is due without resentment.

Taxes and revenue. “Taxes” (phoros) were direct taxes, on land and persons, the tribute paid by subject peoples; “revenue” (telos) meant customs, tolls and duties on goods. Pay both honestly.

Respect and honour. “Respect” is phobos, literally fear, reverence; “honour” is timē, the regard due to a person’s position. Taxes are the easy half. Respect and honour are harder, because they are owed to a person, sometimes one you did not vote for and do not admire. Peter, writing probably under the same emperor, said it in three words: honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). Paul does not say honour the ones who deserve it. He says pay what is owed to the office. And there is one to whom all honour is due without reserve: the Lamb who was slain, worthy to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12).

Must I pay taxes that fund things I believe are wrong? Yes. Jesus and Paul both told believers to pay taxes to Rome, knowing that Rome funded idol temples and gladiatorial games, and that its power could be, and soon would be, turned against the church. When you pay what is owed, the responsibility for how it is spent rests on those who spend it, not on you. You remain free, and often obliged, to speak, vote and campaign against what is wrong. But withholding a lawful tax is not one of the means Scripture gives you.

Is it wrong to reduce my tax bill? Not if you do it honestly. Using the allowances and reliefs the law itself provides is not cheating; the lawmaker meant them to be used. What is wrong is evasion: hiding income, inventing expenses, taking cash to keep it off the books, or bending the truth on a form because no one will check. A useful test is whether you could explain what you did, plainly, to the tax inspector and to your Lord. If you would rather not, you probably already know the answer.

How can I honour a leader I believe is doing real harm? Honour the office and treat the person with basic dignity, while telling the truth about his actions. You may disagree firmly, criticise policies, and vote him out. What you may not do is mock, sneer, invent, or speak of him with contempt, because he bears God’s image and holds God’s appointment. Above all, pray for him, as Paul told Timothy to pray for kings under Nero (1 Timothy 2:1–2). It is very hard to go on despising someone you are honestly praying for.

In everyday life. Honour is mostly kept or broken in private: in how you speak about the people in power when you are among people who agree with you, in the car, at the meal table, in the group chat. Speak of them there as people you pray for.
verseByVerse.note: “Taxes” were direct taxes; “revenue” meant customs and tolls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Love Fulfils the Law: Put on Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The move from taxes to love is sudden but logical: both are debts owed to those among whom we live. But love is a debt we keep paying and never finish paying. Paul’s claim is bold: love fulfils the whole law. That does not make the particular commandments irrelevant; it names their root.

The section closes with the urgency of the time. It is time to wake, to lay aside the works of darkness and to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. The Christian life is not moral self-improvement but being clothed in Christ, day by day, until the change is complete. Notice in verse 13 where the vice list ends: with arguing and envy, set beside the drunken procession in the street.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law
