Romans 13:8–10 sums up the second table of the law, our duties to our neighbour: love your neighbour as yourself. This does not replace the law with a vague sentiment. It names the principle from which all the law’s particular demands flow. The Reformed tradition has insisted that love and law are not opposites: love is the motive, and the law is the guide.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Verse 14 was the sentence Augustine read in the garden in Milan in AD 386, when he could not break free from sexual sin; it came to him as divine command and divine grace at once, and it still convicts, commands and strengthens. Now: The urgency of verses 11–14 belongs to every age: this life is short, Christ’s return is certain, and the works of darkness are not fit clothing for children of light. The way back from a wasted day is open today, through confession to the Christ who is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Owe no one anything. The move from taxes to love is not the change of subject it appears to be: “Pay to all what is owed to them” (v. 7), “Owe no one anything” (v. 8). Paul has been talking about debts all along, and now he names the one debt that never clears.

Except to love each other. Every other obligation in this passage can be discharged. This debt is charged again every morning, to the same people, at the same rate; Augustine called it the debt we always pay and always owe. It never clears because it answers a love that never ran out: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

The one man who owed nothing. There was once a man who owed no one anything: he kept the whole law and left nothing unpaid. And he chose to become the greatest debtor in history. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9): he took on himself the debt of sin we owed to the justice of God and paid it in full. So we can never finish paying the debt of love, because we pay it out of what he gave; and it can never ruin us, because the debt that could have ruined us has been cleared.

Has fulfilled the law. Love does what the law requires toward others. The law is like the plans of a building; love is the building itself, standing in the shape the plans described.

For the commandments. Paul lists the second table of the Ten Commandments, our duties to our neighbour: the seventh, sixth, eighth and tenth (Exodus 20:13–17; Deuteronomy 5:17–21). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add you shall not bear false witness; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it. Paul is not reducing the faith to being good to people; the first table, our duty to love God, is simply not his subject here, and Jesus called it the first and great commandment (Matthew 22:37–38).

You shall not covet. The list ends with the one commandment nobody can see you break, the one that undid Paul himself (7:7–8). You can satisfy the other three by not doing things; you cannot satisfy this one without something happening inside. Love, like coveting, lives in the heart before it reaches the hands.

Summed up. “Summed up” (anakephalaioō) means brought together under one head, the word Paul uses in Ephesians 1:10 of God uniting all things in Christ: every duty to your neighbour has one heading. The words come from Leviticus 19:18, tucked among practical laws about harvests and wages. Jesus lifted them out and called them the second great commandment, on which, with the first, hang all the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 22:39–40; Galatians 5:14).

Does “as yourself” command us to love ourselves first? No. It assumes the care for ourselves that everyone already has: no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it (Ephesians 5:29). We feed ourselves when hungry, defend our own reputation, excuse our own faults and want the best for our own future. That care becomes the measure of what we owe our neighbour. The command is not to build up self-love but to give others what we naturally give ourselves, which is the golden rule turned into a single word (Matthew 7:12).

Where Christians differ: is borrowing wrong? Some take owe no one anything to forbid all borrowing, including mortgages and loans. This commentary’s view: Scripture does not forbid borrowing as such; it regulates it (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–8; Psalm 37:21; Matthew 5:42). Jesus told his disciples not to refuse the one who would borrow from them, which would be strange if borrowing were sin. The context here is paying what is due, and the command is to pay what you owe when it is due and not leave debts unpaid. What Scripture condemns is failing to repay: the wicked borrows but does not pay back (Psalm 37:21). It also warns that the borrower is the slave of the lender (Proverbs 22:7), so wisdom avoids unnecessary debt. A Christian may take a mortgage or a loan he can repay, should keep its terms exactly, and should be slow to borrow for what he cannot afford.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we decide for ourselves what love requires. Whenever someone says love permits what God’s law forbids, Paul’s list answers him: love does not commit adultery, does not take a life, does not steal, does not covet. The commandments tell love where to go, and love supplies the power to go there.

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37): anyone whose need God puts in your path, beginning with the nearest and reaching to the stranger and the enemy. (See Matthew 22:39 for the fuller answer.)

Does loving my neighbour mean I must always say yes? No. Love seeks the other person’s real good, and sometimes that means saying no: refusing to fund an addiction, to cover up a lie, or to go on enabling sin. Love does not require you to stay in danger. A person suffering abuse is not failing to love by getting safe and seeking help; the abuser is the one breaking the law of love. What love rules out is the cold no that protects only my comfort. Ask: which answer genuinely serves this person before God?

In everyday life. Bring to mind the person in your church you find hardest: not an enemy, just the one you would rather not sit near. The debt is owed to him this week at exactly the same rate as to the people you like, and unlike a tax it is paid in person. It is easy to arrange a life so that this invoice rarely arrives; arrange this week so that it does, paying out of the love Christ first gave you: a call, a meal, a word of thanks.

parallels.desc: love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love does no wrong. The commandments of verse 9 are negative, and the negative form is a mercy. Positive definitions of love are hard to check, but the question “Have I done this person wrong?” has a plain yes or no.

A floor, not a ceiling. But it is only a floor, the least that love does. A man can go a whole year wronging no one and loving nobody. Paul set the ceiling a chapter earlier, where love blesses the persecutor and feeds the hungry enemy (12:14, 20), and love is patient and kind, bearing, believing, hoping and enduring all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). Verse 10 tells you where love starts, not where it stops. There has been one perfect fulfilment of the law of love on the earth. Christ never did his neighbour wrong, and he did not stop at the floor. He went to the ceiling and beyond it, touching lepers, eating with sinners, washing the feet of the man who would betray him, praying for the soldiers driving the nails.

The fulfilling of the law. “Fulfilling” (plērōma) is fullness, the complete expression of a thing: love is what the law looks like lived from the heart. This is the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). To fulfil the law is not to set it aside but to do what it was always asking for.

Fulfilled in us. Paul has told us how it comes about: God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, and condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit (8:3–4). When a believer does his neighbour no wrong, and then does him good, the law is not being kept by a moral achiever. It is being fulfilled by the Spirit of Christ in someone Christ has bought.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a feeling of love is enough; love shows itself in keeping God’s commandments (John 14:15). Nor can we earn God’s favour by loving well: love is the fruit of our justification, not its root.

How can I love someone I feel no affection for? Begin with what love does, not with what it feels. Scripture commands love, and a feeling cannot be commanded, but actions can: do this person no wrong, speak well of him, ask God’s blessing on him, and do him one concrete good. Feelings very often follow obedience rather than leading it. And you are not left to manufacture this alone. God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (5:5). Ask him for it, honestly, about this particular person.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. — Romans 13:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides this you know the time. “Time” is kairos: not clock time but the decisive season, the age between Christ’s first coming and his return. And Paul says you know it. His readers are living as though they did not.

In the flow. “Besides this” ties the coming day to everything before it: love your neighbour (vv. 8–10), and do it knowing what time it is. Christians who know the day is near have no time for contempt (14:10).

Wake from sleep. Sleep here is spiritual drowsiness: carelessness, ease in the world, drifting with the culture (1 Thessalonians 5:6–7; Ephesians 5:14). Nothing in the room changes when a person wakes; Paul is not asking for new circumstances, but for someone awake inside them.

Salvation is nearer. Salvation here is its completion: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and final glory (8:23–24). The Christian does not walk away from his salvation as the years pass; he walks toward it.

What “salvation is nearer” does not mean. It does not mean believers are not yet saved, or that their salvation is still in doubt. Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses: we have been saved from sin’s penalty (justified, 5:1; Ephesians 2:8); we are being saved from sin’s power (sanctified, 6:22); and we shall be saved from sin’s presence, when Christ returns and our bodies are raised (8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). Here Paul means the third, and it is as certain as the first, since those he justified he also glorified (8:30).

Salvation with a face. What draws nearer each day is not only an event but a person. Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him (Hebrews 9:28). That turns this verse from a scolding into a summons: a sleeper woken for an arrival, and no one wants to sleep through the arrival of the One he loves most.

The night is far gone. The night is this present evil age; the day is Christ’s return. The Christian lives in the overlap of the ages: the old age of darkness and death is passing, and the new age of light and life has already broken in with the resurrection of Christ. To live in the works of darkness is to dress for a night that is already ending. The night has been long. It began in a garden when the first man hid from God. But there has been a light on the horizon since another garden, where a tomb was found empty at early dawn, and the morning that began there cannot be stopped. Christ is the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16), the herald of a day that will have no night in it, when God himself will be our light (Revelation 22:5).

Cast off and put on. Both are clothing verbs, like taking off night clothes in the morning, or a soldier arming for the day (Ephesians 6:11–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). “Put on” is the same verb as in verse 14: to put on the armour of light is to put on Christ himself. The word rendered armour (hopla) is the word translated instruments in 6:13, instruments for righteousness. The Christian is not given a costume for the daylight. He is given equipment for a fight.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong about the timing? Some say Paul expected Christ to return within his lifetime and was mistaken. This commentary’s view: Paul taught that the day is near, meaning that it is the next great event in God’s plan, with no date given, so that every generation must live ready; he did not claim to know the date (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). He also says that a final rebellion and the man of lawlessness will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so near does not mean that no prophecy remains, but those things are not a timetable to calculate. Since Christ’s first coming, we have been in the last days (Hebrews 1:2). The time is short whether Christ returns tomorrow or in a thousand years, since with the Lord a thousand years are as a day (2 Peter 3:8). And the sentence is not a calculation but a comparison, and it is true every time it is read: salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. It was true for Paul. It is truer for you than it was for him. And for each of us the day arrives at our own death if it has not arrived before, which no one has ever had grounds to think was far off. His return will be one visible, public event, not a secret rapture, followed by the resurrection of all the dead and the last judgment. Many earnest Christians expect a secret rapture first (an unseen coming to take believers away before a final tribulation); this commentary reads the passages on his coming (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17) as one loud, visible return, and honours those who read them otherwise.

Should I be afraid of the day? Not if you are in Christ. For the unbeliever the day is judgment; for the believer it is dawn. Paul calls it salvation, the morning after a long night, the moment the Bridegroom comes for his bride. The fear that is right is the sober fear of being found asleep, which drives us to wake up; the fear that is wrong is the dread of rejection, which Christ has removed (8:1). If you are trusting him, the day that is drawing near is the best day of your life.

So what do I actually do differently because the day is near? Three things. Keep short accounts: do not leave sin unconfessed or quarrels unreconciled, as if there were all the time in the world. Spend your life on what will last: people, the gospel, faithfulness in your calling, rather than things that will burn. And hold everything else loosely: possessions, ambitions and grievances look very different in the light of morning. Nearness is not a reason for panic but for wakefulness and for joy.

In everyday life. Look at two stretches of the day nobody plans and nobody sees: the last hour before you sleep and the first minutes after you wake. That is where the dressing of verse 12 actually happens. Tomorrow, give the first minutes of the day to the Lord who is coming, before the phone gets them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. — Romans 13:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk properly. “Properly” (euschēmonōs) means decently, becomingly, fit to be seen in daylight with nothing to hide. There are things people do at one in the morning that they would not do at eleven, in the same street. The Christian is a person for whom it is always, in effect, eleven in the morning.

Not in orgies and drunkenness. Three pairs of night sins follow, and the sting is in the order. First, sins of excess: “orgies” (kōmoi), the drunken processions through the streets that were a familiar feature of Roman nights, and drunkenness.

Not in sexual immorality and sensuality. Second, sexual sins. “Sexual immorality” is koitai, literally beds: sexual sin. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is unrestrained lust, shamelessness, the point at which a person no longer even bothers to hide.

Not in quarreling and jealousy. Third, sins of relationship: strife and envy. The list begins where a first century reader would expect a vice list to begin, and then, without any change of tone, ends with arguing and envy. That is aimed at the respectable. The man who has never been drunk, whose sexual conduct is beyond reproach, but who cannot let a disagreement go, who keeps score and needs to be right, is named in the same breath as the drunk in the street. Paul does not grade them. We do.

Unpaid love on a Friday night. These are social sins, every one: they are done in company or need a second party by definition. The argument that began at verse 8 with the debt of love is still running. The vice list is what unpaid love looks like on a Friday night: using people for pleasure, or resenting them for what they have.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Believers have already put on Christ, once for all, at their conversion, signed in their baptism: as many of you as were baptised into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). Now they must put him on daily: take on his character, live consciously in union with him, and let him be the clothing others see (Colossians 3:10–14). This is not pretence but identity. You do not put on a set of values. You put on a Person: the Lord who rules you, Jesus who saves you, the Christ promised from of old.

Wearing another man. There is hardly a stranger instruction in the New Testament: that a man should wear another man, and be recognised by him rather than by anything of his own. It completes what began at 12:1–2: there the body was presented to God; here it is dressed in Christ and the flesh is refused its supplies.

Make no provision. “Provision” (pronoia) is forethought, from the same root as the verb of 12:17, give thought to do what is honourable. You plan for good in a calm hour, and you plan for the flesh in a calm hour too, usually without admitting it: the route home that passes the place, the app left installed, the second bottle bought just in case, the evening arranged so that being alone is inevitable. Most falls are not decided at the moment of temptation. They are prepared at the moment of provisioning, days earlier, when it felt like nothing at all. “The flesh” here is not the body as such but our fallen human nature with its sinful desires, which still pulls at the believer even after he has been made new in Christ (7:22–23).

Augustine in the garden. In the late summer of AD 386 a North African professor of rhetoric sat weeping in a garden in Milan, thirty-one years old, intellectually convinced of Christianity for some time and unable to break with a sexual habit. As a young man he had prayed in the notorious form: give me chastity and self-control, but not yet. He heard a child’s voice from a neighbouring house, chanting what sounded like a game: tolle lege, take up and read, take up and read. He went back to where he had left a book of Paul’s letters, opened it, and read the first passage his eye fell on. It was this one. Augustine writes in his Confessions (8.12) that he neither wished nor needed to read further. At the end of the sentence, it was as if a light of certainty flooded his heart, and all the darkness of doubt vanished.

Which clause did it. It was not a doctrine he had lacked, but obedience to a plain command. Augustine had been saying not yet; Romans 13:14 is God’s answer: now. And behind the child’s voice and the open book was the sovereign grace of God, which does not wait for a man to be ready but makes him ready, and which turned that weeping professor into one of the greatest teachers of grace the church has known.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all celebration or wine is sinful. Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding (John 2:1–11), and Scripture speaks of wine that gladdens the heart of man (Psalm 104:15); what is forbidden is excess and the loss of self-control. Nor does “make no provision” mean the body or its desires are evil in themselves; God made them good. It means refusing to plan for their misuse.

How do I actually put on Christ, day by day? Begin each day by remembering who you are: united to Christ, forgiven, clothed in his righteousness. Then fill your mind with him in his Word, so that you know what he is like and can recognise his ways. Pray, asking him for his patience, purity and kindness for the particular situations of the day ahead. When a temptation comes, ask, what does the Lord Jesus look like here, and do that, by his strength. Meet with his people and come to his table, where he feeds his church with himself by faith. Putting on Christ is not a technique but a relationship lived in the open.

What if I have removed the provisions and still fall? Then come back to Christ at once. Removing provisions is wise, but it is not what saves you; Christ is. The Christ you put on was never your own good record, so a fall does not strip him off you. Bring the fall straight to him, for the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin, and we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 1:7; 2:1). Then look honestly at what led to the fall, because there is often another provision you had not noticed, and tell a trusted Christian friend, because sin grows in secret and weakens in the light. Falling again does not mean you are not a Christian. Making peace with the sin and no longer fighting it would be the danger sign.

In everyday life. Name one arrangement in your life whose only real function is to keep a door open: an app, a habit, a place, a route home, a friendship that always ends the same way. Close that one thing this evening. You do not do it by willpower alone, for the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you (8:11) and is the one at work in you as you do it.

For worship. He was stripped so that there would be something for the guilty to wear. The soldiers gambled for the last thing he owned, while he was in the act of clothing the world. The Son of God hung in the daylight, bearing the shame of every work of darkness ever done in the night, so that sinners could be dressed in his righteousness and stand unashamed in the light of God. He has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). And the One we put on is the very One who is coming, so that on the day of his appearing he will find his people already dressed in himself.
verseByVerse.note: Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.<sup>2</sup>Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.<sup>3</sup>For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval,<sup>4</sup>for he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.<sup>5</sup>Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience.<sup>6</sup>For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing.<sup>7</sup>Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.<sup>8</sup>Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.<sup>9</sup>For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,” and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”<sup>10</sup>Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.<sup>11</sup>Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed.<sup>12</sup>The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.<sup>13</sup>Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy.<sup>14</sup>But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Romans 14 and 15 deal with a real quarrel in the Roman church: Jewish believers who still kept the food laws and holy days of Moses, whom Paul calls the weak, and Gentile believers who felt free of them, whom he calls the strong. The particular questions have changed since, but the tension has not: what I am free to do, and what love asks me to do for my brother.

Paul does not settle it by imposing the scruple (the hesitation of a tender conscience) on the free, or by brushing the scruple aside. He counts himself among the strong (15:1), yet his concern is to protect the weak, and to keep either side from wounding the other with contempt or condemnation. Love, willing to limit a lawful freedom for a brother’s sake, rules the whole section.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The section opens with a command that has two sides (v. 1): welcome the brother with a tender conscience fully into fellowship, and do not make the welcome an occasion for arguing him out of his scruples. Paul’s examples, vegetables and special days, belong to first-century Rome, but they show the typical sin of each position: the strong are tempted to despise the scrupulous, the weak to condemn the free.

The argument runs in four steps. Each believer is another Master’s servant, and that Master will hold him up (v. 4). Both sides act in honour of the Lord and give thanks to God (v. 6). Christ died and rose to be Lord of the dead and the living (v. 9). And all will stand side by side before the same judgment seat (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Things indifferent and the conscience

Reformed writers use the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, the ground Romans 14 covers. In them Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean, and a conscience the gospel has freed need not be bound again. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that the strong must use their freedom with care for the weaker conscience, not yielding to every scruple for ever, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Rome the tension was between Jewish and Gentile believers over food laws and the calendar. Paul does not end it by naming the winners; he points both groups to the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation has its own version: alcohol, entertainment, dress, styles of worship. The principles hold: welcome the brother whose scruples differ; do not despise; do not judge; each will give account to God, not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 14:1–15:13 deals with a quarrel in the Roman church over matters Scripture leaves free, such as foods and special days. The strong must not despise the weak; the weak must not judge the strong; God has welcomed both, and all will stand before his judgment seat (vv. 1–12). The strong must not use their freedom to make a brother stumble, for the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (vv. 13–21). And no one may act against his conscience (vv. 22–23). To settle a quarrel about menus and calendars, Paul reaches for the largest things he knows: God’s welcome, Christ’s death and rising to be Lord, and every knee bowing to him.

The setting. The weak probably included Jewish believers who kept the food laws and holy days of Moses, and perhaps Gentiles who avoided meat for fear it had been offered to idols (as in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10). Some, unable to be sure, ate only vegetables, as Daniel did in Babylon (Daniel 1:8–12). Jews had been expelled from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2). When Jewish believers returned after his death in AD 54, they probably found congregations now largely Gentile, and the shared meal at the heart of early Christian fellowship had become a place of tension.

In the flow. Romans 14 is not a change of subject. From 12:1 Paul has been showing what life looks like in the light of God’s mercies, and here the love that fulfils the law (13:8–10) meets its hardest test. If God justifies Jew and Gentile alike, by faith (3:29–30), the church cannot divide them over the menu.

Weak in faith. Everything in this chapter depends on getting one thing straight. “Weak in faith” does not mean weak in trusting Christ for salvation, and it does not mean lax or half-hearted. It means not yet fully persuaded of the freedom the gospel gives in such matters. It is the man with more rules, not fewer: the one who cannot eat the meat or ignore the day without his conscience objecting. We instinctively call the strict Christian the strong one; Paul’s labels run the other way. Read the chapter with the usual assumption in place, and every instruction in it lands on the wrong person.

The weight of the word welcome. “Welcome” (proslambanō, receive, take to oneself) means accept fully into fellowship, not merely tolerate. Paul uses it four times in this section: here; in verse 3, where the reason is that God has welcomed him; and twice at 15:7, “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you”. The hospitality asked for is not politeness at the edge of the room. It is the kind God has already shown to the person you find difficult.

A bruised reed he will not break. The welcome Paul asks for is the welcome Christ gives. He does not break the bruised reed or snuff out the smouldering wick (Matthew 12:20), and a weak conscience is exactly such a reed. Years after Pentecost, Peter still could not bring himself to eat what the law called unclean, and he said so to the Lord himself (Acts 10:14). Christ did not despise him. He showed him the vision three times, patiently, until Peter understood that God had made clean both the food and the Gentiles who ate it. The strong are asked to treat a scruple the way the Lord treated Peter’s.

But not to quarrel over opinions. “Opinions” (dialogismoi) are reasonings, debatable thoughts. Do not welcome someone in order to argue him out of his scruples. It is possible to receive someone warmly while fully intending to work on him, so that the hospitality is a tactic and not a welcome, and the person on the receiving end can always tell.

Only vegetables. The strong believe all foods are clean (v. 14; Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). A scrupulous Jewish believer in Rome could not easily verify how an animal had been slaughtered or whether the meat had come through a temple, so he found that the only way to be certain was to eat no meat at all. That is what a tender conscience usually does: it over-corrects, because it cannot bear the risk.

Where Christians differ: what counts as a disputable matter? Some apply this chapter to every disagreement, including doctrine and morality. This commentary’s view: Romans 14 concerns things that Scripture does not command or forbid, matters indifferent in themselves (the Greek term is adiaphora). It does not cover the gospel itself, which Paul defends fiercely (Galatians 1:8–9), or clear moral commands, such as sexual purity (13:13). Where God has spoken plainly, we do not treat it as an opinion. Where he has not, we give liberty, for God alone is Lord of the conscience (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2).

How do I tell a disputable matter from a real sin? Three questions sort them. Does Scripture command it or forbid it? Is the gospel itself at stake? Is anyone being told that he must do this to be right with God? Where the answer to all three is no, this chapter governs, and the strong bear with the weak. But where Scripture calls something sin, no appeal to liberty or conscience can make it a disputable matter. And where the gospel is at stake, the strong must not yield: when false brothers wanted Titus circumcised as a condition of acceptance, Paul says he did not yield in submission even for a moment (Galatians 2:5). Bearing with a weak conscience is love; letting it rule the church is not.

What are the disputable matters today? Rarely meat sold in temples. Today they are more likely to be alcohol, the keeping of Christmas and Easter, styles of music in worship, which Bible translation to use, schooling choices for children, dress, diet, films and novels, social media, or how strictly to keep Sunday. On all of these, sincere believers who love the Lord reach different conclusions. The list will change from generation to generation; the principle does not. Where God has not spoken, no Christian has the right to speak as though he had.

I think I am the weak brother. Is that an insult? No. The term names one thing only: a conscience not yet free in a matter where God has in fact granted freedom. It says nothing about your sincerity, your salvation or your love for Christ. The man Paul describes is scrupulous precisely because he is afraid of displeasing God, which is not a contemptible reason for anything. And look at whom this chapter is written to protect. Nearly every command in it is aimed at the strong, on your behalf. Paul does not spend a single verse telling you to hurry up.

For worship. Before there was any question of whom we would welcome, God welcomed us. We came with the wrong opinions, the wrong history and a great deal of sin, and he did not receive us on condition that we first agree with him about everything. The Lord who receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2) has set a table where the scrupulous and the free sit side by side, both of them there for one reason only: he wanted them. The welcome of God is wider than our opinions, and warmer than our hearts. So welcome the brother whose scruples you do not share: sit with him, and let the conversation be about Christ, not the scruple.
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not despise. The temptation of the strong is to look down on the weak as narrow and legalistic. “Despise” (exoutheneō) is to count as nothing. The two sins are assigned precisely: the one who eats is told not to despise; the one who abstains is told not to judge. Freedom does not tempt a person to condemn; it tempts him to find the other man faintly ridiculous: the raised eyebrow, the anecdote told later about how strict so-and-so is.

Do not judge. The temptation of the weak is to condemn the strong as worldly or compromising. “Pass judgment” (krinō) here means condemn. Scruple does not tempt a person to sneer; it tempts him to convict. Neither party is usually in any danger of the other’s sin, which is why each so easily believes himself innocent.

For God has welcomed him. If God has accepted him in Christ, who are you to reject him? What unites Christians is not agreement on secondary matters but the fact that the same God has received them all. The brother you are tempted to despise or condemn sits at your table because God himself pulled out the chair. Underneath both sins lies the same hunger: to feel secure by being better than somebody. The scrupulous man is tempted to rest on his strictness, the free man on his insight, and either way religion has quietly become a pedestal. The gospel takes the pedestal away. God’s welcome rests on Christ, not on anyone’s menu, so no one at the table needs to stand on anyone else.

Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? “Servant” (oiketēs) is a household servant, so the picture is of someone else’s home. You may think another family’s arrangements peculiar; you do not walk into their kitchen and start correcting their staff. Not because standards do not matter, but because it is not your household and they do not take their orders from you. Every believer is Christ’s servant, not yours.

He will be upheld. The verse ends somewhere unexpected. Paul does not say the servant may well fall and that will be his own affair. His confidence runs toward the very person you were worried about. The Master is Christ, who died and rose to be Lord of his people (14:9). On the night Peter would deny him, Jesus told him that he had prayed for him, that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32). Peter fell, and stood again, because he was held. Every believer on earth is upheld, at this moment, by hands that do not tire and do not let go. The Master of the house holds every one of them, and he has never yet dropped a servant he took into his house.

The relief hidden in this verse. Much of the anxiety Christians carry about other Christians is a quiet doubt whether God is managing them properly. He is. You may pray for your brother, love him and talk with him. You do not have to hold him up.

Does this mean Christians must never judge? No. Paul forbids condemning a brother over matters God has left open. Elsewhere he commands the church to judge sin among its members (1 Corinthians 5:12–13), pronounces a curse on those who preach another gospel (Galatians 1:8–9), and at the end of this letter tells the Romans to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine they have been taught (16:17). The question is not whether to judge but what: sin and false teaching, yes; another believer’s conscience on a disputable matter, no.

In everyday life. Think of a believer whose practice differs from yours on something Scripture does not settle, and notice which reflex arrives first: the urge to laugh, or the urge to convict. That tells you which of the two groups you are actually in, whatever you would have said about yourself. Confess it to the Lord who welcomed you both, and find something kind to say about that brother to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Special days. The days in question were probably the Sabbath and the Jewish feasts and fasts (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16). Some believers still kept them as special; others considered all days alike.

Fully convinced. “Fully convinced” (plērophoreō) means filled up to full assurance. Paul does not say the matter is unimportant, and he does not say do as you please. Whether you use the freedom or keep the scruple, you must have thought it through. That rules out a position many of us hold without ever having thought about it, simply because it is how we were raised, or what our church does. Paul is not asking everyone to reach the same conclusion. He is asking everyone to have reached his own, which is a more demanding request than it sounds.

Paul’s restraint. Paul is not neutral; he is persuaded that nothing is unclean (14:14). Yet here he defends the right of a man to reach the opposite practical conclusion and act on it before God. He will argue for his view. He will not make it a rule for others. That is apostolic authority used with great gentleness, and a model for every pastor and parent.

In honour of the Lord. Both sides can act for Christ, and the test Paul offers is not what a person does but whom he does it for: is it done for the Lord? The Lord in this chapter is Jesus (14:9), who said that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28). So the Jewish believer who still keeps the seventh day keeps it in honour of its Lord, and the Gentile believer who does not is free because that same Lord has given the rest that the day pointed forward to: rest from trying to earn God’s favour, because his work is finished (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Both are standing before the One the day was always about.

He gives thanks to God. Then the common ground, and it is not agreement. It is thanksgiving. Two men do opposite things at the same table and both of them say grace over it, and Paul treats that as the decisive fact about both.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day. Some say this verse proves no day is special for Christians. Others hold that the fourth commandment, given at creation (Genesis 2:3) and part of the moral law, binds Christians to a strict Sabbath observance, now on Sunday, and that this verse speaks only of Jewish ceremonial days. This commentary’s view: the Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ, who is our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10; Matthew 11:28). In Colossians Paul lists Sabbaths among the shadows whose substance is Christ, and in this verse he lets a believer treat every day alike, which many find hard to square with a binding weekly Sabbath; Christians who hold the Westminster and 1689 view read this verse as speaking of the Jewish feast days rather than the Lord’s Day. Christians are not bound by the Sabbath laws of Moses, and Paul leaves Jewish days to conscience. But the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, the day of Christ’s resurrection, was the day the early church gathered for worship (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). Gathering with God’s people on that day, resting from ordinary work where possible, and giving it to worship, is a great privilege and a wise rhythm, a gift Christians gladly set apart out of joy and wisdom, not a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The Westminster and 1689 view, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment (the Westminster Confession 21.7–8; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.7–8), is held by many godly brothers, who keep it in honour of the Lord and deserve respect, not contempt.

What about Christmas and Easter? They belong to this chapter. A church may keep them gladly, as days to rejoice in the birth and resurrection of the Lord, and many believers find them a rich help to worship. Others, especially in some Reformed traditions, have declined to keep any holy day beyond the Lord’s Day, wanting nothing in worship that Scripture does not command. Both can do it in honour of the Lord. What no one may do is bind another’s conscience: neither by treating the man who keeps Christmas as compromised, nor by treating the man who does not as a killjoy.

How do I become fully convinced? Not by waiting for a feeling. Read what Scripture actually says on the matter, and what it does not say. Ask why you do what you do, and whether you could give a reason from God’s Word. Talk it through with mature believers, including some who disagree with you. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Then reach a conclusion you can thank God for, and live by it with a clear conscience, while remaining teachable. Being fully convinced does not mean you can never change your mind. It means you are acting from conviction now, not from pressure or confusion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regular gathering for worship is optional (Hebrews 10:25). The day may be a matter of conscience; meeting with the Lord’s people is not.

In everyday life. Before any choice in a disputed area, ask: can I actually thank God for this specific thing, out loud, without the sentence going strange in my mouth? The question is not whether I can defend it, or find someone who agrees. If you can thank him, go ahead with a clear conscience. Liberty that cannot say grace over what it is doing has stopped being liberty, and scruple that cannot thank God for the freedom it is declining has become something other than conscience.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of us lives to himself. The principle beneath all of this: no Christian is his own master. Every choice, what to eat and what day to observe, but also every life decision, is made in the presence of the Lord to whom we belong. The verse is often quoted to mean that no one is an island. That is true, but it is not Paul’s point; the next words say to whom we live, and it is the Lord.

To the Lord. All of life, and death itself, is lived toward Christ: for him, in his service, under his eye. “To the Lord”, “to the Lord”, “the Lord’s”: three times in a single verse. Both parties keep claiming to be right; Paul keeps answering that neither of them is his own. That settles a dispute between equals without deciding which of them is correct. It decides who has the right to rule them both.

We are the Lord’s. This is our great comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism opens with this truth, and cites this passage for it: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ (Question 1).

Into your hands. The Lord to whom we live and die first walked the road he asks us to walk. He did not please himself (15:3). He lived to do the will of the One who sent him (John 4:34), and he died to the Father too, with the words of Psalm 31 on his lips: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). So the Christian who dies to the Lord is not stepping into the dark alone. He dies into hands that were pierced for him.

Where this sentence has ended up. The sentence “whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” is read at gravesides and said quietly in hospital rooms at three in the morning. And Paul wrote it about a disagreement over vegetables. That does not make the verse smaller; it is the point of it. He puts the largest thing he knows underneath the smallest possible quarrel, which shows how seriously he takes the damage the quarrel can do.

What does it look like to live to the Lord on an ordinary day? It means asking, about the ordinary things, whom am I doing this for? Work done for him is done honestly and well even when no one checks (Colossians 3:23). Money is spent as a steward, not an owner. Time, including rest, is received as his gift. Relationships are handled as his business, because the people are his. It does not mean thinking religious thoughts every minute. It means that nothing in your life is a private zone where he has no say, and that is not a burden but a freedom: you no longer have to be your own god.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To this end. To settle a dispute about dinner, Paul has gone to the death and resurrection of the Son of God, not as an illustration but as the actual argument. This is what his death and resurrection were for: Christ died to purchase those enslaved to sin and death, and rose to rule them as the living, reigning King.

Lord of the dead and the living. Christ’s rule reaches beyond the grave. Believers who have died are still his (1 Thessalonians 4:14–16), and believers alive now are his. By dying and rising he won the right to rule over all (Philippians 2:8–11; Acts 2:36). The believers you have buried have not passed beyond his rule. Christ went into the one country from which no ruler had ever returned, and he came back, and he came back holding the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). He rules both countries, because he has lived in both.

Both sides disqualified. If the purpose of the cross was that Christ should be Lord, then every attempt by one believer to take charge of another’s conscience in a matter God has left open intrudes on the very thing Calvary was meant to secure. The strong man imposing his freedom and the weak man imposing his scruple are making the same mistake, from opposite ends. Both are trying to sit on a throne that was bought with blood for someone else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ became Lord only at his resurrection, as if he were not God before. He was always God the Son. But as the God-man and Redeemer, he received the lordship he won by his death and resurrection.

Where are believers who have died? With Christ, consciously, now. They are not asleep in the sense of being unaware, and they are not in some place of further cleansing. The Lord of the dead keeps them near him: Paul longed to depart and be with Christ, which he called far better (Philippians 1:23), and he spoke of being away from the body as being at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their bodies rest in the grave awaiting the resurrection; their souls are with him, under his rule and in his joy. Scripture describes their death as sleep because it is temporary and peaceful, not because they have ceased to know.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you pass judgment on your brother? “Or you, why do you despise your brother?” To the weak: why judge? To the strong: why despise? The Greek carries a weight the English cannot show: both questions begin with an emphatic “you”. Paul turns to each party in the room in turn, like a man pointing. And note the word “brother”, twice. You are not arguing with an opponent. You are family.

The judgment seat. The judgment seat is the bēma, the raised stone platform in a Greek city from which a magistrate gave his ruling. Paul had stood before one himself, in Corinth, when Gallio dismissed the case against him (Acts 18:12–16). In 2 Corinthians 5:10 he calls it the judgment seat of Christ, for God judges through Christ (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). We will not be judges there; we will be judged. So we should not take the judge’s seat now. At the judgment seat the strong and the weak stand exactly level. The same Lord who will sit on the judgment seat once stood before Pilate’s, silent, condemned for us. The One we will bow to is the One who bowed his head on the cross and gave up his spirit.

Every knee shall bow. The words come from Isaiah 45:23 (with as I live from Isaiah 49:18), spoken by the God who has just said there is no other. Paul elsewhere applies the same verse to Jesus, at whose name every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11), a sign of how fully he counts Jesus as the one God of Isaiah. So at the end you will bow before him, beside the brother you were correcting. And that is the argument: the judge’s seat is already taken. Every act of judging another believer over an open question is an attempt to sit somewhere that already has someone in it.

Will believers be judged? Yes: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But not to decide whether they are saved. That was settled when they believed: whoever believes does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24; Romans 8:1). What is examined is their life and service. Some will receive reward, and others will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be condemned at the judgment. There is no condemnation for those in Christ (8:1). Nor does every knee bowing mean that all will be saved. Believers will bow in worship and joy; the rest will bow because they must, acknowledging too late the Lord they refused, and will go away into eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). The bowing is universal; the salvation is not.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give an account. “Account” (logos) is a reckoning, like an account book. “Each of us”: personally, individually. “Of himself”: not of others. Whatever else is asked, you will not be asked about your brother’s choices in matters of conscience (Matthew 12:36; Hebrews 4:13).

No comparisons in court. This removes the defence many of us have quietly prepared. Nearly every account we give of ourselves is comparative: I am not as strict as him, I am not as careless as her. It works in conversation, because there is always someone available to be worse. It will not work on that day, because the other party will be busy giving his own account, about himself.

The Judge who is also the advocate. The One who receives the account is the Lord Jesus, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22). That is the comfort folded inside the warning. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2), the one whose sacrifice has met God’s just anger against them in full. The account is real. But it will be read in the presence of the One who bore its worst lines on the cross, and who speaks for the one giving it.

If I am justified, why should the account concern me? Because it is real, and because your Father cares how his children live. The account is not a trial to decide whether you will be condemned; that was settled at the cross. It is more like a son showing his father what he did with what he was given. It should make you serious about how you live, not afraid of rejection. And it should free you from comparison, because you are not being measured against your brother, only seen by your Lord, who knows your weakness and remembers that you are dust (Psalm 103:14).

In everyday life. Try describing your own spiritual condition to God without mentioning another Christian, a church you left, a movement you disagree with, or a generation you think has gone wrong. Just yourself, to God, before the Lord who has already answered for you. What remains is what you will actually give account of on that day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second half of the chapter moves from forbidding judging and despising to the positive duty of the strong: limit your freedom where using it would lead a brother to sin against his conscience (v. 13). Paul’s ground is the cross: the weak brother is the one for whom Christ died (v. 15). The reason for holding back is what the kingdom of God is about: righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, not food (v. 17).

Verse 14 is the pivot: nothing is unclean in itself, yet it is unclean for the man whose conscience says otherwise. Verses 19–21 give the working rules in the language of building, v. 22 tells the free man to stop parading his liberty, and v. 23 closes with a sentence that has travelled far beyond its setting.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian liberty and the law of love

Freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is freedom from the bondage of sin and law, for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother’s conscience misuses it as surely as legalism does; it is just as self-centred, only pointed in another direction.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Much of the meat in a first-century market had passed through a pagan temple (compare 1 Corinthians 8–10). The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul’s principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother’s conscience. Now: The strong Christian is tempted to treat freedom as a badge of maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be handled with care. Maturity shows itself less in using freedom than in being willing to limit it for love.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer. Paul now turns from the judgment seat to the dinner table, and from the weak to the strong. He is not merely telling the two sides to live and let live. He is asking the strong to take responsibility for the spiritual welfare of the weak.

Decide instead. Verse 13 uses the same Greek verb (krinō) twice, which the English hides: let us no longer judge one another, but judge this instead. Paul does not tell the Roman Christians to stop making judgments. He tells them to make one about themselves: resolve never to put an obstacle in a brother’s path. The urge to pass verdicts is not switched off. It is turned on ourselves.

What a stumbling block is. A proskomma is the thing your foot catches on; a skandalon first named the trigger of a trap, and in the New Testament it means whatever trips a person into sin. Neither word means giving offence in the modern sense. The damage is not that the weak brother is annoyed by your steak. It is that he eats one, against his own conscience, because you made it awkward not to, and something inside him gives way.

Persuaded in the Lord Jesus. Paul sides with the strong, and speaks by Jesus’ authority, not personal preference. Behind it very probably stands his Master’s own ruling, the day Jesus said that nothing entering a man from outside can defile him, to which Mark adds the comment, “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). (The KJV reads that phrase as part of Jesus’ saying; most modern Bibles take it as Mark’s comment.) The food laws, which had marked Israel out as holy for centuries, were fulfilled in Christ. “Unclean” (koinos) means common, ritually impure.

Unclean for him. Our care for the weak depends on the second half of the verse. In itself the food is clean. For that man, eating it really does defile. Paul does not say the weak brother is imagining his problem.

Conscience creates obligation, not reality. Believing meat unclean does not make it so. But conscience does bind. It can be mistaken, yet a man who acts against it has done wrong even when the act itself was harmless, because he did what he believed God forbids.

So how do I help a brother with a weak conscience? Never by pressure. If the problem is that he thinks it unclean, the only real remedy is that he should come to think otherwise, and that is done by teaching, time and the example of people he trusts. Getting him to do the thing while he still believes it wrong does not free him. It only teaches him to ignore his conscience. So be patient, open the Scriptures with him when he wants to, live your own freedom gently, and leave the timing to the Spirit. Some people never change their mind on the matter, and that is all right; Paul never says the weak must become strong before they are welcome.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sin is whatever someone thinks it is, so that morality is relative. Paul speaks only of matters indifferent, like food. Murder is unclean whatever anyone thinks.

For worship. The Lord Jesus spoke one sentence, and the menus of the world were opened. Every table became a place where Jew and Gentile could sit together, because the One who fulfilled the law had come. He has made the unclean clean: lepers, sinners, Gentiles, us. And the One who sets his people free teaches them to use their freedom tenderly, for he had authority over every law and every table, and he used it to serve rather than to be served (Mark 10:45).

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if your brother is grieved by what you eat. “Grieved” (lypeō) means pained, hurt: his conscience is wounded, perhaps because he is drawn into doing what he thinks is wrong, or because he watches a brother he loves do what he believes dishonours God.

You are no longer walking in love. The strong man in this scene has broken no rule; his theology is correct and his dinner is lawful. He has simply stopped walking in love somewhere between being right and being at the table. You may be right about food, but you are wrong about love. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

The one for whom Christ died. Christ gave his life for this brother; will you not give up a meal for him? He died for the scrupulous believer with his long list of things he cannot do, and for the free believer who finds him tiresome. He died for each of them by name, and he will lose neither. “Destroy” (apollymi) is the word used across the New Testament for ruin and perishing. Paul could have said upset, or set back. He chose the word for wreckage, and attached it to a plate of food.

What destruction looks like. It is rarely a single catastrophe. It is a man persuaded to act against his conscience once, in company, to avoid looking foolish, and a conscience overridden once is easier to override the second time. What has been damaged is his conscience, the very thing by which he says no to any sin.

Where Christians differ: can someone for whom Christ died be destroyed? Some Christians, often called Arminian, use this verse to argue that Christ died for people who will finally perish, and that a true believer can be lost; they want the warning heard at full weight, and in that they are right. This commentary’s view: Paul is warning the strong about the real tendency of their actions: what they do could lead a brother into sin and spiritual ruin. The warning is real and must be taken seriously. But God uses such warnings to keep his people. Elsewhere Paul is clear that those for whom Christ died will certainly be saved (5:8–10; 8:32–34). Christ died effectively for his sheep, and none of them will be snatched from his hand (John 10:11, 28). This is definite atonement (Christ’s death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died) and the perseverance of the saints (all who truly believe will be kept by God to the end). The man who wrote that nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God (8:39) is not contradicting himself over dinner. He is doing what Scripture consistently does with real dangers: naming them at full strength, to people who are in a position to cause them. The point here is ethical: treat your brother as someone precious to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak can control the strong by complaining about everything. The concern is a brother who might be led to sin against his conscience, not one who simply disapproves. A Christian who uses his scruples to rule the church, or who demands that his preferences become everyone’s law, is no longer the weak brother of this chapter. He is closer to the false brothers to whom Paul would not yield for a moment (Galatians 2:5).

How do I know whether my freedom is actually hurting someone? Watch and ask. Is there a believer in the room whose conscience forbids this, and who might follow your example against it? Is he a new Christian, or someone fighting a particular battle, perhaps with alcohol or gambling, for whom your freedom could reopen an old door? Has he told you it troubles him? If you are unsure, you can simply ask him privately and gently. Most of the time the answer is clear, and the cost of restraint is small: an evening, a meal, a glass. The brother is worth far more.

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spoken of as evil. The good in danger of being spoken ill of is the liberty itself, a true gift of the gospel. Used carelessly, it will be criticised, literally blasphemed. A right thing, handled without love, becomes the very thing people point at as evidence that the doctrine produces bad men.

Not eating and drinking. The kingdom of God is his rule, present now in Christ and coming in fullness. Its heart is not food.

Righteousness, peace and joy. Righteousness: right standing with God and right living. Peace: with God and with one another. Joy: delight in God. All three are the Spirit’s work in us (Galatians 5:22), and that is why the strong can actually do what this chapter asks: the Holy Spirit now lives in them, and his power, not their own resolve, makes such love possible. And they are not only private inward states. Peace here is peace between the two parties at the table; joy is the joy of a brother who has not been trampled; righteousness is doing right by him, not winning over a menu. Paul is describing what a room looks like, not only what a soul feels like.

All three through our Lord Jesus Christ. Each of the three has already come in this letter through Christ: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ (3:22), peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (5:1), and rejoicing in God through our Lord Jesus Christ (5:11). So the kingdom is not a mood or a programme. It is life under the King who died and rose, and the Spirit bringing his gifts to the very table where two believers disagree about the menu.

Does this mean our freedom does not matter? No. Christian liberty is precious; Christ bought it, and Paul fought for it all his life (Galatians 5:1). But it is a means, not the goal. Freedom exists for love, worship and joy, and the moment it is used to wound a brother or to win an argument, it has forgotten what it is for. Prize your freedom enough to protect its good name.

In everyday life. Suppose someone observed your congregation for a month with no access to its statement of faith. From what generates heat after the service, and what people are known for, what would he conclude it was about? Every generation keeps a list of things the kingdom is not made of, longer than Paul’s: how people vote, what they watch, the precise vocabulary used about matters on which we already agree. If the answer is not near righteousness, peace and joy, it is near food and drink, whatever the modern equivalent has turned out to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever thus serves Christ. “Thus” means by living for righteousness, peace and joy rather than for food. This is how we serve (douleuō, to serve as a slave) Christ. And such service is acceptable to God not because it is flawless, but because it is offered through the Son: spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). There was one Servant whom the Father fully approved (Matthew 3:17), who laid aside what he was entitled to for others (Philippians 2:6–7). The believer who gives up a freedom for a brother walks in his steps, and is accepted in him.

Acceptable and approved. “Approved” (dokimos) means tested and found genuine, like a coin that has been weighed. Even the watching world (12:17), which understands little of our doctrine, recognises that kind of love when it sees it.

Pursue peace. “Pursue” (diōkō) is a word for chasing hard: peace has to be chased; it does not come simply by keeping out of arguments. And upbuilding (oikodomē) is a builder’s noun. A congregation is a site with work going on, where every action adds a row of bricks or removes one (1 Corinthians 14:12). A church that pursues peace is only echoing the God who pursued it first, and who came looking for us when we were his enemies.

The better question. The instinctive question about a disputed freedom is: am I allowed? Here the answer is usually yes, which is why the question is useless. Paul substitutes another: what will this build? A thing can be entirely permitted and still take a wall down.

Does pursuing peace mean I should never disagree? No. Paul himself has just told the strong that he agrees with them (v. 14). Pursuing peace means disagreeing in a way that builds: speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), choosing the right time and place, listening before answering, refusing to caricature the other view, and never letting a difference on a secondary matter turn into a break in fellowship. Some peace is false, bought by silence about sin or the gospel. But most quarrels in churches are not about the gospel, and on those, the person who makes peace is called a son of God (Matthew 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The work of God. The work of God is your brother, or the church God is building in him and around him. “Destroy” (katalyō) is the builder’s opposite of verse 19: to demolish what has been put up. Someone else has been building in that man, patiently, for years, and the warning is about walking onto that site with a hammer over a question of lunch.

Created in Christ Jesus. The work has a name: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2:10). Whatever God has done in that scrupulous believer, he has done in Christ, and he means to finish it on the day of Christ (Philippians 1:6). The strong believer who presses his freedom on a weak brother is swinging a hammer at something Christ put his own hands to, at the cost of his own life, and Paul asks whether any dinner is worth that.

Everything is indeed clean. Paul never takes back his view to keep the peace. But he adds at once that “it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats.” Being right is not enough. How you use your rights matters.

Meat or wine. Love may mean giving up a right altogether, at least in certain company. Wine is mentioned perhaps because it too was used in pagan offerings. This verse has been quoted, especially since the nineteenth century, as a standing rule about alcohol, and read that way it turns the chapter upside down. Paul does not say wine is unclean; he has just insisted that everything is indeed clean (v. 20). What he says is that abstaining is good where it prevents a brother stumbling: freely chosen, for that occasion, and for somebody else’s sake.

Why the restraint cannot become a law. The moment the strong man’s self-limitation is made a law binding every believer, it has stopped being love and become the very thing this chapter forbids: a scruple imposed on another man’s conscience. The chapter asks the free to restrain themselves. It never asks them to make their restraint a rule for everyone.

Where Christians differ: alcohol. Some say this verse requires total abstinence from alcohol for all Christians. Others say Christians can drink freely regardless of others. This commentary’s view: Scripture presents wine as a gift of God (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11) and forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; 13:13). Drinking in moderation is a matter of Christian liberty. But love will gladly give it up where it would cause a brother to stumble, for instance around someone struggling with alcohol. Those who choose to abstain may do so for the Lord, and should not judge those who drink moderately.

Should I tell people that I am holding back for their sake? Usually not. The practical form of this verse is smaller and harder than a policy. It is the decision, made quietly and usually noticed by nobody, that at this table, with this person, on this evening, you will not have the thing you are perfectly entitled to have. And you will not announce that you are not having it, which is the part most of us fail. A sacrifice that is advertised turns into a rebuke, and makes the weak brother feel like a burden. If he asks, answer simply and kindly. Otherwise let love work in silence.

What if a friend is fighting an addiction? Then this verse applies with full force. If someone near you is recovering from alcohol, gambling, or any other bondage, your freedom in that area should be laid down gladly whenever you are with him, and probably for longer and more widely than you think necessary. Do not make him the one who has to ask. Ask yourself what would make it easiest for him to stand, and do that, without fuss. That is not legalism. It is love carrying a brother’s burden (Galatians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between yourself and God. The faith here is your conviction about liberty. Enjoy it before God, without making it a test of fellowship. Paul is not telling the strong to hide their convictions; he has just stated his own in the plainest terms (v. 14). What he forbids is the display. Some people do not so much enjoy their liberty as show it off, and it satisfies them fully only when the scrupulous are watching.

The Son who paid the tax. Jesus once did exactly this. Asked whether his teacher paid the temple tax, he explained to Peter that kings do not tax their own sons, so the sons are free. Yet, so as not to give offence, he sent Peter to find a coin in a fish’s mouth and paid for them both (Matthew 17:24–27). He held the truth about his freedom without surrendering it and without parading it, and the strong believer is asked to keep his liberty the same way.

Blessed. “Blessed” means happy, in God’s favour. A clear conscience is a great gift (Acts 24:16). The happy man can do the thing and then simply get on with the evening: no rehearsing of the justification, no wondering at midnight whether it was all right.

A mercy for the scrupulous. Many sincere Christians conduct a running trial of themselves over things God has not forbidden, and no verdict ever settles it. Paul calls the man who is free of that “blessed”: God regards a settled conscience as a gift, not as laxity.

Can a quiet conscience be wrong? Yes, and the guard matters, because the sentence can be misread as: if you feel fine, you are fine. Paul is speaking of a conscience taught by the gospel, not of one that has simply gone quiet. Scripture knows the other kind: the conscience that stops objecting because it has been ignored for long enough, consciences that are seared (1 Timothy 4:2). The absence of self-accusation is a blessing when it comes from clarity. It is a symptom when it comes from numbness, and the difference is usually visible to everyone except the man himself. The safeguard is to keep your conscience under the Word, and to listen when wise friends raise a concern.

Isn’t keeping my convictions private a kind of hypocrisy? No. Hypocrisy is pretending to be what you are not. Paul is not asking you to pretend to scruples you do not have, or to deny your view when asked. He is asking you not to parade your freedom where it would wound. A man who does not order a drink at a meal with a brother who struggles is not lying; he is loving. Your convictions remain yours, openly held before God, and you can explain them gently to anyone who sincerely wants to know.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith in Christ should be kept private. Paul speaks only of convictions about matters indifferent. The gospel itself is to be confessed with the mouth before the world (10:9–10).

In everyday life. Ask whether there is any freedom you enjoy more when someone disapproving is watching. If so, quietly drop the display. The freedom was Christ’s gift to be enjoyed before God, not a point to be scored.

For worship. A clear conscience is not something we could ever have given ourselves; our consciences had every reason to condemn us. Then the blood of Christ cleansed our consciences from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14), and there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). So the believer can lie down at night in peace, not because he is innocent but because he is forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has doubts. The word (diakrinō) means to waver, to be divided in mind: the root Paul used for judging in verse 13, here turned inward on a person at war with himself. He is eating the thing while one half of him objects, and Paul says the verdict on that is already in.

Not from faith. Faith here is a settled conviction before God that this is right. The food was not wrong (vv. 14, 20). He is condemned for acting against his own conviction, not for what was on his plate.

In the flow. The chapter began with the one who is weak in faith and ends with the rule that whatever does not come from faith is sin, fitting a letter about a righteousness that is by faith from first to last (1:17). And 15:1 picks the argument up at once, climbing to Christ, who did not please himself (15:3).

Whatever does not proceed from faith. A general principle: if you cannot do something in confidence that it pleases God, do not do it, for acting against conscience trains you to ignore God’s voice. Augustine used the sentence against the idea that the virtues of unbelievers are truly virtuous, and the Reformers took it up as proof that no act, however decent, pleases God apart from faith in Christ (Hebrews 11:6; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both 16.7). The principle really does reach that far.

The one life lived wholly from faith. Why should faith decide whether an act is sin? Because faith is the hand that rests on Christ, and God is pleased with what we do only as we are in him.
