There has been only one human life lived wholly from faith: Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2), who never once acted against his Father’s will. We never obey like that, not even in our best acts, but his perfect obedience is counted as ours, so those who belong to him are accepted in his name, and failure does not undo their standing. So the question at the table is never only whether the food is clean. It is whether I can do this as one who rests in Christ.

So are the good deeds of unbelievers worth nothing? Not worth nothing to people. When an unbeliever feeds the hungry or tells the truth, he does what God commands, and his neighbours are truly helped; God restrains evil and blesses the world through such kindness. But those deeds are not done from faith or for God’s glory, and so they cannot make the doer right with God or earn his favour (Westminster 16.7; 1689 16.7). That is not a sneer at decent people, because it is the same verdict on every one of us. Even the believer’s best works are accepted only because he is accepted in Christ. No one, religious or irreligious, stands before God on his own record. All alike need a righteousness that is not their own (3:21–22).

Does this mean I am sinning whenever I am unsure? No. The verse terrifies people, and the terror is usually caused by reading it out of the room it was written in. It does not mean that every action not preceded by a conscious act of faith is damnable, or you would sin every time you changed gear. It does not mean you must feel certain before you may act; feelings of certainty are not faith and often accompany foolishness. It does not mean that being unsure about a hard question is itself sinful; Paul has just spent a chapter making room for people who are unsure. What it does mean, in context, is this: do not do the disputed thing while you believe it to be wrong. A man eats what he thinks is unclean, because the company made it awkward not to, and the eating is a small act of unbelief: he has acted on the pressure of the room rather than on his conviction before God.

The cure is not paralysis. Verse 5 already gave it: each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The answer to doubt is not to stop acting but to stop being divided: to be taught, to reach a settled position and then act from it, which is more work than either abstaining or complying. The Lord does not drive his children; he leads them. He teaches the conscience he has cleansed, and he is willing to take years over it.

Textual note: the doxology. Many later manuscripts, the majority of surviving copies, place 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14; one early papyrus places it after 15:33; the oldest and best manuscripts have it at the end of chapter 16, where the ESV, the KJV and most Bibles print it.

How do I train my conscience? By putting it under God’s Word. Read Scripture widely, so that you know both what God commands and what he leaves free; many tender consciences are bound by rules that came from a family, a church culture or a past fear rather than from the Bible. Ask, of each scruple: where does God say this? Learn from mature Christians, past and present. Pray for understanding. And be patient: a conscience grows the way a person grows, slowly. Never force it to go faster than conviction, and never let it fall asleep.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.
