15.title: Unity, Hope, and the Mission of Paul
15.overview:
Romans 15 brings three threads together: the end of the argument about the strong and the weak (vv. 1–13), Paul’s account of his mission to the Gentiles (vv. 14–21), and his travel plans and request for prayer (vv. 22–33). What holds them together is the reach of the gospel: Christ’s own self-giving (vv. 1–3), the nations brought in as the Old Testament foretold (vv. 9–12), and Paul’s ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named (vv. 20–21).

The strong who bear with the weak are not doing something heroic; they are following their Lord, who did not please himself (v. 3). And Paul frames the whole argument in prayer: the God of endurance and encouragement, of hope, and of peace is the one who gives the unity he asks for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Example of Christ and the God of Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now names himself among the strong, and does it only to put their duty first (v. 1). The strong have no right to demand that the weak keep up with them; they owe it to the weak to carry them, to build them up and to seek their good (v. 2). The model is Christ, who did not please himself and on whom the insults aimed at God fell (v. 3, quoting Psalm 69:9).

Verse 4 explains why Paul settles a dispute about food by quoting a psalm: the Old Testament was written for later readers, and what it produces is hope. Verse 7 is the summit of everything since 14:1: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, a welcome none of them deserved. Verses 8–9 show how one Christ serves two peoples: to Israel he brings promises kept, to the nations sheer mercy, so neither may look down on the other. Then a chain of quotations from the Law, the Writings and the Prophets shows that the nations’ praise was the hope of the whole Old Testament, and the section ends in prayer to the God of hope (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ, the pattern for bearing with the weak

Paul grounds the duty of the strong in Christ himself (15:3). This is more than copying a good man’s example. Christ is Lord, he rules by serving, and his self-giving is the source of ours. When Paul tells the Galatians to bear one another’s burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2), that law is this pattern: the One who bore what he did not owe, so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 was not an abstract hope. The Roman church was divided: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people of different classes and nations. Now: Believers who have every reason to be divided, by race, class, culture or politics, worshipping together with one voice, still commend the gospel powerfully.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. In verses 1–13 Paul finishes the argument about the strong and the weak begun in 14:1: the strong must bear with the weak, as Christ did not please himself (vv. 1–6); all must welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, for Christ came to serve the Jews and to bring the Gentiles to praise God (vv. 7–12); and he prays that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace (v. 13). In verses 14–33 Paul begins to close the letter. A quarrel about dinner ends in the throne room, with every nation singing.

Who are the strong and the weak? Chapter 14 has introduced them. The weak are believers, most likely many of them Jewish Christians and those influenced by them, whose consciences would not yet let them eat certain foods or ignore certain holy days (14:2, 5). The strong are those who understand that in Christ nothing is unclean in itself (14:14) and feel free. Paul is not describing weak faith in Christ against strong faith in Christ; both are trusting the same Saviour. He is describing how much freedom a conscience has grasped on matters God has left free. And the weak are not the people with the worst morals. They are often the most careful people in the room.

We who are strong have an obligation. Paul counts himself among the strong, and at once says that being strong brings a duty, not a privilege. The word (opheilō) is a debt word, and it runs the length of the letter: Paul a debtor to Greeks and to barbarians (1:14), owe no one anything, except to love each other (13:8), and here the strong owe the weak. They thought their knowledge made them creditors. It makes them debtors.

To bear with the failings of the weak. “Bear with” is too polite for the verb. Bastazō means to pick up and carry, the word Paul uses for carrying one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2) and John uses of Jesus carrying his own cross (John 19:17). Not tolerate. Carry. The strong are to get underneath the weak and take the weight.

He took our illnesses and bore our diseases. The strong are not asked to do anything Christ has not first done for them. Matthew, quoting Isaiah 53, says of Jesus healing the crowds that he took our illnesses and bore our diseases (Matthew 8:17), using this same verb for carrying. He went on carrying until he carried the cross itself, and on it he bore our sins in his body (1 Peter 2:24). Every strong believer in Rome had first been a weak thing picked up by Christ. So when Paul tells him to shoulder a brother’s scruples, he is not inventing a burden. He is asking a man who has been carried to carry someone else.

Their failings, not their convictions. Look at what Paul calls the thing being carried: not their views but their failings (asthenēmata), their weaknesses, their scruples and tender consciences. Paul does not soften his opinion in order to be kind. He has already said plainly that nothing is unclean in itself (14:14), and he says here that the weak brother’s scruple is a weakness. He simply refuses to treat being right as permission to leave the man behind. He does not pretend the other man is right to keep the peace, nor tell him he is wrong and consider his duty done. He thinks the weak brother mistaken and picks him up anyway.

And not to please ourselves. Strength is for serving others. Every gift God gives, whether knowledge, maturity, health, money or a robust conscience, comes with a direction attached, and the direction is outward.

For his good. Pleasing the neighbour does not mean flattering him, but seeking his real good: “to build him up” (oikodomē, the word for putting up a house). Paul is not commending the anxious habit of becoming whatever the people around us want; if he were still trying to please people, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). Pleasing aimed at his growth is love. Pleasing aimed at his approval is fear, and the two look alike from outside.

What if the weak brother is using his scruple to run everyone else? This is a real situation, and Paul himself faced it. Bearing with a tender conscience is different from surrendering to a man who turns his scruple into a rule for the church or a test of salvation. When false brothers demanded that Titus be circumcised, Paul did not yield for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:3–5). The difference lies in what is being claimed. A weak brother says, I cannot do this with a clear conscience. A legalist says, you cannot be right with God unless you live as I do. The first you carry gently, often for years. The second you resist, kindly and firmly, because the gospel itself is at stake. And both are to be loved.

Does this mean I can never use my freedom? No. Paul’s point is not that the strong must live permanently by the weakest conscience in the church, but that they must never use their freedom in a way that wounds a brother or draws him into sinning against his conscience (14:15, 20–21). Most of the time your liberty harms no one, and you may enjoy God’s gifts with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). The question is not whether this is allowed, but who is at the table and what it will do to him. Keep your freedom between yourself and God (14:22) when using it would hurt someone, and use it freely when it would not.

In everyday life. Picture the person in your church whose conscience is tighter than yours. Christ carried you, and his Spirit in you makes you able to carry that brother. Ask what carrying him would look like, as opposed to merely managing him: a meal planned around what he can eat with a clear conscience, a joke about his scruples left unmade.

For worship. There is only one truly strong One in the universe, and he did not use his strength to please himself. Through Isaiah the Lord told his people that he had made them and would bear them, carrying them from the womb to grey hairs (Isaiah 46:3–4). In Christ he kept that word in the most literal way: the Son took our flesh, shouldered our sins and carried them up a hill outside Jerusalem. He has never set his people down since, and he never will. That is the glory of God in Christ: omnipotence that bends low, owes us nothing, and carries us anyway.

parallels.desc: bear one another’s burdens

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ did not please himself. The supreme example, reached for in the middle of a discussion about vegetables: no question is too small to be settled at the cross. He came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45); though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). The cross is both the motive and the measure of Christian self-giving. And where we fall short of that measure, as we all do (James 3:2), his perfect obedience stands in our place (5:19), so our halting self-giving is accepted for his sake.

A whole life of interruptions. Put flesh on the phrase. It meant crowds arriving when he had gone away to be alone, and compassion on them anyway (Mark 6:31–34). It meant a conversation at a well when he was tired and thirsty (John 4:6–7), no place to lay his head (Luke 9:58), and washing the feet of men who would run away that same night (John 13:5). The interruption was never treated as an interruption, because the people who caused it were the reason he had come.

The reproaches fell on me. Paul quotes Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the suffering righteous one, which the New Testament applies to Christ again and again (John 2:17; 15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 11:9–10). The “you” is God. The “me” is Christ. The insults were aimed at the Father, and they landed on the Son. The mockery at the foot of the cross, the spitting, the crown of thorns: every one of them was meant for God, and every one fell on Christ. He bore the scorn and hatred the world aims at God, and at Calvary he bore far more: the curse that our sin deserved (Galatians 3:13). He carried a burden infinitely heavier than any the strong are asked to carry.

The same psalm twice. Psalm 69 supplied the judgment on those who rejected the sufferer in 11:9–10, and here the example for those who follow him. The one who bore the reproach is either your pattern or your judge.

How can a psalm of David be about Christ? David wrote Psalm 69 out of his own suffering, as a king hated without cause. But David was more than a private man; he was the anointed king, the one through whom God had promised a greater Son (2 Samuel 7:12–16). His sufferings were a sketch, and Jesus is the finished portrait. The disciples saw it the day he cleared the temple and remembered that it was written, zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17), the first half of the very verse Paul quotes here. The Spirit who spoke through David knew whose voice would finally fill the psalm (Acts 2:30–31; 1 Peter 1:11). So when Paul reads the psalm as the words of Christ, he is not reading into it something that is not there. He is reading it the way its Author meant.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ had no joy. He went to weddings and dinners, and for the joy set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). Nor does it mean Christians must say yes to every request. Jesus withdrew to pray and refused to be made king by a crowd (John 6:15). He did not please himself, but neither did he please everyone. He pleased his Father, with the good of others always in view.

parallels.desc: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our instruction. Paul has just settled a pastoral dispute by quoting a psalm, and this sentence says what he thinks he is doing every time he reaches back into the Old Testament. The whole Old Testament was written for Christians too (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Timothy 3:16): the man who wrote Psalm 69 was describing his own misery, and was also, without knowing it, writing for a mixed congregation in Rome a thousand years later. God wrote all of it down, centuries in advance, for us: for readers he already knew by name, who would need on some ordinary morning to be told that he keeps his word.

Endurance, encouragement, hope. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is steadfastness under weight; “encouragement” (paraklēsis) is comfort and exhortation together, the voice of one who comes alongside. Both come through the Scriptures, and their goal is hope. Paul does not say the Scriptures were given to produce knowledge, or even obedience, but hope. That is only true because of what they record: a long series of occasions on which God did what he said he would do, generally later and stranger than anyone wanted. Abraham waited twenty-five years for a son; Israel waited four centuries in Egypt and seventy years in Babylon. Every time, God kept his word.

Why endurance comes before hope. You do not read the Bible and instantly feel hopeful. You find that the waiting in it is nearly always longer than seems reasonable, and slowly become the kind of person who can wait. Endurance trained in that school grows into hope (5:3–5).

Written about him, for us. Paul’s own use of Psalm 69 (15:3) shows what he means: he heard in David’s words the voice of Christ. That is how the Old Testament instructs: not mainly by giving us heroes to copy, but by showing us the One its every page is leaning towards. When the risen Jesus opened the Scriptures to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, their hearts burned within them (Luke 24:32). The hope Scripture gives is hope in him, because every promise God kept through those long waits was a step on the road to the cross and the empty tomb, and the God who kept those promises in Christ will keep the rest.

May the God of endurance and encouragement. Having said that Scripture gives endurance and encouragement, Paul calls God the God of endurance and encouragement. The book gives what its Author is. That is also a caution: a person can read the words without ever meeting the God they reveal (John 5:39–40).

One mind about Christ. Harmony is literally to think the same thing, as in 12:16. Unity is not uniformity of opinion on food, but one mind about Christ. The strong and the weak will go on disagreeing about the menu; Paul prays that they will be of one mind about the Lord who welcomed them both, so that their shared praise is louder than their disagreement.

If the Old Testament was written for us, do all its laws still bind us? Not in the same way. Everything in the Old Testament is for our instruction, but not everything in it is a command addressed to us. The ceremonial laws, the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1), which is exactly why the strong in Rome were right that foods are clean. The civil laws governed Israel as a nation and teach us their underlying justice. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows us God’s will for every person (13:8–10; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both 19.3–5). So read every page asking what it shows you of God, of Christ and of his promises, and you will find instruction even in Leviticus.

What if I read the Bible and still do not feel hopeful? Keep reading, and change what you are looking for. Hope in this verse is not a feeling you get from a passage on a good morning; it is a settled expectation that grows as you watch God keep his promises page after page. Read the long stories, not only the comforting verses: Joseph, Ruth, the exile and return, and above all the Gospels, where the darkest Friday is followed by Sunday. Pray the psalms of lament, which are in the Bible precisely for people who cannot feel hope yet (Psalm 42; 88). And read with others, because encouragement often reaches us through a brother’s voice reading the same words.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one voice. The goal of unity is worship. “Together” (homothymadon) is the word Luke uses of the first believers praying and breaking bread (Acts 1:14; 2:46), and “with one voice” is literally with one mouth. Two chapters of conflict resolution end not in a settlement or even agreement, but in a room full of people who still disagree about the disputed thing, making one sound. Every time a church sings with one voice, the strong and the weak and the people who will never agree about the menu, heaven hears the sound the cross was meant to make: one family, praising one Father, through one Son.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is not a general deity to whom Jews and Gentiles bring their separate religions; he is the Father of Jesus, known through Jesus. The strong and the weak share what matters most: the same Father, through the same Son.

Welcome one another. Verse 7 is the summit of an argument that has been climbing since 14:1, and the way to see it is to follow one verb. “Welcome” (proslambanō) means to receive someone into your company, into your home and your table. In 14:1 the strong were told to welcome the man whose conscience was tighter than theirs. In 14:3 the reason given was that God has welcomed him. Here the same word arrives twice in one verse, and now it runs in every direction at once, “welcome one another”, with Christ himself as the standard.

As Christ has welcomed you. And that standard is not vague, because this letter has already spelled it out. Christ welcomed you while you were ungodly (4:5), while you were still weak (5:6), while you were still a sinner (5:8), while you were an enemy (5:10). That is the measure now laid against your dealings with the believer whose views on a secondary matter irritate you. He did not welcome the promising or the nearly persuaded. He welcomed the ungodly, the weak, the enemy, while the welcome was still being refused. He opened the door to us when we were barring it from the inside, and he did not wait for us to become presentable. Which removes the last available excuse. Nobody in Rome was being asked to welcome someone worse than they had been when they were welcomed. Nobody since has been.

For the glory of God. The welcome is not primarily for the comfort of the person received. It is for God’s reputation. A church where people who would never otherwise sit together eat together is a living advertisement for the grace that brought them there.

Does unity mean we have to agree about everything? No. Paul is describing a church that still disagrees about food and days, and he prays for one voice, not one opinion on every question. Christians must agree on the gospel itself: who Christ is, what he has done, and how a sinner is made right with God (Galatians 1:8–9). On secondary matters, such as the matters of conscience in chapter 14, or how to school children, or styles of music, or whether to drink wine, believers can hold different convictions and still worship side by side. Even on weightier differences, such as baptism, where churches must decide their own practice, we can honour brothers who differ as true brothers in Christ. The mark of maturity is not that you have no convictions, but that your convictions do not stop you singing with someone who holds different ones.

Who counts as someone Christ has welcomed? Anyone who credibly confesses Jesus as Lord, trusts him alone for salvation, and is not living in open, unrepentant sin. You do not have to see into his heart; you receive what he professes and how he lives. That includes the believer who is socially awkward, the one from a very different background, the new convert whose life is still a mess but who is fighting, and the one whose politics you find hard to bear. If Christ has received him, the table belongs to Christ, and you are not its doorkeeper.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant to the circumcised. Verse 8 explains how Christ welcomed both. “The circumcised” are the Jewish people. Christ became not their teacher only, but their servant (diakonos), a word often used of someone who waits at table. Christ came first to the Jews, born under the law (Matthew 15:24; Galatians 4:4). And Paul is writing to a Gentile-majority congregation already warned against arrogance toward Jewish believers (11:18): the Lord they worship took the role of a servant to the very people they are inclined to look down on.

God’s truthfulness. Truthfulness (alētheia) is God’s faithfulness to his word. By coming to Israel, Christ proved God true to his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; every promise of God is answered Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who swore an oath two thousand years before Bethlehem kept it to the letter, in the land, the tribe and the line he had named.

For his mercy. Then comes a careful difference: promises confirmed for the circumcised, mercy for the Gentiles. Israel had promises to be kept, and the nations had none: they were strangers to the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12). Mercy to the nations was always God’s plan, for he swore that all nations would be blessed in Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 22:18). But that oath was sworn to Abraham, not to them, so the Gentiles receive as people with no claim: by mercy alone.

A rebuke and a comfort. That is a rebuke and a comfort in the same sentence, depending on who is reading. For the Gentile believer tempted to feel like the main story: you are here on mercy, and mercy by definition was not owed. For the Jewish believer watching his people’s privileges apparently pass to strangers: the promises were not cancelled, they were confirmed, and Christ took the servant’s place to do it. Both have reason to praise, and neither has reason to boast. God is truthful, for he kept every word he swore. God is merciful, for he gave what he never swore. And Christ is the place where both meet: the faithfulness of God to Israel and the mercy of God to the world, joined in one servant, who now leads every nation in praise of his Father.

Praise among the Gentiles. Paul quotes Psalm 18:49 (also 2 Samuel 22:50), David’s song of victory. In Christ, the Son of David, the line becomes his own: the Messiah stands among the Gentiles and leads their praise, as Hebrews puts it, “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). When a Gentile church sings, it is joining a song its King is already singing.

Were the Jews not saved by mercy too? Yes. Paul’s contrast is about the route, not the ground. Every Jew who was ever saved was saved by mercy; the promises themselves were mercy, given to a people who did not deserve them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8), and Paul has spent chapters 9 to 11 insisting that Israel’s salvation rests on God’s gracious choice (11:5–6). The difference is that Israel had been given the promise in advance, so Christ’s coming showed God keeping his word. The Gentiles had been given no such word to hold, so his coming to them could only look like sheer kindness. Both are mercy. One is mercy keeping a promise; the other is mercy with nothing to keep.

parallels.desc: I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again it says, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice, O Gentiles. The words come from Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Greek translation, at the end of the Song of Moses. This is the third time Paul has quoted that song in the letter (10:19; 12:19). The song God gave Israel about their own unfaithfulness and his faithfulness turns out to contain the Gentiles as well.

With his people. Not instead of them, not in a separate room. Alongside, in the same congregation, singing the same thing: the picture Paul has been trying to produce in Rome for two chapters, and Moses got there first.

Why the nations can sing. These quotations rest on Paul’s claim that Christ became a servant to the circumcised so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (15:8–9). Moses and the psalmist summoned the nations, but they could not bring them; for centuries the call went out and only a few, like Ruth and Naaman, came. What turned the summons into a song was Christ. Psalm 117 gives the reason for praise: the LORD’s steadfast love and faithfulness. In Jesus that steadfast love took flesh and that faithfulness was kept, and through his blood the nations who had no promise were brought near (Ephesians 2:13).

Psalm 117. The second quotation is Psalm 117:1. It is the shortest chapter in the Bible, two verses long, and the whole of it calls the nations to praise the God of Israel. The reason it gives is his steadfast love toward us, that is, toward Israel. What God does for his people is meant to set the whole world singing.

The whole Old Testament agrees. Paul has taken one quotation from the Law (Deuteronomy 32), two from the Writings (Psalms 18 and 117) and one from the Prophets (Isaiah 11, in v. 12): every division of the Hebrew Bible. The nations praising Israel’s God is not a Christian innovation laid over the Old Testament. It is the Old Testament’s own hope, finally coming true. God announced it in the Law, sang it in the Psalms and promised it in the Prophets, and for centuries it was a hope held by a single nation on a strip of land between the desert and the sea. Now it is being sung on every continent, in thousands of languages, by people whose ancestors bowed to idols of wood and stone.

Does with his people mean there are two peoples of God? No. There is one olive tree, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs, into which believing Gentiles are grafted alongside believing Jews (11:17–24), and in Christ there is one new man where once there were two (Ephesians 2:14–16). Gentiles do not get a separate covenant or a separate hope. They join Israel’s worship, praising Israel’s God through Israel’s Messiah. What God will yet do for the Jewish people as a whole is a question Christians answer in different ways from chapter 11, and Paul leaves room for a future mercy to Israel (11:25–32). But there is only ever one family of faith, and one song.

In everyday life. Pray Psalm 117 today, slowly; it will take you less than a minute. Then pray for a nation where Christ is not yet praised. The Son of David, who by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9), is still gathering that choir: ask him to raise up a church there that sings Psalm 117 in its own language.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always intended Gentiles to praise him.

parallels.desc: rejoice with him, O heavens
praise the LORD, all nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again Isaiah says. From Isaiah 11:10 in the Greek translation, the last of Paul’s four quotations and the one to which the others lead: Christ is the one through whom the Gentiles enter the praise and hope of Israel’s God.

The root of Jesse will come. Jesse was David’s father; the root of Jesse is the promised king from David’s line (Isaiah 11:1). Isaiah’s image was a dynasty felled like a tree, cut off at ground level, and a green shoot coming up out of the dead wood. Jesus is that root and offspring of David (Revelation 5:5; 22:16).

Life out of a stump. That picture is worth holding onto, because God very often works this way, and it is almost never the way we would have chosen. A shoot out of a stump is not a rescue of the tree. It is life on the other side of the loss, from the same root, and unrecognisable to anyone who was hoping the old thing would simply be repaired. By the time Jesus was born, David’s line had dwindled to a carpenter in Nazareth. Nobody looking at Joseph’s workshop would have seen a throne. The tree that God plants out of a stump will never be cut down again.

He who arises. “Arises” (anistamai) is one of the New Testament words for resurrection. In Isaiah it means to rise up to rule, but Paul may well have heard more in it: the shoot from the stump rose from the dead, and the risen Christ rules the nations.

The Gentiles will hope. To hope in him is to rest your whole future on him: to look to Christ for what the nations once sought from their idols, safety, meaning and life beyond death (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). And Paul ends the chain of quotations on the word “hope”, which his prayer in the next verse takes up: “May the God of hope fill you” (15:13).

Why is Jesus called the root of Jesse, not just a branch? Both are true, and Scripture uses both. Isaiah 11:1 calls the coming king a shoot from the stump of Jesse and a branch from his roots: he grows out of David’s family as its descendant. But Isaiah 11:10 calls him the root of Jesse, and Jesus himself says, I am the root and the descendant of David (Revelation 22:16). He is David’s offspring according to the flesh (1:3), and David’s source and Lord as the eternal Son (Matthew 22:41–45). The family tree that produced him was itself kept alive by him. He comes from David, and David came from him.

How can Christ rule the nations now, when the world looks so godless? His rule is real now, but it is mostly hidden, like a seed in the ground or yeast in dough (Matthew 13:31–33). He reigns over all things for the sake of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22), restraining evil, overruling the plans of rulers, and gathering his people from every nation through the preaching of the gospel. Every new believer in a closed country is a sign of his rule. One day it will be visible to everyone, when he returns in glory and every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11). Until then, we trust what we cannot always see, and the headlines are not the measure of his reign.

In everyday life. Look at the stump in your own life: the thing that has been cut down, the plan that failed, the family line or the ministry that seems finished. God’s way has often been to bring a shoot out of exactly that kind of dead wood. Do not demand that he repair the old tree. Ask him for life from the root.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line.

parallels.desc: the root of Jesse, of him shall the nations inquire

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the God of hope. A benediction, a prayer of blessing, closes the whole argument of the letter. The case that began at 1:16 with a gospel that is the power of God for salvation ends here, not in a conclusion but in a prayer.

Not the God who recommends hope. The God of hope: not the God who recommends it or requires it, but the God whose own name it is, and out of whom it comes. Hope is not a mood he asks his people to work up. It is something he has in himself, without limit, however dark the situation looks. And this hope has a name. Paul’s prayer follows straight on from Isaiah’s promise that the Gentiles will hope in the root of Jesse (15:12). The God of hope fills his people by giving them his Son: Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:27). Christian hope is not a wish about the future. It rests on a Person who already holds the future, and who lives in those who trust him.

Joy and peace in believing. Joy and peace are two of the marks of the kingdom (14:17), and the verb is fill: not trickle, but fill. All joy. And the joy and peace arrive “in believing”: not afterwards, as a reward for having trusted well enough, but as we trust.

A mercy to a particular reader. Paul does not command them to abound in hope. He asks God to do it to them. Nobody in this verse is being told to cheer up, and nobody is being held responsible for producing a feeling they cannot find in themselves. For the believer in a dark season, that matters enormously. The verse is not a standard you are failing to meet. It is a prayer someone is praying for you.

Abound in hope. “Abound” (perisseuō) means overflow: more hope than circumstances justify, by the Spirit’s power (5:5; 8:24–25). And the hope is not optimism, which is a temperament. It is expectation grounded in what has been argued for fourteen chapters: a verdict already passed, a Spirit already given, a Son already raised, a love from which nothing in creation can separate us (8:38–39).

How is Christian hope different from wishful thinking? Wishful thinking says, I hope it will turn out well, with no particular reason to think it will. Christian hope says, I know how it will turn out, because God has promised it and Christ has already risen. In the New Testament, hope is certainty about something not yet seen (8:24–25). Its object is definite: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, the glory of God, the new creation (5:2; 8:18–23). Its ground is definite: the character of God and the finished work of his Son. It may not tell you how next month will go. It tells you, with full assurance, how everything will end, and that you will be there.

What if I believe but do not feel joy and peace? Then you are in the company of many faithful saints, and this verse is still for you. Feelings can be dimmed by illness, grief, exhaustion, depression or long trial, and none of those mean your faith is false. Keep doing the believing: keep looking to Christ, keep hearing his word, keep praying even when the words are thin. Joy and peace come in believing, but they do not always come on our schedule. Ask God for them plainly, as Paul did. If darkness lingers, speak to a pastor or a trusted believer, and do not be ashamed to seek medical help where it is needed. The Spirit’s work is often deeper than our feelings can register.

In everyday life. Pray this verse for yourself and for someone you love, by name. Then write down one fact from Romans that is true of you whether you feel it or not: no condemnation (8:1), nothing can separate (8:39), all things for good (8:28). Read it aloud when the day gets hard. You are not manufacturing hope; you are standing where the Spirit pours it.

For worship. The God of hope is not running low. He fills people who cannot manufacture hope, by a power that is not theirs. The grave was the strongest argument against hope that has ever been made. He answered it on a Sunday morning, and he has not needed to argue since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from exhortation to his own story and plans, and the turn is less abrupt than it looks. He says he is satisfied about the Roman church and has written by way of reminder (vv. 14–15), then describes his mission in priestly language: he is a minister (leitourgos) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, bringing them to God as an offering sanctified by the Holy Spirit (v. 16). Mission, on this view, is worship.

From Jerusalem to Illyricum he has fulfilled the ministry of the gospel (v. 19), not because everyone has believed but because churches now stand in the key cities to carry the work on. So he looks west, to Spain, the edge of the known world, and asks Rome to help send him there (v. 24). First, though, he must go east to Jerusalem, at real risk, carrying the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers there (vv. 25–28). He ends by asking the Romans to strive together with him in prayer (vv. 30–33) for three things: deliverance in Judea, acceptance of the gift, and a joyful arrival in Rome. All three were granted, none in the form he pictured: he reached Rome in chains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as priestly worship

In 15:16 Paul pictures his mission as priestly service: the nations offered to God, made acceptable and holy by the Holy Spirit. Evangelism is therefore not merely a strategy or a duty but an act of worship. That vision has moved many missionaries, from the pastors Geneva sent into France to William Carey in India.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ministry from Jerusalem to Illyricum took perhaps fifteen years of hard labour. Paul mentions none of its cost here; he states that the work is done and looks to the next frontier. Now: There are still peoples and places where Christ has not been named. Not every Christian is called to go, and settled ministry is no lesser calling, but the whole church shares Paul’s concern that the unreached should hear, by sending, giving and praying until all nations have heard.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. With verse 14 the argument of the letter is complete, and Paul takes up again the threads of 1:8–15: their faith, his calling to the Gentiles, his longing to visit. The theology of chapters 1 to 15 is framed by a mission: Paul explains the gospel to the Romans partly because he wants them to help him carry it west (15:24).

Satisfied about you. “Satisfied” (peithō) means persuaded, confident. Paul has told this church not to be arrogant (11:18), not to think too highly of itself (12:3), not to despise or judge (14:3), and not to please itself (15:1). He now says he is persuaded about them, and that they are competent to instruct each other without him.

Able to instruct one another. Goodness (agathōsynē) is moral excellence and kindness. To instruct (noutheteō) is to admonish, to set someone’s mind right by warning and teaching. Ordinary church members are able to counsel each other from God’s word, for they already have the Spirit, the Scriptures and one another.

By way of reminder. Paul admits he has been very bold. But he calls what he has written a reminder, which treats them as people who already know the heart of it (2 Peter 1:12–13). We do not usually drift because we have never heard the truth, but because we have stopped hearing it.

The word of Christ dwelling richly. What equips ordinary believers to counsel one another? Paul’s answer elsewhere is Christ himself: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom (Colossians 3:16), with the same verb for admonishing that he uses here. The knowledge that fills the Roman church is knowledge of the Son who died and rose (1:3–4), and the reminder Paul has written is fourteen chapters about what Christ has done. That is why the church never outgrows reminders. The Lord gave his people a meal to keep eating in remembrance of him (1 Corinthians 11:24), because the cure for drift is never a new truth. It is the same Christ, held up again.

Because of the grace given me by God. His apostleship is a gift of grace (1:5; 12:3), and the commission creates an obligation to speak even to those who already know, because the gospel is too important to take for granted.

The hard thing, and then the honest praise. Most of us, having said the hard thing, either apologise for it afterwards or leave it there with no kind word. Paul says it at full strength and then tells them plainly the good he sees in them, and he means it, or the sentence would be worth nothing.

If members can instruct one another, why do we need pastors? Because God gives both, and they do different work. Christ gives pastors and teachers to the church to equip the saints for the work of ministry (Ephesians 4:11–12), and elders are charged with teaching, guarding the flock and answering for souls (Acts 20:28; Hebrews 13:17). But the goal of their teaching is a church in which everyone can speak the truth in love to everyone else (Ephesians 4:15–16). A healthy church is not one where the pastor does all the counselling. It is one where a believer struggling on Wednesday is helped by a friend who opens the Bible with him, long before the problem reaches the pastor’s study.

I do not feel able to counsel anyone. Where do I start? Start smaller than you think. Instructing one another in this verse is not delivering lectures; it is bringing God’s word to bear on a friend’s life with goodness and knowledge. Know the gospel well enough to remind someone of it. Listen first, and ask what is really going on. Point to a promise or a command that fits. Pray with them there and then. Be honest about your own struggles. And know when to say, this is beyond me, let us ask the elders together. Most faithful counsel in the history of the church has been given over kitchen tables by people who would never have called themselves counsellors.

In everyday life. Consider the most recent difficult thing you told a fellow Christian. Could you, that same day, have named three genuine strengths in him out loud? If not, the correction may still have been true, but it was not coming from where Paul’s came from.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A minister to the Gentiles. “Minister” here is leitourgos, a word for priestly or public service. Paul puts three temple words into one sentence: he is a leitourgos, he is in priestly service, and what he brings is an offering. The whole verse is written in the language of the altar.

The man who could never be a priest. Paul was of Benjamin (11:1; Philippians 3:5), not Levi. The one role in Israel closed to him by birth is the one he now uses to describe his life’s work. In that he follows his Lord, who was from Judah, a tribe of which Moses said nothing about priests (Hebrews 7:14), yet is the great high priest who offered himself. Paul can carry the Gentiles to God only because Christ has already brought them near by his own blood, and the offering is acceptable because it is presented through him. Christ is the priest who offered himself; the Spirit is the fire that sanctifies the offering; the Father receives it with delight.

Priestly service. “Priestly service” (hierourgeō) means to act as a priest. His altar is the gospel; his offering is people. Not his preaching or his sufferings: the converts are the sacrifice. Paul’s job description is to bring to God the very offering he told them to make of themselves, a living sacrifice (12:1).

Sanctified by the Holy Spirit. The offering is the Gentiles themselves, as Isaiah foresaw when he saw the nations brought as an offering to the LORD from every land (Isaiah 66:20). Once unclean in Jewish eyes, they are now “sanctified”: set apart for God and made fit for his presence, not by circumcision but by the Spirit. Under the old covenant an offering had to be without blemish, and God refused the blind and lame animals Israel brought to his altar, because he is a great King and his name is to be feared among the nations (Malachi 1:8, 14). Only the Spirit could make a crowd of former idolaters an offering such a God would receive, and in Malachi the same God promised that his name would be great among the nations (Malachi 1:11). This is also a powerful argument against the scruples of the weak: if God accepts the Gentiles as a holy offering, no Christian may treat them as unclean.

Reason to be proud. “Proud” (kauchēsis) is boasting, glorying: not personal vanity but the joy of a craftsman whose work has been effective, grounded entirely in Christ Jesus. By the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that ministers are priests offering sacrifices of atonement, as in Roman Catholic teaching on the Mass. Christ’s sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Paul’s priestly language is a picture of evangelism. All believers are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5).

Is evangelism only for missionaries and pastors? No. Paul had a unique apostolic calling, but every believer belongs to the royal priesthood that proclaims the excellencies of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9). Not everyone is a preacher, but everyone is a witness: ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). For most Christians that means the neighbour, the colleague, the relative and the friend, prayed for by name, loved patiently, and told the gospel plainly when the door opens. And everyone can support those who are sent, by prayer and giving, as Paul is about to ask the Romans to do.

Is it wrong to feel proud of something God has done through me? Not if the pride is the kind Paul has here: glad, grateful and pointed at Christ. There is a sinful pride that says, look what I did, and a holy gladness that says, look what Christ did, and he let me be there. The test is where the credit goes, and how you feel when someone else gets it. If you can rejoice as much over fruit in another person’s ministry as in your own, your boasting is in Christ Jesus.

In everyday life. If bringing people to Christ is a duty, it competes with other duties and loses to most of them. If it is priestly work, carrying an offering to God, then it belongs with worship, and the question stops being whether you have time for it. Think of one person you long to see brought to God; pray for them as a priest would, and look for one opening to speak of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God.

parallels.desc: they shall bring your brothers as an offering

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Christ has accomplished. Paul has arranged the sentence so that he cannot be its subject. Christ acts; Paul is only the one he works “through”. This is not false modesty, which would refuse to mention the work at all: Paul reports his in detail, place by place. He simply makes sure that Christ is named as the one who did it. Christ walked those Roman roads in his servant, he spoke through his servant’s mouth, he opened hearts in Lystra and Philippi and Corinth that no preacher could open.

To bring the Gentiles to obedience. The obedience of faith (1:5; 16:26): the letter opens and closes with the phrase, and it describes the goal of all mission. Not decisions recorded, but nations brought to bow to Christ in trust and obedience.

By word and deed. Paul’s message was spoken, and his life embodied it: working with his own hands, caring for the churches.

Signs and wonders. Paul did miracles that confirmed his message (Acts 14:3; 19:11–12). But the final phrase matters most: the power of the Spirit of God, the power behind word, deed and sign alike, who opens hearts and brings the nations to obedience.

From Jerusalem to Illyricum. Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic (modern Albania, Croatia and nearby). Jerusalem to Illyricum is the whole eastern Mediterranean, well over a thousand miles, covered on foot and by ship over years that also held the beatings, the shipwrecks and the sleepless nights he lists elsewhere (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). None of that appears here. He names the two ends of the journey and moves on.

Fulfilled. “Fulfilled the ministry of the gospel” needs reading carefully, because it plainly does not mean that everyone in that region had believed. It means he had fully preached the gospel there, planting churches in key cities that could reach their own territory. Paul’s definition of a finished job is not a converted population. It is a living church in place, doing what he would otherwise have stayed to do.

Where Christians differ: signs and wonders today. Some teach that signs and wonders like those of the apostles should accompany all gospel preaching today. This commentary’s view: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). They confirmed the apostolic message as Scripture was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and the canon complete, the miraculous sign gifts have ceased as a regular part of ministry. God still answers prayer and can heal and work wonders as he pleases, but the gospel is now confirmed by the written word. This is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters (those who believe all the gifts continue today), many of whom love Christ deeply and read 1 Corinthians 12–14 as a pattern for every age.

Does God still heal today, then? Yes, and Christians should ask him to. What has ceased is the apostolic gift by which particular people worked signs at will to confirm a new revelation. What has not ceased is God himself, who hears the prayers of his people. James tells the sick to call the elders, who are to pray over them and anoint them, and the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15). Sometimes God heals, quickly or slowly, with or without medicine, which is also his gift. Sometimes he does not, and gives grace to bear the weakness instead, as he did for Paul (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Either way, pray boldly and leave the answer with him.
verseByVerse.note: Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
My ambition. “Ambition” (philotimeomai) is built from the words for love and honour: to aspire, to make something your aim and point of pride, as in 2 Corinthians 5:9. Paul does not apologise for having an ambition or convert it into something more modest. He simply points it somewhere: at the places where the name of Christ has never been said out loud. Ambition is not the problem in a Christian; ambition pointed at the wrong thing is. The builders of Babel wanted to make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4). Paul wanted to make Christ’s name known where it had never been heard. That is the difference between an idol and a calling: the same energy, aimed at a different name.

Not where Christ has been named. Others could water where he planted (1 Corinthians 3:6, 10). His gift was to take the gospel where no one had yet preached it, leaving behind a church that would reach its own region.

Those who have never been told. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:15, the last verse before Isaiah 53, the passage about the one wounded for our transgressions, by whose stripes we are healed. Paul lifts his mission statement out of the song of the suffering servant, the part where the nations who were never told finally see. That is the God we worship: one who does not wait for the nations to seek him, but sends his word to the ends of the earth, to people who had no idea anyone was looking for them.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to make settled ministry look second-rate. Paul is describing his own calling, not issuing a universal rule; he himself stayed in Ephesus three years (Acts 20:31). And somebody has to stay, as Timothy did at Ephesus, doing the long, unnoticed work of a pastor. The ambition commended is that the unreached should be reached, not that every Christian should be restless.

What are unreached peoples, and what can I do from here? An unreached people is a group, usually defined by language and culture, among whom there is no church strong enough to evangelise the rest without help from outside. Many of them have no Bible in their language and have never met a Christian. Most of us will not go to them, but every one of us can share Paul’s ambition. Learn about one such people and pray for them regularly and specifically. Give to missionaries working among them. Welcome internationals in your own town, since many come from places where the gospel is hard to hear. Encourage the young people in your church who sense a call. And ask God whether he might be calling you.

In everyday life. Ask what your ambition is. Not your plan for the week, but the thing you would most love to see happen before you die. If the name of Christ is nowhere in it, ask God to reshape it.

parallels.desc: that which has not been told them they see

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So often hindered. The verb (enkoptō) means to cut in, often explained from the breaking up of a road so that no one can pass. Something has been across the road, repeatedly, for years. Paul names his pioneer work as the reason, without complaint, though he had already told them of the delay at the start of the letter (1:13) and it has lasted “many years” (v. 23).

No longer any room. A sentence that would be absurd from anybody else. The eastern Mediterranean is finished, in the sense already given (v. 19): planted with churches that can do the rest.

The Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. Luke lets us see who stood across Paul’s road at least once. On his second journey the Holy Spirit forbade them to preach in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them into Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7). The closed road led to Troas, the man of Macedonia, and the churches of Philippi and Thessalonica. Even when Satan hindered him (1 Thessalonians 2:18), the risen Lord was ruling his servant’s steps. Paul could wait for Rome because he knew whose hand was on the map.

How do I know whether God is hindering me, or I am just giving up? Ask what is actually across the road. Paul was hindered not by fear or idleness but by faithfulness: there was gospel work in front of him that had to be done first. So look at your own delay honestly. If what keeps you from the thing you long for is a real duty God has placed in front of you, then the delay is his, and you can wait without guilt. If what keeps you is fear, comfort or sin, then call it by its name and repent. And in either case, keep the desire alive in prayer, as Paul kept praying for Rome for years (1:10). God often brings a long-held desire to pass at the moment it can do the most good.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spain. Spain is easy to read as just another destination. It was not. Spain was the far western end of the Roman world: beyond it the map ran out and the Atlantic began. When Paul says Spain, he is naming the end of the earth as his generation understood the phrase, and he says it in the same breath as a request for travelling expenses.

To the end of the earth. That goal was not Paul’s invention. It was the risen Lord’s last word before he ascended: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Christ had told Ananias that Paul was his chosen instrument to carry his name before the Gentiles (Acts 9:15). And behind both stands Isaiah 49:6. Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32), and Paul applied that same promise to his own mission (Acts 13:47): the Servant’s light carried by the Servant’s servants. Spain was Paul trying to obey his Lord’s sentence to the last word.

Helped on my journey. “Helped on my journey” (propempō, send forward) was a technical term for missionary support: supplies, money, companions (Acts 15:3; 3 John 6). Part of Paul’s purpose in writing Romans was to win their support for Spain. He evidently thought that the way to raise support for a mission was to explain the gospel at length.

Your company. “Enjoyed your company” is literally to be filled with you (empiplēmi): Paul expects the Roman Christians to do him good. To him they are not only a supply base.

Did Paul ever reach Spain? We do not know. Acts leaves him under house arrest in Rome and stops. Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says he reached the limits of the west, which many have taken to mean Spain, and it may. The honest position is that the last plan recorded in the letter is the one plan whose outcome the New Testament never reports. And there is something to ponder in that. A man lays out an ambition at the end of his greatest work, and the record simply does not say whether he got there. Most faithful lives end that way: with the last thing unresolved on the page, and the accounting done somewhere else.

Is it right for missionaries to ask for money? Yes, when it is done openly and for the sake of the gospel. Paul asks plainly here, and the New Testament commends churches that send gospel workers on their way in a manner worthy of God, since they go out for the sake of the name (3 John 6–8). Paul sometimes refused support where it would have hindered the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12, 15–18), but he never thought supporting missionaries was second-class work. Those who give become partners in the mission (Philippians 1:5; 4:15–17). So when a missionary asks for help, do not hear it as begging. Hear it as an invitation to share in the work.

For worship. The gospel has always been heading for the ends of the earth, because the God who sent it intends to be worshipped there. It has gone far beyond Spain, to continents Paul never imagined, carried by people who were helped on their journey by churches that loved them. Whether or not Paul reached Spain, Christ did. And the Lord of the harvest records every faithful plan, finished or unfinished.
verseByVerse.note: Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul ever reached it is uncertain; early tradition says he did.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going to Jerusalem. Paul is almost certainly writing from Corinth (16:1, 23). He intends to go west, and the first thing he is going to do is travel some eight hundred miles in the opposite direction, carrying money, to the city where he asks prayer to be delivered from the unbelievers (15:31). He is postponing the mission of his life to hand over a relief fund.

A contribution for the poor. The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem took years to gather (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9). “Contribution” is koinōnia, fellowship, sharing. The Jerusalem church had been through famine (Acts 11:28–30) and was probably cut off from much of the society it had left. The unity of Jew and Gentile that Paul has argued for across this letter was about to arrive in Jerusalem in a bag, carried by representatives of the nations chapter 11 said had been grafted in.

Have been pleased. His word for the givers, twice in two verses. The Macedonians gave out of extreme poverty, begging for the privilege (2 Corinthians 8:1–4). The gospel had made poor Greeks glad to give to poorer Jews.

Setting his face toward Jerusalem. Luke tells this journey in a way that recalls another. Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Paul, carrying this gift, went constrained by the Spirit, knowing that imprisonment and afflictions awaited him (Acts 20:22–23), and his friends said, let the will of the Lord be done (Acts 21:14), words that echo Gethsemane. Christ went up to Jerusalem to give himself for his people; Paul goes to serve them, carrying the fruit of that self-giving.

Should Christians help poor believers first, or the poor in general? Both, with a particular care for the church. Paul says, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). A family looks after its own members first, not because it does not care about the neighbours, but because they are family. So churches should make sure no believer among them, or in poorer churches elsewhere, goes without, as this collection did. And Christians should also be known for mercy to the poor around them, whoever they are, as the good Samaritan was (Luke 10:29–37). The order is especially, not only.

For worship. Our Lord Jesus Christ, though he was rich, for our sakes became poor, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is the fountain from which the whole collection flowed: Greek believers gave gladly to Jewish believers they would never meet, because they had been made rich by a Jewish Saviour who gave everything.
verseByVerse.note: The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem was a major project of Paul’s later ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They owe it to them. The giving is glad, and it is also a debt: the last appearance of a theme that has run through the letter (1:14; 8:12; 13:8; 15:1). Once again the debt is owed to people the debtor might have looked down on.

Their spiritual blessings. The gospel, the promises, the Messiah, the Scriptures: all came to the Gentiles from the Jews (9:4–5; 11:17–18). “Share” is koinōneō, from the same root as “contribution” in verse 26. This deflates Gentile self-importance, Paul’s target since chapter 11: the nations did not generate their own faith. Salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22): Jesus said it himself, to a Samaritan woman at a well, and moments later told her that he was the Messiah (John 4:26). The greatest of Israel’s spiritual blessings was not a book or a rite but a Person, a Jewish man from Nazareth, through whom the riches of God came to the nations. A Gentile church sending relief to Jerusalem is a congregation admitting in public where it got what it has.

Material blessings. Literally, fleshly things: here simply bodily needs such as food and money, with no thought of sin. “Be of service” is leitourgeō, priestly service, the word family of verse 16: giving money is a form of worship (Philippians 4:18). The exchange is deliberately uneven. You cannot return a gospel. What you can do is send money, as the fitting response to a gift that cannot be repaid.

What it does not mean. The verse is not a general rule that teachers must be paid by those taught; Paul argues that elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:11–14). Here the debt is owed by the whole Gentile church to the mother congregation.

Do Gentile Christians today owe something to the Jewish people? A debt of gratitude, certainly. Every Gentile believer worships Israel’s God, reads Israel’s Scriptures and trusts Israel’s Messiah. That should rule out every trace of contempt for Jewish people, which has disgraced the church too often in its history (11:18–20). It should move us to love, to pray for their salvation as Paul did (10:1), and to share Christ with them humbly. The particular debt in this verse was owed to Jewish believers in need, so its closest application is generous care for Jewish Christians and for the poor among God’s people. Christians differ on how this relates to modern politics, and the verse does not settle those questions.

In everyday life. Name three people who carried the gospel to you: who taught you, baptised you, wrote what fed you. Then give something back, gladly: money to a ministry like theirs, a letter of thanks to one still living, or time given to pass on what they gave you.

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having sealed this fruit. This is the literal Greek behind the ESV’s “delivered to them what has been collected”. A seal certified a thing as genuine and complete, like goods signed for on delivery. Paul intends to see the gift safely into their hands himself. And it is called fruit: the fruit of the gospel, grown in Greek soil and brought home to the root.

The fullness of the blessing of Christ. The blessing of Christ is everything Christ gives (Ephesians 1:3), and Paul expects to bring it in full because he brings Christ himself in the gospel. He is right, and he has no idea what it will cost. He was arrested in Jerusalem within days (Acts 21), spent two years in custody at Caesarea, was shipwrecked off Malta, and came into Rome in chains some three years later (Acts 28:16). Every word of the prediction held. None of the arrangements did. The plans of a man can be overturned in a single afternoon in the temple courts, and the purpose of God cannot be overturned at all. Even as a prisoner, he came in the fullness of Christ’s blessing (Philippians 1:12–13).

Unhindered. Paul has twice said he was hindered (1:13; v. 22). Luke ends Acts with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, and the last word of the narrative in Greek is unhindered (Acts 28:31). The obstruction was to the man, never to the message.

Is it a lack of faith to make plans? No. Paul planned carefully: routes, timing, support, even a three-stage itinerary across the whole Mediterranean. Scripture commends forethought (Proverbs 21:5; Luke 14:28). What it forbids is the arrogance that plans as though tomorrow belongs to us. Instead you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15). Behind much anxious planning lies the desire to hold tomorrow in our own hands, which is in the end a wish to be God; Paul planned hard, but he left the steering to the Lord. So plan as well as you can, pray over the plans, hold them with open hands, and when God changes them, trust that his route is better than the one you drew. Paul’s confidence was not in the itinerary. It was in Christ’s blessing, which no change of route could remove.

In everyday life. Think of a plan of yours that went wrong in the last few years and ask honestly: what came through it anyway? Not everything that went wrong was secretly good. But the blessing of Christ was not one of the things you lost.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the love of the Spirit. The love the Spirit produces in believers, which binds them together across the miles. The Trinity is present in verse 30: Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.

A frightened apostle. Take the request at face value. The apostle who wrote chapter 8 is frightened. He is about to walk into a city where people want to kill him, and he writes to a church he has never met to ask them to get into the struggle with him. The great apostle believed he needed the prayers of ordinary believers he had never seen.

Strive together. “Strive together” (synagōnizomai) means wrestle together. The root is agōn, a contest, from which we get agony; Paul uses its relatives of Epaphras, always struggling on behalf of his church in his prayers (Colossians 4:12). Prayer, in these words, is hard work, done alongside somebody, on their behalf, at a distance.

Watch with me. Paul is not the first to walk toward Jerusalem asking friends to pray. In Gethsemane Jesus took three disciples aside, told them his soul was very sorrowful, even to death, and asked them to remain there and watch with him (Matthew 26:38). Luke adds that, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly (Luke 22:44); these verses are missing from some early manuscripts, so some Bibles bracket them. His friends slept. He wrestled alone and said to the Father, “not my will, but yours, be done”. Because he went through that struggle unaided, Paul can appeal by our Lord Jesus Christ for a struggle shared. The Lord who had no one to strive alongside him has made a people who strive alongside one another.

Delivered from the unbelievers. Many in Jerusalem hated Paul as a traitor to the law (Acts 20:22–23; 21:10–14). He also feared the Jewish believers might refuse a gift from Gentiles out of suspicion about his ministry (Acts 21:20–21): that the very gift meant to show unity might be rejected.

How God answered. Hold the requests against what happened. He asked to be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea. He was seized in the temple and would have been beaten to death had Roman soldiers not run down and taken him into custody (Acts 21:30–33), and later the Romans protected him from a plot to kill him (Acts 23:12–35). He was delivered, into arrest. He asked that his service be acceptable to the saints. Luke says the brothers received him gladly (Acts 21:17), and mentions the money only once, in passing, in Paul’s defence before Felix (Acts 24:17). And he asked to come to Rome with joy. He came in chains, at the empire’s expense, and the last picture Luke gives us is of him welcoming all who came to him, preaching for two years (Acts 28:30–31). He got the joy. He did not get it in the shape he asked for.

Not a glib answer. This needs saying carefully, because it is one step away from a cruel thing to say to someone who is suffering. This is not the cheap assurance that every unanswered prayer is secretly a better answer. Paul lost years to that arrest, and the man asking here for a safe journey did not get one. What the passage shows is narrower and more honest: that God answered every one of these petitions, and answered none of them in the manner requested, and that Paul’s ministry was not diminished by the difference. Several of his letters are traditionally dated to his imprisonment.

If God has already planned everything, why pray? Because God has planned the prayers too. He ordains not only what will happen but the means by which it happens, and prayer is one of his chosen means (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both 5.3). Paul believed God was sovereign over every step of his journey, and he still begged the Romans to wrestle in prayer, because he knew God works through the prayers of his people. Prayer does not change God’s mind; it is the way God has chosen to bring his good purposes to pass, and the way he draws us into his work. When you pray for a missionary’s safety, you are not interfering with providence. You are one of the means providence is using.

In everyday life. Take a prayer of your own that you consider unanswered, and ask what actually happened next: not to your circumstances, but to you and to the people around you. Sometimes the honest answer is still that it was a loss and you are waiting; Paul wrote chapter 8 about groaning. But sometimes the answer arrived under a different name and was not recognised.
verseByVerse.note: These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By God’s will. All Paul’s plans depend on it (1:10). He wanted to arrive rested, on his way to Spain. The will of God would bring him there by a road of violence, prison and the sea. He wrote the words anyway, and the words held.

Refreshed in your company. “Refreshed” (synanapauomai) means to rest together. The man who has carried the churches on his heart for twenty years wants nothing more from Rome than to sit down with them and be renewed.

The God of peace. A benediction. The God of peace is the God who made peace with us through Christ (5:1). Peace with God is more than a calm feeling: it means the war is over. We were his enemies, under his just anger (5:9–10); now, justified by faith, we are reconciled and welcome. He is also the God who gives peace within the church, between strong and weak, Jew and Gentile (14:19; 16:20). His peace surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7).

The names of God in this chapter. It is worth collecting the titles this chapter has given God, because they form a pattern. The God of endurance and encouragement (v. 5). The God of hope (v. 13). The God of peace (v. 33). Three times Paul names God by the exact thing the people he is writing to need: a divided and weary church needs the God of endurance and encouragement, a discouraged one the God of hope, an anxious one the God of peace. That is not a literary habit. It is how Paul prays: he does not merely tell God what to provide; he addresses him as the one who already is what the situation lacks. And it means the last thing the argument of Romans leaves in the room is not a doctrine but a presence.

Peace is the right last word. The letter began with a courtroom: wrath revealed from heaven, every mouth stopped, the whole world accountable to God (1:18; 3:19). It arrives here at “the God of peace be with you all”, and the word “all” matters: the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, the ones who eat and the ones who do not. The hostility the letter opened with has been dealt with in both directions, between God and man, and now between the people sitting in the same room. Both were dealt with in the same place. He himself is our peace, Paul says of Christ, who made Jew and Gentile one and reconciled both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16).

What if church drains me rather than refreshes me? Then you are not alone, and the verse still shows the goal. Paul expected to be refreshed by Christians, and God means his people to be that for one another (Philemon 7, 20). But churches are made of forgiven sinners, and some seasons are hard. Look for refreshment where it can be found: one or two believers you can pray with honestly, a small group, a friendship around the Bible. Ask whether you come expecting only to give, or only to receive; both starve a soul. And if something in your church is genuinely harmful, speak to the elders. But do not give up meeting together (Hebrews 10:24–25), because the God of peace usually sends his refreshment through his people.

For worship. The God of peace is no negotiator brokering a truce between parties who meant well. He made peace with enemies, at the cost of his Son’s blood. And he did not make it and leave: on the night before the cross the Son said, peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you (John 14:27). He has never taken it back.

As it is written, “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”<sup>10</sup>And again it says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.”<sup>11</sup>And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”<sup>12</sup>And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope.”<sup>13</sup>May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.<sup>14</sup>I myself am satisfied about you, my because of the grace given me by God<sup>16</sup>to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.<sup>17</sup>In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.<sup>18</sup>For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed,<sup>19</sup>by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ;<sup>20</sup>and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.<sup>28</sup>When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you.<sup>29</sup>I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.<sup>30</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf,<sup>31</sup>that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,<sup>32</sup>so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company.<sup>33</sup>May the God of peace be with you all.
