16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Romans 16 is often treated as an appendix, a list of greetings to skim. It is more than that. The twenty-six people Paul names in vv. 3–15, with several households besides, give a portrait of the Roman church: women who worked hard in the Lord, co-workers who risked their necks for Paul, households of powerful men, and many names common among slaves and freedmen.

The chapter also warns against those who cause divisions contrary to the doctrine the Romans were taught (vv. 17–20), for the unity the gospel creates needs guarding as well as love. And the letter ends where it began, with the gospel: the doxology of vv. 25–27 gathers up its great themes and gives glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the longest list of greetings in Paul’s letters, and a window into the earliest church: slaves and free, women and men, Jews and Gentiles, all members of one body.

Phoebe (vv. 1–2) very probably carried the letter from Corinth to Rome. Paul calls her a servant (diakonos) of her church and a patron (prostatis) of many, himself included. Much of the list is made of ordinary names, and the last two clusters have no description at all. That is the honest shape of the church in every century: a few remembered for something, most remembered only for being there. The holy kiss (v. 16), a greeting that belonged chiefly to family, declared that these strangers were now family in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The church as the new humanity

Romans 16:1–16 puts names and faces to the argument of chapters 1–15. The lack of distinction between Jew and Greek (10:12), the olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted (11:17–24), the command to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed us (15:7): all are visible in the list. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a new kind of community.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: By the standards of the first-century world the mixing in Romans 16 was startling. Social boundaries in Rome were sharply kept, and eating with inferiors could bring shame. Now: A church whose members all share one race, class or income, especially by design, should ask whether it has stopped short of what the gospel creates.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Romans 16 closes the letter. Paul commends Phoebe, who probably carried the letter (vv. 1–2), and names twenty-six people in Rome (vv. 3–16). He warns against those who cause divisions, and promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan (vv. 17–20). His companions send greetings (vv. 21–23), and a great doxology gives glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ (vv. 25–27). The letter that began with wrath against ungodliness ends with a room full of forgiven people and a sentence that breaks off into worship.

Why should I read a list of names? Because this is where the doctrine becomes visible. Paul has spent fifteen chapters arguing that God justifies the ungodly (declares guilty people righteous in his sight, for Christ’s sake, 4:5), shows no partiality, and makes Jew and Gentile one family in Christ. Chapter 16 is what that looks like on the ground: a wealthy patroness, a tentmaking couple, slaves with common names, a man probably linked to Herod’s family, a city treasurer and a man called Fourth, all greeted as brothers and sisters. Read the names slowly and you are looking at the church Romans 1–15 creates. You will also find that God remembers people the world forgets, and that is a doctrine too.

Our sister Phoebe. A letter of commendation (synistēmi, to recommend) let travelling believers be trusted and received (2 Corinthians 3:1). There was no post for private correspondence, and the roll containing Romans very probably went to Rome in the luggage of the woman introduced here.

The voice in the room. The bearer of a letter commonly read it aloud and answered questions about it, standing in for the sender. When the congregations of Rome first heard about the potter and the clay, and nothing being able to separate them from the love of God, they very possibly heard it in Phoebe’s voice.

A servant of the church at Cenchreae. Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth (Acts 18:18). “Servant” is diakonos; the ESV notes that it can be rendered deaconess. Because Paul ties the word to a particular congregation, it points to a recognised role there, not just to a helpful person.

A servant like her Lord. A chapter earlier Paul used the same word of Christ, who became a servant (diakonos) to the circumcised (15:8). Whatever Phoebe’s office, her service bore the family likeness of her Lord. And the Romans are to welcome her “in the Lord”, as Christ has welcomed them (15:7), not for her wealth or standing. Every name in this chapter is greeted on that ground.

A patron of many. “Patron” (prostatis) means benefactor, protector: probably a woman of means who used her wealth and influence to support Paul and others, supplying money, housing and introductions. It is the only appearance of the noun in the New Testament. The apostle to the Gentiles is on record as having been somebody’s dependent, and he is not embarrassed to say so.

Where Christians differ: Phoebe and women in church office. Some argue from Phoebe that women may hold any office in the church, including elder or pastor. Others deny that Phoebe held any office at all. Among those who agree on the eldership, some take her title in its general sense, others see her as a deaconess serving especially among women, and others as a deacon in the same office as 1 Timothy 3:8–13, reading 1 Timothy 3:11 as speaking of women deacons. This commentary’s view: Phoebe was an honoured servant of her church, and she may well have held a recognised role of service, which some Reformed churches call deaconess (compare 1 Timothy 3:11). The office of deacon is one of practical service and mercy, not of governing or teaching the church with authority. The New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor, with its authority to teach and rule, for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). This is the complementarian view: men and women are equal in worth and in Christ (Galatians 3:28), with different callings in the church and home. Egalitarian Christians, who hold that every office is open to women, read these texts differently out of a real desire to honour women’s gifts, and they are to be respected as brothers and sisters. Phoebe’s example shows how highly Paul valued women’s ministry, and churches should honour and use women’s gifts fully within Scripture’s pattern.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women’s service is second-class. Paul begins his greetings by commending a woman who held a recognised place of service in her congregation, funded the apostle, and was trusted with what may be the most important letter he ever wrote.

What do deacons actually do? Deacons care for the practical needs of the church so that the elders can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. The pattern is usually traced to Acts 6:1–6, where seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom were appointed to ensure that widows were not neglected in the daily distribution of food. Today that means things like caring for the poor and sick, organising practical help, looking after buildings and finances, welcoming newcomers and coordinating mercy. Their qualifications are mostly about character (1 Timothy 3:8–13). It is not a lesser calling: those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in the faith (1 Timothy 3:13).

So how can women serve in my church? In more ways than most churches use. Women in the New Testament host churches (Lydia, Acts 16:15), fund the mission (Luke 8:1–3), carry apostolic letters (Phoebe), labour in the gospel alongside Paul (Philippians 4:2–3), explain the faith privately to men and women alike (Acts 18:26), teach and train younger women (Titus 2:3–5), and pass the faith to children (2 Timothy 1:5). In a complementarian church, women can lead ministries of mercy, teach women and children, counsel, organise, show hospitality, pray in the gathering, and serve in recognised roles of service. What is reserved for qualified men is the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church. A church that keeps that boundary but leaves its women’s gifts unused has obeyed half the chapter.

In everyday life. Think of one missionary or gospel worker who is a stranger somewhere, or carries a heavy load, and ask what a patron would do with what God has given you: a room, a meal, a gift, an introduction.

For worship. The God who gave his church this letter did not send it by angel. He sent it in the hands of a sister from a harbour town, who had used her money to support his servants, and he has kept her name in his book ever since. He saw every coin she gave and every traveller she sheltered. He is a God who notices, and who remembers.
verseByVerse.note: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The ESV notes that “servant” can also be rendered “deaconess.” Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome. A patron was a benefactor who supported others with her resources.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Prisca and Aquila. Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila, tentmakers like Paul, had returned to Rome after Claudius’ expulsion of the Jews (Acts 18:2) was lifted. Paul met them in Corinth and took them to Ephesus, where they taught Apollos the way of God more accurately and hosted a church (Acts 18:18–26; 1 Corinthians 16:19).

The order of the names. The wife comes before the husband, as in four of the six places where the couple appears (here and in Acts 18:18, 26; 2 Timothy 4:19). In a world that ordered such things carefully, she was probably the more prominent of the two, by standing or by gift. Paul notices, and does not mind.

Greater love has no one than this. Paul calls them fellow workers (synergoi) in Christ Jesus, not his helpers: they served the same Lord, and the work was his. And the risk they took looks like Christ’s own love. Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13), and then he laid down his own life. A tentmaking couple who put their necks under the blade for a friend were showing, in a small way, the love first shown to them at the cross.

Risked their necks. Literally, laid down their own necks: the posture of a man on an executioner’s block. We do not know when this happened; it may have been the riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41). Paul does not explain, so his readers evidently knew the story.

All the churches of the Gentiles. By saving Paul, they served all the churches he founded. Every Gentile believer reading Romans owes something to a couple who were willing to die for the man who wrote it.

How does Priscilla teaching Apollos fit with 1 Timothy 2:12? Egalitarian Christians (who hold that every church office is open to women) see her as proof that Paul placed no limit on women’s teaching. But look at what Luke says she did. With her husband she took Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). That was private instruction by a couple, not the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that 1 Timothy 2 reserves for qualified men. The complementarian reading honours both texts. Women may and should teach the faith: to other women (Titus 2:3–5), to children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and in private conversation like this with men too. The office of elder and the preaching of the church belong to men. And Paul’s greeting shows how highly he valued her.

What does it look like for a married couple to serve together? Priscilla and Aquila worked the same trade, opened the same home, taught the same young preacher and risked the same danger. Their marriage was not a retreat from ministry but a base for it. For couples today that might mean opening your home to a Bible study, having students or lonely people at your table, mentoring a younger couple, or working side by side in a church ministry. It means praying together for the church, not only for yourselves. And it means a husband who leads with self-giving love and a wife who is honoured as his fellow worker, both of them looking outward together.
verseByVerse.note: Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of Jews ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church in their house. Churches met in homes; buildings set apart for Christian worship appear only in the third century. Rome probably had several house churches (vv. 5, 14, 15). The church (ekklēsia) is the people: a whole congregation in someone’s front room, no sign, no address anybody would recognise, and from those rooms the gospel spread through the empire.

Beloved Epaenetus. Paul does not greet a congregation in the abstract. He greets a man he loves.

Firstfruits of Asia. Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey, with Ephesus its chief city. The ESV’s “first convert” is literally firstfruits (aparchē), a sacrificial term: the first of the harvest brought to God as the pledge that the rest is coming. It fits Paul’s picture of himself as a priest bringing the Gentiles to God as an offering (15:16). Epaenetus may have been converted through Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, which would explain why he is greeted next to them.

Firstfruits for Christ. The harvest is Christ’s. A generation later the risen Lord appeared to John, standing among the seven golden lampstands, the churches of Asia (Revelation 1:12–13, 20). The province where Epaenetus once stood alone had become a place where Christ himself walked among his churches.

The loneliness of being first. Somebody in every place has to be the first: no church to join, nobody who has done it before him. Epaenetus was that man in Asia, and the region became one of the great centres of early Christianity. When God begins a work, he does not stop at the first. He sows a single seed in a pagan province, and he means the whole field.

Is a small church meeting in a home a real church? Yes, if it has what makes a church a church. A church is not defined by its building or its size but by its marks: the gospel truly preached, the ordinances of baptism and the Lord’s Supper rightly administered, and a people under the care of qualified elders, gathering regularly for worship and holding one another to account in love (Acts 2:42; 14:23; Hebrews 10:24–25). A dozen people in a living room with these things are a church. A thousand people in an auditorium without them are not. Whatever its size, a church should be connected in fellowship with other faithful churches, as the house churches of Rome were connected to each other and to Paul.

In everyday life. If you are the only believer in your family, your street or your workplace, remember Epaenetus. The first is never the last if God has planted him there. Pray for the harvest of which you might be the firstfruits.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary, who has worked hard. “Worked hard” (kopiaō) means toiled to the point of weariness, the word Paul uses of his own apostolic work (1 Corinthians 15:10). It appears three times in this chapter, and every time it is attached to women: Mary here, and Tryphaena and Tryphosa, and Persis, in verse 12.

He noticed. Paul does not say what any of them did. He says how hard they did it, and that he noticed, and he wanted a church across the Mediterranean to know their names. That matters a great deal to a person whose work is of a kind nobody sees. The Lord keeps a record of every weary hour spent in his service.

Andronicus and Junia. “Kinsmen” here means fellow Jews (9:3). The two were probably husband and wife. The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias, a man’s name, but Junia, a common Roman woman’s name, is more likely. The early church read it as a woman’s name almost without exception, John Chrysostom among them, and the masculine form Junias has not been found in any ancient inscription or writing.

Fellow prisoners. They had been in prison with Paul at some point, or for the same cause (2 Corinthians 11:23).

Well known to the apostles. The Greek phrase can mean “well known to the apostles” (ESV) or “outstanding among the apostles” (ESV note). Either way they were held in high regard by the church’s founding leaders.

In Christ before me. They became Christians before Paul’s conversion, usually dated around AD 33–34, so they were among the very first believers, perhaps from Pentecost (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome). And the two words “in Christ” hold the whole of salvation. To be in Christ is to be joined to him by faith, so that his death counts as yours and his life becomes yours: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). While Paul was still breathing threats against the church, these two were already in Christ, and could even have been among the people he was hunting. Then the risen Lord stopped him on the Damascus road and asked, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). To strike at those in Christ was to strike at Christ. Now the hunter is in Christ too, and calls the hunted his kinsmen and fellow prisoners.

Where Christians differ: was Junia an apostle? Some say Junia was a female apostle, and so women may hold any office. Others insist the name must be male, or the phrase must mean only “known to the apostles.” This commentary’s view: The ESV reading, well known to the apostles, is grammatically defensible, though many scholars prefer outstanding among the apostles. But even if the phrase means outstanding among the apostles, the word apostle is used in the New Testament in two senses: the unique apostles of Christ (the Twelve and Paul), who had seen the risen Lord and laid the church’s foundation; and messengers or missionaries sent by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25). Andronicus and Junia could only be apostles in the second sense, as travelling missionaries, as Barnabas is called an apostle in Acts 14:14. This does not overturn the New Testament’s teaching on eldership (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), nor does it reopen the apostolic office, whose foundational work ended with the apostles of Christ (Ephesians 2:20). What it does show is a woman who shared Paul’s chains for Christ and was honoured by name for it.

What if my service goes unnoticed? Then you are in the company of Mary, and of most of the faithful people who have ever lived. Paul noticed Mary, yet we still know nothing about what she did, only that she worked hard. God does not need your work to be seen in order to reward it. Your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4), and God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10). Serve for his eye, not for applause. And make it your habit to do what Paul did here: notice the hidden labourers in your church and thank them by name.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias (a man’s name). Andronicus and Junia had become believers before Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ampliatus. Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome, and Ampliatus is found in inscriptions of the imperial household. Such a man had no standing in the Roman world. Paul calls him my beloved in the Lord, and puts him in a letter read aloud in every century since. That is the grace of God: he passes by the great houses and calls their slaves his beloved. A tomb in one of Rome’s oldest Christian catacombs bears this name in unusually careful lettering; whether it is this man cannot be shown.

Urbanus. A common Roman slave name (from urbs, city), and our fellow worker.

Stachys. Stachys means ear of grain. Three names in two verses, two of them called beloved.

The kind of church the doctrine produces. This is why the chapter is not an appendix. God justifies the ungodly and shows no partiality (2:11), and here is what that looks like: an apostle listing a slave among the people he loves, by name, for the record. It also searches the heart. If my sense of worth rests on whom I know and who knows me, a church like this feels like a loss of status; if it rests on being known and loved by Christ, it feels like home.

The Lord’s freedman. Everything Paul says of these men is said in the Lord or in Christ, and the phrase changes their status at the root. He told the Corinthians that a slave called in the Lord is a freedman of the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:22). For Ampliatus that meant he might still answer to a human master on Monday, but sin and death no longer owned him, and no master on earth could stand between him and his Lord (6:18, 22). Rome counted Ampliatus as property; Christ counts him as his own, bought with a price and set free. And the Lord who did it had first taken the form of a slave himself (Philippians 2:7), and died by crucifixion, the death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels. That is why the apostle can call a slave beloved without condescension. In Christ they stand on the same ground, owned by the same Master, and loved by him.

How can a church make people of low status truly belong? By treating them the way Paul treats Ampliatus: by name, with affection, as co-workers. That means more than being polite on Sunday. It means asking the cleaner, the refugee or the man with no job to serve alongside the professionals, not only to be served. It means eating in each other’s homes. It means choosing leaders for godliness, not for wealth or polish (James 2:1–5). It means praying for and visiting the people who will never be able to repay the visit. A church where everyone in leadership looks the same, earns the same and lives in the same streets should ask whether the gospel has finished its work there.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apelles. “Approved” (dokimos) means tested and proved genuine, like metal that has come through the fire and proved real. Paul gives him only one phrase, perhaps the best one a Christian can receive.

Approved in Christ. Not approved by the church, but approved in Christ. The only life ever tested at every point and found true is Christ’s, tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). A believer’s faith survives the fire because it is joined to him (1 Peter 1:7). Apelles went through something that could have broken his faith, and it did not break, because Christ held on to him (John 10:28).

The family of Aristobulus. The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably include slaves and freedmen of important men. Aristobulus may have been the grandson of Herod the Great, who lived in Rome as a private citizen; when such a man died, his slaves often passed to the emperor while keeping their old master’s name.

Herodion. A fellow Jew, whose name suggests a link with the Herod family. If so, a member of the household of the family that killed John the Baptist and mocked Christ is greeted as a kinsman and a brother, a few lines from a slave and a woman who works too hard.

The family of Narcissus. Narcissus may be the powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, forced to commit suicide in AD 54. “Those in the Lord”: only some in that household were believers. The faith often spread through that city not by converting a great house but by taking root among its servants, a few at a time. A few years later Paul would send greetings from those of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22).

What if I am the only Christian in my home or workplace? Then you stand where these believers stood, and Paul thought you worth greeting. Live as one approved in Christ: faithful, honest, hard-working and kind, so that you adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:10). Do not hide your faith, but let your life speak before your words do, as Peter tells believing wives with unbelieving husbands (1 Peter 3:1–2). Pray daily for the people around you by name. Find fellowship elsewhere, in a church where you are known and fed, because you cannot be the only light in a dark house without being refuelled. And remember that God has often begun his work in a household or an office through one believer who simply stayed faithful.
verseByVerse.note: The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included their slaves and freedmen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Possibly sisters. Their names mean dainty and delicate, yet they were hard workers (kopiaō) in the Lord; Paul may be smiling as he writes it.

Persis. Persis means Persian woman, perhaps a former slave. Paul says she “has worked hard”, in the past tense, which may mean her years of strength are behind her, and Paul has not forgotten them.

Rufus. Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene. Mark, who probably wrote his Gospel for the church in Rome, names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus, as people his readers knew (Mark 15:21). If so, the man who carried Jesus’ cross had a son in the Roman church, and the woman who mothered Paul may have been Simon’s wife. The cross Simon was forced to carry became the cross that saved his family. Simon’s burden was the picture of discipleship: the cross laid on him to carry behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), as every follower is to take up his cross daily and follow (Luke 9:23). “Chosen” (eklektos): elect, or perhaps choice, outstanding.

His mother and mine. She had cared for Paul like a mother, perhaps in Antioch, where men from Cyrene were among the church’s leaders (Acts 11:20; 13:1). It is one of the warmest things Paul ever wrote, and it is over in a moment. Consider the man writing it. Paul had no wife and no household. He had been flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned once and left for dead (Acts 14:19), shipwrecked, hungry, cold and short of clothing (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). And somewhere in all that, a woman took him in and treated him as her own: fed him, presumably made him rest, possibly told him off.

She is not named. Paul identifies her only as somebody’s mother. To anyone who has quietly done that for a Christian worker and assumed it counted for little: the apostle put it in Scripture.

What does chosen in the Lord mean, if every believer is chosen? Paul may mean simply that Rufus is one of God’s elect, as every believer is, and is saying it of him warmly. Or he may use the word in its other sense, choice or outstanding, as we speak of choice fruit. Either way, it rests on the truth Paul has taught in this letter: that God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them, but in love (8:29–30; 9:11; Ephesians 1:4–5). That is not a cold doctrine. Here it is a term of affection. To be chosen in the Lord is to be loved by God from eternity, and every believer may say it of himself with wonder. Christians have long differed over what election rests on, some seeing it as God’s foreknowledge of faith; this commentary follows the reading of Romans 9 that it rests on God’s free love alone, while honouring brothers who read it otherwise.

Can I be a spiritual mother or father if I have no children? Yes, and the church badly needs you to be. Rufus’s mother was a mother to a man who was not her son. Paul called Timothy his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), and Jesus promised that those who leave family for his sake will receive mothers and brothers and children a hundredfold in this age (Mark 10:29–30). Single and childless believers can be the steadiest spiritual parents a young Christian ever has. Have someone younger to your table regularly. Pray for them and their particular battles. Ask how they are really doing, and listen. Teach them what you have learned of Christ, and let them see your faith in hard days.

In everyday life. If you are older and your days of hard labour are past, like Persis, your prayers, your counsel and your example are still labour in the Lord.

For worship. The God who chose Rufus before the world began is the God who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6). He gave a homeless, beaten apostle a mother in the faith. His Son promised that he would not leave his people as orphans (John 14:18), and here is the promise being kept, in a house in Rome.
verseByVerse.note: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions as if known to his readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asyncritus and the brothers. Probably a house church, or believers who lived or worked together. These two verses differ from everything before them. The names arrive with nothing attached: no “my beloved”, no “who has worked hard”, no “approved in Christ”. Just the names.

Philologus and the saints. Another group, perhaps another house church; Philologus and Julia may have been husband and wife. We know nothing else about a single one of them. And behind both clusters stand the ones not named at all, “the brothers who are with them”, “all the saints who are with them”: rooms full of people reduced to a phrase.

All the saints. They are saints not because they had done anything remarkable, but because they were sanctified in Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), and brothers because the Son is the firstborn among many brothers (8:29). Nobody in these two verses has a title or a story. Every one of them has the two names that matter, saint and brother, and both were given by Christ.

The names. Paul names twenty-six people and greets twenty-four of them directly (Aristobulus and Narcissus are named only for their households). Seven of the twenty-four are women, and two more women are greeted without their names. He knew so many in a city he had never visited because believers travelled, and many had met him elsewhere.

The real proportion of the church. A handful of people are remembered for something. Rather more are remembered only as having been present. The overwhelming majority are not written down anywhere, and every one of them got up on ordinary mornings and believed and was faithful and died. Paul could not know he was putting Patrobas and Olympas into the Scripture of the church. The record that matters is kept in heaven, and it has room for every name. Patrobas and Olympas are unknown to history and known to God, and the same is true of most of the saints who have ever lived.

Among so many believers, does God really know me personally? Yes. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). He knows the number of the hairs on your head (Matthew 10:30) and has engraved his people on the palms of his hands (Isaiah 49:16). Paul’s list of unknown names is a small picture of a great truth: God does not love his church in bulk. He chose each one, Christ died for each one, and the Spirit dwells in each one. On the last day you will not be lost in the crowd; you will be known, and welcomed by name. Rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

In everyday life. Picture the faces in your church and pray for five people you rarely speak to, by name. And if you feel like one of the unnamed, take heart: you are the kind of person the church has always mostly been made of, and God has not lost track of you.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A holy kiss. A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends, on the cheek. Holy: pure, expressing the love of brothers and sisters in Christ (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26). And the words “one another” carry the weight. In a congregation that has argued about food and days, and contains a member of Herod’s circle, several slaves and a wealthy patroness, that is the gesture of family, extended across every barrier the ancient world had built.

All the churches greet you. Congregations in Corinth and Philippi and Ephesus, many of whose members had never met anyone on this list, send their love to a church Paul has never visited.

The churches of Christ. The only place in the New Testament where this exact phrase appears. The churches are not Paul’s, nor their members’, but Christ’s, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). That is why strangers in Corinth can greet strangers in Rome as family, and why the kiss is holy. By the second century Christians gave it just before they shared the bread and cup.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The command is repeated (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Peter 5:14), but what it commands is the warmth, not the form. In Paul’s world a kiss was an ordinary family greeting; Paul makes it holy, a greeting between brothers and sisters in Christ. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may still be used; where it does not, a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What is not optional is greeting one another as family, and always in a way that is holy: pure, appropriate, and safe for everyone, especially children and the vulnerable.

What if I find greeting people at church hard? Many believers do, whether from shyness, anxiety or past hurt, and Paul is not commanding you to become the loudest person in the room. Start small. Learn three names and use them. Greet the person sitting nearest you before or after the service. Look for the newcomer standing alone, because they are probably more nervous than you. If conversation is hard, a warm handshake and a simple “it is good to see you” obeys this verse. Ask God to help you, and remember that the people you greet are your family in Christ, not an audience judging you.

For worship. Christ has made one family out of strangers: a slave and a city treasurer, a Jew and a Gentile, an apostle and a woman who mothered him. Every Sunday, in every time zone, the churches of Christ greet one another across oceans. That is no human achievement. It is the work of the Son who was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before the closing praise, Paul inserts a sharp warning (vv. 17–20): watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine the Romans have been taught, and avoid them. After two chapters on bearing with one another over disputed matters, he is not undoing that welcome; these are people who serve their own appetites and deceive by flattery. The way not to be deceived is not to become worldly-wise about evil but to know the good well (v. 19), and the God of peace will soon crush Satan under his people’s feet (v. 20).

A second greeting list follows, from Paul’s companions in Corinth (vv. 21–24), among them Tertius, the scribe who wrote the letter (v. 22). Then the doxology (vv. 25–27) gathers up the letter: the gospel, the mystery now made known to all nations, the obedience of faith, the phrase that opened the letter (1:5) and now closes it, and glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ. The letter that began with Paul as a slave of Christ ends with everything returning to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The mystery revealed: one gospel in both Testaments

Romans 16:25–27 returns to 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets. The Old Testament is the gospel in promise, the New the gospel fulfilled. The mystery kept secret for long ages was something the Old Testament was carrying all along: the nations brought into God’s people, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. Calvin’s principle applies: the two Testaments are one Bible and one gospel of grace, given in different ways but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning against divisive teachers stands at the end of Paul’s fullest statement of the gospel. Teaching as deep as this, on election, freedom and grace, can be twisted into a weapon, so the warning belongs here. Now: Every generation has its smooth-talking teachers who use the language of theology to build a following. Paul’s instruction still stands: watch them, avoid them, and trust the God of peace (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. — Romans 16:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch out. A sudden warning, after all the warmth. “Watch out” (skopeō) means keep an eye on, mark. Divisions (dichostasiai, standing apart) means splitting the church into parties. The divisive teacher is not to be debated endlessly or accommodated in the hope that he will improve. He is to be identified and avoided, not with contempt, but with the clear sight of people who know what they have been taught.

In the flow. The warning guards what the greetings have just displayed: a church of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and patrons, made one by the gospel. Chapters 14 and 15 told the Romans whom to welcome despite disagreement; this verse tells them whom not to follow. And “the doctrine that you have been taught” recalls the standard of teaching to which they had become obedient from the heart (6:17).

Contrary to the doctrine. “Obstacles” (skandala) are things that trip people into sin. The problem is not differences over food (chapter 14), but false teaching that undermines the gospel. The test is not whether a teaching is new or old, or whether most people hold it. It is the apostolic teaching Paul has spent fifteen chapters expounding. The community that has this letter has the measuring rod. Teachers who serve their bellies come and go, and their factions crumble; the church built on the apostles’ doctrine still stands after two thousand years, because the Lord Christ is its master and it serves him.

Avoid them. “Avoid” (ekklinō) means turn away from: do not give them a platform or follow them (Titus 3:10).

Their own appetites. Literally, their own belly, the organ of appetite (Philippians 3:19). Verse 18 tells you how to recognise them, and the marks are not doctrinal so much as personal. Whatever is being said at the front, something is being fed at the back: money, or a following, or the pleasure of being the one who sees what others have missed. And the contrast is exact. The Lord they claim to serve is the one who did not please himself (15:3), who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). A teacher whose message keeps circling back to his own appetite has shown, whatever his words, that he is serving a different master.

Smooth talk and flattery. “Smooth talk” (chrēstologia, fine words) and “flattery” (eulogia, nice speech). False teachers are often charming. And the method named is not argument. The divisive man in Paul’s description does not begin by attacking the church; he begins by being remarkably nice to you. He tells you that you are more discerning than the others, that you have noticed what they have not. Flattery is the tool because it recruits: you cannot build a faction out of people you have insulted. His targets are named too. “Naive” (akakoi) means innocent, unsuspecting, without guile. Not fools. Good-hearted people who assume others mean what they say, which is why Paul goes on to ask them to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil (16:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding every Christian you disagree with. This verse is easily abused. Paul has just spent two chapters commanding these same people not to separate over disputed matters (14:1–15:7). He cannot be undoing that a chapter later. Disputed matters call for patience; false teaching against the gospel calls for watchfulness.

How do I tell a false teacher from a Christian who simply disagrees with me? Look for all three marks Paul gives, together. First, the teaching is contrary to what the apostles taught: it denies or distorts the gospel itself, who Christ is, his atoning death and resurrection, justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, or the call to holiness. Second, the man is serving himself: his teaching keeps leading back to his money, his following or his importance. Third, he works by flattery and private recruiting rather than by open argument. Someone who holds a different view of a disputed matter and says so plainly is the person chapter 14 told you to welcome. Someone who is quietly assembling a party around himself is the person this verse tells you to walk away from. The difference is not how strongly he disagrees. It is what he is building.

Who am I to call anyone a false teacher? It would be arrogance, if the standard were our own opinion. But Paul measures teachers by the doctrine you have been taught, the gospel God gave through his apostles, not by anyone’s taste. Every serious community draws a line somewhere: a pharmacist who handed over whatever was asked for rather than offend the customer would not be humble but negligent, and Paul’s warning is about smooth words that pass for sound teaching (v. 18). The truly arrogant thing is to treat the gospel as ours to revise. And the same standard judges the one who uses it. Paul has just told the Romans not to judge or despise a brother over disputed matters (14:10), so the person who enjoys calling others heretics should search his own heart first: the pleasure of being right can become an idol too.

What does avoiding them involve? Do I cut them off? It means refusing them influence. Do not sit under their teaching, buy their books, follow their channels, invite them to speak, or let them recruit you or others. If such a person is in your church, the elders must deal with it, warning him and, if he will not repent, removing him from fellowship (Titus 3:10–11; Matthew 18:15–17). You should not run your own private campaign. But avoiding is not hating. Paul tells another church not to regard such a person as an enemy, but to warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Pray for him, speak the truth to him when it is right, and long for his repentance. The door to his return should always stand open.

In everyday life. Take the voice that has most influenced your thinking this year, a preacher, a book, a podcast, and ask whether it works by making you feel more discerning than your church. Flattery, from anyone, is one of the surest signals that somebody wants something from you.

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your obedience is known to all. Their faith was famous (1:8). Paul warns because he loves what he sees, and he wants it kept.

Wise and innocent. To be wise as to what is good is to know the good and do it well. To be innocent (akeraios, unmixed, pure) as to what is evil is to have no part in it and no taste for it. Jesus said to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16). You do not need to taste evil to understand it.

Satan crushed. The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden: the offspring of the woman would crush its head (Genesis 3:15), often called the first gospel promise, here in the last chapter of Romans. Christ has already won the decisive victory at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and the false teachers, Satan’s agents (2 Corinthians 11:13–15), will be defeated.

The God of peace who crushes. The verb is violent, to break in pieces, and it is attached to the title Paul has just used of God (15:33). Peace is not made by leaving the hostility in place. It is made by dealing with what caused it. A God of peace who could not crush anything would have no peace to offer.

Under your feet. Christ himself crushed the serpent’s head at the cross. Yet Paul does not say under Christ’s feet. He tells a mixed, quarrelling congregation of slaves and patrons and former idolaters that the last act will happen under their shoes, because they are united to the Victor. The God of peace, who made peace by blood, will grind the enemy under the feet of the very people the enemy once held captive.

Soon. “Soon” (en tachei, quickly, without delay) does not set a date. Some of it may come quickly: every time false teachers are exposed and a church is preserved, Satan tastes defeat in advance. The final crushing comes at Christ’s return: salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed (13:11). It has been two thousand years, and that has to be faced honestly. Paul did not miscalculate. He means that the outcome is fixed and that Christ’s return is the next great event in God’s plan, however long the wait turns out to be, though Scripture names things that will come before it (2 Thessalonians 2:3). With the Lord one day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8–9), and the wait will seem short in the light of eternity (8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17).

A word for the tired. For the reader tired of waiting, groaning inwardly with the whole creation (8:22–23): the groaning is real. But Paul does not write “may God crush”. He writes “will”. The outcome is settled; only the waiting is left.

Grace be with you. A benediction: the letter began with grace (1:7) and returns to it.

How can I be innocent about evil without being naive? Know the good thoroughly, and do not go looking at evil to understand it. Those who are trained to spot forged banknotes learn the genuine note so well that a fake stands out at once. In the same way, the believer who knows Scripture, the gospel and the character of Christ deeply will sense what is false, without needing to immerse himself in it. That means being careful about what you watch, read and scroll through, not out of fear but because you do not need to be expert in sin. It also means being wise in the good: honest about how temptation and manipulation work, alert to flattery, and willing to ask a mature believer when something feels wrong.

Why has Satan not been crushed yet? He has been decisively defeated, and he is not yet destroyed. At the cross Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15); Satan is a beaten enemy who still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, unable to stop the gospel going to the nations (Revelation 20:1–3). Every time someone is converted, his house is plundered (Mark 3:27). God delays the final blow because he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, and the full number of his people is still being gathered (2 Peter 3:9). When the last of them is in, Christ will return, and the serpent will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10). This commentary reads the binding of Revelation 20 as describing the present age (the amillennial view, which takes the thousand years as the time between Christ’s two comings); many faithful Christians expect a future thousand-year reign, and all share the hope of his final victory.

In everyday life. Leaning on the Spirit who is at work in you, choose one way to grow wise in the good: a book of the Bible, a mature Christian to learn from. And choose one thing to be innocent of: an app, a channel or a kind of entertainment you do not need to know so well.
verseByVerse.note: The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden.

parallels.desc: he shall bruise your head

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy. Paul’s closest companion and spiritual son (Acts 16:1–3). Others seek their own interests, Paul says elsewhere, not those of Jesus Christ, but Timothy had proved his worth (Philippians 2:21–22).

Lucius, Jason and Sosipater. Fellow Jews. Lucius may be Lucius of Cyrene (Acts 13:1), Jason the man who hosted Paul in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5–9), and Sosipater the Sopater of Berea who set out with the collection (Acts 20:4). Three Jewish co-workers in a largely Gentile mission: the very unity Paul has been describing, standing beside him as he writes.

In the flow. The first list (vv. 3–16) showed the church in Rome; this second list shows the church around Paul in Corinth. The same gospel has made the same kind of family at both ends of the road Phoebe is about to travel.

Tertius. Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down. It is the only moment of its kind in the New Testament. For hours, likely across several sittings, a man has been taking down the words of Romans as Paul spoke them, and at the end he stops and adds a greeting of his own.

Three and Four. Tertius means Third, and a verse later Quartus means Fourth: ordinary Roman names taken from numbers, common among slaves and freedmen. The last stretch of this great letter contains two men called Three and Four, one of whom physically wrote it. God chose a man named Third to set down in ink the gospel of justification by faith, and then let him sign his name in the margin of Scripture. The word of the Lord endures for ever, and some of it is in Tertius’s handwriting.

Greeting in the Lord. What joins a scribe in Corinth to strangers in Rome is that both are united to the same Christ. And his pen has carried for hours the gospel concerning God’s Son (1:3–4), the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ (3:22), the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (8:39). Every line Tertius wrote was leading to Christ, and so is his greeting.

Paul’s own hand. Paul often signed in his own hand at the end (Galatians 6:11). Using a scribe does not lessen the letter’s authority: the words are Paul’s, inspired by the Spirit.

If humans wrote the Bible down, how is it God’s word? Because God was at work in the whole process. Scripture is breathed out by God (2 Timothy 3:16): men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). God did not bypass their minds, personalities or circumstances. Paul’s logic, his warmth, his grief for Israel and his list of friends are all truly his. But God so superintended what they wrote that the result is exactly what he intended to say, without error. The scribe’s pen, the apostle’s voice and the Spirit’s breath all worked together. That is why we can read Romans as Paul’s letter to Rome and, at the same time, as God’s word to us (Westminster 1.2, 1.4; 1689 1.2, 1.4).

In everyday life. Think of the behind-the-scenes servants who have brought God’s word to you: translators, the person at the sound desk, the Sunday school helper. Thank one of them. And if your own work for Christ is mostly holding the pen for someone else, do it with joy. Tertius never preached Romans, but the church has been reading what he wrote down ever since.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius. Probably the Gaius whom Paul baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14), host of Paul and, it seems, of the whole church there.

Erastus, the city treasurer. “City treasurer” (oikonomos tēs poleōs): a public official. An inscription at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a public square at his own expense in return for his office as aedile. He may be the same man.

The whole argument in one room. Set the three men in this verse beside each other and the argument of the letter is standing in one room. The city treasurer, the host of the whole church and the man named after a number send a joint greeting, on the same footing, and the only title Quartus needs is brother. Outside that house Roman society gave such men almost nothing in common. That is what Paul meant when he said God shows no partiality (2:11) and that there is no distinction (10:12). He did not mean it as a sentiment. He meant that a room would exist in which it was simply true, and he is writing from one. And the footing is Christ: there is neither slave nor free, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). Rank had not stopped existing in Corinth, but every man in that room owed everything to the same Saviour and had nothing he did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7). The Saviour took the lowest place so that the high and the low could stand on level ground at the foot of his cross.

How should a wealthy or powerful Christian relate to poorer believers? As Gaius and Erastus did: as a brother, and as a steward. Paul tells Timothy to charge the rich not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). James tells the rich brother to boast in his humiliation, because he too will fade like a flower (James 1:9–11). In practice, that means opening your home, using your influence for the vulnerable, giving quietly and generously, and never expecting deference in church. In the congregation, your position counts for nothing; your service counts for much. And the poorer brother is to honour you without envy, as a fellow servant of the same Lord.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, insert verse 24, with this benediction. The earliest and best manuscripts do not have it, so the ESV leaves it out of the text, and it is shown here from the margin. If your Bible skips from verse 23 to verse 25, that is why. It appears to be a copyist’s repetition of the benediction already given in verse 20, and the instinct was sound: grace is how this letter starts (1:7), and grace is how it should stop.

Grace with you all. Grace (charis), the free favour of God in Christ, runs through the whole letter: the grace of apostleship (1:5), of justification (3:24), in which we stand (5:2), that abounds all the more where sin increased (5:20), of election (11:5), of gifts (12:6). And it is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, because grace is never handed out apart from him: the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ (5:15). With you all: strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, slave and free.

Can I trust that my Bible says what was originally written? Yes, with great confidence. The New Testament is by far the best-attested book of the ancient world: thousands of Greek manuscripts, some from within a few generations of the apostles, besides early translations and quotations by early Christian writers. Because there are so many copies, the occasional slip of a scribe can be seen and corrected by comparing them, as here. Modern Bibles are open about the few places where manuscripts differ, which is a sign of honesty, not weakness. And no doctrine of the faith rests on a disputed reading. God has kept his word pure in all ages by his singular care and providence (Westminster 1.8; 1689 1.8).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary:
The doxology. The letter ends with a long sentence of praise (vv. 25–27) that gathers up the great themes of Romans and mirrors its opening (1:1–5).

Textual note. Many later manuscripts put this doxology after 14:23, one early papyrus puts it after 15:33, and a few have it twice or not at all. The oldest and best manuscripts put it here, at the end of the letter; some scholars doubt it was part of Paul’s original, but its words fit Romans closely, echoing 1:1–5. Nothing in the text of Romans is in doubt because of this; the question is only where the closing praise stood.

Able to strengthen you. “Strengthen” (stērizō) means establish, make firm, and it closes a loop. Paul told them at 1:11 that he longed to come and strengthen them. He could not do it yet, and when he finally arrived it would be in chains. So the letter ends by handing the task over. What the apostle wanted to do and could not, God can do without him.

My gospel. The gospel entrusted to Paul (2:16), not a different one. It is not merely information about Christ; it is the power by which God strengthens his people (1:16).

The mystery kept secret. A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (11:25; Ephesians 3:4–6): here the gospel of Christ, especially that Jews and Gentiles together would be saved through faith in him. Through the promise to Abraham, the exodus, the law, the kings and the exile, God was holding something back that he fully intended to say. The nations were in God’s plan before Israel was a nation (Ephesians 1:4).

Now disclosed. Revealed in the coming of Christ, and explained by the prophetic writings, the Old Testament (1:2; 3:21). The prophets spoke of it, but its full meaning was hidden until Christ came. And there is a deliberate paradox here: a mystery kept secret for long ages which has nonetheless been made known through the prophetic writings. Secret, and in writing the whole time. Chapters 9 to 11 demonstrate it. Hosea and Isaiah and Moses and the Psalms were saying that the nations would come in. It was on the page in every synagogue. What was missing was not the words but the event that makes the words plain, and once Christ had come, Paul could go back through the same scrolls and show that they had been saying it all along. A mystery in Paul’s sense is not a puzzle nobody could solve. It is something that could not be seen until God did the thing it was about.

The command of the eternal God. The mission to the Gentiles is not Paul’s idea, nor the church’s strategy (Matthew 28:19). It is the decree of the God who has no beginning and no end, carried out in time.

The obedience of faith. The same phrase as 1:5, framing the whole letter. The first and last paragraphs of Romans say the same thing; everything between is the argument for it.

Does the obedience of faith make obedience part of what saves us? No. Paul means the obedience that faith is and the obedience faith produces: to believe the gospel is to obey God’s summons, and those who believe go on to obey. It is the same phrase as in 1:5, and the whole letter between those two verses has argued that we are justified by faith apart from works (3:28). Obedience is the fruit of faith, never its price.

How does God actually strengthen me? Through the gospel, as this verse says, and by the ordinary means he has appointed for it. He strengthens you when the gospel is preached and you hear it with faith; when you read and meditate on Scripture; when you pray; when you come to the Lord’s Supper and see Christ’s death set before you; and when fellow believers speak the truth to you in love. He works by his Spirit through these means, often quietly, so that you may not notice the strengthening until you find yourself still standing in a trial that once would have flattened you. So when you feel weak, do not look for something new. Go back to the old gospel, and to the means God uses to apply it.

For worship. Every page of the Old Testament was written by someone who did not know how the story would end, and who was carried along by Someone who did. And he is able to strengthen you. Not the apostle, who could not reach Rome when he wished; not you, who cannot keep yourself standing; but him, who has never once let one of his own fall out of his hand.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the only wise God. Only God is truly wise, and his wisdom is seen in the plan of salvation, which no one could have imagined (11:33); Christ crucified is himself the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24–25). All of Romans has displayed it: the wisdom that designed salvation through the cross, so that God could be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26), and included the Gentiles through Israel’s stumbling.

The sentence that breaks. Read verses 25–27 as one sentence and it does not quite resolve. It begins “Now to him who is able to strengthen you”, adds clause after clause, and never completes the thought in the expected way, arriving instead at glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ. Paul set out to say something about God and could not get to the end of the subject, and the sentence gives way under the weight and turns into worship.

He has done this before. At the end of chapter 11 the argument about Israel ran out into “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (11:33). The reasoning goes as far as reasoning can, and then the only thing left is to give God glory. That is not the failure of the theology. It is what the theology is for.

Glory through Jesus Christ. Christ is the one through whom God is glorified, and through whom our praise reaches God. To give God glory adds nothing to him, but gladly confesses that all the credit for salvation is his. The letter that began with the gospel of God concerning his Son (1:1–3) ends with glory to God through his Son.

Amen. So be it, truly. The letter began with a man calling himself a slave, set apart for a gospel promised beforehand, sent to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations (1:1–5). Sixteen chapters later, through wrath and justification and no condemnation and the olive tree and the weak brother and the greetings from Three and Four, it ends on the same three things: the gospel, the nations, and the obedience of faith. Nothing has been added to the first paragraph. The letter has only unfolded what it held.

What does it mean to give God glory through Jesus Christ? It means that all our praise reaches the Father by way of the Son. We cannot come to God on our own merit, and our worship, even at its best, is mixed with sin. But Christ is our great high priest, who lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and through him we continually offer up a sacrifice of praise (Hebrews 13:15). So when you pray or sing, you come in his name, trusting that he presents your praise to the Father, cleansed and accepted. It also means that God is most glorified in what he has done in Christ: the cross and resurrection are the brightest display of his glory there will ever be.

I have read Romans. What now? Do what Paul does at the end: worship. Then live out the letter. Rest your whole confidence on Christ’s righteousness, not your own (3:21–26). Fight sin as one who is dead to it and alive to God (6:11). Walk by the Spirit, assured that nothing can separate you from God’s love (8:38–39). Present your body as a living sacrifice (12:1). Welcome the brother who differs from you (15:7). Support the spread of the gospel to the nations (15:20–24). And come back to it. Romans is not a book to be finished but a book to be lived in, and the church has found for two thousand years that it never runs dry.

For worship. To the only wise God. In the end there is no one else to give the glory to: not the reader, who contributed nothing; not the apostle; not the church, which exists only because of what God has done. One God, who found a way to be just and to justify the ungodly, and who is gathering a people from every nation into one family through his Son. From him and through him and to him are all things, and the letter’s last word is not an argument. It is Amen.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae,<sup>2</sup>that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.<sup>3</sup>Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,<sup>4</sup>who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.<sup>5</sup>Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.<sup>6</sup>Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.<sup>7</sup>Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.<sup>8</sup>Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.<sup>10</sup>Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus.<sup>11</sup>Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.<sup>12</sup>Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.<sup>14</sup>Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.<sup>15</sup>Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.<sup>16</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.<sup>17</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them.<sup>18</sup>For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.<sup>19</sup>For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.<sup>20</sup>The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.<sup>21</sup>Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen.<sup>22</sup>I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.<sup>23</sup>Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.<sup>25</sup>Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages<sup>26</sup>but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—<sup>27</sup>to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
